16475-the-great-round-world-and-what-is-:
This December 16, 1897 number of The Great Round World, a children's current-events paper, tells young readers they are living through history. Cuba, Turkey, Haiti, and Hawaii are making stirring chapters, and Austria has joined the procession with an episode that will fill an exciting page of its history. The voice of the people, the paper says, must now be heard.

The issue explains the news in plain, lively language for school readers, with pictures to match. It shows how American children learned world affairs in the 1890s: as an unfolding story they were part of. Collectors of children's periodicals will find it a bright survivor.
22719-old-fort-snelling-1819-1858:
Marcus L. Hansen wrote Old Fort Snelling, 1819–1858, a history of the famous frontier post at the meeting of the Mississippi and Minnesota rivers. The catalog record gives no year. Fort Snelling guarded the upper Mississippi, hosted fur traders and soldiers, and stood at the center of early Minnesota history.

The preface tells the book's own story: the work began as research at the State University of Iowa and was accepted as a graduate thesis in June 1917. At the urging of Dr. Shambaugh of the State Historical Society of Iowa, Hansen enlarged its scope, consulted many new sources, and rewrote the whole manuscript. The result is a documented history of the fort's first four decades. Hansen later became a leading historian of immigration, and his care with sources shows here.
27366-a-journey-in-russia-in-1858:
Robert Heywood of Bolton, England, wrote this privately printed account of his 1858 journey to Russia, first read as a lecture at the Bolton Mechanics' Institute. Members of the institute asked him to publish it so their families and fellow workmen could share what he had learned, since Bolton traded heavily with St. Petersburg and Moscow.

Heywood describes the two Russian capitals as a visiting English manufacturer saw them in 1858, with an eye to commerce as well as to sights and customs. The short volume gives a plain, firsthand picture of Russia just before the great reforms of the next decade. It suits readers who like travel writing grounded in trade and daily life.
34558-defending-the-island-a-story-of-ba:
James Otis tells how two settler children held their home in a tale issued by Dana Estes and Company at Boston in 1904. The scene is Bar Harbor, on Mount Desert Island, in 1758.

Six chapters carry the fight: the island, the first assault, a day of suspense, an attack, fire, and the wreck. Picture captions show the children's work. Susan stands guard at the gateway. The children build platforms inside the stockade. A girl cries that the attackers shall not have the smallest chicken inside. Otis pauses at the start to give a few plain facts about the island's people. Champlain named it Mons Deserts for its thirteen rugged mountains, seen twenty leagues at sea. Otis wrote scores of such tales for young readers.
35558-the-middle-period-1817-1858:
John W Burgess wrote The Middle Period, eighteen seventeen to eighteen fifty eight, for The American History Series. Charles Scribners Sons in New York issued the book with a copyright of eighteen ninety seven and a fresh issue in nineteen ten. Burgess taught politics and law at Columbia University in New York and led its faculty of political science. Maps aid the text. He gave the book to the memory of Julius Hawley Seelye.

Chapters trace how the old Republican Party grew more national in aim. They then treat the gain of Florida, slavery before eighteen twenty, and the making of Missouri as a state. Later chapters treat the vote of eighteen twenty four, the United States Bank fight, and nullification. Abolition and party growth close the span. Students get a clear frame for four full decades of United States growth and strife.
48310-stephen-h-branch-s-alligator-vol-1:
Stephen H Branch's Alligator began with volume one, number one on Saturday, April twenty-four, eighteen fifty-eight. The paper sold for two cents. Its contents list promises alligators first, then Branch's own alligator, then his farewell to his country. A piece from the New York Times of eighteen fifty-five rounds out the bill.

The lead item reprints a letter from the New York Herald of eighteen forty-nine. Emigrants aboard the Crescent City write from Chagres, New Granada. They hail the passengers as men of talent from every section of the Union. All are armed to the teeth, the letter jokes, which warns them to respect each other. Branch's sheet mixed satire, news, and self-promotion.
48930-stephen-h-branch-s-alligator-vol-1:
Stephen H Branch published his Alligator at New York as a two-cent weekly. This issue is volume one, number two, dated Saturday, May 1, 1858. The contents promise a life of Branch himself, a tale of Fra Diavolo and his Italian brigands, a piece on ice cream, and a warning called Our Country's Ruin.

The life opens in boyhood. Young Stephen dresses his friend John Horsewell in his brother's new clothes and quarrels with him on the road. He repents at twilight, and the two ride to Boston with forty cents to learn a trade. The paper is a wild, personal miscellany, half memoir and half fun, from a famed New York character.
48931-stephen-h-branch-s-alligator-vol-1:
Stephen Branch's Alligator, volume one, number three, is the New York comic weekly for Saturday, May 8, 1858, priced at two cents. Truth Whips Fiction leads the contents, a warning tale against the snares of music and fiction. A pale student in Natchez, ruined by midnight oil, recovers among figs and flowers and marries.

Ice cream, Supervisor Blunt, and fun, sun, and shade fill the short pieces. Branch praises his brethren of the press and prints his own life in instalments. His prose runs wild with lists, verses about thin shanks, and battles of sacred pugilists. The Alligator was Branch's one-man paper, half sermon and half squib, and wholly his own.
48932-stephen-h-branch-s-alligator-vol-1:
Stephen H Branch's Alligator, Volume One Number Four for Saturday, May 15, 1858, was sold at two cents. Contents list Let Dad and Son Beware at page two and Advents and Public Plunderers at page three. The Mayor and Charley and a Life of Stephen H Branch fill the issue. A front print shows the Alligator title with Branch's name.

The lead piece warns Peter Cooper and Mayor Tiemann as old friends of George W Matsell. It charges that Tiemann was elected on condition Matsell be restored to his old post. Cooper, Gerard, and Kingsland are said to work for that restoration. Matsell is charged with conspiring against Wood, who saved him from the scaffold. Perjury and alienage convictions are hurled in the attack prose. The paper is a fierce personal and political sheet of its day in New York.
49020-stephen-h-branch-s-alligator-vol-1:
Branch's Alligator, volume one, number five, for Saturday, May 22, 1858, is a two-cent paper, entered for copyright in 1857 by Stephen Branch at New York. Its contents are short and loud: a Life of Stephen Branch, Let the Firemen Stand to Their Guns, and Lamentations of a Grahamite. And a piece headed For American Youth to Read, and for Thieves and Traitors to Ponder.

The life, in this portion, is a schoolboy confession. Branch had the itch; his room-mate Terry caught it. The doctor, Plympton, let the secret out: Terry must have caught it from Branch, as it is just like yours. A cannon ball through the window, Branch writes, could not have thrilled his frame like that disclosure. He told Terry the whole story; Terry mildly chided him, forgave him, and proposed they room together and apply the itch ointment before the same fire.
49021-stephen-h-branch-s-alligator-vol-1:
Branch's Alligator for May 29, 1858 is volume one, number six of a two cent weekly paper. Stephen Branch published and largely wrote it himself. The contents promise matter for boys and girls, wives and husbands, and venerable men. A life of Stephen Branch stands in the contents. A piece called Legislative Robbers follows it. The lead article attacks corruption in New York justice.

Judge Russell and Superintendent Tallmadge have their corrupt antecedents exposed. The founders of straw bail are dissected to their marrow bones, the heading boasts. Branch writes as an insider who shared their deeds of villainy. His narrative begins in 1841, in a Fulton Street law office. An orphaned office boy there wins his sympathy and free teaching. He boards the boy and follows his fortunes through the city. Confession, gossip, and reforming zeal fill Branch's strange little paper.
49051-stephen-h-branch-s-alligator-vol-1:
Branch's Alligator, volume one, number seven, dated Saturday, 5 June 1858, is a two-cent New York weekly of personal attack and confession. Stephen Branch entered its copyright in 1857. The contents promise his own life story, an article on Peter Cooper's avarice and infernal forebears, and the early poverty of the three Napoleons of the American press: Bennett, Greeley, and Raymond.

The life opens at Andover, where Branch courts by letter a girl of his native city. Girls in Providence were fairer and richer, he owns, but her father had been a boy with his father, and she loved him as a sister loves a brother. She followed him to balls, church, and parties, and a day seldom passed unseen. Branch swears Juliet never loved Romeo more hotly.
49052-stephen-h-branch-s-alligator-vol-1:
Stephen Branch published his Alligator as a two-cent weekly paper of attack and satire. This is volume one, number eight, dated Saturday, June 12, 1858. The contents promise a review of three great New York editors. James Gordon Bennett, Horace Greeley, and Henry Raymond are the targets.

Branch calls the trio extremely vicious and begins with Bennett as the biggest villain. He claims years of writing for their papers for little or no pay. His abuse is total: face, speech, grammar, and morals all come under fire. Other items treat a coming war with Britain, a display of crinoline, and Branch's own life. The paper is a curiosity of the rough personal press of its day, kept for its venom and nerve.
49053-stephen-h-branch-s-alligator-vol-1:
Stephen H Branch fires a two-cent weekly blast at a rival editor in number nine of volume one, dated Saturday, June 19, 1858. The paper's name, the Alligator, states its bite.

The contents promise James Gordon Bennett's editorial career first. Incomparable Meanness, Spectres and Hobgoblins, and The Way New York is Bamboozled follow. Startling Revelations and a life of Branch himself close the list. The lead piece turns Bennett's hiring of a boy into a stage dialogue. Johnny Kelly stands barefoot in rags before the great Herald editor. Bennett grills him on his birth and his love of Washington. The boy's grandfather told him of Washington's greatness before dying. Branch's paper was short-lived and libellous. It survives as a raw sample of penny-press warfare.
51556-the-mentor-the-cradle-of-liberty-v:
The Mentor for July 1, 1918, volume six, number ten, serial number 158, sold at twenty cents a copy, takes Faneuil Hall in Boston for its subject. Albert Bushnell Hart, professor of government at Harvard University, writes the number. It opens with a meditation on liberty as older than law, government, or the state.

Hart tells how Peter Faneuil, a rich young merchant of Huguenot descent, offered to build Boston a market house at his own cost and charge. His architect, John Smibert, added a hall above the stalls, and the building was finished in 1742. The chamber over the market became the town hall, in demand for patriotic debates and banquets, until fire gutted all but the walls in 1761.
54806-stephen-h-branch-s-alligator-vol-1:
Stephen Branch's Alligator for Saturday, June 26, 1858, is the tenth number of a New York weekly paper. The paper sold for two cents a copy. Branch entered it for copyright in 1857 and put his own portrait at its head.

The number leads with the Life of Stephen Branch, told in the first person. One tale recalls a youth at Westport, Connecticut, who boarded on Bleecker Street and clerked on Pearl Street. A gift of fine books tests the young man's caution and his guardian's word. Other heads name Supervisor Blunt and Paul Julien, a last talk with Madame Sontag, and the editorial career of James Gordon Bennett. A poem dated June 15 and pages of adverts fill out the sheet.
54818-stephen-h-branch-s-alligator-vol-1:
Branch's Alligator, volume one, number eleven, for July 3, 1858, is one issue of Stephen Branch's scrappy New York weekly. The contents open with a life of Branch himself, then a melodious fragment and a piece called Human Devils. James Gordon Bennett's editorial career gets an article, and Peter Cooper's funny little grocery groggery at the corner of the Bowery another.

Branch, a job printer turned scourge, filled his paper with attacks on the city's great men, editors first of all. The Alligator snapped at Bennett of the Herald above all. Such personal journalism was the sport of the penny press age. Single issues survive as specimens of a vanished newspaper warfare. Branch wrote as if libel law were a rumor. His paper is funny, scurrilous, and very New York.
54834-stephen-h-branch-s-alligator-vol-1:
Stephen Branch's Alligator was a two-cent weekly paper, and this is volume one, number twelve, dated Saturday, 10 July 1858. Branch filled his sheet with attacks on the famous and the powerful, and the contents list names Bennett, Barnum, and Gerard as villain figures. A Fourth of July piece mourns a decline in American honesty and love of country.

Other items promise scandal and exposure, in the loud style of the penny press at its roughest. The paper mixed politics, gossip, and abuse, and sold on shock. For modern readers, this issue is a sample of the rowdy New York press of the 1850s, when a small editor could make a name by biting every hand in sight.
54877-stephen-h-branch-s-alligator-vol-1:
Stephen Branch published the Alligator, a two-cent New York weekly paper, and this file holds the issue of Saturday, July 17, 1858, volume one, number thirteen. Branch filled his paper with his own life and feuds. The contents promise a life of the editor himself, a primary election sketch from 1820, a piece on the editorial career of James Gordon Bennett, and a column simply called Fools.

The opening article tells how Branch breakfasted with Horace Greeley at the Graham House. A man named Goss brought Frederick Douglass and a lady to the table and seated them nearby. Goss kept Black boarders and joined their anti-slavery talk. Branch stared, Greeley ate his bran mush with a sly glance, and the young editor retired feeling the house had changed. The Alligator was a personal, combative little paper, and this number shows its method: memoir, gossip, and opinion printed for two cents.
54894-stephen-h-branch-s-alligator-vol-1:
Branch's Alligator, volume one, number 15, is dated July 31, 1858. Branch published the two cent weekly himself. Contents promise his own trial and national degeneration. A lime kiln man and Mayor Tiemann draw headlines. Bennett, Greeley, and Raymond are named together as press powers. The lead piece is a mock scene: Fanny's Parlor. James Gordon Bennett knocks softly at the dancer's door. Fanny unlocks it and bounds to his knees. Kisses are traded for puffs, in her own arch words. Fill the theatre every night, and she will love him dearly.

Jewels for Bennett's wife sweeten the bargain, the dialogue says. Wyckoff manages her fame offstage. The satire paints newspaper praise as bought goods. Branch wrote for readers who liked scandal in dialogue form.
54978-stephen-h-branch-s-alligator-vol-1:
Stephen Branch's Alligator was a small New York weekly paper, and this is issue 17 of its first year, dated August 14, 1858, priced at two cents. Branch printed much of his own case and views in its four short pages. The lead item sums up his trial for libel.

Counsel's closing words, Branch's own remarks, his sentence, and press views fill the front page. Short bits follow on alligators, a plea, and ads at the back. The sheet is a sharp taste of the bold, lone-wolf press of the 1850s, where one man could be writer, subject, and cause at once.
55004-stephen-h-branch-s-alligator-vol-1:
Stephen Branch's Alligator is a single issue of a New York weekly paper, volume one, number eighteen, dated Saturday, August 21, 1858. It sold for two cents. The Alligator was Branch's personal sheet, famous in its day for its libel suits and its feuds with the rest of the press.

The transcriber's table of contents lists the number's matter. Opinions of the press come first: extracts from other papers about the Alligator's libel case, which Branch lays before his readers with pride. An immortal petition follows. Then comes the news that Frank Leslie has again been arrested. Advertisements close the sheet. The paper is a specimen of the rowdy personal journalism of the eighteen fifties, when an editor's quarrels were his stock in trade and his front page.
55007-stephen-h-branch-s-alligator-vol-1:
Stephen Branch's Alligator for Saturday, September 11, 1858, volume one, number twenty-one, sold at two cents, is a comic paper full of short squibs. The table runs from What Peter Said and A New Scheme to The Tail of the Cable and Cable Jollification. The cable is the new Atlantic cable, and its celebration at the Crystal Palace fills the number.

The lead piece mocks Peter's speech at that celebration, noting that the speeches were printed before they were delivered. Peter, it says, sparkled and snapped like an aurora borealis, better charged than the cable itself. He called the cable the umbilical cord that binds the mother continent to the child, and praised the indomitable Cyrus Field who inspired the work.
55015-stephen-h-branch-s-alligator-vol-1:
Stephen Branch's Alligator for Saturday, September 25, 1858, volume one, number 23, sells at 2 cents and leads with Early Boyhood and its Merry Pastimes. Branch recalls the woman's school at four and a desperate descent on the sugar bowl. He recalls too the two cents he always got on the Fourth of July if he had been good.

He remembers his mother's death, a blast of lightning that felled him while whittling on the summer green, and schoolboy walks with his brother William. The number also holds Stephen and his Adult Pupil, a mournful scene of Branch in his cell at Blackwell's Island, and a page of advertisements.
55090-stephen-h-branch-s-alligator-vol-1:
Stephen Branch's Alligator, volume one number twenty, is a newspaper issue dated Saturday, September 4, 1858. It cost two cents. Its motto runs: and they stoned Stephen. The paper argues its editor's own case, for Branch writes from inside a penitentiary.

Scripture tells how Stephen, preaching truth to the Pharisees, was stoned. In modern days, the paper says, they have stoned Stephen another way. Branch, guiltless of any crime save free opinion, was set to labour in a quarry with felons and thieves. The warden, Fitch, pleaded that duty compelled him. The Alligator challenges him to show one word of his instructions that makes such labour compulsory.
56815-w-kent-co-s-annual-catalogue-octob:
W Kent and Company's Annual Catalogue, dated October 1858, is a London bookseller's list of new and illustrated works. Kent carried on the Fleet Street business late David Bogue's. The catalogue opens with the season's gift books, priced and described for the trade and for buyers.

First comes The Loves of the Poets, a series of steel engravings of ideal beauty. Eminent artists drew them, and Tennyson and Wordsworth supply illustrative text. The price runs from twenty one shillings plain to forty two coloured. Tennyson's Miller's Daughter follows, with seventeen steel engravings and a portrait of the author. Such catalogues were the book trade's engine before advertising grew loud. A year's publishing hopes stand here in columns: art books, poetry, and the illustrated volumes that filled Victorian drawing room tables.
56992-stephen-h-branch-s-alligator-vol-1:
Stephen Branch's Alligator, volume one, number fourteen, is a satirical weekly dated Saturday, July 24, 1858. The price was two cents. Its lead piece, a Conference of Methodists, is a mock dialogue among the Harper brothers. John, Wesley, and Fletcher Harper lament desperate times and poor returns on advertising.

An evil genius and a good genius interrupt the talk. Jack Harper reports an interview with James Gordon Bennett, the rival editor. Jim Harper fans himself and calls for ice water at the news. Branch, a gadfly editor, stuffed his paper with parody, gossip, and attacks on the great New York publishers. One issue shows the bite that made the Alligator feared and short-lived.
59688-chiricahua-national-monument-1958:
Chiricahua National Monument is a National Park Service guide to a small park in the Chiricahua Mountains of southeastern Arizona. The cover shows tall columns of rock in the Balanced Rock area. The guide calls the place a mountain island in a desert sea: steep, wooded ridges rising from brown grassland, filled with pinnacles and spires carved from volcanic rock.

Inside, the text tells how the rocks formed. Long ago, blast after blast laid down layers of volcanic fragments, which later earth movements lifted and cracked. Wind and running water then wore the cracks into towers, balanced rocks, and shapes like beasts and men. The guide also notes the trees, shrubs, and birds of the canyons. Visitors in the late 1950s used booklets like this one to plan walks and to learn what they were seeing.
60992-the-letters-of-richard-ford-1797-1:
Rowland Prothero edited The Letters of Richard Ford, covering the years 1797 to 1858. Dutton issued the book in New York in 1905, with portraits and plates. Ford was the great English writer on Spain of his age. His letters begin at Seville in November 1830.

Ford lived in Spain for three years, at Seville and in the Alhambra. He writes of Spanish politics, roads, and the execution of Torrijos. Back in England he settled at Heavitree, near Exeter, and wrote for the Quarterly Review. His Handbook for Travellers in Spain, after delays and a suppressed first edition, made his name. Letters trace the making of that book, his marriages, and his art, down to his death.
62534-roberts-chester-guide-1858:
Hugh Roberts published this guide to Chester in 1858, revised by John Hicklin, editor of the local paper. The Royal Agricultural Society's visit that July prompted the new edition. Forty-six engravings and a plan of the city fill the book.

Chapters walk the visitor through Chester's history: Roman remains, the walls, the gates, and the castle. The famous Rows, covered shopping galleries, get their own section. The cathedral and churches follow, with Eaton Hall and its park at the end. Cab fares, hotels, and distances serve the practical traveler. Hicklin hoped the book would serve strangers as a useful memorial of the old city. It is a complete Victorian guide, proud and thorough.
63175-the-sia-1894-n-11-1889-1890-pages-:
Matilda Coxe Stevenson wrote The Sia, a report for the Smithsonian's Bureau of Ethnology on the Sia pueblo folk. Their cosmogony opens the study, how the world and its peoples came to be. Cult societies follow, with their rites for rain and healing told in full.

The Snake, Giant, Knife, and other societies each get their rain rites, with songs for rain and for the sick set down word by word. Childbirth, death customs, and myths close the book, among them tales of Coyote. Plates show the village and its plaza. Students of the southwest get a deep, early record of a pueblo world.
65917-crater-lake-national-park-oregon-1:
Crater Lake National Park, Oregon is a visitor guide issued by the National Park Service under Secretary of the Interior Fred Seaton. The catalog dates it to 1958. Its cover shows Wizard Island with Llao Rock behind it, the classic view of the lake.

The guide opens with a welcome, then tells of the lake's discovery and its geological story. Sections cover wildlife, forests, and wildflowers, with a map of the park. Later pages list what to see and do, how to reach the park, and where to stay or camp. Notes on the Mission 66 program and on visitor fees date the booklet. It is a neat sample of park service writing at mid century.
70418-maritime-enterprise-1485-1558:
Maritime Enterprise, 1485 to 1558, by James Williamson, studies English sea trade and discovery under the early Tudors. The Clarendon Press at Oxford published the book in 1913. A frontispiece shows an English warship of the years 1514 to 1545, copied from a Cotton manuscript.

The chapters begin with Henry the Seventh and his commercial policy, then set out how English trade was organized. Two chapters follow the Cabot voyages, John Cabot's of 1497 and 1498 and Sebastian Cabot's after them. An early colonial project, the growth of commerce, and the fall of the Hansa come next. The book closes with the English in the North Sea and with France, Spain and the Mediterranean. Williamson wrote the standard account of how English merchants and sailors first pushed out into the Atlantic world.
aelian-works-hercher-1858:
Claudius Aelianus, a Roman-era Greek with a storyteller's ear, left two great stores of lore. Aelian's works, in Rudolf Hercher's 1858 edition, gather all that survives of him in one set. Seventeen books On the Nature of Animals stand first in the file.

Beside them sit the Historical Miscellany, a heap of short tales and facts, plus his letters and fragments. Bees, elephants, kings, and fools pass through his pages in bright, brief scenes. Naturalists mined him for animal lore; tale tellers mined him for plots. Hercher's edition is the full Aelian in one scholarly home.
allibone-critical-dictionary-english-lit:
Samuel Allibone, a Philadelphia bookseller and bibliographer, published Volume One of his Critical Dictionary of English Literature in 1858. It covers authors from A to J. The full work notices some 30,000 British and American writers.

Each entry gives the author's life, a list of works, and judgments gathered from reviews and histories. Forty subject indexes help readers find writers by theme, from poetry to voyages. Allibone labored for years among his own vast book collection. The dictionary became the great Victorian bio-bibliography, the first place to learn what an author wrote and what critics said of it.
arxiv-2412-00158:
E Santos wrote a 2024 paper for the Pierre Auger Collaboration on open cosmic ray data and public classes. The observatory shares data under the FAIR principles: findable, accessible, interoperable, and reusable. A new portal launched in 2021 carries a tenth of all recorded events. A catalog of the hundred most energetic events is included.

Each data set carries its own permanent identifier. Notebooks on the portal let visitors rebuild famous results step by step. That dual design serves both researchers and the public. International masterclasses use the same data to teach students. Open data widens the multi-messenger astronomy effort beyond the team.
arxiv-2412-01058:
Tom Kimpson and co-authors show, in a 2024 paper, how to strip a mains power hum from data in the hunt for steady gravitational waves. Detectors that listen for these waves, such as LIGO, show long, thin noise lines in their data. A true signal that lands on a line is often thrown out, lost to the search. The mains line sits at 60 hertz in the United States. Their fix borrows a noise-cancel trick from electrical work, built on a fast least-squares update.

They pair the fix with a hidden Markov model, a standard search tool that tracks a signal whose tone can drift. A fake signal, set to cross the mains line, was missed before the fix in both fake and real LIGO noise. After the fix, the line fell by 20 to 40 decibels and the signal stood out. The pair can save signals once lost.
arxiv-2412-01458:
Michael Stadlhofer and co-authors track energy flow as clusters form in this 2024 physics paper. Breaking molecules apart with light is well studied, but forming bonds with light is not. Starting conditions for growth have been hard to set with precision.

The team used helium nanodroplets loaded with magnesium atoms as a clean stage. Fast light pulses excited the atoms, and electron spectra watched the response in real time. A delayed signal at about one picosecond marked the shift from a loose foam-like layout to a compact cluster. Fitting put the change near four hundred fifty femtoseconds. Collisions of excited atoms seem to pool energy into high states.
arxiv-2412-01558:
Dhiman Paul, Md Rizwan Parvez, Nabeel Mohammed, and Shafin Rahman built a model that finds video highlights and moments. Their paper, from twenty twenty-four, tackles two linked tasks at once. One task flags the best parts of a video. The other finds the span that matches a text query. Past joint models were weak at cross task links and at matching video with text.

Their model, VideoLights, adds parts to refine features and align the two tasks. A fusion network joins video and text both ways. A feedback path lets each task help the other. They also used a large vision-language model to enrich the features. Tests on three known sets put the model ahead of prior work.
arxiv-2412-01758:
Hvozd, Patsahan, Patsahan, Kalyuzhnyi, and Holovko study how ionic liquids behave when trapped in porous matter in two thousand twenty-four. Ionic liquids are salts that flow at room temperature, and their gas-liquid balance shifts inside pores. The team treats the question with theory rather than lab work.

Two models differ in the shape of the charged molecule: a bendy chain in one, a stiff rod in the other. Each model mixes paired and free ions inside a disordered bed of hard spheres. Rod-shaped ions gave lower turning points for both heat and density, and a narrower band where liquid and vapor coexist. The work is the first theory pass at rod-shaped molecular ions in such pores.
arxiv-2412-01858:
Siddhant Dutta and co-authors present a 2024 framework that joins quantum computing with privacy-locked group learning. In federated learning, many sites train one model without sharing raw data, and full homomorphic encryption lets them merge updates while still coded. The catch: coded merging often dulls the merged model. Their design adds a quantum mixture of experts that reads several data types at once.

On mixed data sets, and on a hard case pairing gene data with brain scans, the quantum experts lifted accuracy, above all for rare classes. The quantum step also offset the accuracy lost to encryption. The authors offer the frame as a way to keep both privacy and performance.
arxiv-2412-01958:
Said Togru, Youssef Sameh Mostafa, and Karim Lotfy test whether rule-based retraining can make image models harder to fool, in a report from two thousand twenty-four. The method uses fixed rules about how a changed input should change the output, called metamorphic relations. Retraining runs in cycles with methods that learn from both labeled and unlabeled images.

Tests used three standard image sets and a mix of ready-made and fresh models. On average the score for toughness rose by about seventeen points for each model. Four named retraining methods were built into one shared frame so runs could repeat with ease. Readers get a hands-on route to tougher vision models for real use.
arxiv-2412-02258:
Marta Victoria, Zhe Zhang, Gorm Andresen, Parisa Rahdan, and Ebbe Gøtske share lessons from a shared rooftop solar project at Aarhus University in Denmark, in a 2024 paper. European law now backs energy communities that let citizens join the shift to clean power. Solar roofs suit that idea well, since panels can sit close to the people who fund them.

Students and staff bought shares in a 98-kilowatt rooftop system split into 900 parts. The university uses the power, and share owners receive a yearly payment in return. The road to launch was rough, and the team list the ten largest hurdles they met. Other campuses and towns can use those lessons to dodge the same snags.
arxiv-2412-02358:
Ainara Saiz-Pérez and co-authors simulate the twin jets of the radio galaxy NGC 1052 to learn why one side can look narrower than the other, in a 2024 paper. Telescope arrays can now trace how these jets pinch into beams close to their black hole. The team ran relativistic fluid simulations of a jet squeezed by its surroundings and shaken by passing shocks.

Synthetic telescope images were then built from the runs, including the blur and limits of a real observing array, and an automated tracker followed jet features. Shocks traveling down a symmetric jet bent its apparent shape enough to mimic the one-sided look of real sources. The work cautions against reading jet asymmetry as proof of lopsided ejection.
arxiv-2412-02658:
Ayush Jaiswal studies moduli spaces of real and quaternionic connections in a 2024 math paper. The work deals with connections on Lie algebroids, a broad setup that links algebra and shape.

Jaiswal proves that the gauge theory moduli space for these connections has a smooth Hilbert manifold form and is Hausdorff. The result extends known work on simple connections for complex bundles over compact complex spaces. Readers get a firm base for studying these spaces with gauge tools. The paper is short and proof-focused, aimed at experts in geometry and algebra.
arxiv-2412-02758:
Guido Carnevale, Nicola Mimmo, and Giuseppe Notarstefano solved a classic control problem from cost measurements alone in 2024. The linear quadratic regulator picks control gains that balance error against effort. Standard solvers need the system's matrices, which are often unknown.

Their method, EXP-LQR, refines a control policy step by step using only a truncated cost read from finite-time runs. Each run perturbs the current policy in an extremum-seeking pattern. No direct knowledge of the system or cost matrices is used. A Lyapunov argument with averaging theory shows the iterates converge fast to a tiny neighborhood of the best gain. Tests on an induction motor control task back the theory.
arxiv-2412-02858:
Labeling tissue images without paired examples is the problem taken up by Arthur Boschet and co-authors in a 2024 paper. Segmenting such images matters for many medical uses, yet labeled data are scarce. The team builds a pipeline that uses image translation between domains that are not paired, so no labels are needed in the target domain at first.

Two ways of making pseudo labels are tested across three image domains that grow less alike. One path trains a model on synthetic data made by translating labeled images into the target style. The team reports a mean Dice score near 0.736 on one data set. The aim is to give human labelers a strong first draft to refine.
arxiv-2412-02958:
Hashim Yamani and Zouhaïr Mouayn derive new families of coherent states for the harmonic oscillator, the workhorse system of quantum physics. Their 2024 paper works within the J-matrix method, which writes it as a tridiagonal matrix in a chosen basis. Following that route, they recover generalized coherent states of Perelomov type, labeled by complex numbers and an integer level.

Expanding these states in number states gives coefficients expressed through Hermite functions. Their combinations turn out to solve the two-dimensional magnetic Laplacian at the matching Landau level, tying oscillator physics to electrons in magnetic fields. The authors then extend the construction to the Morse potential, the standard model of a vibrating molecule. Coherent states are the most classical quantum states available; new families enlarge the toolkit for optics and molecular science at once.
arxiv-2412-03058:
Models must flag inputs unlike any they trained on, and Yifan Wu and co-authors revisit an energy-based way to do that flagging, in work from twenty twenty-four. Past methods lean on hand-made odd sets or heavy data tricks, which often miss real odd inputs. Their frame makes odd-like samples by simple changes to normal ones.

Those changed samples build an energy wall between normal and odd inputs during training. A new loss rule, drawn from that wall idea, sharpens the split. Tests across many standard sets matched or beat top rival methods. The team argues simple changes can stand in for costly hand-made odd sets, a swap that makes the flagging step cheaper and broader.
arxiv-2412-03158:
Nouhaila Innan, Alberto Marchisio, Mohamed Bennai, and Muhammad Shafique build, in 2024 work, a quantum neural net that calls who should get a loan. Banks need sharp calls to weigh risk and fit loans to clients, yet money data run wide and tangled for old tools. Their net runs on quantum rules, with a dropout trick inside the circuit to curb overfit.

On one rich data set the net called loan fitness with near-total accuracy. A sweep of tune methods found the best setup. Stress tests then shook the net with set kinds of quantum noise, and it held up well. The team frames the work as a base guide for quantum tools in money calls.
arxiv-2412-03558:
Zehuan Huang and co-authors introduce MIDI, a method to generate a full three dimensional scene from one image in a 2024 paper. Older routes rebuild scenes, fetch ready objects, or generate objects one by one in stages. MIDI instead extends a trained image to object model into a multi instance diffusion model, which creates many objects at once with correct spatial relations.

A new attention mechanism captures how objects interact and cohere, inside the generation step itself. Inputs are partial object images plus global scene context, and object completion is modeled directly. Training uses a small set of scene level data plus single object data to keep general skill. Tests on synthetic, real, and stylized scenes show top results.
arxiv-2412-03658:
Esha Bhatia, Sayan Chakrabarti, and Sovan Chakraborty test, in a 2024 paper, whether altered gravity can explain the star motions in a ghostly galaxy. The galaxy, NGC1052-DF44, is an ultra-diffuse system ruled by dark matter under the standard view. The team instead fit its velocity spread with three modified gravity models and no dark matter halo.

The models are MOND, with its fixed acceleration scale; an f(R) model built from a stretched curvature term; and a quantum-gravity-inspired model where the gravity constant runs with energy. All three could match the observed spread. Only MOND and the running-G model, though, stayed competitive with the standard dark matter fit. Letting the orbit mix vary, rather than assuming round symmetry, kept the race close.
arxiv-2412-03858:
Hao Hao and co-authors argue that unevaluated solutions still hold value in costly optimization tasks. In such tasks, testing one solution can consume huge resources. Surrogate models stand in for most tests to save cost.

Evolution guided only by tested solutions loses diversity fast. Populations grow too alike across successive generations. That sameness weakens the operators that breed new candidates. The team adds top predicted but untested solutions to selection. Surrogate scores pick which untested candidates join the pool. Better spread then yields stronger next generations. Tests across operators and surrogate types confirm the gain. The trick is cheap and broad in scope. It asks for no new tests and no extra gear, which makes it easy to add to tools that labs already run each day.
arxiv-2412-04258:
Thermophotovoltaic cells turn heat glow into power, and the metal grid on the cell's front face can quietly eat into the yield. Jeyar and co-authors model that grid honestly, as a metal grating inside a full three-part theory, instead of the usual shortcut that just blanks out the covered area. Their method reads the light power the semiconductor actually absorbs, which lets them define the cell's efficiency more soundly.

In the near field, the grid's effect on absorbed power, and thus on electrical output, is large, and its behavior departs strongly from the shortcut's predictions. The authors argue contact design deserves full modeling in these devices.
arxiv-2412-04358:
Oscar Key and four co-authors evaluated faster ways to find the largest values in a data array in twenty twenty-four. Picking the exact top k values forces a whole array to be funneled through one merge step, which wastes the parallel power of AI chips. Bucketed methods split the array into groups and take the top values of each group, giving an answer that is close but not exact.

The team studied the design choices of this method family with both theory and tests on real tasks. Their test cases come from sparsity methods for language models, which use top-k picks to keep only the most important weights or signals. They also released a fast bucketed top-k tool for PyTorch. The trade is small accuracy loss for large speed gains on parallel hardware.
arxiv-2412-04558:
Maria Mihaela Trusca, Mingxiao Li, and Marie-Francine Moens present a 2025 model for editing images by action words. Normal editing tools insert, remove, or alter objects in a still image. Their aim is to make the edit show an action instead. A person or object should change pose or place to depict that action. The look of the objects should stay the same through the change. Training data came from video frames shot before and after real actions.

The model learns to spot what makes one action differ from another in a scene. Tests showed large gains over past editing tools on such tasks. The model could also reason about a starting scene and build its end state. That skill lets a single photo serve as the first frame of an action. The authors see action-aware editing as a step beyond static touch-ups.
arxiv-2412-04658:
William Compton, Max Cohen, and Aaron Ames teach safety filters to see around the gap between simple and full robot models, in a 2024 paper. Control barrier functions keep machines inside safe bounds, but they are far easier to build for a reduced model than for the real machine. Enforcing the simple model's safety on the full one can break it.

Their predictive barrier checks rollouts of the full model and adds a learned cushion to the safety condition. Proof shows the layered setup stays safe. The cushion is learned in massive parallel simulation with randomized conditions. A hopping robot ran the method in hardware, staying safe without needless caution.
arxiv-2412-04758:
Matt MacDermott, James Fox, Francesco Belardinelli, and Tom Everitt present a 2024 paper that defines a measure of goal-directedness. Judging whether a system truly pursues a goal matters for AI safety and for the philosophy of agency. Their measure, called MEG, works inside causal models and step-by-step decision settings. It builds on a known frame from inverse reward learning, where goals are inferred from behavior.

MEG can score a system against one known goal, a set of candidate goals, or a set of outcome traits. The authors prove the measure meets several traits a good measure should have. They also give methods to compute it and test them on small cases. A shared yardstick could help labs rate how goal-driven an AI system is before it is trusted with open tasks.
arxiv-2412-04958:
Lea Ibele and co-authors present a chemistry paper from 2024 on simulating excited molecules. When light excites a molecule, its atoms move while electrons hop between energy surfaces. A common simulation lets each atom path run on its own and hop when rules say so. That scheme suffers from fading coherence, blocked hops, and clashes between its parts.

The team's scheme couples the paths so they move as one swarm. The swarm as a whole keeps its energy fixed, and paths share energy when a hop occurs. That single change tackles all three flaws at once. Tests on two light-driven molecules gave sound results for electron and vibration traits over time. The authors base the scheme on an exact split of the full quantum problem.
arxiv-2412-05258:
Schulik and Owen use a helium line trio to read big world outflows in this twenty twenty-four paper. Close big worlds leak gas that cools as it spreads in space. That cool fall can pack the trio state past plain counts.

Inside, flow sims show the trio glut springs from cool gas acts. The glut may solve one world's wide line tale in past reads. Those reads then prove the leak runs as true flow, not still gas. The pair also maps which falls feed or drain the trio state. Far worlds past a set gap lose trio depth to drift splits.
arxiv-2412-05458: Pereira and Vachaspati test in twenty twenty-four whether a special electric field pattern in a gauge theory can hold steady under small disturbances. The theory pairs a force field with a scalar field that sources electric patterns unlike standard ones. They probe the pattern for growing wobbles that would tear it apart. They find a region of settings where the pattern is stable. Where the scalar field has a negative mass term, the pattern splits into two branches, and one branch proves unstable.
arxiv-2412-05558:
Feng Li, Jiusong Luo, and Wanjun Xia build WavFusion in 2024 for speech mood reads that blend sound with text. Speech alone blurs mood lines, yet past blends gloss over how modes play on each other. Their frame pairs a strong speech coder with a gated cross-mode watch and a like-trait gap loss.

Tests on two bench sets, IEMOCAP and MELD, beat past top frames on mood calls. The gains back fine cross-mode play and trait-sharp codes as the levers that count. The work adds a clean path for joint speech mood reads.
arxiv-2412-05858: Alon Agin and Barak Weiss show that the Dirichlet spectrum is always an interval, in a math paper from 2024. The spectrum, defined by two earlier authors, collects values tied to matrices and to norms in two spaces. In the smallest case it was already known to be an interval. The pair extend that result to all sizes but the trivial one, and to all norms, and they show that kindred spectra are intervals too. Their proof adapts an argument of Khintchine from 1926.
arxiv-2412-05958:
Adem Ait and co-authors extend a business process language so it can model work shared by people and AI agents, in a 2024 paper. Language models now power agents that solve hard tasks, and teams of agents do better still. Yet mixed human and agent flows are hard to specify with care.

Current process languages lack the parts needed to say who owns each task and how choices get made. The extension adds those concepts to the BPMN standard and gives them a matching picture notation. The team built the extension into an open source editor shared on GitHub. The paper is exploratory and invites wider trials.
arxiv-2412-06058:
Luigi Verdiani and Wolfgang Ziller study geometric equations on a special class of spaces in this 2024 mathematics paper. The spaces, called cohomogeneity one manifolds, have a symmetry group that moves almost every point in a full orbit. One orbit is singular, and the hard work happens near it. The authors set up starting-value problems for curvature-based equations there.

They show that solutions exist near the singular orbit for preset Ricci curvature, and for the Einstein and soliton equations. Each solution is pinned down by finitely many free constants. A simplifying assumption keeps this first part tractable; the general case is promised for part two. The results extend a toolkit used to build new examples of curved spaces with special properties.
arxiv-2412-06258:
Li Yin and co-authors wrote this sports analytics paper, published in two thousand twenty-four, on tracking players in three-on-three basketball. Players collide, cross, and look alike, so trackers swap identities and coaches lose clean movement data.

The team paints each player with a virtual marker, a pose-based tag learned from body shape rather than jersey color. Active learning keeps the hand-labeling bill low while the marker model improves. The markers are stamped onto video, poses are pulled out with steady identities, and boxes are derived for scoring against standard trackers. On their new three-on-three data set, the method scored well above rival trackers, with zero identity switches. Manual fixes during training also dropped. The authors see the approach serving any multi-agent analysis where bodies tangle, from sports to animal groups.
arxiv-2412-06758:
Daniel Beaulieu and co-authors test a quantum learning method for forecasting what drug-like molecules will do, in work from 2024. Standard quantum methods need slope checks on quantum gear, which can fade and stall training. The reservoir method skips that step, since the quantum part is not tuned directly.

The team fed molecule traits into the quantum reservoir and read the results with a simple layer. As data sets shrank, the quantum method held up better than standard tools, a trait that suits drug work where data are scarce. A mapping check also showed the quantum-touched data formed clearer low-dimension patterns. The authors see promise for small, costly data sets in drug hunting.
arxiv-2412-06858:
Dongwei Wang and Huanrui Yang present Noise Perturbation Fine-tuning, a 2024 fix for fragile weights in model compression. Quantization shrinks language models for cheap serving. A few outlier weights react badly to that squeeze. Keeping them at full precision breaks hardware efficiency.

Their method finds the outliers and shakes them with random noise during light fine-tuning. The shaking flattens the loss surface around those weights. Tamed outliers then survive quantization with less damage. No special mixed-precision handling is needed afterward on the serving hardware. The trick aims at smooth deployment on plain hardware.
arxiv-2412-07458:
Del Pezzo surfaces are a classic testing ground in algebraic geometry, and Karol Palka and Tomasz Pełka chart the open versions of them in a 2024 paper. Their objects are rank-one log del Pezzo pairs: a bumpy projective surface with a boundary divisor removed, leaving an open surface whose structure they want to name.

The theorem says the smooth part of that open surface almost always fibers in lines, either the full affine line or the punctured one. The fibration then extends over a resolution of the whole surface. Exceptions cluster in characteristics two, three, and five, where small-prime arithmetic misbehaves. In characteristic zero the result sharpens a known structure theorem of Miyanishi and Tsunoda. Along the way the authors classify the rational curves that anti-canonical geometry allows on the smooth loci of these surfaces.
arxiv-2412-07558:
Riccardo Scotti and five co-authors set out a hybrid quantum-classic method to merge many clusterings of a data set into one strong one. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-four.

Clustering splits data into groups, but each method has weak spots. Merging the results can patch those spots, and the merged form is of wide use. The team casts the merge task in two known hard forms. One suits atom-based quantum machines, and one suits quantum annealers. They test the method first on a fake of the atom machine, then on a next fake built on tensors. The aim is to let quantum gear take on a core data task.
arxiv-2412-07658:
Anubhav Jain and co-authors rethink negative prompting for image models in a 2024 paper. Text-to-image tools can make harmful content, so users steer them away with a negative prompt naming what to avoid. That steering can collapse when a tricky prompt makes the two predictions nearly the same.

When the gap vanishes, suppression fails and the unwanted concept can appear. Their method, TraSCE, steers the sampling path with a fixed anchor and local guidance instead. It needs no retraining and acts at generation time. Tests in the paper show stronger suppression in the collapse regime. The work matters for safe public image tools.
arxiv-2412-07958:
Shambhavi Krishna and co-authors published this web agent study in 2024. AI assistants that browse the web usually reread and rethink every page at each step. That repeated parsing is slow, costly, and error-prone on dynamic sites. The team proposes PAFFA, a method that plans actions ahead of time. It needs no training for a specific task. Instead it builds an action library from the base model's own knowledge of how websites work.

The library is reused across tasks in two ways. One mode spots the key interactive elements shared by many sites. The other explores a new site once, in depth, and stores what it learns for later visits. In tests, PAFFA cut inference tokens by eighty-seven percent. It also slightly beat the baseline on step accuracy, scoring 0.57 against 0.50. Because explorations update the library, the system adapts to unseen websites.
arxiv-2412-08258:
Maps of research topics help scientists search, sort, and link a fast-growing literature, but drawing them by hand is slow and costly. Tanay Aggarwal, Angelo Salatino, Francesco Osborne, and Enrico Motta test in this 2024 paper whether large language models can do part of that work. The task is to judge how pairs of topics relate, a step at the heart of building such a map.

The team built a gold standard from an engineering word list and asked models to label topic pairs as broader, narrower, the same, or unrelated. They tested seventeen models, open and paid, large and small, under four styles of prompting with no examples. Scores were high for the best systems, and even small trimmed models did well once their settings were tuned. The results suggest machines can draft topic maps that humans then refine.
arxiv-2412-08458:
Saraswata Chaudhuri and Jonathan Hill study how to estimate the average effect of a treatment in a 2024 paper. A common method weights each person by the inverse chance they got the treatment. When some chances sit near zero or one, those weights explode and the estimate becomes unstable and slow to settle.

The authors trim the final weighted value itself in a small, adaptive way, rather than trimming people by their traits. They also correct the bias that trimming can cause when the spread is uneven. In simulated tests their method kept bias and error low while cutting only a few extreme values.
arxiv-2412-08658:
Debasish Mohanty and co-authors release an open-source pipeline that invents new polymers in a paper from 2024. Polymers serve everywhere from car parts to implants. Labs can only cook a small set of building blocks, which caps the search for better plastics. Computer generation can roam far wider.

The pipeline joins three parts: discriminator networks that judge candidates, generators that propose them, and query filters that keep the best. It targets chosen traits, such as ionization potential. The discriminators beat prior top models after architecture tuning. Generators produced fresh polymers inside the wanted trait range. Open code lets any lab extend the hunt for materials that no one has synthesized yet.
arxiv-2412-09458:
Kamal Aghazade and Ali Gholami speed up full waveform inversion, a method that images the Earth's subsurface from waves recorded at the surface, in a 2024 paper. The method is powerful but slow, since classic algorithms wrestle directly with both the wavefields and the Earth model. Their dual approach flips the problem around.

In the new framing, the Lagrange multipliers, weights that enforce the wave equations, become the main unknowns. Once those are estimated well, the Earth model follows simply. The background model stays fixed, so one costly matrix factorization per frequency serves the whole run. Borrowed acceleration tricks sharpen convergence further. On standard test models for both sound-like and elastic waves, the dual method settled faster and with fewer computations than the classic approach.
arxiv-2412-09658:
Cheng Mei and co-authors present SEGT, a transformer built to spot objects in lidar point clouds for the nuScenes driving benchmark. Point clouds are sparse and irregular, awkward for standard attention. Their design spreads the voxels into several ordered fields, each laid out by a different expansion rule. Group attention then reads each field on its own terms.

The model fuses the fields' features by alternating the expansion strategies. That shuffle lets it catch spatial patterns no single layout shows. On the nuScenes test set it scored 73.9 on the detection scale, rising to 74.5 with test-time augmentation. The report states the method placed first on that leaderboard.
arxiv-2412-09858:
Charles Xu, Qiyang Li, Jianlan Luo, and Sergey Levine present a 2024 paper on training robot generalists with data made by learning, not by people. General robot policies can adapt to many tasks, but their skill leans on the quality of their training data. Human demos are costly and often clumsy.

Their method uses trial and error learning to create high quality practice data. A specialist first masters tasks such as plugging in connectors and fitting parts. Its best runs then become training data for the generalist. In real world tests, generalists trained this way beat those trained on human demos by up to forty percent in success rate. They also adapted better to new tasks.
arxiv-2412-10258:
Hao-Chiang Shao and co-authors build, in a 2024 paper, a tool for spotting copy-move forgery in microscope images. Faked experimental images have become a public worry as fraud cases surface. Duplicated patches can hide in background tissue, tiny objects, or both, and may never have appeared in training data.

The authors recast detection as finding regions within one image that mirror each other. Their network, CMSeg-Net, scans features at several scales and compares regions against themselves. Attention modules highlight the duplicated areas, even unseen attack types. The paper also supplies a dataset for the task. Reliable forgery screens protect the published record that other scientists build on.
arxiv-2412-10558:
Mohammad Reza Samsami and co-authors test in 2024 whether bigger language models are harder to fool. A model must weigh what it knows against what the prompt claims, and prompts can lie. The team fed models of several sizes, all from one family, deliberately misleading context.

Larger models resisted the deceptive prompts more, leaning on their stored knowledge when the context clashed with it. They also followed honest instructions better than small models, so the resistance is not mere stubbornness. The effect seems to come from richer use of hints inside the prompt, not from memorizing answers. Size, the authors argue, buys a kind of judgment.
arxiv-2412-10958:
Hao Chen and nine co-authors squeeze images into a handful of soft tokens in a 2024 machine learning paper. Generative models train faster on compact image codes. Hard codebooks waste capacity in each latent token. Their tokenizer blends several codewords softly into each token.

A full photo of standard size fits in 32 tokens. Larger images need only 64 tokens in their setup. Reconstruction quality stays high despite the tight squeeze. Generation speed leaps by up to fifty-five fold on big images. Quality scores stay competitive with much slower rivals. Training the generators also takes fewer passes to converge. The fully smooth design keeps gradients flowing throughout.
arxiv-2412-11158:
Pengqian Lu and co-authors catch data drift before it shows up in the error rate. Their 2024 paper addresses concept drift in streaming data, where the world changes under a deployed model. Standard detectors watch mistakes, but early drift often shifts the data while accuracy holds, so the alarm rings late.

Their alternative watches prediction uncertainty. Theory shows the uncertainty index moves whenever drift occurs, even with a stable error rate. It also moves whenever the error rate does, catching everything the old signal caught plus more. A detector built on adaptive bucketing of the index followed. Tests on synthetic and real datasets confirmed earlier, more reliable detection. In production systems, the cost of drift is the lag before anyone notices. A detector sensitive to the model's own hesitation shortens that lag.
arxiv-2412-11358:
Catherine Falvey and co-authors count special matrices in a 2024 paper in algebra. The entries come from a ring of integers modulo a prime power, a setting full of zero divisors that break field rules. They ask how many square matrices over this ring can be diagonalized within the same ring.

The finite-field version of the count is known, but zero divisors make the ring version much harder. The paper sets up the enumeration problem and explains where the difficulty enters. Such counts matter for combinatorics and for coding and cryptography over rings. The authors position their work among recent studies of matrices over finite rings.
arxiv-2412-11658:
Gaurav Aggarwal and Anish Ghosh bound the packing dimension of sets of singular matrices, in a 2024 mathematics paper. Singular matrices are those that Diophantine approximation handles unusually well, and their size on fractal sets was largely uncharted. The authors give the first upper bounds for the weighted versions of these sets.

Intersecting the sets with fractals still yields bounds, and even the unweighted matrix case is new. For plain row vectors their results widen the known family of fractals. The proofs lean on homogeneous dynamics, bounding how orbits of lattice points under diagonal flows escape on average. The paper extends fractal approximation theory into matrix territory.
arxiv-2412-11758:
Gabriel de Jesus and Sérgio Nunes build search tools for the Tetun language in a 2024 arXiv paper. Tetun, spoken in Timor-Leste, lacks the basic resources that web search needs. The team set out to create that foundation and test how well retrieval can work.

They built a stopword list of 160 words, a stemmer with three variants, and a test collection with 59 topics and many documents. Tests compared many strategies on titles and full text. One simple title-based strategy beat the baseline clearly, with faster runs and better scores. The resources are public to support future Tetun search research.
arxiv-2412-12358:
Samy Ateia and Udo Kruschwitz present a web system for biomedical question answering with sourced answers, in a 2024 paper. Their system grows user queries using a language model. It then searches domain literature and drafts replies. Citations link each claim to its source document. Generated queries stay visible for user editing.

Two answer styles are supported: short paragraphs and cited text. The design grew from a strong run in a biomedical search challenge. Few-shot prompting drives the expansion and extraction steps. Transparency is the headline feature for professional users. Searchers can inspect and steer the machine's queries. Code is public, and a live demo runs online. The authors target researchers who need trustworthy scientific answers. Domain focus sets the tool apart from general chatbots.
arxiv-2412-12458:
Pairs trading bets that two stocks which usually move together will snap back when their prices drift apart. Jirat Suchato, Sean Wiryadi, Danran Chen, Ava Zhao, and Michael Yue model that drift with the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process, a standard model of a value pulled back toward its mean. They test the model against a naive strategy that uses a rolling window for its mean and spread.

The physics-flavored model read signals and trends well. On a risk-adjusted basis, though, it lost to the simpler rolling-window approach. The authors blame pairs whose relationship itself wanders over time, plus the difficulty of tuning the model's settings. Their verdict is preliminary but pointed: fancier math does not guarantee better trading.
arxiv-2412-12558:
Factoring large numbers is the hardness that underpins RSA encryption, and quantum circuits for it usually demand huge resources. Gregory Kahanamoku-Meyer, Seyoon Ragavan, Vinod Vaikuntanathan, and Katherine Van Kirk present in 2024 a far leaner circuit. It factors a broad class of integers: numbers built as a squared prime times a smaller factor. Their classical hardness is expected to match RSA-type problems, though RSA numbers themselves are excluded.

For these numbers the circuit uses near-linear gate counts with space and depth below linear, a first for a classically hard factoring problem. The engine is a space-efficient quantum method for computing the Jacobi symbol in superposition, building on an older quantum squarefree-decomposition algorithm. The same trick extends to greatest common divisors and modular inverses. The authors note no classical shortcut exploits the small second factor, so the quantum speedup here is genuine.
arxiv-2412-12858:
Wang and co-authors build a speech command recognizer that runs on brain-like spiking networks, aiming at low power use on small devices. Spiking networks fire only when signals arrive, which suits sound over time, but long sound clips force many time steps and raise the cost. Their 2024 system, SpikeSCR, mixes global and local structure to learn speech patterns well across long clips.

A second method then teaches a leaner version of the network in stages, from easy to hard material. That staged teaching cut time steps by sixty percent and energy use by about half, while scores stayed close to the best rivals. Tests ran on three standard speech command data sets. The authors offer the pair as a route to practical voice control on edge hardware.
arxiv-2412-13258:
Zarattini, Andreon, and Puddu ask where gas-poor galaxy clusters sit inside the cosmic web, in a 2024 paper. Clusters with faint X-ray glow hold less hot gas than bright ones. The team took twenty-nine clusters from a carefully unbiased sample and measured each one's distance to the spine of its nearest filament, the great strands along which galaxies gather. They then compared distances with mass, gas fraction, and brightness.

Faint clusters sat, on average, farther from filaments than bright ones, with middling clusters in between. Very few faint clusters came within two megaparsecs of a spine. A statistical test could not fully rule out chance, and the authors say so. They speculate that filaments shield clusters from their central black hole's outflows, letting gas fall back sooner. A larger sample is needed to settle the idea, they conclude.
arxiv-2412-13358:
Mark de Berg, Arpan Sadhukhan, and Frits Spieksma study the tradeoff between stability and accuracy in graph choices as vertices stream in. Two tasks rule the study. One is a dominating set, a guard set that sees all vertices. The other is an independent set, with no two chosen vertices linked. A dynamic method is stable if each new vertex costs it only a few swaps. Their 2024 work maps what stability can buy.

For both tasks, near-perfect accuracy forces huge swap counts, on the scale of the whole graph, even on bipartite graphs of low degree. When arrival degree is capped, stable methods do far better. A method with one swap per step reaches a modest ratio, and one with three swaps does leaner still. A method with swaps on the scale of the cap reaches a flat ratio. Independent set methods extend to full dynamic graphs as well.
arxiv-2412-13458:
Jie Pan and co-authors slide stacked carbon sheets in a wavy pattern to wake a slant in their flow traits. The trait, a Berry curvature dipole, needs a break in the neat lattice of the sheet. Twisting one sheet against the next can break it, yet flat slides of one sheet on the next tend to snap back. Their 2024 plan slides the sheets in a wavy, locked way that holds.

A corrugated base sets that wavy slide as the sheets grow or rest. Simulations show a large dipole from a small slide. The dipole can run a hundred times the span of the slide itself. Slide span and charge gaps between sheets tune the size by hand. The team pitches the wavy base as a bench-ready route to strong flow traits in carbon stacks.
arxiv-2412-14158:
Text-to-video models make striking clips but give filmmakers little say over the camera. Xi Wang, Robin Courant, Marc Christie, and Vicky Kalogeiton build AKiRa, an add-on kit that trains a camera adapter on top of an existing video generator. The adapter follows a detailed camera model, so users can steer motion and optics together, including focal length, lens distortion, and aperture.

With that control, a generated scene can zoom smoothly, bend into a fisheye view, or soften its background into bokeh while the action continues. Tests show the kit combines several optical effects in one clip and beats earlier methods at following the requested camera behavior. The authors present it as a step toward video generation that respects the craft choices directors use to guide mood and attention, rather than leaving the virtual camera to chance.
arxiv-2412-14258:
Florian Girelli, Jianhui Qiu, and Céline Zwikel write a 2024 paper on gravity at the edge of flat space. Far from all mass, spacetime flattens, and waves that reach that edge reveal a huge symmetry group. The breaking of that symmetry yields special modes that shape how scattering is computed.

In the usual metric picture those modes must be added to the phase space by hand. The team instead uses teleparallel gravity, a twin account of the same physics built on a frame field and a flat connection. They place the special modes inside that flat connection in a natural way. Phase space tools then link the setup to a known rule for charges at the edge.
arxiv-2412-14358: Nikiforov, Baushev, and Barkov studied how the squashed shape of a collapsing ball of matter affects its fall into a black hole. Their ellipsoid has no pressure and starts with a set stretch. They show the smallest size reached during collapse scales as a near-universal power of that starting stretch. They also estimate which starting settings send the ellipsoid straight into a black hole.
arxiv-2412-14558:
Bruno Fernando Aceves-Martínez and co-authors compare two math statements about patterns in whole numbers in a 2024 paper. Ramsey theory studies patterns forced by any coloring of number pairs. One restricted form uses only colorings that ignore shifts. Hindman type results promise sums inside one color class.

The team shows the restricted Ramsey form and the adjacent Hindman statement carry equal strength. The verdict holds under two lenses, proof strength and computing power. Higher dimensional cousins of both statements get the same treatment. Such matches help logicians sort the hidden cost of pattern theorems. The work ties two lines of combinatorics into one neat equivalence.
arxiv-2412-14758:
Alexander Gheorghiu and David Pym lay mathematical foundations for reductive reasoning, the backwards style of logic used in most everyday and machine reasoning. Deduction moves from premises to conclusions. Reduction runs the other way: starting from a goal, it asks what premises would be enough to reach it, as in planning how to meet a friend by noon.

The paper gives a semantic account of reduction operators, the backwards counterparts of inference rules. It covers how to represent these operators, how they drive a reasoning process, and what makes one of them valid. The authors argue this paradigm spans activities from formal proof search to ordinary planning. Their analysis aims to put a widely used but under-theorized style of reasoning on firm ground.
arxiv-2412-14958:
Kristof Schmieden and co-authors study, in a 2024 paper, how a niobium nitride coating behaves in a superconducting radio frequency cavity set inside a strong magnetic field. The cavity belongs to a new experiment hunting for axions, hypothetical particles that may make up dark matter. The search needs a cavity that keeps a high quality factor while sitting in the field that coaxes axions to reveal themselves.

Their cavity, coated with the nitride, was tested at a resonance near 8.4 gigahertz in a 2.5 tesla field. As the field rose, the surface resistance rose with it. That lowered the quality factor, meaning more energy leaked per cycle. The pattern matched earlier cavities made with a related tin compound. The result tells the axion hunters what performance to expect, and what to improve, in the magnetic setting.
arxiv-2412-15058:
Hallee Wong and co-authors present MultiverSeg, a tool that lets researchers outline structures across a new biomedical image set without starting over on each picture, in a 2024 paper. Segmenting a novel dataset normally means hand-tracing every image or having labeled examples from the same task already, which new studies lack. MultiverSeg takes the user's clicks, boxes, or scribbles on the current image, plus every image labeled in the session, as context.

As the context grows, each image needs fewer interactions to reach an accurate outline. Against a state-of-the-art interactive segmenter working image by image, MultiverSeg cut clicks by thirty-six percent and scribbles by twenty-five percent at the same quality bar. The tasks were new to the model. The authors release code and model weights. They pitch it at labs that face a fresh segmentation task every project.
arxiv-2412-15258:
Salman Faroz presents a disease-focused AI embedding model in this 2024 paper. Embedding models turn text into numbers so computers can compare meaning. General medical models spread their learning across all of health care. As a result, they blur the fine differences between diseases. Faroz trained a model only on disease material.

The training set was built for the purpose, with disease write-ups, symptoms, and question-answer pairs. Tests on disease-specific data sets followed. The new model beat general medical models at spotting disease context. It also separated look-alike diseases more cleanly. Such a tool suits search systems that fetch exact disease facts for doctors or chatbots.
arxiv-2412-15358:
Machine learning models hunger for images, and one way to feed them is to generate more. Abdullah Al Rahat and Hemanth Venkateswara propose a generation recipe in a 2024 paper that keeps synthetic images close to real ones. Plain text prompts, they note, drift away from the target domain.

Their method, Mixing Visual Concepts, builds fresh text embeddings out of captions from real images. A pre-trained diffusion model is then fine-tuned, conditioned on both real images and these mixed embeddings. The result is batches of new images that vary while staying faithful to the source data. On benchmark classification tasks, training with these images beat leading augmentation techniques. The authors test both coarse changes, like scene type, and fine ones, like object detail.
arxiv-2412-15658:
The ATLAS Collaboration reports a 2024 measurement from lead nuclei smashed together at high energy. Such crashes make a hot mix of quarks and gluons. The team measured how charged particles spread around the crash axis. Two patterns, classed as second and third order, were tracked across a wide range of speeds and crash types.

Data came from the ATLAS detector in 2018. The second pattern stayed positive up to very high particle speeds. The third pattern stayed positive to a lower range, with some method effects at the top end. At high speed, most particles come from jets that lose energy in the hot mix. The results probe how that loss depends on path length.
arxiv-2412-15858:
Abhimanyu Susobhanan presents, in a 2024 paper, a software package for timing pulsars and sorting signal from noise. Pulsars are spinning neutron stars whose pulses arrive with clock-like regularity. Tiny delays in those arrivals can betray passing gravitational waves and other physics.

His package, Vela, is written in Julia for speed and built in modules for clarity. A Python companion handles file reading, clock corrections, and solar system tables using an established timing tool. A strict test suite guards the package's reliability. The paper explains the design and walks through its use. Fast, trustworthy timing tools are the workhorses behind pulsar astronomy's biggest claims.
arxiv-2412-15958:
Valerio Bertone, Michael Fucilla, and Cédric Mezrag sum heavy-quark mass effects in proton part maps in a 2024 arXiv paper. Part maps tell how a proton's push is shared among its quarks and gluons. Lab-made maps at odd angles must be matched to the standard maps, and heavy quarks bend that match. The team works out the one-loop fix with the mass kept whole.

The result holds at all scales of the mass term and shrinks to the known light case at zero mass. Code then turns a proton map into its charm twin map. The size of the mass fix is weighed at the close.
arxiv-2412-16358:
Mikael Yeghiazaryan and co-authors craft in 2024 texture and shape attacks that fool vehicle detectors in fake overhead images. Air view detection is already hard from clutter, small size, shade, and blocks. Attack tests show how far that trust can bend under set real-world limits.

Texture attacks cap resolution, area, and color range to stay practical. Shape tweaks are graded beside them for attack power. Three detector designs face the attacks in wide tests, which expose a clear trade: practical tweaks bite less, and strong ones look less real. Code and data ship with the study.
arxiv-2412-16458:
Amir Ayati, Hugh Burton, and Stijn De Baerdemacker present a quantum chemistry method that repairs broken spin symmetry, in a 2024 paper. Simple mean-field calculations often break spin rules to capture electron correlation. The broken answers then mix spin states wrongly. Their method projects the constrained solutions back onto proper spin states. A non-orthogonal interaction scheme carries out the projection.

All spin recouplings allowed by the standard rules are included. The constrained starting points can be tuned pair by pair. That tuning trims the cost of full projection greatly. Tests used systems of four, six, and eight electrons. Both strong and weak correlation regimes were covered. The authors aim for accuracy near costly methods at mean-field-like prices. Spin restoration at this level may widen access to hard molecules.
arxiv-2412-16858:
Aifeng Li and co-authors model cosmic rays from spiral galaxy sources in 2024. Cosmic rays are fast particles that rain on Earth from space. Their energy spread and arrival slant carry clues about their sources. The Milky Way is a spiral galaxy, so sources should follow its arms rather than a smooth disc.

The team uses a spread model where travel ease varies by place, with unlike halos inside and out. A nearby source is added to explain odd hardening in the spectra. Arrival direction patterns across a wide energy span are also matched. The work tests whether spiral sources plus one neighbor fit the data.
arxiv-2412-17158:
Vasiliki Koutra, Olga Egorova, Steven Gilmour, and Luzia Trinca describe MOODE, a 2024 software package for designing experiments that must serve several masters at once. A good experiment answers many questions cheaply, and those goals compete: precision for one effect can starve another, and a design should also leave room to check its own fit. The package, written for the R statistics system, builds compound criteria that blend such aims in stated proportions.

Depending on the design's shape, it searches with point exchange or coordinate exchange algorithms until the design nears optimal. Two case studies of differing complexity show the package in use, from setting the criteria to reading the resulting design. The authors target practicing statisticians who have felt the pinch of single-goal design tools. The name is the method: multi-objective optimal design of experiments, made runnable.
arxiv-2412-17958:
Andreas Brandhuber and co-authors study how spinning bodies bend the gravity waves they shed while spiraling toward merger, in a 2024 paper.
