Their tools come from effective field theory, which treats gravity with methods borrowed from particle physics. Two special triple-curvature terms sit at the center of the work. The team asks how those terms change the pull between two spinning objects lined up by their spins.

Working step by step from scattering amplitudes, they find corrections to the classic Newtonian pull. They then derive how the bodies' quadrupole shapes shift, and from that the power carried off by gravity waves. Waveforms change in step, at least to first order in spin. The paper closes by weighing how these effects compare with tidal stretching, a rival source of waveform change.
arxiv-2412-18058:
A classic pairing in combinatorics turns each shuffle pattern into a grid shape, and two summaries of the same shuffle can be compared. Martha Du Preez and co-authors ask which grid shapes can arise from shuffles built of exactly two cycles, in this 2024 paper.

They answer with a coloring construction. Mark the boxes of a candidate shape in a careful way, and a shuffle with the wanted cycle split and shape can be assembled from the marks. The paper gives the full list of possible shapes for the two-cycle case. The result tightens a link between cycle structure and tableau shape that researchers have only recently begun to probe.
arxiv-2412-18758: Cai Heng Li and Luyi Liu open a series on highly symmetric maps drawn on surfaces in a 2024 paper. A map here is a graph laid out on a surface, and the team focus on maps whose symmetry moves any directed edge to any other. Their goal is to classify maps where the edge count and a surface value called the Euler characteristic share no common factor. This first paper builds the framework and completes the case where the symmetry group is solvable, constructing many new regular examples.
arxiv-2412-18858:
Olga Krivorotko, Tatiana Zvonareva and Andrei Neverov ask which parameters of a spatial COVID-19 model can truly be recovered from case data. Their SEIR-HCD model spreads people through space by diffusion while tracking infection, hospital, critical and death states. Global sensitivity checks with the Sobol method and a Bayesian approach narrowed the ranges of the unknown values.

Case, critical and death counts alone could not pin down the diffusion rates that set how fast people move. Those rates need extra information about the process itself. The study warns model users which knobs their data can and cannot set, a guard against false confidence in epidemic forecasts.
arxiv-2412-18958: Johann Cigler and Hans-Christian Herbig prove a guess about a family of polynomials. Their 2024 paper concerns spread polynomials, a set that shows up in a modern reworking of trigonometry. The guess states how each of them splits into factors. The pair give a full proof of the split and show how the factors can be worked out in practice. They also tie the split to the way Fibonacci numbers break into primitive parts. The result links a young branch of geometry-flavored algebra to a classic number sequence.
arxiv-2412-19258:
Cycle convexity in graph products is studied by Anand and co-authors in a 2024 paper. In this setting, a set of vertices is called cycle convex if adding any outside vertex creates no cycle through that vertex inside the set. Two numbers matter here: the hull number, the size of the smallest set whose hull is the whole graph, and the convexity number.

For strong and lexicographic products, the hull number is always two. For Cartesian products, the team gives tight bounds and a closed formula when the factors are trees, which extends a known result for grid graphs. They also prove that deciding whether the hull number is at most a given value stays NP-complete even for bipartite Cartesian products, settling an open question.
arxiv-2412-19658:
Buzzi, Luo, and Yang study how the count of top-chaos states shifts when a smooth surface map is nudged in this twenty twenty-four paper. Such maps twist a surface in a smooth, two-way way, and some reach high chaos. Each map has states that reach that top chaos level, and their count can jump as the map shifts.

Inside, the team works with maps whose chaos beats a bound set by their smooth grade. They prove the count of top states can only fall, not rise, when such a map is nudged a bit. The count stays fixed near a map just when each top state can be tracked through small nudges. Then the limit points of those states stay in the top class as well. The facts are new even for the smoothest maps.
arxiv-2501-00558:
Xavier Emery, Moreno Bevilacqua, and Emilio Porcu introduce new families of correlation functions in a 2025 statistics study. Correlation functions describe how values at nearby places in space relate, including how smooth a random process is and how far its influence reaches. Most standard families only allow positive correlation.

Their two new families also allow negative dependence, known as a hole effect, while keeping control of smoothness and range. Both generalize famous older models, which appear as special cases. The authors also link the two families to each other. Tests on estimation and prediction show how the added flexibility performs on real tasks.
arxiv-2501-01158:
Farshad Noravesh and five co-authors use sentence structure graphs to pull events from biomedical text, in a 2025 paper. Event mining names who does what to whom in research prose. Many tools lean on the shortest path between words in a parse graph. Dropping one word from that path can flip the call. The team instead feeds the full graph to a graph network.

Each word is embedded with help from its graph neighbors. A test that removes the graph shows how much it adds. Scores rose clearly with the graph in place. The full model edged past prior top models on several data sets. The authors back full parse use over path shortcuts.
arxiv-2501-01258:
Shanlin Huang, Gengsheng Wang, and Ming Wang studied in 2025 when a quantum wave can be fully read from a small watching region. Their wave runs under a simple pulling force that grows with distance. The question is which regions are good enough watch posts, and how the reading cost grows as the time window shrinks.

The authors prove reading works over any time span, however short, and give the cost as a clear formula. They also pin down which regions qualify and show that a half-line never does, unlike for stronger forces. Their proof joins a new spectral bound with a compactness argument and classic estimates.
arxiv-2501-01458:
Wang, Murugesan, and Rohatgi hunt for genes that drugs can target, using the web of protein interactions, in a 2025 paper. Finding druggable genes early saves years of lab work. Protein interaction networks hold clues, but they are huge and sparse.

Earlier methods folded the network in indirectly and lost detail. The new framework, GAN-TAT, embeds the network directly in its learning. On the Tclin benchmark it reached an accuracy score of 0.951, the best among rivals. Clinical evidence backed many of its nominated genes. The code is public. The authors frame it as a practical aid for drug discovery teams.
arxiv-2501-01558:
Dylan Sam, Marc Finzi, and Zico Kolter predict a black-box language model's correctness by asking it follow-up questions. Their paper from twenty twenty-five treats the answers' probabilities as a fingerprint of the model's state. A linear probe trained on those fingerprints calls right and wrong answers with care. The trick needs no access to the model's guts, only its API.

The follow-up probe even beats white-box probes that read internal activations. It also flags models that were secretly bent by a hostile system prompt. Code bugs planted the same way surface too. Swapped models behind an API can be told apart by their follow-up style. The authors pitch the method as a monitor for models that serve inside bigger autonomous systems.
arxiv-2501-01858:
Russell Brown, Landon Gauthier, and Daniel Faraco study an inverse problem for a higher order elliptic operator in this 2025 paper. The main part of the operator is the polyharmonic operator, a power of the Laplacian, and lower order terms with rough coefficients are added. The team asks whether boundary data can pin down those coefficients.

They prove that the map from the coefficients to a certain bilinear form is one to one, so distinct coefficients give distinct data. A focus of the work is getting this result while assuming little smoothness of the coefficients. Knowing the bilinear form is the same as knowing the Dirichlet to Neumann map. It is also the same as knowing the Cauchy data of solutions. That ties the result to the usual forms of boundary measurement.
arxiv-2501-01958:
Hyunwook Kim and co-authors survey computer methods that swap recipe ingredients, in work published in 2024. Swaps help cooks meet diet rules, allergies, and bare shelves. A good swap must weigh taste, kitchen role, and health fit at once, which makes the search hard. AI tools now take the task on in many forms.

The survey sorts the field by data sets, methods, and the context each tool weighs, from nutrition to flavor pairing. It also sorts the uses served and grades how safe and clear the tools are. The authors point to hybrid logic-plus-learning designs and knowledge graphs as the next steps.
arxiv-2501-02158:
Liu, Lin, Wu, and Zhou present a computer vision method, published in 2025, for rebuilding people and their surroundings from ordinary web videos. Knowing how a person moves through a scene matters for predicting what they will do next. Lab systems capture this well with special gear, but they fail on casual single-camera footage. The team's method, called JOSH, starts from rough estimates made by existing tools. It then refines the scene, the camera positions, and the person's motion together.

The key trick is contact. Where a foot or hand touches a surface, the person and the scene must agree. Using those contact rules as constraints ties the two halves of the problem together. Tests show the joint approach beats rebuilding each half alone. The work brings lab-grade capture of human-scene interaction closer to everyday video.
arxiv-2501-02258:
Muneto Nitta and Kunihito Uzawa wrote in 2025 about a proposed rule that limits what kinds of universes a theory of quantum gravity can allow. The rule, tied to de Sitter space, puts a harsh bound on allowed settings. They asked what happens when the motion of the driving field is taken into account, not just its resting values.

They extended the rule to cover that motion and applied it to a model of cosmic inflation driven by a slow field. The allowed range of settings came out wider than under the older rule. The authors note the wider bounds could matter for building models that pack extra dimensions into small spaces.
arxiv-2501-02558:
Minoo Dolatabadi and four co-authors teach a neural network to predict its own location errors. Their 2025 paper targets LiDAR map matching for self-driving cars. Matching scans to a map can misfire where scenes repeat or thin out. Fusion filters need honest error estimates to weigh each sensor.

The team built a fresh way to generate training data for error spread. A network then predicts the covariance of each match's error. Fed into a Kalman filter, the estimates sharpened location accuracy by two centimeters. In this field, two centimeters is a large gain. The method needs no hand-tuned error guesses. Self-aware error bars make sensor fusion steadier on real roads.
arxiv-2501-02858:
Toomas Tahves and co-authors present a transformer model that fuses camera and laser data for traffic scenes, in this 2025 paper. Self-driving cars must outline road users such as cyclists, pedestrians, and signs. Each sensor alone has blind spots, so fusion helps.

Their models use the self-attention trick of vision transformers to blend the two feeds. They sort a wider range of object classes than prior fusion work and were tested in varied weather. Results were strong overall, but dark and rainy scenes still caused errors. The authors call the models a strong step for driving perception, with more work needed for harsh conditions.
arxiv-2501-03558:
Jin Lim and co-authors reported in 2025 new sightings of a rare trick of light in the shells of dying stars. Ultraviolet photons from a hot central star strike hydrogen atoms and bounce off shifted into visible red, a Raman scattering signature. The team took high-resolution spectra of twelve young planetary nebulae at a Korean observatory.

Two more nebulae joined the detection list, making four with measured profiles. The hydrogen shells drift outward at roughly thirty kilometers per second against the glowing core. Light modeling put the shells near a hundredth of a solar mass, matching a slow giant wind. Conversion rates varied fourfold among the four. The authors say the feature is a clean probe of the neutral remains of stellar old age.
arxiv-2501-03658:
Emilio Barucci, Adrien Mathieu, and Leandro Sanchez-Betancourt model a market maker who faces fad-driven prices in 2025. Prices drift from true value in short bursts, and both informed and uninformed traders arrive at rates that shift with the fad. The maker sees orders but not who sent them or the fad state.

Both full and partial sight versions of the control task are solved in the paper. The team prices the worth of sight and the cost of liquidity as the share of informed traders shifts. Fit steps from market data and gains over fad-blind plans close the work.
arxiv-2501-03758:
Richard Morton and co-authors wrote a paper from 2025 on waves in the Sun's outer air, watched with a new solar telescope. The waves, named Alfvénic waves, run along magnetic field lines in the hot corona. Low-speed waves there were found over the past decade. The new scope sees far finer detail, far faster, and with less noise than older tools.

The team read a glowing iron line in the corona, one frame per second. The wobble of that line showed the known slow waves and a new, faster band as well. That fast band should have been damped lower down, per some models, so its presence tests those models. The fast waves also carry less energy than the slow ones. The wobbles showed no link to brightness shifts, which fits waves that squeeze nothing as they pass.
arxiv-2501-04158:
Julien Carron and co-authors work out how to detect the rotation that gravitational lensing imprints on cosmic microwave light. Sharper polarization maps are arriving from new telescopes. Reading lensing well is key to hunting primordial waves.

Three estimators are treated together in one frame. One reads polarization rotation, another the lensing field's swirl. A third is the standard gradient lensing method. All perform best where local polarization patterns are strong. Delensing boosts each of them substantially. The team forecasts noise for current and planned surveys. South Pole data should catch the effect soon. Cross-checks with galaxy maps add confidence to the hunt. It is a plan for the next round of sky scans.
arxiv-2501-04258:
Rui Wang and Tamar Schlick ask how large the space of RNA shapes might be in a 2025 paper. RNA molecules fold into loops and stems that decide their jobs. Drawing those folds as graphs lets a computer list every shape a chain of a given size could take.

The pair generated all hundred-thousand-plus graphs for small sizes, then compared them with shapes seen in real RNA fragments. Only a tenth of a percent of the possible graphs are known in nature. Using spectral fingerprints and clustering, they sorted the rest into likely RNA-like and not. The census hints at a vast, mostly unexplored shape space for drug and nanotech designers.
arxiv-2501-04558:
Xiao-Yue Xu and co-authors wrote this 2025 paper on teaching a neural network the physics of quantum noise. Quantum computers today err too often, and learning-based fixes can cut those errors, but black-box models need huge training sets and scale badly. The team wanted a model that knows how noise piles up as a circuit deepens.

Their network, NNAS, is built around that accumulation pattern, layer by layer, giving it a physical shape rather than a generic one. Across tests it beat current methods on accuracy, cost, and training size. For deep circuits, where fixes usually fail, it cut errors by more than half. It also learned from at least ten times less data, thanks to its built-in grasp of the noise pattern.
arxiv-2501-05058:
AI models that mimic the Gulf of Mexico's surface waters are built by Leonard Lupin-Jimenez and co-authors in this 2025 paper. Regional ocean models face tangled coastlines, inflow at the edges, and long-term drift when built with standard deep learning. The team wanted forecasts that stay physically sensible for decades.

Their framework rolls the ocean surface forward on its own at eight-kilometer detail. A second, physics-guided model then sharpens the output to four kilometers and corrects its biases. The system held accurate averages and variability over long runs, with no unphysical drift. It also kept short-term forecast skill. The authors present the pairing as a template for other regional seas.
arxiv-2501-05258:
Daniele Cipollone and co-authors hunt software flaws in GitHub issue reports in a 2025 paper. GitHub issues are the notes coders file about bugs and wishes for a project. Some notes hint at a real security flaw long before an official alert goes out. Reading them by hand does not scale. The team asks if language models can sort the notes on their own.

They built a fresh data set of issues tagged for flaw relevance. Then they tried a range of sorting methods, from classic learning to transformer models. The results show the approach can work in real settings, the authors say. Early flags could shrink the window in which a flaw can be exploited. Their frame is built to be cheap to run and easy to scale.
arxiv-2501-05358:
Magagnin and five co-authors present a study from twenty twenty-five on a better test for antiferroelectric films. Such films flip their internal charge pattern under voltage, unlike standard ferroelectrics. A classic pulse test mixes switching currents with background currents. Their revised protocol separates the two, allowing clean reads of key values. They apply it to zirconium oxide films of varied thickness. Thicker films hold more leftover polarization, a sign of stabler domains. Their switching thresholds fall as thickness grows.

Repeated cycling shows a wake-up gain that later fades from fatigue. Thicker films degrade faster in those cycles. The authors link the trends to defects, grain size, and wall pinning in the films. They call the protocol a key tool for this material class.
arxiv-2501-05458:
Maria Nareklishvili and co-authors review model generation in a paper that sorts the field by purpose. They group such models into three classes: guessing what would have occurred under another treatment, recovering unknown values from simulated data, and forming forecasts of future outcomes.

One math result, the noise outsourcing theorem, sits under all three views. Within it, the authors develop a Bayesian method that trains a quantile neural network on fake value-outcome pairs to read off beliefs. An Ebola spread model shows the method finding sharp beliefs at far lower cost than sampling approaches, without awkward design constraints.
arxiv-2501-05658:
Hidetoshi Nishimori, writing alone, shows that a magnetic phase thought stable can collapse when disorder is correlated. His 2025 paper studies an Ising spin glass, a magnet with random competing links between spins. For the classic versions with uncorrelated disorder, the ferromagnetic phase, where spins align, survives random fields in three or more dimensions.

Nishimori adds spatial correlation to the disorder and proves the opposite: the aligned phase becomes unstable under random fields in any dimension, given a chaos property in the standard model. The same instability can be traced to bond chaos. He also argues the phase can persist under symmetry-breaking fields when the standard model keeps its spin glass phase. The results show how strongly correlation in disorder reshapes magnetic order.
arxiv-2501-05758:
Imre Péter Tóth proves a bus puzzle in a solo 2025 paper. Empty buses wait at a station, and a fixed count of riders boards at pure random, each picking any bus with even odds. Common sense might say more buses spread riders out and thin the crowd. Tóth shows the reverse: the more buses there are, the more likely it is that at least one rider ends up alone.

The claim is stronger than a chance bump: the count of lone riders grows with the bus count in the strict sense of random order. The proof leans on Stirling numbers, the counts of ways to split a set into blocks. Tóth notes the puzzle has no short proof known, despite work by many experts.
arxiv-2501-05858:
Tiago Mendes-Neves, Luís Meireles, João Mendes-Moreira, and Nuno de Almeida study, in a 2025 paper, how Portuguese football clubs scout young players across the map. Portugal exports more football talent, in net transfer terms, than any other country, and its academies drive that trade. The authors ask where clubs look for youth talent and which search patterns pay off.

Their data set spans recent decades of youth and senior football, with player birthplaces and first grassroots clubs. Bigger clubs scout over a wider area, and strong senior teams seem to draw more youth investment. Regions with no professional club are often left unserved. Some clubs gained ground by recruiting outside their home district, the Algarve among them. The authors argue that data can sharpen where clubs spend their scouting effort.
arxiv-2501-06058:
Fu and co-authors design a learning system for teams of unlike robots that must coordinate. Existing designs force a trade-off. One shared network for all robots learns fast but limits how differently each robot can behave. A separate policy per robot is flexible but costly and generalizes poorly. Their system, CASH, uses hypernetworks to generate a shared policy that adapts to each robot's stated capabilities, such as speed and payload.

In tests spanning imitation learning and two kinds of reinforcement learning, on both simulated and real robot platforms, CASH produced suitably varied behavior per robot. It beat the baseline designs on performance and sample efficiency, and it handled robots and team mixes it had never seen in training. It also used far fewer learnable parameters. For multi-robot work, the paper offers an architecture that keeps the sharing benefits without flattening the differences between machines.
arxiv-2501-06158:
Seul Lee and co-authors present a single model that can do many drug design tasks in 2025. Drug design has many steps, from making a new compound to improving a known one. Most past models could do only some of these steps. Their model, called GenMol, builds compounds from small parts called fragments.

The model fills in parts in any order, which speeds up sampling. A trick that hides and remakes parts helps it search for better compounds. A guide method steers the search toward a goal. In tests it beat an older text based model on new designs and on goal based tasks. The team shares the code for others to use.
arxiv-2501-06258:
Mikhail Terekhov studies how pre trained neural networks can help a learner that must pick actions and learn from rewards, in a thesis paper from 2025. When rewards are modeled by a deep network, good bounds on loss have needed huge networks. Terekhov asks whether a head start from prior training lets small networks learn well.

The setup treats the last layer of the network as a straight score and the rest as a fixed feature builder that starts from the pre trained weights. A new method first fits the last layer, then trains all weights in a joint pass. Under clear conditions on the head start, loss grows more slowly than the time span. Tests in code back the bounds and chart how much early search the method needs.
arxiv-2501-06358:
Matthew Doty and co-authors measured how eccentric planet orbits can be before a system flies apart, in a 2025 paper. They used the California Kepler Survey and a machine learning stability tool called SPOCK. The sample held 126 systems with many planets each. For every system, they found the orbit stretch tied to a fifty-fifty stability chance.

Short N-body runs confirmed those values. The team then hunted what predicts the safe stretch. The tightest planet-pair spacing ratio mattered most. Safe values sit far below the stretch that would crash two planets directly. Such limits sharpen theories of how planet systems form.
arxiv-2501-06558:
Alessandro Santoni, Enrique Muñoz, Hartmut Abele, and Benjamin Koch wrote a paper in two thousand twenty-five about testing a variant of relativity with ultracold neutrons. The variant, called Very Special Relativity, allows a preferred direction in space. Ultracold neutrons bouncing in gravity form a sensitive probe, used by a known experiment.

The authors compute how the neutron energy levels shift in an accelerated frame under this theory. At the leading order they find no real change beyond a trivial mass shift, so mass equivalence stays intact. At the next order, time-dependent effects tied to the preferred direction appear. Using the experiment's sensitivity as a yardstick, they set a first rough bound on the neutron parameter and suggest spin-flip setups.
arxiv-2501-06658:
Sanjit Kakarla, Conrad Borchers, and colleagues compare two AI graders for open-ended answers in tutor training in a 2025 education study. Trainee tutors answer equity scenarios in free text, and judging those answers needs sensitivity to context. A large commercial model brings broad knowledge but cannot be fine-tuned freely, while an older encoder model learns the local rubric yet knows less about the world.

Few-shot prompting of the large model is tested head to head against fine-tuned smaller classifiers. The comparison tells training programs which grader to trust for nuanced, values-laden responses where a careless score can teach the wrong lesson.
arxiv-2501-06958:
Peerasait Prachaseree and Emma Lejeune study in 2025 how tangled fiber webs carry force. Such webs underlie tissues and many made materials. Under load, only a few fibers bear most of it, chaining into paths that stiffen the whole. Which web shapes make which paths was poorly mapped.

A computer model with exact bending beams stands in for the webs. Two targets guide the work: how lone chains and full webs behave, and whether a readable formula can predict web stiffness from shape alone. The team finds the strain point where chains and webs suddenly stiffen, they report, and checks their formula against the model. A shape-to-strength rule would let engineers design webs on paper before growing or weaving them.
arxiv-2501-07058:
ZeKe Xiao, Qin Wang, Hammond Pearce, and Shiping Chen wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It tests how well large language models can find flaws in smart contracts, the code that runs deals on blockchains.

Such flaws have cost users dearly, and hand checks are slow. The team ran five top models on contracts in Solidity version nought point eight, newer than the code most past work used. A well-made prompt cut false alarms by over half. But the catch rate for some flaw kinds had fallen hard next to older code. The drop traces to the models keying on shifts in new libraries, the authors find.
arxiv-2501-07158:
Wassim Kabbani and co-authors judge face photo quality by the whites of the eyes in this 2025 paper. Face recognition systems first grade incoming photos, and those grades must be fair across skin tones. The sclera, the eye's white, barely varies with ancestry or complexion. The team tested it as a neutral measuring ground.

They checked three standard quality traits there: dynamic range and over- and under-exposure. Across a dataset spanning many demographic groups, sclera readings carried the same utility as skin-based ones. Error-versus-discard curves confirmed the fairness gain. The authors propose the eye region as a fairer basis for quality checks at enrollment.
arxiv-2501-07458:
Rolf Pfister and Hansueli Jud present a 2025 paper that asks whether a top AI system's high test score means it is truly intelligent. The system scored very high on a benchmark meant to measure general intelligence. The authors build on that benchmark creator's split between skill at set tasks and intelligence itself.

They define intelligence as reaching varied goals in varied worlds, efficiently, with little prior knowledge. The benchmark's tasks, they argue, can be cracked by mass trial of fixed moves, which the system does with huge computing power. Most real-world problems cannot be pre-tested that way. On their reading, such trial-based skill is not a path to general intelligence.
arxiv-2501-07558:
Jakub Gajarský and co-authors prove a limit on how graph classes can be transformed into one another, in a 2025 paper. Logicians study transductions, rule-based ways to rebuild one structure from another using a fixed recipe. The question here is whether flat, planar networks could ever be reworked by such recipes into three-dimensional grids.

The answer is no, and not just for planar graphs: no class of graphs drawn on a surface of bounded shape can produce 3D grids this way. To prove it, the authors invent slice decompositions, a new way of cutting graphs into layered pieces. Any class reachable from bounded-genus graphs must look like a mild reshaping of a class that admits such slices. The result draws a firm line in the map of graph transformations.
arxiv-2501-07858:
Mokarrama, Shaikh, and Alhoori trace how youth research shows up in United States policy papers in a 2025 study. Policy cites scholarship unevenly, and the youth topic is a telling case of which studies cross into lawmaking.

The team ask which youth topics get cited most, what traits lift a study's citation odds, and how well policy topics match research topics. The mapping exposes where youth issues genuinely enter policy and where they stall outside. Findings feed the wider push to involve young people in choices that shape their lives. Three questions guide the whole inquiry. The study also weighs the broader tie between academic research and the drafting of policy.
arxiv-2501-07958:
Igor Konnov and co-authors report in 2025 on machine-checking the rules of the Ethereum blockchain's new agreement protocol. Agreement rules keep many computers locked on one shared record, and one key promise is that honest users can prove fault when safety breaks. The team picked this protocol for its importance and for the hard checks it poses.

They rewrote the official Python rules by hand in a formal language and checked them with a model checker. Layers of simplification tamed the huge state space, and two other tools cross-checked the work. No safety breach appeared in small setups of up to seven checkpoints. The study shows how much expert hand work still aids such checks.
arxiv-2501-08858:
Artur Lacerda, Laetitia Bettmann, and John Goold study, in a 2025 letter, the energy cost of moving a small quantum system from one steady working state to another. A system held in a steady state already wastes energy just staying there; changing states adds its own cost on top. The authors use a framework that separates those two costs and ask what the cheapest possible path between states looks like.

For slow changes, they show the extra cost is set by a kind of distance in the space of settings. That distance ties to a standard quantum measure of how sharply states can be told apart. Following the shortest paths under that measure gives the least wasteful change, which they demonstrate on a simple three-level heat device. They also derive a limit on the standing cost that holds even for fast changes.
arxiv-2501-09358:
Wanli Xie merges grey system theory with the calculus of time scales, in a 2025 paper. Grey system theory models systems where information is uncertain or incomplete, a common state in real data. Time scales offer one framework that covers both continuous time and discrete time, rather than treating them as separate worlds.

The merged model, called the Grey System Model on Time Scales, is offered as a robust tool for hybrid systems. Such systems mix events that unfold smoothly with events that jump at set points, so their time domains vary. Xie presents the construction as a way to analyze those mixed cases inside one model instead of two.
arxiv-2501-09558:
Latour and five co-authors measure metal content in stars of globular clusters in a 2025 astronomy paper. Globular clusters hold several generations of stars, and whether even the first generation varies in iron content has become a hot question. The team used spectra of more than eight thousand giant stars in twenty one Milky Way clusters.

Each star was assigned to the first or later population using space telescope photo catalogs. In nearly all clusters, metal content within the first population rose with a color based marker. The spread ranged widely and grew with cluster mass. Later population stars showed equal or tighter spreads than first population stars. The results inform how clusters formed their stars.
arxiv-2501-09658:
Tianrui Xu, Anjun Chu, Kyungtae Kim, James Thompson, Jun Ye, Tilman Esslinger, and Ana Maria Rey wrote a 2025 physics paper proposing a new kind of atomic clock. Their design builds a symmetry protected topological phase, a state of matter prized for its robustness, inside an optical lattice clock. Such clocks offer long coherence and very fine spectral detail.

The authors lay out a tunable setup in a tilted lattice and a probing method much like Rabi spectroscopy. The method can read out the distinct topological traits of the state. They then show how the state's built in protection against flaws could sharpen clock and interferometer sensitivity. The proposal links two active fields, precision measurement and topological matter, in one device.
arxiv-2501-10658:
Guoyu Li and co-authors present a 2025 paper on faster deep learning hardware. Neural networks keep growing, which raises the cost of running them on chips. Shrinking number formats helps, but plain formats cannot go below one bit per value without breaking down.

The framework, called LUT-DLA, turns network math into lookup tables using grouped values instead of single ones. A training method called LUTBoost converts normal models into table form in stages. Tests show large gains in power and chip area over prior designs, with only small drops in accuracy. The team also maps how model and hardware choices trade off, so designers can tune the setup for each use.
arxiv-2501-11058:
Francesco Lorenzi and Luca Salasnich study solitary waves in multimode optical fibers in a 2025 paper. Such fibers carry many light modes at once, and their pulses can hold together as solitary waves in space and time. Exact equations are heavy, so a variational shortcut is valuable.

Using a nonpolynomial Schrödinger model, they derive a simple one-dimensional action for each mode family. The equations of motion come out in a clean form for any mode numbers. They also find the critical power at which a pulse collapses. Stationary profiles from the full equation check the shortcut. Fiber designers get fast estimates for a complex system.
arxiv-2501-11358:
Tian-Wei Wu, Ming-Zhu Liu, and Li-Sheng Geng predict a new exotic particle in a 2025 physics paper. The catalog title is tangled in raw formula code, but the head states the claim cleanly: a bound state of three heavy mesons with rare quantum numbers. Such molecule-like states have reshaped hadron physics over the past two decades.

Using an interaction strength drawn from real data rather than a fitted model, the authors find the three-body state bound at a stated mass near 4310 mega-electronvolts. It barely mixes with ordinary charmonium states, which makes it a clean test case. They name a decay channel at a major collider where hunters could look for it.
arxiv-2501-11558:
Bruno Casella, in a solo paper from twenty twenty-five, graded the speed cost of safe enclaves for federated learning. Such learning trains across many sites with data kept home. It still faces poison and spy attacks on models and data. Hardware enclaves can shield both, but the old kind caps memory and fights the coder. A new kind wraps a whole virtual machine, which eases port of old code.

Casella ran fed learn loads in such VM enclaves and read the tax: time, memory, and throughput next to bare runs. Readers who must keep training private get a count based read on what the shield costs in speed.
arxiv-2501-11658:
Joshua Brown and Gordon Ogilvie explain how gas discs can turn turbulent while staying formally stable, in a 2025 paper. Massive, cool discs around young stars should form rings by gravity. Yet even slightly lighter discs often grow spirals and turbulence. Linear theory says those discs are stable. The mismatch has puzzled theorists. Simulations show turbulence depends on how fast the disc cools.

The authors find solitary wave solutions hiding in the stable regime. These axisymmetric lumps sit just above the uniform disc in energy. They exist near the instability threshold in three dimensions. The lumps themselves should break up under sideways wiggles. That breakup offers a path into full turbulence. The mechanism is subcritical: finite disturbances, not tiny ones, trigger it. Disc models for planet formation gain a new ingredient.
arxiv-2501-11858:
A model that chats about pictures may still fumble at acting in a world. Zhili Cheng and co-authors build EmbodiedEval in 2025, an interactive benchmark that grades multimodal language models as embodied agents inside simulated 3D scenes. Its 328 tasks span 125 scenes across navigation, object handling, social interaction, and questions about attributes and space.

Top current models fell far short of human performance. The failures map where embodied skill lags: acting over time, not just describing a frame. The team open-sources the data and simulator so developers can train against the gaps instead of guessing at them.
arxiv-2501-11958:
Yao Du and co-authors build materials in 2025 that learn to change shape, much as living things adapt. Engineered shape-shifting materials exist, but they are fixed at design time and cannot learn new moves. The team applies a contrastive learning scheme in which the material updates its own local stiffnesses from shown examples.

Shown target shapes, the material progressively learns to take them on. It can forget old shapes and learn new ones in sequence, learn several shapes that break the usual symmetry of response, and learn shapes with multiple stable states. Those skills let samples grip objects by reflex and crawl. The authors present physical learning as a design route for adaptive materials and robots.
arxiv-2501-12158:
Dominique Malicet and Graccyela Salcedo study random dynamical systems on a circle that never settle onto a finite orbit. In such systems, a map of the circle is chosen at random at each step, so motion mixes chance with rotation. The authors focus on cases with no finite orbit, where no point returns to its start after finitely many steps in a repeating way.

They characterize the long-run shape of the motion through invariant sets built from finite unions of arcs. For each steady statistical regime, they describe where the average orbit accumulates and study a weight function that records how much time the system spends around the circle. Links between the minimal sets of the system and those of its inverse are also established. The results serve pure research on random dynamics.
arxiv-2501-12258:
Patel, Quarles, and Cuntz test in twenty twenty-five which moon and submoon orbits can survive around known giant planets. Claims of moons beyond our solar system are growing, and a claimed moon may even host its own submoon. The team ran body-by-body simulations for a star-planet-moon system based on one claimed case, then added a fourth body as a submoon.

Most of the tested space for the moon case proved stable. The submoon case split into stable and unstable zones with clear resonance patterns, which they traced to slow secular effects. Two further systems were checked in three-body form, and one in four-body form. The authors offer the work as a template for future cases.
arxiv-2501-12458:
Neslihan Alan and co-authors carry out the first photometric study of the eclipsing binary V517 Cam in a 2025 paper. Eclipsing pairs are prized because their light curves reveal the stars' masses and sizes directly, and this system had never been analyzed in detail.

The team combined the TESS satellite's light curve with new ground-based observations in four color filters from a national observatory telescope. Their modeling gives a primary star of about one and a half solar masses with a smaller companion, a distance of a few hundred light-years, and a young system age. The companion still appears to be contracting toward the main sequence.
arxiv-2501-12858:
Bogdanov studies, in a 2025 paper, a system of equations tied to self-dual conformal structures, a topic in geometry and integrable systems. The system is fairly new in the literature and belongs to the class of dispersionless integrable systems. Such systems are valued because they admit many exact methods for building solutions.

The paper focuses on reductions, ways to shrink the full system into simpler ones that still keep its core structure. The author works through several characteristic reductions using the Lax pair, the hierarchy structure, and the dressing scheme. These reductions are then used to construct solutions of the original equations. A related type B system is also presented, and its links with the main system are examined.
arxiv-2501-13058:
David Lehavi and Brian Osserman solve a camera geometry problem in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. The perspective n-points problem asks where a camera is, given points in space and their images. Their fast, accurate solution tackles the four-point case with a new split of the problem.

First, they place new points along the camera rays so that distances between them match the original points as closely as possible. That step turns the problem into an absolute orientation task, which has an explicit formula solution. Their coordinates use squared distances and dot products to stay orientation-free. Tests showed an order of magnitude speed gain over top methods, at similar accuracy under noise. The split also speeds seed rejection in RANSAC.
arxiv-2501-13558:
Francesco Di Sario and co-authors introduced this 2025 method for shrinking 3D scene data at flexible quality levels. Modern 3D scenes are built from millions of soft blobs, and new blob types keep appearing. Most shrinkers are built for one type and one file size, forcing a fresh run per size. Their framework, GoDe, works with any backbone design.

It ranks blobs by importance and nests them into layers, from a coarse base to fine detail layers. One tuning pass readies all layers at once. A decoder can stop at any prefix of the stream and still render the scene. Across five backbones and three benchmarks, the method matched rivals on quality while rendering and decoding faster. One file now serves many bandwidth needs.
arxiv-2501-13958:
Qinggang Zhang and co-authors survey graph-based methods for tailoring large language models in work from 2025. Standard search pulls flat text to help a model answer. That approach struggles with hard expert questions and scattered sources.

The survey explains how graphs, which link facts as nodes and ties, can help. Linked facts support deeper questions, cleaner merging of sources, and faster work at scale. The authors sort past systems, compare their strengths, and note open problems. Readers new to the area get a map of the field. Specialists get a shared set of terms and a guide to what to try next.
arxiv-2501-14158:
Mojtaba Safari and co-authors review how deep learning is speeding up MRI scans. MRI gives rich views inside the body without radiation. Its flaw is time: long scans discomfort patients and blur images when they move. Compressed sensing cuts scan time by sampling less data and rebuilding the image from the sparse set.

The review sorts deep learning methods that merge with that trick. Some learn the rebuild end to end, some unroll classic math steps into a network, and some learn across sites without pooling patient data. Gains in speed and sharpness are charted with the datasets used. The authors point to open needs and keep a public list of new work.
arxiv-2501-14358:
Minjie Tang, Photios A Stavrou, and Marios Kountouris estimate a system's state without knowing the channel. Their 2025 paper targets remote monitoring over wireless MIMO links, where classic Kalman filtering demands perfect channel knowledge and heavy computation.

Their scheme skips channel estimation entirely. Sensors send the surprising part of their readings, the gap between measurement and expectation, merged over the air in analog form. A constant-gain filter, tuned offline by a staged approximation method, does the estimating at low cost. The team proves a stability condition in closed form using drift analysis. Simulations show the lean scheme beating several standard approaches, which the authors offer for sensor networks that cannot afford channel tracking.
arxiv-2501-14558:
A. D. Helgeland and colleagues measure the speed and size of plasma blobs drifting across the edge of a tokamak. They compare ordinary and high-performance operating modes. The blobs are filamentary bursts in the scrape-off layer, the thin region outside the confined plasma. They carry heat toward the walls. Using gas puff imaging on the Alcator C-Mod device and an improved timing method, the team tracks outward radial motion in three plasmas. One is ohmic; two run in high-confinement regimes. A stochastic model interprets the fluctuations as overlapping uncorrelated blobs.

In every regime, large-amplitude filaments dominated. They moved outward at several hundred meters per second, up to about a thousand. Blob speeds and sizes barely changed between ohmic and high-confinement operation. Burst shapes and spectra were nearly identical too. The stubbornness of edge turbulence across regimes is the practical message for reactor wall design.
arxiv-2501-14658:
Maria Chudnovsky and co-authors bound tree decompositions for barred graph classes in a 2025 math paper. The fifth in a series, the work bans line graphs of gridded wall subdivisions, a split claw shape, and a matched pair graph. Such bans often tame hard problems.

For any fixed ban size, each barred graph on n vertices splits into a tree of bags whose largest free sets grow only like a small power of log n. That bound makes maximum weight independent set and kin problems run in quasi polynomial time there. A balanced separator near few vertices anchors the proof.
arxiv-2501-14758:
Yun-Chieh Cheng and three co-authors study how each new MacBook Pro release turns related accessories into electronic waste. Port changes between models break compatibility, stranding chargers, adapters, and docks that still work. The team compared ports and fit across generations to find which items fall obsolete.

They then weighed the environmental cost of that churn and the economic hit to buyers, makers, and the wider industry. Options for reuse, recycling, and safer disposal are explored as ways to cut waste. The authors argue that rapid progress forces new consumption habits. Their study pushes for product design and waste practice that keep pace sustainably.
arxiv-2501-15258:
Yiling Pan, Zhixin Xu, Bin Wang, and Bailin Deng present a geometry processing method in this two thousand twenty-five paper. A ruled surface is swept out by a moving straight line. Such surfaces are prized in architecture and engineering for how plain they are to build. Past work has matched odd shapes with developable surfaces, but general ruled surfaces have had less study, and past methods set bounds on the shape. This work takes on freeform meshes.

First, a group-sparsity step reshapes the mesh close to a form made of ruled parts, piece by piece, with a tangent field that shows the ruling lines. Next, seams that split smooth sets of rulings are pulled out and used to build the first rulings. A last step shifts ruling spots and angles to hug the shape sought. Tests on shapes of many kinds and topologies showed it matching freeform shapes.
arxiv-2501-15358:
Three kinds of ultracold bosons in a one-dimensional trap can arrange themselves in many ways, depending on how strongly each kind repels itself and the others. The four authors map the full ground-state phase diagram for a few repulsively interacting bosons of three species held in a harmonic trap. They solve the many-body Schrödinger equation with an improved exact diagonalization method that handles strongly correlated few-body systems from first principles.

The study covers all combinations of intra- and interspecies interaction strengths, from the ideal limit of no interaction to near the hard-core limit. Unique ground-state traits emerge under strong repulsion, tied to correlations, coherence, and spatial localization. The results show how the three clouds share space, separate, or stack as the couplings change.
arxiv-2501-15658:
Noah M MacKay gauges the drag of the hot quark soup made in atom smashes in a 2025 paper. Drag traits test deep maths of the strong force and the harsh states of such smashes. His frame treats the soup as a mix of glue bits and quark kin at full heat rest.

Each kind adds its own share to the soup's drag in the frame. Run traits for mass and grip shift with heat, and a cool path tracks time. Drag and its heat share both rise with quark kin in, then fall as the soup cools.
arxiv-2501-15758:
Bao Nguyen, Binh Nguyen, Duy Nguyen, and Viet Anh Nguyen present a two stage guard for language model outputs in a 2025 paper. Models can slip into harmful or toxic text, and the team aim to catch and fix such slips from inside. First, an ensemble of layer by layer classifiers learns to detect bad content from the model's activations. The training uses a smoothed version of a risk aware score.

For flagged content, steering policies then adjust the attention heads at each layer. The policies are computed with a principled optimization that promises minimal disturbance while guaranteeing the edit works with high probability. Across several models and data sets, the method beat baselines at cutting undesirable output. The authors frame activation surgery as a precise, internal alternative to output filtering.
arxiv-2501-15958:
Maria Gritsevich and co-authors estimated how much mass comet 12P/Pons-Brooks threw off in its 2023 and 2024 outbursts, in a 2025 paper. The comet flared fourteen times on its way toward the sun. Two more bursts followed after its closest pass. The team built a numerical model of the ejections.

Their model centers on ice turning to gas through the porous nucleus. Burst brightness and the active surface area drive the mass estimate. A classic magnitude law converts brightness into scattering area. Two ices, water and carbon dioxide, were tried in the runs. Knowing ejected mass helps track how comets wear down over returns.
arxiv-2501-16158:
Alexander Korochkin, Dmitri Semikoz, and Peter Tinyakov trace how the Milky Way's magnetic field bends the paths of the most energetic cosmic rays. Their 2025 paper compares four leading models of the galaxy's ordered field. Ultra high energy cosmic rays arrive from space with their origins blurred by these bends.

The team fires simulated particles through each model at three rigidity levels, five, ten, and twenty exavolts. Predicted bends differ from model to model across the sky. The authors pinpoint which field parts, disk, halo, or spiral arms, cause the bends in each region. They also weigh the modeling doubts and how better field maps could sharpen the hunt for cosmic ray sources.
arxiv-2501-16758:
Bob Johnson and Michael Geller combine two learning styles to manage city traffic in this 2025 paper. Traffic data is huge and shifts fast, which strains central control systems. Central systems also raise privacy worries, since raw data must travel to one place.

Their method, meta-federated learning, keeps data on local devices and shares only model updates. A meta-learning layer lets the system adapt to new traffic patterns without long retraining. In a simulated network of smart traffic devices, the method beat older models on accuracy and response time. It also adjusted well when traffic patterns changed suddenly. The authors present it as a scalable template for smart cities and other live systems.
arxiv-2501-16858:
Benedikt Jahnel, Lukas Luchtrath, and Christian Monch study when an infection-like process can die out on a one-dimensional random network, in work from 2025. The network starts from the integer line and adds long-range links at random. Contact processes on such networks can either survive for good or fade away, with a sharp threshold between the two.

The authors give conditions that guarantee a fading zone exists, so the threshold is real and not trivial. Their results cover scale-free geometric random graphs with any well-behaved degree pattern, a wider class than past methods could handle. For one classic graph type, their condition is exact. For long-range percolation on the integers, they confirm a standing conjecture about when the threshold is nontrivial. The work widens the map of survival thresholds on random networks.
arxiv-2501-16958:
Xiaodan Zhou and co-authors reweigh whether redlining caused part of today's air pollution gaps. Their paper from 2025 starts from studies linking the 1930s housing bias maps to current fine particle and nitrogen dioxide levels. Plain links may hide bias, since records from before the policy are thin.

The team joins the old maps with 2010 pollution data and rebuilds the missing pre policy state from 1940 census proxies: joblessness, rent, and Black population share. A latent factor frame, in space and out, supports a causal read under broad assumptions. Redlined zones showed notably higher nitrogen dioxide today. Fine particle gaps were smaller. Los Angeles and Atlanta showed the strongest effects of the cities studied.
arxiv-2501-17358:
A clinical trial can borrow control patients from old data, but borrowing badly biases the verdict. Zhiwei Zhang, Jialuo Liu, and Wei Liu sort the borrowing methods that rest on outcome regression in a 2025 paper. They describe three: an augmentation method, a G-computation method, and a weighted regression method.

Each strikes a different bargain between bias and variability, especially when paired with a propensity model for who got which treatment. Simulations pit the trio against each other and against existing down-weighting and stratification approaches, and weighted regression comes out favorably among the model-based options. Two worked examples, from urology and infectious disease, show the methods on real hybrid studies. The authors give trial designers a map of which bargain suits which risk.
arxiv-2501-17458:
Cristiano Cantore and Edoardo Leonardi ask how the mix of central bank and state policy shapes how households save, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Their model has three kinds of households that hold assets with mixed ease of sale. The key gap is the extra return people need to hold a hard-to-sell asset instead of state debt.

The authors find two forces that push that gap in rival ways. One force comes from state supply of debt, and the other comes from households saving to guard themselves. Which force wins turns on the policy mix and on the kind of shock that hits the economy. Readers get a fresh way to think about how joint policy steadies growth.
arxiv-2501-17658:
Óscar Mata-Carballeira and co-authors give a method to judge ride comfort from driving style, with green driving in view. Their paper from 2025 responds to two shifts at once: self driving cars turn drivers into passengers prone to motion sickness, while pollution from cars still harms health and climate.

A self organizing map sorts drivers by the causes of their poor comfort and poor green scores, using data from an instrumented car. Each driver then gets plain language tips matched to their style, to raise engagement with the system. The authors project gains of up to about fifty eight percent in comfort measures. Greenhouse gas output could fall by up to about forty seven percent, they estimate.
arxiv-2501-17958:
Tianrui Xiang, Gregory Eyink, and Tamer Zaki trace where swirl in a fluid comes from in 2025. In frictionless flow, swirl can be tracked like a material line through time. Viscosity breaks that clean picture by spreading swirl out.

The authors offer a new fixed-frame method based on an adjoint variable. That variable encodes how earlier swirl was carried, tilted, and stretched into the target value. It also handles swirl injected at solid walls. They prove the method matches a random-path view of the same question, then apply it to turbulent channel flow.
arxiv-2501-18558:
David Bolin, Damilya Saduakhas, and Alexandre Simas wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It builds log-Gaussian Cox processes on metric graphs, a way to model event counts on networks such as roads.

The fields at the core solve fractional stochastic equations right on the graph. A new likelihood shortcut skips the need to approximate the field itself. With exact finite laws for smooth cases, the method stays both fast and sound, with proven rates for the posterior. It ships in an open R package tied to a Bayesian engine. A case on road crashes in Saudi Arabia, over a huge road net, flags the risky stretches by exceedance odds.
arxiv-2501-18658:
Pieter Miedema, writing alone in 2025, set out a theory for how the first structures in the universe formed. The work rests on a standard model of an expanding universe, treated with full relativity. He first shows that measures for clumps in energy and in particle counts can be defined in only one sound way.

With a frame chosen, the theory tracks how a clump bends space near it, how fluid moves under its own gravity, and how heat-based clumps help growth. Just after matter and light split apart, brief drops in one part of pressure let clumps grow fast. They then grew more slowly toward the masses and birth times seen for the earliest structures.
arxiv-2501-18958:
A new ladder of imaginary universes for set theory is built in a 2025 paper by Douglas Blue, Paul B. Larson, and Grigor Sargsyan. The rungs are called Nairian models, models of the Axiom of Determinacy arranged in a hierarchy by strength.

Forcing over the simplest such model yields a universe where a strong forcing axiom holds while certain square principles fail. Richer rungs extend the failures higher, and another model makes the first uncountable cardinal behave like a supercompact one. Three corollaries follow, including consistent failures of a long-standing iterability conjecture for inner model constructions. The authors argue these results mark real barriers to pushing inner model theory past a key threshold.
arxiv-2501-19058:
Haoying Zhou and five co-authors improve control of a surgical robot arm in a 2025 paper. The arm belongs to a newer research version of the da Vinci surgical system, whose redesigned structure makes gravity impossible to ignore, unlike the older model. Heavy gravity offsets hurt accuracy and slow responses.

The team first builds a full movement model of the new arm. Then they identify its dynamic parameters from data and use the fitted model to cancel gravity's pull in the controller. The work extends earlier model based control research from the older robot to the upgraded hardware. Better gravity handling matters for the growing community using this open surgical platform for research.
arxiv-2501-19258:
Shumin Que and Anton Ragni add video to speech synthesis in a 2025 paper. One written line can be spoken many ways, with stress and rhythm shifting by context. Text and past speech alone miss cues that a face or scene could give. Many uses, such as dubbing, already have video at hand.

Their model, VisualSpeech, feeds visual and text features into prosody prediction for text-to-speech. Tests show the added visual stream improves rhythm modeling, they report. The synthesized speech sounds more expressive as a result. Sample audio is posted online. The work opens a route to livelier synthetic voices for video content.
arxiv-2502-00058:
Karishma Thakrar and Aniket Chauhan map the social world of open-source developers in a 2025 paper. On GitHub, a star is a small vote of admiration, and twelve thousand developers' starring habits weave a network with real structure. Reading that structure could serve community builders and trend watchers.

The team models the network with graph neural networks. One model sorts developers into communities by their tastes, web building versus machine learning. Another predicts which developers should connect, recommending edges from similarity. Both tasks scored well in experiments. The results show admiration patterns can reveal tribes and likely friendships in the world's biggest code bazaar.
arxiv-2502-00158:
Keeping a large language model current means two jobs at once: adding new facts and erasing unwanted ones. Binchi Zhang and co-authors show those jobs often clash, and that stored facts can sit too sparse or too dense. Their fix, LOKA, stores updated knowledge in a codebook of memories instead of inside the model itself.

Related facts are grouped into the same memory slot by a similarity-aware mapping. Separate slots serve editing, unlearning, or both, steered by a conflict score. At question time, a learned router picks the right memory and plugs it in. Wide tests, the team reports in 2025, show the codebook handles updates without the usual conflicts.
arxiv-2502-00258:
Hongyi Liu and co-authors present ProxSparse, a learned way to choose which weights to prune from large language models, in a 2025 paper. Pruning in a fixed pattern speeds models up, but common mask-picking rules work layer by layer with hand-set heuristics and miss the global picture. ProxSparse turns mask choice into a smooth optimization problem, so the mask can be explored gradually.

Once the mask is set, no further weight training is needed. Across seven widely used models, the learned masks beat earlier semi-structured pruning methods by clear margins. The authors argue that treating pruning as learning, rather than rule-following, gives smaller, faster models that keep more of their skill.
arxiv-2502-00458: Joshua Jackson and David Swinarski present a 2025 arXiv paper on the worst destabilizing direction for a class of unstable curves. In geometric invariant theory, an unstable point has a single most destructive one-parameter subgroup, identified by Kempf. The authors study Chow points of toric rational curves with one single-branch singularity. They recast the hunt as convex geometry: find the closest point of a polyhedral cone to an outside point. The answer carries a combinatorial description that holds once the embedding dimension grows large.
arxiv-2502-00558:
Robot teams that cannot phone home often must still cooperate, and Sydney Dolan and co-authors teach them to work asynchronously. Their system lets each agent learn when and what to communicate over a changing graph of contacts, using graph transformer networks to write the protocol. Links exist only while agents are actually in touch, so the method copes with rare, irregular messages.

In navigation and task tests the asynchronous teams matched leading synchronous baselines on success and collisions while sending about twenty-six percent fewer messages. The saving matters where bandwidth or stealth is scarce: disaster zones, underwater, or contested airspace. The authors show that good communication discipline, not constant chatter, is what multi-agent learning needs.
arxiv-2502-00858:
Manjie Xu and co-authors present a 2025 arXiv paper on home robots that learn unspoken user preferences. Instructions like "prepare an apple" leave choices open: wash or cut, and where to place it. The team built a benchmark, Preference-based Planning, with 5,000 test groups and 290 preferences at three levels, from action details to ordering rules.

Their framework, InTU, first states the inferred preference in words, then plans from that statement. Models planned well when handed the true preference but stumbled when they had to infer it from behavior videos. Spelling the preference out first improved results and helped transfer to new scenes.
arxiv-2502-01058:
Zhang, Guo, and Wang set out a magnetometer, a gauge for magnetic fields, built on a single giant emitter tied in at many points, in work from twenty twenty-five. A giant atom sheds light at a rate that hangs sharply on its frequency. In the model, a bias magnetic field tunes that frequency in step. The emitter crosses its own light paths at the tie points, and that self-interference steepens the slope of its loss curve.

The slope grows in a straight line with the count of tie points, by design. The gauge can feel fields as faint as ten to the minus eight or nine tesla per root hertz. That reach dwarfs gauges built on small emitters much like it. Self-interference is the key edge in the plan. If built, the gauge would widen the uses of giant emitters in fine gauging work.
arxiv-2502-01358:
Andreas Habring, Alexander Falk, and Thomas Pock propose a new sampling method in their 2025 paper. Sampling means drawing random points that follow a chosen pattern, a task at the heart of much data work. Their method is modeled on the way image generators slowly turn noise into a clear picture.

They build a chain of patterns that start out easy to sample and grow closer to the hard target pattern. Parts of the target's cost curve are swapped for smoothed forms to make each step tame. A slow cooling style process then walks samples from the easy start toward the target. The paper backs the method with theory and shows tests as well. Good samplers help in fields from physics to image repair, where the target pattern has sharp or rough parts.
arxiv-2502-01758:
Gianluca Teza and co-authors review odd cases where hot systems cool faster than warm ones in a 2025 paper. The Mpemba effect has been noted since ancient times in water. Like effects now appear in many lab systems, from grains to quantum setups. All share a twist where starting farther away can mean arriving sooner.

The review sorts the water cases and kin effects into a clean frame. Stochastic heat theory, motion theory, and phase change views each add a lens. New predictions include a reverse effect where cold heats faster than warm. Uses range from better cooling plans to heat engines and sampling tools. The survey is built as a self contained entry point.
arxiv-2502-01858:
Akshar Chavan, Rudra Joshi, and Marco Brocanelli rethink energy use in ground robots in a 2025 paper. A delivery or patrol robot's battery limits how long it can work. Past work split the problem in two: saving energy on board, and assigning tasks across a fleet, with the two sides making clashing assumptions.

The team measured how computing speed and driving speed jointly change energy draw and task performance on their own prototype robot. Their system, PECC, predicts energy use so a robot can plan to finish its tasks inside a fixed budget. Joining the two views could stretch each charge without dulling performance.
arxiv-2502-02158:
Young stars in the Carina Nebula complex are mapped by Göppl and Preibisch in a 2025 paper. The authors use Gaia DR3 astrometry and photometry to study the spatial spread and clustering of young stellar populations across the complex and the full Car OB1 association. They also search for new candidates for massive OB stars in the region.

First, the team made a new census of high-mass stars, with a catalog of hundreds of stars whose spectral types and Gaia parallaxes fit membership. A clustering algorithm then found fifteen clusters and groups, four of them new. Most clusters show signs of expansion or contraction. The whole association also expands as a whole. Readers get distances, motions, and ages for a major star-forming region.
arxiv-2502-02258:
Qi Chen, Di Wu, and Zhifei Zhang settle a long-open question about when flow over a flat plate turns unstable, in a 2025 paper. Boundary layer flow can sprout Tollmien-Schlichting waves, the first stirrings of turbulence. Theory long posited a neutral curve: for wave numbers between its two branches, unstable waves exist. A landmark 2016 work built those waves rigorously but left the curve itself unconfirmed.

The authors confirm the neutral curve exists. Their route solves the governing Orr-Sommerfeld equation with finer tools, borrowing ideas from triple-deck theory. That lets them construct the waves in a neighborhood hugging the curve itself. The result tightens the mathematical foundations of how smooth flow begins to break down.
arxiv-2502-02358:
Guo, Hu, Soh, and Zhao introduced MotionLab in twenty twenty-five, a unified system for generating and editing human motion. Motion work in computer vision usually splits into separate tools per task, which wastes effort. Earlier unifying attempts used outside signals to guide generation but could not edit motion.

Their Motion-Condition-Motion paradigm frames every task with three parts: a source motion, a condition, and a target motion. MotionLab learns the mapping between source and target using rectified flows, guided by the condition. Parts include a transformer tuned for conditional editing, a rotation encoding that keeps source and target in sync, instruction modulation per task, and a curriculum for learning many tasks together. Tests across benchmarks showed strong generalization and speed.
arxiv-2502-02458:
Qianhao Yuan and co-authors present in 2025 SAISA, a build for image text models that cuts both training and use costs. Two past builds split the trade: one trains cheap and runs dear, the other runs cheap and trains dear. The key gap lies in how image bits attend to each other.

A test showed that image to image attention adds near nothing, so the team cut it. Their build feeds image traits straight into lean self attention blocks. At the same size as a known base model, run cost fell by two thirds and training cost by a fourth. Scores held in the same range.
arxiv-2502-02558:
Sam Young, Yeon-jae Jwa, and Kazuhiro Terao teach a model to read particle tracks in a neutrino detector by hiding and guessing parts of the data, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Liquid argon chambers image particle paths in fine three-dimensional detail, but labeled training data come from simulations that can bias results.

Their autoencoder learns from unlabeled real images, masking chunks of the point cloud and predicting missing energies. Fine-tuned on only a hundred labeled events, it matched a supervised champion trained on over a hundred thousand. Its attention maps even separated individual particle tracks on their own. The team released a million-event dataset to push foundation models for this physics.
arxiv-2502-02658:
Four astronomers report new findings from 2025 on fast-moving stars that plow through gas in space and leave curved shock fronts behind them. The stars studied are hot O and Be stars that were thrown out of their birth places and now travel at high speed. The team set out to find shock fronts and bubbles that earlier surveys had missed.

Working from a Gaia-based list of runaway stars, the authors searched heat images from the WISE survey and checked old radio data. They found nine new shock fronts, three bubbles, and one mixed case. About a quarter of the O stars showed such fronts, far more than the Be stars. Radio checks gave mixed results, so deeper radio work is still needed.
arxiv-2502-02758:
Hugo Carrillo, Alberto Mercado, and Roberto Morales solve a double puzzle in wave physics: recovering two unknown fields at once. Their work appeared in twenty twenty-five. The setting is a Schrödinger equation, the core equation of quantum mechanics, in a form that does not conserve energy.

The system has mixed edge rules, one of them changing over time in what is called Wentzell form. From a single measure of flow at the edge, the authors show both unknown fields can be pinned down with a firm stability bound. Their proof uses a classic method for inverse problems and a weighted estimate built from a distance-like function. The result says one good measurement carries enough information for both unknowns.
arxiv-2502-02958:
Youssef and four co-authors wrote a position paper in twenty twenty-five warning that editing the facts stored inside large language models is a safety risk the field has largely missed. Editing tools can change one stored fact, such as a capital city, while leaving the rest of the model mostly untouched.

The authors note that these tools are cheap, easy to find, and hard to spot after the fact, which makes them inviting for bad actors. They sketch ways edits could plant false claims or weaken a model's guardrails. They also point out that edited models can be uploaded and shared with no checks at all. Low public and institutional awareness makes the danger worse, they argue. The paper calls for research on tamper-resistant models and for stronger safeguards across the places where models are shared.
arxiv-2502-03458:
Tim Johnston and co-authors proved a sampler works without smoothness in two thousand twenty-five. Langevin sampling walks downhill with added noise. Classic theory demands smooth, bowl-shaped targets. Many real targets are rough or kinked. Their simple algorithm skips costly smoothing tricks. A one-sided geometric condition replaces smoothness instead.

Even jumpy log-gradients fit the new condition. Convergence guarantees come in Wasserstein distance. The bounds are explicit, not just eventual. The sampler doubles as an optimizer with risk bounds. Rough posteriors in statistics become fair game. Computation stays light without envelope machinery. The result widens where Langevin methods can be trusted.
arxiv-2502-03558:
Rodrigo Becerra Silva and five co-authors study how light excited carriers move in thin ribbons of a special material, in a 2025 paper. The material is a topological insulator, which conducts on its surface but not inside. Understanding fast carrier motion in it matters for spin control with light and for new light based devices.

Using a microscope method with very short light pulses, the team watched carriers spread far faster than normal. At low temperature and low carrier density, they traveled up to ten micrometers in a few hundred trillionths of a second range, at speeds far above those of ordinary carriers. Motion was fastest in the purest samples and slowed as temperature rose. The authors discuss hot carriers and paired states as possible causes.
arxiv-2502-03758:
Yibo Xu and co-authors defend image networks against adversarial tricks in this 2025 paper. Tiny crafted changes can fool a network while looking harmless to people. Prompt-based defenses, which add learned cues, are cheap but often spread their focus too thin.

Their defense builds prompts from two spectra of the image: phase, which carries shape, and amplitude, which carries strength. Each class gets both kinds of prompt. During training, prompt weights shift toward whichever kind proves more robust. At test time, prompts are picked per image. The method ties the defense to the semantic patterns that matter most for each class.
arxiv-2502-03958:
Jiaojiao Zhang, Jiang Hu, and Mikael Johansson propose a new algorithm for federated learning in a 2025 paper. In federated learning, clients train a shared model on their own data, which can differ widely. The target problems here are non-convex and have a composite form, a hard mix.

Their method splits a key operator step from communication, so clients talk to the server less often and send one vector per round. Local updates fight client drift. The team proves two rates of convergence under stated conditions. Tests on synthetic and real data beat leading methods. The work targets settings where bandwidth is dear.
arxiv-2502-04158:
Supranta Boruah, Michael Jacob, and Bhuvnesh Jain use one diffusion model for two jobs in cosmology: faking weak lensing maps and rebuilding real ones. Weak lensing maps show how gravity from unseen matter bends light, but the observations are noisy. Models trained only to simulate usually cannot reconstruct, and models trained to reconstruct cannot simulate.

The team applies diffusion posterior sampling, which steers a simulation-trained model with the actual data. The standard version gave biased maps, so they softened the data's pull during the early sampling steps. The fix yields sharp mass maps, finer than an arcminute, with the right power spectrum and realistic non-Gaussian features. The authors point to uses in making simulation-grade maps, estimating errors for higher-order statistics, and finding filaments, voids, and clusters in noisy shear data.
arxiv-2502-04258:
A mild brain injury can hide from standard scans, yet a magnetic sensor array called MEG picks up its traces. Jian Zhang and Gary Green tackle a statistical snag in using those scans: the control data are lumpy and uneven, so the usual case-versus-group tests mislead. Their method compares one patient against many controls in a way that tolerates that mess.

The procedure first builds a source map from the scan's frequency data. It then tests region by region for abnormality, choosing its cutoffs by cross-validation. A similarity step adjusts for how unlike the controls are from each other. The authors back the method with theory and show it beating standard nonparametric tests on simulated and real injury data, especially when the data break normality.
arxiv-2502-04358:
Elliot Meyerson and Xin Qiu argue, in a 2025 position paper, that teams of language model agents need the same cost accounting that algorithms have always used. Builders now split hard problems among many model based agents, choosing roles by gut feel, the way a manager staffs a human team. Nobody knows how close those splits sit to optimal.

Treat one forward pass of a model as the atomic unit of cost, they propose, and the orchestration itself becomes analyzable. The inner workings of any single model stay a black box, while the efficiency of the decomposition shows in asymptotics. Stop picturing models as people, the authors urge, and start counting passes; that is how agent systems will scale to their limit.
arxiv-2502-04558:
Lu and four colleagues probe a robot control model for hidden symbol like states in twenty twenty-five. The model turns camera views and words into arm actions, but works as a black box. The team read its inner layers while it did pick and place tasks. Simple probes decoded object traits, spatial relations, and action states from those layers.

Decoding topped ninety percent accuracy for most states and layers. Object states did not sit earlier than action states, against the team's guess. They wired the readouts into a reasoning shell for live state checks. The blend lays ground for robot control that can be watched and trusted more, they argue.
arxiv-2502-04858:
