Franz Matejcek and a large detector team lay out how to build a vertex detector in a 2025 paper. The detector sits closest to the target in the CBM experiment at the future FAIR facility in Germany. It must track slow particles with fine precision. Layers must stay extremely thin, work inside a vacuum, survive strong radiation, and sit in a strong magnet.

Special CMOS pixel sensors called MIMOSIS do the sensing. The paper covers material choices, prep steps, assembly methods, and quality checks. Work is aimed at a pre-series build and first running in 2028. The design joins tight physics needs with harsh working conditions.
arxiv-2502-05658:
Guillermo González-García and co-authors map in a 2025 theory study when noisy many-body quantum systems stay simple enough for classical computers to mimic. Their models pair particles with smooth Gaussian links, rougher on-site twists, and local noise: loss, gain, and dephasing. The question is where noise wins and the state stays a blend of simple states.

For fermions, dephasing above the twist strength keeps the state a Gaussian blend at all times. For bosons, loss and gain above the link strength keep it separable. Above such lines, a fast classical sampler exists. Yet each family still surprises the other side of the line.
arxiv-2502-05858:
Sergey Komech and Jonathan Mosheiff introduce a new family of error-correcting codes built from alphabet permutations, in work from 2025. Error-correcting codes protect data by adding structure that survives noise. A key measure is list recoverability, which asks how well a code can be decoded when each position offers a small set of candidate symbols.

Their codes start from one fixed word and apply random permutations symbol by symbol, again and again. With a well-mixing choice of permutations, the code is almost surely list-recoverable with list sizes near the best possible. Older linear codes need far larger lists at the same rate. Fully random codes match the performance but need vast randomness and offer no structure. The new codes need only modest randomness, a structured route to near-optimal recovery.
arxiv-2502-06258:
Language models are trained only to guess the next word, yet Zhichen Dong and co-authors argue they quietly plan whole answers in advance. The team probed the models' internal states, the numbers computed while reading a prompt, and found those states already encode features of the reply that has not been written yet. The hidden plan covers structure, such as length and number of reasoning steps, content, such as which character a story will feature, and behavior, such as how confident the answer will be.

The authors also track how this planning grows with model size and how it changes as generation proceeds. Their point is practical: if a model has already sketched its answer internally, reading that sketch could make systems more transparent. It could also give developers a handle for steering answers before they appear.
arxiv-2502-06458: Yu Shi recalls the early work of Chien-Shiung Wu on entangled photons, in a note first shaped for a 2022 talk. Wu is famed for a landmark test of a physics law, yet her photon work came first. Guided by Chen Ning Yang, the note traces how Wu made entangled photons from electron and positron clashes, and what the tests showed. It formed the base of a speech at a meeting for the 110th year since the birth of Wu, and of a few pieces on the subject in Chinese.
arxiv-2502-06558:
Bob Krekelberg and Alison Liu wrote a 2025 paper on the FirstFit algorithm for colouring intervals as they arrive, one by one, with no view of the future. Each interval must get a colour no overlapping interval holds. They sharpen the count of how many colours this greedy rule can ever be forced to use.

A new counting trick finds, for each interval, a critical neighbour that trims past overcounts. With whole number endpoints the bound is tight at twice optimal. In general it lands near seven thirds of optimal. Online colouring models tasks like assigning rooms or channels on the fly.
arxiv-2502-06658:
To trust a trained model, it helps to ask what inputs would make it behave in a chosen way. Kıral, Aydın, and Birbil build a tool that answers such questions by generating whole distributions of inputs. Each question is written as a guidance function that steers the generation.

With it, users can conjure the inputs a model would label a certain way. They can find where two models disagree, where small parameter nudges flip the output, or where predictions turn risky. The framework works across classification and regression tasks and across model types. Rather than probing with single examples, it maps regions of behavior. The authors offer it as an inspection instrument for model auditing, debugging, and comparison.
arxiv-2502-06858:
Six authors improve the translation of plain language into Bash shell commands in this 2025 paper. Bash, the Linux command line, has complex syntax, and language models can draft commands from plain requests, but judging their output has been hampered by bad test data.

The team built a hand checked test set of 600 instruction and command pairs and a training set of over forty thousand pairs, far larger than past sets. Their new check for whether two commands do the same job, mixing execution with model judgment, reached 95 percent confidence. Tests showed that parsing, examples, training, and constrained decoding can raise accuracy by up to a third.
arxiv-2502-07058:
Zixin Tang and five co-authors present a 2025 paper on measuring whether language models treat varieties of the same language unequally. Models train mostly on dominant varieties, so others may be served worse. The team proposes a cheap benchmarking trick: international review sites hold comments about the same hotels, at the same ratings, written in different varieties of one language. They built such a matched set for Taiwan Mandarin and Mainland Mandarin.

Six large language models were tested on sentiment analysis of the reviews. Every model performed worse on the Taiwan variety. Because the reviews describe the same stays at the same scores, the gap cannot be blamed on topic or tone differences. The authors offer the method as a low-cost way to audit fairness across language varieties. They warn that speakers of non-dominant varieties quietly get a worse product.
arxiv-2502-07458:
Karlo Lelas and Robert Pezer solve a classroom classic with friction turned up: a harmonic oscillator slowed by three kinds of damping at once. Constant-magnitude friction, drag linear in velocity, and drag quadratic in velocity can all act together, and the paper derives approachable formulas for how the swing amplitude decays under any weak mix.

The derivation needs only the undamped oscillator and one idea: energy drains at the rate the total damping force does work. Checked against exact numerical solutions, the approximations track the motion excellently across experimentally sensible damping strengths. The authors aim the treatment at undergraduate teaching, showing how far energy bookkeeping and basic technique can carry a problem that looks like it needs heavy machinery.
arxiv-2502-07558:
Anton Savostianov, Michael Schaub, Nicola Guglielmi, and Francesco Tudisco slim down higher-order networks in a 2025 paper. Simplicial complexes capture group interactions beyond pairs, but real ones grow dense and costly. Sparsification swaps them for lean stand-ins that keep the spectrum close. Their probabilistic method picks which pieces to keep using local densities of states, a physics style probe.

Those probes estimate each piece's effective resistance, which sets its sampling odds, they show. A kernel ignoring split avoids degenerate spectra in the math. Error bounds pin down the running cost. Tests on filtered Vietoris-Rips complexes, a standard shape family, show the method holds up.
arxiv-2502-07658:
Wenhao Wu and ten co-authors redesign recommendations for a person-to-person shopping platform in a 2025 paper. On China's largest such marketplace, most listings are one-off items from individual sellers. Once an item sells, it vanishes, so classic recommenders starve for interaction history.

Their system first groups products into interest units by category, image, and meaning. Recommendations then operate on those units rather than fleeting single items. Two stages connect the unit level to final suggestions for each shopper. The shift keeps signals alive even as individual listings churn. Tests on the platform's data back the approach. The design suits any marketplace where stock is unique and short-lived, from vintage goods to local classifieds.
arxiv-2502-08058:
Parsa Moradi, Hanzaleh Akbarinodehi, and Mohammad Ali Maddah-Ali laid groundwork in 2025 for coded computing beyond its usual narrow tasks. Coded computing spreads work across servers with built-in backup math, so slow or cheating servers cannot ruin the result. Old designs fit only tidy tasks like matrix products.

Their scheme covers a wide class of tasks and still holds when a share of servers act as enemies. They prove the average error shrinks fast as servers are added, under mild assumptions. They also show no scheme in this frame can withstand more enemies than theirs does, a sign the design sits at the limit.
arxiv-2502-08358:
Markus Faulhuber, a solo author, collects results on when Gabor systems are secretly the same in a 2025 paper. Gabor systems build signals from shifted and modulated copies of one window function, a backbone of audio and signal analysis. Two such systems can look different yet be unitarily equivalent, meaning a clean transformation converts one to the other. The paper gathers what is known about spotting that sameness using operator pairs and global isometries.

The methods are then turned on Gabor systems built from Hermite functions, classic bell-shaped modes. Faulhuber supplies fresh proofs of some known results, tidying the arguments. A final outlook takes up double over-sampling, a regime where the system samples well past the usual density. The piece is a synthesis for specialists in time-frequency analysis.
arxiv-2502-08458:
Counseling research built on English sessions may not carry over to other languages, since culture and speech habits differ. Aylin Gunal and co-authors take a first step on that question in this 2025 paper. They built MIDAS, a dataset of motivational interviewing sessions in Spanish, drawn from public videos and marked by experts.

The annotations tag counselor moves such as reflections and questions, the core tools of this counseling style. With the dataset, the team compared counselor behavior in Spanish and English sessions. They also trained classifiers in single-language and mixed-language settings to code counselor behavior on their own. The work opens a path for studying therapy talk beyond English and for tools that support Spanish-speaking counselors.
arxiv-2502-08758:
Ghazal Kasalaee, Ali Hasanzadeh Karkan, Jean-François Frigon, and François Leduc-Primeau wrote a 2025 paper on making neural networks for wireless precoding cheaper to run. Massive MIMO systems use many antennas, and learned precoders can beat classic methods. Their computing and energy costs, though, block wider use.

The authors built an energy model that counts both memory access and calculation in learning hardware. They then compressed the networks with mixed precision training, where numbers are stored at varied bit widths, plus an automated search over network shapes. On ray traced data from varied base station sites, compressed precoders reached up to thirty five times the energy efficiency of a standard method at equal quality. Site conditions changed the gains, so the paper also sets a benchmark.
arxiv-2502-08958:
Ciyuan Peng and six co-authors built a brain graph reader that respects how real brains are wired in a 2025 paper. Brain scans can be drawn as graphs of linked zones. Real brain graphs have hubs and tight modules, with most zones close by short paths. Past AI readers skip that shape, so their maps of the brain ring false.

Their transformer marks each zone by how much it steers traffic across the whole graph. Its attention step also honors the brain's split into working modules that still talk to each other. On three test sets the model beat top rivals at tasks such as spotting brain disorders. The team says shape true maps make the calls more trustworthy.
arxiv-2502-09258:
Upadhyay, Saini, and Sethi wrote a methods paper in twenty twenty-five on cleaning up a known bias in supernova cosmology. The galaxies that host these exploding stars drift with their own motion, called peculiar velocity, and that drift skews the distance estimates used to measure how the universe expands.

The usual fixes rebuild the drift from maps of galaxies, which assumes a cosmology in advance, or pad the error bars using rough shortcuts. The authors instead built a Bayesian method that fits the expansion model and the drift correction at the same time. It treats the problem as fitting a curved relation with errors on both axes, dropping the straight-line shortcut. They checked the method on simulated data at the sharpness of current and future surveys, then on a real supernova sample. The approach offers a cross-check on standard corrections.
arxiv-2502-09358:
Lucas de Oliveira Silva and four co-authors present a 2025 study of a harder version of a classic graph problem. The classic problem asks whether a list of numbers can be the connection counts, or degrees, of a graph's corners. That version is solvable fast. The new version adds cut constraints: for chosen groups of corners, the number of edges leaving the group must match a given size, on top of the degree list.

The authors prove the problem stays fast when every constrained group has at most three corners. With groups of four, it becomes as hard as problems believed to have no fast solution. The hardness holds even when every corner needs just one edge. The result draws a sharp line between the easy and hard forms of the problem.
arxiv-2502-09858:
Kexin Huang and co-authors automate the testing of bold claims in this 2025 paper. Many real claims are broad and hard to test head-on. Language models now propose claims in huge numbers, and they often invent facts, so hand checks cannot keep up.

Their system, Popper, follows Karl Popper's rule that claims should face attempts to prove them false. Model agents design and run tests aimed at each claim's testable parts. A staged testing method keeps the false-alarm rate strict. The work offers a way to screen machine-made claims at scale, with rigor that hand review cannot match.
arxiv-2502-09958:
Alexandr Prishlyak builds methods to tell surfaces apart by their shape type in a 2025 paper. The work is the third part of a series on shape invariants for systems that change over time. Part one set out the base ideas of the field, and part two laid out the block-like structures the theory uses.

Part three gives step methods that read a surface from a mesh of blocks or cells. The steps name the key traits: how the surface joins up, whether it has a front and back, its hole count, and how many edge loops it holds. The same frame sorts the type of maps and flows on the surface, the author shows.
arxiv-2502-10058:
Qingliang Meng and four co-authors rethink how language models are trained for speech to text work. Stock speech language models train left to right to match code that builds word by word. That bars them from use of right side words while they learn. Their MTLM plan joins train in one way and in both ways through three aims.

The joint train lets the model take in rich word trends from both sides. It stays fit with plain code steps. It also backs more than one code plan. They are light join and re score of pick lists in each way or both. Tests on the LibriSpeech test set show the way beats one way train in a firm way. That holds through code plans. The team sets MTLM out as a bendy lift for the language model stage of speech paths.
arxiv-2502-10358:
Luke Jeffreys and Carlos Matheus bounded the size of orbit graphs for origami surfaces in 2025, in a corner of geometry that studies flat surfaces folded from squares. Acting on such a surface with a group of stretch and shear moves generates a graph of related surfaces, and its diameter measures how far apart two cousins can be.

Earlier work sorted these orbits for one family of surfaces, and later authors reused the same machinery for two harder families tied to Prym forms. Jeffreys and Matheus turned those sorting methods into explicit diameter bounds for all three settings. Each bound grows like the orbit size to the two thirds power, times a log factor. The result ties the classifications to hard numbers.
arxiv-2502-10558:
Younghoon Kim, Sumanta Basu, and Samprit Banerjee detect emotional stress in therapy patients from phone-sensor streams. They cut the streams into segments where the stress signal actually lives. Their data mix passive sensing, such as movement and phone use, with self-reported stress. The patients are middle-aged and older adults in mood-disorder therapy. Some also live with chronic pain. Global machine learning smears the link, because sensors and stress connect only in short windows. Writing in twenty twenty-five, their algorithm first finds change points in the passive streams. It then keeps segments where sensor behavior and self-reports move together distinctively. Predictors are trained on those co-segments.

Applied to a real clinical study's data, the approach identified stress periods more accurately than standard models. The unit of analysis shifts from single moments to episodes, matching how stress actually unfolds.
arxiv-2502-10758:
Shashwat Singh and three co-authors probe fuzzy dark matter with bent gravity waves in a 2025 paper. Gravity bends both light and the waves from merged black holes as they cross a heavy halo. Fuzzy dark matter, made of ultra-light bits, packs its halos around dense cores called solitons, unlike the smooth halos of cold dark matter.

Wave bends leave tone-linked marks in a wave's shape when the bend is soft. Low-mass fuzzy halos mark waves in ways cold halos do not, and a core leaves its own print. A space wave watch called LISA could read those marks and split the two dark forms.
arxiv-2502-11258:
Thanushon Sivakaran and En-Hui Yang use an information measure to sharpen language model training, in a 2025 paper. The measure is conditional mutual information, a gauge of how much one signal reveals about another. It had rarely been applied to large language models. The pair test it in two directions for classification tasks.

First, they fine-tune a model while keeping the measure low, to boost its solo performance. Second, they raise the measure while training a small student model from a larger teacher. Their setup adapts a framework first built for image tasks. On a standard language test suite, both directions beat their baselines on most tasks. Information theory gains a firmer place in model building.
arxiv-2502-11358:
Ziyou Jiang and six co-authors proposed AutoCMD in twenty twenty-five, a dynamic attack on language model systems that call external tools. An attacker who compromises a tool can inject commands that trick the model into leaking sensitive information to it. Earlier attacks used fixed commands, which adapt poorly as conversations and tool chains evolve, and so get caught.

AutoCMD mimics the familiar: it learns, from open-source systems and a few target examples, what information upstream tools legitimately handle, then crafts theft commands that blend in. In evaluations it beat baselines on theft success rate by over thirteen points and transferred to new systems. The authors also propose four defenses that effectively blunt the attack, mapping both sides of this vulnerability.
arxiv-2502-11458:
Eleven authors, led by Jiecheng Zhou, test whether large language models can be trained with very low-precision numbers. Training these models costs a great deal, and using fewer bits per number can cut that cost. The FP4 format uses just four bits, but it risks errors because it can store only a small range of values.

The team's scheme gives different parts of the model different precision levels, matched to what each part can handle. It also uses fine-grained scaling and a planned schedule for when each precision level applies, which keeps training stable. In their tests, models trained this way reached accuracy close to that of models trained with wider formats, at a lower cost in theory. The authors say the scheme prepares the ground for future chips built to handle FP4 math.
arxiv-2502-11658:
Antoine Boutet and Victor Morel survey young smartphone users about how they share location data and what risks they see, in a paper from 2025. Phones collect location that can reveal home, work, and daily habits. Apps and service firms pass that data on in ways users may not grasp.

Just under one hundred young adults took part. The team compared what people said they did with what their settings showed. About half of the group undercounted the apps that could reach their location data. A third had forgotten to withdraw access they no longer wanted. A demo tool then showed what could be inferred from their own traces. More than half were surprised by what it revealed. The authors call for clearer, easier privacy tools.
arxiv-2502-11758:
Stephen Overall and John Southworth train a model to pre-read eclipsing binary light curves for expert fitting. Detached eclipsing binaries yield star masses and sizes with rare precision. Survey missions like Kepler and TESS flood archives with candidate curves. Human fitting cannot keep pace with that flood.

Their EBOP MAVEN model inspects a light curve and guesses the fitting inputs. A formal code, jktebop, then does the careful final analysis. Good starting values cut wasted fits and expert hours alike. The goal is a catalogue that matches the true abundance of systems. Machine triage thus feeds, rather than replaces, exact stellar physics.
arxiv-2502-12158:
Mingchen Shao and co-authors use large language models to mine social factors from clinical notes and tie them to heart failure readmissions, in a 2025 paper. Heart failure sends millions back to hospital within a month. Social conditions like housing and transport drive many returns. Those facts hide in free-text notes, not tidy database fields. Manual chart review cannot scale to find them.

Language models extracted social determinants from the notes. Regression then linked each factor to thirty-day readmission. Tobacco use and limited transportation stood out among the signals. Care teams gain a list of fixable risks. Social work referrals could target the flagged patients. The method turns dormant text into planning data.
arxiv-2502-12258:
Xuesong Liu and Emmett Ientilucci wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It presents SmokeNet, a lean model that traces smoke plumes in images for safety and environmental watch.

Finding plume edges fast guides blast checks, fire response, and rule enforcement. Past models are heavy and stiff when smoke changes shape. SmokeNet mixes convolutions at many scales with a light attention plan that looks from many angles. A loss tuned per layer steadies the learning. Four data sets test it, one a fresh quarry blast set the team shares. Scores stay high while the cost stays low. That balance suits field gear with small budgets of power and chips.
arxiv-2502-12358:
Tavernarakis and co-authors describe a sharper way to sense tiny motion in a 2025 physics paper. Their setup pairs a focused laser beam with a thin tapered lever that bends as it moves. Rather than read the beam with a simple split sensor, they shape the light first and study many output modes at once. The goal is to push the measure close to the quantum limit.

Shaping the beam raised the signal to noise level about 350 fold, a gain of 25.5 decibels over the standard method. The result sits close to the best precision quantum rules allow. The authors argue the method opens fresh room for both finer sensing and tighter control of how light and motion interact. Small labs that track faint forces stand to gain from the approach.
arxiv-2502-12858:
Reward models grade the answers of large language models and steer them toward replies people prefer, but the grading itself can be biased. Joel Mire and co-authors test one such bias in this 2025 paper: whether reward models score text in African American Language worse than the same content in White Mainstream English. The team built a framework for checking dialect bias and applied it in a case study.

Across several tests, the models matched human choices less well on African American Language texts, by about four points of accuracy on average. They often ranked the mainstream version above the dialect version, and they steered chats toward the mainstream form even when users wrote in the dialect. The authors argue this stage of model building deserves more scrutiny for fairness.
arxiv-2502-12958:
Jun Zhang and co-authors devise and then block a poisoning attack on federated recommender systems in a 2025 paper. In such systems, user devices train a shared model without sending raw data. Attackers can twist their updates to push chosen items. Past attacks needed model details or prior knowledge, limiting real use.

Their attack, PIECK, mines which items are popular by watching how embeddings shift in training. It then pulls target items toward popular ones, with an added trick that fakes user profiles for strength. Common defenses failed against it. The authors add two training penalties that curb both tricks while keeping recommendation quality.
arxiv-2502-13458:
Xiaofei Wen, Wenxuan Zhou, Wenjie Jacky Mo, and Muhao Chen build a guard that thinks slow for chat safety in a 2025 paper. Guards now lean on rule screens or one-pass sorts, which miss fine breach kinds. Their guard learns from big models' writ notes that stand by each safe tag.

Fine tune on note-rich data lends the guard a slow, wary think style, they show. Plain outs let users read why a call went each way in the tests. Top mean grades on a set of safe benches crown the runs.
arxiv-2502-13658:
Faheem Ullah and colleagues mine the job market to answer a practical question: what skills does a cybersecurity career actually require? Attacks keep rising, demand for defenders follows, and would-be entrants lack a clear map. The team analyzed over twelve thousand job advertisements. Nearly forty-nine thousand developer forum posts added a practitioner's view.

Communication and project management topped the soft skills. Technical skill demand varied far more between roles, from analyst to architect, than soft skill demand did. Java emerged as the most commonly used programming language in the field's postings. The authors aim the findings at two audiences. Career changers get a target list for their preparation. Universities get evidence for which skills their degrees should teach. Role-specific breakdowns keep the advice from going generic.
arxiv-2502-13858:
Shiyang Zhang and co-authors test how well a sky survey can spot faint dwarf galaxies near our own in a 2025 paper. Such dwarfs are old, small, and rich in dark matter, so they test ideas on how galaxies form. Knowing what a survey can and cannot see is key to reading its finds.

The team builds fake dwarfs, plants them in fake survey images, and tries to find them again. Image-level fakes catch flaws that list-level fakes miss, such as blends and split errors. Tight far dwarfs are lost more often than lists suggest, since they merge into one blob in the image step.
arxiv-2502-14258:
Yein Park and colleagues located the attention heads that handle time in language models in a 2025 paper. Facts change: a champion or office holder this year differs from last year, and models must answer for the year asked. Circuit analysis revealed specific heads, dubbed temporal heads, that specialize in time-specific recall across several models, though their addresses differ from model to model.

Switching those heads off damaged recall of dated facts while leaving timeless knowledge and general question answering intact. The heads react to written-out year phrases as well as numerals, so they encode time itself, not digit patterns. Editing the heads' values even changed the model's dated answers, opening a surgical route to updating stale facts.
arxiv-2502-14458:
Aviv Bick and co-authors introduce Llamba in 2025, a family of fast language models built by distilling larger ones. They start from Meta's Llama-3 models and pour their skill into the Mamba design, which reads text in a leaner recurrent way. The family comes in three sizes, from one to eight billion parameters. A method called MOHAWK guides the transfer between the two designs.

The models answer faster and handle much larger batches than transformer models of like size. Their test scores stay close to the originals. The transfer used less than a tenth of a percent of typical training data. The team also tuned the models for phones and edge devices.
arxiv-2502-14758:
Cagliari and co-authors bound the size of first-era lumps from quasar maps. The mark fNL sizes how far first mass spread strays from smooth. Their maps come from the eBOSS DR16 quasar set in full. Two counts join: a paired count and a triple count of spread. Best weight picks squeeze the most fNL facts from the pair count. Stock weights drive the triple count in their runs.

Fix terms for whole and ray-based count warps join the frame. The ray fix shifts marks the most of the two in tests. Bounds land from minus 6 to 20 at the 68 mark. That span beats the past pair-count span by near 16 percent. A low-quasar-pull case gives minus 23 to 14 in its place. Both spans track the counts the team first sketched.
arxiv-2502-14958:
Anthony Rey and co-authors build a map of quantum phases in this 2025 paper. Phase transitions between magnetic states can pass through unusual critical points. Some of those points are called deconfined, because their behavior defies the standard picture. The team designed a lattice model of spin-half particles with triple mirror symmetry.

The model hosts four gapped magnetic phases and one broad gapless phase between them. Switching between gapped phases can run through a critical point or through the gapless phase. That phase acts like a hub joining four special critical points. Math arguments and heavy computer simulations together charted the map. The setup gives theorists a clean test bed for exotic transitions.
arxiv-2502-15158:
Khanh Le and Duc Chau improve streaming speech recognition in a 2025 paper. Chunk based systems read speech in blocks, which is fast and simple, yet they see only past and current sound. Tasks that need a peek at future sound suffer under that limit.

Their design adds a time shifted attention that brings in future context in a controlled way. A dynamic mask sets how much right side context each part may use. On a standard speech set, word error rates fell by a tenth or more in relative terms. A full pipeline keeps user felt delay low and still allows batch runs, which suits live products.
arxiv-2502-15558:
Competitive programming contests, where student teams race to solve coding problems, draw far fewer women than men in Brazil. The authors document strategies used to raise female participation in these programming marathons. Their work is documentary and exploratory, gathering the inclusion actions tried so far and the results they produced.

The actions include affirmative steps and inclusion efforts aimed at girls and women in computing. The authors argue such steps form an important move toward gender equity in the contests, even though female participation still lags well behind male participation. They frame the collected strategies as a record other organizers can draw on. The catalog title is in Portuguese; the text head gives the English title used here.
arxiv-2502-15658:
Marek Rogatko and Paritosh Verma ask, in a 2025 paper, whether light given off near a black hole could betray a hidden dark sector. Their dark matter model couples the familiar Maxwell field to a second, hidden gauge field, the dark photon model. The coupling also shapes how a black hole in this theory becomes magnetised.

They follow a heavy particle that carries both a visible and a hidden charge as it circles a round, weakly magnetised black hole in its equatorial plane. Such a particle sheds synchrotron radiation as it turns. The team computed the radiated power and the energy loss rate. They then looked for marks that the dark sector leaves on those quantities, which future readings could in principle catch.
arxiv-2502-15758:
Machine learning systems slip quietly into production and rot there, unless an organization grades their quality like it grades code. Angelantonio Castelli, Georgios Christos Chouliaras, and Dmitri Goldenberg propose a maturity framework in 2025, a ladder of quality levels with an open assessment method to place a system on it.

The authors draw on large-scale adoption experience at Booking.com, where the framework was put to work across many teams. They report quality trends improving as the method spread, and business outcomes that followed. Challenges and lessons from that rollout fill much of the paper. The goal is an industry-usable standard for reliability and reproducibility in applied machine learning.
arxiv-2502-15858:
Sebastian Stober and Tim Dornis examine in 2025 copyright law for training generative AI models. Note that the text's byline order differs from the catalog listing, and the text governs here. Training needs vast data, often scraped from the web, and much of it is copyright protected material.

United States developers rely on fair use, while Europe leans on a text and data mining exception. The authors argue neither defense fits generative training, which differs fundamentally from mining. Memorization of training data raises separate copyright problems. They outline fair practices and a role for their research community in the debate.
arxiv-2502-16058:
Milton Jair Santibañez-Armenta and co-authors model the black hole at the center of our galaxy in a 2025 paper. Telescope images show a dark shadow ringed by bright light. Bright spots and flicker in the ring are still not well explained.

The team tests one idea: a second, smaller black hole sits on the line of sight and blocks part of the view. Their image, made for the observed wavelength, shows bright hot spots like those seen. The model sets the gap between the two holes and gives mass values for each. The work offers one testable account of the bright pattern, apart from gas effects alone.
arxiv-2502-16158:
Pengyan Wang writes a 2025 math paper on symmetry in fractional equations. The equations involve a p-Laplace operator stretched across distance, so each point feels the whole space. Solutions to such equations often turn out symmetric and monotone, but proving it is delicate. Wang first proves a maximum principle for functions that are antisymmetric across a plane.

That principle powers a moving-plane argument, giving a fresh proof of symmetry for the elliptic case with gradient terms. With the right starting data, the same tools yield symmetry at every moment for the time-dependent version, on both open space and bounded regions. The methods should export to many problems with nonlocal operators.
arxiv-2502-16258:
B Q Song, J D H Smith, and J Wang derive a formula that computes electric currents in superconductors straight from the underlying wavefunctions. Their 2025 paper explains that the standard BCS wavefunction is complex, with correlations and changing particle numbers, so physicists usually describe currents through coarse order parameters instead. Their formula avoids that detour.

One part of the current comes from the Berry phase, a geometric property of the wavefunction, and matches a group velocity form that survives even with strong correlations. A second part is driven by pairing itself, arising from the correlated pairs of electrons. The authors note parallels with insulators, hinting at one frame for charge flow at both extremes of conductivity.
arxiv-2502-16358:
Jamshid Mozafari and three colleagues present a 2025 paper arguing that wrong answers deserve respect. Language models are judged on correct answers, yet plausible-but-wrong candidates are exactly what multiple-choice tests need as distractors and what robustness checks use to probe models. Existing datasets rarely score how plausible each wrong answer is.

Their dataset, PlausibleQA, holds ten thousand questions with one hundred thousand candidate answers. Each answer carries a plausibility score and a justification, plus nine hundred thousand pairwise comparison justifications refining the scores. Human checks validated the labels. Experiments show plausibility-aware methods generate better distractors and sharper robustness assessments. The authors release the data as a resource for evaluating how well models separate the nearly-right from the right.
arxiv-2502-16458:
Five authors build Transformer networks in 2025 to read asteroid spectra for a planned probe mission to a near-Earth asteroid. The mission needs the rock type, surface shine, and mix before close work and sampling. Three networks split the tasks, one for class, one for shine, and one for mix.

Class calls hit about 97 percent on a four-way split and about 96 percent on an eleven-way split. Shine error for S-type rocks stayed near 0.03 on mean. Mix forecasts also tracked the true spectra closely, and the platform was run on six asteroids as a demo.
arxiv-2502-16558:
Xiaoyang Wang and seven co-authors use deep learning to search for high-temperature superconducting ternary hydrides, in work from 2025. The search space is vast, since many element mixes and crystal forms are possible. Their framework links large-scale structure search, physics-based screening and prediction of critical temperatures.

About 36 million structures across 29 elements were explored in the study. The screen found 144 candidate materials with predicted critical temperatures above 200 K and good stability at high pressure. Of these, 129 compounds across 27 new structural types are reported for the first time. The method offers a scalable way to search complex hydride systems.
arxiv-2502-17258:
Xiangpeng Yang, Linchao Zhu, Hehe Fan, and Yi Yang presented VideoGrain in 2025, a tool for editing video at several levels of detail. Users may want to change a whole class of object, one object, or just a part of it. Two main faults block that: text prompts land on the wrong areas, and features blur together.

VideoGrain works without new training, by tuning how the model pays attention across space and time. It boosts each local prompt on its own area and cuts cross-talk with other areas. It also helps each area keep its own traits. Tests on real scenes gave top results, the authors report.
arxiv-2502-17558:
Joao Barata and Enrique Rico simulate, in a 2025 physics paper, a high-energy probe smashing through dense matter in real time, mimicking what happens inside nuclear collision experiments. Their stage is a simplified one-dimensional version of quantum electrodynamics with mass.

Three regimes appear as target density grows. A thin target lets the probe fly nearly straight. A medium one lets it pass while stirring the matter locally. A dense one acts like a black wall that stops it cold. Energy loss grows in step with path length through the medium, and entanglement measures expose how probe and matter mix. The team also sketches a route to quantum simulators.
arxiv-2502-17958:
Wei Xun and co-authors show how stacking and strain can switch on exotic magnetism in flat materials in 2025, using team framing for the author list. A new magnet type splits spin states without net magnetism. That trait suits low power, fast devices. The team asks how layer stacking and strain steer such states.

Symmetry rules tie spin splitting to four symmetry patterns in layered stacks. Stacking alone can flip one test material from plain to exotic magnetism. It can also flip it from insulator to metal. Strain adds a bundle of piezo effects across charge, valley, and magnetism. Rich topology phases appear as well. The work gives design rules for spin and valley devices.
arxiv-2502-18158:
Mauricio Cruz Reyes, Richard Anderson, and Susmita Das cataloged in 2025 the pulsing stars known as Population II Cepheids in the Milky Way's globular clusters. These old stars swell and shrink in steady cycles, and their cycle length tracks their brightness, which makes them distance markers. The team sorted true members from look-alikes across the clusters.

Their final list holds eighty-eight confirmed stars and forty-four candidates. Most confirmed stars fit the known brightness pattern for their type, and matches with another major catalog agreed in nearly all shared cases. Sky survey catalogs miss a fair share of these stars in crowded clusters, the team warns.
arxiv-2502-18358:
Oliver Rice and Christopher Prior test what a neglected layer of the Sun's atmosphere does to models of solar eruptions, in a 2025 paper. Magnetic fields above sunspots are usually extrapolated upward from the surface, skipping the cool, dense chromosphere that lies between surface and corona. The layer is thin and hard to model, so it is often left out. The authors built driven simulations of an erupting active region with and without it.

Including the layer changed events far above it: eruptions came later and released more magnetic energy. A thin boundary layer steering a huge eruption is a warning to forecasters. Space weather predictions built on field models may need this layer after all, despite the modeling cost.
arxiv-2502-18558:
Sky surveys must sort fleeting events, like exploding stars, from huge data streams, and the next giant survey starts soon. Rithwik Gupta and co-authors show in this 2025 paper that old models can be retrained cheaply for new data through transfer learning. A sorter trained on simulated events from one survey was adapted to real events from the same survey.

The adapted model needed 95 percent fewer labeled real events to match a model trained from scratch. Moving the sorter to the coming LSST survey's simulated data kept 94 percent of baseline skill with only 30 percent of the data. The upshot: good sorting should be ready early in the new survey, not years in.
arxiv-2502-18658:
Programming assistants that wait to be asked are safe; ones that jump in may help or may derail. Kevin Pu and co-authors built Codellaborator, a probe agent that offers help based on what the programmer is doing. They tested three levels of boldness with eighteen users: prompt-only, proactive, and proactive with visible presence and context.

The proactive versions sped work up but also broke flow. Showing what the agent was doing and why repaired much of the damage. It also raised awareness of its process. The study weighs speed against control, ownership, and understanding, and argues that proactivity must adapt to how programmers actually work.
arxiv-2502-19058:
Hao Liang and co-authors build a test that checks whether AI can catch flaws in synthetic math data. Synthetic data now trains much math skill in large models, but flaws in the questions or worked answers rot its worth. Their 2025 set holds 2,000 sound questions, 2,000 flawed ones split by flaw kind, and 2,000 worked answers with flags. Each item was checked by hand.

The team ran 14 large models and three scoring models on the set. Even strong math models fell well short of a full score, most of all on fine flaw kinds. Math-tuned models did not beat plain ones at the audit task: skill at solving did not mean skill at checking. When flaw kinds were given as hints, fixes to bad items rose in a clear, firm way. The set aims to make synthetic data cleaner at the source.
arxiv-2502-19158:
Yijiang River Dong, Tiancheng Hu, Yinhong Liu, Ahmet Ustun, and Nigel Collier test tailored training for language models in a 2025 paper. Standard training from human likes assumes all users want the same thing. That hides the views of small groups and can skew what the model learns to favor.

Tailored methods train a taste profile for each user instead. The team built a test frame that grades not just skill but fairness, side effects, and flex as tastes split apart. Eight methods were run on three data sets. Score gaps reached 36 percent when users disagreed hard. Tailoring could also bend safety by up to 20 percent, a risk the frame helps catch.
arxiv-2502-19458:
Yue-Liang Wu builds a general theory that folds gravity into the standard model of particles through new spin based forces, in a solo work from 2025. The framework rests on a spin related spacetime with several gauge symmetries stacked together. New interactions appear, including forces tied to spin, chirality, and scale.

Gravity enters through an equation drawn from the non commuting derivative of that spacetime. The graviton appears as the field of a gauge force, and both gauge and geometric forms of the gravity equations are derived. A heavy new boson is cast as a dark particle candidate. The theory aims to reveal what the author calls the dark side of the universe.
arxiv-2502-19758:
Ashkan Soleymani, Behrooz Tahmasebi, Stefanie Jegelka, and Patrick Jaillet study how a learning model can respect exact symmetries in its data without slowing to a crawl, in a 2025 paper. Many tasks have built-in symmetries, such as rotations that should not change an answer. Older tricks either break the exactness or take too long, and some do not fit the kernel methods they study.

Given access to facts about the shape of the input space, their method learns in reasonable time and honors the symmetries exactly. Its error matches that of plain kernel learning without the symmetry demand. The proof draws on geometry, spectra, and optimization, and one side result may serve other problems.
arxiv-2502-20058:
Shining intense laser light into gas can multiply its frequency many times over, a process called high-order harmonic generation. Saga Westerberg and co-authors run the first systematic test in this 2025 paper of how the laser pulse's length affects the yield.

Using a compact cell that tunes pulse length while keeping everything else fixed, they swept from very short to moderate pulses. For each brightness there was a best length, and it was not always the shortest; dimmer light favored longer pulses. Simulations matched the pattern, blaming the interplay between the gas interaction and phase matching. The result explains old reports of the effect with very long pulses.
arxiv-2502-20158:
Yating Yu and co-authors tackle bias in open vocabulary action recognition in a 2025 paper. Models that start from a strong image text system can spot actions named in words, even new ones. Yet that starter model favors still cues, so video models lean on static shortcuts and fail on novel actions seen in new contexts.

Their framework, Open-MeDe, uses meta learning to improve generalizing from known to open classes and to debias image to video transfer at low cost. A cross batch scheme trains the model to adapt fast to later data, which smooths learning and eases static bias. Averaging over the training path gives final weights that hold up on both familiar and novel data.
arxiv-2502-20258:
Amr Mohamed and co-authors present a 2025 study on how language models distort facts over repeated passes. Models now write much of the web's content. Their outputs feed back as inputs for later text. The children's game of broken telephone shows how chained retelling warps a message. The team tests whether models warp facts the same way. Translation chains serve as the test bed.

Distortion grows with each round, as in the human game. Language choice and chain complexity steer how fast facts degrade. Prompt design can slow the decay, though not stop it. Content teams get a warning backed by tests: recycled model text drifts. Drift matters for news, summaries, and training data built from web text. The study gives the drift a name, a measure, and a partial brake.
arxiv-2502-20758:
The authors wrote a study from 2025 on whether a group of large language models can check each other's work. In most tests, answers are scored against a known right answer. For hard new work, no such key may exist. The team asked four well-known models to write and solve hard problems in chance and odds, at a level meant for advanced study.

They then used tests of group accord to see how much the models agreed with each other. Some models wrote clearer problems and agreed more with the group. One model varied more and agreed less with the rest. The team argues that accord among unlike models can flag which answers are more safe to trust. It can also help judge the worth of the problems themselves.
arxiv-2502-20858:
Xiaochuan Liu and co-authors teach a model to predict where a person will look while listening, in a 2025 paper. Most gaze research studies silent viewing: free browsing, searching, or answering questions about a picture. In daily life, though, ears guide eyes, and sounds pull attention across a scene. The team built a dataset for this audio-guided setting with twenty thousand gaze points from eight viewers.

Their framework, EyEar, blends three forces on the eye: its own tendency to keep moving as physics suggests, the pull of visually striking regions, and the pull of what the sound means. A new scoring method compares predicted gaze patterns against real ones fairly. Predicting listening gaze matters for virtual characters that should look alive, and for interfaces that follow attention without a camera on the eyes alone.
arxiv-2502-21058:
Vitor Ferreira, Érica Fornaroli, and Javier Sánchez read the base traits of free skew growths of rings, in a 2025 math paper. Such growths build wild term rings with many shift rules at once. When the growth stays whole, prime, or fits in chain rings was not yet set in one place.

Kind marks for the growth rings come in more than one form. Whole trait marks rest on the base ring and its shift rules. Chain fit marks join the set with their own tests in the work. Prime trait marks close the trait list for the growth kind. Ring staff gain a trait map for wild term builds.
arxiv-2502-21258:
Robin Heinonen, Luca Biferale, Antonio Celani, and Massimo Vergassola test how well Bayesian search strategies find a scent source in turbulent air, in this 2025 paper. The problem matters for flying insects and for machines that must track a leak or plume. Bayesian methods such as infotaxis are known to work well, but earlier tests assumed each whiff of scent was independent of the last.

The team simulated a turbulent flow and tracked particles released from a point source, under several strengths of steady wind. From the simulations they extracted how encounters with the scent spread through space, then built search policies on those statistics, including space-aware infotaxis variants and quasi-optimal policies. The quasi-optimal strategies still beat the heuristics when a steady wind blew, but not when the air was still. The authors also study how to set search parameters such as sampling rate and detection threshold.
arxiv-2503-00258:
Guangsheng Bao and co-authors wrote a 2025 paper on how to detect text that an artificial intelligence model helped to write. Existing detection studies are scattered, with no shared framework. The team first sets out a hierarchy of risk levels for AI involvement, from a light touch to a fully fabricated text. Each level forms its own detection task.

Their method splits a text into two parts: its content, meaning what it says, and its expression, meaning how it says it. They find that content stays stable when the expression is altered, which makes content a strong signal for detection. On the highest-level tests, their two-part method beat the best earlier detectors by a wide margin on a standard curve score. It also won on a well-known difficult test set. The team released their data and code for free reuse.
arxiv-2503-00358:
Smruti Dash, Kedar Khandeparkar and Nipun Agrawal wrote a 2025 paper on spotting cyber attacks on smart power grids with little labeled data. Digital controls make grids efficient but open to attack. Classic detectors need many labeled cases, which miss novel tricks. Their method learns from both labeled and unlabeled meter data.

It pairs consistency checks with self-labeling that weighs its own uncertainty. A staged teaching plan improves those self-labels over time. On public data sets, detection accuracy reached near ninety-nine percent even with unknown samples mixed in. False alarms dropped sharply as well. The team pitches the method for real grid defense.
arxiv-2503-00458: Thomas Rimbot, Martin Jaggi, and Luis Barba explore in a 2025 study how machine learning might serve sport climbing. They build a tool that shows move sequences on a given boulder problem so climbers can judge them. They then ask whether a model can predict the next moves from the holds alone, trying three transformer designs. Results so far are not conclusive, the team says, but the work is a first step for this kind of aid in climbing and lays ground for more.
arxiv-2503-00958:
Milad Alshomary and co-authors identify authors by reading every layer of a transformer, not just its final one. Their 2025 paper tackles authorship attribution, deciding who wrote a text. Different layers of these models capture different linguistic signals, from surface habits to deeper style, and most systems throw most of them away.

The full-layer approach was tested on three data sets, in-domain and out-of-domain. Using all layers made the attributions much more robust when the test text came from a new domain, setting new best results. The layer-by-layer analysis also shows which stylistic features live where, a map of how machines internalize a writer's voice.
arxiv-2503-01258:
Osamura and co-authors test how coupling between layers shapes skyrmion crystals in 2025. Skyrmions are tiny swirls of magnetic spin. In some crystals they pack into a neat lattice. The team studies a stacked triangle lattice with frustrated spin links, using large Monte Carlo runs.

They try both aligned and opposed coupling between the layers. The skyrmion crystal stays stable at finite fields and warmth in both cases. Weak opposed coupling, though, makes it less stable. The phase map looks much like maps for flat models and for long-range models. One glass-like effect seen in a long-range model does not appear here. That gap hints that long-range links may be needed for that effect to arise.
arxiv-2503-01658:
Youngbin Choi and co-authors present a way to tailor language models to each user in a 2025 paper. People want unlike things from the same model, yet learning each person's taste from few ratings is hard. Their method, called CoPL, borrows an idea from film and shopping sites: learn from patterns across users.

A graph links users to the replies they liked, which helps guess tastes even when ratings are sparse. Small expert modules are mixed to balance shared taste with each person's own bent. New users can be served with no fresh training at all. Tests on a feedback data set beat prior tailored reward models.
arxiv-2503-02058:
Dana Rubin and co-authors introduce a model that designs RNA molecules together with their three-dimensional shapes, in a 2025 paper. RNA carries messages, catalyzes reactions, and regulates genes. Designing new RNA could unlock therapies and biotech tools. Most generators produce either the letter sequence or the shape, not both at once.

Their model, RiboGen, generates the two together. It pairs flow methods for continuous shapes with a discrete version for letters. Its network respects three-dimensional symmetry, so rotations do not confuse it. Samples came out chemically plausible and self-consistent. Designing sequence and structure in one pass may beat pipelines that bolt the two steps together.
arxiv-2503-02258:
Phones and laptops pull attention out of the room, and wearable augmented reality could either deepen that pull or heal it. Tram Thi Minh Tran, the sole author, studies her own technology habits for four weeks to find out what presence feels like in daily life. Twenty experiences with phones, laptops, and fitness trackers were documented in varied settings.

The first-person record reveals fine-grained patterns: some uses scatter attention, others anchor it. From those patterns the author draws design lessons for wearable AR. The key idea is personalized, context-aware nudges that return the wearer to the physical surroundings. The study joins the digital well-being debate with lived detail. It argues AR should be judged by whether it reconnects people to where they are.
arxiv-2503-02358:
Xinyu Wang, Bohan Zhuang, and Qi Wu test vision-language models as game players in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Standard benchmarks, like image question answering, miss many skills these models need. Games instead demand perception, rule following, and multi-step reasoning in a structured setting.

Their framework sorts play into four tasks: perceiving the scene, answering questions, following rules, and playing end to end. Extensive experiments expose current limits. Models stumble on long, structured outputs and on dense visual detail. The authors release code and data in public. They argue game play gives a fuller picture of model cognition than static benchmarks.
arxiv-2503-02658:
Inge Helland argues that quantum style probabilities deserve a place in ordinary statistics, in a paper from 2025. The catalog title adds a running head note. New work on quantum foundations rests on postulates that, the author claims, also make sense for large scale settings, and one such approach is laid out in depth.

The reasoning behind the Born rule, which assigns the probabilities, is presented for that framework. A list of possible statistical uses is given and discussed. One sketched idea uses a quantum model to shrink complex models, with a classic regression method appearing as a special case. Decision theory built on quantum probability is also covered.
arxiv-2503-02958:
Dylan Huson and co-authors reprocessed starlight data for 220 million stars from the Gaia mission, in a 2025 paper. Their model reads each star's spectrum and returns its heat and surface gravity across a huge range, from cool young stars to hot giants. For the first time, it handles stars not yet settled into adult life, and its gravity readings can hint at their ages.

Scanning the nearby young stars, the team found a new group of more than a thousand stars east of the Scorpius-Centaurus region. The group, named Ophion, is already falling apart, with members drifting without shared motion. Better ages for nearby stars may rebuild the recent birth history of our corner of the galaxy.
arxiv-2503-03158:
Thanh-Dat Nguyen and co-authors wrote this 2025 systematic survey on debugging machine learning systems. ML software breaks in ways ordinary software does not, thanks to its probabilistic guts and mixed pipelines of data, training, and code. Many fixes have been proposed, yet no map showed which faults the field actually tackles.

The team gathered the technical literature and sorted each paper by the fault it targets and the technique it uses. The result is a taxonomy pairing fault types with the debugging methods built for them. Interviews with developers then exposed the faults nobody has fixed yet. One headline finding: only about forty-eight percent of the fault space has drawn real research attention. The survey closes by pointing at the neglected gaps.
arxiv-2503-03358:
Buchbinder and co-authors compute a high order correction in a supersymmetric model in this 2025 paper. The model, the massless Wess-Zumino model, is a basic testing ground for supersymmetry. The quantity they chase is the chiral effective potential, a function that encodes the model's low energy behavior.

A famous non-renormalisation theorem bans diverging corrections to this potential. In the massless case, though, finite corrections survive, and the team computes them at three loops. Only three supergraphs contribute to the pure chiral part. Two come out finite on their own, and the third needs only a one loop counterterm tied to field renormalisation. The result gives a rare exact handle on how the model's low energy behavior shifts at high order.
arxiv-2503-03558:
Yuna Kato and five co-authors automate the camera alignment behind a clever surgical video system. Several cameras ride on the surgical light so that at least one sees past the surgeons' hands and heads. But every time the light moves, the cameras' geometry changes, and someone must realign the feeds by hand.

Their algorithm detects the frames where the light is moving, recalibrates the cameras geometrically, and picks the least occluded view moment by moment. The output is a stable virtual single-viewpoint video of the operative field. Quantitative comparisons beat conventional approaches, and a user study with medical doctors confirmed the improvement. The goal is occlusion-free surgical video without a technician in the loop.
arxiv-2503-03858:
Informal currency markets can be read as limit order books, Alejandro García Figal, Alejandro Lage Castellanos, and Roberto Mulet show in a 2025 study. The case is the Cuban informal currency market. The authors scraped data from websites and social media about bid and ask intentions in that market, then modeled those intentions with the standard microstructure tool.

That frame lets them study liquidity, stability, and volume profiles. They then use the Avellaneda-Stoikov model to explore what a market maker would do in this informal setting. Adding such a maker improved the quality of the market in their analysis, lifting its structure and bid-ask dynamics. The findings may help policymakers who must intervene in informal markets with limited resources.
arxiv-2503-04158:
Telling whether two quantum particles are entangled, linked in a way no classical pair can be, often relies on test gadgets called entanglement witnesses. Dariusz Chruściński and co-authors study a paired form of these tests in this 2025 paper. A recent paper had guessed that no pair of top-quality tests could both catch the subtlest kind of entanglement, the kind that survives a partial flip.

The authors show such a mirrored pair does exist for two multi-level particles. Both tests are optimal and both catch that bound entanglement. The construction also stretches to higher dimensions. The result uncovers new structure in how these witnesses fit together, against the earlier guess. It sharpens the toolkit for certifying quantum links.
arxiv-2503-04458:
Graham and Weigel count the quantum tax on lone waves of unlike twist loads, in a study from 2025. A soliton is a lump of field that holds its shape; its twist load is a whole count of how the field winds. Past its plain mass, void shake adds a tax, the top quantum fix.

For two-part lumps in one space span, both mass and tax grow in straight lines with the twist load, with a small fixed step each. That step pair rules the bind: by the stuff's marks, all high-load lumps bind, or none do. The straight law holds even when lumps smear far from lone form, a fact hid from bound-state reads alone.
arxiv-2503-04558:
Alexander Chen, Martin Luepker, and Yajie Yuan introduce Aperture, a simulation framework for plasma near black holes, in this 2025 paper. Around dim galactic centers, thin hot plasma is best modeled by tracking particles directly, which demands heavy computing. Aperture runs that particle method on graphics processors and respects Einstein's gravity.

The paper details its particle pusher, field solver, and charge-keeping schemes, with tests for each. The team then simulates spark gaps in the magnetic zone of a black hole. Where a gap seems to sit, and how it evolves, depends on the observer, a result that settles clashes between earlier one- and two-dimensional studies.
arxiv-2503-04758:
Sasa Maric, Sonja Maric, and Lana Maric examine ChatGPT as an education revolution in a 2025 paper. AI tools are entering every facet of life at speed. Education faces claims of total transformation from such tools. Entire courses could in principle be built and graded by AI.

The paper weighs practical impacts on learning and thinking skills. Course design, assignments, and feedback could all run faster with AI. Dynamic fields like computer science suit continuously updated material. New disciplines may emerge while old degree models face challenge. Positives and negatives are examined across applications. Problem solving and cognitive ability effects get special attention. The authors treat adoption as a critical step toward a new era. Their stance is largely welcoming with noted caveats. Educators gain a survey of stakes and scenarios.
arxiv-2503-04858:
Kejia Chen and co-authors present a self-teaching method to align vision-language models in this 2025 paper. Such models are steered by training on triplets: an image, a better answer, and a worse answer. Human-made preference data are diverse-poor and costly, which limits how well models can be aligned.

Their framework, called SHAPE, turns plain image-text pairs into preference triplets with no human labels. For each pair, varied views of the image are joined with a summary text to form the winning answer, while the original text serves as the loser. The model then improves in rounds. Tests across twelve benchmarks and several model families show clear gains, the authors report.
arxiv-2503-05158:
Ruisong Xia, Hao Liu, and Yongquan Xue track how a famous flicker in a distant galaxy's X-ray glow swells and fades on short timescales. Their 2025 paper studies RE J1034+396, the galaxy with the strongest known X-ray quasi-periodic oscillation. Long-term drift of the signal was known; its quick swings inside one sitting were not.

The team gathered twelve long telescope sittings and ran a wavelet analysis on them. The signal's strength pulsed in both soft and hard X-rays on a scale of about 17,000 seconds. When the hard-band flicker showed, the soft glow ran clearly higher, and the two tracked each other with a short lag. The lag itself shifted across sittings. The authors read the tie as a link between the soft and hard parts of the corona.
arxiv-2503-05458:
Designing a fresh peptide that binds a chosen protein can speed drug discovery, but the search spans both chemistry and shape at once. Lars Meuser, Alexandros Patsilinakos, and Pietro Faccioli take a physics-based route in this 2025 paper, with no training data at all. Their multi-scale framework mixes classical computing with a quantum annealer, a machine built for hard searches.

The annealer quickly proposed varied candidate binders for several protein targets, atom by atom. The proposed chains and their binding poses matched experiments well. The authors say this shows that even today's early quantum machines can power physics-based drug design. The approach aims to cut the cost and time of finding new peptide drugs from scratch.
arxiv-2503-05658:
Manuel Morales-Alvarado and co-authors analyze scientific output in high energy, cosmology, and particle astrophysics across Latin America. The study uses the field's open INSPIRE database for its records. Seven decades of regional research enter the analysis.

Output growth is compared with the rest of the world. Country tables cover papers, citations, and researcher counts. Impact is weighed against population and research spending. Development levels add further context to the rankings. Team patterns within the region and abroad are mapped. The gender gap in the field is tracked over time. The report gives funders a rare regional evidence base. It also spotlights rising groups across the continent.
arxiv-2503-05858:
Jiachen Luo, Huy Phan, Lin Wang and Joshua Reiss wrote a 2025 paper on reading emotion from speech by fusing sound and text. Subtle feeling shifts are hard to catch from either channel alone. Their method stacks three modules. One models how the two channels connect, using an encoder-decoder shape.

A second module sharpens what each channel adds to the other. A third trims cross-channel noise while keeping true correlations. Two standard emotion data sets hosted the tests. The fused system beat the best prior baselines on both. The authors credit the layered attention design for the gain.
arxiv-2503-05958:
Guzman-Olivares, Quijano-Sanchez, and Liberatore present in 2025 a light method to pick the right sense of a word from its context. Large chat models still lag humans at such sense judgments, which matter for sound reasoning. Their frame recasts the task as telling clusters apart in a meaning network.

The network is refined from a public sense bank with group algebra tools. Tests across many sense benchmarks gave top scores for all languages and tasks in their account. Gains held for single word classes and for low resource languages. The model also used far fewer parameters than rivals, which cuts cost for wide use.
arxiv-2503-06358:
Idan Shenfeld, Felix Faltings, Pulkit Agrawal, and Aldo Pacchiano wrote a 2025 paper on tuning language models to each user. Most training with human feedback assumes all users want the same thing. That leaves no room for tastes that differ from one person to the next, which the authors set out to change.

Their method treats each user's reward as a mix of a few base reward parts. With about ten replies from a user, the method can guess that user's mix and shape the model's replies to match. Tests with made up and real users showed a clear gain. In human checks, their replies won against plain GPT-4o replies two times out of three.
arxiv-2503-06858:
The Starobinsky model is a leading account of inflation, the rapid expansion thought to have shaped the early universe. Subhendra Mohanty, Sukanta Panda, and Archit Vidyarthi showed in 2025 that the model makes a testable prediction. Its extra scalar field, the scalaron, decays into gravitons during reheating, and that decay uses a coupling fixed by the model with no free choices.

The decay fills the universe with gravitational waves at very high frequencies, far above what current detectors hear. Resonant cavities that convert gravitons to photons could reach that band, the authors argue. Detecting such waves would give direct evidence for this inflation model, a rare chance to test ideas about the universe's first moments.
arxiv-2503-06958:
Chihiro Oguri and Mao Shinoda study a math question about patterns on a grid in a 2025 paper. They look at the hard square shift, a set of grid patterns with a ban on some neighbors. The question is whether the best patterns stay best when the scoring rule changes a little.

In one dimension, such stability is known to hold. In two dimensions, a past case based on Robinson tiling showed it can fail. Oguri and Shinoda study a nearest-neighbor system with a helpful filling property and positive variety. Their main result shows stability does hold there, which helps map where the two-dimensional case differs.
arxiv-2503-07358:
Yiqing Xie and co-authors published a computing paper in 2025 on building testable coding environments at the level of whole code repositories. Checking generated code needs running feedback, but building whole repositories is hard for humans and models alike. Their method, RepoST, isolates a target function and its needs into a separate script for sandbox testing. That cut in complexity allows scale.

With it they built a training set of thousands of functions from hundreds of repositories. Training on its feedback raised scores on two code benchmarks. They also built an evaluation set and benchmarked a dozen code models. The authors offer both sets as resources for repository-level generation.
arxiv-2503-07458:
Lajos Diosi, writing alone, offers a 2025 paper on a proposed test of whether gravity is classical or quantum. A hybrid equation that joins quantum motion with classical gravity is known to break causality, the rule that effects cannot outrun their causes. In cosmology that flaw is often set aside, but lab tests of the equation are now within reach.

Diosi cites a simple proof that neither classical nor quantum dynamics can be nonlinear under their standard readings. He then shows that a planned light-based experiment would predict a fake action at a distance on a single probe. The planned test may thus probe the causality flaw directly.
arxiv-2503-07658:
Zuhair Al-Johar writes on set theory in a short 2025 paper about Cantorian and non-Cantorian sets. The work sits inside a system called NF, a version of set theory with its own rules for which sets exist.

In that system, a set is called Cantorian when it behaves in a certain well-behaved way with respect to counting. From outside the system, the two kinds of sets match in number, so a simple count cannot settle which kind is more common. Al-Johar sets out a plain test for phrasing the question inside the system, where the key term is hard to define. Under that test, he proves there are more non-Cantorian sets than Cantorian ones.
arxiv-2503-07758:
Tomasz Romanczukiewicz and Yakov Shnir wrote a 2025 physics paper on quasi Q-balls, lump like waves that leak energy as they live. A Q-ball is a stable ball of field held by a conserved charge. Here the setting has no mass threshold, so the lumps radiate and decay over long spans.

Two models are compared. One reshapes the standard Q-ball potential in a rational way. The other traps the lump in a box with walls that let waves out. Both lumps decay alike at first. In the last stage they split: the boxed lump turns into a linear resonance, while the reshaped model lump fades by a power law. Wall rules also shift the lump spin rate into complex values.
arxiv-2503-08358:
Md Faizal Karim and co-authors release, in 2025, a large dataset for robots that grasp with two arms. Two arms are needed for big objects that demand stable, coordinated holds, yet training data for that setting was scarce. Their set holds sixteen million dual-arm grasps, each checked under sharpened force rules.

A benchmark adds three hundred objects with about thirty thousand grasps tested in a physics simulator. That gives a fairer way to judge grasp quality than geometry alone. A classifier trained on the data beat leading methods by a clear margin, with higher success and better generalization to new objects. The resource targets a gap in robot manipulation research.
arxiv-2503-08558:
Robots trained by imitation can fail in ways nobody rehearsed, and catching the failure live is hard when no failure examples exist for training. Chen Xu and co-authors take on that problem in a 2025 paper. Their system, FAIL-Detect, learns only from successful demonstrations.

The method squeezes the inputs and outputs of the policy into scalar signals that track failure and uncertainty. It then treats detection as spotting out-of-distribution moments in that signal stream over time. A second stage applies conformal-style statistics to call the failures. The modular design separates signal building from detection, so parts can be swapped. The authors aim at trustworthy deployment of robot policies around people, where a missed failure can hurt someone.
arxiv-2503-09058:
Machines can learn visual features without labels by matching two views of the same image, but such systems risk collapse, where every image maps to the same point. Byeongchan Lee and Sehyun Lee work in the positive-only family of methods, which dodge collapse through lopsided networks: a source encoder that learns and a target encoder that follows. They ask whether the contrast idea can live inside that design.

Their answer is guided stop-gradient, a tweak that quietly builds contrastive pressure into the asymmetric setup without needing negative examples. Applied to two benchmark methods, SimSiam and BYOL, the tweak steadied training and lifted performance. It also kept learning stable with small batches, and the networks did not collapse even when the usual predictor part was removed. The authors present the method as a simple addition that makes self-supervised training hardier.
arxiv-2503-09258:
Guilherme Almeida, writing alone, offers a 2025 math paper on equations that govern certain curved spaces used in physics. These spaces carry a rich structure tied to quantum theory and to systems that can be solved exactly. A set of equations, extended to cover cases with a boundary, frames that structure.

Almeida starts from spaces built over Hurwitz spaces, which catalog branched covers of a sphere. He uses a known recipe that assigns a special function to each such space. His result shows that parts of those functions obey the extended equations. The method gives a fast route to the equations for any space of this family.
arxiv-2503-09358:
Jiushen Cai and co-authors present language models that standardise clinical reports of fundus eye images, in work from 2025. Eye doctors' reports vary in format, terms, and style, which blocks data integration and confuses automated systems. The team built a bilingual standard terminology for eye findings and common clinical descriptions.

Their first model was fine-tuned on an augmented dataset that simulates clinic scenarios and learned strong standardising behaviour, but covered a narrow disease range. A second model was then trained on standardised data generated by the first, plus matched English data, covering far more cases. It achieved report-level standardisation for the first time in this setting. In tests, it beat rival language models on the bilingual task. Model checkpoints are public.
arxiv-2503-09458:
Viktor Harangi settles a conjecture on splitting the edges of random regular graphs into star-shaped pieces, in a paper from 2025. A k-star is a bundle of k edges that share one vertex. A decomposition covers every edge with such stars, no overlaps and no gaps.

One clear bar exists: a decomposition needs a large independent set, a set of vertices with no edges between them. Two thresholds frame the question, one from that bar and one from where decompositions truly exist. A past conjecture held that the two thresholds match. Harangi proves it for large degree: decompositions exist for all k above half the degree and below the independent-set bar, and even at the bar for most degrees.
arxiv-2503-09858:
Nataliya Balabanova and co-authors model how media coverage shapes whether AI gets governed well, in a 2025 paper. Four actors interact: developers, regulators, users, and the press. Using game theory about how strategies spread, plus runs acted out by language models, the team tested what happens under different rule regimes. Two levers stood out: reporting that rewards good oversight, and user trust that follows commentators' advice.

Sharp reporting, they find, can act as soft oversight, probing developers or watchdogs where formal rules are absent. Both the math and the model runs show trustworthy AI emerging only under the right mix of rewards and costs. Good commentary is not free, and its price matters. The authors conclude that governing AI well means managing commentators' rewards too.
arxiv-2503-09958:
