Liu and six colleagues propose Progressive In-Context Alignment for language models in twenty twenty-five. In-context learning teaches a model a task from examples in the prompt. How those examples shape token representations was unclear for alignment tasks. The team finds the learned task function is stored in the separator token.

Once the first response tokens are set, the examples become redundant, they show. Their method first runs a few shot stage and extracts that stored vector. A zero shot stage then uses the vector alone to guide generation. No further examples are needed in that stage. Tests beat standard in-context learning and matched tuning based alignment methods. The training free method also cut time cost in their experiments.
arxiv-2503-10358:
Zirun Guo and Tao Jin present a 2025 paper on teaching image generators one personal concept after another without wrecking what came before. Tools that learn a pet or a face from a few photos usually train on all concepts at once. In real use, concepts arrive in sequence, and later training can erase or blur earlier ones.

Their system, ConceptGuard, fights both failures with three tools: shifted embeddings, prompts that bind each concept to its own token, and a penalty that guards old knowledge. A priority queue tracks how important and how recent each concept is. Across wide tests, the authors report clear wins over all rival methods on both numbers and sample images.
arxiv-2503-10758:
Mohamad Shalaby, Antoine Bret, and Federico Fraschetti simulate shocks in magnetized space plasma in a 2025 paper. In such shocks, particles rather than collisions do the work of slowing a supersonic flow, and these fronts light up supernova remnants and other cosmic sites.

Running a one-dimensional particle code, the team varied the field strength that ions feel. Strongly magnetized shocks compressed less, heated unevenly in a stable pattern, and accelerated fewer particles. Weakly magnetized shocks, by contrast, spawned downstream instabilities from that uneven heating. This first part of a series maps how magnetism governs the physics of the shock jump itself.
arxiv-2503-11158: Ulrich Jentschura studies the tiny energy shifts that radiation imprints on an electron circling in a strong magnetic field, in a paper from 2025. These are quantum cyclotron states, the levels of an electron bound in a trap. He shows, by direct calculation, that the leading radiative correction is the same for every level. It does not depend on which state the electron sits in. So the shift is better read as a change to the electron's mass itself. The field inside the Penning trap sets its size.
arxiv-2503-11258:
The black hole at our galaxy's core flickers fast, while its spiral shroud stays calm, and that calm can calibrate the flicker. Ezequiel Albentosa-Ruiz, Iván Martí-Vidal, Ciriaco Goddi, and Alejandro Mus build that trick in a 2025 report. Their data come from the ALMA radio array.

Steps run from a first image, to shroud-only maps, to a two-part fit per time slice. The fit returns the core's flux at each moment. Brightness curves follow for total, polarized, and circular light. One April 2018 run shows the method at work. The script runs inside the field's standard CASA package.
arxiv-2503-11358:
Mihalchenko and Novikov present a method for pulling faint cosmic signals out of messy foreground glow in this 2025 paper. The cosmic microwave background carries tiny spectral distortions that encode early universe physics. Foreground sources blur those signals with shapes that are hard to pin down.

Their Least Response Method cuts response to all plausible foregrounds at once. It also keeps the response to the true signal fixed and trims photon noise. Tests against a known map-cleaning method show clear gains. The team also find the best operating temperature for the telescope optics. Cleaner spectra would sharpen tests of how the early universe cooled and heated.
arxiv-2503-12158:
Optimal control of a noisy system whose state depends on the whole crowd's average behavior is a hard math problem. Bowen He, Juan Li, and Zhanxin Li study it in this 2025 paper, for equations where the usual smoothness demands are weakened to a monotonicity condition. Both the dynamics and the cost take mean-field form, depending on the state's distribution.

The authors derive the stochastic maximum principle, a necessary condition that any best control must meet, for a convex set of controls. With extra convexity on the Hamiltonian, they prove the condition is also sufficient. Along the way they settle existence and uniqueness for the related mean-field equations, and they give examples showing their results reach beyond earlier work.
arxiv-2503-12258:
Myisha Chowdhury and co-authors stretch scarce battery data with a generative model in a 2025 paper on predicting lithium-ion capacity. Knowing how a battery will fade matters for safety, but cycling batteries to death for training data is slow and expensive, and much data stays locked away.

Their recurrent conditional generative adversarial network invents realistic extra charge-discharge histories, conditioned on the capacity level so the fake data ages correctly. Memory-based generator and judge networks learn the time patterns in the signals. Across six batteries from two public benchmark sets, training on the enriched data improved capacity forecasts over using the raw records alone.
arxiv-2503-12358:
In-Chang Baek and four co-authors presented IPCGRL in twenty twenty-five, a method for generating game levels from written instructions using reinforcement learning. Designers increasingly want generative tools they can steer with plain language. Their system pairs a learning agent with a sentence embedding model that turns instructions into compact task codes.

Fine-tuning the embeddings for the task sharpens how level conditions are packed into those codes. On a two-dimensional level generation task, IPCGRL improved controllability by up to about twenty-one percent over a general-purpose embedding method. It also handled unseen instructions better, gaining about seventeen percent in generalization. The approach widens the kinds of input a procedural generation system can take, promising a more flexible dialogue between designer and generator.
arxiv-2503-12458:
Luc Scharenberg and co-authors report first results from pairing a pixel chip called Timepix4 with gas-based particle detectors, in work from 2025. The chip has a large active area and links through its back, so chips can tile four sides with no dead gaps. That pairing opens new options for tracking particles.

With one detector type, the team sorted events by shape, took X-ray pictures, and gauged energy and timing at once. In parallel, they built the chip into a second detector frame that boosts the signal. Early bench tests of the build went well. The paper reports the state of the wiring and tests, plus model studies of how signals form in the device.
arxiv-2503-12758:
Zhifeng Wang, Renjiao Yi, Xin Wen, Chenyang Zhu, and Kai Xu present a model that creates angiography images without contrast dye. Their 2025 paper tackles a trade-off: dye makes blood vessels visible for diagnosis, but it brings extra radiation and health risks for some patients.

Earlier methods worked slice by slice and broke the continuity of vessels in three dimensions. Their model builds a state space that follows the tree shape of vessels, then joins it with a diffusion generator. A pre-trained vision tool helps keep vessel structure consistent across scan types. Tests on varied angiographic data sets checked the approach. Clean synthetic angiography could spare patients dye exposure while keeping the vessel maps doctors rely on.
arxiv-2503-12858:
Duke Nguyen, Aditya Joshi, and Flora Salim adapt language understanding models to dialects at test time in a 2025 study. Models are usually trained on standard American English, then judged on Indian, Singaporean, or Nigerian English, whose grammar and vocabulary shift noticeably. Labeled dialect data are scarce, so retraining for each variety is impractical.

Test-time adaptation adjusts the model using only the unlabeled inputs it is currently reading. That makes it attractive for dialect settings, where new text arrives with its variety baked in. The authors test how far such adaptation closes the dialect gap on understanding tasks, a fairness question for global English tools.
arxiv-2503-12958:
Yunbo Li, Jiaping Gui, and Yue Wu add explainable privacy to federated learning in a 2025 paper. The head title names the method FedSVA. Federated learning trains a shared model across many devices without pooling raw data. Differential privacy adds noise to shield each person's data, but blind noise wastes accuracy. Their idea is to set the noise by each attribute's true influence.

Shapley values, a fair-share measure from game theory, score how much each attribute drives training. Attributes with more influence get noise tuned to their weight. The authors prove the scheme keeps its privacy promise and that training settles. On two image data sets, the method gave the best balance of privacy and accuracy among rivals. It also resisted attacks that try to rebuild private images from the model.
arxiv-2503-13158:
Bernd Zimmering and co-authors presented this 2025 paper on modeling systems pushed by an outside force. Such forced systems show up in engineering, finance, and nature, and their response mixes inner motion with the push itself. Delays between push and response make the modeling harder still.

The team propose Laplace-Net, a neural method that uses the Laplace transform to split the problem into parts. Inner dynamics, outside inputs, and starting values are handled apart, which makes the model easier to read and reuse. When the forcing changes, the model can be retrained quickly for the new signal. On eight test data sets, it beat leading rivals on accuracy and held up on inputs it had never seen.
arxiv-2503-13658:
José Antonio Nájera and Harry Desmond ask in 2025 whether ways of measuring distance in space agree with each other. Such measures do not rely on redshift, and they support much work on galaxies. The authors build a test that checks measures of the same galaxy against each other, using a large NASA database.

Of the methods they could test, only a small share gave results that matched their own past work and the work of others. A few methods, such as those based on masers and some bright stars, did well. The authors also check Cepheid measures and find no hidden error there, while warning that many methods still need work.
arxiv-2503-14158:
Eduardo Abi Jaber and a co-author present a new model for how market volatility bends and moves, in this 2025 finance paper. Traders read risk from the smile, the curve that option prices trace across strike prices. A good model must match that curve for stocks and for volatility bets at once. It must also match how sticky the curve is as prices shift.

Their model writes volatility as a fifth-degree formula built on two hidden drivers. Each driver drifts back toward its mean at its own speed, yet both follow the same market shocks. The authors show it fits surface data for the SPX index and the VIX across terms from days to over two years. It also copies a known quirk where past moves shape later swings.
arxiv-2503-14358:
Chao Wang, Giulio Franzese, Alessandro Finamore, and Pietro Michiardi study a mismatch problem in AI image making, in this 2025 paper. Rectified flow models draw pictures from text prompts, and they lead the field. Still, their images often get details wrong: colors land on the wrong object, counts go astray, or items sit in the wrong place.

The team built RFMI, a tool that gauges how much a picture and its prompt share, using the image model itself rather than outside helpers. They then fine-tuned a model on its own outputs, keeping only pictures with high shared scores. Tests on a mid-size public model showed better prompt match while picture quality held steady. Since no extra data sets or scoring models are needed, the recipe could transfer to other flow-based image tools.
arxiv-2503-14858:
Kevin Wang and co-authors scale self-taught robot learning by stacking networks a thousand layers deep, in work from 2025. In this setup, no rewards or demos are given. The agent must explore on its own and learn to reach goals it is told. Most past work used shallow nets of two to five layers.

Depth up to over a thousand layers lifted scores on a contrast-based method by two to fifty times. Gains beat other goal-based rivals on fake walking and handling tasks. Depth did more than raise scores: the moves the agents learned changed in kind. The team shares code and a project page for the work.
arxiv-2503-15358:
Thomas Pickard and co-authors present a shared task in a 2025 paper on idiom understanding across text and images. Idioms mean more than their words say, and models still stumble over them. The task, part of a yearly evaluation workshop, asks systems to read idioms in both words and pictures and in several languages.

Teams faced two sub tasks: rank images by how well they match an idiom's true or literal sense, and predict the next image in a sequence. The best entries reached human level scores. Winning recipes joined large pre trained language and vision models in expert mixtures, with repeated queries to smooth over weak spots. The data sets stay public for future work.
arxiv-2503-15558:
A large team from NVIDIA presents models that reason about the physical world and pick next steps for robots in plain words, in a paper from 2025. Body bound smart systems must see a scene, grasp how it works, and act in long chains. The models are trained to think in long word chains that end in a clear move call.

The team first lays out what such thought must hold, split into world sense and body choice. World sense is ranked in a tree of space, time, and force facts. Body choice is laid on two axes that span tasks from grip to route. Trained models score well on tests of both kinds. The authors share the build as a base for robot thought.
arxiv-2503-16158:
Shenbin Qian and three co-authors craft tricky Chinese test words to probe whether translation quality checkers really protect emotional tone. User-generated content often carries feelings that a translation should preserve. Emotion-focused evaluation models exist, but their robustness had not been stress-tested.

The method generates emotion-related homophones, words that sound alike but differ in writing and meaning, guided by self-information from information theory. These homophones were observed to trigger emotion-losing translation errors. Human judges rated the generated words, and the new method matched their judgments better than an existing generator. The team then used the words, with manual translations, to perturb texts and expose weaknesses in evaluation models.
arxiv-2503-16358:
Nicholas Fleming-Vázquez measures how fast a chaos theorem kicks in in this two thousand twenty-five paper. The weak invariance principle says wild deterministic motion, watched long enough, mimics random wandering. Knowing the limit is not enough; users need the error at finite times. Fleming-Vázquez proves error rates for maps that stretch unevenly, losing grip in places. The observables can point in several dimensions at once.

Models include the famous Sinai billiard and certain smooth chaotic systems. The rate follows a clean power law in the time span. Even some slow-mixing invertible maps, long left out, are covered. The work grows out of the author's doctoral thesis. Dynamicists and probabilists share the audience.
arxiv-2503-16558:
Micky Nnamdi and co-authors report a three year trial of problem led learning for biomedical engineering in the age of smart software, in a paper from 2025. The method, built on real problems, has shaped the field since the early years of this century. Merging deep training in smart tools into set courses is hard, thanks to mixed student roots, scarce mentors, and private health data.

The trial ran from 2021 to 2023 with close to two hundred fifty students at a joint program of two large schools. Teams tackled true health data problems in mixed groups. Gains showed in sixteen student papers, warm peer marks, and fresh methods for real tasks. The authors map a path that other departments can scale.
arxiv-2503-16758:
Robin Ming Chen, Feimin Huang, Dehua Wang, and Difan Yuan study whether sharp flow boundaries in elastic materials hold up under small disturbances. Their 2025 math paper concerns vortex sheets, surfaces where a compressible flow slides past itself. The setting is three-dimensional elastic flow, where the material also stretches and springs back.

Earlier work showed weak forms of stability for such sheets. The team now tackles the full nonlinear problem. They isolate outgoing wave modes into a closed system and build energy bounds despite a loss of smoothness. A key insight is that the non-parallel stretch of the material restores control at the boundary. Tricky spots where wave roots and poles collide get a refined treatment.
arxiv-2503-16958:
Kim, Kwon, and Baek wrote in twenty twenty-five about simulation methods for active particles that respect thermodynamics. Active particles power their own motion and form dissipative structures. Finite-size effects in such systems are strong, so efficient simulation matters. The challenge is discretizing space and time without breaking the physics. They propose two kinetic Monte Carlo methods for active lattice gases. Both reproduce the correct continuous dynamics in the limit.

One method follows conventional Kawasaki-style updates. The other adds a state-dependent factor to the jump rates. That factor captures self-propulsion speed more accurately in their tests. Error shrank linearly as the time step shrank. At high activity the improved method gained accuracy by a squared factor. Proofs and extensive simulations support the claims. The tools should help study energy costs of active matter.
arxiv-2503-17058:
Gunjan Yadav and co-authors study single photon scattering in 2025 in a topological waveguide tied to a driven atom system. The atom has a three-level shape, like the Greek letter lambda. Such setups can act as switches for single photons, a key part for quantum networks.

The team works out a formula for how much light passes through, for three points where the atom can attach. At two points the result does not depend on topology, while joint attachment does. With a weak control field the system acts as a perfect mirror in all cases. As the field grows, the pass window splits in known patterns. The joint case adds a sharp Fano shape, fit for a tunable switch or a fine sensor.
arxiv-2503-17358:
Jerred Chen and Ronald Clark turn motion blur, the smear in fast-moving shots, into a clue for how the camera moved. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Robots and headsets often lose track of position when the camera swings fast. Standard pose tools fail on blurred frames.

From one blurred image, their model predicts a full flow field and a depth map. A least-squares step then turns those outputs into the camera's speed and spin. The result acts like a reading from a motion sensor chip. To train the model, they built a large set of shots with fake blur drawn from real indoor scans. Fine-tuning on real footage sharpened it further. On real tests it beat leading rivals at gauging both swing and drift.
arxiv-2503-17858:
Jack Buttcane verifies in 2025 a set of conjectures about special functions tied to the group of four by four invertible matrices. The functions, of Bessel type, arise in number theory and harmonic analysis. A prior paper set out the expected pattern for the general case, and this one checks it for the first hard case.

Most of the conjectures hold in general for this size. Two fail for single special elements. One interchange of integrals claim looks false in its strong form, though a weak form is proved. For another element, the standard series solutions may not span all solutions of the equations. Buttcane discusses what sharpening of the growth theorem would fix the identification, and proves the needed forms in the exceptional cases.
arxiv-2503-18058:
Minghao Li and Ling Yang wrote this 2025 mathematics paper on the sorting of special curved surfaces inside compact three-dimensional spaces. The surfaces at issue are called isoparametric hypersurfaces, and they are studied through a related notion called a transnormal system. The authors ask which such systems can exist on a compact space of dimension three, and how the systems behave when one space covers another.

Working in terms of equivalence classes, the pair show that spaces carrying one key type of system must match, at least locally, one of six standard shapes. They also find classes that hold no system of that type at all. That gap sets these systems apart from a close cousin in geometry, and it gives later work a clear map of what is possible.
arxiv-2503-18158:
Members of the LUX-ZEPLIN collaboration report new limits on dark matter boosted by cosmic rays in a 2025 paper. Xenon detectors have led the hunt for heavy dark matter particles that bump atomic nuclei. Light particles below one giga electron volt scale leave recoils too faint for standard searches. Cosmic rays can strike such light particles and speed them up.

Boosted particles would then hit the detector with enough energy to register. The team searched their xenon chamber data for that boosted signal. No claim of detection frames the paper, which sets fresh bounds instead. Those bounds narrow the space where light dark matter can hide. Other underground searches can build on the same boosted idea.
arxiv-2503-18458:
Luchao Wang, Qian Ren, and colleagues address stray artifacts in three-dimensional scene reconstruction in a 2025 computer vision study. A popular method builds scenes from many small soft blobs fitted to photos. Loose blobs, called floaters, often hang in empty space and spoil both shape and appearance.

The authors trace floaters to vanishing opacity gradients once blended colors reach a false balance against the background. Their framework splits rendering into two paths, one enforcing depth based geometry and one refining appearance on that stable base. A dual opacity design keeps the two jobs apart. The goal is clean reconstructions without floating debris.
arxiv-2503-18558:
Leavitt path algebras turn a graph into an algebra, and their internal multiplication groups hide surprising structure. Bui Xuan Hai and Huynh Viet Khanh prove in this 2025 paper that, over number fields of characteristic zero, these groups always contain free subgroups that are not merely cyclic.

A free subgroup behaves like words built from two letters with no relations, so its presence signals rich, wild structure inside the algebra. The authors also describe how to write down generators for such subgroups directly from the graph. The result holds for any unital, noncommutative algebra of this kind, giving algebraists a concrete handle on its symmetries.
arxiv-2503-18758:
Yunus Can Gültekin and four co-authors settle a question about neural decoders in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Neural networks have been proposed to decode error-correcting codes, with single-label and multi-label designs each claiming near-optimal results on short codes. Whether they can truly match the best possible decoding was open.

The authors prove that certain versions of both designs can always realize optimal decoding, for any code. Their architectures are fixed by the codebook itself, with binary weights and no training needed. Tests on three classic short codes confirm optimal performance with simpler designs than earlier proposals. A catch remains: the approach explodes in size for longer codes. Optimality, they show, is achievable but not yet practical at scale.
arxiv-2503-19258:
Hui Chen, Liangyu Liu, Xianchao Xiu, and Wanquan Liu unmix satellite rainbow images with a factorization that learns its own map of neighbors in this 2025 paper. Each pixel in a hyperspectral image blends several materials, and unmixing names the parts and their shares. Standard factorization methods lean on first or second neighbors and need hand tuning.

Their method builds links at several orders at once, near and far, and lets the data set the link strengths by itself. Two kinds of sparsity keep the answer clean: one prunes the material shares, the other isolates noise into its own matrix. An alternating solver with closed-form steps does the work. On fake and real scenes the method beat its rivals at recovering the true materials. The authors pitch it for mapping land cover, minerals, and crops from orbit.
arxiv-2503-19458:
Shujuan Li, Yu-Shen Liu, and Zhizhong Han present a 2025 method for rebuilding open surfaces from photos taken from many angles. Open surfaces, like a torn sheet or a shell, are hard to model because they have edges and no clear inside.

Their method fits thin, flat two dimensional spots onto the surface and learns a field that gives the unsigned distance to it. Self checks and slope based rules guide the spots both near and far from the surface. New limits keep the training stable near the surface line where slopes grow tricky. Tests on standard sets and real data showed gains in accuracy, speed, and sharp detail.
arxiv-2503-19558:
Jacco Terwel and co-authors search old sky survey data for late glows from stellar blasts found before the survey began, in a 2025 paper. The Zwicky survey has watched its sky patch for years, so past events hold long records. A late glow can betray a blast wave striking gas shed long ago.

They scanned more than seven thousand past transients, mostly supernovae. One case fit a late strike on a thin, far shell of modest mass. Five cases fit fresh flares in galaxy cores near the old sites. Two cases stayed unclear. The many blanks bound how often such shells occur. The work shows the reach of long survey records.
arxiv-2503-19758:
Wang and Gu present a 2025 quantum computing paper on a shortcut for hard logical gates that skips magic state distillation. Fault-tolerant machines need non-Clifford gates to complete their toolkit, and the standard route brews costly magic states. Their scheme runs the hard gate directly on one error-correcting code, then teleports the result into the main circuit. A joint measurement across two codes forms the bridge.

Skipping the brewing step cuts overhead from multiplicative to additive growth. A worked example joins a 3D color code to a surface code of equal strength. The authors argue the savings matter as machines scale toward useful sizes.
arxiv-2503-20258:
Six authors led by Jiaheng Zhou teach a lean video network to read medical ultrasound clips with few labelled cases. Ultrasound film is a core clinic tool, yet labelled sets are scarce and film is hard to mine. Their net, built on the Mamba line, keeps the 3D shape of film so space and time links stay clear. A ring of global tokens pools the wide scene in each pass.

Pre-training hides parts of clips and makes the net guess them, a self-taught warm-up. The hide plan chains space and time gaps to fit many clip kinds. Tests on four sets, across two scan tasks, put the net at the top of its class. Skill held up with few labels, a key draw for real wards.
arxiv-2503-20358:
Radek Zavorka and co-authors compare ways to cluster radio echoes inside a car cabin at millimeter waves, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Cabin links face safety stakes and car-to-car talks. A known echo model with fading clusters fits the cabin too.

Measured echo profiles from inside a car fed the race. A sparse reweighted method ran against the classic k-means split. The work sets up which tool reads cabin echoes best. Trusty links start with knowing where echoes bunch. Readers in car radio get a methods check for a tight, metal room on wheels.
arxiv-2503-20458:
Iwan Praton and Weiran Zeng published a paper in 2025 on amicable shapes drawn on graph paper grids. Two polygons are amicable when each one's perimeter equals the other's area, a numerical friendship like that of amicable number pairs. Restricting the corners to whole-number grid points sounds mild, yet it trims the possibilities hard.

The authors settle the two simplest families completely. Among lattice triangles there is exactly one amicable pair. Among lattice rectangles there are exactly five pairs. Short lists like these are satisfying in themselves, and the counting methods may extend to richer polygon families. The result is a reminder that simple rules on grids can still hide exact, finite answers.
arxiv-2503-20858:
Silvio Fortuné and four co-authors trace how galaxies switch star birth off and on across cosmic time. Their paper, from two thousand twenty-five, uses the Magneticum Pathfinder simulations. The standard story says galaxies form stars steadily, then quench for good. Recent observations hint the truth is messier. The team follows central galaxies in the highest-resolution run of the suite.

They sort each galaxy's path by its place on the star formation main sequence. A major share of galaxies cycle through long quiet and active phases, each lasting billions of years. Only a small share of field galaxies stay active the whole way. Gas inflow and the wider setting both shape these cycles. The work widens the standard story from one slow fade to many phases.
arxiv-2503-21358:
Uffe Hogsbjo Thygesen and Kasper Kristensen show a fitting method in a 2025 paper on ecology models. Equations with random noise fit natural systems well, since they join first principle rules with real uncertainty and measurement error. Fitting them, though, is often hard and slow.

A classic shortcut, the Laplace approximation, can do the job when used with care, the authors show. Extra hidden states are added between observation times, and step rules estimate how the system moves. Hard cases get full attention: curved dynamics, noise that grows with the state, and nonstandard error shapes. Worked examples show the method in action for ecology time series.
arxiv-2503-21658:
Thijs Hazenberg and four co-authors simulated iron dust flames to see whether sudden changes in fuel loading can shake them, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Iron powder is a candidate clean fuel, burned and then recycled as oxide. Using a validated model of a Bunsen-style flame, the team flipped the burner upright and upside down and jolted the particle feed.

Neither orientation changed the flame's answer, and the jolts excited no instability at all. The authors credit a missing feedback loop: in gas flames, heat release raises temperature, which raises heat release. Iron particles burn at a pace set by oxygen diffusion, which barely feels temperature. That decoupling, they argue, makes iron flames unusually calm.
arxiv-2503-21858:
Michal Moravec and co-authors probe electron flow in two layered metals in 2025, in a regime where electrons fly straight rather than scatter. In narrow channels cut into these metals, flow already breaks the rules of bulk behavior because the surface that electrons spread over is lopsided. The team now adds a magnetic field to that regime.

Channels ran along two crystal directions and across many widths, in both metals. Resistance under the field split from the bulk pattern, more so in narrower channels and by direction, they report. A classic theory tied the effect to the field bending how electrons bounce off channel walls. Some role for bulk scattering stays open. The work shows micro-scale flow can read out the shape of a metal's electron surface.
arxiv-2503-21958:
Kibon Ku and co-authors wrote this paper, published in two thousand twenty-five, on making 3D models of plants without moving the camera. In fast plant labs, plants ride conveyors or turntables past fixed sensors, so the usual trick of walking a camera around the subject does not work.

Their method flips the setup: the plant rotates on a pedestal while one camera stays still. Software first estimates poses as if the camera had moved, then trains a neural radiance field, a model that learns the scene from photos. A cropped region of interest keeps stray background out. The result is a dense point cloud of about ten million points with near-perfect scores on their checks. The authors say fixed-camera setups can serve costly, delicate sensors like hyperspectral cameras. Speeding up the pose step is their next goal.
arxiv-2503-22058:
Lukas Scarfe, Yingwen Zhang, and Ebrahim Karimi demonstrate a high-capacity form of quantum key distribution, in this 2025 paper. The head titles it as spatial mode encoding for quantum key distribution. Quantum key distribution lets two parties share secret keys with security backed by physics. Encoding in the position and momentum of photons packs far more data per photon.

The pair of photons is entangled, so measuring one prepares the other at a distance. Each side picks a basis at random, position or momentum, and matches yield key bits. The demo reached 5.07 bits per photon with ninety modes, and a top rate of 0.9 kilobits per second with 361 modes. With brighter sources and better cameras, the team projects nine bits per photon at two thousand modes. The paper sets benchmarks for future quantum networks.
arxiv-2503-22358:
Meghyn Bienvenu, Diego Figueira, and Pierre Lafourcade rethink, in a 2025 database theory paper, how to assign blame to facts when a query answer comes out true. A popular game-based score is elegant but brutally hard to compute, even for simple queries. The authors propose a new family of scores built from weighted sums over the smallest fact sets that already force the answer.

Their scores meet the intuitive fairness demands one would list. A surprise theorem shows each of them is secretly the game score of a suitably built game. Better still, they are cheap to compute for wide query classes, including unions of simple patterns. The paper maps where the cheapness holds and where it breaks.
arxiv-2503-22458:
Shengyue Guan and five co-authors survey how researchers judge chat agents over long, multi-turn talks. Their survey appeared in twenty twenty-five. Language model agents now hold conversations, use tools, and recall context, so scoring a single reply no longer tells the whole story.

The authors reviewed nearly two hundred fifty sources in a structured way. They build two linked maps. The first lists what to judge: task success, reply quality, user experience, memory, planning, and tool use. The second lists how to judge: human scoring, automatic metrics, mixed methods, and models judging themselves. Older scores like BLEU and ROUGE sit beside newer methods built for live dialogue. The maps give builders a shared frame for fair tests.
arxiv-2503-22558:
Lorenzo Clemente decides deep traits of polynomial control systems with exact, terminating algorithms. The paper from twenty twenty-five studies systems whose input enters in affine form and whose state flows by polynomial rules. Four traits are in view: being zero, being equivalent, ignoring input, being linear, and being analytic. Chen-Fliess series give each system a unique generating series.

Classic work by Fliess mirrors each trait in the series' combinatorics. Those series match a class called shuffle-finite, a nonlinear kin of rational series. Recent results on such series decide their core traits by algorithm. Clemente extends those results and ports them back to systems. A closure result on support restrictions is proved on the way. The work serves formal checks of control systems in full rigor.
arxiv-2503-22858:
Koryukova and co-authors watch a distant quasar flicker through interstellar plasma in a 2025 paper. The quasar 2005+403 shines through the turbulent Cygnus region. Radio light curves from the RATAN-600 dish span years of daily data. Plasma lenses along the path bend and scatter the signal, causing extreme scattering events.

Strong events appear in 2011, 2015, and 2020, each lasting four to five months, they report. Six events in a row occur across 2015 and 2016. Joint fits size the main lens at about 0.6 astronomical units, moving fast across the sky. The fits also recover the quasar's own true size once scattering is stripped away.
arxiv-2503-23458:
Karan Mukhi, Georg Loho, and Alessandro Abate compute the total flexibility of groups of small energy devices, in a 2025 paper. Batteries, heaters, and car chargers can shift when they draw power, which helps the grid absorb wind and solar swings. Sellers of that flexibility must state the group's range exactly, a sum that is usually too hard to compute.

The team shows these range sets belong to a shape family called generalized polymatroids, whose sums can be found exactly and fast. Uniform groups get even shorter forms. They add a solver over the sums and a way to split a group promise back to single devices. Tests beat older methods on both speed and exactness.
arxiv-2503-23558:
Piyush Pallav and co-authors test a way to see inside buildings and monuments without cutting into them, in this 2025 paper. Their tool is muon tomography: cosmic particles called muons pass through matter, and denser parts block more of them. By counting what gets through, the team can map hidden differences inside a structure.

Their setup, nicknamed MARS, uses overlapping detector paddles that are easy to obtain. They probed samples of common building materials and compared the readings with computer simulations. The match was good in every test. The authors argue the simple rig can serve for non-destructive checks of civil and industrial structures.
arxiv-2503-23958:
Nima Torbati and five co-authors automate the reading of melanoma tissue images in a 2025 paper. Melanoma is the deadliest skin cancer, and diagnosis rests on spotting tissue regions and classifying cell nuclei in stained slides. Most computer methods handle tissue and nuclei as separate jobs, which can waste information.

Their multi stage framework feeds each stage the other's context, unifying both tasks. On a public challenge dataset it took second place in one track and first in the other, with strong overlap and classification scores. Tests on an outside dataset showed the method travels well to new data. Step by step ablation confirmed each part of the framework earns its place. Code is public.
arxiv-2503-24058:
Bogomila Nikolova, Moritz Göb, Kilian Singer, and Peter Ivanov propose a new quantum device built from a single trapped ion in a tapered trap. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. The taper makes the ion's sideways and lengthwise motions talk to each other. That talk bends the sideways motion into a Kerr-type behavior.

The strength of the bend is set by the trap's tone settings. Such bent motion enables a class of gates that round out the full set for continuous quantum computing. A wobbling electric field can also squeeze the sideways motion, thanks to the same bend. The team further maps the tone spread of ion chains in such traps. Stronger bends widen the gaps between tones, which should allow faster gates. The design offers a fresh route to non-Gaussian quantum tools.
arxiv-2503-24258:
Lorenzo Tronchin, Tommy Löfstedt, Paolo Soda, and Valerio Guarrasi team up rival image generators for medical data in a 2025 paper. Synthetic medical images must be faithful, diverse, and cheap to make. Single GANs often collapse to a few modes. That collapse leaves real data patterns uncovered.

The team pick an ensemble of GANs by multi-objective tuning. The tuning balances fidelity against diversity across the set. Each chosen model adds a distinct contribution with little overlap. They tested 22 GAN designs across three medical datasets. Sampling training epochs gave 110 model variants to choose from. The ensembles made richer, more useful synthetic images.
arxiv-2504-00058:
Modern software is often built from many small services that talk to each other, and spotting faults in such systems is hard. Lahiru Akmeemana and three co-authors tackle the problem in a 2025 paper. They first build a dataset called RS-Anomic from an open-source shop application, recording performance measures and response times under normal running and under ten kinds of faults.

Their model, GAL-MAD, combines graph attention with a memory network to follow links between services and changes over time. A further step uses SHAP values to point at the faulty service and explain the likely cause. In tests, the model beat leading rivals on accuracy and recall, and its explanations gave operators clear leads to act on.
arxiv-2504-00258:
Francesco Capone and co-authors present a 2025 paper on a tiny superconducting device called a Josephson junction. Early theory promised that paired electrons would flow through it without loss, like an ideal conductor. The team asks whether that promise survives quantum fluctuations and the resistive paths that real devices always include.

Using both pen-and-paper methods and a Monte Carlo simulation, they study the junction under two bias schemes. Ideal conduction turns out to be fragile: fluctuations and dissipation each spoil it. Stronger dissipation drives a phase transition of a classic type. Charge and phase fluctuations near the transition behave in ways that defy the standard picture of a superconductor-to-insulator switch.
arxiv-2504-00558:
Marek Vaško, Adam Herout, and Michal Hradiš build a data set for finding faces in digitized historical newspapers in a two thousand twenty-five computer vision paper. Archivists need faces linked to the text around them, but modern detectors fail badly on old scans.

Off-the-shelf tools reach only about twenty-four percent mean average precision on old documents. The authors annotated by hand twenty-two hundred images from nineteenth- and twentieth-century newspapers, adding eleven thousand bounding boxes with facial landmarks in the style of the Wider Face data set. Retrained detectors from several families improve greatly in their tests. Ablation studies across detector sizes chart the detection and landmark accuracy now within reach on archival material.
arxiv-2504-01158:
Mark Lewis and Andrew Summers count graph shapes that can arise from the character degrees of a finite solvable group. Their 2025 paper builds on work by Pálfy, who showed that when such a graph splits into two parts, the part sizes obey a strict inequality. The authors ask a counting question: how many size pairs can meet that rule?

They work out that count in full. They also fix a target number and count how many graph orders admit exactly that many valid size pairs. The results pin down which split shapes the inequality allows at all. Work of this kind maps the limits on how the arithmetic of a group can look. It gives later studies a checklist of possible and impossible degree patterns.
arxiv-2504-01458:
Ask a computer a question about a place and it needs more than facts; it needs to grasp location, shape, change over time, and how features relate. Jian Wang and co-authors built GeoRAG to give language models that geographic grounding. They assembled a knowledge base from 3,267 sources, sorted by multiple agents into seven geographic dimensions, yielding over 875,000 question-answer pairs. A classifier first tags what kind of question is being asked, a retrieval evaluator then picks the most relevant passages, and tailored prompts feed them to the model.

Across several base models, GeoRAG beat conventional retrieval-augmented systems. The authors pitch the design as a template for grounding language models in other specialist fields, not just geography.
arxiv-2504-01658:
Venus Rai and Andreas Michels reported in 2025 a hidden scaling pattern in how magnets scatter neutrons. Inside bulk ferromagnets, defects bend the magnetization into long waves whose size shifts with the applied field. The authors define a scaling length that captures those waves and split it into a field part and a fixed part tied to the grain structure.

Old neutron data from several magnets collapse onto one curve when the axes are scaled by that length. Scaling turns messy scattering patterns into a single law, giving materials scientists a sharper ruler for reading magnetic texture.
arxiv-2504-01858:
Jake Miller, Edward Cackett, Mike Goad and Kirk Korista report six months of photometric reverberation mapping of the active galaxy PG 2130+099. Light echoes across wavelengths measure the size of the glowing continuum region around the black hole. Past campaigns disagreed on whether that size matches a standard thin accretion disk.

Their robotic telescope data give the fastest sampling and widest wavelength cover yet for this galaxy. The inferred region is larger than the simplest thin disk prediction, as in many active galaxies studied lately. A flux-flux analysis found a variable part much like a disk plus a steady part with extra emission in one band, perhaps from hydrogen. Lag may grow with brightness, though past lag errors are too large to be sure.
arxiv-2504-02158:
Jaehoon Choi and co-authors build digital twins for drone training in a 2025 paper. Drones learn to spot people and objects from flight footage, but real footage is costly and narrow. A twin world, rebuilt from real scenes, can mint fresh training views on demand.

Their method, UAVTwin, rebuilds backgrounds with a splatting method that scatters soft 3D blobs. Synthetic people with varied looks and moves are dropped into those scenes. Two add-ons, an appearance model and a mask refiner, fight the blur that moving people cause. Render quality beat recent rivals by a clear margin. Detectors trained with the twin data gained up to about fourteen percent on a standard score.
arxiv-2504-02958:
Many particle measurements are fit at once to bound new physics by the CMS Collaboration in a 2025 paper. The catalog record lists no creator, while the head names the CMS Collaboration. The frame is the standard model effective field theory, where effects of heavier physics appear as dimension-six operators with coefficients called Wilson coefficients.

Seven sets of CMS measurements are fit together. They probe Higgs boson, electroweak vector boson, top quark, and multijet production, using proton-proton data from the Large Hadron Collider. Electroweak precision data add complementary bounds. Individual limits on sixty-four coefficients are obtained, plus limits on forty-three linear combinations. Readers get a broad, joint picture of where new physics could still hide.
arxiv-2504-03058:
Kevin Church and co-authors present a 2025 mathematics paper on stable cycles in ecosystems of competing predators. A periodic orbit is a loop of population rises and falls that repeats. The authors build a method to prove that whole families of such stable loops exist, not just single examples.

Their technique turns the hunt into a zero-finding problem, then defines a Newton-like operator that should contract near a computed approximation. They derive checkable inequalities on that operator, and a computer verifies them with interval arithmetic, making the proof rigorous. Applied to an ecosystem with a saturating feeding response, the method settles a stable connection problem posed in 1981. The approach does not force parameters into a corner and should travel to other systems.
arxiv-2504-03358:
Ryan Kellermann and co-authors audit the hidden error sources in lattice QCD estimates of inclusive decay rates. Their 2025 paper works on decays of a strange-charm meson into a lighter strange system. Such totals are harder to pin down than single-particle channels.

Two error types get close study: cut-off error in energy sums, and box-size effects when several particles share the final state. Splitting ground-state and excited-state parts gives better control of both. A polynomial method keeps the cut-off error in check. A model of two-body final states gauges the box-size effect. The authors present the checks as a template for cleaner inclusive decay work on the lattice.
arxiv-2504-04058:
Anirban Mukherjee and Hannah Hanwen Chang argue that agentic AI blurs who made what, past the reach of law. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five; the pack row gives no title or year, so the text head is the source. Such systems chase goals on their own, shift plans as they learn, and vary run to run. Deep research tools are their case in point.

They name the trait a fluid, chance-led autonomy. Human and machine shares in a joint work melt into one stream that cannot be split back. Authorship, patent, and liability rules all lean on that split, so they strain. The pair urge that law treat the shares as one, not from morals or money, but because split counts cannot be made in practice.
arxiv-2504-04458:
Bashir Alam and co-authors tackle lopsided training data in medical image segmentation, in this 2025 paper. When the region a model must outline is tiny or rare, standard training losses copy the skew and the model's borders drift. Their fix, CALF, is a loss function that adapts to the data at hand.

The method gauges skew with statistical shape measures, then reshapes training and switches loss behavior on the fly. Tested on four large public brain tumor datasets, the approach improved outlines over standard losses by clear margins. The authors frame it as a general remedy for skewed medical datasets.
arxiv-2504-04958:
Satoshi Ejima, Kazuhiro Seki, Benedikt Fauseweh, and Seiji Yunoki develop in 2025 a probabilistic way to run imaginary-time evolution on quantum hardware. The technique, a staple of classical simulation, steers a quantum state toward its lowest energy. Their version works both in exact state-vector simulation and in shot-based runs that estimate values from repeated measurements.

Tests on a Heisenberg chain probed which starting states converge best. The method then ran on a trapped-ion device for a standard magnet model. The team also explores error mitigation inside the scheme, weighing what near-term machines need to make the approach practical.
arxiv-2504-05058:
Machine unlearning promises to delete specific facts from a trained language model, for privacy or safety, but Aravind Krishnan, Siva Reddy, and Marius Mosbach show that not all facts delete equally. Forgetting that Montreal is a city in Canada is treated by today's methods exactly like forgetting a private phone number. The authors test whether the two are really alike, and find a strong pattern: how often a fact appeared in training data decides how hard it is to remove.

Frequent knowledge resists unlearning. The team also uncovered a measurement trap: judging success by the model's probabilities disagrees with judging by what it actually generates, and the gap widens in larger models. They argue unlearning methods and evaluations must account for training frequency, or privacy deletions may be declared that never really happened.
arxiv-2504-05258:
Adrián Bazaga and co-authors teach language models to reason better about time. Models often stumble on event order, durations, and how events relate across a timeline. Their 2025 paper introduces TISER, a framework that first has the model build a timeline, then reflect on it in rounds.

Each reflection pass lets the model catch order slips and fix its chain of thought. The method leans on test-time scaling: longer reasoning traces at answer time, bought with compute rather than retraining. Results hit state-of-the-art levels on several temporal benchmarks, including test sets drawn from new domains. The traces also stay readable, so a reader can audit how the answer was reached. AI researchers get a recipe for steadier time sense.
arxiv-2504-05358:
Chen, Mao, Li, and Shangguan built this legal prediction system in twenty twenty-five. AI tools that predict court judgments often lean on huge archives of past cases. They also underuse the reasoning power of modern language models. The authors borrow the debate stage of a real trial to structure the task.

Several model agents argue the case from opposing sides. A separate checker scores how reliable each round of debate is. Feedback from the checker steers later rounds. The setup needs far fewer past cases than older methods. In comparative tests it beat both general and legal-specific models. The authors present debate plus feedback as a light, dynamic route for legal AI.
arxiv-2504-05858:
Ramcharan Meena and Rajendra Dhaka study a ceramic that can carry sodium ions, a trait wanted for solid-state batteries. Their 2025 paper varies the recipe by swapping some zirconium for titanium, in four small steps. The base is a NASICON-type material, a known family of fast ion movers.

X-ray fits show all four mixes share the same slanted crystal form. Heat-driven conduction follows the classic rising curve, and the energy needed to start it grows as the swap shrinks the cell. Charge storage gauges over heat and frequency show two relaxation paths with unlike start energies. Both the storage fits and the impedance fits point to a spread-out, non-ideal relaxation, with grain and grain-edge parts.
arxiv-2504-05958:
Mischa Huisman and co-authors propose a 2025 control scheme to guard cars that drive in linked groups. Such cars use cruise control that adapts with help from nearby cars. False data fed into a sensor can fool the system, so the team builds a way to spot and work around such an attack as it happens.

Their scheme runs matched copies of the controller, each fed by a distinct set of sensors. When all is well the copies agree; a split flags a bad sensor by a vote. The system then swaps to a sound copy and resets the flawed one. Test runs in simulation show the plan can keep the group safe.
arxiv-2504-06158:
Saad Wazir and Daeyoung Kim present a 2025 image model for marking biomarkers in medical scans. Such marking is key for biotech work, but shifts in shape and staining blunt many models. Data are also scarce, which makes the hand-off of traits between the model's halves a weak point.

Their nested U-Net design fuses traits at many scales and adds attention steps that stress key channels and zones. That mix keeps fine detail while holding the wide scene in view. Tests on four datasets, plus part-removal checks, show the design beats top past methods.
arxiv-2504-06958:
Xinhao Li and co-authors presented VideoChat-R1 in 2025, a model that watches video and chats about it. Video is hard for such models: events stretch over time, and tracking things across frames strains them. Reward-based tuning had lifted text reasoning, so the team asked if time-aware rewards could lift video sense as well. They tuned the model on several space-and-time tasks at once.

The tuned model set new best marks on time-based tests. Its score for finding when an event happens jumped by about thirty-two points, and object tracking rose by a like amount. Plain question tests also improved, and chat skill stayed intact. At run time, the model now hunts for time clues before it answers. The authors offer the method as a data-light way to build video agents that hold up in the real world.
arxiv-2504-07258:
Robin Harper and co-authors study how error-corrected quantum gates fail in this 2025 paper. Mid-circuit measurements read out error data and drive logic in quantum computers. Those reads can also inject noise of their own.

The team used a heavy-hex code on a superconducting qubit array. Idle errors during readout badly hurt a quantum memory at first. A shallower syndrome circuit they designed improved the memory a lot. A stability test then showed how readout errors cause logic failures. More readout rounds helped stability but left more time for decay. Simulations matched the device results and fingered measurement noise as the main limit.
arxiv-2504-07458:
Good and Linder study a flipped version of anti-de Sitter space through the lens of a moving mirror, in a 2025 paper. Anti-de Sitter space is a curved spacetime beloved by theorists. Inverting its parity gives a mirror world with odd properties.

In the flipped space, the mirror produces particles with positive energy flux. The total energy stays finite, unlike the usual case. The particle spectrum follows a Whittaker shape, close to but not quite thermal. The authors also derive the matching spacetime metric. It resembles de Sitter space yet stacks repeated causal regions with horizons. The work tests how mirrors mimic exotic gravity.
arxiv-2504-07758:
Shuangfan Zhou and co-authors present a joint method for cleaning up and enlarging polarised images, in a 2025 paper. Polarisation cameras capture light at several angles in one shot, but their raw output is a mosaic that must be rebuilt into full colour images. That rebuilding step adds errors in the very measures users care about, such as how strong and at what angle light is polarised.

Past methods either rebuild the image without raising its resolution, or enlarge a rebuilt image and carry its errors along. The new method does both jobs at once, straight from the raw mosaic. Tests on made-up and real data gave top results, the authors report, with more accurate polarisation measures. Downstream tasks that rely on polarisation also worked better with its output.
arxiv-2504-07958:
Hanxue Zhang and eight co-authors present DetAny3D, a foundation model that spots any object in 3D from a single camera view, even objects and cameras it never saw in training. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Labeled 3D data are scarce, which starves direct training. Two-dimensional models, by contrast, are rich with visual knowledge.

DetAny3D borrows that 2D wealth through two modules. One aligns features from several 2D foundation models into a shared form. The other maps those features into 3D while keeping early training steady. Users prompt the model for the objects they want found. Tests show top results on unseen classes and new camera setups. It even beats most rivals on familiar data. Uses range from rare-object spotting in driving to open-world robotics.
arxiv-2504-08058:
Arthur Choplin and three co-authors model how an intermediate neutron capture process in giant stars creates actinides and short lived radioactive nuclei. Asymptotic giant branch stars host mixing events where protons plunge into hot layers and trigger rapid neutron captures. Stellar models span low masses and a wide range of metal content.

A large nuclear network of more than a thousand isotopes is coupled to transport during those ingestion events. Models with very low metal content can synthesize actinides, at times above solar levels. One iron isotope yield scales with metal content, while five other radioactive yields peak near a shared metal level. Barium isotope fractions also vary with mass and composition. The results inform the origin of heavy elements in old stars.
arxiv-2504-08458:
Esther Johnsen and co-authors present a faster way to predict how materials absorb X-rays at their inner electron shells. These spectra act as fingerprints for elements and chemical states. The single-particle methods work well for the deepest shell, but the next shells tangle with spin-orbit coupling, an interplay of spin and motion.

Their method keeps the single-particle picture and adds an explicit empty core state, a fixed spin-orbit split for each level, and a fitted energy shift. Predictions land on the true energy scale at a fraction of the cost. Against a heavy method that runs forty times slower, the new approach matched experiments as well or better for molecules. Solids agreed well with X-ray and electron energy-loss spectra. The authors note one gap: patterns from electrons interacting in groups lie beyond any single-particle method.
arxiv-2504-08658:
Giovanni Brigati, Jean Dolbeault, and Nikita Simonov reviewed stability results in twenty twenty-five for logarithmic Sobolev inequalities. These are key estimates in analysis and probability. They say entropy is held in check by energy. Stability asks a sharp next point. If a function is near equality, must it be near an optimizer? Does that hold in strong norms, or does it fail?

The review sets versions side by side on Euclidean space. It uses Lebesgue and Gaussian measures for that space. It weighs how moment assumptions shift the picture. The authors give new, direct proofs. They give counterexamples too. They take up stability of a logarithmic uncertainty principle as well. The piece maps where quantitative stability is proven. It maps where it breaks. It notes which forms should get the field's focus next.
arxiv-2504-08858:
Zinnat Hassan's thesis investigates traversable wormholes in modified theories of gravity in 2025. The pack record's title is garbled, but the text itself is a study of wormhole spacetimes where exotic matter at the throat is described by an anisotropic energy-momentum tensor.

Solutions are built in one modified gravity theory under several equations of state, and their viability and stability are checked in depth. A quantum correction principle is applied to Casimir wormholes to see how its parameter shapes the geometry. The thesis also covers wormhole shadows and light bending with dark matter present. Work in a second gravity theory rounds out the study.
arxiv-2504-09358:
Zhi Wang and three co-authors build DoorBot, a robot system that opens unseen doors using touch feedback, in work from 2025. Doors vary in look, mechanism and swing direction, which defeats vision-only and open-loop plans. Their design pairs a task planner with a manipulation controller in a closed loop, so force signals during a push or pull steer the next move.

The system was tried on twenty doors across different buildings, none seen in training. It opened nine in ten successfully. The authors present touch-guided adaptation as the key to generalizing, and suggest the same frame for other hinged and jointed objects in open-world settings.
arxiv-2504-09558:
Weiye Xu and co-authors present a 2025 smart fabric system with no battery, no chip, and no wires sewn in. Rigid parts and power cells make smart clothes hard to wash, wear, and make at scale, and they add to e-waste. The team's cloth senses touch and shape through woven resonant circuits alone.

A nearby coil pair sends power across a small air gap and reads the cloth's signals back. The authors built a math model of the full circuit, then an algorithm that turns shifts in the system load into sensor values. Sims and a user study show the cloth can host many sensor types at once. The work points to softer, greener wearables.
arxiv-2504-09758:
Stephane Tchuiaga develops new ways to measure distance between flows that stretch and fold in a chaotic but steady way, in a paper from 2025. Such flows are a core topic in the study of motion and change. A good distance should reflect the cost of bending one flow into another.

Tchuiaga proves key traits of the new measures, such as completeness and good behavior under smooth changes of shape. Near flows in this distance have close values for entropy, growth rates, and mixing speed. The paper also defines a new class of rough flows that keep key traits of the smooth ones. The work gives tools for sorting and comparing such systems.
arxiv-2504-09858:
Wenjie Ma and five co-authors question whether reasoning language models really need their long thinking step, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Top reasoning models write out lengthy chains of thought before answering, and that habit is credited for their strength. The team tested a leading distilled model with the thinking stage switched off by a simple prompt.

Judged at equal token budgets, the no-thinking mode beat the thinking mode across seven hard test sets, from math to coding, above all when budgets were tight. Making many quick no-thinking tries and picking the best answer worked even better, matching slow thinking at a fraction of the wait. The authors argue the field should rethink how much visible reasoning is truly needed.
arxiv-2504-10058:
Mendonça, Di Marzo, and Abdennadher reviewed in twenty twenty-five data co-ops as a fair way to hold and rule shared data. In a co-op, folks own and rule their data as a group by vote. That sets it apart from trusts, shared pools, and unions that hold data in other ways.

Uses span health, farms, and build work, they note. Blocks are hard group work, growth to scale, and low drive from parts. New rule forms, sound tech, and ways to line up group aims are needed. They back co-ops as a last-ing, fair frame for the data age.
arxiv-2504-10458:
The authors present GUI-R1, a vision-language model trained to operate software interfaces as an agent. Most interface agents learn by supervised fine-tuning, which demands huge training sets and still generalizes poorly to unseen screens. Inspired by reinforcement fine-tuning in reasoning models, the team trains with rewards instead. Their framework rests on a unified action space that describes interface actions by shared rules across platforms.

Training uses a small, carefully curated set of about three thousand examples spanning Windows, Linux, MacOS, Android, and the web. A policy optimization method updates the model from its own trial results. Across eight benchmarks on mobile, desktop, and web, the model beats prior leading systems while using only a tiny fraction of their data. The authors argue reinforcement learning with a unified action model holds large promise for real interface tasks.
arxiv-2504-10958:
Dictionary learning builds a rich set of building blocks so that any input can be rebuilt from just a few of them. Alexander Köhler and Michael Breuß tried in 2025 to turn that trick toward a new job: telling geometric shapes apart.

Their early tests show the choice of solver behind the method matters a great deal for how well shapes are recognized. With the right solver, accuracy looks promising. The authors present the work as a first step, suggesting that a tool long used for rebuilding images could also serve for sorting them. More trials would be needed to judge how far the approach can go.
arxiv-2504-11058:
Aamar Abbas, Touqeer Ahmad, and Ishfaq Ahmad model daily rainfall with a single distribution that handles dry days and deluges together, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-five. Rain data are awkward: many days record exactly zero, while the wet tail stretches to dangerous extremes that hydrology cares about most.

Standard practice picks a threshold and models only what exceeds it, leaving the bulk and the tail in separate worlds. The proposed zero-inflated extended generalized Pareto model folds dry days, light rain, moderate rain, and extremes into one framework. Its tail index mirrors the classic extreme value distribution, so tail behavior comes built in rather than bolted on. Covariates can enter through generalized additive structure, though the current version treats days independently. Estimation runs by both maximum likelihood and Bayesian methods. Simulations and real data applications test the fit.
arxiv-2504-11258:
Liam Welsh, Udit Grover, and Sebastian Jaimungal model carbon offset credit markets with learning agents in a 2025 paper. Governments cap emissions and fine excess, but firms can buy offset credits from carbon-cutting projects instead. How firms trade those credits shapes real climate outcomes.

The authors characterize the market's Nash equilibrium for finitely many firms. Because exact equilibria are computationally hard, they estimate them with a reinforcement learning method built for games. Simulations show learning agents find the equilibria and that firms abiding by them save real money. Market designers gain a testbed for rules before those rules govern actual emissions.
arxiv-2504-11358:
Liu and four co-authors built this detector in twenty twenty-five for prompt injection attacks on AI apps. Attackers hide instructions inside inputs to hijack a language model's output. Detectors must flag poisoned inputs, but attackers adapt to evade them. The authors frame the contest as a game between attacker and defender.

Their method, DataSentinel, fine-tunes a model to catch injections crafted to slip past it. Training alternates between strengthening the attack and strengthening the detector, a minimax loop. A gradient method solves that loop in practice. Tests across datasets and models showed strong catches of both known and adaptive attacks. The authors offer the game view as a sturdier base for defense.
arxiv-2504-11658:
Nanshan Jia and three co-authors use language models to sharpen product suggestions, in a 2025 arXiv paper. Many shops already run a base tool that learns from click history. Bolting a big language model straight on raises doubts about why it picks what it picks. The team instead uses the model as a side helper that mimics sales logic in plain terms.

The helper reads item traits that people can grasp and builds a guided code for each item. That code merges with a slimmed form of the base tool's code, and the mix feeds the final picks. Tests across tasks show gains of roughly ten to fifty percent on standard scores. Case studies, the team adds, show the picks are easier to explain too.
arxiv-2504-11758:
The Anh Bui wrote a mathematics paper in two thousand twenty-five on function spaces tied to Bessel operators. Bessel operators are math tools that show up in problems with round or radial shapes. Bui builds the theory of Hardy spaces and related BMO-type spaces for a version of the operator that works in many dimensions at once.

The paper then turns to higher order Riesz transforms, a family of operators linked to the Bessel operator. Bui shows that the transforms belong to a well understood class called Calderon-Zygmund operators. He also proves that they stay bounded, meaning controlled in size, on the new Hardy and BMO-type spaces he defines.
arxiv-2504-11858:
Joël Mathys, Andreas Plesner, Jorel Elmiger, and Roger Wattenhofer synthesize blood vessel data in two thousand twenty five. Brain vessel networks matter for stroke research and flow studies. Pulling their topology from microscopy images is hard. Labeled training data are scarce and accuracy demands are high.

Their pipeline builds synthetic sets that mimic real vessel networks. Stages run from abstract graphs to masks to full images. Two 3D U-Net stages then detect nodes and predict edges. Fine tuning on five hand labeled samples lifts edge scores a lot. Automated extraction looks close to practical use now.
arxiv-2504-12158:
Many objects in mathematics look almost like monoids: a set with a unit and a multiplication obeying laws that almost match. Paul Blain Levy and Morgan Rogers ask when such a look-alike deserves the name. Category theorists already define monoids inside monoidal categories and multicategories, but stubborn examples — relative monads, the sequencing of a programming semantics — fall outside both.

The authors generalise in two stages. First they use left-skew multicategories, which allow the leftmost factor of a multiplication to be special; that covers relative monads. Then they build a bi-skew framework where both ends can be distinguished, covering cases like categories on spans and call-by-push-value sequencing. In the general setting they prove a coherence result: their monoids match the unbiased version of the concept. The paper redraws the boundary of a basic algebraic idea.
arxiv-2504-12358:
Artificial intelligence is seeping into nuclear research and operations faster than anyone is tracking its risks. Aditi Verma and Elizabeth Williams call for governing this spread before surprises force the issue. Their proposal has two parts. One is an anticipatory governance system for AI across the nuclear sector. The other is a global AI observatory to make that foresight real, watching what models are deployed where and for what.

The paper sketches the observatory's shape by borrowing from science and technology studies, public policy, and futures research. Safety, security, and safeguards consequences of embedded AI are the blind spot the observatory would illuminate. The authors argue a watching brief, held globally and early, beats scrambling after an incident in a sector where mistakes carry unusual weight.
arxiv-2504-12458:
Jansen Pereira, Giovani Valdrighi, and Marcos Medeiros Raimundo teach gradient boosting to mind subgroup fairness while it learns. Predictive models can quietly disadvantage marginalized groups defined by traits like gender and race. The team folds fairness directly into the boosting objective. Standard losses for classification and regression share the stage with a min-max fairness term that guards the worst-off subgroup.

Each boosting round solves a primal-dual pair for that combined objective. The theory shows the algorithm converges under mild conditions. The generic frame adapts to several fairness concepts, binary and subgroup alike. Experiments back the claim of a powerful, flexible approach. Rather than auditing a finished model for bias, the method bakes the fairness pressure into every tree it grows. Justice, here, is an optimization term, not a postscript.
arxiv-2504-12658:
Chunyan Li and co-authors report in this 2025 paper a new way for sluggish systems to fall out of equilibrium balance. Glasses and similar materials age and diffuse with extreme slowness, and why their time averages part from group averages was murky. The team studies systems whose spread grows only with the log of time.

In such systems, rare events grow rarer as the system ages. Those events barely move the averages, yet they stretch the system's own clock, so time and group averages of spread split apart and two distinct long-run distributions appear. The pattern differs from the classic Lévy picture. The authors offer the mechanism as groundwork for far-from-equilibrium matter.
arxiv-2504-12758:
Kyriakos Stylianopoulos and George Alexandropoulos show that a giant antenna array can act as a trainable learning machine in the air itself, in this 2025 paper. In their setup, the wireless channel supplies the random hidden layer of a classic fast-learning design, and the receiver's analog combiner becomes the trainable output. No digital crunching and no transmitter preprocessing are needed. The air does the computing.

Tests across several datasets cleared ninety percent classification accuracy with only milliseconds of tuning, where normal methods take seconds to minutes. Performance held under rich fading when the receive array was large. The authors frame huge future antenna systems as double agents: radios that also think at the edge, cheaply enough for tiny devices.
arxiv-2504-13058:
Cynthia Zastudil and five co-authors review research on neurodiversity in computing education, in a 2025 survey. Fair access for students with autism, dyslexia, or ADHD shapes who joins the computing workforce. The team searched the literature and found near two thousand papers, of which just fourteen fit their rules. They coded each paper for methods, participants, and type of contribution.

Interviews were the most common method in the hands-on studies. Many papers gave teaching advice with little hard proof behind it. Reports often skipped key details, such as how many people took part. The authors call the field young and thin. They point to three needs: test active learning, learn more about these students' own views, and design teaching tools with them, not just for them.
arxiv-2504-13158:
Stewart N Ethier, a solo author, asks how to test a gambling claim in a 2025 paper on craps. Some players say that setting the dice and throwing with care can sway the results and beat the house. A fair test needs a clear model of what such control would look like in data.

Two models from the gambling literature are used, each with a dial for the level of control. Four test scores are proposed and compared: the share of sevens, the share of pass line wins, the average length of a hand, and a ratio test on hand lengths. The setup can test both no control at all and control below a set level.
arxiv-2504-13358:
Omar Tsai and co-authors present a tool that hunts security flaws in GraphQL interfaces, the query systems behind many finance, shop, and social apps. Their 2025 paper notes that the worst flaws need chained steps, such as make, delete, then read, which standard scanners miss since they test each call alone.

The tool maps how calls depend on each other, then builds chains aimed at known flaw kinds. On a live finance system it flagged eight possible flaws with no login or docs in hand. On a shop system with known bugs it replayed all four cited access flaws. Across public systems its coverage far beat two rival tools, and it found chained flaws the rivals missed entirely.
arxiv-2504-14158:
Yuan Feng and Li Zhou study refinement orders for quantum programs, in a paper from 2025. Refinement lets builders grow a rough specification into working code step by step, with each step keeping correctness. An order on programs is what makes those steps safe.

For classical code the theory is old, but quantum programs lacked a full account. The pair cover definite and chance-allowing programs, under both full and partial correctness. They test three kinds of quantum claims: sharp yes-no claims, graded claims, and sets of graded claims. For definite programs, two of the claim kinds match a known order on quantum operations. Chance-allowing programs line up with classical domain ideas.
arxiv-2504-14258:
Think of a bus network where every link runs on a repeating schedule. George Mertzios and three co-authors model such systems as periodic temporal graphs, where each connection appears once per period and the design task is to assign its time slot. They measure quality by stretch: how much longer the fastest timed route becomes, against the plain map distance.

The authors ask which stretch values can be guaranteed. They give approximation methods and hardness results, including a simple polynomial-time method whose guarantee always beats the trivial one and sometimes finds the optimum. They also study a repair version, where an existing schedule may be changed on at most a few links. The repair version proves hard in one sense, yet solvable with effort growing in the number of changes.
arxiv-2504-14758:
Trung-Phuc Vo and co-authors study the fine structure of photoelectron Kikuchi diffraction patterns and how they change with energy, published in 2025. These faint patterns help probe phase changes and strain in materials, and in photoemission work they can disentangle crowded data and pinpoint where an electron came from. In the hard X-ray range they are hard to detect and model.

Simulations covered core-level emissions from germanium and silicon surfaces across a wide energy range, using multiple-scattering theory with a one-step photoemission model. That route avoids the cluster-size troubles of older methods. The computed networks of faint lines track how patterns evolve with energy. The authors aim to strengthen structural analysis that rests on these patterns, in both microscopy and spectroscopy settings.
arxiv-2504-15058:
Jiayin Liu, Shijin Zhang, and Yuan Zhou solve a geometry problem about the shortest paths on curved spaces that open out like a cone at large distances. These spaces, called asymptotically conical manifolds, widen toward an ideal edge far away. The authors ask whether, for any two opposite points on that far edge, a single straight-line path in the curved sense runs across the space and links the two points.
