They prove that such a path does exist under clear conditions on the space. The space must have a positive rate of opening, its angle must avoid a set of special values, and its distance map must behave well. They also bound how many directions the path can bend in. The result extends a classic question about flat surfaces, the Plateau problem, to this wider class of curved spaces.
arxiv-2504-15158:
Maria Chiara Angelini, Louise Budzynski, and Federico Ricci-Tersenghi (2025) study what happens when two copies of the same puzzle are tied together. The puzzle is random hypergraph bicoloring, a standard constraint satisfaction problem. Each copy must color its nodes with two colors under random rules. A ferromagnetic coupling rewards the copies for agreeing. Using the cavity method on combined variables, the authors solved the coupled model's solution space.

Coupling lowered the density at which solutions shatter into isolated clusters. That shattering is where search algorithms slow down badly. The change also softened the transition itself, from abrupt to gradual over a wide range of coupling. Belief propagation, a common solver, converged differently near the softened transition. The results carry a puzzle of their own: coupled copies should favor dense solution regions, yet clustering arrives sooner. The authors call for closer study of algorithms and reweighting tricks near such transitions.
arxiv-2504-15458:
Brandon Le and Dustin Keller extract, in a 2025 paper, measures of the proton's inner structure from scattering data using quantum-inspired neural networks. The measures, called Compton form factors, come from deeply virtual Compton scattering, in which a high-energy probe bounces off a proton. The data set is from Jefferson Lab, and the maths frame is the standard twist-2 formalism.

On fake data, the quantum-flavoured networks often beat classic deep networks on accuracy and gave tighter error bars at like complexity. The team built a score that says which kind of network suits a given fit. They then ran local fits on the real data and a global fit across sets, matching earlier global studies. The method is pitched as a sharp extra tool for mapping the proton.
arxiv-2504-15558:
Some samplers change as they run, because the prior they draw from keeps learning from the samples so far. Fan, Ko, Loureiro, Lu, and Shen study one such scheme: a Langevin diffusion that samples a Bayesian linear model while its prior keeps updating by a fit to the samples seen. A companion paper set out the high-dimensional limit for how the prior and the samples move together.

Here the authors study that limit when the posterior is smooth enough to mix well. They show the sampler settles, on a time scale that does not grow with dimension, to a fixed state given by a small set of scalar equations. The prior lands on a key point of a simpler free-energy formula, and the work gives a fresh proof that the simpler formula is exact.
arxiv-2504-15658:
Lachlan Dunn wrote this mathematics paper, published in 2025. It tightens the known upper bound on Brun's constant, a famous number built from the twin primes, prime numbers that sit two apart, like five and seven.

Brun's constant adds up the reciprocals of every twin prime pair. Unlike the sum over all primes, this sum settles to a fixed value, but its exact size is unknown. Firm bounds that assume nothing extra were already known. Dunn proves the first firm bound that leans on the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis, a major unproven claim about prime numbers. Under that assumption, the constant comes out below 2.1594. The result shows how a big conjecture, if true, sharpens what can be said about twin primes.
arxiv-2504-15958:
Yao and six co-authors present FreeGraftor, a method to place a subject from a photo into new AI images with no training, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Subject-driven generation must keep identity true while following text prompts. Tuning methods are slow and costly, while instant methods often lose the subject. FreeGraftor grafts features across images to bridge that gap.

Semantic matching finds matching parts between reference and draft images. A position-aware fusion step then blends those details in. A new noise start preserves the subject's shape for better matching. Tests show higher fidelity and better text fit than rival instant methods. The method extends to scenes with several subjects at once.
arxiv-2504-16058:
Hendrik Müller and Sanjay Bhatnagar speed up radio image cleaning in twenty twenty-five. Radio interferometers produce data that must be deconvolved to form images. The classic algorithm for this is CLEAN, the de facto standard. New telescopes bring far larger data, higher resolution, and wider dynamic range, straining existing pipelines.

Multiscale CLEAN variants beat the classic on quality but cost much more compute. The authors combine ideas into a new algorithm, Autocorr-CLEAN. It fits clusters of CLEAN components rather than single points. The autocorrelation function informs how those clusters are shaped. The goal is variant-level quality at closer to classic speed. Readers who reduce radio data get a deconvolution built for the coming data flood.
arxiv-2504-16658:
Ole-Christian Engstrøm and three co-authors release an open data set on sprouting barley in a 2025 paper. Malting depends on even germination, so tracking how each kernel sprouts over time is valuable. The data set follows 2,242 single kernels through the process.

Every kernel was imaged before wetting and then every 24 hours for five days. The images come in three kinds: normal color, near-infrared spectra, and near-infrared hyperspectral images, each with masks that outline the kernels. Each kernel is labeled as sprouted or not at every step. Because the background is black filter paper, simple threshold methods can cut the kernels out. The set supports work on predicting sprouting time from images or spectra.
arxiv-2504-16858:
Hanwen Du, Bo Peng, and Xia Ning present DiffTOD in a 2025 paper on steering chats toward a set goal. Guiding a talk to a target takes strategy, and step by step planners can stack errors and act with short sight. Their frame plans the whole path at once instead.

Dialogue planning is cast as making a full trajectory under guidance toward the goal. A diffusion language model scores how likely each full path is to land well. Three guidance tricks fit unlike target types and can swap at test time with ease. Tests in three goal chat settings show strong long horizon planning. The method beat step wise rivals and bent well to complex scenes, the team report.
arxiv-2504-17058:
Rahul Vishwakarma, Shrey Dharmendra Modi, and Vishwanath Seshagiri add hard statistical promises to fake data made by generative models. Fake data are widely used when real data are private or scarce. Yet makers could not say how close their fakes sit to the true spread, which bars use in high-stakes fields.

Their framework threads conformal prediction, a method that gives error bounds without assuming a data shape, through a rival-network generator. Four flavors of the conformal method are built in. The result is fake data with stated limits on how far it may stray. That guarantee can unlock uses in medicine and finance that now stay closed. The team names the system Conformalized GAN. It trades a little freedom for a promise that can be checked.
arxiv-2504-17258:
Md Ashiqur Rahman and Raymond Yeh generalize a core image-network step in a 2025 paper. Downsampling shrinks feature maps to widen a network's view and cut computing cost. Networks that respect symmetry, such as rotation, need a version of this step that works on general groups, not just grids, and that blurs before shrinking to avoid artifacts.

They give a method to choose a fitting subgroup for any group and shrink rate, plus a band-limit rule for the anti-aliasing blur. On plain cycles their method matches the classic filter-then-shrink recipe. Tests on image tasks show better accuracy, better kept symmetry, and smaller models when the new step is built in.
arxiv-2504-17558:
Giuliano Orso and co-authors study a single impurity atom moving in a one dimensional gas of fermions, a system known as a Fermi polaron. The impurity is drawn to the gas by a short range pull, and the team ask how much of its lone particle character survives.

Using exact methods and computer sampling, they find that share falls to zero as the gas grows large, in line with a known view of such gases. A simpler guessed form, though good for energy and mass, wrongly keeps the share above zero. They also track how the impurity shifts the spread of the gas around it.
arxiv-2504-17658:
Marcela Grcic and two co-authors worked out in 2025 a theory of lopsided disks around pairs of stars. Gas circling a star pair can hollow out a center that sits off-center and slowly turns. Such steady states can be read as trapped waves in a bowl-shaped field set by the pair's gravity and the disk's own pressure. One ratio, of pressure pull to gravity pull, rules the wave set.

The team solved the problem at several levels of detail, from sharp-edged disks to smooth ones. Thinner disks and more equal star pairs host more wave modes. For thin disks, the main mode hugs the gravity peak inside the hollow, while thick disks anchor it at the hollow's rim. Their results match computer simulations well, including a halving of rates in three-dimensional disks.
arxiv-2504-17758: The MicroBooNE team gives the first study of how well a neutrino's direction can be rebuilt from quasielastic-like events in its detector. The paper came out in two thousand twenty-five. MicroBooNE is a liquid argon time projection chamber that tracks hits in fine detail. The events they use leave one muon and one proton. They check how far the rebuilt muon-proton system sits from the known direction of the beam. It is tied to sub-GeV oscillation studies for DUNE.
arxiv-2504-17858:
Idel Waisberg, Ygal Klein, and Boaz Katz revisit two star pairs with the most stretched orbits known, using fresh observations from their closest approaches in 2023 and 2024. Very eccentric binaries, pairs whose orbits are nearly hairpins, are oddly rare among systems whose eccentricity can be measured. Earlier work claimed one of the pairs, Zeta Boötis, had an eccentricity above 0.99, the record.

With interferometric data from the VLTI/GRAVITY instrument, the authors find Zeta Boötis sits at 0.980450 instead, still the second-best constrained value known. Its closest approach is about 0.818 astronomical units. They blame the old overestimate on a degeneracy that haunts orbit fitting for such extreme pairs. The second pair, Eta Ophiuchi, measured 0.93077, and its earlier mass estimate was also too high. Both pairs should slowly circularize as their stars age and swell.
arxiv-2504-18058:
Sijia Cheng, Wen-Yu Chang, and Yun-Nung Chen study how shopper personality changes chatbot sales talks in a 2025 paper. The team typed simulated customers by the Myers-Briggs scheme and let a pretrained sales agent talk with each type at large scale. They then graded the chats for task success, smoothness, and fit.

Clear patterns emerged: some personality types finished purchases more often and kept talks natural, while others stalled the agent. The results show a one-style agent serves unevenly across personalities. The authors release their persona simulators as domain-free tools for other researchers. They argue future sales agents should read and adapt to customer temperament.
arxiv-2504-18258:
Three researchers studied in 2025 how positons, rippling lumps of voltage, travel down a modified electrical transmission line. Earlier work covered solitons and rogue waves in such circuits. Positons resemble solitons but fade slowly with a wobbling tail, holding energy in place while spreading gently.

By recasting the circuit equations into a classic wave equation, the team found second- and third-order positons and followed their journeys. Both kept their height and width over long spans, promising stable signaling. Circuit settings that tune the lumps' size were also mapped for future designs.
arxiv-2504-18458:
Wenyi Xiao and Leilei Gan teach vision-language models to think fast or slow as the question demands. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, presents FAST-GRPO. Reward training often makes such models write long chains for every task. Length grows, but accuracy barely does, and tokens are wasted.

Tests first show that answer length and data mix shape results in a usable way. Two scores then rate how hard each question is. Rewards favor the right length for the difficulty, and a safety term scales with it too. Across seven reasoning tests, accuracy hit top marks. Token use fell by a third to two-thirds versus slow-only rivals.
arxiv-2504-18558:
Danehkar revisits the nearest known tidal disruption event, a star torn apart by a black hole in the galaxy NGC 4845, and its faint aftershocks, in a paper from 2025. The 2010 flare, IGR J12580+0134, was followed in X-rays in 2011. Hoping the radio cycle pointed to a repeat, the author won nearly a year of NICER monitoring from March 2023.

The new watch caught small X-ray flares in spring 2023, far weaker than the original event. Statistical decomposition tied both the old blaze and the new flares to an absorbed power-law glow, with a whisper of hot plasma. The flares likely mark feeble feeding by the galaxy's black hole, a low-luminosity active nucleus rather than a second disruption. The study keeps the nearest case on the books.
arxiv-2504-18958:
Ataei, a solo author, models stock market volatility through a Financial Chaos Index in a 2025 paper. The index uses tensor and eigenvalue methods to capture shared swings among asset prices. Market volatility is known to behave in distinct regimes.

Data from the early nineteen nineties to the end of twenty twenty-three fell into three regimes of low, middle, and high chaos. Each regime differed in stress, spread, and persistence. The author then used sentiment-based predictors in an elastic net model to forecast implied volatility, tracked by the VIX. Shifts in economic, financial, policy, and geopolitical uncertainty strongly predicted volatility. The work links market structure to forward-looking expectations.
arxiv-2504-19158:
Sijia Xiao and co-authors present a system that helps survivors of online harm make sense of what happened to them, in work from 2025. Harms such as cyberbullying and sexual harassment are widespread on social media. Standard moderation removes content but often ignores survivors' own needs and agency.

Drawing on restorative justice, their system guides survivors through reflective questions, offers tailored advice drawn from similar survivors' stories, and lets users map a plan on interactive sticky notes. A controlled experiment found the structured process improved sensemaking over an unstructured one. The authors argue the approach builds community awareness and a support network among survivors. They also discuss design lessons, such as giving guidance while keeping survivors in charge of their own story.
arxiv-2504-19358:
Fldzhyan, Saygin, and Straupe wrote this physics paper, published in 2025. It proposes a new layout for programmable photonic circuits, chips that steer light to multiply matrices, a core task in both classical and quantum computing.

Large light-based circuits suffer from losses, hardware errors, and hard programming. The authors build on an overlooked fact: any matrix, even one that does not preserve length, can be written as a sum of two length-preserving ones. Circuits built from that sum stay shallow, at low depth, and can be programmed by formula rather than by search. Earlier designs could not offer both traits at once. The new circuits keep the perks of the standard approach based on splitting matrices into rotations and scalings. The authors present the design as a clear step up for light-based matrix multiplication.
arxiv-2504-20058:
Ambedkar Dukkipati and four co-authors build data sets and tests for stock forecasting that uses outside knowledge, not prices alone. Their work appeared in twenty twenty-five. Prices move with company links, policy shifts, wars, and the wider economy, and all of those change over time.

No public data captured that web, so the team built time-stamped knowledge graphs for the stock market. Their method treats events on those graphs as sparks in a Hawkes process, a model where one event raises the odds of others. The learned patterns rank stocks by expected returns over several holding spans. In wide tests, the rankings beat rival baselines. The authors offer the data and benchmarks for others to build on.
arxiv-2504-20658:
Dell'Anna, Montibeller, and Boato (2025) introduce TrueFake, a dataset of the newest AI-generated images as they actually circulate online. Synthetic pictures are widely used to spread misinformation. Sharing through social networks compresses them, erasing the traces detectors rely on. Most test collections ignore that real-world damage. TrueFake holds 600,000 images, made with top current generators and passed through three social networks.

The authors use the collection to benchmark leading fake-image detectors under realistic, hard conditions. Their experiments show how social media sharing degrades detection. They also identify which detectors and training strategies currently work best. They argue that forensic tools should be judged in conditions that mirror real use. The dataset is offered as a shared yardstick for that purpose.
arxiv-2504-20758:
Naratip Santitissadeekorn and co-authors reconstruct who influences whom from nothing but counts in bins. Many real systems report event counts per interval rather than timestamps: crimes per week, emails per day. The team builds network inference for such data on multidimensional Hawkes processes, where each node's activity excites others.

An ensemble algorithm on an expectation-maximization backbone handles batched counts, with a majorization trick that lets the linear Hawkes fit run in parallel. Sequential data get a Bayesian treatment whose rank-one covariance update keeps the cost down. Synthetic tests confirm recovery of the hidden network, and email traffic between European academics provides a real-world proof. The authors frame strong recovered links as the key influences worth an analyst's attention.
arxiv-2504-20958:
Steffen Wittrock and co-authors unveil a microscope for spin waves that sees the shortest ones yet. Magnons are quantized ripples of ordered spins, and at nanometer wavelengths their interactions turn rich and strange. Catching them has been the bottleneck. Their 2025 paper introduces magnon momentum microscopy, a soft X-ray scattering method that images magnon crowds across momentum space.

The method is sensitive enough to catch magnons interacting with each other, not just traveling alone. Applied to yttrium iron garnet, the standard magnonic material, it revealed a variety of nonlinear couplings never seen before. The tool is element-specific and sees into the bulk, not just the surface. Spintronics researchers get eyes for a regime they could only compute before.
arxiv-2505-00158:
Ribeiro, Lui, and Wolf add a restraining sensor to a stabilization scheme for simulating swirling compressible flows, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-five. Large-eddy simulations resolve the big whirls and model the small ones. But sharp shock waves can spawn fake oscillations that ruin the run.

The standard fix adds artificial viscosity and heat conduction where the flow has sharp gradients. That added diffusion can also smear real vortices, especially the low-pressure cores that dominate many flows, and spoil turbulence statistics. The authors' sensor restrains the artificial shear diffusivity so it acts near shocks but holds back around vortical structures. Their solvers use high-order compact finite differences, prized for fidelity. The aim is stability without paying for it in blurred physics. The model targets vortex-dominated flows in aerospace and propulsion work.
arxiv-2505-00358:
Albert Ge and co-authors present in 2025 a method called R and B for mixing training data for large models at lower cost. Older mixing plans group data by source or task, which can miss fine shades of meaning. They also grow costly as the number of groups rises.

R and B first regroups data by how close items are in meaning, making finer groups. It then balances the mix with a matrix built from group slopes seen during training, with no extra checks needed. Tests on five data sets show it matches or beats top mixing plans with very little added compute time.
arxiv-2505-00458:
Onur Mutlu, Ataberk Olgun, and İsmail Emir Yüksel argue that computing must be redesigned around memory, in a 2025 paper. Memory now dominates energy use, cost, and slowdowns in modern systems. Data-heavy fields like machine learning make the strain worse. Two scaling problems drive the crisis, they say. Device-level memory is hard to scale, and system performance gains have stalled.

The root cause, they argue, is treating memory as a dumb store. A memory-centric design lets memory manage itself. Known glitches like RowHammer could then be handled inside the memory. Computing inside memory chips could also lift speed and efficiency by orders of magnitude. Adoption hurdles are discussed frankly. The authors sketch an evolutionary path from today's machines to the new design.
arxiv-2505-00658:
Mohammed Saif and Shahrokh Valaee design resilient drone networks aided by reconfigurable intelligent surfaces in a two thousand twenty-five telecommunications paper. The surfaces can be virtually partitioned to create several relay links at once.

User equipment reaches blocked but reliable drones through these surface-aided links, with multiple users sharing one drone via non-orthogonal multiple access. The authors derive exact and approximate signal-to-interference-plus-noise formulas for aligned and non-aligned beams. Their two-step scheme clusters users by channel gain, associates drones by reliability, then partitions surfaces optimally. Simulations show connectivity gains of thirty to forty percent over traditional drone schemes.
arxiv-2505-00958:
Vahid Shamsaddini and Amin Rahimian tell two kinds of contagion apart in a 2025 paper. A simple one spreads through a single contact, as many infections do. A complex one needs support again and again from peers before a person takes it up.

To tell them apart from data on real spread is hard in practice. Other forces at work, and the way each person acts, can blur a plain test. Extended persistent homology, a tool from topology, reads the shape of the spread itself. Its signatures split the two kinds with high accuracy in tests. How the network's shape shifts over time holds the key clue. Readers see a shape-based tool answer a question that plain counts struggle with.
arxiv-2505-01258:
Chu and co-authors present PnPBO, a plug-and-play framework for a two-level kind of machine learning problem called bilevel optimization. In these problems one task sits inside another, such as tuning a model's settings while the model itself trains. Random sampling makes the math noisy, and each noise-handling method used to need its own proof.

PnPBO lets different stochastic estimators be swapped into one shared single-loop design, with a moving average added for one class of estimator. The authors prove the whole family reaches the best possible sample cost, matching ordinary single-level training. Tests on benchmark problems backed up the theory, settling a long-open question in this field.
arxiv-2505-02158:
Ioannis Avgerinos and co-workers tackle pickup and delivery routing with time windows and mid-route transfers, in a 2025 paper. Vehicles may hand loads to each other along the way, and every stop has a strict time window. That combination makes planning much harder than the classic problem.

Their exact method uses logic-based Benders decomposition and improved optimality gaps on all known benchmarks. For larger cases, a refined large neighborhood search gives near-optimal answers and scales well. They also built an instance generator to fill a gap in test data. On moderate sets the exact method closed the gap fully, while the search method stayed close on the largest sets.
arxiv-2505-02258:
Emir Esenov and four co-authors use physics-informed neural networks to read the electrical response of insulating materials, in a research paper from 2025. Such response data guide the design of insulation for high-voltage gear. Raw curves are hard to interpret because several processes unfold at different speeds.

Engineers usually fit the data with simple circuit models. The authors instead train a network that respects the circuit equations while it fits. On synthetic data with added noise, the network recovered up to five unknown circuit values accurately, with little tuning. It also recovered a hidden temperature curve from data taken at several temperatures. They see wide use for this approach.
arxiv-2505-02458:
Anouar Kouraich, Chokri Manai, and Simone Warzel show one quantum glass melting into another at the limit. Their 2025 paper deals with p-spin glasses in a crosswise magnetic field, where each spin talks to p others at once. As p runs to infinity, the free energy of the glass is proven to meet that of the quantum random energy model.

The proof weds tools for non-commuting quantum parts to the shape of extreme dips in the classical glass. Past results on the classical free energy get a review, and guesses for the first quantum corrections are stated.
arxiv-2505-02958:
Nina Beskrovnaya and co-authors use X-ray brightness to weigh the stellar winds feeding massive binary pulsars, in a 2025 paper. In these systems a neutron star sweeps up wind from a giant companion. The captured mass rate sets the X-ray luminosity. That link lets astronomers infer wind speed limits. The neutron star must catch material that moves slowly enough.

Across the studied systems, winds in the orbital plane stay within a few hundred to a thousand units of speed. That range runs two to four times slower than the star's fastest outflows. The result holds for Be-star systems and supergiants alike. Slower in-plane winds reshape accretion models. Binary evolution theorists gain firm numbers to test.
arxiv-2505-03058:
Wei Liu, Joshua Lockyer, and Suchita Kulkarni test how well a collider search can see particles from a hidden sector, in a 2025 paper. Hidden Valley theories posit a shadow world of particles that rarely touch ours. Long-lived members would decay far from the collision point, showering inside the muon system. A CMS search targets exactly that signature.

The team simulated the search across a parameterized theory space. Lifetimes were left free to keep limits model-light. Sensitivity proved broad across the sector's scale and mass ratios. It depended only weakly on the sector's color and flavor counts. Exact numbers hinge on modeling choices, which the authors flag plainly. The study also caps how strongly a mediator could couple to the hidden quarks.
arxiv-2505-03258:
W Esmail, A Hammad, and M Nojiri present a 2025 paper on IAFormer, a leaner transformer network for sorting particle collision data. Detectors record each collision as a spray of particles, and finding the interesting events means modelling how particles relate. Earlier particle transformers do this well but carry heavy costs in size and compute.

IAFormer's attention is steered by fixed, boost-proof measures of each particle pair, which slashes the parameter count. A second trick, sparse differential attention, lets the network spend its effort on the informative particles and skip the rest. The result matches the best known accuracy while running more than ten times cheaper, the authors report.
arxiv-2505-03358:
Marios Michael, Eugene Demler, and Patrick Lee wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It gives a rival account of light tests on the cuprate YBCO, where terahertz pulses seem to wake a superconducting mark far above the true transition.

The mark had been read as proof that the pump built pair coherence up to the pseudogap heat. The authors posit that local pairs, with phase links of a few lattice steps, sit there all along at rest. The pump, by parametric boosting of the Josephson plasmon, aligns the currents between the layers. A Floquet frame then fits the data. No pump-made coherence is needed, but the pseudogap must hold local pairing at rest.
arxiv-2505-03458:
Nicolas Rubido and co-authors sort Alzheimer disease from healthy aging using moving brain networks, in a 2025 paper. Brain scans can map which regions act together over time. Most studies freeze that map into one still picture. This team also built time-varying maps, which catch networks as they shift.

Data came from a large Alzheimer cohort with patients, mildly impaired people, and healthy controls, matched by age and sex. Still and moving maps were built from resting scans using a standard brain atlas. Healthy and mildly impaired people looked alike at the region level in both views. Alzheimer patients stood apart more clearly. Some links differed steadily, while others flickered near the amygdala and related areas.
arxiv-2505-03758:
Nuclear physics runs on the EXFOR library, a vast store of measured reaction data gathered over decades. Naohiko Otuka, Vidya Devi, and Osamu Iwamoto built a set of utility programs, called ForEXy, to work with that library more flexibly. At its core are converters between the library's classic format and a new JSON format the team designed.

Companion codes handle the store's storage, bibliography, and dictionaries. To show the package in action, the team used it to gather the measured fission cross sections of neptunium-237 for fast neutrons. They built the uncertainty correlations between those measurements from the library records. Those matrices then fed a fresh evaluation of the cross section across energies from 100 keV to 200 MeV. The work gives evaluators a modern toolchain for turning raw experimental archives into the numbers reactor and safety studies rely on.
arxiv-2505-03858:
Alireza Khayatian, Anil Vullikanti, and Aritra Konar present a 2025 method for finding the main pattern in a network without exposing private links. The pattern, called the principal component, helps spot key nodes and dense groups, but network data is often sensitive. Standard privacy methods add so much noise that the answer becomes useless, or they run too slowly on big graphs.

Their method first checks, in a private way, whether a given graph is well behaved, and only then releases an answer with light noise. It runs about as fast as the non-private calculation. On real networks with up to three million nodes, it ran about 180 times faster than a leading older method. The work also yields a private method for finding the densest small subgraph.
arxiv-2505-04258:
Pietro Bonazzi and co-authors fuse two camera kinds to warn drones of coming crashes. Their 2025 paper joins standard color video with event cameras, which report only pixel changes and react very fast. Two encoder arms read each stream, and a self-attention step blends the reads to call crash time and place.

On a shared test set at fifty calls per second, the fused model beat single-stream models by a small mean margin, and by more at longer range. Event-only reads beat color-only reads by wide margins on time error, at like cost. Shrunk event models trade a bit of accuracy for big savings. The gains cost more memory and math, a fair price for safer flight, the authors suggest.
arxiv-2505-04358:
Arthur Grundner and co-authors cut cloud errors in a climate model in a 2025 paper. Cloud rules are a top source of doubt in climate outlooks. Pure data-driven rules can be hard to read and hard to fit into big models.

First, the team slot a clear cloud rule, found by symbolic search on fine storm simulations, into a global air model. Next, an automatic tuner resets the mixed model against Earth data in staged runs. Cloud bias fell sharply over the Southern Ocean and over low-cloud coasts. The tuned model stayed steady under strong warming. The work shows clear rules plus tuning can lift model trust.
arxiv-2505-04558:
Wenzhao Liu and co-authors noted a structural find in 2025 about optimal answers to the travelling salesman problem. Neural solvers often fail to broaden to tours of new sizes or new point layouts, because they do not learn the underlying rules of good answers. The team looked for such a rule in the geometry of optimal tours themselves.

They identify what they call the Purity Law: in optimal tours. The prevalence of an edge grows exponentially as the points around it become sparser, a bias toward local thinness that held across many test instances. Building on it, their training method, Purity Policy Optimization, steers a neural solver's buildings toward that law during training. Tests showed it plugs into popular solvers and boosts their generalization without adding cost when solving.
arxiv-2505-05158:
Tiago de Souza Farias, Lucas Friedrich, and Jonas Maziero review machine learning with multi-level quantum systems in a 2025 survey. Qudits generalize qubits beyond two levels, offering larger state spaces in a single unit. That room allows richer data encodings, more compact circuits, and problems with many-valued structure that qubits handle awkwardly.

The review concentrates on variational algorithms and quantum neural networks built from qudits. Recent experiments show the hardware maturing toward practical use. The authors weigh where qudits beat qubits on expressivity and resource cost. For readers entering quantum learning, the survey maps a fast-moving alternative to the standard binary picture.
arxiv-2505-05758:
Azim Ospanov, Farzan Farnia, and Roozbeh Yousefzadeh present a proof-repair system in a 2025 paper. Writing proofs that a formal checker like Lean accepts is hard for language models; the usual fix is to sample thousands of attempts until one passes. Their system, APOLLO, instead fixes broken proofs step by step.

A team of agents reads the checker's complaints, repairs syntax, isolates the failing sub-goals, calls solvers, and asks the model to retry only the stuck parts on a small budget. Fixed pieces are rejoined and rechecked, looping a set number of times. On a standard benchmark, APOLLO set a new best score for small models while using fewer than a hundred samples.
arxiv-2505-05958:
Paolo Verme's 2025 paper stress-tests the models used to predict poverty when income data go missing. Such predictions drive real policy: who receives aid, where poverty maps are drawn, and how surveys are patched. Verme takes clean data with no gaps and corrupts it on purpose, hiding incomes in different patterns and amounts. He then asks classic statistical models and machine learning methods to recover the true poverty rate.

Because the true answer is known, every method can be graded honestly. Random forest, an ensemble of decision trees, gave the most consistent and accurate predictions across most scenarios. But not all: certain missing-data patterns still favored other approaches. The paper gives practitioners a concrete guide to which tool to trust under which kind of data loss, instead of a blanket endorsement of machine learning.
arxiv-2505-06058:
Beatrice Brienza, Anna Fino, Gueo Grantcharov, and Misha Verbitsky study the shape of a special class of geometric spaces in two thousand twenty-five. These spaces, called strong HKT manifolds, carry three complex structures at once plus a metric with a twist. The team asks what forms such spaces can take when they are closed and finite.

They prove that a wider class of such spaces, with full symmetry group, must in fact be of the simpler Kahler kind. A like result holds for strong HKT spaces as well. For spaces built from solvable groups, they prove a strict form and sort all cases where a key twist stays parallel. They also add a new leaf structure for these spaces and show that in eight dimensions the closed ones are always Hopf bundles.
arxiv-2505-06358:
Barber and co-authors announce a fourth, inner planet in the young TOI-2076 system. Young multi-planet systems let astronomers compare worlds born under the same conditions. TOI-2076 already held three planets of 2.5 to 4 Earth radii on 10 to 35 day orbits. The new planet is smaller, at 1.35 Earth radii. It circles in just 3.02 days, inside the others. All four are targets for space telescope air studies.

The team also re-dated the star system from spin, lithium, and star charts. TOI-2076 and its companion system are about 210 million years old. The find urges fresh searches of known systems with newer data.
arxiv-2505-06558:
Andreas Knüpfer and Timothy Callow make a popular data versioning tool work on supercomputers, in this 2025 paper. Big simulations need version control for data and recipes that a machine can rerun exactly. DataLad, built on git, offers both, but clashes with batch schedulers.

Their extension resolves the clash with the SLURM scheduler. Many jobs can now share one data repository at the same time without corrupting it. The fix also dodges wasteful habits that parallel file systems punish. The result brings tidy, reproducible workflows to high-performance clusters. The result brings tidy, reproducible workflows to high-performance clusters and their shared storage systems.
arxiv-2505-06758:
Henrik Ingo wrote this 2025 paper looking back on eight years of speeding up an open-source tool. Apache Otava detects change points in performance test data, the moments when the speed of a system truly shifts. Its code grew at firms like MongoDB, DataStax, and Confluent, written by engineers who barely coordinated yet kept optimizing as they went.

A trick for the common case, where new points simply append to a series, marks the seventh generation of speedups. Together the layers of work made the tool run some eighteen thousand to three hundred thousand times faster than the textbook original. The gains nearly allow live change detection while a user browses results. Ingo frames the history as a case study in unplanned, compounding craft.
arxiv-2505-06858:
Tianyu Chen and seven co-authors fix a weakness of Fourier neural operators, the workhorse neural solvers for partial differential equations. These models learn in the frequency domain, but high-frequency signals are sparse and usually truncated by a fixed pattern. The lost detail hurts high-resolution inputs and long-term forecasts exactly where accuracy matters.

FreqMoE first learns the low-frequency weights, exploiting the dependence of high frequencies on low ones. A sparse upward-cycling strategy then grows a mixture of experts that extends those weights into high-frequency regions. Across regular and irregular grids it gained up to about seventeen percent accuracy while using a fiftieth of the parameters of a dense model. Long-term prediction stayed stable, and the scheme ports to other operator variants.
arxiv-2505-07158:
Locking up high-definition video in real time is a race against the clock, and the usual way of scrambling images is too slow. Dong Jiang and five co-authors blame diffusion, the step that chains each pixel to the ones before it and forces slow, repeated passes. Their method drops diffusion entirely and leans on the extreme sensitivity of the SHA-256 hash: change one bit of a frame, and the hash changes completely.

Computer and graphics processors split the work, with one graphics thread per pixel, so a single pass of mixing and XOR reaches the needed security measures. On their test server, full high-definition video at 30 frames per second encrypted in about 26 milliseconds per frame, with strong statistical scores. They present the protocol in 2025 as delay-free bit-level protection.
arxiv-2505-07358:
Pongwit Srisangyingcharoen and Jongruk Pukdee compute basic string amplitudes in a 2025 theory paper. They work out the two-point scattering strength for both open and closed strings at the simplest level. In a strong-coupling style limit, the results take a shape that mirrors how a field crosses a curved anti-de Sitter space from wall to wall.

Open and closed strings give matching expressions, which is striking. Yet the effective coupling for each is set by a different kind of worldsheet curvature, one based on path length and one on surface bending. Readers get a hint that open-closed duality may carry a geometric side worth probing.
arxiv-2505-07558:
Rei Higuchi and Taiji Suzuki propose a new way to align language models with human taste in a 2025 paper. Standard alignment leans on a fixed model of how people rank answers. That shortcut has a flaw: feed it more data and the model may still never settle on what people truly prefer.

Their method, DDRO, skips the ranking model entirely. It directly estimates how much more likely preferred answers are than unpreferred ones, and trains toward that ratio. The authors prove the method is statistically consistent, meaning it does approach true preferences as data grows, whatever shape those preferences take. Benchmark tests put it ahead of standard alignment methods.
arxiv-2505-07658:
Derks and five colleagues study error control codes for quantum computers with noisy readouts in twenty twenty-five. Quantum bits are fragile, so codes must check for errors again and again as they run. These codes are set by a schedule of checks. The team asked how to tune that schedule when the checks themselves add the most noise.

They found that repeating checks helps when readout noise dominates. When other noise rules, repeating checks gains little. They also built a broader score that counts both qubits and check rounds. How results were decoded mattered a lot: a smarter decoder turned the worst code into the best in one case.
arxiv-2505-07758:
Maurice Genevieva Almeida studies balanced colorings of graphs where every vertex sees each color equally among its neighbors. His 2025 paper sets the number of colors to an odd prime count, written as 2k+1. Each vertex of a graph gets one of those colors. The coloring counts as balanced when, for every vertex, its neighbors split evenly across all colors. That is a strict demand on the graph's structure.

The paper establishes a range of results for common families of graphs. Some families are shown to admit such colorings. Others are presented with the property established case by case. The work sits in combinatorics, where parity and divisibility often decide what colorings can exist. By fixing the color count to a prime of a set form, the study links number theory with graph structure.
arxiv-2505-07858:
Siyuan Yan and co-authors work out scaling laws for speculative decoding, a trick that speeds up large language models by letting a small draft model propose tokens that the big model checks. Speed matters most for reasoning models that think in long chains. Yet how decoding speed scales with training and size was not known.

They prove log-linear laws linking the draft's acceptance rate to three factors: pretraining tokens, draft size, and batch size. Guided by the laws, their system coordinates all three dimensions for popular model families. It accepted drafts far more often than leading rivals and doubled decoding throughput in a production inference engine. The work turns an ad hoc trick into an engineering discipline.
arxiv-2505-08058:
Chris Forrester and Octavia Sulea present Hypernym Mercury, a text compression method aimed at cutting the token count of language model prompts, in a 2025 white paper. The scheme rewrites words using hypernyms, which are broader terms that cover a narrower word's meaning. By shrinking each word's semantic field and rebuilding the text later, the authors aim to cut tokens by over 90 percent.

The authors report that the compression can stay lossless and that the level of detail can be tuned. They tested it on open data, including Bram Stoker's Dracula from Project Gutenberg, at the paragraph level across genres and models. The paper's results suggest the savings hold up beyond a single text or system.
arxiv-2505-08558:
Thermodynamics for systems driven by coherent light gets a new framework from Max Schrauwen and co-authors in a 2025 paper. The head title adds the word thermodynamic to the catalog form. At the nanoscale, fluctuations and quantum effects matter, and heat and work depend on which degrees of freedom can be accessed, so no unique framework exists in general.

The authors derive a framework for coherently driven systems where the output light is assumed accessible. The resulting second law is strictly tighter than the conventional one. It demands that output light be more noisy than input light. Several established models illustrate the framework. A three-level maser is reinterpreted as an engine that reduces the noise of a coherent drive.
arxiv-2505-08758:
Nikita Nemkov presents a 2025 quantum computing paper on barren plateaus, the flat landscapes where variational quantum algorithms go to get lost. On a plateau, the training signal shrinks exponentially, and three causes are known: global observables, entangled starting states, and overly expressive circuits. Nemkov builds simple statistical models for each cause instead of wrestling with deterministic ones.

In the models, trouble is nearly certain: random global observables create plateaus with probability exponentially close to one. A sharper result follows for two observables at once: each hides its useful signal in its own exponentially small corner of parameter space, and the corners barely overlap. That independence, Nemkov argues, should rethink how warm starts and other rescue strategies are designed for plateaued circuits.
arxiv-2505-08958:
Quantum networks will link distant users by sharing entanglement, a fragile quantum connection that is hard to create over long distances. Tasdiqul Islam, Md Arifuzzaman, and Engin Arslan used reinforcement learning in 2025 to decide which links to entangle and when to swap those links onward. Older methods solve a heavy optimization each time, which is too slow for real-time requests.

Their learning approach ran twenty times faster than linear programming. Two extra ideas helped: saving unused entangled links for later requests, and swapping entanglement ahead of time on busy path segments. Together these raised request success substantially in simulations, by up to about half for the proactive step.
arxiv-2505-09158:
Xiaohan Jiang, Yuanyuan Pan, Yang Zhang, and Ye Xiong study light waves in lattices that leak energy. Their twenty twenty-five paper uses microcavity lattices with strong loss, called non-Hermitian systems. Most states in such a lattice fade fast, yet one chosen excited state can keep moving in a coherent way.

In a one-dimensional lattice, that state shifts sideways from where it was injected. The shift is a hallmark of a point gap in the spectrum. In two dimensions, the packet spreads into a V shape whose arms can be steered by geometry alone. The team reads this as a way to steer light with no change to the device structure.
arxiv-2505-09358:
Bingxin Ke and seven co-authors set out Marigold, a plan to turn text to art spread models into tools for close art work. Models like Stable Diffusion learn rich sight facts from huge sets of shots with words. Marigold tunes such a model, with small change to its build, for tasks like depth gauge from one eye. It also fits tasks like face tilt calls and splits of a shot into its base parts.

Train uses small made up data sets on a lone art card through a few days. That keeps the shift cheap to run. In spite of the light purse, Marigold hits top zero shot scores on its goal tasks. The work says that train to make art is a base too scant used for class tasks of read. A page for the work comes with the set out.
arxiv-2505-09858:
Danush Kumar Venkatesh and co-authors make synthetic surgical videos to fix skewed training data in a 2025 paper. Tools that guide surgery learn from video, but some actions and events appear rarely, so models learn them poorly. The team generate extra videos for those rare classes with a diffusion model guided by text prompts.

Their method works in two stages, first building the look of each frame and then adding timing links so motion stays smooth. A sampling step then keeps only the fake videos that fit best. When these videos were added to training, models got much better at spotting surgical actions and predicting events during operations. The team share their code in public for others to use.
arxiv-2505-11058:
Baraq Ghaleb and William Buchanan surveyed in 2025 how homomorphic encryption, which lets computers compute on data while it stays encrypted, can leak secrets through side channels. Side channels exploit implementation quirks like timing differences, a flaw class that has bitten older ciphers before. Fully homomorphic schemes rest on lattice mathematics, whose implementations carry their own leakage risks.

The paper sorts side-channel attacks on these systems into a clear categorization. Case studies show what concrete implementations reveal, from key material to plaintext hints. Countermeasures are reviewed for each weakness. The authors warn that mathematical strength alone does not secure a deployment. As encrypted computation moves into machine learning services, they argue, implementation hygiene deserves the same scrutiny as the cryptography itself.
arxiv-2505-11158:
Xing Hu and co-authors published a review in 2025 on diffusion models for hyperspectral image work. Such images record many bands of light and are used in remote sensing, farming, and checks on the environment. The data are hard to use because they are large, noisy, and full of repeated detail.

The review sorts recent methods into groups and compares them with older tools. It covers tasks such as cleaning noise, making more data, sorting images, and finding odd spots. It also looks at change over time and damage after a disaster. High cost and shaky training are noted as open limits, with paths for future work.
arxiv-2505-11358:
Jaume Llabrés and co-authors sort phase changes in opinion models into families in a 2025 paper. Voter models track how opinions spread and lock in across a network. Nonlinear versions, where groups sway more than lone voices, show rich transition types.

Several models with twin absorbing states map onto one canonical form, sharing a generalized voter transition. Adding a noise term that kills the absorbing states extends that form. The phase map then shows two transition lines, one smooth and one abrupt, meeting at a tricritical point. Many noisy models map onto this same map. Finite-size scaling above and below a key dimension confirms the shared classes.
arxiv-2505-11658:
An astronaut falls toward a planet with no air to slow her, and gravity strengthens as she drops, so her speed does not follow the simple constant-acceleration rules. Scott Scharlach tackles this Falling Astronaut Problem with the hyperbolic tangent, a smooth curve that switches between regimes, joined with basic motion equations. An earlier paper gave time as a function of position but no formula for position over time. The new work derives an approximate position formula that students can actually use.

The paper then turns to teaching. Scharlach discusses how building the approximation can deepen student understanding of motion with changing acceleration, a topic textbooks often rush past. He also points to uses beyond the classroom, where quick approximate formulas beat exact but unusable ones.
arxiv-2505-11758:
Vision language models can learn new classes from just a few sample images, but they stumble when classes look alike. Sriram Mandalika introduces SCAN in 2025, a framework that fights that confusion at the moment of guessing. Older methods pushed down all wrong classes evenly, though the classes most likely to be confused differ from query to query.

SCAN narrows its push to the few most confusable classes for each query, using contrast prompts that spell out how those classes differ. A built in weight also balances image and text evidence without hand tuning. Across eleven test sets, SCAN beat prior prompt and adapter methods, with the largest gains on fine grained sets. It also held up when labels were noisy.
arxiv-2505-12058:
Koc presents in twenty twenty-five a featherweight test kit for quick health checks of language model pipelines. Full benchmarks are slow and costly, which breaks the fast loop developers need while tuning prompts. The kit pairs a tiny hand-checked English question set with a generator that mints matching packs in any language, domain, or difficulty.

Ready packs already cover ten languages, and each ships with standard metadata and plug-in files for common test tools. A full run adds only seconds to a pipeline yet catches prompt template faults, tokeniser drift, and tuning side effects early. The author released the framework openly. It aims to give teams a unit-test style safety net for daily model work.
arxiv-2505-12458:
Many integrals in mathematics and physics blow up at special points, and the pattern of those blow ups carries deep information. Martin Helmer and Felix Tellander study integrals of Euler-Mellin type, a family that includes every scalar Feynman integral from particle physics. Their goal is the spectral decomposition of the singularities, for both the integrand and the finished integral.

For each side they give two explicit constructions of the characteristic variety and characteristic cycle, the geometric objects that encode where and how things go singular. From those, the singular locus of the integral, known in physics as its Landau singularities, can be read off. Along the way they provide a simple method to compute a local geometric quantity called the Euler obstruction, and from it the Euler characteristic of a related space.
arxiv-2505-12758:
Matias Quintana and co-authors survey a thousand people across five countries on how city streets look and feel, asking whether who you are changes what you see. Urban perception studies usually average everyone together, hiding group differences. Their balanced sample rated street images on classic scales like safe and beautiful, plus new ones like green and walkable.

Demographics and personality clearly shifted the ratings. Where a person lived colored their judgments further. Machine learning models trained on existing global data leaned too rosy, overestimating the pleasant scales and underestimating the bleak ones compared with people. The authors argue planners need perception data that respects local and personal differences, and release their dataset for that purpose.
arxiv-2505-13058:
Gabriel Bena, Maxence Faldor, Dan Goodman, and Antoine Cully push in a 2025 paper neural cellular automata toward universal computation. Grid automata with local rules can compute anything, as the Game of Life proves. Learned continuous versions raise whether that power survives the move to smooth rules.

Their model, objectives, and training schemes steer learned rules toward general computing. Basic parts come first, matrix products and transposition trained as grid behaviors. The climb ends with a neural network emulated inside the automaton that sorts handwritten digits. That emulation runs in the grid state itself, not as an outside readout. The work lays a path toward analog general purpose computers grown by training.
arxiv-2505-13258:
Jingyi Ren and co-authors introduced TRACE in 2025, a method to make language model answers show their evidence. Systems that search documents before answering often give replies with no clear path back to the sources. That hides errors and wastes the context that was retrieved.

TRACE trains models with reinforcement learning to give structured answers with explicit citations. Rewards cover evidence relevance, format, and accuracy, and a merging strategy keeps training steady across those signals. On three hard question sets, TRACE raised accuracy by ten to thirty percent and matched top commercial models. Tests on new tasks showed the skill carried over. Code was made public with the study.
arxiv-2505-13358:
Nimrod Berman and co-authors look for a faster way to run diffusion models, the image generators that build a picture step by step. That step-by-step process gives good results but costs a lot of computer time. The team wants a model that can produce a clean image in one step instead.

Their approach, called the Koopman Distillation Model, rests on an old math idea for turning curved motion into straight motion in a new space. The model maps a noisy input into that space, moves it forward with a simple learned rule, then decodes it into a clean sample. Tests on standard benchmarks show results that rival other fast methods.
arxiv-2505-13458:
Bandar Siddani and co-authors present a multiscale method for simulating dense flows of grains, in work from 2025. Coarse models of sand-like flows are fast but rely on closure rules that are often crude. A linked fine model can supply those rules, yet running it everywhere is far too costly.

Their method trains neural networks on fine simulations to stand in for the closure rules. A group of networks also estimates its own uncertainty at each point. Where the estimate looks unreliable, the system runs fresh fine simulations and updates the networks. The networks are shaped to keep the coarse model well behaved. Tests on sloped flows and a collapsing column of grains in three dimensions show the method stays accurate while cutting cost sharply.
arxiv-2505-13858:
Gonzalo Constante-Flores, Hao Chen, and Can Li enforce hard rules in deep learning in twenty twenty-five. Deployed models in safety-critical settings must satisfy strict constraints. Physical laws, fairness rules, and safety limits are examples. Standard networks have no built-in way to guarantee such limits.

Regularization and projection fixes are limited, costly, or lack guarantees. Their framework is model-agnostic and handles input-dependent linear constraints. A task network pursues prediction accuracy. A safe network, trained with decision rules from robust optimization, ensures feasibility. The final prediction mixes the two networks convexly. That mixture guarantees constraint satisfaction during training and deployment alike. Readers get predictions that cannot cross the lines their domain forbids.
arxiv-2505-14058:
Copulas let statisticians study how random variables depend on each other apart from their individual distributions. Ratio-type copulas are prized for their flexibility in modeling joint behavior. Ziad Adwan and Nicola Sottocornola focus on the separate kind, where the dependence function splits into a product of one-variable functions. They revisit a theorem that states when such copulas are valid and generalize it to broader settings.

They also examine when the theorem can be reversed, for concave generating functions, and they propose new assumptions that secure validity where the old ones fell short. The results refine the theory of separate copulas and widen where it can be used, from pure mathematics to finance, risk management, and machine learning.
arxiv-2505-14158:
Sanjay Govindan, Maurice Pagnucco, and Yang Song steer language models toward a chosen year in a 2025 paper. Models learn facts from mixed eras, so they may answer a question about 2022 with facts from later years. The team test activation engineering, a method that nudges the model's inner signals at run time instead of retraining it.

They grounded three versions of one model family at set points in time and varied which inner layers received the nudge and how prompts were phrased. Gains reached forty-four percent under relative phrasing and sixteen percent under explicit dates. That matched a fine-tuning baseline while costing far less compute and needing no prepared data sets. The result points to cheap, reversible time control for chatbots.
arxiv-2505-14258:
Ivan Ridkokasha and co-authors link two views of how matter is spread in the young universe, in a paper from 2025. One view is the full three dimensional spread of matter at small scales. The other comes from the Lyman-alpha forest, the pattern of absorbed light in spectra of distant quasars, which is only a one dimensional trace.

The flux trace is shaped by heat, pressure, and the motion of gas, so the link to matter is not direct. The authors work out how the power patterns in the two views correspond despite those twists. A firm link matters because the small scale matter pattern carries clues about dark matter and other basic physics. The forest is one of the few tools that can reach those scales outside galaxies.
arxiv-2505-14358:
Shobhana and colleagues presented a passive method in twenty twenty-five for measuring how long web services take to respond, without touching the client's device. Operators need that number to spot slowdowns and attacks, but return traffic often takes a different road back, hiding the timing.

Their system, PIRATE, watches only the outgoing requests at a middle point. Some requests trigger follow-ups, and the gap between such a causal pair stands in for the round-trip delay. The trick works even when packet headers are encrypted. In tests on a realistic web application, the estimates landed within one percent of the true client-side delay. Plugged into a load balancer, the measurements cut the slowest responses by thirty-seven percent. The authors say the method gives operators client-grade insight with no probing traffic and no client software.
arxiv-2505-14458:
Imon Banerjee, Vinayak Rao, and Harsha Honnappa build a gauge in a 2025 paper for how a steered chain moves from state to state. Such chains run through time study, trial-based learning, and probe work. Old gauge tools assume free samples and a known smoothness grade, both false when a hand steers the chain.

Their gauge adapts as it learns and asks for no prior smoothness grade. It also makes no call on how the steering hand acts, even when that hand has memory. The build rests on fresh work in free-form gauge craft. Field teams gain a tool that fits real steered data.
arxiv-2505-14658:
Giovanni Rolandino and co-authors wrote a 2025 paper on a dry electrode grid that reads the fine movement signals of the hand from the skin, with no gel. The signals are the small electrical sparks of the arm, read in a dense grid. A known network then estimates the position of the hand from them. Gel electrodes are the norm, but they dry out, cost, and irritate.

The team built the dry grid with just two rows of electrodes. They ran it head to head with a gel setup, through the same position network. Skin-contact checks weighed two side effects: voltage division and power-line hum. The position estimates of the dry grid matched those of the gel setup, and at times beat them. A spread check showed the two rows lose little information. The team presents them as a cheap, friendly path for prosthetic and rehabilitation gear.
arxiv-2505-14758:
Issak and co-authors turn ethics into pictures in 2025 to probe how AI image tools carry moral ideas. Ethics theories shift over time, and so do the models, which makes each a moving lens on the other. Talks with ten ethics experts first set the base: the theories sorted into five families.

Images made from those families became a gallery shown back to the same experts. Eight themes surfaced, the team reports, with morality, society, and learned links at the center of how the theories came out in pictures. The work sits in a young field that uses art to question tech. It warns that image models soak up social habits along with ideas, so their pictures of right and wrong need a critical eye, not trust.
arxiv-2505-14858:
Fernando Coutinho, Nicolas Lizarralde, and Fernando Lizarralde control two robots building metal parts together in a 2025 paper. The process, wire arc additive manufacturing, lays down weld metal layer by layer, usually with the part kept flat.

Flat building fails on complex shapes, leaving overhangs and stepped surfaces. The authors' scheme steers the welding torch over the growing part while a second robot tilts the workpiece. Each new layer is kept aligned with gravity, which improves quality. The control method plans the torch path in the part's own frame while tracking orientation in the world frame. Parts with tricky geometry were built in a two-robot cell to prove the approach.
arxiv-2505-14958:
Bingying Dai and co-authors forecast mutation effects on proteins in a 2025 paper. Swapping one amino acid can break or boost a protein, but the space of swaps is vast and lab tests are slow and dear. The Potts model reads family history to score how sites in a protein lean on each other.

Past Potts fits cut corners with a mean-field shortcut and dropped the protein's shape. The new frame keeps the shape facts and solves the model in high dimensions with firmer grounds. Better scores could rank which swaps to test first. That ranking speeds work on enzymes and drug targets.
arxiv-2505-15458:
Felipe Hernández maps exactly which infinite linear patterns must appear inside any reasonably dense set of integers, in this 2025 paper. Density here is upper Banach density, a generous measure that counts a set as substantial if some long stretches of it are thick. A shift of the set, sliding it along the number line, is allowed before hunting for patterns.

Two famous results framed the question. Szemerédi's theorem guarantees arithmetic progressions of any length in such sets, and a recent density finite sums theorem, by Kra, Moreira, Richter, and Robertson, guarantees rich additive configurations. Hernández's article describes all possible infinite linear configurations that a shift of any positive-density set must contain, settling both predecessors as special cases of one picture. The result belongs to density Ramsey theory, the study of order forced by size alone.
arxiv-2505-15558:
Chen and co-authors build Robo-DM, a toolkit for storing and serving the huge data sets used to teach robots. Modern robot learning feeds on recordings of remote-controlled demonstrations, mixing video, text, and numbers from several cameras. Such data is bulky to curate, ship, and load. Robo-DM packs it into a self-contained format built on a standard media container.

Compression shrinks the data by up to seventy times with slight loss, or about three and a half times with none. Smart caching speeds up loading far beyond a rival framework. A model trained on the heavily compressed data still performed a pick-and-place task as well as before. The authors offer the open-source toolkit as plumbing for the era of giant robot data collections.
arxiv-2505-15658:
Šárka Nečasová, Tong Tang, Emil Wiedemann, and Lu Zhu prove energy conservation for weak solutions of the inviscid primitive equations. Their paper from twenty twenty-five works on a bounded domain, the setting of ocean and atmosphere models. Onsager-type smoothness terms are assumed. A prior result on domains with walls guides the path, but this system adds fresh snags.

The vertical velocity is barely known, which starves key estimates. Corner points in the domain add more trouble. The team brings new ideas to clear both. A side result gives a term that rules out stray energy loss as viscosity fades. The work ties a famous turbulence idea to a workhorse model of geophysics. Energy bookkeeping for rough flows gains a firmer base.
arxiv-2505-15758:
Leon Wichette and co-authors published this quantum error correction study in 2025. Quantum computers need error-correcting codes, and judging a decoder's quality means simulating countless failures. A known mapping turns such codes into models from statistical mechanics, where partition functions summarize ensembles. The authors define a ratio of these functions that gives the success chance of one optimal decoding strategy.

They contrast that ratio with a second quantity tied to a different decoder, and show the two are not the same. The gap between them hints that the best decoding boundary may extend beyond the usual phase boundary. Working through the toric code under bit-flip noise, they show ratios can be estimated from far fewer samples than failure counting needs. That efficiency matters most at low noise, where failures are rare and precious. A look at the color code rounds out the analysis.
arxiv-2505-16258:
Aashish Anantha Ramakrishnan and co-authors presented IRONIC in this 2025 paper on spotting sarcasm in posts that mix images and text. Sarcasm is hard for machines because the words often mean the opposite of what they say. Most current tools need heavy task-specific training to catch it.

IRONIC instead reasons in steps about how the image and text relate, checking reference, analogy, and tone. It learns from examples in the prompt rather than from retraining. Across several baselines, the method reached the best scores yet on zero-shot sarcasm spotting. The authors argue that borrowing ideas from language and mind research makes machine reasoning stronger.
arxiv-2505-16358:
Gur Keinan and Omer Ben-Porat model the tug between a platform and its creators over sharing work with generative AI. Creators choose how much quality to invest and whether to let the platform's AI learn from their content. The platform, in turn, can share its AI-driven revenue to coax consent.

Their 2025 paper centers on full-sharing equilibria, where every creator agrees to share. Such outcomes please both theory and practice, and the pair find when they can exist. A surprise link to the prisoner's dilemma shapes the analysis. They also solve, in quick form, for the revenue split that best serves the platform while holding the sharing pact. Simulations trace how the split moves creator welfare.
arxiv-2505-16558:
Xin Wu and co-authors present a 2025 arXiv paper on hyperon decays through the lens of flavor symmetry. Hyperons are heavy cousins of protons and neutrons, and their two-body decays without leptons test the Standard Model's quark rules. The team sorts the weak Hamiltonian into SU(3) symmetry pieces and builds decay amplitudes two ways, by symmetry components and by topology diagrams.

Corrections for the strange quark's mass enter systematically. A global fit to current data pins down the unknowns and predicts branching ratios and asymmetries for several channels. One channel, a sigma decay, sits more than a standard deviation from experiment, a hint the authors flag for new physics.
arxiv-2505-16758:
Qian-Xi Zhao, Jian-Jun Dong, and Zi-Xiang Hu measure the statistics of work done on strongly linked electrons. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Quantum work fluctuates when a system is driven out of equilibrium. Correlated electrons resist the usual analytic tools. Their testbed is the Ising-Kondo model of heavy fermion materials. A Monte Carlo framework does the heavy sampling.

The method builds the moment generating function of work step by step. Mean work, irreversible work, spread, and skew all follow from it. At low temperatures these quantities kink sharply at the metal-insulator transition. Heat smooths the kink into a crossover. Work statistics thus flag the phase change. Thermodynamics gains a fresh diagnostic for correlated matter.
arxiv-2505-16958:
André Pedroso Kowacs, writing alone, settles a question about smoothing operators in a 2025 math paper. The setting is a compact Lie group, a smooth space with a group structure, such as rotations. An operator is globally hypoelliptic when it forces any rough solution of its equation to be smooth everywhere. Systems of such operators, acting together, are harder to judge.

The author starts from a recent result for operators on vector bundles over such spaces. He derives a clean condition that is both needed and enough for a whole system of left-invariant operators to have the smoothing trait. The proof stands on its own, without the bundle frame. He also gives easier-to-check conditions for a large class of cases. Those rest on lower bounds for the smallest singular values of the matrices that encode each operator.
arxiv-2505-17358:
Chinmay Talegaonkar and co-authors turn a relative depth model into a metric one using blur, in a 2025 paper. Marigold, a diffusion model, judges depth order well but not real distances, and it fades on unfamiliar scenes. The trick needs no retraining: shoot the same view twice, once with a small and once with a wide aperture, and let defocus blur betray the true scale.

At run time the method tunes the model's scale settings and noise seeds against a blur formation equation. On a self gathered real dataset it beat standing zero shot metric methods in both numbers and judged quality.
arxiv-2505-17458:
Guiquan Sun, Xikun Zhang, Jingchao Ni, and Dongjin Song teach graph models that keep learning without forgetting. Real graph data, full of mixed entity types and relations, change constantly, but a model retrained on new tasks tends to erase what old tasks taught. In such graphs, old knowledge hides not just in the target nodes but in their typed neighborhoods and relation-specific responses.

Their framework, HERO, replays a few chosen nodes together with compact, rebuilt neighborhoods, since replaying nodes alone provably skews the old lessons. A distillation step also aligns the model's predictions and its semantic responses with its past self, and a look-ahead step keeps it flexible for the new task. Across four data sets and three model backbones, HERO matched or beat the best rivals while forgetting competitively little.
arxiv-2505-17658:
F O Schumann and co-authors sharpen pictures of magnetic domains taken with a photoelectron microscope near the light threshold. Such images often come out faint, which hides the domain pattern on a surface. The team finds the fix in symmetry and in picking which electron paths reach the detector.

Careful placement of a contrast aperture selects electron momenta that carry the magnetic signal. Symmetry reasoning shows why that pick boosts both domain selectivity and brightness contrast. The team tests the idea on an iron surface and matches measured images against photoemission calculations. The match proves the method works in practice. Sharper domain images help labs study thin magnetic films used in sensors and memory, where domain shape rules device behavior.
arxiv-2505-17758:
Wang Chen, Hongzheng Shi, and Jintao Ke present HRSim, an open simulator for high-capacity ride-sharing services. Cities hope pooled rides can cut congestion and emissions, but testing pricing, matching, and fleet rules needs a testbed that mirrors real streets at scale. Older platforms often lack size, flexibility, or open access. The catalog title carries a funding note, so the plain head title governs here.

HRSim builds on real road networks and demand data, and simulates pricing, routing, matching, and empty-car repositioning as drivers and riders act. Its parts can be swapped, and it covers both pooled and solo ride modes. A live visual module tracks performance while a run proceeds. Built-in exact and shortcut solvers let it handle large fleets. Demo runs cover emissions counting, scaling checks, and strategy trials, work published in 2025.
arxiv-2505-17858: Yossi Bokor Bleile and co-authors wrote a 2025 math paper on tunnels between separate parts of a cell complex, a shape built from simple blocks. Work in chemistry drives the question, since such tunnels matter in molecules. They give a formal way to define these links using homology, and a method to find when each tunnel is born and dies as the shape grows.
arxiv-2505-18158: Ivan Mikhailov uses asymptotic dimension to compute distances between infinite spaces in this 2025 math paper. The distance at issue is the Gromov-Hausdorff distance, which measures how far apart two metric spaces are in shape. Mikhailov shows that for some unbounded spaces the value can be found by this route. He works the plane against the integer lattice as an example: there, the Gromov-Hausdorff distance equals the plain Hausdorff distance between the two. Short results of this kind give concrete values in a theory where exact distances are rare.
arxiv-2505-18258:
Luisa Lucie-Smith and eight co-authors rethink how the birth of galaxies reshapes the cosmos. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five. Gas blown out by young stars and black holes, called feedback, changes how matter clumps. Most studies measure this by comparing the clumping in full simulations with gravity-only ones.

This team instead tracks the growth histories of dark matter halos, the clumps that host galaxies. They ask which halo groups each kind of cosmic probe really sees. One probe, based on fast gas motion, sees far smaller halos than X-ray or lensing probes do. Feedback had its strongest effect when halos reached a certain mass, at whatever age. That insight can sharpen how future surveys correct for galaxy effects.
arxiv-2505-18458:
Xuanhe Zhou and co-authors survey in a 2025 review the two-way street between large language models and data management. Data work feeds the models: gathering, cleaning, deduplicating, storing, and serving the text they train and retrieve on. In return, the models are becoming engines inside data systems themselves.

The survey maps both directions in detail, from KV-cache handling and checkpointing to model-driven data cleaning, discovery, and query rewriting. Multi-agent setups and retrieval-grounded prompting recur as themes. For builders of either field, the message is that the two now design each other.
arxiv-2505-18658:
Pankaj Kumar and Subhankar Mishra survey how to make large language models robust in a 2025 paper. A robust model gives steady, sound answers across many inputs, even when inputs are odd or hostile. Failures in live use can mislead users, so the stakes are real for work and public tools.

The survey first sets out what robustness means and how models fail. It then sorts the sources of weakness into flaws in the model, flaws in the data, and attacks from outside. Next it reviews the main fixes on offer, and the tests and scores used to judge them. The authors close with gaps in current testing and paths for new work.
arxiv-2505-18758:
Alexander Conzelmann and Robert Bamler present a method to shrink stored neural networks in a 2025 paper. Growing model sizes strain small devices such as embedded sensors. Compression can help, as long as performance stays close to the original model. Their framework works after training and joins quantization, which reduces number precision, with entropy coding, which packs the result tightly.

They extend a classic layer wise loss with a cost term for the storage rate, estimated by a simple quadratic form. Exact local solutions follow a classic brain surgeon method for pruning and tuning. On several vision networks, the method cut bit rates by twenty to forty percent at the same performance as a leading codec. Code is shared in public.
arxiv-2505-18858:
Maeva Guerrier and co-authors present a robotics paper, published in 2025, on using formal safety rules as teachers for learning robots. Reinforcement learning robots usually get one harsh penalty and a reset when they stray somewhere unsafe, which hides the lasting harm of staying in danger. When the authors instead charged a steady penalty without ending the episode, standard learners stalled, fenced in by accumulated losses.
