Their remedy brings in control barrier functions, rules with proven guarantees that steer a robot away from forbidden zones. Three blends of the rules with standard learners taught safer behavior and better performance. Trials in simulation and on a real four wheeled robot supported the approach.
arxiv-2505-19058:
Chung I Lu, Julian Sester, and Aijia Zhang make reinforcement learning cautious about model error. Their 2025 paper tackles Deep Q learning for continuous state spaces, where the true rules of motion are uncertain. Their robust version plans against the worst plausible transition within a ball around a reference model.

Solving the robust Bellman equation directly is hard, so they dualize and smooth it with a Sinkhorn distance term, then fit the result with deep networks. The recipe turns the standard Deep Q Network into a worst case optimizer. A portfolio task built on S&P 500 data shows the method working in practice. Convergence guarantees and an error breakdown into clear parts round out the theory.
arxiv-2505-19458:
Akiyoshi Tomihari and Ryo Karakida wrote this 2025 theory paper on self-attention, the core part of modern language models. Much past work studies attention layers through an energy score that falls as the state updates. That view needs strong limits, such as symmetry, which real models may not meet. The authors instead study the dynamics with no energy score assumed.

Their tool is the Jacobian matrix, which tracks how small changes in the state grow or fade. They show that the normalization step keeps the dynamics tame, and that Lyapunov exponents place the system near a critical state. That near-critical state, they argue, tracks strong inference, and they build training methods on the idea.
arxiv-2505-20058:
Yihong Lin and co-authors present a pipeline to rebuild a 3D hand mesh from one photo in a 2025 paper. Hands bend in many ways, depth is ambiguous, and fingers hide each other. Past methods were slow or awkward at placing mesh points in space. The new pipeline predicts point positions directly.

It first draws 2D cues from the image to guide the 3D task. A spiral decoder then refines the mesh in layers that adapt weights to point positions. A region layer polishes each hand zone by its physical traits. On the FreiHAND benchmark, the method beats prior real-time systems by a clear margin.
arxiv-2505-20158:
Timur Sağlam and Larissa Schmid test how well code plagiarism detectors stand up when copied code is scrambled by machine. Their 2025 paper deals with programming homework, where copying is a steady problem. Detectors shrug off simple scrambles, but deep scrambles that reshape code while it keeps its behavior can slip past. Past checks of added defenses used a narrow set of attacks and skipped AI-made scrambles.

The team pits two defenses against a wide range of attacks, both rule-based and AI-made, across many real data sets. Millions of code pairs were compared. Both defenses caught far more scrambled copies, and they even spotted AI-written code better, though not built for that task.
arxiv-2505-20558:
Ware and Young rank the stars a future space telescope should visit first in its hunt for living worlds. The planned Habitable Worlds Observatory will photograph planets directly, at great cost in time per target. A good target keeps a planet in the mild habitable zone for billions of years.

Their method computes the chance that each orbit has stayed in that zone for two billion years, the time Earth took to oxygenate its air. They applied it to 164 candidate stars. The score peaked for stars a bit older than the Sun's family, around three to four billion years. The hottest stars looked unlikely to host such a steady zone today.
arxiv-2505-20758:
Ying Huang, Tingjian Luo, and Youde Wang settle when a class of Schrödinger equations has ground states in a 2025 paper. The equations mix two diffusion operators of different orders and carry a nonlinearity that varies in space, a combination arising in optical and quantum models. Ground states are the lowest-energy standing waves, and their existence depends on the mass regime.

Working through constrained variational problems, the authors prove existence, non-existence, and long-range behavior across subcritical, critical, and supercritical masses. Some existence results are sharp, marking exact thresholds. As a byproduct, they obtain many bound states at prescribed mass. The paper gives this equation family a nearly complete map of when its basic waves exist.
arxiv-2505-20858:
Jason Chui, Daniel Cremers, and co-authors give a chance based way to align photos into three dimensional scenes from a cold start, in a 2025 paper. Classic alignment needs sharp start values and known lens traits. New dense match tools give rich pairs but with noise that breaks old track rules.

Their way treats scene points as soft clouds and weights each pair by trust. A pose graph with smart link cuts keeps the whole scene in line. A twin guess rule clears mirror traps. Tests beat both classic and learned tools on truth and held up in wild scenes.
arxiv-2505-21058:
Search engines learn ranking from big teacher models, but which part of the training recipe earns the gains was muddy. Andrew Parry and two co-authors pull the recipe apart in 2025, separating how training examples are chosen from how their labels are written. Popular pipelines had grown baroque, stacking a dozen models with murky data origins.

Theory shows the two choices bend the model along independent axes, and augmentation can fix a biased ranker under stated conditions. Experiments deliver a surprise: hard example mining, a hero of older training styles, can be useless or harmful under distillation. The entropy of the teacher's rankings steers learning more than the sampling does. The authors urge simpler, cheaper recipes aimed at the real levers.
arxiv-2505-21758:
Maria Patrou and six co-authors hunt for wasted energy in supercomputing in a 2025 paper. Exascale machines draw enormous power, and even small efficiency gains save real money and carbon. Modern chips let operators cap power separately for processor and graphics units, but knowing where to set the caps is the puzzle.

The team tested two ways of judging the trade-off between speed and energy on a physics simulation running on a current superchip. One metric blends speedup, energy, and delay; the other measures distance from an ideal point in a multi-goal space. Adjusting graphics power caps task by task, while steering power between the two units, improved energy use for some tasks. The authors are modest about the wins: for a mostly compute-bound code, savings are targeted, not huge. Their groundwork points toward self-tuning power management in future systems.
arxiv-2505-22758:
Aniruddha Nrusimha and co-authors present, in 2025, a way to run large language models faster when requests arrive one at a time. Most optimized software targets big batches, where computing power dominates. In low-batch settings, memory traffic and the overhead of launching many small operations dominate instead, and those cases matter for edge devices and snappy services.

Their system, FlashFormer, fuses the model's entire forward pass into a single program kernel, removing launch overheads and streamlining memory flow. Across model sizes and compression settings, it delivered solid speedups over existing inference kernels. The work argues whole-model fusion is the right shape for low-batch serving.
arxiv-2505-22858:
Sanjoy Kundu, Shanmukha Vellamcheti, and Sathyanarayanan Aakur recognize activities from a wearer's view in a 2025 paper. First person video is open ended: the next action may be one the system never saw. Their framework, ProbRes, searches a large label space with a jump diffusion process. Commonsense priors shape that space so the search stays sane.

Vision language models refine guesses as evidence comes in. The stochastic search balances exploring new labels against exploiting likely ones, skipping full enumeration. Tests ran across several open world benchmarks. A search that stays cheap while staying open could help glasses and robots name what their users are doing, even when the activity is new.
arxiv-2505-23258:
Haojie Jia and four co-authors present SealOS Plus for securities trading systems in two thousand twenty-five. Trading systems now run as microservices, which strains resource plans. Delays grow and chips sit idle under old schedulers. Exchanges demand replies in tens of milliseconds.

Their stack adds three parts to a container platform. A deep reinforcement learner schedules resources on the fly. A three level cache speeds common trading steps. A memory based net predicts load ahead of time. In live use at an exchange, chip use rose high. Reply times fell and peak throughput hit a strong rate. Results met the strict demands of the floor.
arxiv-2505-23358:
Reem AlJunaid and Muzammil Behzad present a model that writes rich, knowledge-filled captions for images. Their paper appeared in 2025. Many caption systems produce bland lines that miss context. Their model replays stored knowledge while it writes, and uses beam search to draft several candidate captions before choosing. Attention modules inside the image encoder sharpen which features the writer sees.

Training schedules smooth the learning process. The authors report gains in both caption quality and recognition of the facts an image shows. The model also handled knowledge ideas it had not seen in training. They present the design as a step toward captions that inform, rather than merely label, useful for search, teaching, and access tools for blind users.
arxiv-2505-23758:
Yusuf Dalva, Hidir Yesiltepe, and Pinar Yanardag give a train free way to blend many lone traits in one shot edit, in a 2025 paper. Lone trait packs teach a maker one face or style at a time. Past blends need retrain or hard clamps that oft break scene sense in the base shot.

Trait zones light up in set spots early in the clean steps of the maker. A first pass maps those zones, then trait packs run just in their zones. Face faith beats past blends while light and fine bits hold. Shot tales with many stars can thus be built fast.
arxiv-2505-23858:
Aashwin Mishra and co-authors outlined a machine learning plan for a major X-ray light source in 2025. The upgraded source, LCLS-II-HE, will be far brighter, and its experiments are growing more complex. Beams must stay within a fraction of a micron over a kilometer-long machine.

Without live feedback and a fast path from data to insight, the team warns, researchers will drown in mostly useless data. Their plan applies learning at each stage: the electron source, the optics, the end stations, and the fast detectors. Examples from accelerator, optics, and user work show how the pieces fit. The aim is to deliver the design performance to users in practice, not just on paper.
arxiv-2505-24258:
Vishal Pallagani, Nitin Gupta, John Aydin, and Biplav Srivastava test if word tools can track a flow in a 2025 paper. Flow is how a mark is born, bent, and kept in a step tale, the base of all plan craft.

Their test turns eight stock flow crafts to asks in plain text. The crafts run from which birth rules a use, to which marks may bear a germ. Three worlds bear them: fare lists, road plans, and made work plans. Near two and a half thousand asks fill the bank. A thought-deep tool led, but at a score of time past its kin. The plain and code tools scored near a coin toss. The authors give the bank as a first gauge of this core skill.
arxiv-2505-24358:
Larger families of cospectral graphs can be built from smaller ones, Abhinav Bitragunta, Hareshkumar Jadav, and Ranveer Singh show in a 2025 paper. Cospectral graphs share the same spectrum, so they cannot be told apart by spectral methods alone. Connected families of such graphs are a useful test bed for what spectra can and cannot determine about a graph's structure.

Their method starts with two cospectral families of given sizes. The size of the new family depends on the Cartesian primality of the input graphs. It can be the product of the sizes, their sum minus one, or the larger of the two, based on how strict the applied conditions are. Under the strictest condition, many new cospectral triplets are generated, and relaxed conditions yield many more.
arxiv-2505-24458:
Tianlong Yu and ten co-authors release a data set for studying how augmented reality and chat models can be turned into tools of social manipulation. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. The set records staged attacks in settings like meetings, classes, and mixers. Sixty people took part across many scripted talks.

Each record pairs headset video and audio with scene context and fake social profiles. It also holds trust ratings and measures of how open each target was to influence. The staged attacks worked at alarming rates: most targets clicked phishing links or took calls. Trust often rose after the talks rather than falling. Guards include scrubbed identities and ethics board approval. The authors offer the set to help build defenses against such attacks. It is shared in public for research use.
arxiv-2505-24558:
Simone Cammarasana and Giuseppe Patanè add a new twist to image networks in 2025. Standard convolution treats all nearby pixels in the same way. Their weighted version folds in a density map that gives each nearby pixel a weight based on its place. The change keeps the same count of learned values and fits current network designs.

The team tests the method on image sorting and on cleaning noisy images. Well known networks gain clear score boosts with the weighted step in place. Run times stay close to the standard step thanks to precomputed maps. The idea also extends to three dimensional scans and to signals over time.
arxiv-2505-24658:
Yeseon Hong and co-authors build a test frame in a 2025 paper for how chat models show empathy over many turns. As models step into tender talks, one warm reply is not enough. Warmth can drift, ring hollow, or swell into mere nodding as a chat runs on.

Their frame grades empathy as a flow shaped by what the user bares, turn by turn. In two studies with more than eighty people, stock replies missed the mark by flat, stock warmth. A self-check prompt eased that flaw but bred a new one: too much agreement. Chat builders gain a lens that sees empathy fail in motion, not just in one shot.
arxiv-2506-00158:
Eli Chien, Wei-Ning Chen, and Pan Li prove a privacy result for a thrifty training method in a 2025 computing paper. Zeroth-order optimization fine-tunes big models by probing outputs instead of storing gradients, which suits private data and small memory. Privacy amplification by iteration gives strong guarantees for gradient methods, but the proof leans on noise spread evenly in all directions. Zeroth-order updates push scalar noise along random directions instead, breaking the argument.

The authors design a hybrid noise scheme and a coupling analysis that sidesteps the broken step. The result is the first convergent hidden-state privacy bound for this method. Better guarantees make private fine-tuning of large models easier to certify.
arxiv-2506-00258:
Qianqi Yan and co-authors test whether multimodal language models notice when something is quietly wrong with a request, in this 2025 paper. Real inputs can point at missing objects, clash with facts, or ask for impossible actions. Success then means spotting the hidden flaw, not just obeying. The team built a diagnostic suite across four real-world failure types and ran six leading models, including top commercial ones.

Models often sailed past the flaw and complied anyway, even when they clearly had the skill to catch it. Direct probing showed the ability was present but suppressed by a drive to please the user. Simple fixes helped a lot, above all forcing the model to ask a clarifying question. The authors frame trust as a behavior problem, not just a skill problem.
arxiv-2506-00358:
Sarthak Kumar Maharana and co-authors present a benchmark for sound-and-vision models under damage in 2025. Models that read both audio and video do well on clean data, yet their strength under real-world shifts is unclear. Older test sets damage only one channel at a time, which misses how faults hit both channels together.

Their set, called AVRobustBench, covers four data sets with 75 paired damage types each. Top supervised and self-taught models lost ground as damage grew worse. Standard fix-on-the-fly methods gave small gains at best. The team adds a simple fix method that joins the two channels while discounting unsure samples, and it improved scores on one data set.
arxiv-2506-00458:
Nina Cohen and Kordel France train computer players for Hanabi, a card game where teamwork is everything and no one can see their own cards. Players hold their hands facing outward, so each person knows everyone else's cards but not their own, and the group must build stacks through limited hints. That hidden information makes the game a test for reinforcement learning, where agents learn from reward.

The authors tried a range of methods, from table-based learners to deep networks, and played them against copies of themselves and other types. Some agents scored best against one partner type, while others adapted to whoever they faced. Overall, methods that learn stepwise value updates beat the table-based ones, and two stood out: a tabular expected-update method and a deep Q-learning agent. The paper maps which pairings produce the most interesting and effective play.
arxiv-2506-00558:
Adrian Azzarelli and co-authors release ViVo, a data set for volumetric video, in a 2025 paper. Volumetric video captures a scene in three dimensions, so viewers can move around inside it. Rebuilding and squeezing such video needs varied, realistic test data. Older data sets lack the range of content found in real production work.

ViVo broadens what diversity means for this field. Scenes vary in human traits like skin and hair, and in tricky sights like glass, shine, and liquid. Each sequence packs many paired color and depth views, plus calibration, sound, masks, and point clouds. The team benchmarked leading rebuilding and compression methods on it. Results showed the set is hard for current tools.
arxiv-2506-00658:
Raina Gao and co-authors introduce, in a 2025 paper, a benchmark for how well language models handle sarcasm. Sarcasm says the opposite of what it means, which makes it hard for machines to read and to produce. Their benchmark sorts sarcasm into seven types, from deadpan and polite to raging and manic.

They labeled entries from an existing sarcasm data set by type. Then they tested models under several prompting styles, from no examples to step by step reasoning. They also propose a new prompt style built on emotion, and a generation method drawn from sarcasm's key parts: a clash of meaning, shock value, and context. The best classifier used the emotion prompts, though its score stayed modest. Human judges liked the emotion based generations much more than plain ones.
arxiv-2506-01258:
Jason Lambe and co-authors estimate the settings of a Hawkes process, a model for events that trigger more events, when only counts per time block are known. With exact event times hidden, the usual likelihood math becomes unworkable. Their 2025 method skips the likelihood and trains a neural network on simulated data instead.

A quick rough estimate from the counts serves as the network's input summary, needing little expert design. The trained network matches the best existing approximate methods on error, while running much faster. A quantile version gives quick uncertainty bands as well. The team apply the method to weekly counts of two infectious diseases, with a seasonal background rate.
arxiv-2506-01458:
Speech technology must handle many languages at once, and shared test challenges drive progress. This short paper describes the systems built at Tallinn University of Technology for the Interspeech 2025 ML-SUPERB 2.0 Challenge. The entry covers two tasks: naming the language being spoken, and transcribing speech in many languages. Language naming uses a hybrid design, pairing a pretrained language embedding model with a light speech recognizer that shares one encoder across languages and keeps a small word model per language.

For transcription, the team keeps three models and picks one per language based on training data and test results. The set includes a finetuned SeamlessM4T, a large multilingual model with custom language adapters, and a zero-shot variant. The combined system takes the top overall score in the challenge. The authors credit the per-language model choice for much of the gain.
arxiv-2506-01658:
Yuxi Cai and co-authors propose a leaner model for forecasting data that arrive as tensors over time, in a statistics paper from 2025. Tensor data stack many dimensions at once, like readings across places, types, and times. Standard factor tricks either lose clarity as dimensions grow or stay fast but hard to interpret.

Their method first splits the response and the inputs with a fast decomposition, then links the two sets of features. A sparse extra term soaks up signals that the low-rank core misses. The authors prove error bounds for their estimates and give a fitting algorithm. Simulations backed the theory, and a study of the El Niño climate pattern showed gains in both forecast skill and clarity.
arxiv-2506-01758:
Ruibin Li, Tao Yang and a team of co-workers wrote a 2025 paper on one model that learns many video and image tasks together. Most generators train for a single job, like text-to-video. Retraining a giant base model for each new task is costly. Their framework pools training data across tasks instead.

A light adapter unifies the varied inputs each task brings. Training mixes images and video in stages, building the model from scratch. Depth maps join as a cue to sense 3D space. Two sizes were trained, each handling over ten tasks. The larger one rivals top open and commercial video engines.
arxiv-2506-01858:
Andrea Quadri, writing alone in a 2025 paper, extends a gauge-invariant way of splitting scattering amplitudes into clean sectors for theories with three-way interaction points. The setting is a broken massive gauge theory with chiral fermions, where unphysical parts of the field must cancel in any real prediction. Tracking those cancellations by hand is notoriously messy.

Using fields that are themselves gauge-invariant and can travel inside loops, Quadri shows the cancellations sort amplitudes into sectors that each obey the key symmetry identities on their own. The construction holds at every order of approximation. It also suggests a fresh strategy for computing the finite correction terms that chiral theories need when no symmetry-preserving shortcut exists.
arxiv-2506-02158:
Ruhana Azam, Aditya Vempaty, and Ashish Jagmohan present a 2025 paper on giving web-browsing agents a memory. Today's web agents start each task from scratch, so they repeat old mistakes. The authors add reflection: the agent writes down what worked and what failed, then consults those notes on later tasks.

Their system, Reflection-Augmented Planning, stores both wins and failures as short self-reflections. When a new task arrives, relevant reflections guide the plan. Scores rose by 11 points overall against the base system. On tasks that had previously failed, the gain reached 29 points. The study shows that lessons from one site can transfer to different tasks. Memory, handled this way, makes web agents less brittle.
arxiv-2506-02258:
Mohd Akhtar and co-authors ask whether Mamba based audio models best recognize emotion in nonverbal sounds such as laughs, cries, and sighs. These sounds carry feeling without words. The authors reasoned that Mamba models, which track state over time, would capture emotional shape more stably than attention based models, which may amplify stray patterns.

Tests with leading models of both kinds backed that view. The team then fused models of the two kinds in a system called RENO. A new training loss aligns the models, and a self attention step blends their strengths. The fused system beat single models and past best results. The study sets a new mark for the task.
arxiv-2506-03158:
Jiahao Qin and four co-authors present a learning framework that handles uncertain features in single and multi-modal tasks, in a paper from 2025. Real data carry noise and missing cues, which degrade model reliability. Mixed sources compound the problem, since each source fails in its own way.

Their method refines uncertainty estimates as training proceeds, rebalances sample influence to keep feature spread healthy, and models uncertainty in cross-source links explicitly. Gains appear across image benchmarks, with large jumps on standard sets. Sentiment tasks that fuse text, audio, and video also improve, as does a multi-modal retrieval task.
arxiv-2506-03258:
April Qiu Cheng and co-authors wrote this astronomy paper in 2025 on fast radio bursts, brief flashes from deep space. As a burst crosses space, loose electrons slow it by an amount called its dispersion measure. Match that delay to galaxy maps, and bursts can trace where matter sits. The catch is bias: some bursts and host galaxies are easier to spot than others.

The team ran fake skies through a large computer model of the cosmos and shot 3,000 test bursts through it. Most biases proved mild. Host traits, follow-up habits, and one survey's known quirks did not skew the signal much. But dropping the most delayed tenth of bursts bent the signal by over half at small scales. Surveys must count and correct that cut, the authors say.
arxiv-2506-03558:
Jiawei Chen and co-authors build multi-turn dialogue data that stays on track, in a 2025 paper. Instruction data for language models is mostly single-turn, and stitched-together conversations drift off context, which lowers task completion in long chats. Their framework first models the intent arc of a whole conversation, assigning it to one of nine well-defined trajectories, so the exchange keeps a goal and a sensible flow.

On that skeleton, a sequence of user queries is generated to match the intent, and the full dialogue is then synthesised under that scaffold. The resulting data set, ConsistentChat, holds about fifteen thousand conversations and over two hundred and twenty-four thousand utterances. Models fine-tuned on it improved chat consistency by twenty to thirty percent on standard benchmarks and raised task success by up to fifteen percent. Both gains beat models trained on existing single and multi-turn sets.
arxiv-2506-03658:
Erika Hausenblas, Boris Jidjou Moghomye, and Paul Andre Razafimandimby wrote this mathematics paper, published in two thousand twenty-five, on simulating a coupled system from biology. The system joins a chemotaxis equation, which tracks cells moving toward chemical signals, with fluid flow equations shaken by random transport noise.

The model itself is already cut into pieces in space, and the authors add a matching cut in time. Their scheme is a semi-implicit Euler method, a step-by-step rule that treats some terms at the old time and some at the new. They prove the scheme is well-posed, meaning each step has a sound solution. They also derive uniform bounds that hold for the step values as the steps shrink. Such bounds are the groundwork for proving the simulation truly closes in on the real system. The setting is a bounded, convex region in three dimensions.
arxiv-2506-03758:
Daniel Palenicek, Florian Vogt, and Jan Peters make a sample-efficient learning method scale better in this 2025 paper. CrossQ learns control policies from few interactions, which matters when data is costly. Raising its update rate, a natural way to learn faster, instead made training unstable.

The team traced the trouble to exploding value bias and growing weights in the value network. Their fix adds weight normalization, which keeps weight sizes in check and holds the learning rate steady. With that change, higher update rates worked reliably across hard control tasks. The method matched or beat rivals on a standard benchmark, including dog and humanoid robots. No drastic resets of the network were needed.
arxiv-2506-03958:
Robert Wimmer-Schweingruber and co-authors report in 2025 Solar Orbiter readings of two interplanetary shocks with time resolution fine enough to catch physics usually averaged away. Energetic particle instruments normally sample far slower than an ion's gyration, smoothing over the microphysics of acceleration. Two shocks crossed in late November 2023 gave a rare sharp look.

The solar wind's proton beam tracked the magnetic field almost instantly, faster than a gyroperiod. Energetic particles flickered on the short time a structure takes to convect past the craft. Such non-equilibrium flickers challenge standard transport models. High-cadence data like these can reveal how shocks really energize particles, step by step.
arxiv-2506-04058:
Bulat Maksudov and co-authors coax a generative model to show its medical reasoning in pictures. To trust an imaging model, clinicians want counterfactuals: the same scan with one feature dialed up or down. The team maps named clinical concepts into the hidden space of a simple autoencoder trained without concept labels.

Directions in that space line up with features such as an enlarged heart, and sliding along them grows or shrinks the trait in the image. Concepts proved stable across data sets. Large pathologies counterfactualized well, while small ones blurred against reconstruction limits, and accuracy did not top baselines. Even so, the authors see a workable route to explanations doctors can inspect.
arxiv-2506-04258:
Vorotyntseva, Levshakov, and Henkel reported in 2025 differential measurements of the electron-to-proton mass ratio toward two molecular clouds near the Galactic Center. This constant, called mu, might vary from place to place, and methanol lines are a sensitive probe. Data came from a thirty-meter telescope working at three millimeter wavelengths.

For the cloud Sgr B2(N), nine methanol lines gave a weighted mean shift that sits below the lab value, with a stated uncertainty. The sign matches an earlier result for the same cloud from a space telescope at higher frequencies, based on two lines. The authors present the pair of results as an indication that mu may be lower in these Galactic Center clouds.
arxiv-2506-04358:
Uditansh Srivastava, Shivam Aryan, and Shaurya Singh propose a risk aware reward for trading agents in a 2025 paper. Reinforcement learning agents learn to trade by chasing a reward score, but single measures like the Sharpe ratio capture only part of what investors want. Their reward blends four smooth terms: yearly return, downside risk, extra return over a benchmark, and a ratio that weighs return against market risk.

Weights on the four terms can be tuned by grid search to match a chosen risk and return profile. The authors derive exact gradients for each term to support gradient based training. They also analyze traits like monotonicity and boundedness. Readers get a modular blueprint for multi goal rewards in trading and beyond.
arxiv-2506-04458:
Xueqiang Xu and nine co-authors present ZOES, a method for pulling named things and their details out of text, in a 2025 paper. Such extraction feeds knowledge graphs, but current tools lean on fixed templates or labelled examples.

ZOES needs neither. It works in three passes: first it enriches a rough guess about an item and its details, then refines the guess, then merges the results into one clean structure. The idea is that the item and its details support each other, so improving one improves the other. Tests in three different subject areas showed that language models using ZOES pulled out fuller structures than the same models working alone. The method should carry over to new fields without fresh labelling.
arxiv-2506-04558:
Yefeng Fan and Simon White build a faster way to fit network models to groups of brain scans, in this 2025 paper. Their models, called exponential random graph models, describe how connections form in a network. Fitting them the standard way is slow because the math resists direct calculation.

The new method trains a neural network to estimate the answer distribution directly, tuned for groups of networks at once. It was shaped for aging brain data from a Cambridge project, where it matched earlier results. The team then scaled it to a larger sample, a step the old method could not handle. The approach may serve network science well beyond brains.
arxiv-2506-05058:
A flat crystal called CrSBr holds magnetism and a lattice that talk to each other strongly, which makes it a test bed for fast spin devices. Yiqi Huo and co-authors used terahertz laser pulses in 2025 to watch that magnet lose its order in trillionths of a second.

The team found two stages. In the first twenty femtoseconds, excited electrons drive the loss directly, tightly linked to the pulse. After that, shaking of the lattice takes over, and one shaking mode stands out. Its electrons relax in about 83 femtoseconds, faster than the usual guess, and its effect on the magnet is outsized. The work maps which vibrations matter, a guide for building light-controlled quantum devices.
arxiv-2506-05158:
Thomas Henzinger and co-authors present a computing paper from 2025 on rules for whole sets of system runs. A single run of a system can be scored, for instance by its mean response time. New kinds of rules score the whole set of runs at once, such as the worst run or the average over a random pick.

The authors build a two-part machine for such rules. One part scores single runs; a second part merges those scores across the set. For yes-no scores, the machines capture rules about sets of runs. For number scores, they capture graded versions of those rules. The paper then studies three basic tasks: scoring a given system, and asking if any or every system meets a threshold. It maps which of these tasks can be solved and at what cost.
arxiv-2506-05358:
Souradip Nath asks whether ChatGPT can spot doctored photos in a 2025 preliminary study. Splicing pastes part of one image into another, and forensic tools usually train for that single job. Nath instead tested the general model GPT-4V off the shelf, with no task training, on a curated slice of a standard splicing data set.

Three prompting styles were tried: asking cold, showing a few examples, and asking the model to reason step by step. Plain asking already passed eighty-five percent accuracy, and step-by-step reasoning gave the most balanced calls on real and fake images. The model caught not only visual glitches but also odd scales and facts that did not fit the scene. It trails specialist detectors, but explains itself.
arxiv-2506-05558:
Andreas Meuleman and four co-authors rebuild three-dimensional scenes from photos on the fly, with no wait after shooting. Their method appeared in twenty twenty-five. Viewpoint-free rendering from photos is now easy, but finding camera poses and training the scene model can take minutes to hours.

Their approach estimates poses fast, using learned image features and a small GPU-friendly adjustment step. It then seeds scene blobs directly where needed and grows them during training, which speeds the fit sharply. For large scenes, blobs are grouped into anchors and parked off the graphics card, then merged as work proceeds. Tests across many data sets show the method matches rivals in quality while delivering a walkable scene as soon as capture ends.
arxiv-2506-05658:
Sobah and d'Almeida prove a solution result for a kinetic gas model in a 2025 paper. The Broadwell model tracks gas particles moving at a few fixed speeds, a stripped-down stand-in for real gas flow. Their version is planar, unsteady, and allows four velocities. They study it in a rectangle over a finite time span, with starting and boundary values that are smooth, bounded, and never negative.

The theorem states that exactly one well-behaved solution exists for that setup. The solution stays non-negative and smooth, with bounded first derivatives, matching the data's quality. Such existence and uniqueness proofs anchor numerical work: a simulation can only be trusted if the underlying problem is known to have one answer. The result extends earlier theory for this classic simplified model.
arxiv-2506-05858:
Jinjuan Wang and co-authors present ChronoTailor, a system that swaps clothing on people in videos while keeping fine garment detail, in a research paper from 2025. Video try-on often flickers or loses patterns as the person moves. Their diffusion-based method guides attention across space and time to hold details steady.

Region-aware guidance steers where edits land in each frame. A fusion step blends features across frames for smoother motion. Multi-scale garment features preserve small visual details, and a pose-alignment step keeps the garment glued to the body. The team also built StyleDress, a dataset of ornate garments in varied scenes and poses, to train and test such systems.
arxiv-2506-06158:
Armand Kassai Koupai and co-authors build a generative solver for physics equations that evolve in time in a 2025 paper. Neural solvers struggle to handle wide parameter ranges and patchy data. Their model, ENMA, works in a squeezed hidden space where future states are grown token by token.

Spotty spatial samples are first coded into even hidden grids by attention, then squeezed further by a layered encoder. At run time the model can lean on past states or on like past runs as context. One-shot fits to fresh equation settings follow from that trick. The frame suits forecasting of flows, waves, and other spread-out dynamics.
arxiv-2506-06458:
Waldemar Holubowski and Slawomir Kusinski extend a classical trick in measure theory to products of perfect sets, in a 2025 paper. Certain families of sets define their own notion of measurable functions. Old theorems say such functions can be reduced to continuous ones on large perfect sets. Those results were built for simpler bases.

The authors define product-wise versions of two such families. For each, they prove analogs of the classical theorems by Luzin and Eggleston. They also give a method that reduces whole sequences of functions to continuous ones. That method generalizes a known extension of two combinatorial theorems. The work serves descriptive set theory, where measurability and continuity meet.
arxiv-2506-06658:
Calvin Luo and co-authors published this robotics paper in 2025. Video generation models trained on expert demonstrations can plan robot actions from text instructions, but they often fail on tasks they never saw. The usual fix is more pre-collected data. The team instead proposes SILVR, a loop in which the model practices on its own: it generates its own task attempts, learns from them, and repeats.

Across rounds of this self-training, performance on new tasks kept climbing. The tests covered a suite of simulated MetaWorld tasks and two real tasks on a robot arm. The loop worked without human reward scores or fresh expert demonstrations. It also beat rival ways of using online experience on both final performance and learning speed. The authors present the loop as a path toward robots that keep improving from their own experience.
arxiv-2506-06858:
Running a large physics simulation many times is costly. Surrogate models stand in for the real thing during exploration. Ziwei Li and co-authors present FA-INR, a surrogate built on implicit neural representations. Such models store a field in network weights, but they struggle with sharp local detail. FA-INR instead uses cross-attention over a learnable memory bank. Capacity flows to where the data need it. A mixture of experts, guided by coordinates, adds efficiency and specialization.

The learned experts divide the simulation domain into an interpretable map. Scientists can spot complex structures from that map. They can also explore parameters locally and run sensitivity checks. Tests support both the fidelity and the interpretability claims.
arxiv-2506-06958:
Chance Jiajie Li and co-authors argued in 2025 that computer models of society need to model thought, not just behavior. Large language models are now used to act out how people and groups respond. Yet most such agents are fed basic facts about a person and asked to produce a likely act, with little inner structure.

The authors propose a frame called Generative Minds, drawn from the study of the mind. It gives agents beliefs that are ordered, can be revised, and can be traced. They also offer a test that checks causal paths, fit to the person described, and steady responses when conditions change. The goal is agents whose reasoning can be followed and trusted.
arxiv-2506-07058:
Larraín-Hubach, Shapiro, and Vodev wrote in twenty twenty-five about how fast wave energy fades near an obstacle when electric and magnetic fields are present. They prove sharp estimates for a magnetic Schrödinger operator with rough, bounded potentials. The same estimates hold outside a non-trapping obstacle with a wall condition. Magnetic potential must vanish in that obstacle case, they note. Applying the estimates gives exponential decay of local wave energy. The potentials themselves decay exponentially at infinity in their setup.

Low frequencies need cutting off in even dimensions for the result. In odd dimensions, no cut-off is needed under a spectral condition. Zero must be neither an eigenvalue nor a resonance there. Sharp resolvent bounds are the technical core of the paper. Such decay results underpin scattering theory and control of waves. The work extends earlier results to less regular potentials.
arxiv-2506-07458:
Yuxin Xiao and co-authors present KScope in 2025, a framework for judging what a language model truly knows. Knowing whether a model knows an answer is hard, and past work mostly tested clashes between memory and given context.

The team define five knowledge states based on whether model answers are steady and correct. KScope applies a ladder of statistical tests to place each case in one state. Across nine models and four datasets, context narrowed knowledge gaps, and traits like relevance guided updates. Summary methods shaped by the findings improved updates across models.
arxiv-2506-07558: Fabian Lander and Diaaeldin Taha present a ray-marching method for drawing flat surfaces in an immersive way in a 2025 paper. Their approach lets viewers explore translation surfaces, mirror rooms, unfolded polyhedra, and translation prisms from inside. It stays fast enough for interactive use. The authors walk through several examples, share practical advice for programmers who want to copy the technique, and discuss using the pictures in public outreach. Their simulations and code are posted online for anyone to try.
arxiv-2506-07658:
Nitin Sharma, Thomas Wolfers, and Cagatay Yildiz build a pipeline that turns raw domain texts into clean tests of what language models know, in a paper from 2025. Fields like law, medicine, and education need honest measures of model expertise. Existing tests are often leaked into training data and lean on multiple choice formats with known biases.

Their deterministic pipeline mines a corpus for domain keywords and related vocabulary. It then builds prompts whose missing word is a domain term, and scores models on completing them. No other model and no paid annotators are involved, so tests can be rebuilt cheaply as data grows. Scores lined up well with an expert made benchmark, and the method compares base and chat tuned models fairly.
arxiv-2506-07858:
Robert Halverson and Ryan Caverly tackle steering for a small satellite that spins to stay stable, in a 2025 paper. The satellite uses magnetic rods that push against Earth's field, saving the power and space that wheels or thrusters would take. The catch is that magnetic steering is weak and changes as the satellite orbits, so the controller must plan ahead carefully.

The team built three planning controllers that predict the satellite's motion with a time-varying model. One accounts for the satellite's position along its orbit, and two refine their guesses step by step, one with straight-line math and one with the full curved math. In tests aimed at holding a steady pointing direction, the full-math version used the least effort, broke no limits, and stayed cheap to run.
arxiv-2506-07958:
Salah Faroughi and Farinaz Mostajeran published this paper in 2025. It studies how a new kind of physics-informed network learns. These networks solve equations from physics, and the variant here builds its layers from flexible curve pieces rather than fixed switches.

The authors apply neural tangent kernel theory, a lens that tracks how a network's behavior shifts during training. They derive the kernel for the new networks, first in plain training and then in the physics setting. Four test equations, from steady waves to a vibrating beam, let them watch the kernel's spectrum evolve. The patterns expose learning habits that the older network style cannot show. They also reveal when splitting the domain speeds learning. The paper is the first full study of its kind for these networks.
arxiv-2506-08458:
Daptari, Montesinos, and Rao study continuity points in dual Banach spaces in this two thousand twenty-five math paper. Banach spaces are complete spaces of vectors with a size measure. Their duals hold all the continuous linear readings of those vectors. On the dual's unit ball, two topologies compete: a weak-star one and a weak one. The authors ask where the identity map between them is continuous.

They find classes of spaces where such points are plentiful, forming a dense set of a special descriptive kind. They also study how the trait passes to higher duals. One result is negative: for von Neumann algebras whose predual has a certain smoothness property, no continuity point exists at all. The paper serves functional analysts who map the fine structure of dual spaces.
arxiv-2506-08558:
William de Vazelhes, Xiao-Tong Yuan, and Bin Gu improve optimization when the answer must be sparse and must obey extra rules, in a 2025 paper. Keeping only a few active variables gives clean, cheap models, but real problems add constraints that the sparse set must respect. Older algorithms demanded a projection formula that may not exist, or promised only local success. Their variant of iterative hard thresholding projects in two steps, tuned to support-preserving constraints.

A fresh trade-off between relaxing sparsity and accepting sub-optimality yields global guarantees on the result. The proof rests on extending a classic three-point lemma to their two-step projector. The guarantees cover plain, random, and derivative-free versions of the problem. Even without extra constraints, the zero-order result beats the prior best, which one author set in earlier work.
arxiv-2506-08758:
Batch size in stochastic gradient methods should grow without replacement sampling, Marco Boresta, Alberto De Santis, and Stefano Lucidi argue in a 2025 paper. Recent methods base their efficiency and convergence on controlling the variance of the gradient batch estimate. That control is usually achieved by increasing the batch size dynamically as iterations proceed and the model nears a solution.

Statistical analyses in that literature often rely on sampling with replacement, which the authors call unrealistic in practice. They study batch selection based on sampling without replacement instead. The new selection still ensures global convergence. It also represents the variance reduction seen in practice more accurately, which leads to a smoother, more efficient batch update scheme for practitioners.
arxiv-2506-09158:
Neslihan Alan, Mehmet Alpsoy, and Yücel Kılıç present the first light study of an eclipsing binary star in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. In such pairs, one star passes in front of the other, causing dips in brightness. Those dips let astronomers measure star masses and sizes directly.

The team combined a space telescope light curve with new multicolor observations from a robotic telescope in Türkiye. Their modeling gave masses and radii for both stars in the pair, plus brightness and surface gravity values. They also estimated the system's distance. The secondary star proved larger but less massive than the primary, a clue to its stage of life.
arxiv-2506-09258:
Vaidotas Simkus and Michael U Gutmann offer a new way to fill gaps in data sets in a 2025 paper. Missing values block many uses of data, and old fill methods strain on hard cases. Their method learns a flow that can grow full rows from the parts that are present.

The team tests the method against nine rivals on two dozen small to mid-size tables. It ties or beats both old and new rivals on a wide range of scores. On time-based data used cold, it ties a close rival on skill and beats it on speed, which makes it a broad first pick.
arxiv-2506-09758:
Zikai Liu and co-authors borrow a mainframe idea to make far memory workable in a 2025 paper. Big old mainframes route disk work through side units called channel controllers, which free the main brain. Far memory pools, linked by new fast wires, promise relief for memory jams, yet no clean handle lets the system software run work near the data.

The team proposes memory channel controllers as that handle. The design needs no change to the main chip, and it rides on the shared-view links the new wires give. That yields a finer, back-and-forth style of near-data work than past designs allowed.
arxiv-2506-09958:
Sushant Gautam, Michael Riegler, and Pål Halvorsen build a harder test for AI systems that answer questions about medical images, in a 2025 paper. Their arena is gastrointestinal endoscopy, and the task is visual question answering over real scope images. Existing datasets are too simple and too clean to predict clinical usefulness, so the team expanded a prior dataset with nearly one hundred and sixty thousand new question-answer pairs.

Language models generated the questions under a systematic scheme, tiered by the depth of reasoning required. The team also dirtied the images with augmentations mimicking real imaging artifacts, so models must be robust, not just accurate. Evaluation runs on two tracks: standard performance, and performance under those perturbations. The dataset follows FAIR principles and is fully public, code included. The authors aim it at developers of clinical decision support who need benchmarks that resemble the mess of real practice.
arxiv-2506-10058:
Mingyu Li, Bjorn Emonts, and co-authors show a twin ring world crash far off, shaped like an owl face, in a 2025 paper. World crashes drive shape change, gas moves, and star birth in young worlds. Twin ring crash forms are scarce, and both rings here host live cores.

Deep shots and wave reads from scores of scopes map the pair. Both worlds show near twin ring forms in the shots. One core shoots a wave jet that hits the crash front head on. A star burst flares at that front with vast cold gas in store. Shock birth from crash and jet may drive the burst.
arxiv-2506-10358:
Electrons in a material carry charge, spin, and orbital motion, and their combined patterns are described as multipoles. Yambe and Hayami lay out the symmetry rules that govern how multipoles interact in crystals. Working through the crystallographic point groups, they find which interactions are allowed by each bond's symmetry. The antisymmetric kind extends the famous Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction, while the symmetric kind extends compass-like couplings.

The allowed interactions can seed unusual ordered states in which several patterns repeat at once, called multiple-Q states. As a worked example, the authors take an antisymmetric quadrupole interaction on a triangular lattice. A triple-Q quadrupole state emerges from it. The paper gives researchers in heavy-fermion, frustrated, and nematic materials a rulebook for predicting such states. Exotic order, they argue, may often trace back to these multipole couplings.
arxiv-2506-10658:
Narges Nemati and Mostafa Haghir Chehreghani make recommender systems tougher against noisy clicks by teaching two cleaned-up views of the same data to agree. Graph-based recommenders pass messages along user-item edges, so junk edges poison them, and they overfit easily. Writing in twenty twenty-five, the pair build two views for each interaction's neighborhood. One view denoises with attention-weighted graph layers. The other comes from a variational autoencoder that regularizes the feature distribution. A mutual learning loss gradually harmonizes the two views during training.

Experiments on several real data sets followed. Predicted ratings grew slightly more accurate. Rankings improved dramatically, by up to about a third on the reported metrics. The contrastive design's common patterns, the authors argue, are exactly what survives noise.
arxiv-2506-10758:
Gutekunst studies a special traveling salesman problem where edge cost depends only on edge length around a ring. Its complexity is a noted open question. A geometric object, the edge-length polytope, offers one attack route. Its corner count turns out to hinge on how n factors. For prime n, corners grow in step with n. For a squared prime, they grow like n to the 1.5 power. For powers of two, the count is superpolynomial.

By contrast, the classic salesman polytope has near n-factorial corners. So brute force over corners is fast for some n and hopeless for others. The split ties a salesman problem to number theory.
arxiv-2506-11158:
Xizheng Yu and co-authors use implicit neural representations to fill in gene activity maps of the human brain in a 2025 paper. Gene expression in the healthy brain is sampled only sparsely, at scattered points. The goal is a full map of any gene at the resolution of single voxels. The team start from a public brain atlas and focus on the top genes linked to Alzheimer's risk.

They adapt implicit representation models, which learn a continuous function of position, to this interpolation task. The pipeline produces quantitative whole brain maps for all the chosen genes. Experiments compare the results against a standard interpolation baseline. The authors present the approach as a tool for spatial transcriptomics, turning sparse samples into complete pictures of where genes act.
arxiv-2506-11358:
Martin Klazar revisits a neat guessing rule from 1975 about proofreading, in a 2025 paper. George Pólya suggested a shortcut: if one proofreader finds a errors and a second finds b, with c errors found by both, the total is about a times b divided by c. The rule feels right, but it lacked a firm basis.

Klazar builds a realistic model of how proofreaders work — each error has its own chance of being spotted — and tests the formula inside it. Tools from the probabilistic method, including bounds on rare large deviations, measure how well the guess performs. He closes by weighing realistic models against purely chance-based ones. The result puts a folk rule of editing on solid ground.
arxiv-2506-11658:
Agúndez, a solo author, models how disequilibrium chemistry and temperature shape each other in exoplanet atmospheres in a 2025 paper. The one-dimensional model solves both at once along the vertical direction. Its reaction network was built from scratch with many species and reactions.

The model was run on five known gas giants and on possible secondary atmospheres. For the gas giants, temperature shifts from disequilibrium chemistry were modest, since the main opacity sources barely changed. One hot Jupiter case hinged on titanium oxide loss under ultraviolet light, which is poorly known. In methane-rich or oxygen-rich secondary air, the effects could be large. Composition type decides the impact.
arxiv-2506-11758:
González-Fuentes and Gómez-Valent rebuild the history of dark energy without locking in a fixed formula shape. Their 2025 paper uses weighted function regression, which averages over expansion orders with Bayesian weights. Standard fits truncate the dark energy formula at first order, a choice that can fake features.

Data from supernova catalogs, the DESI survey, and the cosmic microwave background feed the rebuild. The shape-free result backs earlier hints of shifting dark energy. Combined data favor a switch from phantom to quintessence behavior at a modest redshift, with crossing odds between about ninety-six and near one hundred percent. A simple steady fall of dark energy density is ruled out strongly. No firm sign of negative dark energy appears late in cosmic time.
arxiv-2506-11858:
Vadim Ustyuzhanin, writing alone, measures the cost of parenthood for Russian workers in a 2025 study. Past work on this topic in Russia relied on simple correlations. This study uses natural variation in family size, from twin births and the sex mix of siblings, to get closer to causal answers.

The central finding is that mothers lose about fifteen percent of employment in the first year after a birth. That penalty then fades fast, falling to about three percent once children reach school age. The long-run penalty is thus smaller than the roughly ten percent seen in rich countries. Fathers showed no steady employment penalty, though they slightly raised their labor supply. The study is the first of its kind for present-day Russia.
arxiv-2506-12358:
Control policies learned by computers may hold private data, and encrypting them can shield that data during use. Jihoon Suh, Yeongjun Jang, Kaoru Teranishi, and Takashi Tanaka build an encrypted policy method in a 2025 paper. They base it on a learning frame that prices each step by its gap from a prior policy.

That frame gives the update math a clean linear shape with no search step. The shape lets strong encryption slot in at low cost. The team bounds how errors from rounding and refresh steps grow as the policy updates. Fake-data runs matched the theory. The work points to control that stays private end to end.
arxiv-2506-12558:
Kubo and co-authors present a way to explain knowledge graph predictions in a 2025 paper. Graph networks that reason along paths score at the top on tasks that fill missing links. Yet users cannot see why a link was predicted, and most explainers target single nodes or whole graphs, not paths.

Their explainer, RAW-Explainer, uses a random walk goal to keep the shown subgraph connected and short. A learned model produces the explanations for many links at once, keeping costs down. A special checker judges small subgraphs fairly, fixing a shift problem in older checks. Tests on standard sets balanced explanation quality with speed, the authors report.
arxiv-2506-12658:
Yi Zheng, Haoyang Tan, and their co-authors demonstrate Raman lasers inside tiny silicon nitride rings. Their 2025 paper notes that silicon nitride is a favored chip material for light based circuits, thanks to low loss and compatibility with standard chip making. Light matter effects that use electron response are well explored on it, but Raman scattering, which uses atomic vibration, is not.

The team shaped the ring and its waveguide so the stored light overlaps the silica cladding where Raman gain lives, while suppressing a competing Kerr effect. The lasers lit at under two milliwatts of input power. They also mapped the trade off between how tightly light is confined and how long it circulates. The results open broadband frequency conversion on this chip platform.
arxiv-2506-13058:
Fast sampling for diffusion models is the subject of a 2025 paper whose head names the work SynBoost, by Hu Yu and co-authors. Diffusion models make images by cleaning noise step by step, which is slow. Cutting steps speeds the process but adds error, and past fast methods have mostly fought one kind of error.

The authors split sampling error into two parts and study how each part changes across steps. Their method blends the current noise estimate with a sharper guess from a larger step, cutting the second kind of error while standard solvers cut the first. The method needs no new training and plugs into existing samplers. Tests on image tasks, in both pixel and compressed forms, showed gains in speed and output quality at very low step counts.
arxiv-2506-13158:
Aswathy K R, Udaya Maurya, Surya Teja Gavva, and Rickmoy Samanta study swirling vortices on a doughnut-shaped surface in a 2025 physics study. The setting is a thin, frictionless fluid film wrapped on a torus, whose curved shape and closed topology change vortex motion. A Hamiltonian description covers the vortices, plus a self-force that comes from the geometry.

For two vortices the authors work out the basic motion, finding several classes of paths for a vortex dipole. Random clusters of same-sign vortices show collective behavior shaped by the surface. Comparisons with quantum superfluid vortices highlight subtle differences between the two settings.
arxiv-2506-13358:
Xiangfan Wu proposes a new way to train language models so they learn from the process of reasoning, not just from final answers, in a 2025 paper. Most training rewards a model only when its last answer is right, which wastes much of what an attempt can teach. Wu's frame, called Socratic RL, rests on thinking hard about why steps fail or succeed. It splits the work between two minds.

In the design, a teacher system reads past attempts, pulls out the causes of errors, and turns them into short guiding points. A student system then uses those points to reason better on later tries. The teacher also improves itself over time through a learning loop, and the student's stored points are pressed into its settings. Wu lays out the ideas, hard parts, and a research plan.
arxiv-2506-13458:
Cristina Mahanta and Gagan Bhatia wrote a 2025 computer vision paper on recognizing human activity in single still photos. A still image lacks motion cues, which makes actions like running versus standing hard to tell apart. Yet still image recognition would serve photo indexing, safety monitoring, and assistive tools.

The authors labeled 285 images from the MSCOCO collection into four classes: walking, running, sitting, and standing. A convolutional network trained from scratch reached only forty one percent accuracy. Fine tuning CLIP, a model pretrained to match images with text, lifted accuracy to seventy six percent. The jump shows that vision language pretraining transfers powerfully to this small data task. The study is small, but the contrast is stark.
arxiv-2506-13558:
Yang and co-authors (2025) present X-Scene, a system that generates large driving scenes for autonomous vehicle development. Diffusion models already synthesize driving data well over time, but building big three-dimensional scenes that stay coherent in space is less explored. X-Scene accepts control at two levels: fine layout direction from user input or text, and broad semantic guidance from user intent enriched by a language model.

The pipeline first builds a 3D semantic map of the scene, then renders matching images and video from several viewpoints, keeping the views aligned. Local scenes are then stretched into large ones by outpainting that extends geometry and imagery from what already exists. The results are lifted into a high-quality 3D representation used for simulation and exploration. In experiments, the authors report clear gains in both control and fidelity over prior scene generation methods.
arxiv-2506-13658:
Koune and Cicirello proposed a physics-based learning model in 2025 for work where only part of a system is known. Several hidden factors can shape a measured response, and building them all into a physics model is often not feasible. Pure data models, meanwhile, may find bloated codes that work poorly on small, noisy data.

Their design splits the hidden code in two: one part holds values that drive a physics model, the other captures all other variation. A training goal stops the data part from overriding known physics, so the first part stays clear to read. Made-up case studies on structures showed the model can separate known physics from other factors.
arxiv-2506-13758:
Camilletti and co-authors built an AI model for European weather in two thousand twenty-five. Large air flow patterns over the Atlantic shape Europe's climate. These patterns settle into a few long-lasting states called regimes. Knowing the regime hints at heat and rain weeks ahead. Past methods linked regimes to surface weather with straight-line math only.

The new model learns curved, complex links instead. It rebuilds monthly heat and rain anomalies from regime indices. Training used past records of both regimes and surface weather. Skill at this task opens a path to seasonal outlooks. Farmers, energy planners, and water managers all use such outlooks. The authors frame the tool as a step beyond linear methods.
arxiv-2506-13858:
Wenzer Qin, Soubhik Kumar, Priyamvada Natarajan, and Neal Weiner present a 2025 paper proposing a gentler route to the seeds of the giant black holes seen in the early universe. Space telescopes keep finding huge black holes surprisingly soon after the Big Bang. Making them from scratch that fast strains standard models.

Their scenario starts with density ripples a bit stronger than usual but too weak to collapse straight into black holes. The ripples still gather dark matter halos very early, while the leftover heat of creation blocks the gas inside from cooling and splitting. Unable to fragment, the gas falls straight in and collapses into a heavy seed. Sample models match the observed counts.
arxiv-2506-13958:
Leonardo Guiducci and co-authors open the black box of a decision transformer variant in a 2025 paper. Elastic Decision Transformers shine at offline reinforcement learning, where an agent learns from stored data alone. Adding intrinsic motivation, a built-in drive to explore, lifts their scores, but no one had mapped how it reshapes what the model learns inside.

The team studies the learned embeddings after training, checking their spread, size, and alignment. Each motivation variant carved a distinct geometry into the embedding space. Links between embedding traits and task success shifted from one environment to the next. The picture that emerges casts motivation as more than an exploration bonus: it acts as a shaping prior, bending representations into forms that suit each world. The authors say such structure echoes patterns seen in brains.
arxiv-2506-14058:
Ali Baheri adds domain rules straight into the update step of offline reinforcement learning, in a paper from 2025. Offline learning must improve a policy from logged acts alone, yet top methods can overrate values or break known rules such as steady rise.

His frame projects each update onto the set of value forms that obey the rules. The joined operator still shrinks in a sound way and settles at one fixed point. A smooth solver layer passes gradients at low cost. On a bid auction test with a known steady rise rule, the method broke no rules and beat two strong rivals.
arxiv-2506-14458:
Xiao-Fu Peng proposes a shared gauge for how macroscopic a quantum state is in a 2025 paper, writing solo. The gauge, beta, weighs how long coherence lasts against the time needed to tell the superposed parts apart for sure. It aims to draw one line between quantum and classical play.

For matter wave interferometers, from electrons to large molecules, beta takes a compact form and stays below one across past data. That read says such tests have yet to near the boundary. Atomic fountain runs score far higher, near 300 at best, which marks them as the richer hunting ground.
arxiv-2506-14658:
Tianyu Yuan and co-authors solve for the time a wandering particle takes to be caught in a trap in 2025. The particle diffuses in three dimensions inside a pull toward a center. A sphere boundary absorbs it on contact. The team solves the survival equation head on. Their sum based answer corrects a past published result.

Computer runs match the new math across a range of settings. From survival they derive the full spread of capture times. A mean capture time formula follows as a sum of terms. Its first terms match a value found by a unlike method in the past work. In the weak trap limit, their first term matches known escape odds for free diffusion.
arxiv-2506-14958:
Mustafa Bakr lays out a way to link far-apart quantum bits in a 2025 paper. Superconducting bits must trade signals to tangle, the link that powers quantum math. Near bits link well, but the tie fades fast with range, which caps chip size.

His plan puts the bits on a surface of tiny switches whose state shifts in space and time. That surface acts as a shared road whose lanes can be tuned to pick out one pair of bits. Two kinds of tangle steps are worked out, one driven at a matched tone and one built from path shape. Test runs hold link quality above 98 percent across centimeter gaps.
arxiv-2506-15158:
Yu Nakayama and Takahiro Tanaka complete a three way swap among minimal models in a 2025 paper. Small conformal theories sort into A, D, and E families. Gauging, a way of folding a symmetry into the theory, was known to swap A with D through a plain flip symmetry, and A with E through a stranger non invertible one.

The missing leg was D against E. The pair show a second non invertible symmetry does that job when gauged. With it, all three families trade places under gauging moves, a full triality. The result tidies a long standing pattern in two dimensional physics. It also shows how non invertible symmetries widen the map of equal theories.
arxiv-2506-15358:
Prathap Rayalacheruvu and co-authors catalog the ices around a young star using data from the James Webb Space Telescope, in a 2025 study. The target is a young stellar object in the NGC 1333 region, where frozen water and complex organic compounds coat dust grains. Splitting the blended light signals into single ices, across a wide range, is still a hard problem.

Their tool, INDRA, strips away background glow and fits all the ice signals at once, then reports amounts and confidence. Results match earlier narrow fits and add new finds, including signals tied to carbon dioxide and ammonium. The work expands the known ice list for this young star.
arxiv-2506-15658:
Jinzhao Sun and Pei Zeng sort the role of chance picks in quantum sum builds in a 2025 paper. Many quantum tools write a hard step as a sum of plain unit steps. Chance picks shrink gate counts and spare qubits in that craft. Their twist stacks sums in layers. The catch: chance sums leave a state no rig can just build, a cross form with two unlike sides.

Past use thus stops at one mark read at a time. A new gauge tool, built on oft checks and resets of a spare qubit, cracks that wall. Fair reads of the cross state and its kin come from it. Sum builds then tie to shadow reads, which grade many marks at once. Three task costs close the case.
arxiv-2506-16058:
Yong Liu and colleagues argued in 2025 that current tests for open-vocabulary segmentation do not truly test open understanding. Such systems must outline any category named in text, using large vision-language models. But the test sets use concepts much like the training sets, with many overlapping classes, so scores flatter the models.

They built a new benchmark, OpenBench, whose concepts differ far more from training data. Known methods scored quite differently on it than on older tests. They also propose OVSNet, which fuses varied features and widens the training space at no extra cost. It reached top results on both older datasets and OpenBench, backing the need for harder tests.
arxiv-2506-16258:
Yisu Wang and five co-authors present a system that speeds video feature indexing inside datacenters in this 2025 paper. Indexing huge video libraries depends on moving feature data efficiently. Doing computation inside the network can help, but varied hardware and tangled paths make it hard.

Their framework, ViFusion, merges many small feature tensors into bigger units as they travel the network. A fusion module at switches and hosts streamlines the flow for indexing jobs. In deployment, the system raised retrieval throughput eight to twenty-two fold at the same latency as leading systems. The authors credit the gains to communication-aware merging rather than faster models. They aim the design at large multimedia datacenters.
arxiv-2506-16458:
Likhitha Annapurna Kavuri, Akshay Mhatre, Akarsh Nair, and Deepti Gupta build SecureFed, a two-phase frame to catch rogue clients in shared learning. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five.

Shared learning guards data privacy, since holders keep their data. But its spread form lets a rogue holder warp the results or wreck the model. In phase one, the frame gathers each holder's update and shrinks its dims to bare odd forms tied to bad acts. Fake data sets score each temp model, to grade how odd it is. In phase two, weights are routed by zones of worth: zones with strong, useful slopes count more in the join.
arxiv-2506-16658:
Wenlong Ji and co-authors bring machine learning forecasts into bandit decision problems in a 2025 paper. A bandit problem asks a learner to pick among options again and again, learning which pays best from sparse live results. In many real settings, rich side data exist before any live trial, and a trained model can turn that data into forecast rewards.

Those forecasts can be biased, since they rest on guessing beyond past data. The authors' algorithm blends the forecasts with live results through a confidence method that needs no prior knowledge of how the two relate. Proofs show it cuts total regret even when the forecasts point the wrong way on average. Tests on model choice and video recommendation backed the math.
arxiv-2506-16858:
Michael Anastos and co-authors strengthen a result about cycles in a randomly thinned hypercube. Their 2025 paper deals with the binary hypercube, a network whose corners link by single bit flips. Each edge survives with a fixed chance, a process called percolation. Past work by the same team showed something striking. Above a modest edge density, the thinned cube typically holds a cycle covering nearly all its corners.

The new result fills in the middle lengths. Under the same conditions, cycles of every even length appear, from four up to nearly the full corner count. Even lengths are the only possible ones here, since the cube's cycles alternate between two corner types. The proof builds on the team's earlier near spanning cycle. Results like this show how robust the cube's structure stays under random damage.
arxiv-2506-17058:
When an ad slot sells to the top bid, the house tells each bidder the least bid that would have won. Sébastien Lahaie, Benjamin Schaeffer, and Yuanjun Zhou ask in 2025 how that hint should work when a whole pod of video ads sells at once. Pod sales carry caps, such as total ad length, so the hint turns into a set of joint bid shifts. Some bids must rise, some may fall, and the winning spread must stay best.

The team show the safe set of shifts is the core of a two-sided team game. For the plain case of one-to-one matching, a linear program draws the set exactly. From it they draw candidate forms of the least-bid hint. Real pod data from a live exchange then let them watch how each hint steers bidding over time.
arxiv-2506-17258:
Jasmin Lim, Dimitrios Pylorof, Humberto Garcia, and Karthik Duraisamy design a twin on screen to run a new type core plant, of the fourth kind. Their test plant cools with fluoride salt and runs at high heat. The twin aims to cut run costs and lift calls. It links the real plant to stand in models, learn by gains, and Bayes calls in a closed loop.

The learn chief sets goal strength while it counts health of parts and wear. A chief named for guide rules holds pump flow and heat caps. Bayes screens fold gauges into the mock runs. Three case works show year long plans for care of the plant. They show truth made more fine with oft gauges. They show real time re set past a shock to the plant. The team claims wide use for more new plants.
arxiv-2506-17358:
Akarsh Aurora and co-authors describe in 2025 a new test rig for fusion magnet materials. Fusion plants need magnets that stay strong and carry heat well while fast particles batter them at very low temperatures. Until now, teams could not watch key traits change during that battering.

The rig pairs ion beams, used to mimic the damage, with a laser method that reads heat flow and surface waves in real time. In a trial run at thirty degrees above absolute zero, copper lost near half its heat flow while its wave speed held steady. The rig can now track how other candidate materials wear down under fusion-like stress.
arxiv-2506-17658:
Qiong Liu, Jianke Lin, Tianzhu Zhang, and Leonardo Linguaglossa present a light network monitor in 2025, under a head title that names it DRST. Modern phone networks run many virtual jobs on shared gear, where fights for resources can slow a service without warning. Direct traffic checks are costly and can be barred by system limits.

Their frame skips direct checks and reuses hardware counters already in the gear, so it barely touches live traffic. It also retunes itself as the system drifts over time, a trait built into its name. The frame is meant to slot into live virtual network setups with ease. For operators, a watch that adds almost no load could spot slowdowns before customers feel them.
arxiv-2506-18158:
Xinzge Gao and three co-authors present a 2025 paper on helping AI agents move between apps on a phone or computer. Such agents often lean on past screenshots or clicks to guess where a task stands, which fails on long, multi-app jobs. The team proposes Chain-of-Memory, a method that stores task state in explicit short-term and long-term memory. The agent records what each action did and keeps screen details that matter.

To teach this skill, the team built a data set of 111 thousand screen-action pairs annotated with memory notes. Agents trained with the method performed far better on cross-app tasks. Smaller models with the memory data matched the memory handling of models ten times their size. The authors plan to release the data and code. They present explicit memory as a missing piece for dependable interface agents.
arxiv-2506-18458:
Noah Oldfield, Christoph Laaber, and Shaukat Ali present, in a 2025 paper, a debugging aid for quantum programs based on checking a qubit's Bloch vector mid-run. Quantum bugs hide well because states are fragile and outcomes probabilistic. Checks during execution can localize faults, but older check schemes need costly mid-circuit measures.

Their tool instead reads expectation values of a few standard operators, which pinpoints faults with low overhead. A companion builder writes the check schemes by itself from the target algorithm. Across hundreds of thousands of test programs, the tool beat the prior best at fault finding, above all as circuits deepened and noise grew. It also ran far faster with less depth added.
arxiv-2506-18558:
Xiaobin Sun, Jian Wang, and Yingchao Xie prove averaging rules for noisy systems that run on two clocks at once, where the fast clock's rules themselves change over time. Many real systems mix a slow trend with fast jitter; averaging replaces the jitter by its mean effect. Their 2025 paper handles the harder case where the fast drift depends on time and only partly pulls back.
