When the slow part's noise ignores the fast part, the slow path converges strongly to the averaged equation. Otherwise they prove weak convergence and name the limit's law.

Such theorems justify the shortcuts modelers already take in climate, finance, and engineering. The authors work under stated assumptions on the coefficients. Their result extends averaging to systems whose fast layer ages as it spins. Rigor here protects every simulation built on the shortcut.
arxiv-2506-18658:
Zhang and co-authors teach a model to write pathology reports from slide images in this 2025 paper. Whole slide images are vast and redundant, and their raw features lack medical meaning. Pathologists, by contrast, reason with prior cases in mind.

Their framework, BiGen, copies that habit. It first retrieves relevant knowledge from a medical knowledge bank by matching the slide's most attended patches. Then a two-stream learning setup uses one learnable token for image features and one for the retrieved knowledge, aligning the two. A decoder merges both streams into the final report. On a breast cancer dataset it improved language metrics by 7.4 percent and a key classification score by 19.1 percent over prior methods.
arxiv-2506-18858:
Layton Hall and three co-authors rethink a basic effect in optics in a 2025 paper. When light passes through a grating or a prism-like device, each color leaves at its own angle, an effect called angular dispersion. Engineers use it to tune the speed and spread of laser pulses. Standard theory treats the angle as a smooth curve over frequency, needing only a few correction terms.

The authors show that a newer class of pulsed light fields breaks that picture. At one special frequency, the angle's rate of change is simply not defined, so the smooth expansion fails there. Describing such beams takes many independent correction terms instead. The paper gives this unruly case a name and a theory. It argues the effect is a general feature to design with, not a defect, for the new wave packets now entering optics labs.
arxiv-2506-19158:
Moffat and Thompson place a known spin group inside a broader complex geometry, in math work from 2025. The group, written SL(2,C) over Z2, is the spin cover of the Lorentz group that rules how spin looks in relativity. Their stage is a four-fold space where lengths can take complex values.

By stretching the metric and link forms into the complex realm, the frame group grows and splits into two twin spin factors. Picking one factor gives back the group they sought, with a shared flip modded out. Paths that bend around trouble spots in the complex plane also give smooth black hole answers with no added matter. The result gives chirality, the left-right split of spin, a clear geometric home.
arxiv-2506-19258:
Rasiq Hussain and co-authors tackled in 2025 the task of reading personality from life story interviews. Questionnaires are the usual tool for measuring the Five-Factor Model of personality. Open-ended narratives are richer but very long, often passing two thousand tokens each. The team wanted language models that can handle that length and still explain their judgments.

Their method has two steps. First, sliding-window fine-tuning of pretrained language models extracts embeddings from the long text. Then recurrent networks with attention combine those pieces and highlight what drove each prediction. Tests against long-context models such as LLaMA and Longformer showed gains in accuracy, efficiency, and interpretability. The authors see narrative text as a strong base for future personality assessment.
arxiv-2506-19458:
Jacques Desmarais and colleagues resolved a long-standing glitch in spin density theory in a 2025 paper. Simulating magnets whose spins point in varying directions produces a torque from the exchange-correlation term, the theory's catch-all for quantum interactions. That torque should vanish or stay physical, but in plain spin-density theory it comes out spurious, because it secretly depends on the spin current, a quantity the theory does not contain.

Their fix works inside spin-current density theory, whose energy obeys an exact combined gauge symmetry. Nonzero torques on twisted solutions are then fenced by that symmetry and never enter the actual spin dynamics, which involve only physical currents and torques. Two decades of confusion trace to a missing constraint.
arxiv-2506-19658:
Yang Xing, Jiong Wu, Yuheng Bu, and Kuang Gong adapt the Segment Anything Model 2 for medical scans without hand-drawn prompts. The vision model segments images well, but it leans on human hints and was trained on photos and video, not scans. Both flaws bite in the clinic.

Their 2025 framework, SAM2-SGP, feeds the model a support set of image and mask pairs. A first module drafts pseudo-masks from those pairs through the model's memory. A second module turns the drafts into boxes and steers attention to the right zones. Low-rank adaptation softens the domain gap. Tests span six imaging types, from fundus photos to ultrasound, in two and three dimensions.
arxiv-2506-19858:
Manrique Camacho, Amanda Cedeño, Luis Barboza, Shu Wei Chou-Chen, Mario Gómez, and Hugo Hidalgo wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It builds a Hurricane Impact Index that scores both the direct hit of a storm and its spread harm, for use in Central America.

Hurricanes rank among the worst natural hazards. Their harm runs past the track line, since heavy rain and strong winds bite far off path, shaped by the lay of the land. The index is built so its parts can be split across time and space. That lets crews map where a storm's force fell hardest and how the harm was spread. The team shows the index at work on the Central American region.
arxiv-2506-20558:
Renyi Zhong and co-authors tackle stale notes in computer code, where a comment no longer matches what the code does. Old notes mislead readers and slow fixes and tests. Past tools for the flaw were trained on sets with many wrong labels, which capped their worth. The 2025 paper of the team first audits those old sets and shows the scale of the label problem.

To fix the base, the team built a cleaned set of high-grade cases for training and tests. On top of it they built a tool that both finds a mismatch and rewrites the note in one pass. The tool hit a top score on the finding task and beat the best past tool on the fixing task by a wide step. Human judges also rated its fixes best. It ran about a third faster than the base model, which suits real use.
arxiv-2506-20858:
Jamil Farhat and four co-authors tackle a radio problem for sensors that talk straight to satellites, in a 2025 paper. The link uses LoRa, a low-power, long-range radio method popular for remote devices.

Low Earth orbit satellites move fast, and that motion bends the signal's frequency, the Doppler effect. The bend is strong enough to spoil LoRa links. The authors propose four ways to estimate and cancel the shift, then compare them in simulations against a perfect no-shift case. They also map the trade-offs with the radio's spreading factor and other settings. Their results point to LoRa setups that can hold a link with a passing satellite, extending coverage to places with no ground network.
arxiv-2506-21158:
Hampus Gummesson Svensson and co-authors make molecule-generating software explore more widely by feeding each training step a deliberately varied diet of examples, in a 2025 paper. In de novo drug design, a reinforcement learning agent proposes new molecules and scores them, but scoring is slow and costly, and the agent tends to collapse onto a few similar answers. Learning from diverse batches pushes back against that collapse.

The team introduces mini-batch diversification: each small batch used for an update is chosen to be varied on purpose. Across their experiments in chemical exploration, the method raised the diversity of the molecules found while keeping their quality high. That pairing matters in drug hunting, where several distinct good candidates give medicinal chemists real choices. The authors suggest the same trick can steady exploration in other costly reinforcement learning problems.
arxiv-2506-21358:
Behrooz Nasihatkon and co-authors label 3D boxes around cars using nothing but an ordinary photo and about ten clicks. Self-driving datasets need millions of cuboid annotations, yet the standard rigs, calibrated LiDAR and stereo cameras, are too costly to scale. Their method, ToosiCubix, asks annotators to mark vehicle parts instead: wheels, badges, symmetric features.

Those clicks become geometric constraints in an optimization that recovers each car's position, orientation, and size up to one scale ambiguity. The solver alternates between standard perspective estimation and least-squares fits. Cheap cuboid ground truth for existing photo collections could unlock 3D training data that fleets already photographed but never measured.
arxiv-2506-21658:
Muhammad Latif and Daniel Whalen ask how far back in cosmic time three great telescopes could spot quasars, in their 2025 arXiv paper. Supermassive black holes sit at the centers of most galaxies, and more than three hundred are already known from when the universe was young. How they grew so fast is still an open question.

Using a cosmological simulation of a billion-solar-mass quasar, the authors compute its infrared brightness for the Euclid, Roman and JWST telescopes across a wide redshift range. Euclid and Roman could find such black holes much earlier than expected in wide surveys, out to very high redshift, and JWST could then confirm them. Together the trio could reveal how these giants evolved.
arxiv-2506-21958:
Muhammad Imran Qureshi writes alone in a 2025 geometry paper. He builds a family of four dimensional shapes called terminal Fano varieties, prized in the sorting of higher dimensional forms. The shapes sit inside weighted spaces at low codimension and carry at worst isolated rough points. Computer algebra played a central role in the search and checks.

The sorting counts 95 families of one kind and 32 of another, split by how their cutting sections behave. Some have no useful linear system at all, others a large one whose section is not the expected smooth type. A full census of such shapes at low codimension gives later geometers a map to test conjectures against.
arxiv-2506-22058:
Baohao Liao, Xinyi Chen, Sara Rajaee, Yuhui Xu, Christian Herold, Anders Søgaard, Maarten de Rijke, and Christof Monz wrote a 2025 paper on a weak point in how language models reason. Long step-by-step reasoning lets models fix their own errors, but it also wastes effort. The team show the very first step of a reasoning chain carries outsized weight.

An error in that first step drags down everything after it, in test after test across leading open and closed models. Their fix is to sample many first steps, score them with a reward model, and keep only the good ones. That cut computing cost by up to seventy percent with no loss in accuracy. The result gives builders a cheap lever: guard the start of the chain.
arxiv-2506-22358:
Kalokyri and co-authors propose giving every medical AI model a passport: a structured, machine-readable record of what it is, what it was trained on, and how it has changed. Health AI is spreading fast, but its paperwork is mostly hand-written documents that cannot be compared or checked at scale, and models carry no verifiable identity. The passport framework captures the full life story, from data collection and cleaning through design, training, and deployment.

The paper also presents a working tool, AIPassport, built inside a European prostate cancer imaging project. The tool gathers the metadata automatically, keeps versions straight, and separates results from the scripts that made them. A lesion segmentation case shows it in action. The authors argue the approach cuts manual documentation effort while raising transparency and readiness for regulators. For hospitals and developers alike, the pitch is trust you can audit.
arxiv-2506-22458:
A cheap, portable air quality box is built by S M Minhazur Rahman and co-authors in a 2025 arXiv paper. The box reads two dust sizes, carbon monoxide, heat, and damp in real time. It sums an air quality index from those reads. A Bluetooth link feeds a phone app on the spot. Small size and low build cost suit homes, streets, towns, and farms alike.

Design, build, and accuracy checks fill the paper. The team weighs what such boxes mean for public grasp, green aims, and rule calls. Cheap live reads could spread where fixed stations never reach.
arxiv-2506-22558:
Blaise Bourdin, Jean-Jacques Marigo, Corrado Maurini, and Camilla Zolesi set out a new model of how stuff cracks, which can hold any round strength rule. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five.

Past crack models let a phase field eat the stuff's stiffness. Here it does not. In its place, the spring energy grows in a straight line past the strength zone. That zone shrinks to nil as the field nears its top. The team works out the model on a cube under edge loads. Its answer is a clean cross crack, when load and jump paths meet a test they state by a known circle tool. They sort strength rules by whether cracks can form.
arxiv-2506-22658:
Shiyang Zhang, Shun-Sheng Li, and Henk Hoekstra test how overlapping galaxies bias cosmic shear measurements, and how two surveys can rescue each other, in a 2025 paper. Weak lensing measures the shapes of millions of galaxies, but blended neighbors corrupt those shapes. The team simulated an idealized grid layout and a realistic random layout for space-based and ground-based surveys.

Blending biased the deep ground-based data most, since its blur is larger. Combining catalogs from both surveys helped: simply uniting all detections reached a higher usable galaxy density than either survey alone. Keeping only sources seen by both surveys still gained about twelve percent, though it wastes data at catalog level. The authors suggest pixel-level joint fitting could exploit shared objects better. Realistic blending, they insist, must feature in any synergy forecast.
arxiv-2506-22858:
Duygu Altinok teaches speech recognition to remember what surrounds a name, so names survive transcription intact, in this 2025 paper. Systems like Whisper transcribe fluently yet mangle named entities and numbers, exactly the details that matter in legal, financial, and medical records. Chunked processing makes it worse: an entity sliced at a boundary loses its context and its formatting.

The fix widens the ear during training. Thirty-second chunks gain five-second overlaps on both sides, making a forty-second window of meaning, while the model still answers only for the central thirty. Entities straddling a boundary are reassigned whole to the right-hand chunk, so they are learned intact. Training data enriched with entity labels teaches type-specific formatting alongside recognition. On the Spoken Wikipedia data set, the method improved entity recognition, formatting, and the semantic measures that track them.
arxiv-2506-23358:
Pawel Renc and co-authors present Federated Timeline Synthesis for training medical AI across hospitals in this 2025 paper. Patient records cannot be pooled freely across institutions. Their method turns each record into a token timeline of clinical events. Each hospital trains a generator on its own timelines and shares only model weights.

A central server uses those generators to synthesize a large shared corpus. A global generator trained on that corpus can simulate future patient paths on demand. Five prediction tasks on the MIMIC-IV dataset tested the approach. Models trained on synthetic data performed about as well as those trained on real data. Privacy, scale, and reuse for trial simulation are the main claimed gains.
arxiv-2506-23658:
The authors re-examine a charge-ordered crystal with synchrotron light in a 2025 paper. This spinel compound pairs copper with iridium and sulfur. At low temperature its iridium atoms form pairs. Charge ordering accompanies that dimer formation.

Powder studies had mapped the low-temperature structure before. Single-crystal diffraction now revisits it with sharper tools. The reanalysis confirms dimer formation and charge order. The ordering pattern itself differs from the earlier report, though. Dimer arrangement inside the unit cell also changed. Structural parameters from the new fit are provided. The authors argue for their structure's validity in discussion. Physical property studies of the compound remain active. A corrected lattice picture redirects that work. Magnetism and transport interpretations depend on the pattern. Crystallography self-corrects through better crystals here.
arxiv-2506-23858:
Jianzong Wu and co-authors introduced VMoBA in 2025, a sparse attention method for video diffusion models. Full attention grows too costly for long, high-resolution video. Past sparse methods often work only as inference shortcuts or miss video's space and time patterns.

Study of trained video models showed strong local patterns, varied query importance, and head-specific focus. VMoBA answers with a layered block scheme that shifts between one, two, and three dimensions, global block choice, and a threshold that sets how many blocks to attend. Training on longer sequences sped up greatly with quality matching or beating full attention, and inference also accelerated.
arxiv-2507-00358:
Yilie Huang and Xun Yu Zhou study reinforcement learning for control problems in twenty twenty-five. Their class of problems runs in continuous time with linear dynamics and quadratic costs. The costs here are indefinite, and the noise depends on both state and control. States are scalar, and there are no running control rewards.

Earlier work on this class used fixed exploration schedules. Those need heavy tuning and ignore how learning is going. The authors propose a model-free method that adapts exploration as it runs. The critic adjusts entropy regularization while the actor adjusts policy variance. Even with that freedom, the method keeps a sublinear regret bound. It matches the best known model-free results for this class.
arxiv-2507-00458:
Zhang and co-authors fix a language gap in voice hiding tools in a 2025 paper. Such tools mask who is speaking while keeping words clear. Most are built and graded on English alone, so other tongues suffer. The team works with Japanese and Mandarin speech and a self-taught sound encoder at the core.

Tuning the encoder on Japanese speech lifted clarity while keeping identity masked. A many-tongue encoder tuned the same way stretched the gains to Mandarin as well. The authors say target-tongue tuning and broad pre-training are both key. Their results point to voice privacy tools that serve more than English speakers.
arxiv-2507-00558:
Huai-Che Shia and co-authors shape dark light modes in a 2025 theory paper. The modes arise when a gas is made clear by control light, letting a probe beam park inside as a slow light blend.

By adding crafted electric and magnetic like potentials, the team carve the blend into set spots. They show the blend can swing between two spots in a clean beat, and can be walked through three spots in a slow, loss proof path. Moving stored light between spots could tune photon memory and shape light on recall. The work is a design study, awaiting lab tests.
arxiv-2507-01058:
Puspendu Banerjee and co-authors bring language AI to the judgment archive of the Calcutta High Court, in a 2025 paper. Courts sit on mountains of verdicts that lawyers must search for precedent and clients must somehow understand. The team built a framework that summarizes judgments and retrieves similar past cases on request.

A summarization model was fine-tuned on headnote summaries written by the court, and a two-step routine preserves the legal context that single-pass summaries drop. The summaries feed a vector database, over which a retrieval-augmented generation system answers questions with matching cases. Tests show clear gains in summary quality over generic approaches. For a judiciary short on time, such tools could turn an archive from a warehouse into a working library, provided lawyers keep verifying what the machine hands them.
arxiv-2507-01158:
Edvige Corbelli and three co-authors find what drives star birth across the M33 disk in a 2025 paper. The spiral's disk forms stars at rates that shift from core to rim. Which local trait sets that rate, gas weight, spin, or pull, was open.

The team built gas heights and weights from light reads and disk math, with dark matter in the count. Fit tools from plain lines to smart forests weighed each trait at scales from fine to broad. Gas squeeze came out on top disk-wide. High squeeze turns light gas into the dense kind stars need.
arxiv-2507-01358:
Hirao, Nozaki, and Tasaka grade three rare unit groups as ball point sets in this twenty twenty-five paper. The groups count two score, four score, and six score points on the ball. A point set earns design rank when set sums kill all wave forms of set grades.

Inside, wave grades that die on each group are found in full for all three. Each group proves the least and lone set of its rank in their tests. One group's rank tale had no past match in the design lore. Grids built on the groups then host wave sums as sum forms. Those sums prove to be shape forms, with dead spans named by rank.
arxiv-2507-01558:
Davis Berlind, Lorenzo Cappello, and Oscar Hernan Madrid Padilla build a Bayesian tool for spotting change-points. Their 2025 paper looks for breaks in a time series where the average or spread suddenly shifts. The tool also reports credible sets, ranges that carry stated confidence about each break's place. Most rival tools give bare point guesses.

For a single break, their method finds the spot at the best possible rate, up to small factors. It stacks single-break models to catch many breaks at once. In tests it matched top rivals on speed and accuracy, with far tighter credible sets. Real uses include ion channel gating in a bacterial cell and rock layers in an oil well log. The tool suits both smooth and count data.
arxiv-2507-01758:
Stevens and Deffner present a 2025 physics letter on the energy cost of quantum gates. Real quantum computers drive gates with classical fields, and those fields carry energy. The authors derive a floor for the field energy a gate needs. That floor links to the gate's expected error rate.

The key trait is entangleability, a Hamiltonian's power to entangle qubits. Gates rich in that trait can run with less field energy, they show. In the limit, a universal quantum computer could run on vanishing energy, but only at the cost of endless complexity. The trade-off frames a design rule for future machines: buy energy savings with entangling power.
arxiv-2507-01858:
Hank Chen and Joaquin Liniado introduce a three-dimensional quantum field theory with an endless symmetry, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. The symmetry generalizes the famous chiral symmetry of a two-dimensional model, now stretched into three dimensions and graded for supersymmetry. Its algebra is an extended loop-like structure with a central term.

By quantizing the theory in radial shells, they build its space of states. A three-dimensional echo of the state-operator link then shows the local operators form a new algebraic structure named after a pasta shape. The authors expect the setup to carry exact methods from two-dimensional theory into three dimensions, a longstanding goal in the field.
arxiv-2507-02058:
Mahsa Sanati and co-authors simulate how the first supermassive black holes grew so fat so fast, in the aftermath of the first stars. Telescopes keep finding giants absurdly early, and the energy from these feeding black holes shapes even dwarf galaxies. The team ran high-resolution zoom-in cosmological simulations following hundred-thousand-solar-mass seeds inside young galaxies.

The suite escalated the physics step by step: no feedback, then thermal feedback capped at the Eddington rate, then richer mixes of thermal, kinetic, and radiative pushback. In every model the seeds still ballooned to about ten million solar masses by redshift eight. Growth, it seems, is hard to stop; feedback's fingerprints lie elsewhere.
arxiv-2507-02158:
Jacob Roberts, Blair Archibald, and Phil Trinder argue that container software should report its own health rather than wait to be asked, in this 2025 paper. Kubernetes, the system that runs fleets of small services, usually polls each container on a timer to check it is alive. Polling needs careful tuning, reacts slowly, and can cry wolf.

Their signal based design lets a container speak up the moment its state changes. A new mathematical model predicts the gain, and six experiments on a standard shop benchmark confirm it. Failures were spotted about eighty-six percent faster than with polling, with no false alarms. Polling's false alarms alone cut availability by about four percent in their tests. The authors urge orchestrators to add signal based health as a standard feature.
arxiv-2507-02358:
Seven authors, led by Anlin Zheng, present Hita in this 2025 paper, a tokenizer that helps machines build images step by step. Autoregressive image models write visual tokens one after another, like words in a sentence. Standard tokenizers chop an image into local patches, so the model starts with little sense of the whole picture.

Hita fixes that with a holistic-to-local scheme. Learnable holistic tokens come first and carry the global shape of the image. Patch tokens follow, adding local detail. Causal attention keeps each step aware of what came before, matching how the model will generate. A light fusion module then steers the flow of information before the tokens are decoded back into pixels. The design aims at images that hang together as a whole, not just as a grid of parts.
arxiv-2507-02458:
Tingyang Shen, He Wang, and Jibo He propose a way to fill data gaps in spaceborne gravitational wave detectors in this 2025 paper. Missions like LISA, Taiji, and TianQin will listen for years to sources such as merging massive black holes. Gaps and glitches in the stream cost information and leak signal across frequencies. Standard fixes, like windowing and smoothing, can bias the estimates of source traits. The authors instead impute the missing stretches with a Kalman filter and smoother.

In their test case, the smoother removed the biases that windowing had introduced. It also ran cheaper than noise inpainting, the main rival augmentation method. The approach treats the signal's own dynamics as the guide for what the missing data should look like. The authors present the method as a robust and efficient option for the data pipelines of space based observatories.
arxiv-2507-02558: The Pierre Auger Collaboration reports, in a 2025 paper, a measurement of the muon content of inclined cosmic-ray air showers. When a high-energy cosmic ray strikes the upper air, it spawns a shower of particles that rains over a wide area. Muons are a key part of that rain and carry clues about the ray's nature. The paper joins two instruments of the Pierre Auger Observatory: the AERA radio array and its water-Cherenkov surface detectors, which together pin down the muon share of slanted showers.
arxiv-2507-02858:
Yuchen Shen, Anmol Singhal, and Travis Breaux test language models as interview helpers in this 2025 study. Software teams learn what to build by interviewing users and clients. Good follow-up questions are hard to craft live: the topic may be new, and speech comes fast. The team asked whether a large language model could suggest follow-ups as good as a human's.

They built prompts on a frame of common interviewer mistakes, and on the speaker's own words. In two controlled tests, judges rated the model's questions on clarity, fit, and new information. The model matched human questions overall. When guided by the mistake frame, its questions beat the human ones. The authors see real-time help as a way to ease the load on interviewers.
arxiv-2507-03058:
Lo Ho Tin studies sums built from powers of harmonic numbers, a classic sequence in analysis. The 2025 paper builds a Dirichlet series from those powers and asks what the series can reveal. Such series link sums, poles, and special constants in one frame.

From the series the author derives new identities for sums with harmonic numbers. Values at negative integers and conduct near poles get close study. Objects akin to the Stieltjes constants also appear. Growth rates for the sums are worked out as well. The author closes with a link between these analytic traits and a possible path toward settling whether a famous constant is irrational.
arxiv-2507-03258:
Zhaorun Lin wrote a 2025 thesis on building voting and auction systems atop blockchains. Smart contracts on Ethereum offer records that anyone can verify and no one can quietly change. Those traits suit settings where strangers must trust the process without trusting each other.

The first design, Blind Vote, is a fully on-chain election method built on blind signatures. Votes stay untraceable while the tally remains open to checking. It matches the safety of earlier methods while using far less gas, the fee unit of Ethereum. The thesis also gives a family of auction methods that hide bidder names and bid values. Both lines of work aim to make on-chain deals cheaper and more private.
arxiv-2507-03858:
Can Zheng and Chung G. Kang design a receiver for a new wireless waveform called affine frequency division multiplexing. Such waveforms must pick the sent symbols out of signals smeared by multipath echoes, and classic receivers either cost too much computing or lose accuracy. The proposed receiver uses variational Bayesian inference, a method that works with an approximate probability picture in place of the exact one.

The receiver estimates the chance of each symbol by shrinking the gap between its approximation and the true posterior distribution. This yields soft decisions, meaning graded confidence values rather than hard guesses. In simulations, the method reached lower bit error rates than zero-forcing, linear minimum mean square error, and message passing rivals. It also converged faster and held up better in complex multipath channels. The authors present it as a low-cost receiver that does not trade away detection quality.
arxiv-2507-04158:
Paolo Santonastaso and Ferdinando Zullo forge new fingerprints for sum-rank codes in a 2025 paper. Coding theory asks when two codes are really the same code in disguise. That equivalence question feeds cryptography. The sum-rank metric, which blends two older metrics, breaks the classic fingerprints.

The authors define fresh invariants: generalized idealisers, a centraliser, a center, and a refined sense of linearity. From these grow nuclear parameters, borrowed from division algebra theory, where they excel at proving codes distinct. A computing framework on skew polynomials, mirroring the matrix setting, makes the parameters computable for known best codes. With them, the team studies equivalence among the largest known families of top-grade sum-rank codes. They offer the method where traditional tools fall short.
arxiv-2507-04358:
Alfakih writes, in a solo 2025 note, on a cleanup task that sits under GPS fixes. A set of points in space yields a matrix of pairwise distances, and such a matrix must meet strict shape rules. Noise in the raw readings can break those rules. His task: given a sound distance matrix and one noisy row of distances, find the closest row that keeps the enlarged matrix sound at the same embedding dimension.

The task grows out of fault checks in GPS, where a bad reading must be flagged and fixed fast. He gives a criterion that spots when a fault is there at all. He then gives three algorithms to find the fix row. One suits the small case of four points. Two more cover five points and up. The note keeps its scope tight: one matrix, one row, exact dimension held.
arxiv-2507-04558:
The XY spin chain is a textbook model that free fermions solve exactly, and Robert Henry and co-authors push it into non-Hermitian ground. They let the model's anisotropy parameter take complex values, which allows two quasi-energies to meet and merge. At those meetings the system hits exceptional points, where two eigenvalues and their eigenvectors coalesce into one. The paper maps how these degeneracies organize, including exceptional point rings tied to PT symmetry.

Such points mark where the usual rules of quantum mechanics bend, since the eigenvectors stop being independent. The work extends a classic solvable model into a playground for non-Hermitian physics.
arxiv-2507-04858:
Antonio Sa Pinto adapts music software to an Afro-Brazilian tradition called Maracatu, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. The task is to spot the exact start of each drum hit in a recording. Maracatu rhythms are dense and complex, so models trained on Western music often fail on them.

He started from two pre-trained networks, one built to find hit starts and one built to track beats. He then fine-tuned them with just five-second labeled clips for each of five percussion instruments. Scores improved sharply, in the best cases by more than fifty points. The beat-based model worked best for instruments that keep time. The best tuning recipe differed by instrument. The approach needs little labeling, which helps traditions that lack large data sets.
arxiv-2507-05058:
Enrico Lattuada and four colleagues write a practical guide to differential dynamic microscopy, a way to read motion from microscope movies, in a 2025 tutorial. Over two decades the method became standard for colloids, polymers, active fluids, and living systems. It extracts the same dynamic correlations as light scattering setups, from an ordinary microscope and camera.

The guide walks through planning, image acquisition, and analysis step by step, aiming to lower the entry barrier for a widening, mixed user base. It introduces fastDDM, the authors' open-source package, whose parallel algorithms cut analysis time by up to ten thousand fold on typical datasets of ten thousand frames. High-throughput workflows become realistic for single labs. The authors frame the tutorial as an invitation: the technique is mature, the software is free, and the applications keep growing.
arxiv-2507-05458:
Robots that serve people need to learn what each person likes, such as a safe route or a fast one. Yi-Shiuan Tung, Bradley Hayes, and Alessandro Roncone wrote a 2025 paper on a method called CRED, which helps a robot learn human reward from ranked paths. Older methods often miss good paths and ask weak questions, above all in long tasks.

CRED makes up new scenes and asks what the reward would be if a guessed taste were the true one. That mix yields a wide, useful set of paths for a person to rank. Tests in a grid world and on real street maps from OpenStreetMap showed better reward learning. The gains also held when the scene changed.
arxiv-2507-05758:
Gaetano Fiore and Fedele Lizzi examine what happens when changing reference frames is itself uncertain, in a 2025 paper. Textbook frame changes, like boosts between moving observers, have exact parameters and form a group. The authors allow the parameters to be smeared out as probability distributions, classical or quantum, and the neat group becomes a semigroup where changes cannot always be undone.

A striking consequence follows: a system can be in a pure state in one frame and a mixed, thermal-looking state in another. They work this out for Galilean boosts in one space dimension. If one frame sits in a thermal state relative to another, a particle at rest in the first appears warmed in the second, a link they discuss alongside the time-energy uncertainty relation.
arxiv-2507-06058:
Marius Cizauskas and co-authors studied in 2025 the spin properties of quantum dots that emit light in the telecom band. These dots were grown by a droplet method rather than the usual strain-driven route. Spin behavior matters because such dots could serve as building blocks for quantum information systems.

Using pump-probe light measures, they found the electron spin factor was about half the usual value for dots grown the standard way. The spin lifetime was about ten times longer than in comparable standard dots. The spread in spin factors was also smaller. The authors credit the more symmetric shape that the droplet method gives. The results make these dots attractive for quantum uses, they say.
arxiv-2507-06158:
Anjelo Gabriel Cruz, Manuel Joseph Loquias, and Jörg Thuswaldner studied addition machines for digit systems built on matrices. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, deals with ways to write vectors as digit strings in a matrix base. The base here is a growing two by two matrix with rational parts. Each vector gets a sole such write, but a tail term from a finite set, the attractor, may stay. When that tail can be set to zero, the system is clean.

The team ties those tails to automata that add digits in the system. Such machines let one check if the clean case holds. Readers in number theory get a bridge between digit writes, tilings, and finite machines.
arxiv-2507-06458:
Arjun Banerjee and three co-authors label every neuron in 2025 inside a protein language model. These models absorb deep biology from amino acid text, but what single neurons encode stayed obscure. Prior probes labeled only samples by hand or through compression tricks.

Their automated pipeline assigns plain-language labels to hundreds of thousands of neurons, each tuned to specific chemical or structural traits. The labels then steer generation: nudging chosen neurons guides the model to proteins with target weight, stability, and shapes like helices and zinc fingers. Comparing model sizes, the labeled maps expose scaling patterns and a structured layout of the neuron space.
arxiv-2507-06658:
Gennadii Iakovlev introduces a new way to measure hostility among political elites using large language models. His 2025 paper argues that comparative research tracks public polarization and party ideology, but rarely the direct evaluations politicians aim at each other. The new Elite Polarization Score fills that gap from parliamentary speech.

The method finds named actors in debate transcripts, pairs speakers with their targets, and scores the sentiment aimed at each one. Scores are then rolled up into party and parliament measures of mutual negativity. Tests on British, Hungarian, and Italian debates spanning up to four decades found no false discoveries. Sentiment estimates landed close to human coding, and the model matched or beat human sensitivity in two of the three countries.
arxiv-2507-06758:
Simon Thelen and Wolfgang Mauerer present a way to pick the best quantum-classical method for a job, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Hybrid methods promise gains, yet their speed and quality are hard to foresee. Users are left unsure which method fits a given problem.

Their frame reads notes placed in the source code to trace key traits of each method. Statistical models then predict which method and settings best meet stated needs. A case study on optimization problems backs the approach with simulation data. The authors argue the same frame fits other tasks, such as simulating physics systems.
arxiv-2507-06858:
Mathias Schulz and co-authors report a two-and-a-half-year study of face recognition drift in a 2025 paper. Over four hundred volunteers of varied backgrounds visited a German test center on a set schedule. Their faces and fingers were captured with several devices under controlled conditions. The local database holds over two hundred thousand biometric samples, handled under European privacy law.

Modern face algorithms scored each visit against the volunteer's earlier records. Scores wobbled more from one day to the next than across the whole study span. Day-level noise, from light, mood, or skin state, may swamp slow aging effects. Test centers, the authors argue, must sample the same people across many days to grade systems fairly.
arxiv-2507-07258:
Rami Darwish, Mahmoud Abdelsalam, Sajad Khorsandroo, and Kaushik Roy let smart-device fleets learn malware detection together without pooling their raw data. Their 2025 paper works in federated learning, where each site trains locally. Standard averaging methods stumble when sites hold skewed, non-overlapping malware mixes, exactly the real-world pattern.

Their framework, FedP3E, swaps summaries instead of data or gradients. Each client builds class prototypes with a Gaussian mixture model, adds noise for privacy, and sends only those compact sketches to the server. Returned global prototypes enrich local training, and synthetic oversampling lifts rare classes. Tests on a standard IoT dataset under realistic skew showed the approach holding up where plain averaging sags. The design keeps communication light while sharing what each site has seen.
arxiv-2507-07758:
Particle beams circling in an accelerator follow rules that bend from the simple linear picture, and those bends were once treated as flaws to correct. Giovannozzi reviews the field of single-particle nonlinear beam dynamics in this 2025 article, tracing it from pioneering work in the 1950s. The review covers how design practice for circular machines has changed over time.

Recent years have brought a friendlier view of nonlinear effects. New concepts describe and model them better, and fresh proposals use them on purpose to steer and shape beams. The article discusses these approaches in detail. It should serve readers who design accelerators and want to turn a former nuisance into a tool for finer beam control.
arxiv-2507-08158:
Differential privacy promises that one person's data barely moves a model's output, but its guarantees are stated against a worst-case attacker. Marika Swanberg and co-authors ask what those guarantees mean against the attackers we actually face, in this 2025 paper. Their unified framework stretches the classic bounds across membership inference, attribute inference, and outright reconstruction.

The bounds cover attacks on many people at once and count near-misses, not just exact hits, using only the privacy settings and the attacker's starting odds. The team tests the theory on language models fine-tuned with privacy and on noisy survey tables. They offer the framework as firm ground for judging real risk from private algorithms.
arxiv-2507-08758:
Mohsen Dehghankar, Stavros Sintos, and Abolfazl Asudeh add fairness constraints to classic geometry tools for summarizing data, in a 2025 paper. Epsilon-nets compress point sets while preserving answers to range queries, and hitting sets cover shapes with few points. Neither had been examined for fairness across demographic groups.

The authors define two fairness notions: keeping group shares as in the input, or hitting arbitrary target ratios. They give a fast sampling algorithm whose fair nets grow only slightly with the number of groups, and a slower discrepancy-based one that outputs smaller nets. Fair hitting set reduces to fair nets, yielding a solid approximation. Under some input distributions, they also prove fair samples cannot exist at all, a useful warning. Experiments confirmed zero unfairness at modest size cost. The work opens computational geometry to fairness-aware data systems.
arxiv-2507-08858:
Sami Achour and co-authors test foundation models for time series forecasting in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Conformal prediction wraps a forecast in an interval with a stated coverage rate. It needs held-out data for calibration, which competes with training data for classic models.

Foundation models forecast with no task training, so nearly all data can go to calibration. The team compares them with statistical models and gradient boosting inside this setup. When data were scarce, the foundation models gave more reliable intervals, thanks to better raw accuracy. Their calibration was also more stable. The scarcer the data, the bigger the edge. Code is shared for replication.
arxiv-2507-08958:
Xiaowen Zhang, Zhenyu Bi, Patrick Lachance, Xuan Wang, Tiziana Di Matteo, and Rupert Croft wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It presents SimAgents, a team of language model agents that pulls simulation settings out of papers and sets up cosmology runs.

Cosmology codes grow ever more tangled, and their settings hide in dense papers with no shared form. Hand translation to scripts is slow and error-prone. SimAgents splits the work among agents that reason on physics, check the software, and run tools, all in set talk. The team built a test set from dozens of past simulations in print. The system scores strongly there. Code and data are public.
arxiv-2507-09058: Zachary Radke proves that well-behaved solutions exist for a family of fluid equations in this 2025 paper. The equations model surface flows driven by temperature-like quantities, a standard model for large-scale weather patterns. Most theory assumes solutions fade away at distance, which excludes broad, uniform states. Radke instead allows states that do not decay. He shows such solutions exist for a short time and are unique, in two kinds of function spaces.
arxiv-2507-09158:
Murthy and co-authors present an automated way to outline spine bones on X-ray images, in a research paper from 2025. Clear outlines of each vertebra help doctors judge spine movement problems and plan surgery. Drawing them by hand is slow, tiring, and prone to error, above all when each bone must be traced on its own.

Their method reshapes a standard image model called U-Net into a sandwich form with two activation functions. It segments chest vertebrae from front-view X-rays and draws each contour. Against the base U-Net, the new design raised the Dice score, a measure of overlap with hand-drawn truth, by 4.1 percent. The authors argue the tool gives faster and more even results than manual tracing.
arxiv-2507-09258:
Liu, Wu, Pan, and Yang tested in twenty twenty-five a dark energy model where dark stuff and dark energy trade flows. The norm model of the cosmos has small clashes with sky data across its long past. Their model lets the sound scale at an early split time set the start state in a neat way.

As the trade strength grows, their count for the present spread rate rises too. That shift helps the clash on that rate a bit, but not in full. The trade leaves a mark on the early sky glow in a thin time span. Chain tests pin down the free parts of the model.
arxiv-2507-10158:
Robots in different places could learn to grasp objects together without sharing raw data, using federated learning. The catch is each robot sees different amounts and kinds of data, which drags down the shared model, especially for robots with little data. The authors propose MTF-Grasp, a multi-tier version of this training. It first ranks robots by quality and quantity of their data. The strongest robots, the top tier, train seed models first.

Those seed models are passed to the remaining robots, giving them a better start than a model trained from scratch on skewed data. The approach is tested on two standard grasping datasets, Cornell and Jacquard, with uneven amounts of data per robot. MTF-Grasp beats the conventional federated setup by up to 8 percent on the quantity-skewed tests. The authors present tiering as a general fix for uneven data in robot fleets.
arxiv-2507-10458:
Morteza Baniasad Azad and Mostafa Arabtash studied a number built from finite groups in twenty twenty-five. Take every element of a group, note its order, and multiply them all: that product is their starting point. They then count its prime factors, with repeats, using the classic omega function, and ask how the count behaves under group operations.

The resulting function mimics the derivative rules of calculus. For a direct product of groups of coprime size, a product rule holds. For a quotient by a central cyclic Sylow subgroup, a quotient rule holds. They also show a non-cyclic group never beats the cyclic group of the same size on this measure. A final bound compares arbitrary groups with a specific linear group at three small primes.
arxiv-2507-10658:
Anupam Bhardwaj and co-authors calibrate the brightness of Mira variables, pulsating giant stars in globular clusters, to give the cosmic distance scale a fresh anchor. Knowing how bright these stars truly are, for a given pulse period, lets astronomers measure distances and pin down the expansion rate of the universe. Independent anchors are precious because expansion estimates disagree.

The team gathered near-infrared time series for fifty-five candidate long-period variables in eighteen clusters spanning a wide range of metal content. Using motions from the Gaia mission and color data, they confirmed forty-one oxygen-rich Miras as true cluster members. Their brightness relations show scatter comparable to other top methods. A solid cluster calibration strengthens the whole distance ladder.
arxiv-2507-10758:
Smart home devices and cameras form easy targets for malware, and spotting bad traffic among the flood is a growing need. Nikesh Prajapati, Bimal Karki, Saroj Gopali, and Akbar Siami Namin compare deep learning detectors for that job in this 2025 paper. The line-up mixes graph-based models, which read the traffic web, with sequence models that read traffic over time.

Seven designs were tested, including a transformer model called BERT and several memory-based networks. BERT came out on top, with accuracy near ninety-nine point nine percent and near-perfect scores on the other standard measures. Attention-based models also did well and offered clearer readings of their choices, though some took long to train. The graph model trained fastest but scored lowest. The authors credit the mix of order and variety in device traffic for the strong results.
arxiv-2507-10958:
Anthony Miyaguchi and co-authors report their team's run at the eRisk 2025 shared tasks in a 2025 working note. The lab's challenges target early detection of mental health risk from online text. Their team, DS@GT, entered two: a pilot task on spotting depression through conversation, and one using time-aware attention models.

For the conversation task, several large language models interviewed in the style of a standard depression inventory and returned structured scores. With no true labels available, the team judged entries by cross-model agreement and internal consistency. Their best run placed second on the official board, with strong marks on the task's agreement-based measures. The note details the prompt design that kept model outputs aligned with the clinical criteria.
arxiv-2507-11258:
Olivier Gasquet's paper on modal logic carries an unusual and candid notice: the proof it set out to present does not work. The paper aimed to show that quasi-dense modal logics have the finite model property, using a path-filtration technique. The author states plainly that the argument contains a major flaw, and that the flaw is unfixable.

The text is preserved as a record of the attempted proof and its failure. Quasi-dense logics are a family of modal logics whose frame conditions generalize density, and the finite model property matters because it often underpins decidability results. A published admission that a promising route collapses is itself useful to logicians: it warns others away from the same dead end and documents where the argument breaks. Readers should treat the paper as a cautionary artifact, not as an established result.
arxiv-2507-11458:
Sameer Sharma, writing alone in 2025, built a matrix tool for sorting entanglement in graph-shaped quantum states. Such states serve quantum error fixing, communication, and computing. His matrix counts links drawn from the graph's control points, where pairs of qubits are joined.

Using entropy as the yardstick, he derived exact formulas for the most entanglement such states can hold. The top value grows with the square of the qubit count, but the pattern splits by odd and even counts. Counts that are multiples of twelve showed extra strength. The framework gives a clean map of how entanglement spreads in large linked systems. The author aims it at the design of future quantum technology.
arxiv-2507-11658:
Karla Arellano-Cordova and a large team study nitrogen enrichment in nearby star-forming galaxies, in a 2025 paper from the CLASSY survey. They measured nitrogen and oxygen abundances directly in forty-five local galaxies with a wide range of traits. The goal was to see what drives the nitrogen-to-oxygen ratio.

That ratio followed the same trend with oxygen seen in other local galaxies, and distant galaxies showed similar values at fixed metal content. Denser gas went with higher nitrogen ratios, which may explain part of the scatter. Galaxies with intense or compact star formation also ran high. Fast outflows linked to higher ratios too, pointing to feedback from stars and black holes.
arxiv-2507-11758:
Schwartz works out formulas for the neutron load that a fusion reactor wall must bear when the fuel nuclei are spin-polarized. Polarizing the fuel can raise the reaction rate and steer where neutrons go, but designers need to know what that steering does to each part of the wall. The formulas cover a torus with a convex cross-section, any fuel polarization, and any local direction of the magnetic field. They can be evaluated very fast.

Because the formulas are fully differentiable, they can sit inside an optimization code that searches for wall shapes with an even neutron load. Example shapes tuned for each main polarization mode are shown. The treatment skips neutron scattering, so the results serve as fast guidance rather than final engineering numbers. For designers weighing polarized fuel, the work turns a slow simulation question into a quick calculation.
arxiv-2507-11858:
Qiwei Chen and Ricardo Constante-Amores compress a turbulent flow into a small model in a 2025 paper. Their test case is heated fluid in a box, a classic convection setup. At strong heating the flow is chaotic and its great circulation flips now and then. The team ask whether a compact state description can hold such a system.

Their framework splits motion into slow and fast parts. Each part is squeezed into a small nonlinear space with its own closed dynamics. Scale separation alone, they show, yields a working low dimensional account of the chaos. Small models that keep rare flips could speed forecasting of like flows in weather and engineering.
arxiv-2507-12058:
Konstantin Slutsky, Mikhail Sodin, and Aron Wennman prove, in twenty twenty-five, equivariant Borel versions of classic theorems in complex analysis and partial differential equations. Equivariant means the construction respects translations: shifting the input shifts the output the same way. Borel means the assignment is measurable, though not necessarily continuous. Their starting point is a Weierstrass-type theorem: each pattern of prescribed zeros gets an entire function with exactly those zeros, chosen in a translation-respecting Borel way. They also study right inverses for three operators: the Laplacian, the heat operator, and a complex derivative operator.

Borel equivariant inverses exist on the free part of each operator's range. The freeness conditions cannot be dropped, and Borel cannot be upgraded to continuity. Proofs use approximation theorems and Borel toasts, measurable analogues of ergodic towers.
arxiv-2507-12158:
Nawshin Mannan Proma and four co-authors present a way to check the safety of self-driving ground vehicles in a 2025 paper. Such vehicles now work in factories and yards where a fault can hurt people. Testing must cover many conditions, and the team wants numbers, not just pass-or-fail marks, on how safe a vehicle is.

They build a grid that lists every relevant setup of the surroundings, then run situation-based tests to learn how likely the vehicle is to move from one setup to the next. Those rates feed a probabilistic model of normal and unsafe behavior. Safety rules drawn from hazard analysis are then checked on the model, which flags high-risk setups and gives measured guarantees.
arxiv-2507-12658:
How small features on the Sun's surface feed the solar wind is far less clear than how its large bursts do. Jeongwoo Lee and five co-authors measure fine motions of bright points along a coronal hole edge in sharp telescope images from Big Bear. They combine the motion, magnetic flux, and lifetime of the open flux tubes involved to estimate the energy carried by each Alfvénic pulse.

Each pulse holds about ten to the twenty-fifth erg, far more than the ten to the twenty-third erg blamed for the magnetic switchbacks seen by the Parker Solar Probe. The pulses also match the switchbacks in how much area they cover at granular scales. The team concludes that such pulses could reach the solar wind with enough strength left to create switchbacks, a new clue to how energy cycles between the Sun and its wind.
arxiv-2507-12858:
Yuki Tomoda, Ichiro Tsuda, and Yutaka Yamaguti present a study of how networks of artificial nerve cells can split into parts with distinct jobs. Their method trains a recurrent neural network while pushing down the shared information between groups of cells. The shared information is estimated with a neural tool, and the network is tested on two tasks.

One task asks the network to hold two bits in memory, and the other asks it to separate two chaotic signals. The team found that the trained networks still did the tasks well while their cells formed clear functional groups. Groups defined by how cells act together appeared before groups defined by the strength of the links between cells. The authors suggest that cells first take on special roles, and that this step then drives the network to rewire itself.
arxiv-2507-12958:
Yu-Yue Cui, Xiao-Mei Tang, Qi Huang, and Rui Chen predict new two-baryon states built from charm and strange quarks. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Dibaryons with heavy flavor are a frontier of hadron physics. The authors use a one-boson-exchange model of baryon forces. Charm baryons pair with light baryons in P-wave motion. Eight coupled channels enter the analysis.

Several molecular candidates emerge with set quantum numbers. Some pair a charmed baryon with a nucleon, others with hyperons. Coupled-channel effects prove decisive for at least one state. Phase shift analysis confirms bound states and flags resonances. One shape-type resonance stands out among them. Experiments gain a target list for exotic hadron searches.
arxiv-2507-13258:
Mariam Arif and co-authors test how spread in particle size harms the order of thin colloidal crystals in 2025. Colloids are tiny spheres that can self assemble into crystals. Uneven sizes can break that order and stop crystal growth. Most past work was by computer. This team runs lab tests with a controlled range of size spread.

Films were dried from drops with set spread levels. As spread rose, order fell as expected. Sharp drops in local order marks came at two spread levels. The pattern fits a model of layer by layer growth like that of crystal films on a base. The results set limits for making crystals from cheaper, less even batches.
arxiv-2507-13358:
Maxwell Siegel builds a Fourier theory for a class of p-adic functions defined by self-similar rules, in a 2025 paper. Let p be an integer at least two and K a global field. An F-series is a function of a p-adic integer that rebuilds itself on each residue class by a simple affine rule. The coefficients of those rules are treated as variables in a ring of formal power series.

He shows that such a function has a Fourier transform, and that the transform survives when relations are imposed on the coefficients. He also shows the same for the pointwise product of the function with itself many times over. These results extend to products of distinct series as well. The work links p-adic analysis with algebra in a functorial way.
arxiv-2507-13758:
Reasoning models are increasingly used as judges of other models' answers, trusted because they show their work. Qian Wang and co-authors show in this 2025 paper that the shown work itself can be rigged: judges favor text that merely looks like reasoning, even when the logic is broken. They call the flaw Fake Reasoning Bias.

Their benchmark, THEATER, builds test cases that dress wrong answers in reasoning costumes, from tiny cue phrases to full fake chains of thought. Seventeen leading models were tried on opinion-style and factual tasks. All were fooled to some degree, and reasoning models were fooled more than plain ones, a more-thinking-less-robust paradox. Simple cues did the most damage, cutting accuracy by up to fifteen percent on the weakest sets. Careful prompting clawed back some accuracy on factual tasks.
arxiv-2507-13858:
Nicolò Brunello and co-authors built InTraVisTo, a tool for peering inside large language models, in a 2025 paper. Models have grown strong but stay hard to predict. A user sees the final words, not the steps that made them. The tool traces how each word forms as it moves through the model layers.

Two views drive the design. One view decodes word states at each layer, so a user can watch a half-formed word sharpen step by step. The other view maps how facts flow between parts of the model with a Sankey diagram, a chart of thick and thin streams. The authors aim the tool at teams who test and ship these models. Clear views of the inner steps may help them spot odd acts and fix flaws before release.
arxiv-2507-14458:
Ching-Hao Chang, Jih-Hsin Cheng, and I-Hsun Tsai study bundles tied to a classic equation from physics and geometry, in a 2025 math paper. Their objects live on three kinds of spaces: flat torus-like spaces, complex projective spaces, and spaces of planes. The equation's solutions come in energy levels, like notes on a scale.

Borrowing a trick from physics, the authors turn higher-level solutions into lowest-level ones, which are easier to describe. That move gives the bundles a natural complex structure and lets them write higher solutions out in full using known special functions. For projective spaces they also give an exact count of how many such solutions exist. The work speaks to questions raised by string theory studies done with computers.
arxiv-2507-14758:
Luyi Ma and co-authors presented a 2025 conference paper on a new way to recommend items to users. Modern recommendation systems can generate a personal list step by step, much like a language model writes text. The catch is cost and clarity: the standard method pays attention to everything at once, which is slow, and its tokens carry little plain meaning.

Their system, GRACE, first turns each user action into tokens enriched with facts from a product knowledge graph, such as category, brand, and price. A chain-of-thought style layout makes the reasoning behind each token clearer. Then a new attention method looks only at selected chunks of the history: near, far, and current parts of the user's journey. The authors report tests showing the design keeps quality while cutting waste. The work aims at recommenders that are both cheaper to run and easier to inspect.
arxiv-2507-15158:
Abbas, Abdel-Ghani, and Maksymov build a computing system for image recognition out of resonant-tunnelling diodes, in a 2025 paper. These diodes are tiny electronic parts whose current bends sharply as voltage rises, a quirk ideal for reservoir computing. In that approach, a fixed nonlinear device scrambles inputs and only a simple readout layer is trained. Edge devices need such lean hardware as AI spreads into real-time, low-power settings.

The team formulate the diode reservoir in theory and simulate it as a circuit-level system. It classified handwritten digits and recognized objects in a fruit image dataset with promising accuracy. Unlike classic reservoirs, the design drops random wiring for a deterministic transform of the signal. The authors present it as a step toward neuromorphic chips that sip power.
arxiv-2507-15358:
Jiahao Liu, Cheng Wang, and Tianshu Bi revisit in 2025 how grid-following converters, the electronics that link solar and wind farms to the power grid, affect the grid's frequency. As spinning generators retire, these converters shape stability more and more, yet their exact influence was murky.

This first part of a two-part study focuses on the center of inertia, the grid-wide average motion that sets overall frequency. The authors build a multi-generator model where converters interact with spinning machines through virtual tie lines. Folding that model into the center-of-inertia frame reveals how converter behavior pushes the shared frequency around.
arxiv-2507-15458:
Asghar Ullah, Tahir Naseem, and Özgür Müstecaplıoğlu work out the best quantum probes for taking a temperature. The hosted text's own title frames the study as optimal strategies for transient and equilibrium thermometry with Gaussian and plain probes. Their 2025 paper compares probe states made in one mode and in paired modes born in a nonlinear crystal.

In the short-time regime, odd-shaped states such as Fock and cat states estimate temperature far faster than smooth Gaussian ones. Entangled pairs reach the signal earlier still. At equilibrium, a squeezed thermal pair beats any single-mode probe. Among readouts, energy measures give the best precision, population gaps come close, and wave-shape measures lag. Squeezing earns its keep by quieting the population gap's noise.
arxiv-2507-15558:
Dzmitry Saladukha and co-authors boost wake-word spotting in noise with many sound lanes in a 2025 paper. Beam aim and noise cut can warp or mute the wake word they guard. Their net takes in a few lanes at once and weighs which lane or mix helps most.

A care web in the net picks the best lane blend per clip on the fly. Tests span a lab set with set terms and a smart speaker set from real homes. Gains are set next to plain routes on grade and cost.
arxiv-2507-15758:
Xingyu Wu and co-authors teach large reasoning models in 2025 to think only as long as a problem deserves. Such models write long chains of thought and waste tokens on easy questions. Outside caps and after-the-fact trimming are blunt fixes. Their method instead builds length sense into the model itself, through two stages of reinforcement learning.

In stage one, the model discovers how long its own successful solutions tend to run for each kind of problem. In stage two, those patterns are placed inside the model's working context as guidance it can consult while reasoning. The model stays free to go long when a problem is truly hard. On math benchmarks, token use fell by up to about forty percent while accuracy rose slightly. Analysis showed the models learned to budget effort by problem difficulty, an emergent habit rather than a hard rule.
arxiv-2507-15858:
Elena Hernández-Martínez and co-authors inspect the hot gas inside simulated versions of our real nearby galaxy clusters. The SLOW project rebuilds the local universe's large-scale structure inside a computer, cluster by cluster. Their 2025 paper, the fifth in the series, reads the intracluster plasma: its pressure, temperature, entropy, and density.

Simulated profiles are set against X-ray and Sunyaev-Zel'dovich data for real local clusters. The real ones sort into strong cool-core, weak cool-core, and non-cool-core systems. The team asks whether the simulated clusters sort the same way, and whether a cluster's merger history explains its core type. Cosmologists get a check on whether our digital neighborhood behaves like the actual one.
arxiv-2507-15958:
Skin lesion checks on small devices get a brain-style chip design from Haitian Wang and co-authors in a 2025 paper. Clinic data shifts and heavy math make phone-grade tools hard to build. Brain-style processors compute with sparse spikes and sip energy, but moving standard networks onto them often breaks.

Their design bounds signal ranges, aligns scaling with low-bit storage, and swaps fragile parts for spike-friendly ones. Light feature tricks and attention modules are chosen so they convert cleanly to chip steps. The result aims for stable accuracy even when lesion classes are lopsided. Field clinics with weak hardware could gain fast, low-power screening if the design holds in trials.
arxiv-2507-16158:
Hui Ye and co-authors present AMMNet in 2025, a network that labels every pixel in remote sensing images using two data types. Satellite views in color show texture, while a surface height model adds shape and height cues. Together they should beat either alone, but merging them usually makes models heavy and redundant.

AMMNet is asymmetric: the two streams are treated unequally, with the richer color stream carrying more of the work. That trims computing cost while keeping the height cues that separate buildings from roads. Tests on standard benchmarks check accuracy against speed. City mappers and land-use analysts get a leaner tool for turning mixed satellite data into land cover maps.
arxiv-2507-16258:
Tram Tran and co-authors study how animals meet autonomous vehicles and robots. Their twenty twenty-five paper notes that self-driving systems now share streets and parks with pets and wildlife. Design so far has focused on humans, with little grasp of animal views.

The team joined three sources: a review of forty-five papers, online study of videos and posts, and talks with eight experts. Five worry zones emerged. Cars can hit animals or fail to spot them. Animal behavior shifts, with stress and avoidance. Service animals face access snags. The work, rooted in animal-computer interaction, argues for design that plans for many species, not one.
arxiv-2507-16358:
Argyrios Christodoulou studies families of maps of the unit disc that are applied again and again in shifting order, in this 2025 mathematics note. Such systems, called iterated function systems, are built here from holomorphic self-maps, smooth complex maps that keep the disc inside itself. The question is what happens at the rim.

Inside the disc, the motion of points under these systems is fairly well understood. The main result gives a condition strong enough to guarantee that the interior behavior extends smoothly to the boundary circle. That extends a known disc theorem, itself a widening of the classical Denjoy-Wolff result, from single maps to whole systems. The proof reshapes norm estimates for composition operators and adds a trick: nudging the system with special disc symmetries that keep control of the rim.
arxiv-2507-17958:
Daniel Carlstrom Schad and five co-authors present VIBE, a two stage transformer that forecasts brain fMRI response from video input. Features from open models for video, audio, and text feed the system. Their work came out in twenty twenty-five.

A fusion transformer merges the streams, and a second transformer decodes them over time with rotary position codes. Training drew on dozens of hours of film data from a shared brain set, pooled across many seeds. Scores on a held in TV season beat those on fresh films, as expected. An earlier build won one challenge phase and placed second overall, the authors note.
arxiv-2507-18058:
A team including Qing-Xin Ji and Hanfei Hou reports multicolor pulses from a single optical pump in a microresonator, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. In microcombs, solitons can drive other modes to produce optical gain. Theory predicted multicolor solitons: phase-locked pulses sharing one location at new spectral positions. The needed dispersion conditions, though, do not occur naturally in conventional microresonators.

The pulses observed here are closely related to that concept. Individual soliton pulses share the same repetition rate and could potentially be fully phase-locked. They arise through interband coupling inside a compound resonator. A regenerative secondary pulse forms in time and space with the exciting soliton. The result is multicolor light from one pump in one device. Such sources matter for applications needing several synchronized colors on a chip.
arxiv-2507-18358: Junyao Pan maps out a family of symmetries of the Cuntz algebras, a central family of operator algebras. His 2025 paper studies permutative automorphisms, which match stable permutations of word strings. The simplest case that is not trivial swaps just two words, and each word has length three. That swap is a transposition, and Pan pins down just when it is stable.
arxiv-2507-18458:
Hiroki Yoshida and Takehito Yokoyama propose a Hall effect powered by gravity-like fields that arise from quantum geometry, in a 2025 paper. The Hall effect bends electric current sideways in a magnetic field. Here the bending force comes not from magnetism but from effective gravitational fields hidden in the geometry of quantum states.

The pair identify four mechanisms behind the effect. Gravity can act through real space, through momentum space, through an anomalous velocity, or through a Lorentz-like force. All four are written with the same geometric symbols used in general relativity. A unified semiclassical framework lets them study the four on equal footing. Model calculations show when a real sideways response can appear. The authors present the effect as a fresh route for probing gravitational ideas inside tabletop quantum materials.
arxiv-2507-18758:
Yifan Liu and co-authors present a faster way to build moving human avatars from video in this 2025 paper. Older methods tune a model for each person, which is slow. Newer feed-forward methods make 3D Gaussians per frame but ignore links across time.

Their Human Gaussian Graph ties each Gaussian to the SMPL body mesh. One layer holds the Gaussians and the other holds mesh points. Steps merge Gaussians that share a mesh point and pass notes between nearby points. That lets all frames inform one shared human model. Tests on new views and new poses show strong results with good speed and reach to new people.
arxiv-2507-19058:
Xia leads a team presenting ScenePainter, a system for generating long, consistent 3D scene sequences, in a 2025 paper. Endless scene generation suits long videos and scene reconstruction. Standard outpainting drifts in meaning as views accumulate.

ScenePainter builds a layered graph of scene concepts and their relations. That graph steers the outpainter to stay faithful to the current scene's content. The graph can also be refined on the fly to add variety. Tests showed the method beating the semantic drift problem that plagues rivals. View sequences stayed more consistent and immersive over long runs. The authors frame relation alignment as the fix for drift. A project page shows examples.
arxiv-2507-19258:
Seok Hyung Lie and Hyukjoon Kwon wrote a 2025 physics paper on a notion of quantum state that spans space and time. A state that holds across both could be a step toward a relativistic quantum theory. The authors give such states a hands on meaning through a measurement scheme that works no matter how regions relate in cause and effect.

They prove that scheme can always be run with interferometry, also called the scattering circuit method. In that frame, the standard state, a state over time form, and the process matrix all merge into one view. The frame lets them model mixed states across time, which matter for memory effects in quantum systems. They also find a fresh space time link born of synced motion under time reversal.
arxiv-2507-19858:
Chia-Ming Lee and eight co-authors published a paper in 2025 on why a CT-scan classifier trained at one hospital stumbles at another, and how fixing the inputs beats fixing the model. Scanners and protocols differ, so the same disease looks different across sources, a domain shift that erodes accuracy. A known pipeline standardizes each scan slice by slice and samples slices by density before the network ever sees them.

The authors dissect why that input-space tidying works: it shrinks the differences between sources while keeping the details that separate diseases, handing the network an easier, more uniform job. Gains held across several architectures, and the approach took first place in a competitive challenge. Preprocessing, often an afterthought, is here the main event.
arxiv-2507-19958:
Sky bursts in the mid spark band lack a watch eye that sees all the sky and points fast and true. Aloisio and co-authors draw such an eye in a 2025 study, a space borne watch for the band from low X to mid spark. Their draw is tuned by the watch's own sky: a low, near plain path round the world.

Full sims of the eye in that sky set its catch. Its true face and catch depth beat like eyes by spans. A live point way, built in the work, points near ten times more fine than the marks such eyes now claim. The draw is pitched as a help for the age of joint sky news.
arxiv-2507-20558:
Hospitals that cannot share patient records can still study survival together if each site shares only safe summaries. Hyojung Jang and co-authors proposed a one-shot federated method for that task in 2025. Their approach builds pseudo-observations from a stepwise survival curve and fits them with an estimating equation, all without pooling raw data or repeated rounds of messages between sites.

The method allows flexible link choices and handles risks that change over time, unlike classic proportional hazards models. A debiasing step shrinks noisy local quirks toward the global estimate while keeping real site differences. Tests on simulations and on pediatric obesity data from a Chicago network of nearly forty-six thousand patients gave robust results.
arxiv-2507-20658:
Jesco Talies, Eric Breitbarth, and David Melching present a training method for trustworthy AI in a 2025 arXiv paper. Their test task is marking crack tips in image data used to study how materials fracture. Deep models can be accurate yet hard to trust in high-stakes science.

Their method, attention-guided training, feeds expert checks of the model's focus back into training. Explanations are scored, and known stress field patterns guide where the model should look. Aligning focus with these physical fields improved the model's reach to new cases. The explanations also grew more faithful to the real physics.
arxiv-2507-20758:
Asking a language model to think step by step, the chain-of-thought trick, plainly improves its answers, but why it works inside the network is murky. Hao Yang and co-authors trace the flow of information backward through the model's decoding, projection, and activation stages. They look for what the written reasoning actually changes.

One finding casts the reasoning text as a pruning device: it narrows the space of likely outputs by leaning on answer templates. The closer the output hugs the template, the better the score. A second finding surprised them: the trick quiets neuron activity on open-ended tasks yet stirs more activity on closed ones. The authors frame these results as handles for designing sharper prompts on purpose, rather than by folklore. Code and data are released.
arxiv-2507-20858:
Louis Esteve and co-authors survey in 2025 how diversity is measured in natural language processing. Diversity is praised in data sets and systems, yet papers use many measures and do not always mean the same thing by the word.
