The authors borrow unified frames from ecology and economics and sort more than three hundred recent papers by four questions: why diversity matters, what it is measured on, where, and how. Simple richness and distance averaging dominate the field, while balance measures are nearly absent. Half the measures in use do not fit the classic frame. The survey ends with advice on shared terms and on stating the values behind each measure.
arxiv-2507-21158:
Nishani Fernando and co-authors design a framework that adapts AI explanations to build fast trust in high-stakes teamwork. In settings like emergency response, people must decide quickly whether to rely on an AI partner. Standard explanation tools give everyone the same output and ask for explicit feedback, which is impractical under pressure.

The proposed framework instead reads the user quietly. Body and behavior signals, such as brain and heart activity and eye movements, feed a model that estimates workload, stress, and emotion. Those estimates are mapped to a personal, shifting trust score. The score then tunes what the explanations show and how they show it, without interrupting the user. The authors present the design as a foundation for explanation systems that fit the user moment by moment. They aim it at time-sensitive work where trust must form in minutes, not weeks.
arxiv-2507-21358:
Jicheng Yuan and co-authors present Collaborative Perceiver, a vision based system that finds 3D objects for self driving, in work from 2025. Top down views built from cameras are cheap and rich in context. Past methods squash object features into that view and lose scene context such as roads and pavements.

Their framework learns object detection and space occupancy together. Occupancy data carry local density, which helps the model read the physical scene. Shared structure between the two tasks sharpens features for both. The authors build dense occupancy truth data to train the system. The aim is fuller perception of the world around the car.
arxiv-2507-21458:
Ayano Nakamura and eleven co-authors probe an unusual Hall effect in a magnetic material, where a sideways voltage appears under a magnetic field in the same plane. Such in-plane effects are prized as probes of quantum geometry inside solids. They worked with thin films of a trigonal antiferromagnet and measured the effect across its magnetic phases on the crystal's main face.

Near zero field they found the sideways signal grows with the cube of the field, a pattern held in both the quiet and magnetically ordered phases. One part of the response faded with temperature in an odd cubic pattern above the ordering point. When a strong field forced the material into a ferromagnetic state, the dependence turned straight and stayed so to high fields. The results clarify how field and signal couple in this geometry, opening new probes of quantum materials.
arxiv-2507-21758:
Arijit Bishnu, Mathew Francis, and Pritam Majumder wrote a 2025 paper on covering point sets with curves. A curve covers a point when it passes through it. Given a field of points, often a grid, how few curves of a set kind can thread them all?

The team sets upper and lower bounds for that count across curve kinds: rising curves, straight lines, box shaped curves, and circles. A converse puzzle joins the work. If a grid of n squared points is threaded by just n lines, what must the point layout look like? Such bounds tie into wider work on how often points and curves can meet.
arxiv-2507-21958:
Casabella, Kastner, and Vlad sort all the graph shapes of a class of tropical curves in this twenty twenty-five paper. The curves come from where two curved faces cross in a warm-math three-space. Each graph stands for a most-worn form of a loop-shaped curve built that way.

Inside, the team finds just over four thousand such graphs in the full class. Each graph has the same count of points and links, which fits the loop form they stand for. The count rests on a huge sweep of ways to split a four-way shape into neat blocks. That sweep ran past four hundred times ten thousand cases in all. The list gives a firm base for more work on these curves.
arxiv-2507-22158:
Subhajyoti Bid and Henning Schomerus split a known flaw in wave spectra in two thousand twenty-five. Some open wave systems show a spot where modes merge. At such spots, states fuse into a single one. When just part of the set fuses, the case was murky. The pair set out rules for these split cases. A neat algebra route made the build quick.

They placed the split spots in the bulk and at the edge. A Lieb grid gave the flat case. A Dirac-type solid gave the three-part one. Sensors prize merged spots for keen response. Split forms may tune that response more finely. The work maps a fresh patch of open-system physics.
arxiv-2507-22458:
Hugo Levy-Falk and a large team study graphene quantum dots on a perovskite crystal in two thousand twenty-five. On this surface the dots clump, unlike in solution or on other bases. That holds even from very thin starting mixes. Small clusters were watched through their spectra over time.

Clusters flip back and forth between a lone dot state and a paired state. On some clusters the glow then jumps up for good. At the same time the glow fades faster than before. The team ties that shift to a shared collective state. Light may drive the dots to organize as they sit on the crystal.
arxiv-2507-22558:
Yuna Oikawa and co-authors teach a language model to draw alloy phase maps in a 2025 paper. Phase maps tell which forms a metal mix takes at each heat. They guide alloy design, yet each map costs lab time. The team built question and answer pairs from an open phase bank and expert checks. They tuned an open language model, Mistral, on that set. The tuned model takes the name aLLoyM.

Two styles faced tests: pick-one-of-four and short free answers. Tuning lifted pick scores by a wide span. The short-answer form could sketch maps for new mixes from parts alone. That skill may speed hunts for fresh alloys. The team freed the short-answer model and the full test set in public. Later teams can grade their own tools on the same base.
arxiv-2507-22658:
Dimitrios Ntalampekos proves, in a solo 2025 mathematics paper, a test for when a set on the sphere can be reshaped into a Schottky set. A Schottky set is what remains of a sphere when open disks are cut out, no two touching. The reshape may bend and stretch but must keep a fixed bound on how far it skews shapes. Such bounded reshapes are called quasiconformal.

His test is neat. The set passes just when each pair of its leftover pieces maps to a pair of open disks under one sphere map with a fixed skew bound. The result covers famed fractal sets such as Sierpiński carpets and gaskets. For gaskets it gives the first reshape rule of this kind. It also contains a past rule for carpets as one case, and drops a separation condition past works leaned on.
arxiv-2507-22758:
Gautam Jajoo and co-authors published a research paper in 2025 on a team of language model agents that judge loan applications together. Credit scoring still leans on rigid rules and old statistics. Their system, MASCA, splits the judgment among specialist agents arranged in layers, mimicking how human credit teams work.

A contrastive learning step tunes how the agents weigh risk against reward. The paper also reads the layered setup through game theory, asking how the agents signal and respond to each other. A bias analysis checks the system for unfair treatment of applicants. On their tests, MASCA beat standard baselines at scoring credit.
arxiv-2507-22958:
Khrulev introduces in twenty twenty-five a benchmark for judging how well vision-language models can grade handwritten maths work. Most tests check whether AI can solve problems. His test instead checks whether AI can read a student's written solution, spot mistakes, and grade it by fixed rules, as a human examiner would.

The set holds just over one hundred scanned solutions from Russia's national school exam, each with an official expert grade. He tested seven modern models from major labs in three modes of use. Results exposed real limits in maths reasoning and in matching human grading rules. The author offers the set as a spur for work on AI-assisted marking.
arxiv-2507-23158:
Yuhan Liu and co-authors study user feedback in human and language model dialogues in a 2025 paper. Deployed models could improve from feedback, but asking directly is disruptive. Implicit feedback hidden in chat logs might serve instead, if it can be harvested reliably.

Using two large interaction data sets, they first analyze when and why users give feedback. Then they test whether using feedback content, not just its positive or negative polarity, improves model performance. Results were mixed: content helped on short, human designed questions but not on longer, complex ones. The study maps both promise and limits of log based learning.
arxiv-2507-23358:
Renato Vukovic and co-authors brought in TeQoDO in 2025, a method that lets a language model build the data store schema for a task-oriented dialogue system by itself. Such assistants answer from an outer data store set up by a clear ontology. This keeps them clear and controllable, but writing that ontology usually takes hand labels or supervised training. Language models alone, relying on memory, are hard to trust.

TeQoDO exploits the model's skill at SQL programming. Given concepts from modular dialogue system design in its prompt, the model constructs a working ontology from scratch as a data store design task. The result beat transfer learning methods at ontology building, and the generated ontology performed competitively on the downstream job of tracking dialogue state. Tests on Wikipedia and arXiv substance showed the method also scales to much larger ontologies.
arxiv-2507-23458:
Cheng-en Liu and co-authors present a 2025 paper on using cosmic ray muons to study both cosmic rays and dark matter. Muons rain through detectors from space, and how much they scatter reveals what they passed through. The team built a tomography system from resistive plate chambers.

Over sixty-three days they recorded 1.18 million scattering events. Fitting the angle pattern separated the cosmic ray ingredients, pinning the electron share to about two percent precision. The same data hunted dark matter that couples to muons. No signal appeared, so they set an upper limit on the scattering strength. For slow one-GeV dark matter gathered inside Earth, the cross-section sits below about 1.61 times ten to the minus seventeen square centimeters, at ninety-five percent confidence.
arxiv-2507-23558:
Tsipinakis and Parpas study Newton's method for a subclass of well behaved functions in twenty twenty-five. Newton's method is a classic algorithm for minimization. Its theory is well developed for self concordant functions. A local analysis for strongly self concordant functions, a narrower class, was missing.

The known quadratic convergence for the wider class applies here as well. The authors ask whether the narrower class enjoys stronger guarantees. They show its quadratic rate differs from the general case. For a wide range of objectives, convergence is provably faster. The region where local convergence holds is also larger. The results close a gap in the theory of Newton's method. They clarify what extra structure buys in practice.
arxiv-2508-00958:
G G L Nashed and Kazuharu Bamba present an exact solution in a modified theory of gravity in this 2025 study. Their theory adds a squared term to a measure of how space fails to stay rigid, called non-metricity. Some past papers claimed no round, symmetric solution exists for such higher-order theories, a claim that would limit their use for stars and black holes.

The authors derive such a solution in closed form. In it, the squared term plays the same role as a cosmological constant, the steady push tied to cosmic acceleration. They also show that adding electric charge to the setup leaves the solution unchanged. The reason is that the off-diagonal parts of the field equations never feel the charge, a neat quirk of this theory.
arxiv-2508-01058:
Sara Yavari and co-authors outline brain tumors on MRI scans by first imagining a scan the patient never had. Their two-stage system starts with a diffusion model that synthesizes one contrast type from three others. Where the real scan disagrees with the invented one, the tumor likely sits, since healthy tissue is predictable and tumor tissue is not. Those disagreement maps then guide a small segmentation network.

The design needs no hand-drawn masks for its main objective, which suits messy multi-center data. On the large BraTS 2021 collection the method scored 93.02 percent on the standard overlap measure for whole tumors, beating its predecessor's marks on the earlier 2020 set. Filtering out empty slices and tuning thresholds balanced missed tumor against false alarms. The authors present the residual trick as a scalable way to find tumors where labeled training data are scarce.
arxiv-2508-01358:
Elijah Adejumo and Brittany Johnson test a stability score for open source code in a 2025 paper. Firms now rest on free code from public stores. A score that gauges if a store will stay sound could guide that trust.

The score joins commit pace, issue fix rate, merge rate, and crowd acts. One hundred top GitHub stores were scored to test the frame in real life. Week pace proved a saner commit gauge than day pace. Swapping means for medians sharpened the stats as well. The work moves the score from pure theory to field proof.
arxiv-2508-01558:
Kun Ding, Ying Wang, and Shiming Xiang present a 2025 method that lets a computer design its own ways to adapt vision-language models. These models link images with text and can be tuned for new tasks, but the tuning methods in use were crafted by hand, which takes time and deep skill. The team's method, EvoVLMA, uses a large language model to write and test candidate methods.

The search runs in two stages, first improving how features are picked and then how scores are computed. Extra tools keep the search stable and fast, among them low-precision code and web-based test runs. In tests with just eight training images per class, a known method gained 1.91 points of accuracy after the search improved it. The authors offer the system as a way to automate method design for models of this kind.
arxiv-2508-01758:
Pinaki Chakraborty, Tristan Caulfield, and David Pym wrote a paper in 2025 on a logical framework for causality and decision-making in systems and security modeling. The framework assumes only minimal structure about the systems it describes.

The authors model systems as transition systems, formal accounts of states and steps between them. They then apply modal logic, a language for what can and must hold over those changing states. The key new tool is an intervention operator built into the logic, paired with a separating conjunction. The operator acts on a what-if change: hold part of the system fixed, and one sees how changing a part changes the whole. Together the tools capture real causal links between parts. The authors also align the framework with a well-known counterfactual approach to causality. Examples, including microservices in spread-out systems, show how it guides local choice.
arxiv-2508-01958:
Alejandro Mata Ali introduces QUDO, Tensor QUDO, and HOBO formulations in two thousand twenty-five. These are optimization forms for combinatorial problems with varied alphabets. QUDO is quadratic and d-ary, its tensor form adds structure. HOBO covers higher order binary cases in the family.

Plain encodings between the forms are laid out with their limits. Worked cases span the knapsack and traveling salesman problems. Five puzzle games show the forms in play as well. Some games had QUBO forms before, redone here in broader terms. The forms suit quantum and quantum inspired solvers.
arxiv-2508-02758:
Yihao Ang and co-authors build the first broad bench for fake crypto price series, in a paper from 2025. Fake series help test trading ideas, but crypto trades all day with wild swings and fast regime shifts that old benches miss.

Their bench, CTBench, draws on more than four hundred tokens. It grades makers on thirteen marks across forecast truth, rank hold, trading gain, risk, and speed. Two tasks check whether fakes keep forecast patterns and whether they keep mean snap back signals for trades. Eight models across five families showed a trade off between true form and real profit.
arxiv-2508-02958:
Daniel Killough and co-authors build a system that describes virtual reality scenes aloud for blind users, in this 2025 paper. Mainstream VR shuts blind people out, and most apps add no access features. Their system, VRSight, works after the fact, with no help from app makers.

AI models detect objects, gauge depth, and read the mood of a scene, then render cues as spatial tones. To train virtual object spotting, the team built a data set of thirty object types from seventeen social VR apps. Nine blind participants used the system inside a popular VR app. They managed social tasks like finding avatars and free seats.
arxiv-2508-03358:
Tiago Canario and co-authors build a 2025 tool called Taggus that maps who knows whom inside Portuguese novels. Pulling a cast of characters and their ties from fiction is a hard language task. Standard tools that spot names and tag grammar were not built for it, and they do worse in languages with little labeled training data, such as Portuguese.

Taggus chains several language steps, led by grammar tagging plus a blend of custom rules tuned for fiction. The authors compare it with ready-made name spotters and with a large chat model. Their pipeline beat both at finding characters and the links between them. Such maps let scholars study plot structure and social worlds in books at a scale no reader could manage by hand.
arxiv-2508-03858:
Charles Wang and co-workers put forth a runtime governance setup for self-running AI agents in a 2025 paper called MI9. Agents that plan and act develop new actions no pre-rollout review can fully foresee. Safety must be supervised while the system runs, not only before it ships. MI9 integrates six parts into one rules that watches and steers agents across varied designs without favoring any vendor's stack.

An agency-risk index scores danger at all times, semantic telemetry records what agents mean, and sign-off is monitored without pause. A finite-state fit engine checks actions against allowed patterns, goal-conditioned drift detection notices objectives sliding, and graduated control steps up responses proportionally. Scenario studies are offered as evidence of full coverage.
arxiv-2508-03958: James Kitchens and Yan Wong introduce, in a 2025 software paper, a tool for drawing ancestral recombination graphs. Such graphs capture the full family history of recombining DNA, and they sit at the heart of population genetics. Their Python package draws the graphs interactively, so a researcher can explore one by hand. The authors show it at work in teaching and in picking through graphs inferred from real data.
arxiv-2508-04158:
Dmytro Uvarov studies tension free strings in curved spacetime in 2025. Integrability is the key that unlocks many string theory puzzles. Full superstring equations are tangled by fields that vary across superspace. A null string, the zero tension limit, offers a simpler case worth solving first.

Uvarov rewrites the null string equations for anti de Sitter space in Lax form. That form is the hallmark of an integrable system. He also gives a twistor reading of the string action in group terms. Solvable limits like this can teach lessons that carry back to the full theory.
arxiv-2508-04758:
Nashed and Eid build a new way to shape curved spacetime in a 2025 gravity paper. They work in a modified theory where gravity comes from torsion, a twist in spacetime, rather than pure bending. Older tricks with one or two added fields could not make general round-symmetric shapes in this theory.

Their fix uses four scalar fields, with added constraints that keep out ghost-like flaws. With that setup, any round-symmetric spacetime can be rebuilt in the theory. They show the method on one sample shape and a version with an extra squared term. The shapes came out sound and free of ghost problems, widening what the theory can describe.
arxiv-2508-05058:
Munguía López and four co-authors study particle bursts in proton smashing at the Large Hadron Collider in a 2025 paper. When two protons collide, the spray of new particles carries a spread of momenta. That spread changes shape as the count of particles grows, a process called hardening.

The team read data sorted by several event counters from the ALICE detector. They worked out spread measures such as variance, Shannon entropy, and heat capacity for each class. Entropy and heat capacity answered in distinct ways to counters at the front of the detector versus the middle, a warning that how events are sorted can skew the lessons drawn.
arxiv-2508-05158:
XiangKun Gong, Wu-zhong Guo, and Jin Xu write a 2025 paper on entanglement across time. Entanglement is usually measured between regions split in space. The team studies regions linked by cause and effect in time instead, where the math takes a stranger form.

Using a real-time replica method, they build the operator that links such regions and compute its measures. In some setups the result acts like an entropy for time-like splits. A matching picture from holography is proposed and checks out in tests. A time-like version of a cross-section measure stays positive in their worked cases. The authors also weigh how far other measures, such as reflected entropy, can stretch into the time-like case.
arxiv-2508-05358:
Fenya Wasserroth and co-authors tested an adjustable sign language avatar in a 2025 study with expert users of German Sign Language. The avatar ran on a head-worn display, and users could adjust some settings. The team asked whether those controls would aid understanding, ease of use, and acceptance.

Users liked having controls, yet scores for understanding and ease stayed low in both modes. Missing mouth shapes and face cues, plus blurred hand shapes, held the system back. Stress ran higher with the adjustable form, and users found the hand gestures for settings hard to learn. The lesson is that avatars must be clear by default before personal controls can help.
arxiv-2508-05858:
Orkan Umurhan and co-authors find a quieter way dust clumps in planet-forming disks, besides the famous streaming instability, in a 2025 paper. Before planets form, dust settles into a thin midplane layer in the gas disk around a young star. Clumping there is the first step toward planetesimals, and the streaming instability is the usual suspect.

In their simulations of the settled layer, filaments of the instability had not formed — yet small-scale clumping still appeared. Particle-rich strands lined up with zones where the gas strains hardest, wrapping gas-only voids that swirl coherently: the signature of turbulent concentration. A scaled particle measure collapsed neatly across settings. Planet building may start earlier and more gently than thought.
arxiv-2508-05958:
Yingzhou Li and Jingyu Liu wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. Its text introduces hierarchical matrices whose blocks are Tucker tensors, a data-sparse way to hold matrices that come from smooth interaction kernels.

Classic hierarchical matrices store off blocks as low-rank forms. Swapping in Tucker blocks, built by high-dimensional sampling and tensor squeezes, cuts the store further. The authors give builds for the matrix and for its product with a vector, at near-linear cost. Head-to-head tests against a sampling-based hierarchical code show smaller stores and at times faster builds, at like run cost. The frame also fits near-even grids.
arxiv-2508-06258:
Byunghyun Ko, Anning Tian, and Jeongkyu Lee present a network for outlining the thigh bone in MRI scans, in a paper from 2025. Exact outlines of the femur guide diagnosis and surgery planning in bone and joint care. Pure two dimensional methods miss context from nearby slices, while full three dimensional methods cost heavy computing.

Their model, XAG-Net, takes a middle path by reading a small stack of slices at once. One part pays attention across slices at each pixel, so fine detail can borrow strength from its neighbors. Another part gates the skip links inside the network to sharpen features within each slice. In wide tests the model beat two dimensional, stack based, and three dimensional rivals on accuracy while staying cheap to run. Ablations confirmed both new parts matter.
arxiv-2508-06458:
Javad Asadollahi, Rasool Hafezi, and Somayeh Sadeghi extend an algebra concept called strong flatness to rings where multiplication order matters. Their 2025 paper leans on universal localization, a method by Cohn for forcing chosen maps to become reversible. The new module class is defined through the localized ring.

Modules, in this branch of algebra, are like vector spaces over a general ring. The team studies chains of these modules and the motions between them. They show that a certain family of exact chains forms a precovering class in that setting. As a result, a natural quotient map between two large categories always has a faithful helper map going back. The work is pure theory, aimed at algebra specialists.
arxiv-2508-07058:
Paul Parsons and Prakash Chandra Shukla study how chart designers frame problems in two thousand twenty-five. Design is often told as solving a fixed problem in a known space. That view stresses craft skill and skips how designers judge and define the task. Work in other design fields stresses framing and joint growth of problem and fix.

The pair ran a mixed study with expert designers. Tasks, diaries, and talks showed how experts frame and reframe their briefs. Tricks used spanned sketching, word images, rules of thumb, and tests of failed tries. Framing went on through the whole task, not just at the start. Results call for models that honor this back and forth.
arxiv-2508-07158:
Shankhadeep Mondal, Deguang Han, and Mohapatra ask which backup description of a signal best limits damage when parts of the signal are lost. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Frames describe a signal with some slack, and dual frames rebuild it. When chunks vanish in transit, the choice of dual sets the error.

The team judges duals by the size of their error operators, under three different size measures. They seek the dual that cuts the average error over all loss patterns of a set size. For the gentlest measure they fully solve the problem for even, tight frames. Rules emerge for when the standard dual is the unique best pick. Links between the three measures are also drawn. The results serve speech, imaging, and any system that must rebuild from partial data.
arxiv-2508-07258:
Andrei Diakonov and co-authors show a chip-scale frequency comb can pass an optical clocks precision down to microwaves in a 2025 paper. Deployable clocks need their exquisite tick divided to usable signals without loss. Kerr microcombs promise that division on a chip, but hour-long steadiness was unproven.

A hybrid lock pins one comb tooth by injection and a second, freely chosen tooth by active control, leaving the pump loose. The two channels split the combs two freedoms cleanly. Over five unbroken hours, a spare tooth held stability at the highest level metrology asks. Pocket clocks gain a credible heart.
arxiv-2508-07558:
Ziqian Wang and seven co-authors built one system for many speech cleanup tasks, in a 2025 paper. Tasks such as noise removal, echo removal, and pulling out one speaker are usually solved apart. That split wastes effort and gives uneven results. Their system, UniFlow, handles all of them in a shared hidden space.

Sound is first squeezed into a compact code by a trained encoder. A transformer then predicts how that code should change. A task tag tells the system which job to do, so most weights are shared. The authors compare three training goals for the generative step. Tests on public benchmarks beat strong task-specific rivals. The design can extend to new tasks with little extra work. The team plans to release its code for others.
arxiv-2508-07658:
Zhang and co-authors present a 2025 interview study on how users feel about AI guessing private traits from their social videos. Visual language models can now infer place, background, and income hints from clips. The team ran deep interviews with seventeen users about that power. Most believed the models could indeed read such traits, often with unsettling accuracy.

Fears centered on unwanted identification, misuse of personal data, and constant watching. Wrong guesses worried users too, since errors can still harm. People described shields they try, from cropping to posting less, but doubted those shields hold. They asked platforms and regulators for openness, control, and safeguards built in from the start.
arxiv-2508-07858:
Christiansen and co-authors count how many carbon monoxide molecules can crowd onto a single foreign atom in copper, in a 2025 paper. Copper catalysts turn carbon dioxide into useful products, and dopant atoms may steer that chemistry. A lone carbon monoxide is the usual yardstick, yet earlier work hinted several can bind at once.

Extending the math to heavier dopants and a dispersion-aware method, the team finds the first molecule binds far harder than on clean copper, then grip fades as more pile on. Four can still out-bind the clean surface. Binding also shoves the dopant outward, sometimes out of the surface entirely. Catalyst designers must plan for crowds, not singles.
arxiv-2508-08058:
Ziad Al-Haj Hemidi, Eytan Kats, and Mattias Heinrich speed up MRI scans in 2025 without losing image quality. Shorter scans cut cost and patient strain, yet fast scans blur structure and add ghost patterns. A newer method rebuilds images with a small network fit to each scan, but it fades at high speed-ups for lack of prior knowledge.

Their method, PrIINeR, feeds that per-scan network with knowledge from models pre-trained on many scans. Two checks keep the result true both to the raw scan data and to the prior-informed rebuild. On a public knee and brain data set, it beat its class and several top learning methods, they report. The code is posted in public for others to test.
arxiv-2508-08158:
Laura Spillner, Rachel Ringe, Robert Porzel, and Rainer Malaka wrote this 2025 study on whether the explanations an AI gives can change a user's mind. Decision support tools explain their advice so users can judge when to trust it and when to push back. That safety net works only if users read the explanations with care.

In an online study, many users spent little time on the explanations and skipped their detail. The authors dig into what made some users linger: traits of the task, the person, and the explanation itself. They trace how that care, or its lack, shaped whether users let the AI move their call. The findings caution builders that an explanation on the screen is not the same as an explanation actually weighed.
arxiv-2508-08458:
Pallabee Das and Stefan Heindorf build explanations for graph neural networks by generating whole example graphs in a 2025 paper. Heterogeneous graphs, where nodes are typed and carry real features, model citations, social ties, and molecules. Networks that classify their nodes predict well but explain poorly, and older explainers cheat by ignoring node features or emitting unrealistic graphs.

Their DiGNNExplainer answers at the level of the whole model: it synthesizes example graphs that show what patterns drive a class. A discrete diffusion process, denoising step by step in the native discrete space, generates graphs whose node features look like real bag-of-words data, not soft averages. Across multiple datasets, the generated explanations proved both realistic and faithful to the model's decisions, beating the standing methods. Honest features, the authors argue, are the difference between an explanation and a cartoon.
arxiv-2508-08558:
Imre Bartos and Zoltán Haiman published this study in 2025. It reads the fingerprints of GW231123, the heaviest black hole merger yet detected. The pair sits in or above a mass gap where standard star collapse should not leave black holes. Both holes also spin very fast, which repeated mergers struggle to explain. The authors find the two spin arrows point much the same way. Yet both tilt well away from the orbit's axis.

That pattern, they argue, points to growth by swallowing gas. Shared, steady accretion can raise masses and spins together while keeping the spins mutually aligned. Gas disks around galaxy-center black holes are a prime setting. A past record merger, GW190521, may share the same story. Sustained feasting, the authors conclude, shapes the most extreme binaries.
arxiv-2508-08658:
Runhua Wang and co-authors present a control theory paper, published in 2025, on sharing resources fairly across a network when some members lie. In decentralized allocation, agents negotiate with neighbors to split a common resource, but compromised agents can poison the process with false messages. The authors frame the tug of war between local choices and global limits as a primal dual optimization problem.

Their algorithms blend adaptive clipping, which trims suspicious messages, with robust aggregation rules that filter what each agent hears. Theory promises tight bounds on both regret, the cost of learning on the fly, and on how far the shared limits are overshot. Simulated power dispatch across a grid confirmed the defenses hold.
arxiv-2508-08758:
Keisuke Hanada and Tomoyuki Sugimoto improve meta-analysis for cases with very few studies in a 2025 paper. A meta-analysis pools results across studies, and a random-effects model allows the true effect to vary between them. With few studies, that spread is often underjudged, so error ranges come out too narrow and miss the stated confidence level.

The authors build their fix inside a broad class of mixed models that can handle counts, rates, and other outcome types. Their method adjusts a profile likelihood with a simplified Bartlett correction, which sharpens the math without hard higher-order terms. Theory keeps the good traits of standard estimators. Computer trials gave near-unbiased estimates with honest coverage. Tests on three past reviews, with three outcome types, worked well too.
arxiv-2508-08958:
Kostiantyn Kucher, Niklas Rönnberg, and Jonas Löwgren tell of a first course for sight-craft adepts in a 2025 paper. The craft of clear charts and views is split by kind: its hands sit in shops of graph craft, of man-tool craft, and of form.

New adepts land in that split house and must draw one map of the whole. The course at a north land school walks them through all the shops in turn. Trips take the class to each crew, from hard sums of light to the dress of news. The authors tell how the course was built to mesh with the rest of adept school. They share what the first run, in the fall of a past year, taught those who would build the like.
arxiv-2508-09158:
Siwen Jiao and co-authors present in this 2025 paper EvaDrive, a self-driving planner that drafts routes and grades them in a loop. Human drivers propose, judge, and revise paths on the fly; most systems split those steps or squash many goals into one score. EvaDrive instead runs a multi-round contest between a path maker and a trainable critic.

The maker blends intent modeling with diffusion-style polish; the critic scores paths on several goals at once, and a Pareto rule keeps the best trade-offs alive. On two standard benchmarks the system topped prior art, and shifting goal weights yielded varied driving styles with no outside preference data.
arxiv-2508-09558:
Jiahui Zuo and co-authors route cables with a robot nail in a 2025 paper. Laying cables is a multi step task in car and cloth plants. Plain two finger grippers can crush or over pull soft cables as they guide them.

An eagle like nail on each finger helps lift cables from flat tops and steer them in hand. One grasp then drives the whole route, not pick and place hops. Vision reads the task state, and set move chunks plan the path off line. Tests with many cables and slots beat pick and place by a wide mark.
arxiv-2508-09758:
Denti and Laura D'Angelo present a software package for grouping grouped data, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Data often nest, as with patients inside hospitals or students inside schools. Ignoring that nesting can bias results and hurt prediction on new groups.

Their R package fits Bayesian models that cluster both single observations and whole groups at once, while estimating each group's own distribution shape. The models share a common set of building blocks across groups, a recent idea in statistics. Heavy computation is handled by fast code under the hood, with both sampling and shortcut inference options for large data. The authors aim to make these models practical for everyday analysts.
arxiv-2508-10258:
Allan Freitas and co-authors prove shape inequalities for charged spacetimes in a 2025 paper. An electrostatic system joins gravity with a static electric field, often on a space that ends at a boundary, and a cosmological constant may add pressure to the whole picture.

The team extends known geometry results to higher dimensions, then proves sharp estimates at the boundary. Their inequalities relate the size of the region to two classic mass measures, one weighing the boundary and one tied to horizons. Such bounds limit what charged, gravitating objects can look like, and they test proposed descriptions of black holes against clean mathematics.
arxiv-2508-10458:
Pooja Chandravanshi and four co-authors engineer a quantum key system in twenty twenty-five. Quantum key distribution promises future-proof secrecy for communications. It is moving from laboratories into real networks. Device imperfections, not protocol math, are now the main obstacle to secure keys.

Their framework implements the BB84 protocol with broader use in mind. Device calibration, synchronization, and optical alignment are treated systematically. Key post-processing gets the same care. A simple sifting algorithm is given that hardware can run easily. Results stress the choice of temporal window, a humble setting with big effects. It trades key rate against the quantum bit error rate. Readers get a builder's guide for turning quantum secrecy into working hardware.
arxiv-2508-10758:
Nicolas Lapautre, Maria Marchenko, Carlos Miguel Patiño, and Xin Zhou adapt a leaner attention method to transformers that read point clouds, in a 2025 paper. Attention, the core of transformers, grows quadratically with input size, which chokes models of big physical systems. A recent architecture, Erwin, handles such data as trees of points. The team grafts on Native Sparse Attention, a method built for sequences, and reshapes it for unordered point sets.

The combined model was tested on three physical data sets: cosmology simulations, molecular dynamics, and air pressure fields. It matched or beat the original Erwin model on each. The team also re-ran the original Erwin experiments to check their build against the published numbers. They argue the pairing widens the reach of transformers for physics, where systems are huge and detail matters at many scales.
arxiv-2508-10958:
Apurba Tiwari and co-authors study black holes in a changed theory of gravity in this 2025 paper. They look at how heat-like traits of these black holes can reveal hidden links among their smallest parts. A curved measure is used as a clue: its sign hints whether those parts mostly pull together or push apart.

The authors write out the heat traits for new black hole cases in four dimensions. They track where the clue measure changes sign or spikes, which marks key points and phase shifts. They find a simpler pattern than in many past cases, with one sign crossing marking a second-order shift. The work offers a direct read on the hidden behavior.
arxiv-2508-11058:
Wentao Mo and co-authors push 3D scene question answering beyond single views in a 2025 paper. Older datasets rarely force a model to combine looks from several angles, and their labels tie text to lone objects. Their new MV-ScanQA set makes sixty-eight percent of questions need multi-view reasoning, far above past sets. A companion corpus, TripAlign, holds one million triplets linking 2D views, object groups, and text.

Their baseline model, LEGO, borrows strength from big 2D vision-language models and pre-trains on TripAlign. It tops the new benchmark and also leads older captioning and question sets, they report. Data and code are public.
arxiv-2508-11258:
Ruicheng Xian, Yuxuan Wan, and Han Zhao make closed language models fairer classifiers in a 2025 paper. Group fairness means a classifier should not systematically favor one demographic group over another. Standard fairness tools retrain the model or tap its inner layers. The most capable commercial models, though, are closed: users can only prompt them and read outputs.

Their framework treats the closed model as a feature source. Carefully designed prompts pull out prediction scores that carry the facts a fairness rule needs. A small, standard fair classifier is then trained on those features, after the model has done its work. The approach needs no access to weights or inner layers. Tests show it brings closed models closer to fairness targets.
arxiv-2508-11558:
Spacetime itself might create particles when it ripples, and a passing plane gravitational wave is the cleanest test case. Nail Khusnutdinov computes the Green's functions for massless scalar and vector fields in that background, in closed form, three independent ways. One route solves the governing equation directly; the other two build the answer recursively through classic schemes from quantum field theory in curved spacetime.

All three routes agree exactly with the standard expansion used in the field. That agreement points to no massless particles being produced by the wave at all. Khusnutdinov also addresses a rival line of work whose coefficient calculations predicted creation, explaining why the closed-form result should stand. The dispute matters because particle creation by gravity underpins ideas from Hawking radiation onward.
arxiv-2508-12058:
Ibrahima Dramé and Etienne Pardoux prove two classic limit results for a broad class of family-tree style growth processes in 2025. In these models, each person's chance of having offspring depends on age and also varies at random from one person to the next. The authors study what happens when the number of founding ancestors grows very large.

They show the whole process settles near a fixed average path, and that random swings around that path follow a known bell-shaped law. The hard part is proving the swings stay tight in the space of jump paths, which they handle with a known test. The results firm up tools used for populations, cells, and spread models.
arxiv-2508-12158:
Judging whether a text is private is slow human work, and language models are being tried as stand-in judges. Stephen Meisenbacher, Alexandra Klymenko, and Florian Matthes test that substitution in a 2025 paper. Ten datasets, thirteen models, and six hundred seventy-seven human raters fed the study. Privacy proved hard even for people, who agreed with each other only loosely. Tastes and values shift what counts as sensitive.

Models still managed to mirror the shared human view fairly well. Reasoning traces from both sides were compared for style. Strengths and limits of model judges are laid out in turn. The authors frame the work as a feasibility map for privacy scoring tools.
arxiv-2508-12258:
Małgorzata Bogdan and co-authors wrote this 2025 statistics paper on learning networks whose links mean conditional dependence, and on finding their hubs. The standard tool, graphical LASSO, penalizes raw precision entries and so changes its answer when variables are rescaled. A newer variant penalizes partial correlations instead, the scale-free quantities that define the graph.

The team put that variant on firm ground. They state a scale-invariant version of the irrepresentability condition and prove it suffices for the method to recover the true graph consistently. The condition is strictly weaker than the one the older method needs, which explains why the new one shines on hub-structured graphs. Two efficient algorithms and an analysis of the underlying nonconvex problem, including when its solution is unique, complete the package.
arxiv-2508-12358:
Haolin Jin and Huaming Chen uncover systematic failures of language models as code reviewers in this 2025 paper. Engineers now ask these models whether code meets a written specification. The authors tested that judgment on standard benchmarks with unified prompts. The models often failed the test in a specific direction: they flagged correct code as failing the requirements or as hiding defects.

Richer prompts made matters worse. Asking for explanations and proposed fixes raised the misjudgment rate further. The team traced root causes in how the models weigh surface cues over the specification itself. They then proposed two prompting strategies that cut the errors. The authors frame the work as the first clear report of this failure mode. Their guidance aims at teams who use such models for review, where a wrong verdict can block good code.
arxiv-2508-12658:
Lucía Martín-Merchán builds new seven-dimensional shapes carrying a special geometric structure in this 2025 mathematics paper. The structures, named for the exceptional group G2, are prized because perfectly flat versions relate to physics theories. Her shapes satisfy every known topological requirement for such a flat version, yet arise where the underlying space cannot host one.

She starts from folded spaces with a mirror symmetry, then smooths their creases with a symmetry-respecting method she develops for this purpose. The resulting manifolds carry the closed form of the structure. She also computes their key topological fingerprints, including a curvature-linked class and subtle product invariants. The work widens the known zoo of almost-flat G2 spaces.
arxiv-2508-12958:
Fabrizio Colombo, Francesco Mantovani, and Peter Schlosser wrote a 2025 math paper on the S-functional calculus for the adjoint of a Clifford operator. Clifford algebras extend complex numbers to higher dimensions, and their operator theory needs its own spectrum and function calculus. Adjoints, the mirror form of an operator, are basic objects whose calculus was not fully charted.

The authors show the adjoint shares the same S-spectrum as the original operator. A key property, bisectoriality, passes from an operator to its adjoint as well. They then link the left calculus of one to the right calculus of the other, through a simple mirrored version of each function. The link holds across bounded, unbounded, and two stronger forms of the calculus.
arxiv-2508-13358:
Zeeshan Ahmed and co-authors attacked the lag problem in phone based speech translation in 2025, where a device must hear one language and speak another almost at once. Splitting the job into a listener and a translator is natural, but naive handoffs pile up delay.

Their streaming translator starts rendering before the speaker finishes, keeping pace by aligning partial text. Cues from the speech recognizer help the translator hold context, and search shortcuts such as timeouts keep the whole chain real time. On a two language conversation setup on device, the system beat baselines on both speed and quality. It nearly matched systems allowed to hear the whole sentence first.
arxiv-2508-13658:
Faruk Alpay and Hamdi Alakkad build a calibrated theory of diffusion across graphs, with constants they can state exactly. Their work appeared in twenty twenty-five. Diffusion smooths signals over networks, and tuning its speed for each graph is essential but slippery.

Their framework blends three known tools: plain Laplacian smoothing, a nonlinear p-Laplacian flow, and a learnable energy drain. For strong nonlinearity they prove sharper decay bounds than standard templates give. They also prove a limit result: no fixed setting can hit universal targets across graphs with different spectra. A calibration algorithm with guarantees answers that limit. Closed-form bounds for key graph gaps and sharp stability constants round out the theory. Small tests confirm the bounds are tight.
arxiv-2508-13858:
A plasma torch with two radio-frequency coils is modeled in a 2025 paper by Loann Terraz, Biruk T. Alemu, and Santiago Eizaguirre. The torch burns argon at normal air pressure, with one coil driven at high frequency and the second at medium frequency.

Using commercial simulation software, the team found the least coil current that keeps the plasma lit. They then varied the gap between the coils and the power of the fast coil, watching how the plasma answered. Readouts include sideways temperature profiles, gas speeds along the axis, and the heat carried out at the end of the second coil. That heat is compared with the heat lost to the tube wall.
arxiv-2508-14358:
Zhujun Li, Shuo Zhang, and Ioannis Stamos proposed HRC-Pose in 2025 for estimating object pose by category from depth data. The task is to predict full pose and size for objects in a known class. Past methods train only on pose labels, missing the smooth continuity of poses, which hurts generalisation to unseen angles.

Their depth-only frame uses contrastive learning so point cloud features keep pose continuity. Rotation and translation are encoded separately and used across the network. A ranking scheme contrasts clouds by rotation, translation, and category differences. On two benchmarks the method beat prior depth-only leaders and ran in real time, suiting real-world use.
arxiv-2508-14758:
Ali Enayat, Mateusz Lelyk, and Albert Visser prove a result in mathematical logic about weak theories of arithmetic. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five. A theory has restricted complexity if its axioms can all be stated within a fixed, low level of logical complexity. A known barrier says no strong enough arithmetic theory can be completed in that restricted way.

The authors work around the barrier by starting from a model instead of a theory. They build models of arithmetic whose full true descriptions do have restricted complexity. Their strongest case covers a weak base theory plus the full collection scheme, a powerful set of principles. The construction shows the barrier depends on the theory's strength, not on arithmetic itself. It is the first paper in a planned series.
arxiv-2508-15458:
M Darcis and co-authors add color to a light sensor used in planet hunting telescopes in a 2025 paper. Imaging an Earth like planet needs extreme contrast, which demands control of the light wavefront to better than a billionth of a meter.

The Zernike sensor they study is very sensitive but answers in a strongly nonlinear way, which limits its range. Using several wavelengths at once, made possible by new photon counting detectors, should steady it. Simulations with a fast fitting method confirm gains: the plain sensor gains range, and wider wavelength coverage brings more photons, which hardens the reading against noise. Large jumps in the wavefront, like petal errors, can also be unwrapped, at some noise cost.
arxiv-2508-15558:
The authors measure in 2025 how fast atoms wander inside two refractory high entropy alloys, and whether the wander is truly sluggish as folklore claims. Such alloys, built from many metals that resist heat, are candidates for turbines and reactors. How atoms diffuse inside them governs creep and stability at high temperature.

The team tracked radioactive tracer atoms of cobalt, manganese, and zinc through single phase samples of the two alloys. Neutron scattering measured how far each kind of atom sits from its ideal lattice spot. Pairing those distortions with the diffusion speeds tests the sluggish story. The title gives the verdict away: diffusion is not sluggish here. Design rules for hot section alloys must rest on measured rates, not slogans.
arxiv-2508-15658:
Su and co-authors built SurGE, a benchmark for testing how well language models write scientific survey papers. Literature grows so fast that hand-written surveys are becoming impractical, and models are being tried as replacements, but no standard test existed. Their benchmark gives each system a topic, an expert-written survey as reference, and the full set of papers that survey cited, drawn from a corpus of over a million computer science papers.

Their scoring framework rates generated surveys on coverage, citation accuracy, structure, and content quality. When they ran a range of model-based methods, including agent-style systems, all fell well short of the human references. The authors conclude that survey writing remains hard for current systems, especially faithful citation and coverage, and they release the benchmark, data, and code openly. The catalog lists a shorter title and one fewer author than the text itself.
arxiv-2508-15858:
Buyl and co-authors ask whether large language models can trust each other, and how anyone would know. As AI systems increasingly work in teams, trust between them may shape how well they cooperate, much as it does between people. The team set out to build trust in controlled ways and to measure it both directly and indirectly.

They built trust three ways: letting models build rapport in conversation, handing them a script showing trust, and adjusting their system prompts. Then they compared what models said on a standard trust questionnaire with how they actually behaved when persuaded or asked to collaborate financially. The two kinds of measure matched poorly, sometimes negatively, so the authors warn that asking a model whether it trusts is deceptive.
arxiv-2508-15958:
Victor Ginzburg proves new results linking sheaf theory to duality for Hamiltonian spaces. His 2025 paper begins with a known pattern: extensions between intersection cohomology sheaves can often be read from plain cohomology groups. He proves a broader version under weaker assumptions than before.

That result is then applied to the derived Satake equivalence, a deep bridge between geometry and representation theory. He describes how the equivalence treats a class of pure objects and finds a new functorial behavior when the underlying group changes. A second thread settles when the symplectic dual of a smooth Hamiltonian variety is normal, covering many standard examples. Coulomb branch duals are also described, and shown to carry only symplectic singularities.
arxiv-2508-16458:
Øyvind Stormark Auestad wrote this 2025 mathematics paper on equations driven by noise. Stochastic evolution equations describe systems that change over time while random shocks hit them: fluids, prices, and fields. Solutions live in a space called L0, where size is measured by probability rather than by a fixed ruler.

Auestad builds a framework for two jobs: judging how smooth those solutions are in time, and rating how fast numerical schemes approach them. The core is a pair of inequalities for stochastic integrals, of the classic Burkholder-Davis-Gundy kind, adapted to weakly integrable inputs. One version feeds a continuity test that yields Hölder smoothness of the integrals. The other gives clean rates for approximations. Linear parabolic equations serve as the test case for both uses.
arxiv-2508-16558:
Bhaskar Dutta, Aparajitha Karthikeyan, Nityasa Mishra, Yago Porto, and Louis Strigari study tiny particles called neutrinos from exploding stars. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five. They ask whether a new kind of interaction, beyond the standard rules, would change the burst of neutrinos sent out when a star in our galaxy collapses.

In the dense matter of the star, this new effect grows with the square of the density. That trait is absent in the Sun or Earth, so a star burst could probe it far more deeply. In one case, it would bring back a sharp peak in the signal that normal rules suppress. A large planned detector called DUNE could spot that change.
arxiv-2508-16958:
Simon Chandler-Wilde and Siavash Sadeghi show that rough obstacles can trap sound without bound, in work from 2025. Sound scattering by a hard obstacle is modelled with the Helmholtz equation plus a radiation rule. For smooth obstacle edges, a key solution size grows at most at an exponential rate with frequency.

The authors drop all smoothness demands on the obstacle shape in their setup. They then build one fixed obstacle where solution size beats any preset growth list. Given any rising frequency list and any faster rising size list, the built shape tops each size at its paired frequency. The result shows that edge smoothness is not a side detail. Roughness alone can drive extreme trapping.
arxiv-2508-17158:
Jack Youstra and five co-authors defend the services that let customers fine-tune large language models, in this 2025 paper. Fine-tuning APIs allow businesses to adapt a model on their own data. Attackers have found they can smuggle harmful training content past filters by encoding it in ciphers, quietly stripping the model's safety training while the data looks harmless.

The authors define the defense problem precisely and release CIFR, a benchmark for this fight. The benchmark scores defenses on two axes at once: keeping the model safe against cipher attacks and keeping it useful for honest fine-tuning. The test set hides some cipher families entirely, to check whether defenses generalize. Their best defense watches the model's internal activations with a probe: it caught over ninety-nine percent of attacks and held up on unseen ciphers. The open benchmark invites others to harden a genuinely two-sided problem.
arxiv-2508-17258:
Filippos Ventirozos, Peter Appleby, and Matthew Shardlow combine AI agents in a 2025 paper on review sentiment. The task sorts opinions by theme: a review may praise food but pan service. Trained models lead the field, but labeled data are scarce and costly for each new domain.

Large language models used with no training offer a way around that cost. The team runs several agents that reason step by step, then merges their answers with a measure of how sure each agent is. Bias in hand labels can make trained models look strong yet fail in new domains. A merged, doubt aware approach aims for results that travel better.
arxiv-2508-17958:
Angelo Passariello's dissertation, from twenty twenty-five, extends a stochastic backscatter model from structured to unstructured flow solvers. The model adds random fluctuations to turbulence simulations, with set correlations in space and time. Those variables come from smoothing a random field, which yields a decaying spatial correlation. The smoothing runs along the three coordinate directions of the grid. That works only for structured solvers, which use regular grids. Unstructured solvers use irregular meshes, common for complex shapes.

Laplace smoothing, a mesh-based averaging, can replace the directional smoothing. But the spatial correlation it produces must be derived by analysis, not assumed. Deriving that correlation is the main goal of the dissertation. The work matters for accurate turbulence modeling in real-world flow codes.
arxiv-2508-18158:
Provakar Datta's doctoral thesis, dated 2025, reports precise measures of how neutrons respond to magnetic fields. When electrons bounce off the parts of an atom's core, the pattern tells where charge and flow sit inside. That response is summed up in form factors. Data at high push, where the bounce is hard, are scarce, since such tests are hard to run.

Datta used the ratio method, which takes the neutron's signal as a share of the proton's and so cancels many errors. Two large detectors at a lab caught the bounced electrons and the struck core parts at once. Data came at five push levels, the last far past the old range. The low points match world data, and the high points stretch the map of the neutron for years to come.
arxiv-2508-18258:
Kegreisz presents a paper from twenty twenty-five on a new optimizer for training neural networks in noisy settings. Popular optimizers lean on momentum to size their steps. Noise and shifting tasks can make those size estimates stale. The new method splits direction from size cleanly. Momentum smooths only the direction of travel. Step size comes from the freshest gradient's magnitude instead. A variant stretches the momentum window over time on a log schedule.

Convergence guarantees match other sign-based methods. Gains show strongly in noisy reinforcement learning tests. Calm tasks stay competitive with standard tools. Simplicity and speed are stressed throughout.
arxiv-2508-18558:
Benjamin Castle, Assaf Hasson, and a third co-author published a paper in 2025 on hidden groups inside tame topological structures. Model theory sorts mathematical worlds by how wildly they behave. Within a broad tame class, the authors draw a line, called topological 1-basedness, between linear and non-linear behavior. They ask what structure the linear side must contain.

For a rich enough structure on the tame side of the line, they prove a type-definable abelian group must exist on an open chunk of the space. That group carries the natural topology as a genuine topological group. The induced structure on it then matches a topological analogue of a classic classification of simple stable groups. Abstract as it sounds, the theorem extends results once known only for narrower families of theories.
arxiv-2508-18658:
Loïc Foissy and three co-authors build a new algebra on decorated rooted forests in a 2025 arXiv paper. Forests here are math objects: sets of rooted trees whose nodes carry labels. Such sets carry rich shuffle and split rules used across algebra and physics.

The team adds a split rule that turns the forest space into a bialgebra of the Moerdijk kind. They give a plain recipe for the split and a mirror form through a fresh notion of matrices that a forest can stand for. In the lens of operated algebras, they set up a wider class where a symmetric rule holds. They then show the flip map of the algebra acts as a Rota-Baxter operator, and they build the free case, which lands on the classic algebra.
arxiv-2508-18758:
Yipeng Zhang and co-authors turn plain questions into query plans for giant tables, skipping SQL altogether. Asking data questions in code bars most people from large data sets. Text-to-SQL helps but inherits SQL's weakness on huge tables and rich analysis. Their framework instead builds a step-by-step plan of operations.

A language model reads the question and grows the plan one operation at a time. Steps run directly on the data, so the model never swallows the whole table. Classic query commands ride along, plus extras like principal component analysis and anomaly spotting. Tests on standard and large science tables back the design.
arxiv-2508-18958:
Matteo Contini and co-authors present a drone-based method for mapping coral in a 2025 arXiv paper. Pixel-level labels over wide reef areas are a bottleneck for machine learning in ecology. Their framework trains a segmentation model from weak labels instead.

Underwater photos give fine-scale class calls, while drone images cover broad areas. Point-level calls become coarse masks that supervise training on the aerial views. A second pass trains on the model's own refined output to sharpen edges. On hand-labeled reef zones, the model reached strong pixel accuracy. New coral classes can be added with ease.
arxiv-2508-19458:
Mahdi Haghifam, Adam Smith, and Jonathan Ullman study a privacy risk in machine learning in a 2025 paper. An attacker may try to tell if one person's data was used to train a model. Most attacks use a set of fresh samples from the same source to make that call.

The authors ask how large that fresh set must be for an attack to work well. They study a clean test case where a model learns the mean of bell-curve data. Their proof shows the set may need to be far larger than the training set itself. That means common attacks may miss real risks.
arxiv-2508-19658: Zbigniew Haba writes in 2025 on how quantum gravity might be framed through a gauge theory with a large symmetry group. The paper treats that theory as a single frame for all forces. In one-loop work, the author shows that Einstein gravity can be seen as an approximation to the gauge theory. The paper also discusses the role of special wave states in the quantization step.
arxiv-2508-20058:
Kaden Bearne, Alexander Duplinskiy, Matthew Filipovich, and Lvovsky build a light sorter in 2025 from a diffractive neural network. Mode sorting splits a beam into its basic shapes and sends each to its own spot, so all can be measured at once. Such sorting serves quantum and classic optics alike.

Their twist is to let the network also choose where the output spots land, not just how the plates bend light. In tests sorting twenty-five beam shapes with three plates, stray light leaking into wrong spots fell from 37.5 percent to 8.7 percent at the same efficiency. Flexible targets beat fixed ones.
arxiv-2508-20258:
Arya Tschand and seven co-authors published a paper in 2025 on using large language models to speed up graphics chip code the way human experts do. Expert tuners win speed by matching a program's memory pattern to the chip's layout, a craft that takes weeks per kernel. Search-based AI tools tune runtimes blindly, without that hardware sense.

Their system feeds the model the workload's access patterns, chip specifications, profiling logs, and notes on past attempts. For one classic matrix kernel it found in under five minutes the arrangement that took experts two weeks. Across ten varied kernels it produced winning layouts for nine, with speedups up to about twofold. The work points toward AI engineers that reason about hardware, not just code.
arxiv-2508-20558:
Chao-Hui Wang and co-authors find layered orbit families around charged black holes in a 2025 paper. Dyonic black holes carry both electric and magnetic charge. Their gravity wells shape the closed paths that matter and light can take.

Turning one coupling dial reshapes the well from a single dip to several dips. What matters is how the metric bends outside the horizon, not how many horizons exist. Extra wells spawn extra branches of periodic orbits that share one winding number. Those branches differ in energy, reach, and stretch while matching in form. Orbit catalogs for exotic holes grow richer than classic charts suggest.
arxiv-2508-21358:
Gagik Tovmassian and a large group of co-authors revisit two odd star systems in this 2025 arXiv paper. The systems, V479 Andromedae and V1082 Sagitarii, are cataclysmic variables, pairs where a white dwarf pulls gas from a companion star. Most such pairs orbit in under ten hours, but these two take far longer, which strains ideas about how they formed.

The team gathered fresh data from ultraviolet and infrared spectra, light-polarization measures, and improved Gaia distances, then matched the stars against computer models of binary evolution. Both donor stars appear swollen enough to fill the space that feeds the white dwarf. The results suggest the donors once lost mass fast, and that magnetic braking drains orbital motion more strongly in these systems than in normal ones.
arxiv-2508-21458:
Kaouther Mouheb and a large team test how to tune a big medical AI model across many hospitals, in a 2025 benchmark study. The task is sorting brain MRI scans by dementia type. Patient scans cannot be pooled freely, so training must be federated. Each site trains locally, and only model updates travel.

Working with a large multi-cohort data set, the team varied three choices: the shape of the sorting head, how much of the base model to tune, and how to merge updates. Head shape mattered a lot. Freezing the base model’s encoder matched full tuning, which saves compute. Smarter merging beat the standard averaging rule. The results guide real rollouts in hospital networks.
arxiv-2508-21658:
Hirofumi Osada and Shota Osada build the motion of infinitely many charged particles in a 2025 mathematics paper. The particles repel each other with Coulomb force, the same force that pushes like electric charges apart, and they also jitter randomly. Their joint motion is described by equations with infinitely many unknowns, one for each particle.

The authors construct this motion in all dimensions from two upward and for all strengths of the repulsion. They prove the equations have strong solutions and that each solution path is unique. Earlier work covered only one special case tied to random matrices. Their new method, based on how the random field's density changes, works beyond that case. The result gives a firm base for studying large charged systems.
arxiv-2508-21758:
Roberto Soler studies how Alfvén waves climb from the Sun's surface to its outer atmosphere, in a 2025 paper. These magnetic waves carry energy that may heat the corona, the Sun's hot outer layer. To get there they must cross the chromosphere, a middle layer that reflects and absorbs much of their energy.

Older theory treated the waves as steady and computed how much is reflected, transmitted, or absorbed. Soler instead simulates waves driven at the surface over time. With fine spatial detail, the transmitted share settled to the steady value after only a few crossings of the chromosphere, across all frequencies. Reflected shares matched well at low frequencies. The check validates steady theory while showing when it can mislead.
arxiv-2509-00058:
Eric Zhang, Li Wei, Sarah Chen, and Michael Wang compare four dysfluency detection models in 2025 on more than raw scores. Dysfluency means breaks in speech flow, such as repeats and blocks in stuttering. Clinics need models that doctors can control and understand, not just accurate ones, before they will adopt them.

Four approaches are weighed on performance, controllability, and explainability across many data sets, with clinician input. Two light models are fast and simple but opaque. One modular model best balances accuracy with clinical clarity. A fourth shows promise but could not be fully rebuilt by the team. The study maps trade-offs that builders must face when speech tools move toward real care.
arxiv-2509-00258:
Erwan Dereure, Emmanuel Akame Mfoumou, and David Holcman assess one-dimensional cluster stability in 2025 by trimming extreme points. Given a sample of independent points on a line, the span shrinks as the most extreme points are removed one by one. The diameter-shrinkage ratio quantifies that relative reduction at each step.

The team derives formulas, with finite-sample corrections, for the expected shrinkage under uniform and Gaussian models. The two curves stay distinct even after moderate trimming. A simple rule assigns each sample to the closer profile, beating the classic likelihood-ratio test in small or noisy samples while staying consistent for large ones. The criterion also plugs into clustering methods to judge stability.
arxiv-2509-00458:
Fabrizio Chinu reports a measurement made with the ALICE detector for the ALICE Collaboration. The work tests perturbative quantum chromodynamics, a method that computes strong-force rates step by step, using beauty hadrons, particles that contain a beauty quark, made in proton-proton hits.

Chinu rebuilds B-zero mesons from their decay into a D meson and a charged pion, using data from LHC Run 3 at an energy stated in the record. The rate he finds, tracked against sideways momentum and rapidity, a measure of direction, is set beside modern calculations. Agreement or gaps here check how well the theory handles heavy quark production.
arxiv-2509-00558: Thibault Damour, writing alone, sums up joint work begun in 2008 with A A Starobinsky. The work was never finished. The pair tried to apply the stochastic approach to quantum gravity. That approach treats long-wave quantum effects as random noise. They focused on infrared effects, meaning effects at very large scales. The setting was an inflationary space-time, an early universe that expands fast. Damour presents the results reached in those first stages. The text preserves ideas from a project that stopped early.
arxiv-2509-00758:
Dongdong Wei, with two co-authors, studies double-layered vacuum bubbles. These bubbles can form during phase transitions in the early universe. The setting has multiple vacua, meaning several stable states. Standard transitions produce single-wall bubbles. Those bubbles expand and collide with each other.

The team uses lattice simulations to evolve the fields on a grid. They show flyover transitions can produce double-layered bubbles. Such bubbles arise by crossing two barriers in a row. The team tracks wall speedup, collisions, and trapped regions. Double-layered bubbles behave quite unlike single-wall ones. The difference bears on signals such as gravitational waves. It also bears on baryogenesis, the origin of the matter imbalance.
arxiv-2509-00858:
Wei-Chun Chen and one co-author, Wei-Hsuan Yu, establish upper bounds for two-distance sets, point sets in Euclidean space or on a sphere whose points use only two distinct distances. Bounding the largest such set is a classic problem in discrete geometry.

Their main recipe is the spectral method: they construct Seidel matrices, matrices that encode the distance relations between points, and apply eigenvalue analysis to derive explicit bounds. For Euclidean space, they bound the cardinality in terms of dimension and the ratio of the two distances. For spherical sets, two bounds are given depending on the sign of a sum of inner products, and one coincides with the relative bound for equiangular lines in one higher dimension.
arxiv-2509-01058:
Health falsehoods spread fast online, and replies that correct them often use words many readers cannot follow. Xiaoying Song, with five co-authors, builds a system that writes such replies at a reading level matched to its audience. Their method joins search-based generation with learning from rewards.

The system first pulls in facts written for a chosen literacy level, meaning how well a reader handles health text. A reward score then blends user likes with plain readability checks, guiding the output toward that level. Tests show the replies were easier to read and more liked than those from rival methods. Song and the team argue this can make public health messages fairer and clearer.
arxiv-2509-01558:
Promotions in online marketplaces do not act on one item alone: treating one product can change the fate of its neighbors. Bram van den Akker studies uplift modeling, a method that estimates the extra profit a promotion causes, under such clustered network interference. Standard uplift methods assume no interference, an assumption whose failure leads to poor policies in real marketplaces.

Van den Akker builds a practical method around an interference-aware estimator, used as a learning objective that gradient methods can optimize directly. Combined with proven response transformation techniques, the framework aims straight at economic outcomes such as incremental profit. Simulations show the approach beats interference-naive methods by a wide margin, above all when interference effects grow. Guidance is also given for adapting profit estimation to settings where items influence each other in clusters.
arxiv-2509-01658:
Zhenyu Wu and seven co-authors present MoTo, an add-on module that lets a fixed robot arm work while its base moves. Fixed arm systems can handle many tasks but cannot travel across a room. MoTo adds travel skill without new training data drawn from moving robots. Vision and language models help the system find where the robot should park.

The method picks docking points near a target object and plans paths for both the base and the arm. Key points on the object and the arm guide the motion so the arm stays in reach. Tests on a standard benchmark and with a real robot beat prior methods on success rate. The gain comes with no extra training examples.
arxiv-2509-02058:
Luca Bianchi, Carlo Marconi, Laura Ares, Davide Bacco, and Jan Sperling join two forms of boson sampling into one scheme. Boson sampling sends light bits through a web of optics to draw hard samples. One form counts single light bits, while the next form uses squeezed light states. A join lets rich states like squeezed light join the more new schemes.

A math frame based on generating functions treats multi bit light under smooth changes in one tongue. Those tools let unlike light based platforms meet and work as one. Code based tests grade the joined sampler on speed, hardness, and scale. Measures of quantum links show the kind of links the mixed scheme can make. The work widens what sampling rigs can try.
arxiv-2509-02458:
Borja Ocejo and nine co-authors wrote a 2025 applied machine learning paper on deciding when to send notifications in a large production system, LinkedIn's. Each message trades user value against fatigue, and choices form a long sequence rather than single steps.

Earlier offline reinforcement learning, such as Conservative Q-Learning, proved unstable and hard to reproduce at scale. The team reframes the learning task with Decision Transformers, which cast policy learning as supervised learning conditioned on target returns. Additions include a multi-reward design for ongoing tasks and quantile-based conditioning on those returns. A production system with circular sequence buffers supports near-real-time decisions. Online tests raised session activity over the older agent while keeping fatigue in check.
arxiv-2509-02558:
Sahel Sharifymoghaddam, Yijun Ge, and Jimmy Lin wrote a 2025 information retrieval paper revisiting BRIGHT, a benchmark of long, reasoning-heavy search queries like those used with retrieval-augmented generation. They supply strong, reproducible baselines inside three open toolkits.

While rebuilding the lexical baseline, the authors found an under-documented detail: BM25 weighting applied to the query side, a variant called BM25Q. On long multi-sentence queries, that variant beat standard BM25 and became the strongest word-based baseline. An audit of the benchmark corpus also uncovered data quality problems, with suggested fixes. Tests on five other benchmarks show the query-weighting gain is mostly specific to BRIGHT. Blending it with standard BM25 gave the steadiest gains overall.
arxiv-2509-02758:
Michael Bouzinier and four co-authors present a 2025 mathematics education paper reviving an ontology-based system for organising Euclidean geometry problems, first built in the 1990s. Geometry trains logical reasoning, yet it has faded from many curricula.

The ontology sorts problems, solutions, and skills into linked facts, objects, and methods, letting teachers track student abilities in fine detail. Its core device is the solution graph, a directed acyclic graph holding multiple solution paths and the skills each step needs. Problem selection can then match teaching goals precisely. The framework was tested in practice by annotating problems numbering in the thousands across three decades.
