External synchronization improves bit-error, frame-error, and signal-to-noise ratios, cutting the frames needed for reliable lock and raising throughput.
arxiv-2604-07458: Ferreira fixes fermion field transformations for two-Higgs-doublet models under a new class of symmetries, dubbed GOOFy, from an unorthodox transformation of scalar, gauge, and spacetime fields. Earlier work showed Yukawa matrix textures can respect those symmetries up to two loops. This paper sets out how fermion fields transform under the new symmetries. New parameter regions invariant under renormalization to all orders emerge, including scalar-fermion interactions, widening the symmetry's reach for model building.
arxiv-2604-07558: Bhattacharjee and four colleagues offer live experience for digital mental health care tools. The feel is made at runtime, not just custom in content. Their GUIDE system makes own content and multimodal formats through rubric-guided making of modular parts. In a study with 237 people, GUIDE reduced stress and gave better user ratings against an LLM-based cognitive reframe control. GUIDE also aided diverse thought and action through varied flows.
arxiv-2604-07658: Cao traces weak long-range memory in linear recurrent models to their decay spectrum. Random starts collapse the smallest gap in that spectrum. Evenly spaced rates also fade over long contexts. His Position-Adaptive Spectral Tapering pairs geometrically spaced decay rates with scaling that stretches the spectrum to the true dependency range. Tests on Mamba-2, RWKV-7, and related models show steadier language modeling and better long-context retrieval.
arxiv-2604-07958: Xu and eight colleagues propose ImVideoEdit, a video editing framework that learns entirely from image pairs instead of costly paired video data. Most editing tasks decouple into preserved temporal dynamics plus selectively modified spatial content. By freezing pretrained 3D attention modules and handling images as single-frame videos, the method separates 2D spatial learning from temporal behavior. Its Predict-Update module pulls out and feeds in spatial differences. Rather than rigid external masks, the module adapts to content, keeping edits precise while motion stays faithful to the source.
arxiv-2604-08058: Celiberti and three colleagues investigate the Jahn-Teller phase transition in LaMnO3 near 750 Kelvin. Runs use machine-learning atomic motion trained on ab initio data. The transition is driven by ordering of the Q2 Jahn-Teller distortion of MnO6 octahedra. That distortion acts as the order marker and sets its order-disorder nature. Local shifts keep moving above that temperature. Results match the experimental temperature trends of structural and phonon traits and highlight anharmonic effects at finite heat.
arxiv-2604-08158: Paspaliaris and 10 colleagues show DustPedia and Local Volume Legacy samples serve as benchmarks for dust change in galaxies. Combined, the samples hold 1011 objects of all shapes, spanning varied stellar masses and star-forming rates, with spectral coverage far UV to far IR. The samples span matching ranges of stellar mass and shapes, ideal to pin down the main drivers of galaxy dust change. Using multi-band survey data, the team fitted spectral energy distributions and estimated real traits, including stellar mass, dust mass and star-forming rate.
arxiv-2604-08358: Gu, Bonilla Ataides, Lukin, and Yelin build a neural decoder for quantum error correction that uses the geometric layout of low density parity check codes. It reaches the tiny logical error rates needed for large fault tolerant programs with modest code sizes at present physical error rates. It also runs fast enough for leading hardware. On the Gross code it cut logical errors to about 17 times below rival decoders, reaching around one in ten billion at a physical error of one tenth of a percent.
arxiv-2604-08658: Baumann and three colleagues uncover a combinatorial pattern behind the rules for wave numbers of massive scalar fields in de Sitter space. Writing the Feynman sums as twisted sums of simple functions, they show the sums reduce to a finite master integral set obeying a first order system. The rules admit a simple graph based picture through graph tubings. That gives a fast way to derive them and an edge view of massive cosmic links, shown in small and large mass limits.
arxiv-2604-08958: Kim and Sreenath address a robotics bottleneck, where gathering real-world training data is costly and risky, by moving experience from a source task to a new target task. Their WOMBET framework learns a world model in the source task and generates prior data from it. That data moves to the target task under an uncertainty-penalized objective that lower-bounds the true return. Tests on continuous control benchmarks show better sample efficiency and final performance than strong baselines, with theory separating mismatch from approximation error.
arxiv-2604-09058: Baeg and Kim tackle long-range guessing, where piling errors, noise growth, and missing real-world fit defeat current models. Diffusion models offer a chance-based frame for doubt but usually rely on mean squared error and miss motion ruled by nature's laws. Their PDYffusion system brings PDE-based controls into a motion-aware model with doubt filter. It settles under the new loss. Tests on several data sets show better CRPS and MSE scores with stable doubt, giving an even, robust answer to the score-doubt trade-off.
arxiv-2604-09158: Güreş and three colleagues compare structuring and problematizing in language-model help for diagnostic reasoning. Novices face biases like jumping to conclusions early and leaning on rules of thumb, and struggle to apply diagnostic methods to new cases. Case-based learning with data tracking and language models pairs lifelike cases with tailored help. Results were driven mainly by case hardness, not prior knowledge or help style. Structuring was linked to more accurate Active and Interactive work, while problematizing drew out Constructive work. Mixing methods best builds diagnostic reasoning.
arxiv-2604-09458: Özyılmaz, Thareja, and Nasser revisit nonlocal games through a representation-theoretic path from Bell locality to quantum pseudo-telepathy. Nonlocal games unify classical, quantum, and wider no-signaling correlations. The authors link the Bell view to math views of nonlocal games and quantum plans. They start from hidden-variable models, the CHSH inequality, and Bell nonlocality as a witness of entanglement needing no device trust. They present nonlocal games via predicate and checker rules, looking at XOR, GHZ, coloring, magic square, and Hardy cases, then compare four views.
arxiv-2604-09558: Hu and nine colleagues introduce VTC, a compiler framework that removes needless data movement from neural-network workloads. Its virtual tensors track movement between compute steps through index maps, instead of shuttling data to and from global memory. A new search routine picks the profitable virtual-tensor plan automatically, and the design works with existing compute kernels across arbitrary operator mixes. On graphics processors it beats current compilers by up to about 2 times, averaging about 1.3 times, while cutting inference memory by up to 60 percent.
arxiv-2604-09758: Zanineli and five co-authors ask whether odors share molecular drivers or emerge from distinct regimes, a question at the heart of the shape-versus-vibration debate. Clear machine-learning models trained on basic markers spanning electric, vibrational, and shape traits reveal odor-wise patterns of feature weight. No single marker class always rules odor guessing. The mix holds across models, hinting no single code captures smell; instead, receptor- and odor-tied links govern it. The results constrain rival theories and offer a guide for mapping odor space.
arxiv-2604-10158: Lin and nine colleagues open up Leela Chess Zero, a top chess transformer whose inner workings are largely opaque. They take apart its MLP and attention modules with sparse stand-in layers that capture the main work. A close case study shows these pathways expose rich, checkable tactical ideas. Three numeric metrics further show side-by-side reasoning matching the policy head's built-in bias. This is the first breakdown of both module types for clarity, and causal tests complete the picture of super-human tactical reasoning.
arxiv-2604-10658: Seck proposes Cognitive Core, a governed decision system for institutional choices like compliance, triage, and authorization appeals. Ordinary AI agents can silently execute wrong calls without flagging them for review. Nine typed reasoning steps, a four-tier governance model with human review as a condition of execution, and a tamper-evident audit ledger structure the design. On an 11-case appeals test it scores 91 percent, against 55 and 45 percent for two baselines. It makes zero silent errors while the baselines make 5 to 6 each.
arxiv-2604-11058: Ren and three colleagues investigate the nonlinear response of flow harmonics to initial eccentricities in the Gubser-flow model. By extending small answers, they derive analytic relations linking them to flows. Their results match the well-known large transverse momentum limit result. They further study a mismatch between the participant and fixed planes. They find standard values acquire a factor set by plane angles, often treated as random noise. This factor can modify the strength and even the sign of the coefficient, making it tied to first crashing nuclei setup.
arxiv-2604-11158: Katoch, Sarkar, and Sen take timelike entanglement rules from one interval to two in a changing holographic model. This extends their earlier work on a single timelike region, now with two regions in play. Where regions do not overlap, timelike mutual information stays positive and a weak monotone rule holds. Subadditivity and the Araki-Lieb rule still hold when intervals overlap. Strong subadditivity, though, generally fails for timelike intervals, as their worked examples show.
arxiv-2604-11358: Klausner and five colleagues update Bayesian inference of a Skyrme energy density functional for neutron star structure, using a Gaussian emulator of the Milano HFBCS-QRPA code to explore a wide parameter space. The calibration adds data sensitive to isospin from calcium and tin chains plus updated giant monopole resonance constraints. Posteriors are further tightened by ab initio neutron-matter calculations and NICER observations, giving consistent crust and core properties for catalyzed neutron stars. Bulk matter parameters come out nearly Gaussian, while several finite-nucleus parameters look clearly non-Gaussian.
arxiv-2604-11458: Stolte, Rahnenführer, and Bommert compare methods for measuring how similar categorical datasets are, judging both detection power and resource use. Edge count tests do well for two datasets, and the constrained minimum distance does even better in some settings. For variables with five categories each, the best method depends on the difference type, with graph-based tests or classifier tests winning. For two samples they recommend the Friedman-Rafsky test; for many samples, the Multi-Sample Mahalanobis Cross-Match test.
arxiv-2604-11658: Gaspari and three colleagues study brain-like computing with optomechanical oscillators. Phase oscillators suit machine learning through built-in nonlinearity and joint sync when coupled. The authors study a network of oscillators pumped in the blue-detuned regime for self-sustained oscillations, propose a theory for their motion, and show how such systems serve brain-like computing. They discuss training and a drum-resonator platform for a real build. Results from modeling an XOR gate with 5 nodes in an all-to-all setup round out the work.
arxiv-2604-11858: Härkönen sets out a scheme for finding which quantities in non-relativistic many-body quantum theory count as truly physical, for molecules and crystals. Two new postulates add: the states that matter are normalizable and stationary. A quantity counts only if unchanged under a chosen symmetry group and Galilean boosts. Superselection rules and quantum reference frames fit in the same scheme. Each truly physical quantity must then draw on more than one quantity that alone fails the test, linking the account to relational quantum theory.
arxiv-2604-11958: Saha conjectures a description of the Chow ring for the universal moduli stack of bundles over hyperelliptic curves, and proves it for rank two and genus two. The proof yields explicit generators and relations, showing the Chow ring is tautological. He also computes the Chow rings of products of universal Jacobians over genus-two curves.
arxiv-2604-12158: Hammoud gives one variational frame joining Kalman-type methods, KL-regularized control, Bayesian filtering and smoothing, and variational data assimilation. He proves identities showing the evidence is the global infimum and the true posteriors are the unique minimizers when they belong to the allowed classes. The frame clarifies targets often mixed up. Strong- and weak-constraint 4D-Var count as MAP estimators under Gaussian assumptions, and the ensemble Kalman filter is exact only in the limit of linear-Gaussian dynamics with infinite ensembles.
arxiv-2604-12358: Jiwan Kim and four colleagues study why cutting visual tokens harms multimodal models on hard reasoning. They trace the failures to a shift in what visual detail matters as answers form. Their training-free add-on, DSTP, keeps pruning matched to those changing needs during decoding. Tests show it recovers much lost accuracy on reasoning tasks and helps simpler image tasks too. The gains come at little extra computing cost.
arxiv-2604-12658: Muhammad Junaid simulates a massive black hole binary in the Leo I dwarf galaxy. Dark matter and stars shape the binary's long-term fate. N-body simulations track the orbit in a realistic Leo I model. Separation shrinks from 300 parsecs to roughly 1 parsec in about 2 billion years. Dynamical friction and stellar hardening drive the shrinkage. The orbit then stalls, illustrating the final parsec problem. Eccentricity grows while inner mass profiles shift modestly. Gravitational-wave models suggest no merger within a Hubble time.
arxiv-2604-12758: Mykyta Kliapets and 30 colleagues catalog variable stars in PLATO's first long-term field, LOPS2. PLATO launches in January 2027. The team sorted 38 million TESS light curves for 6 million sources. Two frameworks did the work: a neural network and a boosted tree ensemble. Combined predictions form the first LOPS2 catalog. Vetting and analysis validate the method. About 72 percent of curves show instrument or pipeline signals. The rest are 3.6 million variables: pulsating, rotating, and eclipsing types.
arxiv-2604-13058: Lee and six colleagues introduce KMMMU, a Korean-native benchmark of 3,466 questions across nine disciplines and nine visual modality types, built from Korean examination materials. The strongest open-weight model reaches 42.05 percent, while the best proprietary model scores 52.42 percent on the harder KMMMU-Adv set. Korean-specific questions show gaps up to 13.43 percent, with failures tied to local conventions and knowledge recall more than to reasoning depth.
arxiv-2604-13258: Pramanik, Maliha, Bastian, and Jha propose Hessian-Enhanced Token Attribution, an explanation framework tailored to decoder-only language models. It combines a semantic shift vector tracking token-to-token effect across layers, Hessian-based response scores catching second-order effects, and KL gap gauging information loss when tokens are masked. The unified design yields context-aware, causally faithful, meaning-grounded credit, and tests show it beats current methods on truth and match with human labels.
arxiv-2604-13358: da Silva and Vassilevich extend the Atiyah-Singer index theorem to non-Hermitian Dirac operators. When an operator anticommutes with a chirality operator, its null space splits into positive and negative parts, and the index is their size difference. For Hermitian operators the theorem keeps this index fixed under smooth changes. Using heat-kernel methods, the authors prove the same fixed index for diagonalizable non-Hermitian operators under ellipticity rules, with the index given by a local integral.
arxiv-2604-13458: He presents the first around-the-clock analysis of jump risk, combining market data with news narratives behind jumps. An open-source reasoning model sorts those narratives. Jump categories show risk premia vary widely, and macroeconomic news carries the largest premium. An annually rebalanced Fama-MacBeth portfolio isolating the most priced jump risk achieves a high Sharpe ratio and significant alphas over standard models. In short, news about the wider economy moves jump risk the most, and a portfolio built on that insight earns well out of sample.
arxiv-2604-13958: Al Ezzi and colleagues show that twisted monolayer-bilayer graphene hosts two kinds of band flattening at once. Global flat bands stabilize states at whole-number fillings, while local flattening lifts degeneracy and breaks symmetry at fractional fillings without opening a global gap. The metal stays conducting, yet anomalous Hall signals reveal broken time-reversal symmetry and valley polarization, making transport a probe of gapless correlated states.
arxiv-2604-14058: Stafford and the CMS collaboration present a first search for new resonances in events with four top quarks in the two-lepton channel. Using 138 inverse femtobarns at 13 TeV and 35 at 13.6 TeV, they find no significant excess. Limits cover vector Z-prime, scalar, pseudoscalar, and ALP mediators, with Z-prime mediators at 50 percent width excluded up to 850 GeV.
arxiv-2604-14658: Koroleva proves a fresh weighted Hardy-type inequality for functions in the Sobolev space W1p, under the assumption that small alternating boundary pieces are where the functions vanish. That classical family is thus widened to functions whose vanishing set consists of small alternating boundary pieces. Hardy-type inequalities relate a function to its derivatives through weights, and this result extends that classical pattern to the alternating-piece setting.
arxiv-2604-14858: Yang and eight others extend ATBench, a benchmark for trajectory safety testing and diagnosis of agent systems, to OpenClaw and Codex. The adaptation analyzes each setting, customizes a 3D safety taxonomy of risk source, failure mode, and harm, and feeds it into the ATBench pipeline as the spec. ATBench-Claw covers OpenClaw chains over tools, skills, sessions, and external actions. ATBench-Codex covers Codex trajectories over repos, shells, patches, dependencies, approvals, and policy boundaries. Emphasis falls on taxonomy tuning, domain risk coverage, and design under one framework.
arxiv-2604-15058: Yang and others study how people share place memories by jointly making heritage objects in VR. Pairs built 3D objects and scenes in VR heritage sites, using GenAI to give shape to memories you cannot touch. Watchers saw partners merge prompts and spots while settling clashing views, and use space itself to show how a place felt in the body. When the AI fell short, people reused its output in new ways rather than stopping.
arxiv-2604-15158: de la Cruz develops a projector-based way to study additive left group codes over finite fields. Classical idempotent codes describe images of projectors that must be linear over the bigger field, too narrow a frame for additive codes. He separates restricted idempotent codes from projector codes built from any projectors, showing the two kinds differ as a rule. The projector view thus widens the theory to cover additive codes the classical frame misses.
arxiv-2604-15658: Mei and five colleagues pin down how far away 56 gas clouds sit in sky from 10 to 20 degrees in Galactic longitude, using the MWISP carbon monoxide survey. For 47 of them, no distance was known before. Clouds picked out by DBSCAN get their range from a color-based method tuned on models and fed by 2MASS and Gaia EDR3 star data, giving 275 to 2,118 parsecs. Dust dimming rises with carbon monoxide glow, but only in a middling way.
arxiv-2604-15858: Ming-Xing Luo gives the first unconditional proof of Weber's conjecture for k up to 12, a claim from 1886 that governs lattice-based cryptography. The conjecture covers the Principal Ideal Problem, freeness of modules over rings of integers, and tight worst-case-to-average-case reductions in Ring-LWE and Module-LWE. Earlier checks for k at 9 and above leaned on the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis. Luo's method joins the Fukuda-Komatsu sieve, the inductive structure of the cyclotomic Z2 tower, and Herbrand's theorem.
arxiv-2604-15958: Bodea, Meisenbacher, and Matthes study where anonymization should sit in a RAG pipeline, the chain of steps behind retrieval-augmented answers. Privacy worries arise when RAG insights risk exposing private data to the model or the end user. Anonymization strips private markers and other sensitive tags, but no prior work asks where along the pipeline it belongs. Testing anonymization at the dataset and at the generated answer, they find privacy-utility trade-offs differ by placement, showing that placement itself matters for risk mitigation.
arxiv-2604-16058: Dihan and Muhtasim present LLMSniffer, a detector that tells AI-generated code from human-written code. It fine-tunes GraphCodeBERT with a two-stage supervised contrastive pipeline, comment removal preprocessing, and an MLP classifier. On GPTSniffer, accuracy rises from 70 to 78 percent and F1 from 68 to 78. On Whodunit, accuracy rises from 91 to 94.65 percent and F1 from 91 to about 95. Plots confirm fine-tuning yields split, compact embeddings. Model checkpoints, data, code, and a live demo are public.
arxiv-2604-16258: Alharbi, Tamma, Payne, and de Berardinis study competency questions generated by large language models, the natural-language questions an ontology should satisfy. Such questions traditionally come from engineers and domain experts working by hand, while generative AI now creates them at scale. The authors build quantitative measures to compare generated questions across domains and models, open and closed, and assess their intrinsic properties such as readability and structural complexity.
arxiv-2604-16658: Sole challenges stories of tempo change in Beethoven performance, arguing for coexisting traditions. Past studies fit regression lines to tempo against year, imposing stylistic evolution. K-means clustering of bar tempo data from over one hundred recordings of five sonatas finds traditions. Every movement holds two, three traditions: slow and fast, each stable across decades. The mid-range cluster dominates each movement with 55 to 70 percent. No slow cluster appears in fast movements, and one drifts, slowing near 3.2 beats per minute. Membership shows no link to performers' backgrounds.
arxiv-2604-16758: Shepherd presents a system detecting, localizing and scoring arrow punctures on archery target faces from only 48 photographs. The pipeline rectifies distorted photos into a standard system, then pairs a frozen DINOv3 transformer with guided upsampling. Only about 4 million of 308 million parameters are trainable, yet F1 reaches about 89 percent with localization error of one point four one millimetres. An ablation shows the CenterNet offset head adds negligible detection gain while degrading localization. Per-image scores return with median error of one point eight percent, and group centroids land within 4 millimetres.
arxiv-2604-17058: Liu links three traits of a memory kernel for open quantum systems: delayed support, upper-half-plane holomorphy, and Hardy boundary control. He gives conditions linking them for the Nakajima-Zwanzig kernel when the system space is finite-dimensional. The paper also derives Kramers-Kronig formulas, treats a perturbative force-fit equation, and proves them in Lean 4, closing with a Jaynes-Cummings check.
arxiv-2604-17258: Yan, Liao, and Ye present a pipeline that cuts onboarding for a new object from one to two days to about 30 minutes. Roboflow annotation trains a YOLOv8 detector, SAM 3D rebuilds the object without a scanner, and FoundationPose tracking uses the generated mesh as its template. The pose drives a Unity planner whose joint commands stream via UDP to a Unitree G1 humanoid. Tests show detection mAP of 0.995, pose precision under about 1 mm, and successful grasps at five positions, with generality confirmed on an automobile-window glue task.
arxiv-2604-17358: Lee, Song, Lee, Kim, and Yoon study voice assistants interrupted by third parties, a case where models confuse a bystander with the main user. They build TPI-Train, a set of 88,000 examples with speaker-aware hard negatives that force attention to voice cues over meaning. Their TPI-Bench then measures interruption handling and speaker discrimination in deceptive settings. Experiments show the design curbs shortcut learning from semantics alone, laying groundwork for sturdier multi-party spoken interaction.
arxiv-2604-18058: Delaney and five colleagues introduce Sonata, a compact latent world model for six-axis trunk inertial sensing under clinical data scarcity. Clinical cohorts often hold only tens to hundreds of patients, a poor match for web-scale training. Sonata, at 3.77 million parameters, pretrains on nine public datasets covering 739 subjects and 190,000 windows, predicting future state, not rebuilding raw traces. Against a matched autoregressive baseline it shows stronger frozen-probe clinical tests, fall-risk prediction, and cross-cohort transfer, while fitting wearable use.
arxiv-2604-18158: Lu, Qian, Jiang, and Zhou ask where prompt-based control of a language model actually lives. They test whether a behavior learned in one routing task can transfer through a fixed interface to another. On small GPT-2 routing tasks, exact transfer through an early interface passes strict necessity and sufficiency checks. Retrained prompts can relearn the same behavior elsewhere only with extra examples, so fixed-interface transfer is stronger evidence of reuse than training success alone.
arxiv-2604-18358: Shen, Xia, Gan, and Yu present LBFTI, a method that rebuilds detailed faces from facial recognition templates, exposing a privacy risk. Templates are meant to minimize stored data, yet inversion attacks can recover faces from them. LBFTI splits faces into foreground, midground skin, and background layers, generating each with dedicated models across three training stages. It beats state-of-the-art methods with a 25.3 percent improvement in TAR, plus better human-perceived similarity in surveys.
arxiv-2604-18558: D'Alimonte and Gassmann prove FK-percolation local event probabilities are evenly analytic in the parameter under suitable mixing rules, with a fast-growing bound. This proves Potts magnetisation analytic in a suitable parameter range, including the Ising case in all dimensions 3 and above in the whole supercritical regime. They also prove analyticity of Potts response with q colours, for any q 2 or above in the whole subcritical range. Finally, they extend this to various items in the FK measure, including the multi-point and cut multi-point link chances.
arxiv-2604-18658: Zhang and Jiang name Owner-Harm, a threat model with eight kinds of agent acts hurting the deployer. They show the gap: a layered setup scores 100 percent true positives and 0 percent false positives on AgentHarm, yet only about 15 percent on AgentDojo injections. A generic-model baseline scores about 63 versus about 59 percent, so the gap stems from brittle symbolic rules per setting. On a 300-case owner-harm set, the gate hits about 75 percent true positives and about 3 percent false positives; a post-check audit lifts true positives to about 85 percent.
arxiv-2604-18758: Purushothama and three colleagues propose an in-context learning approach for translating Coptic to English, a low-resource setting, augmented with syntax from Universal Dependencies parses. Building on bilingual dictionary glosses for vocabulary items, they test raw parser outputs, plain-English verbalizations of parses, and targeted guidance for hard constructions found in subtrees. Syntax alone helps less than dictionary glosses, but combining the two yields significant gains across model sizes. The combined method sets new state-of-the-art results for Coptic translation.
arxiv-2604-18958: Xiong and three colleagues study the small finitistic dimension of commutative rings through flat homological algebra. Using modules with finite projective resolutions, they set out the flat dimension's basic traits, step by step. They prove change of rings results for it, covering quotients, polynomial extensions, and local bounds. They then describe the small finitistic dimension in these terms and derive matching quotient, extension, and local bound results.
arxiv-2604-19058: Zhang and three colleagues demonstrate a photonic stepped frequency radar using dual Brillouin lasers in one fiber cavity. The design suppresses phase noise and enforces uniform steps at once, solving a challenge for existing architectures. Brillouin suppression plus common mode rejection on mixing cuts phase noise, while evenly spaced cavity resonances set step uniformity. The system produces an X-band waveform spanning 1.31 GHz, improving phase noise over 23 dB at a 100 kHz offset against a low cost oscillator. It thus frees output quality from driving electronics noise.
arxiv-2604-19258: Doi, Ohzeki, and Ricci-Tersenghi rework the Daydreaming learning rule, which strengthens stored patterns while damping false attractors in Hopfield memory models, for biased patterns. They build the update on a centered representation, with its own retrieval dynamics and energy function. Against the centered pseudo-inverse rule, their centered Daydreaming gives wider basins of attraction, so stored patterns are recovered from more starting states.
arxiv-2604-19658: Jian, Stoura, Scandella, and Chatzi build a label-free self-taught tool that spots structural damage from vibration alone. It separates true damage from shifts caused by changing loads and weather. Their design uses an autoencoder with two hidden codes, one trained to ignore non-damage effects through a variance-invariance-covariance rule called VICReg. The goal is reliable readings even when operating conditions shift, rather than readings that confuse weather and load changes with real harm.
arxiv-2604-19758: Düzkar presents ThermoQA, a three-tier testbed of 293 open-ended engineering thermodynamics problems covering property lookups, component analysis, and full cycle analysis. Ground truth is computed with CoolProp 7.2.0 for water, R-134a, and variable-cp air, and six leading models are tested across three runs each. Claude Opus 4.6 leads the combined ranking at 94.1 percent, with GPT-5.4 and Gemini 3.1 Pro close behind, while gaps between tiers run far wider for weaker models.
arxiv-2604-20958: Jarvis and colleagues present 608 spectroscopically confirmed members of GD-1, one of the longest and coldest stellar streams in the Milky Way. The members come from the first three years of DESI observations. The sample doubles the earlier heterogeneous haul. Fresh tracks in position, proper motion, and radial velocity span more than 100 degrees. A mixture model splits the stream into a cold thin strand and a hot cocoon. The cocoon holds about 30 percent of members, its spread fitting about 11 billion years of heating by dark-matter clumps.
arxiv-2604-21158: Michael Reitz and three colleagues compute two-dimensional spectra for molecular polaritons, hybrids of molecules and trapped light, using a semiclassical method in the many-molecule limit. By varying input-field strengths and phases, they separate the nonlinear pathways behind single- and double-quantum signals. The method matches measured single-quantum spectra, explains the short-time bleach puzzle, and shows how anharmonicity marks the double-excitation manifold.
arxiv-2604-21358: Shapiro links ribbon graphs on Riemann surfaces to meromorphic functions mapping them onto the sphere. A ribbon graph avoiding a function's critical points maps to an immersed graph. Conversely, any immersion of a multigraph without vertices of valence 1 or 2 lifts to a surface with a meromorphic function realizing it. For genus-g surfaces he builds spanning ribbon graphs of any smaller prescribed graph genus, including planar cases. Self-intersection counts, he shows, cannot be controlled by surface genus alone, and he gives general lower bounds.
arxiv-2604-21458: Jun Ye puts a HEOM solver into closed-loop qubit calibration, exposing bath structure that Markovian fits hide. The Ramsey channel carries the headline. The Markovian fit hits an exponential ceiling, while HEOM recovers a revival envelope whose primary coherence time beats the Markovian reference by at least 13 times at 95 percent bootstrap confidence. Rabi contrast falls slightly below an exact solve on a noise-limited grid, backing rather than proving the signature alone. The loop adds about 10 microseconds of scheduling overhead per protocol, a tiny latency penalty.
arxiv-2604-21558: Michele Botti and colleagues study a dual mixed nonconforming scheme for a generalized Darcy-Forchheimer model of flow through porous media. Past the older Girault and Wheeler scheme, they allow nonquadratic nonlinear rules, mixed uneven edge rules, and rougher flow tensors. They build schemes of each order. They prove convergence under weak smoothness claims using new Sobolev trace bounds for broken spaces, give each-order error bounds, and test the schemes by computer across rule types and solvers.
arxiv-2604-21758: Nielsen and ten colleagues demonstrate a passive photon-sorting circuit built around a solid-state quantum emitter in a waveguide. Scattering in the emitter supplies the nonlinearity that linear optics lacks, letting the circuit sort one- and two-photon components with 62 percent success. The same system enables Bell state measurements at 57 percent post-selected success without extra photons, above the 50 percent linear-optical limit, and could pass 65 percent with design improvements.
arxiv-2604-22058: Weingartner links error terms in estimates for smooth- and rough-number counting functions. He then uses this link to bound the error term in de Bruijn's Lambda approximation for counting smooth numbers. The bound comes from Fan's explicit upper bound on the error term in a de Bruijn-type estimate for counting rough numbers.
arxiv-2604-22258: Angino and five colleagues test a neural network that spots gaseous microemboli, tiny gas bubbles that can complicate heart procedures, in ultrasound recordings taken during surgery. Their U-Net model, tried on eight recordings from eight patients, beat classical spot detection and a simpler two-dimensional network while staying fast enough for live use. Under cross-validation it reached 92.55 percent precision and about 81 percent recall, and on bubble-free external recordings it mostly produced empty masks, suggesting few false alarms.
arxiv-2604-22558: Wang and 11 colleagues present SOLAR-RL, a training scheme for multimodal language-model agents navigating graphical interfaces. Offline reinforcement learning leans on static step-level data and misses whole-trajectory meaning such as task completion and execution quality. Online learning captures long-term dynamics at high interaction cost and environmental risk. Their semi-online approach folds global trajectory insight into offline learning instead. It rebuilds rollout candidates from static data, spots the first failure point with per-step validity signals, and assigns dense step rewards shaped to trajectory-level quality.
arxiv-2604-22658: Shi and five colleagues present PASR, pose-aware 3D shape retrieval from occluded single views, a hard task of growing importance. Existing approaches map point cloud features into vision-language spaces with contrastive learning, or learn one shared 2D-3D space. Such whole matches are hard to read, limiting toughness and use. PASR frames retrieval as feature-level analysis-by-synthesis, distilling knowledge from DINOv3 into a 3D encoder. Pose-conditioned 3D projections aligned with 2D maps bridge real images and synthetic meshes. Inference optimizes the same way.
arxiv-2604-22958: Zaninotto and three co-authors study the inverse problem for preference-based argumentation, which extends Dung's abstract argumentation by ranking arguments. Preferences turn attacks into defeats, and each reduction method yields its own abstract framework. The inverse question asks whether some ranking of arguments can produce a desired labeling under a given semantics. Across the four most widely used reductions under complete semantics, the answer can usually be found in polynomial time, with uses in elicitation and explanation.
arxiv-2604-23258: Ahadi and Sarshar simulate four-mode cluster states with linear, square, and T-shaped layouts for measurement-based quantum computing. Using symplectic maths and covariance matrices, they model how each graph shape drives quadrature links and nullifier rules. Stronger squeezing boosts target links and curbs anti-squeezing noise, with T-shaped graphs showing a stronger central link like GHZ behaviour. They introduce the Correlation Concentration Ratio, which weighs edge links against total links. The index offers a tool for ranking layouts and designing larger clusters.
arxiv-2604-23958: Carmosino, Dang, and Jackman show that gate elimination proofs, the main tool for lower bounds on general Boolean circuits, can be turned into algorithms that find errors. Given a circuit too small to compute a function, their refuters produce an input where it fails, covering cases from XOR and multiplexers to affine dispersers. For XOR they go further, characterizing optimal circuits so that even a circuit matching the bound can be refuted when it errs.
arxiv-2604-24058: Sharma and Balram test whether modular Hamiltonian methods can reliably pull topological numbers out of a wavefunction. Working with a lattice model of fractional quantum Hall states, they extract quantities for the Laughlin and Moore-Read states and watch them converge to expected values. Convergence slows as correlation length grows, so reliable extraction demands large systems. Their results support modular methods as a sound route to topological content, given enough size.
arxiv-2604-24258: Liu and five colleagues describe the SVOM Ground Support System, a critical part of the mission's ground segment. Its main tasks cover running payload operations, receiving, preprocessing, and managing science data. Built on the Chinese Space Science Satellite Project Ground Support System design, it handles mission planning, data reception, status monitoring, and product processing. The system supported SVOM's launch and on-orbit operations.
arxiv-2604-24458: Taye offers a heat-based account of why warm-blooded animals tend to rack up about a billion heartbeats in a lifetime, a pattern noted long ago but left without a physical reason. He links each beat to a fixed slice of entropy, a measure of energy spread. A lifetime total then stays near constant even as body size changes. Size scaling cancels out in his algebra, and a correction tied to activity, temperature, and hazard explains why some groups live longer than the rule predicts.
arxiv-2604-24558: Matthews and five colleagues replace the single reward per option in hierarchical reinforcement learning with whole spaces of behaviours, letting a controller blend reward functions to shape richer policies. Tested in the NetHack Learning Environment, the method, called Hierarchical Behaviour Spaces, performs strongly. Follow-up tests trace its edge to wider exploration rather than deeper long-term planning, a result that cuts against common wisdom about why hierarchy helps.
arxiv-2604-24958: Winecki and Nandi integrate video into the Vega grammar for data graphics. Video is now used with standard data for interactive exploration. They name three kinds of video display: sync, annotation and transformation. A split-signal design links Vega's instant dataflow to video player state. Compile-time detection of scrubbing lets encoding-aware tweaks lift responsiveness up to 4 times. Repurposed VOD protocols transform videos in real time. Updates stay under 200 milliseconds even for multi-hour compilations.
arxiv-2604-25258: Liu and Dayanikli study rumor control in large networks with Stackelberg graphon games. One side promotes its preferred news over other news. They define the Stackelberg equilibrium and characterize the Nash equilibrium with a forward-backward system and prove existence. They also formulate a two-principal model, each promoting her own news. Finally, they propose a bi-level algorithm for multi-leader equilibria, and tests show rivals produce strong opinion divisions.
arxiv-2604-25358: Parolari, Faccioli and Ballan put forth a closed-set test, C-Bench, that splits key skills with varied prompt and layout twists, and an open-set test, O-Bench, for real-world prompts and layouts. They also build one shared scoring rule that joins meaning and place scores into a single mark. With these tests, they rate six layout-led diffusion models on 319,086 images, setting a rank with fine splits for text and layout fit. Fine checks across settings and prompt twists show strengths and limits.
arxiv-2604-25758: Sharma and Mandal study transport in two-dimensional Dirac systems with tilted cones, shaped by strain-induced pseudogauge fields. Their pseudo-Landau levels differ from standard ones: they disperse with momentum, giving finite longitudinal group velocities. Using a semiclassical Boltzmann framework, the authors compute electrical, thermoelectric, and thermal responses in the linear regime. Those responses gain nonzero longitudinal parts. They also test the Mott relation and the Wiedemann-Franz law. The work unifies tilted spectra and deformation in quantum transport, with clear testable signatures.
arxiv-2604-25858: Chandrupatla and two colleagues map, empirically, when transformers succeed at in-context learning on Gaussian-mixture binary tasks. Theory had set conditions for in-context linear classification, but the scaling behavior was poorly characterized. Building on Frei and Vardi, they vary input dimension, example count, and pretraining task count in a controlled synthetic setup. They also track benign overfitting, where models memorize noisy labels yet generalize well on clean tests. Sweeps across geometry and training exposure reveal the regions where in-context learning works and where it fails.
arxiv-2604-26058: Sarode, Patil, and Joshi define and study S-Noetherian lattices, a generalization of Noetherian rings to lattice theory. Their central equivalence states that a ring is S-Noetherian exactly when its ideal lattice is S-Noetherian in the lattice sense. They also prove a Cohen-Kaplansky type theorem. It characterizes S-Noetherian lattices by the compactness of their S-prime elements. Finally, they introduce S-primary elements, proving that S-primary decomposition exists and is unique in this setting.
arxiv-2604-26258: Yu, Young-Bum Kim, and Yoon Kim tackled the hand-built bottleneck in LLM workflows, chains of calls to language models that pursue a goal together. They framed workflow design as bilevel optimization: an outer loop shapes the overall sketch, while an inner loop tunes each call one by one. Both loops learn from textual gradients passed layer by layer. The discovered workflows matched strong baselines built by hand or by machine.
arxiv-2604-26758: Kumar and twelve colleagues study uneven magnetism and field changes in orthorhombic TbAlGe crystals. The compound is a topological rare-earth compound with the highest ordering temperature in its series. With one rare-earth site in three-way layout, it shows antiferromagnetic changes at 40 and 8 kelvin in zero field. Metamagnetic changes cascade only for fields along the a-axis. Resistivity, magnetization, heat capacity, and transport data up to fields over 41 tesla map the magnetic phase diagram and tie local 4f magnetism to roaming topology.
arxiv-2604-26858: Üsten and three colleagues replace the fixed desired walking speed in crowd models with a motivation that shifts over time. Grounded in expectancy-value psychology, each agent's drive responds to closeness to the goal, position among neighbors, and how much the goal matters. That drive jointly steers speed, gap-closing, and spacing. Tested in simulated waits before a bottleneck and against concert-entry data, the dynamic model reproduces the real pattern of front agents taking less space, which a static baseline misses.
arxiv-2604-27058: Chase and Labib introduce Clifft, an open-source simulator for exact classical runs of fault-tolerant quantum circuits. It shifts the dominant exponential cost from total qubit count to a dynamic active subspace, factoring the state into an offline Clifford frame, an online Pauli frame, and a sized active vector. Costs then track peak active virtual dimension, growing on non-Clifford steps and shrinking on measurement. Clifft nears standard tools in pure limits while beating GPU near-Clifford simulators by orders of magnitude on low-magic benchmarks.
arxiv-2604-27358: Sun proposes Safe Bilevel Delegation, a framework for runtime hand-off when language model agents pass subtasks to subagents. Hand-off becomes a bilevel problem: a network learns safety-efficiency weights, while an inner loop tunes policy under a safety rule that holds with high probability. A hand-off degree slides between human override and autonomous execution. Sun proves safety monotonicity, inner-policy convergence, and an accountability bound across chains. He specifies datasets, baselines, and test plans for medical AI, financial risk control, and tutoring, with tests still planned.
arxiv-2604-27558: Hirvi and three colleagues extend Monte Carlo methods to compute frequency- and time-domain Jacobians for optical tomography. They are sensitivity maps, and methods for both domain versions were incomplete. Their approach derives them in a perturbation Monte Carlo framework, built in the MCX simulator and checked against the diffusion approximation in neonatal head models. Monte Carlo and diffusion agree well only in high-scattering regimes, showing Monte Carlo's value for low-scattering tissue.
arxiv-2604-27658: Battestini and five colleagues develop a model for particle therapy effects, extending the GSM2 model beyond Poisson assumptions. The model extends GSM2's damage stage to larger scales, covering cell groups with set shape and working layout. Its single-cell detail covers energy dose, tissue variety, organ volume effects, cell types, and oxygen gradients across beam types, strengths, and LET values. The work shows how physics and surroundings interact in healthy-tissue side effects, and highlights chemical variety in tumor response.
arxiv-2604-27858: Vu and Saito prove a universal limit on resetting a physical system, a task the third law of thermodynamics already bars from reaching absolute zero in finite steps. They link the error of any classical or quantum reset map to its geometric complexity, a measure folding in time, energy and control effort. Perfect resetting would therefore demand unbounded complexity, a bound holding across both classical and quantum regimes.
arxiv-2604-28058: Li and colleagues design multilayer grating couplers that move several independent waves from free space onto a chip, respecting real foundry rules. Minimum feature size proves the dominant constraint, and forcing robustness to over- and under-etching also steadies efficiency against other fabrication flaws. Larger features cost only moderate efficiency, leaving simple scaling laws for layer counts and thicknesses intact.
arxiv-2605-00158:
Jaewon Jeong, Pan-Yang Su, S. Shankar Sastry, and Anil Aswani study how to pay an agent whose effort cannot be watched. Their setting is a linear control system with noise, where an agent picks one of two controllers. One controller costs the agent more to run than the other.

The team designs a payment rule that makes the agent choose the controller that best serves the system's goals. They frame the design as a constrained optimization problem under risk aversion. For a payment made at a set time, the best rule sets the amount by a likelihood ratio test, a standard statistical check. They show the scheme at work on power grid frequency control and on body weight programs.
arxiv-2605-00558:
Argianto Rahartomo, AmirHossein Jamshidipoor, and Mohammad Ghafari propose a graphical password scheme built on a simple ritual: pick and sort. Instead of typing a secret, the user chooses visual elements and arranges them inside a grid. The number of chosen elements and the size of the grid are configurable, and the pictures can be tailored to particular groups, such as children.

A preliminary study with a prototype found the scheme easy to learn and flexible to deploy. Logging in takes longer than with conventional methods, since the interaction itself is the password. The authors argue that cost can be acceptable where speed is not critical: for services used only rarely, or as a secondary authentication step guarding a primary one. The work contributes a design and an early usability read, rather than a full security evaluation.
arxiv-2605-00958:
Bob Osano develops a mid-scale formulation of equilibrium statistical mechanics, working between the small-scale and bulk levels. The build starts from coarse-grained occupation-number sectors of one-particle phase space. A mid-scale partition function is built by averaging the small-scale Hamiltonian over all set-ups that fit a given occupation profile, for both spatial and phase-space cells.

In the fine-graining limit, the build converges to the canonical Gibbs partition function, and it stays compatible with interacting many-body systems. Osano shows thermodynamic extensivity is equal to asymptotic factorisation of the mid-scale partition function, while leftover links between cells generate smaller corrections. The formalism offers a mathematically consistent bridge between small-scale Gibbs theory and mid-scale thermodynamics.
arxiv-2605-01158:
Jacob Morrison and two co-authors provide a detailed breakdown of the environmental cost of a full language model development pipeline, beyond pretraining alone. Green reporting usually focuses on training one final model. Their case covers it through supervised fine-tuning, preference optimization, and reinforcement learning for the Olmo 3 family, in instruction-following and reasoning variants at two sizes.

Those models are far more expensive to post-train than tuned counterparts, driven by reinforcement learning rollout generation. Project work including experiments, failed runs, and ablations accounts for the large majority of total compute. Total estimated energy, emissions, and water use are reported, with water driven by power production rather than cooling. The authors call for fuller disclosure standards.
arxiv-2605-01258:
Hyunho Cha, Chae-Yeun Park, and Jungwoo Lee study how to squeeze quantum states through a narrow bottleneck and rebuild them with the least possible loss. Quantum autoencoders do this squeezing, and the question is how wide the circuits must be to hit the best possible score.

One extreme uses narrow but limited circuits, and the other uses fully general maps that can do anything but carry too many parts. The team prove a middle path always works. For any spread of pure states, an encoder with a set number of extra qubits can match the best score any general pair can reach. That count is also shown to be a hard floor for some sources. On the rebuild side, simple isometric decoders are best for several clean cases, but one clear counterexample shows they do not always suffice, though tests suggest the gap is tiny in practice.
arxiv-2605-01658:
Sergey A Denisov disproves the strong form of a conjecture in nonlinear harmonic analysis. The setting is the Dirac equation with a square-summable potential, a model where waves scatter off a background that fades at infinity. The objects under study are its Jost solutions, the waves with clean behavior far away.

Denisov studies the transmission coefficient, which records how much of a wave gets through, and builds a maximal function from the argument of that coefficient. He proves the maximal function is unbounded. That failure carries the headline: the strong version of the nonlinear Carleson conjecture does not hold, for Dirac equations and for the Krein systems tied to them. Counterexamples of this kind redraw the map of what estimates analysts can hope to prove in nonlinear scattering.
arxiv-2605-01958:
Rami Atar studies many interacting Brownian particles on a half-line, where interaction happens only when particles hit the boundary at zero. Each particle moves randomly, reflects at the origin, and feels pushes from the boundary time of the others. For a fixed set of interaction weights, the system forms a reflected Brownian motion in the positive orthant.

Atar first treats the uniform case, where every pair shares the same weight. Global well-posedness holds when that weight stays above a threshold. He then proves propagation of chaos, meaning particles become nearly independent as their number grows, with a limiting nonlinear reflected process. Part of the uniform range was known before, and the paper extends it.
arxiv-2605-02058:
Nadia Khoury and Pierre-Emmanuel Jabin give quantitative rates for the mean-field limit of interacting particle systems. As particle number grows, the system should approach a mean-field description, and the question is how fast marginals and correlations converge. Their framework uses duality and a hierarchy of dual cumulants tied to the particle dynamics.

For second-order Vlasov systems with pairwise forces that are only square-integrable, they first derive the natural fluctuation-scale rate. An iterative argument on the hierarchy then improves that to the optimal mean-field rate and gives robust bounds on dual cumulants, at the cost of stronger smoothness on the force. Those bounds transfer to direct cumulants, refining knowledge of correlations and departures from independence.
arxiv-2605-02158:
Aaron Lutheran, Srijan Das, and Alireza Tabarraei generate near-optimal material layouts for structures with a diffusion transformer, avoiding repeated physics solves. Classic topology methods, such as SIMP, run a finite element analysis at every step, which makes large or real-time design costly. Their model learns to produce a layout directly from the problem statement.

Conditioning comes in two forms. Stress and strain fields are fed in as spatial maps, while scalar facts such as load position, load size, and target volume share enter through adaptive normalisation. Training used thirty thousand two-dimensional structures optimised by SIMP. Results in the paper compare the generated layouts with physics-based designs for accuracy and speed.
arxiv-2605-02358:
Sarvagya Somvanshi, Mohan Xu, Rakhi Chadalavada, and Nathan Canera predict which Reddit posts will go viral by adding real-world trend signals to post features. Past models lean on static text and structure, ignoring how outside attention shifts over time. The authors ask whether exogenous signals can add predictive power beyond the post itself.

Their model, ViralityNet, fuses title and body embeddings, structural metadata, and learned subreddit embeddings. A temporal cross-attention block queries a daily sliding-window matrix of trend terms, built from the strongest Wikipedia pageview spikes in preceding days. A post counts as viral if it passes the ninetieth percentile of engagement for its subreddit and a minimum score. The design tests trend timing as a virality signal.
arxiv-2605-02658:
Xiayang Li, Kuo Gai, and Shihua Zhang explain, with evolutionary game theory, why deep networks learn shortcuts. Shortcut learning means a model leans on easy, non-essential traits in the data instead of the real signal. Its roots in training dynamics lacked a formal account, which this paper supplies by defining core and shortcut features precisely.

Data samples are cast as players, and their neural tangent features as strategies, with core and shortcut subnetworks assumed to exist. Plain gradient descent and its stochastic form settle into different stable states: the first mainly trains the shortcut subnetwork, the second the core one. A continuous stochastic equation then traces how data noise and optimization noise shape shortcut bias. The theory offers a principled view of how to reduce the bias.
arxiv-2605-02758:
Chupao Lin and ten co-authors report the first integrated electro-optic modulator for ultraviolet light on a thin-film lithium tantalate platform. Fast UV modulation matters for quantum information work, portable atomic clocks, and secure communications that use sunlight-blind channels. Visible and infrared platforms are mature, but UV modulation has stayed with bulky crystals.

A compact lumped-electrode design reaches a record-low voltage-length figure at a near-UV wavelength, a gain of up to four orders of magnitude over bulk devices on that measure. The chip also shows strong light extinction, low insertion loss, and a small footprint with short electrodes. Measured bandwidth was limited by the test detector, and the authors argue the design itself supports far higher speeds.
arxiv-2605-02958:
Xulin Hu and four co-authors trace how a language model's refusal to comply is built up inside the network, and use that trace to detect jailbreak attempts. Standard analysis reads refusal from a single static direction in the final layers. Attacks can suppress that end signal, which raises the question of whether the refusal process leaves earlier marks that survive.

Causal tracing finds a sparse upstream activation pattern, a refusal trajectory, that often persists even when the final signal is suppressed. Their detector works on raw hidden states from a chosen layer window, with no heavy machinery. Across three model families it improved detection on several attack types at a fixed operating point. Tests against adaptive attacks and encoded inputs map where the method holds and where it thins. Trajectory monitoring is promising, not settled.
arxiv-2605-03158:
Benjamin M. Ampel and Sagar Samtani release HackerSignal, a large dataset linking hacker forum talk to the full life cycle of software vulnerabilities. Threat analysts need to connect early chatter, exploits, advisories, and fixes, but those records usually sit in separate silos.

The set holds millions of deduplicated documents from dozens of sources across eight layers and more than three decades, linked by shared CVE identifiers. Three benchmark tasks are shown: cross-source linkage, exploit type classification, and forward-in-time generalization with disjoint vulnerabilities. Leakage checks, audit packets, and governance notes ship with the release for careful use.
arxiv-2605-03758:
Zihong Cheng and Fa Peng Huang study whether dark matter could have been produced by bubble collisions during a first-order phase transition at the end of inflation. The transition happens in a spectator scalar sector whose potential depends on the inflaton, so bubbles form faster as inflation ends. The authors first map where vacuum decay is led by the Coleman-De Luccia channel and the transition completes.

In the viable regime, elastic self-scatterings spread the spectator particles' momenta efficiently, while their decay into dark matter is the main channel moving the population into the dark sector. The final abundance combines direct production in bubble collisions with later decays of spectator particles. Competing number-changing processes stay too slow compared with cosmic expansion.
arxiv-2605-03858:
Jaeyun Lee and four co-authors introduce MCJudgeBench, a benchmark for judging language model judges on multi-constraint instructions, constraint by constraint. Judges are usually scored on whole responses, yet real instructions bundle several demands that can each pass, partly pass, or fail. Each benchmark instance pairs an instruction and a candidate response. It adds an explicit constraint list and per-constraint gold labels.

Controlled perturbations of responses and variants of the prompt let the protocol separate two kinds of inconsistency. One is intrinsic, under stochastic decoding. The other is procedural, under prompt changes. Across proprietary and open-source judges, strong overall scores did not guarantee sound detection of the rarer partial and negative cases, and higher correctness did not always mean lower inconsistency. Reasoning improved correctness but not stability across the board.
arxiv-2605-03958:
J. Sumaya-Martinez proposes a Fisher-informational reformulation of physical time, in which clock time is not a fundamental substance but an emergent calibration of how distinguishable physical states become along a causal order. Clocks, on this view, do not measure time itself; they are reproducible processes whose distinguishable states correlate with other events. The framework defines a causal-informational parameter as a summed Fisher-geometric distance along a trajectory in state space.

In classical systems the parameter comes from the Fisher information metric; in quantum systems it uses quantum Fisher information with the Bures and Fubini-Study geometries. The manuscript distinguishes model-dependent from quantum Fisher information. It clarifies how Schrödinger dynamics gets recast. It gives examples including a qubit clock and a decay process, and a Fisher-based measure of clock quality.
arxiv-2605-04158:
Rohit Ghosh and four co-authors show that analogue gravity effects in fluids that accrete are not an artifact of the linear theory. Analogue gravity uses fluid flows to mimic spacetime geometry. Here the system is spherical accretion onto compact objects. The fluid has a relativistic, mixed equation of state. Its adiabatic index varies with position. The authors extend the acoustic metric into the nonlinear, higher-order regime.

They show the perturbations obey a covariant wave equation. The equation lives in an effective acoustic spacetime with nonlinear corrections. That makes the analogue geometry move rather than stay fixed. So the acoustic horizon can shift inward or outward. The shift depends on how large the swings in density, temperature, and mass accretion rate are. The result gives a truer framework for studying such spacetimes in such flows.
arxiv-2605-04358:
Zhenhan Huang and three co-authors propose a search-based method for spotting images made by generative artificial intelligence. Photorealistic fakes raise misuse concerns, yet trained detectors are costly and often fail on new kinds of data, while training-free methods have been weaker.

Their method looks inside a model's intermediate layers and compares how an image's internal representation changes when the image is slightly perturbed. Real and generated images react differently, and that gap drives the detection. On two broad benchmarks the method beat both trained and training-free rivals, with the largest average gain on the harder forensic set.
arxiv-2605-04458:
Bryan Li and eight co-authors automate a tedious step in evaluating long, citation-backed reports produced by retrieval-augmented systems. Evaluators break a topic into small nuggets of required information, often written as question-answer pairs, but building those sets by hand scales poorly, especially across languages.

Their pipeline generates nugget sets in three stages, grounding each question in the source documents so the answer is attested in the collection. Separating the question from its possible answers allows finer scoring of what a report covers. The work aims to make report evaluation reusable for new topics and multilingual collections.
arxiv-2605-04658:
Wei Cheng and Jiahui Hong survey a framework that unifies gradient flow ideas with Hamiltonian dynamics. It is used to study Hamilton-Jacobi equations. Those equations are central to mechanics and control. The survey emphasises how singularities travel through solutions and connects the theory to weak KAM theory, optimal transport, and mean field control.

Beyond reviewing known results, the authors construct generalised special curves. They use a minimising movement scheme. They then pass to a weak limit using Young measures. They also lift the dynamics of strict singular curves to a flow on trajectory space. They prove its only steady measures at the critical value are exactly the projected Mather measures. That is a new dynamical description.
arxiv-2605-04958:
Federica Fieramosca and four co-authors test fast computer simulation of indoor Wi-Fi signals as a way to locate people without asking them to carry a device. Human bodies disturb radio waves, and those disturbances can reveal position. Measuring real rooms for every design is costly, so a trustworthy simulation baseline would help planning.

Their compact full-wave setup produces maps of received signal strength and checks the patterns against controlled settings. The maps reproduced the main spatial features and interference structure, though simple material descriptions left some gaps. The authors propose diffraction-aware refinements and present the approach as a pre-measurement reference for designing device-free sensing systems.
arxiv-2605-05158:
P Taylor-Burdett and five co-authors present a device for switching a permanent magnet's field on and off with very low power and very low noise. Many experiments need magnetic fields that are both ultra-stable and switchable. Wires are switchable but noisy, while existing ways to switch permanent magnets need large pulses and waste power, especially at high switching rates.

Their Saturable Electronic Reluctance Switch routes the magnet's flux through a nonlinear ferromagnetic circuit. The field ramps smoothly with current up to a threshold, then holds constant, shielding stability from current noise and avoiding demagnetisation. The authors expect far lower power per switching cycle than existing approaches, plus robustness to fabrication errors.
arxiv-2605-05758:
Biomedical researchers lean on specialized tools daily; language models mostly cannot use them. Xin Gao and four co-authors build BioTool, a dataset for teaching models to call biomedical tools properly. Earlier efforts relied on prompting tricks and a handful of tools, which caps what an agent can actually do in a lab workflow.

BioTool covers 34 frequently used tools gathered from real research practice, with examples formatted for fine-tuning. Training on it should move models from describing procedures to executing them through the right tool with the right arguments. The dataset is meant to close the gap between general-purpose tool use and specialist biomedical practice.
arxiv-2605-05858:
Simulating how magnetization evolves carries a constraint: its length must never change. Changjian Xie compares two numerical schemes for the continuity-equation form, asking whether an extra projection step is needed at all. Its own structure keeps the length fixed, since the motion is always at right angles to the magnetization.

Xie discretizes the equation and tests an implicit Gauss-Seidel method against a semi-implicit backward scheme. The test checks accuracy and whether the constraint survives in practice. The study answers a practical coding question: enforce the constraint by projection, or trust its geometry.
arxiv-2605-05958:
Peilin Zhan and four co-authors work on knowledge tracing, the task of estimating what a student has mastered over time. Learning logs are not random samples, since exercises are recommended and chosen in biased ways. Most tracing methods ignore that bias, so their mastery estimates skew and errors feed into later recommendations.

The team build a doubly robust method that joins a propensity model with an error imputation model. It stays unbiased if either part is right, a classic strength of that design. They then show that estimator variance builds up over a learning sequence and destabilizes training. A temporal smoothness term controls that variance in their framework, and tests on real benchmarks show gains across several tracing backbones.
arxiv-2605-06158:
Zhengchunmin Dai and seven co-authors study backdoor attacks that stretch across many sessions of a language model agent. A multi step attack may need chances that appear in different sessions, such as access to target data or the right tool. To exploit them, the attack must keep state, store partial results, and branch on current conditions like a small program.

The authors model such attack programs as Mealy machines and build a sub backdoor for each transition. Training trajectories for the parts are combined so one fine tuned model learns all local behaviors, linked later through persistent memory. Across four models, complete programs succeeded at high rates in two agent environments. The results show end to end cross session attack programs are feasible, a risk defenders must plan for.
arxiv-2605-06658:
Weiqing Xiao and nine co-authors present Relit-LiVE, a framework that relights videos under new illumination without needing camera poses. Neural relighting usually decomposes a video into intrinsic scene parts first, but that decomposition is unreliable on real footage and errors pile up as distorted materials and flicker. Their key move is feeding raw reference images directly into the rendering process.

A single diffusion process jointly generates the relit video and per-frame environment maps aligned to each viewpoint, enforcing consistency between geometry and lighting. That supports moving lights and cameras naturally. Experiments beat leading relighting and neural rendering methods on synthetic and real benchmarks, with uses in material editing and object insertion.
arxiv-2605-06858:
Jose Falla and Ilya Safro add counterdiabatic driving to quantum portfolio optimization. The Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm searches for good portfolios, but real budget and risk constraints tangle the search. Their constrained variant builds its ansatz from approximate gauge potentials. These come from nested commutators between the portfolio problem Hamiltonian and a mixer that preserves total weight.

Tests compare the approach against standard mixer, Grover mixer, and penalty-based versions of the algorithm. At fixed circuit depth, the counterdiabatic version steadily achieves better ratios under the constraints. The work suggests shortcut ideas from adiabatic control can buy optimization quality without deeper quantum circuits.
arxiv-2605-07158:
Junseon Yoo audits a core assumption behind scientific search tools: that embedding similarity reflects real relatedness. He built an expanded citation graph over millions of papers and split it into sub-fields and finer research agendas. Four leading embedding models were then tested on whether their nearest neighbors share those groupings.

The models did reasonably at the broad sub-field level but failed at the agenda level, where most retrieved papers were off-agenda. The failure appeared across eight domains and all models. A simple citation-count reranking recovered much of the missed signal, suggesting embeddings miss agenda-level structure that citation graphs carry, a concrete warning for scientific retrieval systems.
arxiv-2605-07258:
M. Kohno and H. Kamada calculate low-energy scattering between a Xi particle and a deuteron using the Faddeev three-body equations. Three candidate descriptions of the Xi-nucleon interaction are tested, one from chiral theory and two from lattice-based HAL-QCD calculations. Phase shifts are reported for two spin states of the combined system.

From the three-body wave functions, the authors compute momentum correlation functions that experiments can measure. Deuteron breakup matters strongly in one spin channel, which earlier treatments could miss. Differences between the calculated correlation functions reveal how strongly the candidate interactions differ, so future experimental data could help pin down the true Xi-nucleon force.
arxiv-2605-07758:
Tiago Ferreira and two co-authors learn weighted automata, using an SMT solver as the engine. Weighted automata assign weights from a semiring to strings, and classic learning algorithms in the Hankel or L-star style are fragile in practice. Their algorithm is built around the semiring and, when it terminates, is certain to return a minimal one.

They prove partial correctness and give a termination condition that covers all finite semirings in particular. In many experiments the learner recovered many minimal machines over finite and infinite semirings. It vastly outperformed a naive baseline. It also stayed competitive with a state-of-the-art algorithm while producing much smaller automata and asking the teacher fewer queries.
arxiv-2605-07858:
Jad Koleilat gives differential linear logic, a proof system that builds in differentiation through links between linear and non-linear formulas, a new categorical semantics. Models of the logic are stated as a pair of Grothendieck fibrations with a tangent functor. They draw methods from the categorical semantics of type theory and fit them to linear-non-linear adjunctions.

The paper is clear about its scope: this fibrational view is a first step toward joining differential linear logic with dependent types. Framing it through tangent structure on fibrations is what makes that joining plausible.
arxiv-2605-07958:
Aaron Gobeyn and two co-authors extend the standard model for superconducting layered coatings used in radio-frequency cavities. The established Kubo model covered superconductor-insulator-superconductor stacks; accelerator builders now stack arbitrary sequences of superconducting, normal, and insulating layers, with losses and dielectric effects that the old model omitted.

The extended model handles any layer sequence and counts all parts, including ohmic losses and dielectric effects. For repeated two-layer structures, the single-repeat setup gives the highest usable field, though those layers can be thinned below the depth fields reach at minor cost. Transition regions between layers are modeled with virtual blended layers, and thicker transitions degrade the peak field. A surface impedance form plugs the model into finite element simulations.
arxiv-2605-08158:
Haopeng Jin, Wenlong Zhao, Tao Yu, Tiankun Yang, and coauthors present HIMMEL, a framework for understanding long videos with multimodal language models. Long video is expensive three ways: decoding dense frames costs heavily, token counts grow with frames, and sparse keyframes miss motion.

HIMMEL splits the work. A few semantic anchor frames go to the costly vision transformer to fix identity and layout. The dense intervals between them are handled by a light adapter that reads compressed-domain signals directly: motion-vector maps, residual maps, and an intra-frame context branch. Motion evidence is gathered without decoding every frame, so long videos become cheaper to process while keeping their movement information.
arxiv-2605-08258:
John deVadoss lays out a design-first architecture for intelligent agents in large firms. Enterprise interest has moved on from generic software agents. It now centers on language model agents that plan and call tools. They keep memory, check their own work, and sometimes write into systems of record. Governance matters, he argues. But it cannot be the organizing idea.

The CEAD reference architecture starts from agent design itself. It covers capability boundaries and how autonomy is split. It covers interaction protocols and authority over tools and data. It also covers memory design, verification, and the human interface. It borrows contracts and registries from service-oriented design. It rejects governance as the primary abstraction.
arxiv-2605-08458:
Jakeb Chouinard examines which radial basis kernels a brain-like representation can build. Spatial semantic pointers encode continuous space in distributed neural activity. Radial basis functions respond by distance from a center. They are the natural currency for merging physical and perceptual information into one space.

Chouinard characterizes the common radial basis kernels that fit the pointer framework. He checks earlier work based on grid cell-like codes. Those codes are the periodic neurons known from navigation research. The analysis shows grid-style representations can realize radial basis kernels. More than that, they are optimal for the job. The result links a neuroscience motif to a machine learning staple.
arxiv-2605-08558:
Muyun Lu, Haoyang Hong, Huazheng Wang, and Ying Lin study decision problems where cheap rough tests can improve with use. Classic multi fidelity bandits assume the gap between rough and exact feedback stays fixed, yet simulators and language model judges get better when calibrated. Their work focuses on two feedback levels where the cheap source grows more informative over time.

Their algorithm, TACC, uses an optimistic rule to decide when cheap sampling still pays and when to switch to exact checks. Theory shows real savings for middling options, and tests on synthetic tasks plus a model judging task probe when continuing cheap trials helps. Experiment design gains guidance for budgets that mix practice runs with costly truth.
arxiv-2605-08658:
Jiang and two colleagues ask how a practitioner stuck with a small, cheap code model should spend extra test time. Their answer, SketchVerify, is a cost performance rule for one model tier, not a universal accuracy improvement. The model lists distinct algorithmic strategies, drafts a partial program sketch for each strategy, and fills each sketch several times.

That yields diverse candidates checked by running them and grouped by fingerprint clustering. Each new sketch explores a different algorithm by design, while each new flat sample likely repeats an existing one. On the hard subset where Lite greedy fails, Lite Sketch with two sketches and five fills recovers 11 of 19 problems, against 5 of 19 for flat sampling. Flat sampling still loses even at roughly triple the budget, while sketching still wins. Across tiers, upgrading still beats sketching: Pro greedy dominates Lite Sketch on pass rate and dollar cost.
arxiv-2605-08758:
Jiaxin Liu, Peng Yang, Yuping Li, and Xinyue Xie coordinate warehouse robots that shuttle totes instead of pallets, a shift driven by online shopping and small batch production. Orders, totes, and robots must be decided in sequence, yet past methods fit one system only. Their OLSF-TRS framework joins structured combinatorial optimization with multi agent reinforcement learning into one general, scalable decision scheme.

On small systems it lands within a few percent of optimal across two layouts. At large scale it beats heuristic rivals, cutting tote movements clearly against strong rule based methods while answering in real time. Warehouse operators gain lower cost, energy use, and steadier throughput from one transferable framework.
arxiv-2605-08858:
Piotr Borycki and four coauthors explain image classifier decisions with prototypes, the this looks like that style of explanation, without needing any of the original data.
