Half and full blinks are recognized indicators of pain and stress, but as micro-expressions they are easily missed by the naked eye and require frame-by-frame video inspection.

The team developed and evaluated three methods on a publicly available dataset. They are a frame-based YOLOv12 object detector, an optical-flow thresholding approach that tracks motion between frames, and a fine-tuned VideoMAE model that reads video clips directly. Their best results reached a macro-F1 score of 0.898 on the harder task of classifying blink type and 0.926 on binary blink detection. A human baseline study underlined why automation matters: even human observers agreed only 73 percent of the time on half-blink labels.
arxiv-2606-05658:
Maharjan, Kaur, and Molyet compare agent-style search pipelines on two contrasting tasks in a 2026 arXiv paper. Search-augmented generation grounds model answers in fetched documents. Standard pipelines fetch once with the raw query, which falters on tangled questions. Their framework splits queries into parts, fetches in rounds, and reflects on results within a bounded loop. Two testbeds check the design: a DevOps knowledge base and a multi-hop reasoning set.

Query splitting gave steady gains on the structured DevOps data, lifting both overall score and ranking quality. On the multi-hop benchmark the same move hurt ranking precision instead. The reflection loop improved citation accuracy but cost substantial response time. Gains in one setting became losses in the other. The authors argue for cost-aware control that turns agentic steps on only where they pay. Uniformly aggressive pipelines, they conclude, waste effort and can even backfire.
arxiv-2606-06058:
Salmani-Zarchi, Rahimi, Faili, and Dousti diagnose why a reinforcement learning method wobbles on instructions in a 2026 arXiv paper. Multi-constraint requests, exact endings, casing rules, word counts, suit verifiable rewards. Yet group-relative policy optimization destabilizes when rewards are discrete and groups score alike. The authors formalize three pathologies of z-score normalization: zero-variance collapse, mean-centering blindness, and low-variance amplification.

MDP-GRPO answers with four stabilizers. Multi-temperature sampling spreads rewards out. Dual-anchor advantages restore gradients when a group is homogeneous. Prospect-theoretic shaping, borrowed from Kahneman and Tversky, bounds updates and punishes violations asymmetrically. An asymmetric KL term completes the package. On FollowBench, IFEval, and a curated set, strict constraint satisfaction improved by up to five points on a Llama model. Training stayed stable with small groups, and abilities held on standard benchmarks. Careful advantage bookkeeping, not bigger models, fixed the instability.
arxiv-2606-06158:
Kevin Dave and co-authors present a cheaper way to compress video for machine use in this 2026 arXiv paper. Video tokenisation turns frames into tokens, compact units that later models process. Adaptive methods spend tokens where a scene changes and save them where it stays still, but many need extra decoder passes or learned estimators to decide. The authors show the needed signal is already visible inside a frozen continuous tokeniser.

Positions whose internal representation barely changes between frames carry almost no new information, so a fixed threshold on that change drops them with no learned allocation network at all. Static scenes then compress steeply while busy scenes keep more tokens, and the rate follows the content itself. A small transformer, LIT, paints the dropped positions back in from those kept. On TokenBench and DAVIS, the method matched continuous-regime rivals at equal keep rates with much lower inference cost.
arxiv-2606-06258:
Shenwei Huang, Yiao Ju, and Yidong Zhou push a famous graph conjecture to two new cases in this 2026 arXiv paper. The Erdős Hajnal conjecture says that any graph avoiding one fixed pattern as an induced subgraph must contain a large clique or independent set. A clique is a set of vertices all joined to each other, while an independent set has no edges at all. The conjecture was recently proved for the five vertex path.

They prove it for two larger patterns built from that path and from the bull graph. One adds a pendant edge to the middle of the path, forming the E graph. The other adds a pendant edge to one horn of the bull. Their proof generalizes the iterative sparsification framework behind the path result, and extends the older Chudnovsky and Safra theorem on the bull.
arxiv-2606-06458:
Alexander Möllers and co-authors teach a model to learn classification tasks from a handful of examples in this 2026 arXiv paper. Multiple instance learning trains on bags of items with only a bag level label, common in pathology slides and satellite images. Labels are scarce in exactly those fields, and ordinary models either overfit or cannot adapt. Their answer is in context learning: pretrain once, then solve new tasks in a single forward pass.

The learner, built on a Perceiver style architecture, was pretrained entirely on synthetic bag data. The team designed several data generators, each encoding a different bias about how bags relate to labels. A model trained on a mixture of the generators inherited their separate strengths. Across twelve multiple instance benchmarks in the low label regime, it achieved the best average ranking, beating supervised baselines that needed task specific training for every problem.
arxiv-2606-06658:
Bhargav Sriram Siddani and co-authors give coarse grained physics a memory in this 2026 arXiv paper. Simulating every particle in a fluid is costly. Modelers instead use stochastic equations for the density, like the Dean Kawasaki equation. Those equations are Markovian, memoryless, and Gaussian. They miss short time behavior and sparse regimes where real systems remember their recent past. The authors learn the distribution of fluxes directly from particle data with flow matching, a generative technique.

Their test case is the Kramers first passage problem, timing how long Brownian particles take to escape. The learned model captured the short time dynamics accurately. It predicted the density's statistical moments better than the Markovian baseline, including higher order statistics at early times. Predictions drift at later times, a limitation the authors state plainly.
arxiv-2606-06958:
Before birth, doctors watch the fluid spaces inside a baby's brain for dangerous swelling. Sayem automates one key measurement in this 2026 arXiv paper. The condition is fetal ventriculomegaly, enlargement of the lateral ventricle. Clinicians judge it by atrial width, measured from ultrasound images.

His network, MVSegNet, first outlines the ventricle, then estimates that width. Manual measurement varies between observers, so consistency matters. Ultrasound also fights back with shadowing, speckle, and weak contrast. The model pairs multi scale feature extraction with boundary aware refinement. It trained on five hundred eighty four expert labeled frames. Against six rival segmenters, it won on boundary and measurement scores. Its overlap score reached about eighty one percent. Width error averaged about three point four millimeters. The model is small, with about two point three million parameters, and runs very fast.
arxiv-2606-07158:
Defenders name attacker groups by their habits, but AI attackers may not keep steady habits. Francesco Balassone and a large team test that idea in this 2026 arXiv paper. Their AI agents posed as five famous state linked hacking groups, including APT28 and Lazarus. They attacked two defended test networks, one business style and one military.

A binary pattern emerged across twenty experiments. All ten enterprise attacks ended in compromise. All ten military experiments were defended or stalled, whatever the persona. In eight enterprise cases, attackers independently turned the defender's own endpoint platform into their control channel. That trick appeared in no threat intelligence profile. Yet checks against official profiles still matched the fake attack chains with fifty five to eighty percent precision. The personas mimicked state tradecraft well enough to fool attribution. If machines can wear any group's fingerprint, habit based attribution collapses.
arxiv-2606-07458:
Israeli and co-authors observe collective light emission from disordered solid-state atom arrays, against expectations, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Quantum metasurfaces made of subwavelength atomic arrays promise strong light-matter interaction for quantum devices. Solid-state emitters were thought unfit here because inhomogeneous broadening, the spread of emitters' frequencies, exceeds their natural linewidth hugely and should destroy the photon-mediated cooperation behind emission. The team used silicon-vacancy centers in diamond, whose broadening is about 100 times the natural linewidth.

Collective effects survived: resonance shifts, changed decay rates, and coherent emission all appeared. The trick was placing many silicon ions at each array site, creating superatoms, local groups where some emitters match across the array and amplify the response. Theory explains how cooperation survives the disorder. The authors argue the result opens subwavelength emitter arrays to any solid-state platform, easing use with nanophotonic devices.
arxiv-2606-07658:
Cepeda and co-authors tackle brain shift, the movement of brain tissue during surgery that makes pre-operative scans misleading, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Their setting is glioma surgery, where removing as much tumour as safely possible improves survival, yet navigation maps drift once the skull is opened. Operating-room MRI can correct the drift but is rare and costly, while ultrasound is cheap and repeatable.

The pipeline turns intra-operative ultrasound into a synthetic MRI, then uses that image to anchor a deformable registration, a warping that aligns the old scan with the patient's current anatomy. In fourteen patients scored against two hundred fifteen expert landmarks, the anchored warping cut mean alignment error from about six point three millimetres to about five point nine. The real gain is the updated whole-brain volume itself, which shows the resection cavity that registration alone cannot represent.
arxiv-2606-07958:
Xin Peng and co-authors rank three candidate shapes for early-universe inflation energy, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Inflation models give the inflaton field a potential energy curve. The simplest family is monomial, rising as a power of the field: quadratic, cubic, or quartic. In cold inflation these are squeezed by the observed limit on gravitational waves. Warm inflation, where the inflaton leaks energy into radiation, relaxes that squeeze differently per power.

The team computes a Bayesian evidence score for each power. They solve the warm background equations with radiation back-reaction and integrate over the parameter ranges. With fifty-five e-folds, the quartic potential wins clearly. The quadratic branch is disfavoured by about thirty-two log-evidence units, a crushing margin, and the cubic by about seven. If low-temperature warm inflation with this dissipation law is right, the data already point strongly to the quartic shape.
arxiv-2606-08458:
Gonzalez, Shovo, and Ayub design a household robot that predicts what its human needs next, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Proactive assistance requires predicting human activities and object usage under noisy conditions. People move things, pets wander through, toddlers rearrange the home. Existing approaches often rely on complex spatio-temporal models that are expensive and sensitive to this noise. Their framework, GLOBE, instead pairs a lightweight statistical predictor with a large language model consulted only when needed.

The predictor is an n-gram Markov model, which forecasts the next activity from recent activity sequences, running efficiently on the robot. Uncertainty guides the language model's involvement. When confidence is low, the model reasons about the situation. When high, the cheap predictor acts alone. To test robustness, the authors introduce HOMER-Noise, a noisy extension of a household dataset simulating disturbances such as objects moved by humans, pets, and toddlers.
arxiv-2606-08558:
Yingcheng Li and Zou construct a universal theory of an exotic phase of matter from measurable ingredients, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Symmetry-enriched topological quantum spin liquids are phases where spins refuse to order conventionally. They form a liquid with topological order, patterns of long-range entanglement, enriched by symmetries.  The authors present exactly that: a microscopic universal theory for these phases in two spatial dimensions.

The theory is deliberately general. It covers Abelian and non-Abelian phases, chiral and non-chiral ones, internal and lattice symmetries, unitary and anti-unitary symmetries, discrete and continuous ones, with or without spin-orbit coupling. The input is concrete: microscopic states containing anyons, the exotic quasiparticles of the phase, plus operators and symmetry actions. The output is a set of data characterizing the universal properties.
arxiv-2606-08658:
Hila surveys how formal knowledge structures meet neural embeddings, and proposes a hybrid future, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Ontologies and knowledge graphs model knowledge explicitly, with named concepts and relations that support crisp logical inference, but they are brittle and hand-built. Dense embeddings, the vector representations behind large language models, capture similarity and context probabilistically but lack explicit, inspectable structure. The paper reviews the ways ontologies and knowledge graphs have been integrated with dense embedding algorithms.

Hila proposes a new frontier: knowledge representation systems that accommodate both kinds of inference in the same representation. The proposal is neuro-quantum-fuzzy systems, which combine neural learning, fuzzy logic's graded truth values, and quantum-neural networks whose contextual behavior models how meaning shifts with context. The paper is a position and survey piece, arguing that the probabilistic-crisp trade-off is a limitation of current representation choices.
arxiv-2606-08758:
Dentelski tests whether a neural quantum decoder's confidence can be trusted like a classical score, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Quantum error correction requires a decoder to infer the logical state of protected information from error syndromes. Beyond a hard decision, some decoders give soft information estimating reliability of the call. For the standard matching decoder, a common confidence measure is the complementary gap, the cost difference between the chosen correction and the best alternative. Dentelski asks whether a graph neural network decoder's output logit can serve as a learned proxy for that gap.

Using a pretrained graph network for the rotated surface code under circuit-level noise, the study compares the network's output with the matching decoder's gap. Post-selection on the network's confidence yields a lower logical error rate than post-selection on the classical gap here. The network assigns higher confidence to many correctly decoded shots.
arxiv-2606-09158:
Junnila, Laihonen, Lehtilä, and Padavu Devaraj count exactly how many strings lie in several error balls at once, in this 2026 arXiv paper. A Hamming ball collects strings within a set number of substitutions of a center, over an alphabet of size q. Intersecting balls matters for DNA data storage and the Levenshtein reconstruction problem, recovering a stored string from noisy copies. Center distances alone were known not to determine the size.

They derive an exact formula for the intersection size of any number of Hamming balls, any radii. It reveals which center properties determine the size. Asymptotics for long strings follow. For 3 balls they give necessary and sufficient conditions, every alphabet size at least 2 except 6, long strings, for the maximum intersection size at a given minimum center distance. The maximum is computable from the formula. The q equals 6 exception is a real arithmetic obstruction: the 3-ball characterization is complete.
arxiv-2606-09558:
Mikele Milia and his co-authors build known gene regulation into a Transformer model for single-cell data in this 2026 arXiv paper. Single-cell RNA sequencing records which genes are active in each cell. Most models treat genes as lone features, so the model must learn all links from data alone. Known biology says which regulator genes switch which target genes on or off.

Their model, scTransformer, limits attention flow to paths that match those known links. Attention is the step where the model weighs links between features. The team tested it on disease-linked single-nucleus data, sorting cells by type. Accuracy reached about ninety-one percent, close to the ninety-two percent of a free-form model. With just one percent of the training data, the guided model won clearly. Its chosen gene sets also stayed far more stable across repeat runs.
arxiv-2606-09658:
Tianyu Ruan and his co-authors ask whether the Muon optimizer teaches models better internal features than Adam in this 2026 arXiv paper. Optimizers steer training by setting each update step. Muon, which reshapes gradient matrices, trains big models fast. Its speed edge is known, but whether its features are better was not.

The team tested models trained each way on bent inputs: smudged images and warped text. Muon-trained models held up best across image nets and transformers alike. Probes on each layer showed wider logit margins, a sign of firmer class splits. When the features were reused on fresh tasks, Muon again won, by direct transfer and by full fine-tuning. Hidden states from Muon models also spanned more directions, a trait called effective rank. A toy proof in a clean setting backs both edges.
arxiv-2606-09758:
Quinn Pfeifer and his co-authors fix a weak spot of learning by copying, without new data or expert help in this 2026 arXiv paper. Behavior cloning trains a robot policy on expert demos, then drops the data at run time. Small slips then pile up, pushing the robot into states the demos never showed. Their DARP method keeps the data in play.

At each step, DARP fetches the nearest demo states to the live one. It feeds the model those states, their actions, and the gap vectors between them and the live state. The policy thus reads local structure, not a blunt global map. No fresh demos, feedback, or task tricks are needed. Gains over plain cloning ran from fifteen to forty-six percent. The wins spanned control tasks and arm work, and held for rich image inputs as well.
arxiv-2606-10158:
Balloli and colleagues explore what different stakeholders need before trusting AI tools for pregnancy-related information, in a 2026 arXiv paper on human-computer interaction and health. AI systems increasingly promise to fill information gaps in maternal health, where timely, accurate guidance matters and preventable deaths show stark racial disparities in the United States. The study centers those social questions instead.

The team ran four synchronous focus groups with twenty-four participants spanning birthing people, clinicians, and health workers such as doulas, social workers, and community health workers. Discussions covered information seeking, experiences with current clinical infrastructure, misinformation, and reactions to an AI factual answering tool used as a design probe. The title question, asking where an answer comes from, captures the trustworthiness ideals participants voiced. Findings aim to guide AI peripartum tools that respect how trust is actually built among the groups who support pregnancy care.
arxiv-2606-10258:
Wang and his team extend a background-removal technique so researchers can test whether tiny collision systems create quark-gluon plasma, in a 2026 arXiv paper on nuclear physics. In particle correlations, collective flow signals the plasma, while nonflow, links from other sources, contaminate the signal. Their method extends the subtraction to multi-particle cumulants, built on how nonflow scales with multiplicity in a many-source picture.

Correlators with the dipolar flow component serve as clean nonflow estimators, since its total value nearly vanishes. Using a nonflow-only test setting as ground truth, they test the subtraction on three targets in oxygen-oxygen and deuteron-gold collisions at two energies. Most nonflow is removed, with residual fractions usually within twenty to thirty percent when mapped to the two-particle level, though the best measure differs by target. The method pushes genuine collectivity tests into the smallest collision systems.
arxiv-2606-10458:
Xu studies a design question in signal processing in this 2026 arXiv paper: how should a quantizer be built when its output must follow a distribution chosen in advance? Quantization squeezes a continuous value into one of a few allowed labels, how signals are stored and sent digitally. Designers usually only minimise distortion, the average error between a value and its label. Here the labels must also appear with specified frequencies, for compression, channels, and privacy.

Xu derives the optimal quantizer and shows it has an explicit form built from cumulative distribution functions, curves tracking how probability accumulates. The best labelling is found by choosing a permutation of the output labels, and the proof leans on majorization, a way of comparing how spread out distributions are. When either the input or the required output is uniform, the optimal rule simplifies to one direct mapping, a closed answer where search is usual.
arxiv-2606-10758:
Cristian-Teodor Neamtu and colleagues trace synthetic speech back to its maker in this 2026 arXiv paper on audio forensics. Detecting fake audio is half the forensic problem; investigators want to know which text-to-speech system made it, including systems never seen in training. The framework learns an embedding space with proxy-anchor metric learning over Wav2Vec2-BERT representations, so samples from one system cluster tightly while unknown systems fall away from every cluster. An architecture-merging step groups system versions into unified classes, cutting confusion between near-identical generators.

On the MLAAD v9 benchmark, spanning 140 systems in 51 languages, attribution accuracy reaches 99.76 percent across 110 classes, and unknown systems are flagged with a false positive rate of 2.04 percent. On the MLAAD v5 splits it doubles the best prior out-of-distribution accuracy and cuts the false alarm rate. Well-clustered embeddings serve attribution and rejection at once.
arxiv-2606-10858:
Fjeldstad, Bueie, and de Wijn rework kinetic theory for dense fluids in this 2026 arXiv paper. Chapman-Enskog theory predicts transport properties such as shear viscosity, but its extensions lean on effective hard-sphere diameters that fit poorly for soft, long-range forces. The authors build a framework around an exchange function tied to the fluid's thermodynamics, and show two existing extensions fit inside it.

Their alternative adds the potential interaction energy that modified Enskog theory omits. Tested on simulated Weeks-Chandler-Anderson and Lennard-Jones fluids across wide density and temperature ranges, mean prediction errors stay between 2 and 4 percent at low and middle densities. The worst cases reach 4.4 percent and 8.1 percent for the two fluids.
arxiv-2606-10958:
Khalatbari investigates the hidden life of graphics cards in this 2026 arXiv paper. Over four years the author combined social science with hands-on research-creation: dismantling, dissolving, rebuilding, and remixing some fifty acquired graphics cards. Fieldwork reached liquid-nitrogen overclockers in Taiwan and urban miners in Ghana, two ends of the same device's world.

Miniaturization, the paper argues, is what lets AI look abstract and placeless, hiding rare metals, assembly labor, and the communities that inherit the waste. Taking cards apart made those material ties tangible in ways reading could not. The work presents making itself as a rigorous way of knowing, aimed at ICT sustainability.
arxiv-2606-11358:
Pandit and Koranga expose a hidden systematic error in neutrino physics in a 2026 arXiv paper. Long-baseline analyses often treat Earth matter effects with a constant-density approximation. Using exact propagation through realistic PREM density profiles, they show this mismodeling does not merely shift the standard appearance probability. It generates correlated biases across all oscillation channels at once, as PMNS unitarity dictates.

Their stochastic analysis finds the muon-to-tau neutrino channel is the most volatile carrier of the geophysical error. At baselines like 5,000 and 7,000 kilometers, the tau channel always carries larger mean bias and variance than the electron appearance channel. Below roughly 4,000 kilometers the CP bias is negligible, under one degree, but grows sharply beyond. A multi-channel joint fit does not help, since the coherent errors favor the same wrong CP minimum. They conclude spatially resolved density treatments are a necessity for future precision facilities.
arxiv-2606-11858:
Yiwen Zhang and four colleagues speed up control of virtually coupled trains in this 2026 arXiv paper. Virtual coupling lets trains run close together, coordinated by radio rather than physical links, raising line capacity. The controller must track a target speed profile while respecting comfort limits and guaranteeing no collisions, all in real time, which makes ordinary predictive control expensive.

Their approach lifts the curved train dynamics into a Koopman space, a transformed space where the dynamics become nearly linear, using closed-form observable functions. Freezing the lifted predictor along the predicted path turns each control step into a quadratic program, a fast standard problem. Safety terms involving squared speed are lifted along with the dynamics. In a simulated two-train metro scenario, the desired gap is nine metres on a line just over two kilometres long. There the method matches a conventional controller's tracking while cutting online computation time substantially.
arxiv-2606-11958:
Di Yang, Jiayi Zhao and Jian Zhou revisit classical formulas for random matrices in this 2026 arXiv paper. Hermitian matrix models are a backbone of random matrix theory, used from nuclear physics to combinatorics. Their connected correlation functions, which describe how eigenvalues at several points fluctuate together, admit determinantal formulas built from a kernel. The authors give a direct proof of those determinantal formulas for connected multi-point functions.

They also supply a new proof that these functions are integrable in the sense of the KP hierarchy. From that viewpoint they re-derive the explicit formula for the affine coordinates encoding the model. Duality for certain hermitian matrix models is proved as well. A concrete dividend appears in the examples: generating functions match classical path-counting sequences, including Dyck, Motzkin and Schröder paths and Catalan numbers. Conjectures in earlier literature about those identifications are now theorems.
arxiv-2606-12058:
Itay Lavie leads a six-author team explaining why attention circuits appear suddenly during training in this 2026 arXiv paper. Induction heads, the transformer circuits that copy patterns from context, underpin in-context learning, and their key component emerges abruptly. The authors build a Bayesian theory of this feature learning.

They study a single-layer softmax attention network trained on a copy task and derive a closed-form posterior over the attention matrix. Reducing it to a low-dimensional order parameter space reveals a genuine phase transition in the amount of training data. Both Bayesian sampling and standard training with the Adam optimiser confirm the transition. The comparison with linear attention is sharp. Softmax attention shows a first-order transition, an abrupt jump, while linear attention crosses a second-order transition and then evolves smoothly. The work gives a first-principles account of abrupt circuit emergence in language models.
arxiv-2606-12158:
C. Gatto and a large collaboration lay out the physics case for REDTOP, a proposed particle experiment, in this 2026 arXiv paper. REDTOP would mass-produce eta mesons, short-lived particles whose decays are tightly constrained by symmetry rules. Rare or forbidden decays would expose physics beyond the Standard Model, the current theory of particles and forces. Earlier experiments gathered about a billion etas. REDTOP aims for about 100 trillion etas, plus about a trillion of the heavier eta-prime partner.

That flood of decays powers two hunts at once. First, light dark matter in the MeV-to-GeV mass range, reached through all four known portals linking our sector to a hidden one. Second, discrete symmetry violations, tiny breaks in rules like charge-parity symmetry that decays can reveal. Its sensitivity matches or beats collider searches in this range, improving key conservation-law limits by orders of magnitude.
arxiv-2606-12658:
Bisht and Agarwal benchmark physics-informed neural networks for chemotherapy drug tracking in this 2026 arXiv paper. Pharmacokinetics studies how a drug's concentration changes over time. Blood plasma levels are easy to measure, but tissue levels, which drive tumour killing and side effects, usually are not. A physics-informed network must obey the known equations of motion while learning, unlike a plain network fitted only to data.

On a standard two-compartment problem, the network matches the clinical estimator and reconstructs the hidden tissue curve, which a data-only network misses by about tenfold. On a harder problem with saturable elimination, where the drug-clearing machinery can be overwhelmed, the clinical formula silently returns meaningless constants. The network instead reveals that the model cannot be identified from plasma alone, and adding two sparse tissue measurements restores most parameters to near their true values.
arxiv-2606-12858:
Wu and colleagues propose Joint Source-Channel-Generation Coding, a generative communication paradigm that swaps the standard decoder with a generative model at the receiver, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Standard systems are built under Shannon's rate-distortion theory, which tunes a generic error metric. Such metrics miss visual perception, so outputs come out blurred or unreal, notably at low rates or in noisy channels.

In the scheme, the received signal is treated as a condition controlling a sampling process from a conditional distribution. This turns communication from deterministic reconstruction for distortion minimisation to controlled generation for mutual information maximisation under perceptual constraints. The authors build a joint training and stochastic sampling framework around this idea, with analysis of both the learning and inference stages. They note a distinct error behaviour: failures appear as semantic mismatch, content that looks plausible but means something distinct, rather than as error.
arxiv-2606-13158:
Castelli and Massazza compute the counting sequence of Z-convex polyominoes by area, extending it further than previously known, in this 2026 arXiv paper. A polyomino is a set of unit squares. Its degree of convexity is the number of direction changes needed for a monotone path inside it to join any 2 of its cells. Z-convex polyominoes are the convex polyominoes of degree at most 2, named for the Z-shaped paths that suffice. Counting polyominoes by area is a hard problem in combinatorial geometry, so restricted classes with tractable enumeration are valuable.

A recent combinatorial approach showed Z-convex polyominoes can be counted by area in polynomial time. By changing some of that approach's combinatorial decompositions, the authors obtain a set of recurrence equations and formulas that can be implemented efficiently. Their C++ program computes the number of Z-convex polyominoes of every area up to n equals 75.
arxiv-2606-13558:
Zhang and colleagues present BitResEdit in this 2026 arXiv paper, a training-free editor for autoregressive generators. Editing an image from an instruction requires controlling what the model samples and where the change lands in the image's code. Editors for these generators work on token streams, features, or output scores, ignoring two structures. One is the per-bit prediction head, which scores each bit of the code. The other is the multi-scale residual code from which the image is assembled. BitResEdit exploits both.

One component tilts the per-bit odds along a contrast between source and target descriptions. Each update stays inside a trust region around the sampler. The other converts the bits into residuals at all scales, gates them with a localisation mask, and reinjects them into generation. They aim for edits strong where the instruction points and absent elsewhere. The method targets bitwise-residual generators such as Infinity.
arxiv-2606-13758:
Ibarra and McQuillan characterise a class of automata with a pushdown store in this 2026 arXiv paper, a republication of a journal article. Pushdown automata read input while using a stack, the last-in-first-out memory that lets them recognise nested structure such as matched parentheses. Finite-turn machines bound how often the stack can switch between pushing and popping. The authors give characterisations of finite-turn pushdown automata in terms of multi-tape finite automata, which have no stack but several input tapes. They extend the characterisation to machines augmented with reversal-bounded counters, counters that change direction only finitely often.

They then use the characterisations to pin down the complexity of the languages they accept. languages of finite-turn machines with reversal-bounded counters lie in a small space class, solvable with logarithmic memory. Such theorems convert questions about one machine model into questions about another.
arxiv-2606-14058:
Zhang's team benchmarks a question driving simulators rarely face: do simulated road users react sensibly when the test vehicle misbehaves? Reactive capability means surrounding agents respond well when the vehicle's behavior departs from the recorded log. Existing benchmarks control all vehicles together and grade by similarity to the log. Their 2026 arXiv paper, ReactSim-Bench, decouples the two: the vehicle follows deviated behaviors while agents respond on their own.

Deviated behaviors come from a planner model, filtered by rules and manual checks, yielding two thousand six hundred thirty-six scenarios in three categories. Scoring uses collision, map-based, and kinematic metrics. Leading models of several architectures, Transformer, diffusion, and next-token prediction, were evaluated. A case study shows the failure mode: when the vehicle merged early, one model slowed too little and collided, another replayed the log and collided, while a third braked in time. Replanning frequency effects are analyzed too.
arxiv-2606-14258:
Piersanti develops a 2026 arXiv mathematical model of grounded shallow ice sheets, broad ice masses resting on land rather than floating. The model couples two changing quantities: the thickness of the ice and its internal temperature, each subject to physical limits. The governing equations are degenerate, meaning they lose their usual form in places, and the temperature evolves inside a domain that itself moves.

The author first builds the model formally, borrowing ideas from diffuse-interface methods that blur sharp boundaries into smooth transition zones. Then, using a penalty method that enforces the constraints approximately, he proves that solutions exist for one version of the model. He notes plainly that the problem's low regularity blocks any standard notion of solution, so the existence result uses a weaker solution concept.
arxiv-2606-14658:
Villavicencio-Garduño and co-authors attack camera-based AI with sound in a 2026 arXiv paper. Acoustic vibration can physically shake a camera and disturb its internal stabilization, pushing the system outside its design conditions. The stabilizer then introduces artifacts into the frame, and vision models misclassify, miss targets, or hallucinate objects that are not there.

Earlier attacks used ultrasound above twenty kilohertz, which fades quickly and limits range. This team instead probes lower, audible frequencies below twenty kilohertz. In physical experiments they resonated a commercial camera at various frequencies and fed the distorted video to an off-the-shelf object detector, YOLO11. Their results show the attacks are viable and identify which image and object features suffer most, informing future defenses for vision systems in vehicles, recognition, and security cameras.
arxiv-2606-14758:
Bilgiç and co-authors explain why explanation maps for vision-language models hallucinate in a 2026 arXiv paper. Explainability tools highlight the image regions behind a model's answer. But they often highlight a big object even when the text prompt names something else. A dog may light up for the prompt cat. That semantic hallucination undermines trust in safety-critical uses.

The authors prove the effect is not one design's quirk. It is a basic outcome of linear semantic leakage in high-dimensional embedding spaces. They build one scheme covering the main explanation methods. Their fix, orthogonal semantic projection, turns the query vector away from distractor concepts. It uses a leftover trait from matching pursuit. The map goes blind to shared features while staying true for right prompts. Theory and tests show the fix cuts hallucination.
arxiv-2606-14858:
Erneta develops a regularity theory for fully nonlinear oblique transmission problems in a 2026 study. Transmission problems describe systems split into two phases, each governed by its own partial differential equation. The two sides meet at a flat interface, where a coupling rule links the full gradient from each side. Earlier work coupled only the normal derivative, so the slanted coupling treated here is more general.

Erneta proves that viscosity solutions, a weak solution concept for such equations, stay piecewise smooth up to the interface. For constant-coefficient equations the solutions reach the best regularity possible on each side of the boundary. The result also extends to equations whose coefficients vary, within a narrower class of solutions. Such results matter because transmission models arise in layered materials, regime-switching economics, and living tissue. Knowing that solutions remain smooth at the boundary makes those models safer to use in computer work.
arxiv-2606-14958:
El Assadi and coauthors release MVEB, a benchmark for video embedding models, in a 2026 study. Embeddings turn video into vectors that support search, grouping, and question answering. Older benchmarks test one skill at a time, so a strong score may hide narrow ability. MVEB instead curates twenty-three tasks from a larger pool of one hundred eighty-four.

The tasks span classification, zero-shot classification, clustering, pair classification, retrieval, and video question answering. The team evaluates thirty-three models across the main embedding paradigms. No single model dominates the whole suite. Models based on multimodal language models lead on classification, clustering, and question answering, while binding models lead on retrieval. Generative models without contrastive training collapse on cross-modal tasks. Paired tests also show audio helps when dataset labels came from both sound and vision, but hurts when labels came from vision alone.
arxiv-2606-15258:
Zhang and coauthors build Mask-Proof, a 2026 pipeline that turns mathematical proofs into graded exercises. Judging a model's proof ability usually means checking final answers or paying experts to grade steps. Mask-Proof instead hides a key formula step inside a proof. The model must reconstruct the missing step from the surrounding context. An LLM-based judge then scores the reconstruction, voting to stabilize its verdict. The pipeline produced a benchmark of two hundred ninety-two problems.

The tasks span thirty-five mathematical fields, from research papers and competition sources. Shortcut-solvable items are filtered out during curation. Seventeen models were evaluated on the benchmark. Reasoning-enhanced models beat standard models by twelve to twenty-seven percent. The judge agreed with expert annotators about ninety-seven percent of the time. That agreement makes proof skill measurable at scale, reproducibly. The authors release the benchmark, annotations, and code for reuse.
arxiv-2606-15558:
Zhang and Chen settle a question in quantum error correction that had stood open for nearly three decades: can degeneracy evade the quantum Hamming bound? The bound is the sphere-packing limit on exact correction of arbitrary qubit errors. Degenerate codes break the usual proof, because distinct correctable errors can act identically on the code space, so error spheres need not be disjoint.

The pair prove that every exact binary quantum subspace code with more than one codeword obeys the bound, with no assumptions of nondegeneracy or additivity. Their argument turns a known linear-programming polynomial into an exact count of intersections between quaternary Hamming balls. Monotonicity in block length and centre separation then reduces everything to a local charging inequality at the shortest length. Degeneracy can merge correctable error sectors but cannot enlarge the bound. The ideas may transfer to other finite-length bounds where degeneracy blocks packing arguments.
arxiv-2606-15858:
Mederski and Zeng prove the existence of ground state solutions for the Born-Infeld-Choquard problem in 2026, a nonlocal equation. Born-Infeld theory caps field strength so a point charge carries finite energy. Its operator is the mean curvature operator of Lorentz-Minkowski space, coupled to a Choquard-type nonlocal term. A relativistic gradient constraint, the gradient never exceeding one in size, makes the energy functional non-smooth, blocking classical variational methods.

The authors build a non-smooth critical point theory on a Pohožaev-type manifold and use it to establish ground states. The abstract theorem is reusable: it also handles strongly indefinite problems. The solutions are radially symmetric and decay monotonically to zero at infinity. Ground states are the lowest-energy states, the natural first candidates for stability analysis. Extending such machinery to this setting widens the class of field equations analysts can attack.
arxiv-2606-15958:
Jackson's lecture notes on quantum measurement and Markov processes, given at Perimeter in late 2025, build the theory of diffusive instruments. Such readings gather data weakly and continuously, so the system evolves as a random process rather than a single collapse. The course builds the tools from scratch: Gaussian Kraus maps, Wiener increments and the Itô rules, Lindblad terms, and the Fokker-Planck-Kolmogorov equation.

Five worked examples carry it: von Neumann measurement, heterodyne and homodyne detection, Barchielli's joint position-momentum case, and the isotropic spin case. The lectures open with a detour through the planimeter, a mechanical area-measurer whose motions embody the Weyl-Heisenberg group. They close on noncommuting quantities measured jointly, where Markov and central-limit results justify the diffusive limit. Problems and recordings make the notes a self-contained entry into the field.
arxiv-2606-16058:
Touloumis proposes a penalized method in 2026 for correlated yes-or-no outcomes, such as repeated patient responses. Generalized estimating equations, or GEE, give population-wide effects for such clustered binary data. Ordinary GEE can break down under separation, where a predictor nearly splits the outcomes perfectly. Small, sparse, or rare-event samples then produce extreme estimates, or fail to converge at all.

The framework adds a Jeffreys-prior penalty, a standard steadying penalty, to GEE while expressing association through marginalized odds ratios. Odds ratios avoid a trap of correlation parameters, whose allowed range shrinks as fitted chances near zero or one. The penalty strength is tunable, with one half as the default. Under working independence, the method reduces to a known penalized likelihood fit with finite estimates. The goal is sound results in the small samples where ordinary GEE is most fragile.
arxiv-2606-16358:
Xie and co-authors expose in 2026 a quiet risk in how AI agents reach language models: the API router in the middle sees everything in plaintext. A router ends the client's secure session and opens its own upstream one, making it an application-layer man-in-the-middle. A malicious router could rewrite agent tool calls, swap dependencies for typosquatted packages, fire attacks only when audits are unlikely, or copy secrets.

Their system, Aegis, seals the router with attested trusted execution environments, hardware enclaves the host cannot peek into. Plaintext handling is confined to a small enclave component, while authentication, scheduling, and accounting stay on the untrusted host. Clients verify the enclave before releasing any plaintext, which can leave only toward destinations fixed by the verified software image. All four attack classes succeed against a plaintext-access baseline router and are blocked by Aegis, including adaptive attacks.
arxiv-2606-16458:
Elmaaroufi and co-authors let coding agents design robot policies in 2026, searching at training time so the deployed robot needs no model calls. Code-as-Policies systems have language models write robot code from perception, planning, and control primitives, but multi-turn generation loops are too slow for real-time control. Their paradigm, Robotics Harness Optimization, has coding agents propose and evolve multi-file policy repositories instead of single functions.

Search runs on reflective feedback from environment reward and execution traces, not human demonstrations. On pick-and-place tasks in LIBERO-PRO, where OpenVLA scores 0 percent and a leading vision-language-action model averages under 13 percent, RHO reaches 45 percent success. That is two and a half times the strongest multi-turn agentic system. On Robosuite it sets a record of 70 percent. Deployment is single-turn: the repository runs as code, with no model in the control loop.
arxiv-2606-16658:
Jain and colleagues test vision-language models as annotation tools for pathology slides in a 2026 study. The first step in slide analysis is foreground segmentation, marking tissue and ignoring empty background. Older tools use hand-tuned rules or trained models that fail quietly on unusual stains, such as Jones silver used for kidney samples.

Their coarse-to-fine method treats tissue detection as a general visual task, not a specialist medical one. Large models trained on broad image collections are asked to judge slides with no task-specific labels. On a new benchmark of renal transplant slides, the method scores best on unfamiliar stains and varies far less across stain types than the best trained rival. Few-shot prompts rescue hard cases in a stress test set. Model review also matches human expert consensus closely, and the labels train small student models that keep quality at lower cost.
arxiv-2606-16758:
Dognini examines the Cass criterion in a 2026 economic theory paper on overlapping generations economies. In such economies each generation trades with the next, and some outcomes waste resources forever. The Cass criterion is an infinite sum test on prices and consumption that checks whether an outcome is efficient.

The paper first defines deep projections of two basic surfaces of consumer theory, the indifference surface and the offer surface. These measure how far the flat trade plane must be bent to reach each surface. One positive factor, built from a multiplier and a utility derivative, captures how much more curved the offer surface is. Using this geometry in a consumption-loan economy gives broad statements on when the Cass test is needed and when it suffices. The results allow unbounded population and endowment paths, and they show the criterion is local in nature.
arxiv-2606-16958:
Mihaila, Skýpalová and Kozák propose a light-based phase plate for electron microscopes in a 2026 optics paper. Electron lenses suffer spherical aberration, blurring probes especially at wide angles, and compact correctors for continuous beams are scarce. Their design corrects the aberration with light rather than extra electron optics.

Inside a near-concentric optical cavity, a standing wave in a vortex-shaped Laguerre-Gaussian mode presses on passing electrons through the ponderomotive force, a push from intense light. The ring-shaped phase shift it imprints has the opposite sign to a normal lens's third-order spherical aberration. For a modest-energy beam at a wide angle, the calculation shows full compensation of a typical lens's aberration, leaving an atom-scale probe width. The reachable phase patterns are limited to what the cavity's modes can form, but the needed vortex mode survives the central hole the beam requires.
arxiv-2606-17058:
Changqing Li and colleagues evaluate language model coding agents on scientific compression kernels in a 2026 computing paper. The SZ family does error-bounded lossy compression: numerically delicate, memory-hungry, control-flow-heavy code. Agents are asked to port and optimize two CUDA kernels for two very different machines.

The targets are NVIDIA graphics processors and Cerebras wafer-scale accelerators, which run a spatial, processing-element-centric model. Results diverge sharply by architecture. On graphics processors, stronger models reach much higher throughput but grow sensitive to prompt precision and guidance. On Cerebras hardware, the hard part is producing runnable programs at all, and models that excel on GPUs can fail outright. Kernel structure matters too: agents improve the modular kernel reliably; the tightly coupled bit-level pipeline resists them. The lesson: judging coding agents for supercomputing must weigh throughput, robustness and failure modes together, not correctness alone.
arxiv-2606-17358:
Lee and colleagues present a 2026 arXiv paper on a privacy hole in language model serving: the tokenizer running on the processor side of a confidential computing setup. Tokenizers turn prompts into tokens through table lookups, and the memory access pattern leaks which lookups happened. Recent work recovered whole user prompts from that pattern on production hardware, yet the standard oblivious memory defence slows tokenization by more than ten times, inflating time to first token noticeably.

Their design, OTRO, builds on square-root oblivious RAM, which is fast per lookup but costly to rebuild at set intervals. Three ideas tame that cost: replicated instances exploiting the read-only tokenizer table, epoch rotation with dummy accesses, and chunked tokenization overlapping rebuilds with GPU work. In tests the added delay stayed small, memory overhead stayed modest, and leakage shrank across model families.
arxiv-2606-17458:
Li and colleagues present a 2026 arXiv paper introducing ICBCBench, a benchmark for deep research agents working in finance, built by an industry consortium. Deep research agents plan, retrieve, reason, and write analyst-style reports, yet existing benchmarks test only closed questions or only open reports. Neither alone captures the retrieval accuracy and end-to-end report quality that real financial workflows demand from such systems before firms can trust them with consequential research tasks.

More than fifty experts from over forty organisations, spanning banks, funds, and universities, helped build the benchmark. A dual-track design joins objective tasks with checkable answers to judged long-form reports scored for expert alignment and citation quality. Tests of leading research agents and language models exposed substantial gaps in complex reasoning and factual grounding. Report quality also lagged industry level, the authors report across the board.
arxiv-2606-17658:
Magar and colleagues present a 2026 arXiv paper on the ground state of a chromium phosphate compound whose spins sit on a distorted triangular lattice, a classic setting for frustrated magnetism. Triangular arrangements prevent all neighbours from aligning against each other at once, and unequal couplings along the triangle's sides reshape the physics. The team grew and measured the material with diffraction, magnetisation, heat capacity, and phosphorus nuclear magnetic resonance, backed by band structure calculations of the exchange paths.

Susceptibility peaks broadly at a few kelvin, signalling short-range order, before true long-range order sets in slightly lower. A spin-flop jump appears at modest field, and saturation follows at a few tesla, as expected for an anisotropic two-dimensional magnet. Resonance spectra confirm the ordered state is commensurate with the lattice. Calculations show one side of each triangle couples far more weakly than the other two.
arxiv-2606-17858:
Hayashi and colleagues turn machine learning back on itself in a 2026 paper, asking whether trained models can be sorted into classes automatically. They focus on one-class classification models, which learn what normal data looks like, since most models can be approximated in that form. Their idea is to represent each such model by the normality ranking it assigns, a kind of fingerprint of its behavior.

Classification then compares those fingerprints with nearest neighbor matching and ranking correlation measures. Experiments show the method sorts models by their training dataset with high accuracy, and it can even tell algorithms apart when datasets share a class. The authors note this makes model sorting largely a form of dataset sorting, and they demonstrate that side on sleep records, proposing one unified tool for models, datasets, and rankings.
arxiv-2606-18058:
Thong and colleagues rebuild protein shapes directly from cryo-electron microscopy images, working from coarse detail to fine, in a 2026 paper. Cryo-EM freezes molecules and images them in huge numbers, but recovering an atomic model from noisy, low-contrast pictures is a hard inverse problem. Their algorithm represents the protein backbone explicitly, through its bonds, bond angles, and torsion angles, which pours strong prior knowledge into the recovery.

Refinement proceeds across scales, settling large structure before fine detail, which steers the fit away from bad local minima. On three datasets produced by a digital twin of an electron microscope, the multiscale method beat single-scale fitting. It won on standard accuracy scores against ground truth, and stayed robust when the imaging model was misspecified. The explicit backbone keeps costs low, since not every atom pair interaction needs modeling.
arxiv-2606-18358:
Tannous and colleagues present an all-reflective design for a field-widened interferometer in a 2026 optics paper aimed at quantum sensing and communication. Such instruments let time-bin encoded light signals interfere even when a beam arrives distorted, as on turbulent free-space or satellite links, without the heavy correction hardware that adaptive optics demands.

Their design builds its imaging system only from mirrors, pairing a spherical concave mirror with a flat one in a compact folded cavity. That choice keeps the device free of color distortion and small enough for resource-limited platforms. In tests the interferometer reached interference visibility above ninety-seven percent for spatially multimode beams, well into the range needed for time-bin qubits. The authors argue the folded layout can also give long path delays in a much smaller footprint.
arxiv-2606-18758:
Jahanbazi and the team adapt federated learning to networks of devices that live off harvested energy, in a 2026 wireless communications paper. Federated learning trains a shared model across edge devices, without pooling their data. But in energy-harvesting Internet-of-Things deployments, stochastic energy arrivals make device participation intermittent, and communication costly. The averaging algorithm gains an error floor, and unstable training, under partial participation.

Their method EH-FedSAG is a server-memory variance-reduced scheme, in the spirit of the SAGA incremental gradient algorithm. It was tested against the energy-harvesting version of the standard baseline, in a unified simulation. That simulation captures battery charging, compute, and transmission costs, across varied energy-arrival chances. EH-FedSAG reached higher test accuracy throughout, with much lower training variance. That held in both homogeneous and heterogeneous data settings. Its edge grew more pronounced when energy was scarce, and data did not match.
arxiv-2606-18858:
Razanajatovo, Cayssol, and Dutreix show how to rebuild the full quantum state of electrons in a material, from the interference patterns around single impurities, in a 2026 condensed matter paper. A band structure is known through energy levels, wave functions, and quantum shape. That shape is held in the quantum geometric tensor. Local probes have struggled to resolve it orbital by orbital.

The team studies two-orbital models on a honeycomb lattice. For on-site impurities, backscattering between time-reversed states maps the density matrix's populations and coherences into distinct orbital contributions. Those appear within quasiparticle interference maps, measured by scanning tunneling microscopy. The contributions transform under different symmetry forms, so they can be pulled apart even with a conventional unpolarized tip. That reveals the density matrix and the quantum geometric tensor of the scattering states. The result turns plain impurities into tomographic probes of band structure.
arxiv-2606-18958:
Wan and colleagues present LiveStack in 2026, a way to simulate a whole cluster of computers before real use. Such tests must run the full, unchanged software stack true to life. They must also run fast enough to try many setups. Past tools model single parts well but fail on the full stack. Tools that stitch parts together are held back by their slowest part.

LiveStack builds on the Linux stack for virtual machines. It has four parts for scheduling, memory, message passing, and control of the whole run. Together they keep real and modeled parts on one shared clock. They also limit how hosts on one machine disturb each other. Tests on database and data jobs show good fidelity and clear speed gains. The authors argue that control of such tests should sit in the core of the system, not in add-on tools.
arxiv-2606-19058:
Lindenschmitt and colleagues propose an atomic handover method for nomadic non-public networks in future 6G systems in 2026. Such networks are mobile and fast to deploy, for uses like emergency response or short events. When such a network moves across unlike infrastructures, both its attachment and its spectrum access may need to change at once. Handling those two changes apart risks drops in service at the worst moment.

Their zero-touch design joins mobility control with dynamic spectrum coordination in a single step. An edge-based spectrum broker works with a cognitive spectrum manager to pick the new network and assign spectrum together. The idea is tested in a MATLAB simulation of a mobile health case. An ambulance carrying its own network moves between public and non-public networks. An atomic handover of this kind could keep critical links seamless while the unit is on the move.
arxiv-2606-19358:
Ma and colleagues introduce WorkBenchMark in 2026, a LEGO-based assembly benchmark for the Smart Manufacturing League. Robotic assembly couples low-level handling with task-level planning under physical constraints. End-to-end learning methods do not yet solve that combination reliably.

The benchmark provides hundreds of tasks across four tiers, built from LEGO Duplo parts. A simulation environment supports development. The team also gives an open baseline that assembles by disassembly, combining language-guided sensing, constraint-based planning, and collision-aware motion. It is tested against zero-shot and fine-tuned vision-language-action baselines on tasks from every tier. The baseline achieves higher success and accuracy across all tiers. Its edge is largest on long-horizon builds. The benchmark gives manufacturing robotics a shared, physical yardstick.
arxiv-2606-20258:
Simon Aagaard Enni, Malthe Stavning Erslev, Karl-Emil Kjær Bilstrup, and Kristoffer Laigaard Nielbo study how public knowledge institutions can keep editorial control when language models mediate access to their collections. Their 2026 paper starts from a worry. Pretrained models arrive already aligned with their developers' values, quietly absorbing the editorial function that encyclopedias exist to perform. The authors ran design workshops with editors at a Nordic public knowledge institution.

Together they designed and built an LLM-enabled encyclopedia interface shaped by editorial standards. The team names this practice editorial alignment: treating the editorial standard as a design artifact that translates newsroom values into alignment objectives for builders. Framing alignment as participatory design, rather than a one-time technical fix, keeps editors in the loop as the system evolves.
arxiv-2606-20358:
Fubin Yan and Kenneth Shum formalize the extended complex plane, Möbius transformations, and the cross ratio in the Lean 4 theorem prover. Their 2026 paper builds the Riemann sphere inside Mathlib. It uses the Option type over the complex numbers, where the extra element plays the point at infinity. On that foundation they define Möbius transformations and their action on the plane. They then prove the basic theory: the transformations form a group, identified with a projective general linear group.

Two landmark facts are verified. A Möbius transformation is uniquely fixed by where it sends any three distinct points, and the cross ratio is invariant under every such transformation. The development runs to roughly six thousand lines of Lean, with about forty definitions and one hundred fifty lemmas. Formalizing this core of complex analysis gives future work a verified base for conformal geometry, hyperbolic models, and modular forms.
arxiv-2606-20458:
Zhenghao Peng and four colleagues pair a slow vision-language model with a fast learned planner for sidewalk robots. Their 2026 paper names the failure they target the trajectory scoring gap. Planners generate good candidate paths in real time but pick bad ones, steering onto grass, toward pedestrians, or the wrong way.

Rather than replacing the planner end-to-end, a vision-language model supplies the high-level scene understanding the scoring function lacks. The fast planner keeps proposing trajectories at full rate while the slower model re-scores them with semantic judgment. The design aims to keep latency low enough for real urban navigation. Better selection among existing candidates may beat generating fancier ones.
arxiv-2606-20558:
The CMS Collaboration reports the first evidence for electroweak production of Z boson pairs with two jets at 13 TeV. The 2026 analysis uses 138 inverse femtobarns of proton-proton collision data. The signal channel has two leptons, large missing transverse momentum, and two widely separated jets.

Events require exactly two same-flavor, opposite-charge leptons, large missing momentum from the neutrinos, and a dijet pair with large rapidity separation and invariant mass. The electroweak production cross section is measured in a fiducial volume. Electroweak ZZjj production probes how the weak force scatters bosons at high energy, a direct test of the Standard Model's gauge structure. Evidence here opens the door to precision studies of this rare process.
arxiv-2606-20758:
OpsCortex, presented in a 2026 paper with no personal byline in the hosted text, is a prototype for self-diagnosing microservice systems. Modern microservice deployments fail in ways that are easy to detect and hard to explain. When a fault spreads along service links, alerts flood in. Engineers must rebuild context that monitoring tools discarded. The authors argue the missing piece is operational memory, not a better detector or a larger model.

Operational memory stores how a system normally behaves, how parts depend on each other, and how it failed before. OpsCortex organizes that memory into four tiers. Root cause is computed directly from a learned dependency graph and the timing of threshold crossings. A large language model is then asked only to explain, confirm, and recommend. Splitting diagnosis from explanation could make automated operations more trustworthy, because the causal claim rests on evidence rather than fluent text.
arxiv-2606-21058:
Caitlin Davis studies multigraded regularity in a solo 2026 mathematics paper on the complete flag variety under its Plücker embedding. A flag variety parametrizes nested chains of subspaces. Regularity measures how complex the equations of an embedded variety are. The multigraded version, introduced by Maclagan and Smith, extends a classic notion to richer grading settings such as products of projective spaces.

Davis proves inductive relationships among regularity regions for the flag variety. Inner and outer bounds on those regions are also provided. Bounds of this kind control the degrees at which computations and vanishing results become effective. Flag varieties sit at the crossroads of geometry, algebra, and representation theory. Sharper regularity knowledge helps researchers predict the cost of working with their equations, and supports proofs where a bound must be known before a geometric claim can be closed.
arxiv-2606-21158:
Tejas Shirodkar and P Narayanan introduce Dead-Direction Signatures in 2026, cheap readings of singular complexity in deep networks. Singular learning theory measures complexity through the shape of the loss surface. The standard estimator, the local learning coefficient, needs a costly sampling chain with many passes per checkpoint. Their readings replace that chain with basic spectral algebra on activation or gradient matrices.

A dead-direction frame predicts a link between activation-side and gradient-side spectra at singular minima. A volume identity based on log determinants counts dead directions. That count tracks the true rank deficit across test cases with varied deficits. Cheap readings could make singular complexity a routine check during training, rather than a research measurement done once. Knowing where a network has dead directions may guide pruning and fair comparisons of model families.
arxiv-2606-21458:
Frederic Berdoz, Luca Lanzendorfer, Antonis Asonitis, and Roger Wattenhofer add a post-training stage in 2026 for speech enhancement language models, systems that clean noisy speech token by token. Such models train on token prediction error, yet they are judged by how speech sounds to listeners, a mismatch like that in text models. The team applies Group Sequence Policy Optimization with rewards taken straight from perceptual quality metrics.

The rewards combine DNSMOS, transcription error, and UTMOS scores, with no learned stand-ins or preference pairs. Applied to the UniSE and GenSE base models, the method reaches state-of-the-art results on the DNS2020 benchmark. Human listeners preferred the multi-metric reward over any single-metric variant, and single-metric training showed the reward hacking, gaming one score while hurting real quality, that composite rewards avoid.
arxiv-2606-21558:
Lydia Bakiri, Jeremy Dubut, and Sergio Mover extend a spatio-temporal logic in 2026 so it can police the communication graphs of moving multi-agent systems. Verifying swarms and fleets means checking properties that entangle space and time, such as how far a message chain can reach. The existing mu-TGL logic handles much of this, but it cannot bound the distance of communication chains or track their length and cost, quantities tied to a network's diameter.

Their extension adds a space horizon operator that bounds chain distance directly. The operator also encodes reachability and escaping modalities the base logic lacked, deepening the space-time entanglement available to specifiers. A centralized offline monitoring algorithm checks the new logic, demonstrated on simulations of consensus-based bundle algorithms, a distributed task allocation protocol used by agent teams.
arxiv-2606-21658:
Lanqing Yuan and Karthik Ramanathan prototype an LLM pipeline in 2026 to keep a dark matter constraint repository alive. Repositories like AxionLimits plot the mass-coupling regions experiments have ruled out. They are vital shared infrastructure, yet they rest on single volunteers who must spot new papers, digitize curves, convert conventions, and write plotting code. Their pipeline watches arXiv, extracts limit curves, integrates them as code, and opens pull requests for human review.

On a 346-paper benchmark graded against the human-curated repository, it names the coupling type correctly for 90.5 percent of papers, with median coupling error of 0.33 dex. Consensus voting over noisy extractions and a convention-canonicalization layer do the heavy lifting. The pipeline is deployed and proposing limits, though none have merged yet, leaving governance of AI-written science data an open problem.
arxiv-2606-21858:
Zhang and colleagues use open city imagery in 2026 to study exposure segregation, the lack of everyday contact between income groups in shared spaces. Movement data can show where mixing fails, but not which physical features of a neighbourhood block or encourage it. Their framework, VISAGE, reads satellite and street-level images with a large multimodal model to judge this separation directly from what places look like.

The study covers 10,030 areas across 31 United States cities, guided by a visual codebook drawn from social theory. Defensible design features such as fences and gated enclosures, together with single-use zoning, predicted higher social isolation. Mixed-use infrastructure predicted more interaction, and the imagery explained much of the pattern seen in travel data, with a correlation of 0.770 between the two measures. Neighbourhoods shaped by inclusionary housing policies also showed distinct visual signatures tied to higher mixing, suggesting such policies visibly reshape the landscape.
arxiv-2606-22158:
Sharma and colleagues propose, in 2026, perception-verified self-training to improve reasoning in vision-language models. Self-training uses a model's own outputs as supervision, but rationales are usually filtered only by answer correctness. That admits visual hallucinations, where the text describes things not in the image, and language shortcuts that ignore the image.

Their framework uses a caption-reasoning-conclusion template that separates perception from reasoning, so each can be checked independently. PerceptEval, a method needing no labels, scores caption quality by alignment with visual and textual elements, replacing missing ground-truth captions. Verified captions plus answer correctness split data into easy, medium, and hard subsets. A two-stage schedule then trains on easy examples first, then rebuilds medium ones using verified captions. Experiments show improvements of up to sixteen percent over standard self-training baselines.
arxiv-2606-22358:
Elver Bajrami's 2026 paper works in complex analysis, the study of functions of complex numbers. It revisits Gabriel's classical theorem, which bounds a function's integral along any convex curve inside the unit disk. The bound uses the function's boundary values, measured in a Hardy space norm. Recent work by Das extended the result to harmonic functions, which are built from two analytic parts.

Bajrami proves versions of the inequality for quasiregular mappings, mappings allowed a controlled amount of distortion. For sense-preserving harmonic mappings in the main class, the constant depends on the distortion level. With no distortion, the estimate recovers Gabriel's sharp analytic constant. As distortion grows without limit, the constant approaches Das's harmonic value. The paper also gives a maximal-function test for wider classes, treats a logarithmic case where the sharp constant carries over, and states Stoilow factorization criteria under boundary distortion assumptions.
arxiv-2606-22458:
Wei Wang proves new identities for Ramanujan's mock theta functions in this 2026 number theory paper. Mock theta functions are strange series that Ramanujan announced in his last letter to Hardy, grouped by order, and they resisted understanding for decades. Wang works with the third-order examples, in particular the functions known as f and omega.

The function f has a classical Appell-Lerch series representation, an identity rewriting it as a simpler sum. Wang establishes a natural generalization of that identity using the theory of harmonic Maass forms, the modern framework that finally explained mock theta functions. Wang then proves analogous Eichler-Selberg type relations for the omega function as well. These relations connect the series to trace-like sums over algebraic data, in the spirit of classical formulas for modular forms. The method, the paper notes, extends to other classes of mock theta functions beyond the third order.
arxiv-2606-22558:
Renata Krupczak, Nicolas Borghini, and Hendrik Roch model oxygen-oxygen collisions at a particle collider in this 2026 physics paper. When two oxygen nuclei collide at high energy, the produced particles flow out with an elliptical pattern called elliptic flow. In heavy nuclei this pattern reflects the almond shape of the overlap zone, but oxygen is small and fluctuations may rule instead.

The team use a fully three-dimensional model combining McDipper with the MUSIC hydrodynamics code, and they reproduce the measured particle counts across centrality and angle. They show the initial elliptical eccentricity is driven mainly by fluctuations in how energy is deposited. It therefore varies considerably from event to event even within one centrality class, and elliptic flow inherits that variation. Decomposing initial states into an average event plus uncorrelated modes, they reproduce the joint distribution of eccentricity and flow using only a small set of modes.
arxiv-2606-22758:
Emanuele Contini and four colleagues ask how many galaxies host a central black hole in this 2026 astrophysics paper. The black hole occupation fraction, the share of galaxies containing one, is a clue to black hole seeding in the early universe. Usually estimated from simulations, its reliability is worth probing.

Using the FEGA25 semi-analytic model on merger trees from three dark-matter simulations, the team varies the mass threshold, galaxy type, box volume, resolution, and redshift. In their model, black holes grow through quasar and radio modes, with no seed population imposed. The occupation fraction rises with stellar mass, but its shape and level depend on the mass threshold and the mix of central and satellite galaxies. Results vary by box. Redshift evolution is not universal: two simulations show one trend, larger-volume boxes the opposite. The inferred fraction, they conclude, is sensitive to modelling choices.
arxiv-2606-22858:
Sannaan Khan and Muhammad U. S. Khan show that fairness audits themselves can be gamed, in this 2026 workshop paper. Machine learning models are checked for bias using fairness metrics and SHAP explanations, which assign credit to each feature. Earlier attacks on these audits left detectable artifacts, which limited their stealth.

The authors introduce Targeted Identity Re-Association attacks, which manipulate a model's outputs step by step without needing access to its internals or features. One algorithm applies small local swaps between neighboring outputs; the other adds tiny randomized shifts to output ranks. Both pushed fairness metrics toward ideal values in their experiments. Crucially, the attacks also confounded SHAP explanations, leaving effectively zero residual attribution for protected features. That is a major stealth improvement over prior work, and a warning that auditing tools need their own defenses.
arxiv-2606-22958:
Ruolan Sun and Pawel Polak align image generators at run time in a 2026 paper. Text-to-image models often need steering after training so pictures match the prompt and human taste. Common steering tweaks one control at a time, such as guidance strength or attention weights. That misses how prompt settings and the evolving image influence each other. Their framework, PG-MAP, treats alignment as one joint optimization problem over both.

Sun and Polak update the conditioning and the latent image together along the whole generation path. A frozen preference reward can guide the updates, with no retraining. Across two diffusion backbones, scores for prompt fit and visual appeal improved. On a flow-matching model, a latent-only version won most head-to-head comparisons against a static baseline. Human raters also preferred its outputs over strong baselines.
arxiv-2606-23058:
Raphaël Delécluse and colleagues forecast where pedestrians will walk next in a 2026 computer vision paper. Crowd prediction must juggle three things: how motion unfolds over time, which scene cues matter, and how nearby people influence each other. Many earlier systems blend those jobs inside heavy attention blocks. That blending costs computing power and blurs what each part does. The team's transformer splits the work into three explicit steps done in sequence.

Delécluse and colleagues first encode each person's motion over time. Compact summaries from a small recurrent unit then let the model fuse added cues cheaply. A final social attention step reasons over time-and-person tokens to capture crowd influence. Tests on three datasets gave top results on two real-world sets and competitive results on the third. Each stage proved its worth in removal tests.
arxiv-2606-23558:
Herrera-Marín builds a stability theory for equations whose dynamics carry memory and switch between regimes, in a 2026 paper on operator theory. Volterra equations describe systems where the present rate of change depends on the whole past, weighted by a memory kernel. Here the kernels are completely monotone, a well-behaved fading-memory class, and a regime process flips the rules over time. Network coupling and Hawkes-type self-excitation, where events raise the chance of more events, add feedback.

For each fixed regime, Herrera-Marín constructs the resolvent family, the solution operator, and proves the system stays well-posed across switches, with explicit bounds. In the commuting case, the stability condition is sharp: every mode is stable exactly when its branching ratio sits below a damping threshold. A second result shows bursts can still amplify along the way, following a power law set by the exit rate.
arxiv-2606-24258:
Saidov and colleagues use X-ray binaries to test a modified theory of gravity around spinning black holes.
