In MOG, modified gravity, an extra parameter strengthens gravity beyond Einstein's description. The Kerr-MOG spacetime describes the resulting rotating black hole. Low-mass X-ray binaries, where a black hole siphons gas from a companion star, offer six well-studied test systems. Their glowing disks report on the spacetime they orbit.

The modified parameter shifts the innermost stable circular orbit. In the Novikov-Thorne disk model, it changes how efficiently gas converts rest mass into radiation. That creates a degeneracy: spin and the gravity parameter can mimic each other in disk observations. Continuum-fitting estimates of radiative efficiency carve allowed regions in the joint parameter space, for each source. Jet power from the Blandford-Znajek mechanism, for two jet speeds, adds an independent constraint, and combining both tests tightens the verdict.
arxiv-2606-24458:
Gray and colleagues rebuild the map of where photosynthesis could work on other worlds, without borrowing Earth's biology. The photosynthetic habitable zone overlaps the classical habitable zone, adding the orbital range where starlight is strong enough to drive photosynthesis. Existing estimates use light response curves from Earth phytoplankton, smuggling in Earth centric assumptions. Their 2026 model is agnostic: a generalised photochemistry grounded in thermodynamics and redox chemistry, with no model creature inside.

A generic reaction couples photon capture to the oxidation of a donor molecule and the reduction of carbon dioxide. Optical properties and reduction rates are optimised against the light spectra of planets around main sequence stars. A genetic algorithm mimics natural selection. Runs predict organisms compensate for reduced light flux by evolving larger light harvesting gear. Gray's team offers the resulting zone as a fairer guide for biosignature searches, asking what physics permits rather than what Earth does.
arxiv-2606-24758:
Faris Alasmary and colleagues present CANDLE, a system that cleans repeated characters from Arabic text. Repetition is ambiguous in Arabic writing. Extra letters can be correct spelling, or casual elongation common in social media posts. CANDLE avoids the dictionaries and analysers that rule based fixes need. It reframes normalisation as a sequence alignment problem. A character based encoder is trained with Connectionist Temporal Classification, a method new to this task.

Three benchmarks test the system: clean newspaper text, curated ambiguous cases, and real social media text. Sentence error rate falls as low as 5.37 percent. The model beats a classification based baseline by a wide margin throughout. For speed, the six layer model is distilled into a two layer student with little loss. Normalised text also helps downstream language models. Tokeniser fertility drops by up to 12.8 percent across several Arabic tokenisers, directly lowering inference costs. Code and models are released publicly.
arxiv-2606-25058:
Deepthi Prabhu and thirty one colleagues present deep imaging of two ultra faint Milky Way satellites, Grus II and Horologium II. Wide field imaging with the Magellan telescopes reaches about three magnitudes deeper than the discovery data. The goal is tighter constraints on distances, luminosities, and structure, plus a search for signs of tidal disturbance. Both systems show colour magnitude diagrams of old, very metal poor stellar populations, about twelve and a half billion years in age.

Grus II sits about 52 kiloparsecs away. Its half light radius is near 103 parsecs, its shape mildly elliptical, and its total brightness extremely faint. Horologium II lies farther out, around 72 kiloparsecs. The measurements rest on photometry deep enough to make the structural fits robust rather than tentative. Prabhu and colleagues deliver the improved parameters satellite studies need.
arxiv-2606-25258:
Polymer fluids remember their recent stretching, and the equations tracking that memory are notoriously hard to control mathematically. Sai Peng develops a new framework for two dimensional viscoelastic flow in 2026, for models with no stress diffusion. Any standard elastic stress law can be split so that, after pressure is absorbed, only a trace free active part pushes on the velocity. Peng shows a weighted energy estimate where the main coupling between flow and polymer shape cancels exactly.

From that cancellation comes an endpoint estimate, plus a decisive extra ingredient: logarithmic smoothness of the polymer configuration that the flow itself generates rather than assumes. Two famous models fall out as special cases. For one, the velocity gradient alone decides whether smooth solutions can be continued; for the other, a squared version of the same quantity plays that role.
arxiv-2606-25658:
A video stream never ends, yet a model's memory must. Fixed budget streaming understanding is the problem Baiyang Song and colleagues at Xiamen University attack in 2026. Their method, CausalMem, needs no training. It keeps a bank of visual tokens. It judges which tokens repeat information already stored. Then it updates the bank through a running semantic basis that tracks the main themes seen so far. The idea mimics how a person summarises a long programme while watching it.

Applied to LLaVA-OneVision and Qwen2.5-VL, CausalMem beat prior methods on streaming and offline video tests alike. Average accuracy rose by a few percentage points. The compression was dramatic: about twelve thousand tokens held an hour of streaming video. That is a better than twentyfold squeeze, in some eighty two megabytes of storage. Careful forgetting, guided by redundancy, beat keeping everything.
arxiv-2606-25958:
Thanh-Nhan Nguyen and Minh-Phuong Tran revisit regularity theory for multi-phase variational problems. Such problems minimize energy functionals whose growth changes from phase to phase. Classical work assumes the modulating coefficients vary smoothly. Nguyen and Tran assume far less. Their coefficients need only belong to a class of Muckenhoupt weights. Those weights may degenerate or blow up, which blocks standard methods.

Localized energy estimates get refined to fit the weaker assumption. An adapted iteration scheme uses the weights' reverse Hölder properties. Main results then follow in sequence. Local minimizers gain higher integrability and local boundedness. Hölder continuity follows as well. The headline result is a Harnack inequality for non-negative local minimizers. The authors note it is the first of its kind for multi-phase problems with Muckenhoupt coefficients. The framework widens regularity theory past smooth-coefficient settings.
arxiv-2606-26158:
Nitya Nadgir leads a team asking what a saturated benchmark can still teach. When accuracy on a benchmark maxes out, the usual move is retirement and replacement. Their case study is CORE-Bench Hard, a test of whether agents can reproduce published computational results. Six more dimensions deserve measurement after saturation, they argue: shortcut-driven validity threats, out-of-distribution reach, efficiency, reliability, model-versus-scaffold credit, and gains from human-agent teamwork.

Saturated accuracy hides real flaws. The shortcuts surfaced were invisible to weaker agents. An improved version and an out-of-distribution suite answer those threats. The revised benchmark still measures efficiency, reliability, and the split between model and scaffold skill. A randomized study of human-agent pairs finds a real-world speedup near twofold. Human-only attempts hitting the time limit make that estimate conservative. Accuracy alone, the case argues, wastes most of a benchmark's information.
arxiv-2606-26258:
Lior Verbitsky and a Princeton-led team report a new family of superconductors built on a predicted parent. An artificial intelligence method had flagged the compound PtPb3Bi as a likely superconductor. The team synthesized its cousins instead: gold, palladium, and rhodium versions of the same structure type, with lead and bismuth sharing one site. Nickel, much smaller, collapses into a different structure and drops out of the family.

Composition tunes itself in a telling way. The lead-bismuth balance shifts across the three compounds to hold the total valence electron count near twenty per formula unit. Superconducting transitions arrive at a few kelvin, highest for the gold member. Resistivity, magnetization, and heat capacity confirm the superconductivity is bulk, not a surface effect. All three are moderately anisotropic type-II superconductors. The family gives heavy-element intermetallic research a fresh platform where site disorder can be dialled.
arxiv-2606-26358:
S. Corley and colleagues forecast how many exoplanets the Rubin Observatory's big survey can confirm by transits. The Legacy Survey of Space and Time will scan the southern sky for ten years. Its cadence, tuned for cosmology, revisits fields in scattered bursts. Transits need the opposite: steady watching. Their framework simulates light curves for planet populations built from Kepler occurrence rates, folded through a galactic star model and the survey's real observing plan.

Confirmation demands are strict. Three full transits must be caught, with signal strong enough to detect, and a periodogram check must pass. Under the current design, yields come out thin. The deep drilling fields may confirm a small number of hot planets around faint red dwarf stars. The wide survey is projected to confirm none. Sparse, multi-band observing starves transit science, the authors conclude, however superb the telescope.
arxiv-2606-26458:
Xiaochen Wang, Bao Hoang, Han Liu, Ting Wang, and Fenglong Ma built MKG-RAG-Bench, a benchmark for retrieval in multimodal knowledge graph systems. Such systems answer questions by fetching facts from a knowledge graph, a network of linked facts. Multimodal graphs mix text with images and other media. Retrieval, the fetching step, is often the weak link.

Existing benchmarks mostly ignore that retrieval problem. The new benchmark draws on two multimodal knowledge graphs. One covers general topics and the other covers medicine. Aligned question-and-answer sets support controlled tests of retrieval and of final answer quality. A language model pipeline built the benchmark. It filters low-value knowledge and writes questions with exact known answers. It also covers varied mixes of media types. The authors use it to compare retrievers and show where multimodal retrieval breaks down.
arxiv-2606-26558:
Sooyeong Kim, David W. Kribs, Michael Nathanson, Rajesh Pereira, and Sarah Plosker study when distant partners can tell quantum states apart. The states are product states, meaning each partner's part is independent. The partners may act locally and exchange ordinary messages. This restricted teamwork is called LOCC. Graphs, networks of points and links, have recently encoded which state sets are distinguishable this way.

Earlier graph work covered one-way communication only. Kim and colleagues extend it to full two-way exchange over finitely many rounds. They derive basic closure properties for the family of distinguishable graphs. Closure properties say which operations keep a graph inside the family. They identify graph classes that guarantee distinguishability and others that rule it out. Worked examples and open directions close the study. The results sharpen a graph-based map of what local observers can and cannot learn.
arxiv-2606-26958:
Berestycki and Klein study heat flow on a random bumpy geometry known as Liouville quantum gravity. That geometry warps flat space using a Gaussian free field, a random height landscape with rough, scale-rich structure. The heat trace sums how heat starting at each point returns there after a short time. The authors focus on the second term of that expansion for the average heat trace over a bounded region.

That second term is governed by a nontrivial exponent fixed by the KPZ relation, a famous formula linking flat and warped scaling. A stronger almost-sure version holds for heat content, a related total-heat measure. Along the way, the team settles a conjecture about averaged short-time heat kernel behaviour from earlier work. They also show every moment of the properly rescaled heat kernel stays finite.
arxiv-2606-27258:
Jackson argues that object orientation, the organising idea behind decades of software design, rests on a flawed split. The founding principle assigns each system function to objects mirroring individuals in the problem domain. Jackson contends that carving functionality along those lines is neither natural nor straightforward. Later methods tried to patch the resulting fragmentation and conflation of functions. Those troubles, he argues, were inevitable consequences of the founding principle itself in this essay from 2026, written for a memorial volume honouring Jean-Raymond Abrial.

An easier path starts by abandoning object orientation altogether. The alternative decouples problem-domain individuals from the modules that partition functionality. Historical discussion reaches back to Abrial's 1974 data semantics work, an early abstract model of objects and relations. That model, Jackson suggests, already hinted the object structure was the wrong path. Software specification and design gain a cleaner foundation when functions are partitioned on their own terms.
arxiv-2606-27358:
Xu and Wang cultivate reusable catalyst states that let surface codes apply fine phase rotations exactly. Fault-tolerant quantum computers need non-Clifford gates, usually synthesised from Clifford operations plus T gates. Their protocol instead grows a special logical state, an eigenstate of a high-period Clifford circuit, directly inside the code. Phase kickback from that catalyst applies the target rotation with no synthesis error at all, in a quantum computing paper appearing in 2026.

A square-root-of-T catalyst is built from a nine-qubit brickwork Clifford circuit. Growth starts from nine distance-three rotated surface-code blocks and proceeds through logical checks, syndrome extraction, and postselection. Even one verification round attains the leading error-corrected scaling. Simulations grow the catalyst to distance-seven blocks with logical leakage around one in a million at the stated physical error rate, needing about seven attempts in the reported runs.
arxiv-2606-27458:
Mizuse and colleagues directly image how the two mirror-image forms of a chiral molecule orient differently while rotating in lockstep. Enantiomers, left- and right-handed versions of one molecule, matter across chemistry and drug science, yet their distinct motions had never been filmed. A femtosecond laser pulse pair sets isolated molecules into unidirectional coherent rotation. For the test molecule, the two forms develop equal and opposite out-of-plane tilts. In the 2026 chemical physics paper, time-resolved Coulomb explosion imaging, with two detectors arranged at right angles, follows the spinning wave packets.

The rotation itself is identical for both enantiomers; only the out-of-plane orientations mirror each other. The pattern persists through early quasi-classical and later quantum regimes, matching simulations closely. Full angular distributions carry richer information than the usual single orientation factor. Real-time observation and control of chiral dynamics in the gas phase opens up.
arxiv-2606-28158:
Ali AlHadi Kalout and seven colleagues take on the Calderón problem, which asks doctors and engineers to map the electrical conductivity inside a body using only measurements at its surface. Sharp borders inside, such as the edge of an inclusion, are the hardest features to recover from limited data.

Kalout's team builds a reconstruction method from physics-informed neural networks, which learn while respecting the governing electrical equations. They excite the surface with randomized wavelet patterns and test two ways of feeding position into the networks. On synthetic data the method recovered the main structures with errors between roughly three and twelve percent. One encoding sharpened localized features, while plain coordinates worked just as well for smoother fields.
arxiv-2606-28358:
Ian van Dort and Maria Heuss open up a language model to watch it decide whether to attach a citation. Retrieval-augmented systems answer questions from fetched documents and add inline citations for trust, but a citation only helps if it faithfully marks where the answer came from.

Van Dort and Heuss use activation patching, swapping internal activations between runs, on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct answering factoid questions. They locate an attributional ensemble, a set of attention heads and feed-forward layers that together drive citation decisions. The circuitry leans heavily on shallow shortcuts, such as matching entities between question and passage, rather than deep checks of what supports the claim. Citations that look reassuring, they warn, may rest on much thinner evidence than readers assume.
arxiv-2606-28558:
Marcin Bienkowski, Joakim Blikstad, Jarosław Byrka, Martín Costa, Yann Disser, and Annette Lutz beat a classical guarantee in submodular maximization, the art of choosing sets with diminishing returns. The incremental version asks for one ordering of all elements whose every prefix is a good solution for its size, useful when the budget itself is not fixed in advance.

The greedy algorithm's competitive ratio, about one point five eight, had stood as the best general guarantee. The team's adaptive scaling algorithm improves it to one point three seven three, a genuine advance after long stagnation. They pair the algorithm with a deterministic lower bound of one point two five, proving no method can guarantee better than that in general. The gap between what is achievable and what is provably impossible narrows considerably.
arxiv-2606-28858:
Letsios and Vitouladitis analyse an axion, a hypothetical light particle, living in de Sitter space, the expanding geometry that models an accelerating universe. Their axion is a massless compact scalar field, whose value wraps around a circle. Quantising the theory, they determine the charges allowed by de Sitter symmetry and uncover an extra ingredient beyond the usual oscillator states.

The axion's zero mode, its uniform component, contributes a quantum-mechanical factor resembling a particle on a ring. The full state space combines that ring factor with the oscillator space. The ring's momentum is the conserved shift charge. A neutral zero-particle state is fully symmetric, while charged ones break some symmetry. Boosted observers thus disagree on particle counts in charged sectors. A Euclidean path-integral view reaches only the neutral sector unless vertex insertions are added. In three dimensions, duality with a photon turns the zero mode into monopole sectors.
arxiv-2606-28958:
Brito and Baquero examine a security hole in teams of language models that share hidden memory instead of just text. In their protocol, specialist agents send short visible commitments to a coordinator while passing along their full KV-cache, the stored internal state from processing context. Sharing that state improved split-evidence reasoning in tests, beating matched text-only collaboration on standard question benchmarks.

The same channel, though, is fragile. A tampered hidden state can look fine in the visible text while quietly steering answers, and random corruption or scaled hidden states collapsed performance near zero. Filters that audit only the visible commitments missed the attacks, and clever adaptive attacks evaded magnitude checks and a learned sanitiser. The authors' working defence sits at the transport layer: a cryptographic manifest binding identity, session, model and payload digest. It accepted all 774 honest payloads and rejected all 295 tampered ones in their tests.
arxiv-2606-29158:
Yang, Zhang, Xu and Zhang examine a rule of thumb for cutting training costs for large language models: the best learning rate obeys a log-linear scaling law in data and model size. If true, the law would let practitioners extrapolate the right rate from small runs instead of full-scale sweeps. Their study trains GPT-2-style models, from twenty-two to over seven hundred million parameters, on up to a hundred billion tokens.

The optimal learning rate bends upward at larger scales, so log-linear extrapolation goes wrong. The bend largely disappears when raw rates are replaced by the effective rate, the step size in normalised weight space. It also fades when extrapolation runs over data rather than model size. They explain the bend through weight norms, which reach equilibrium slowly when the optimal rate is small. Tests with an optimiser controlling the effective rate support this.
arxiv-2606-29558:
Bedratyuk studies the graph algebra, an algebraic structure whose monomial basis is indexed by the simple graphs over a fixed vertex set. The same algebra describes pseudo-Boolean functions on the Boolean cube. 

Two symmetry structures act on this algebra. One comes from the Lie algebra sl2, generated by operators that add or delete a single edge. The other comes from renumbering the vertices. Bedratyuk proves the algebra with its sl2 action is a tensor power of the standard two-dimensional module, and he decomposes it into irreducible pieces. Primitive spaces, the kernels of the edge-deletion operator, match two-row Specht modules. The two actions commute, so graph invariants inherit the sl2 structure. The classical count of non-isomorphic graphs by edge number gains a finer refinement.
arxiv-2606-29658:
Tian proposes a transfer learning framework that borrows strength from related datasets without ever seeing their raw data. Transfer learning improves a target task using knowledge from source domains. Existing theory mostly assumes a known link function, or some other linear structure, and requires direct access to source data.

His method rests on the single-index model, where outcomes depend on one combined score passed through an unknown curve. Only summary statistics cross from each source, derived through a generalized Stein's lemma, in a single one-time communication. That design preserves privacy and avoids harm from differing unknown link functions across domains. A multilayer perceptron, guided by the index estimated from the transferred statistics, captures the flexible nonlinearity and limits overfitting. Experiments on synthetic and real-world data show consistent improvements over generalized linear model based approaches.
arxiv-2606-29758:
Hwang and Kim propose PS-PPO, a cheaper way to run critic-free reinforcement learning from human feedback for large language models. Critic-free methods are popular for their simplicity, but a trajectory-level signal spread across all tokens makes every update costly.

Prefix-Sampling PPO exploits that temporal redundancy. A prompt-conditioned cutoff distribution picks a cutoff point for each trajectory. The update then backpropagates only through the sampled prefix. An importance-weighting correction keeps the truncated gradient estimator unbiased relative to the full-trajectory objective. Experiments show big reductions in training compute and in peak GPU memory, with accuracy comparable to strong baselines.
arxiv-2606-29858:
Wang and four colleagues ask why the training loss of language models falls so smoothly as models and data grow, following clean scaling laws. Their answer looks at learning token by token, a token being a word piece.

Fitting S-shaped curves to each token's loss over training, the team finds that learning is concentrated in short transitions: each token is picked up at a fairly definite time. Across more than one hundred training runs, the spread of these learning times rebuilds the overall loss curve along the time, data, and model axes. The runs reach six billion parameters and 300 billion tokens. Using the signal to reshape the training mix then cut the loss eleven percent faster.
arxiv-2606-30058:
Comparing the pose of two objects needs a shared reference frame. Tom Fischer, Martin Sundermeyer, Adam Kortylewski, and Eddy Ilg let such a frame emerge by itself. Traditionally, canonical frames required costly manual pose annotation. That bottleneck limits how many categories models can cover. Their method learns from ordinary object videos instead.

Training is self-supervised on one hundred sixty thousand in-the-wild videos. The only guidance available is noisy camera poses from structure-from-motion. All sequences pass through one shared geometric bottleneck. That bottleneck is a coarse canonical mesh with no category detail. The model learns dense matches from image pixels to this mesh. Per-sequence alignments are estimated from the noisy geometry. A common frame then emerges from multi-view consistency. On category-level pose benchmarks, accuracy rivals methods using full pose supervision.
arxiv-2606-30158:
B. Dudás, G. Papp, G. Barnaföldi, and G. Bíró, writing for the Bergen pCT Collaboration, build a compact deep learning pipeline for proton computed tomography. This imaging method needs fast, accurate tracking of each proton. Traditional distance-based matching fails under scattering and track crossings. It is also too slow for clinical image formation. Lightweight neural networks offer a faster route.

The pipeline has two stages working in sequence. A tracking module predicts each proton's expected hit in the next detector layer. That prediction acts as a physically informed prior for matching. Ambiguous tracks get flagged and dropped from the final analysis. A second network estimates each incoming proton's kinetic energy. Training data come from the OpenGATE simulation toolkit. The energy estimates prove accurate enough for current reconstruction methods. Deep learning parallelism keeps the whole pipeline within clinical time limits.
arxiv-2606-30258:
Boshko Koloski, Xiangjian Jiang, Senja Pollak, Blaž Škrlj, Mateja Jamnik, and Nikola Simidjievski steer small tabular foundation models with curated domain knowledge. Such models predict from tables after pretraining on synthetic tasks. In niche domains, data are scarce, high-dimensional, and distributionally shifted. Carefully built specialist methods can still beat the general models there. Knowledge graphs from those domains sit unused by default.

Their fine-tuning recipe, KnowsTFM, injects that relational knowledge during adaptation. Structural attention priors are derived directly from the knowledge graphs. Parameter-efficient low-rank updates carry the rest of the fine-tuning. Nanoscale variants of two tabular model families serve as testbeds. Injecting structural knowledge yields meaningful gains in specialist settings. Gains on general-domain tasks, by contrast, are only marginal. Continual fine-tuning of frontier models can collapse pretrained knowledge, they warn.
arxiv-2606-30458:
Wenjie Qian and six colleagues improve finding people in surveillance photos from text descriptions when image quality varies wildly. Text-to-image person search matches a written description to gallery photos. Real cameras produce mixed sharpness in one gallery. Low resolution destroys fine details the text mentions. Mixed galleries also warp the similarity rankings themselves. The authors name these two failure modes explicitly.

Evidence Reliability Collapse covers the unreliable degraded visual tokens. Ranking Distribution Drift covers the distorted neighborhoods across resolutions. Their framework, CRST, answers with three modules. Resolution-conditioned reasoning estimates which tokens can be trusted. Text-guided refinement restores discriminative cues from the description. A transfer step borrows sharp-image neighborhood structure to steady low-resolution ranks. Three standard benchmarks test the approach. Ultra-low-resolution accuracy rises by about five to six points on average. Sharp-image performance is preserved at the same time.
arxiv-2606-30558:
Marcos Escartín Ferrer, Giorgio Leoni and Conchita Martínez Pérez study even Artin groups. Their work appeared in 2026. Artin groups are built from graphs. Their generators are linked by braid-like relations, and the even case limits those relations to even lengths. Right-angled Artin groups are well understood. General Artin groups are not. The trio ask which cohomological facts survive the move to the even family. Cohomology gives algebraic measures of a group's shape.

For certain even families, they compute the cohomology ring. In the FC case, they also describe the pro-p completion. That is a way of rebuilding a group from its finite p-power shadows. They determine its p-Zassenhaus restricted Lie algebra too. A rigidity result follows. If two even Artin groups of FC type are isomorphic, then their defining graphs agree. Agreement holds in the p-part for every prime p.
arxiv-2606-31358:
Zhu and three colleagues screen thousands of crystals for a fast optical route to switch magnetism on and off. Linearly polarised light pulses were proposed to magnetise some non-magnetic semiconductors, yet few candidate compounds were known, so tests stalled. The team search the MC3D database of real inorganic crystals with first-principles methods.

Nearly 440 non-magnetic semiconductors develop spin polarization under such pulses through a light-induced exchange-driven instability. The crystal field setting and the orbital character at the band edge decide how strong the effect is and which magnetic order forms. Clear chemical and periodic trends emerge, giving experimentalists a shopping list rather than a guess. Magnetisation switching with femtosecond pulses, the results argue, is common rather than exotic.
arxiv-2606-31458:
Roth and three colleagues study how students learn performance analysis for parallel programs, and test a tool built to lower the barrier. Courses on message passing with MPI need cluster practice, yet professional analysis tools assume deep knowledge of clusters, resource managers, and common parallel faults. Students often stall before they learn anything about speed.

Their EduMPI tool gives a simple graphical interface that runs student programs on a cluster for them. It draws MPI communication almost in real time, placed by where each process sits in the machine, so load imbalance and bottlenecks show up visually. A user study against established professional tools finds EduMPI lowers entry barriers and builds an intuitive feel for parallel performance, raising its teaching value.
arxiv-2606-31558:
Shimizu, Ghioldi, Ronning and Batista derive design rules for rare-earth quantum magnets whose exchange interactions behave almost like the simple, direction-blind Heisenberg model. Such quasi-isotropic magnetism is prized for hosting quantum spin liquids and topological textures, yet the strong spin-orbit coupling in rare-earth ions usually makes exchange strongly directional instead.

Working from a multiorbital Hubbard model with degenerate perturbation theory, the team studies cerium and ytterbium insulators with edge-sharing octahedra. Isotropic exchange comes mainly from virtual hopping inside the ground-state Kramers doublet, while anisotropy comes from processes involving excited multiplets. The resulting rule is practical. Quasi-isotropic exchange is favored when the ground doublet has strong maximal-angular-momentum character about the axis perpendicular to the superexchange plane, . That pattern matches studied ytterbium materials.
arxiv-2606-31758:
Shaukat and three colleagues propose PIFLUX, a way to locate single fluorescent molecules with few-nanometre precision across a wide field of view. Standard localization microscopy is limited by photon counts. Patterned methods such as MINFLUX reach about one nanometre but address one molecule at a time, while SIMFLUX keeps a wide view with only a modest precision gain.

PIFLUX interferes counter-propagating gap plasmons, waves bound to a metal surface, with a normally incident optical field. Shifting the plasmon phase moves the illumination pattern without changing its fine period. A Cramér-Rao analysis gives precision matching MINFLUX and doubling SIMFLUX over a micrometre-wide field. A maximum-likelihood estimator confirms the gain on a synthetic nuclear pore complex.
arxiv-2606-31858:
Baltag and Smets design a logic for knowledge about data values, not just facts. Agents may know a proposition, or they may know the value of a variable such as a key or password. Conditional versions capture what an agent would know about a value if given extra information, and counting operators bound how far a group can narrow the possibilities.

On that static base, dynamic modalities model data-exchange events. Gaining access to a source hands over everything stored there at once, covering public sharing, private announcements and even secret hacking of a database. Complete axiomatizations are provided for the resulting logics. Decidability and co-expressivity results round out the analysis of the framework.
arxiv-2606-31958:
Bhatia and three colleagues propose learning robot tasks in prompt space rather than action space. Generalist robot policies hold broad skill repertoires from pretraining. Standard reinforcement learning tunes raw actions, which only works when the base policy already starts near a good action distribution. Long-horizon tasks outside the pretraining mix break that assumption.

Semantic Action Reinforcement Learning treats the policy's language instructions as the action space. Adjusting prompts elicits skills the policy already owns, so exploration stays structured and meaningful. Grounding each prompt in the behavior it actually induces lets skills compose into solutions beyond zero-shot reach. Across real-world settings and simulated benchmarks, SARL adapts vision-language-action behavior to complex tasks and beats existing deployment-improvement methods.
brought-home-pg7358:
Hesba Stretton's Brought Home is a Victorian tale of a quiet market town, a rectory and a woman's duty. Upton is so quiet that London's stir seems hard to believe, though the city lies little more than an hour away by a branch line with only three trains each way daily.

Chapters follow Upton Rectory, Ann Holland, a baby's grave, town talk, the rector's return, and a husband and wife in sad days. A colonial curacy, self-sacrifice, farewells, a long voyage and a near shipwreck carry the story toward its close. Stretton writes with the moral earnestness of her popular tales, and readers of Victorian domestic fiction will find Brought Home affecting.
cardano-metoposcopia-1658:
Girolamo Cardano reads fate in the brow in Metoposcopia, his vast Latin work of 1658, set in print at Paris. Cardano was a healer, sage of sums, and gambler of famed note. He holds that the lines of the brow are writ by the stars at birth. Each line, cross, and scar marks health, wealth, rank, and the hour and kind of a man's death in his scheme.

Eight score draws of brows fill the book, each with its gloss. The scheme is false, yet its craft stuns. The text is the brow lore's great store. Sages still cite its plates.
cia-0000009758:
Bodies believed to be those of twelve American prisoners of war were found in the Viet Cong's Duy Xuyen district, a January 1973 report states. Duy Xuyen lies in Quang Nam province, on South Vietnam's central coast. The discovery came as the Paris accords were being signed.

A find of this size could close a dozen cases at once, if identification held. Officials had to test the claim carefully before telling any family. The report's careful wording, possibly twelve, shows that caution at work. It preserves a grim discovery at the exact moment the war was supposed to end.
cia-0000009858:
An assertion about many captured American pilots, its ending cut off in the heading, fills an April 1966 item with two deleted sections. The deletions hide the claimants, as the censor's marks show. What survives is the claim's shape: many pilots, captured, and something asserted about them.

Files like this one frustrate readers, yet they still testify. A claim large enough to file in 1966 mattered to the men tracking prisoners then. The redactions mark where the public record stops, not where the story does. Preserved as released, the item shows both wartime reporting and later secrecy at work.
cia-0000011758:
Che Guevara had vanished from public life in Cuba. In August 1966 the CIA issued a statement on his status and on Havana's timetable for spreading revolution. Guevara, the Argentine doctor turned guerrilla, had helped Castro win power and then disappeared from view. Rumors placed him fighting in Africa or preparing a new campaign in Latin America.

The statement reports what the agency believed about where Che was and what he meant to do. It also lays out Cuba's plans for exporting revolution to other lands. Within a year Guevara was dead in Bolivia, which makes the paper a record of the hunt.
cia-0000013858: A senior American pilot, a lieutenant colonel, was captured in Thanh Hoa Province, and a CIA note dated June 4, 1967, records it. Senior rank made a capture stand out in the files. A high ranking prisoner held strong value for the north, both for news value and for what he knew. The note marks his entry into the prison system.
cia-0000014658: Headquarters wished to pass on material about a convicted spy's case, in a CIA file dated April 1, 1956. The title keeps the spy unnamed in the open line. Passing case material between offices was the daily flow of the spy files. Even a cover note like this shows how long the big cases stayed alive on paper.
cia-0000014758: The pro-Cominform Communist Party in Trieste is tracked in a CIA file dated January 5, 1953. The file leans on CIC reports, from the Army's counter intelligence arm. Trieste was a disputed port city, split between east and west claims. Party moves there mattered because the city's fate hung in the balance.
cia-0000015258: Bolivia's reports clashed on the details of a fallen object, in a CIA file dated April 3, 1978. Two days of claims had already muddied what came down and where. Clashing reports were the norm for falls in far country. The file preserves the muddle before any team could reach the site.
cia-0000015358: An item for the Director's log fills a CIA file dated March 2, 1953. The title does not say what the item was. The Director's log noted matters thought fit for the top man's eye. A saucer era item reaching that log shows how high the subject could rise in the building.
cia-0000015458: Comments and suggestions from the UFO panel fill an undated CIA item filed in 1953. The panel was a group of scientists asked to judge the saucer evidence for the government. Their added remarks show experts refining what should be done next. Even without a firm date in the catalog, the entry holds the tone of that first official review and its advice.
cia-0000026758: The outlook for Iraq is forecast in a CIA paper dated in 1957. Iraq was then a kingdom allied with Britain, ruled in the name of a young king. Within a year the monarchy was destroyed in a bloody coup. Read with that knowledge, a calm outlook paper from 1957 shows how fast the ground of the Middle East could shift under careful men.
cia-0000037158:
Caucasian prisoners were transferred by truck from Thanh Hoa to Quang Ninh province, a CIA record dated February 1, 1982 reports. Thanh Hoa lies south of Hanoi, and Quang Ninh far to the northeast. A truck convoy between them was a long and notable move.

The record preserves the reported transfer as a piece of prison-system movement. Tracking where prisoners were held, and when they were moved, helped test other claims. The file shows analysts building a picture of a hidden system from single glimpses. Each convoy report added a line to a map drawn mostly in the dark.
cia-0000040058:
Peru's Armed Forces Command issued a communique on a killing, in a CIA record dated March 2, 1987. A communique is the military's formal public statement on an event. Peru was then fighting the Shining Path insurgency across much of the country.

Inside, the command's own wording sets out the official account of the killing. Such statements were how the military spoke to the public during the war. The file preserves the official line at a set date. Readers can set it beside press and human rights accounts of the same years, and judge how the command chose to present its actions.
cia-0000045158:
The FMLN claimed credit for killing Marines, in a CIA record dated May 5, 1985. The claim concerned the Zona Rosa killings in San Salvador. Guerrilla claims of this kind were issued to be believed and feared.

Inside, the rebels' claim of responsibility is preserved as made. Owning the attack told Salvadorans the rebels could strike at will. It also dared Washington to answer in the war's daily contest. Claims like this one were answered, in time, with more aid and more advisers for the government. The file holds that boast from May 1985, set beside a companion communique record from the same attack in this same group of files.
cia-0000045258:
From Panama, Ungo denied any link with the negotiations, in a CIA record dated September 2, 1985. Distance was the point of his denial's dateline. An exile leader in Panama could not be running talks in San Salvador.

Inside, his clearing of his own name is preserved as issued. Denials from abroad carried a special need to be believed. His hosts, his allies, and his enemies all read this one closely. The file holds the Panama denial among the case's many disavowals. Each one drew the map of who would, and who would not, be tied to the crime.
cia-0000049058: The second part of the file on the legal case involving Hans Christ survives in a CIA item from 1983. The same item touches on the forming of a new Salvadoran group, its title cut off before naming it. Case files like this one advanced in pieces, each part adding a hearing, a ruling, or a delay.
cia-0000049258: The Latin America warning and forecast meeting of February 1990 is preserved in a CIA item from that year. Warning meetings were where analysts told their bosses what to watch: coups, offensives, and collapses they saw coming. The record shows the region as the watchers framed it, one month into a new decade.
cia-0000049358: El Salvador: Political Difficulties Persist heads declassified CIA document 0000049358, dated September 4, 1982. The item, noted for the Truth Commission, records that political difficulties in El Salvador were continuing. Its plain heading is the main evidence it offers, a short dated sign that the country's problems remained unresolved in the agency's reporting during that year.
cia-0000075258: Military prospects in El Salvador are the subject of declassified CIA document 0000075258, dated January 3, 1991. Marked for the Truth Commission, the paper looks ahead at the military's position. It is a brief declassified outlook item whose title states its forward focus, part of the agency's closing sequence of Salvadoran assessments before the war's end phase.
cia-0000096658: Mao Tse-tung and His Associates; Uneasy Alliance is the title of declassified CIA document 0000096658, dated August 5, 1968. The heading pairs the leader and his circle with a strained partnership. Readers get a short declassified paper on that leadership group, its subtitle carrying the paper's judgment in two words, uneasy alliance.
cia-0000102958:
Imprisonment in a prison and corrective labor camp in Tashkent, Uzbek SSR, is the first item in declassified CIA document 0000102958, dated November 2, 1986. The heading spells the city Tashket. A second item follows in the title, but its subject is cut off.

The summary says suspects waited in investigative prisons before trial, while most convicted inmates went to labor camps. Camps were grouped as general, reinforced, and severe, based on security and inmate privilege. Notorious or important convicts could stay in prison, where guards kept a closer watch. The text also notes Uzbek inmates usually kept to themselves.
cia-0000108158: Current Situation and Probable Developments in Finland During 1954 is the heading on declassified CIA document 0000108158, dated January 3, 1964. The catalog date and the heading disagree by ten years: the file is dated 1964, the title says 1954. That mismatch stands on the face of the record itself. The brief record is a Finland outlook item with a dating puzzle.
cia-0000109058: The Che Guevara Diary is the short subject of declassified CIA document 0000109058, dated November 5, 1967. The heading names a diary tied to Che Guevara, in four plain words. No place or campaign is named in the title itself. The brief record is a diary item, filed a month after Guevara's death in Bolivia in October 1967.
cia-0000119758: An October 1956 CIA chronology lists the principal events of the Hungarian Revolution from October 23 to November 4. Timelines assembled while events still moved became the first draft of the uprising's history, and this one lays the revolution out day by day. A day-by-day list gave officials a shared spine of fact during arguments about response, and it still serves readers as the uprising's basic timetable.
cia-0000126958: A July 1968 CIA special memorandum examines the split in the AD party and what it meant for Venezuelan democracy. Accion Democratica, the country's leading party, was breaking apart from within. The memo weighs how that feud threatened the party system holding the country together. Party splits in a dominant-party system move the whole state, and the memo's concern was that Venezuela's young democracy might crack along with its strongest party.
cia-0000132158: Dated January 1991, Iraq-Kuwait situation report 475 covers a deleted section and first political reactions to an event the heading loses mid-phrase. Whatever drew the reactions was removed by the censors. The report preserves the rest of that day's watch. Deleted passages are marked rather than hidden in these releases, so readers can see the shape of the missing piece even where its words are gone.
cia-0000132758: Venezuela's stance on the Cuban problem fills a CIA paper dated May 1, 1960. Caracas was still making up its mind at that stage of the quarrel. The stance would harden into open hostility within about two years. For now the paper catches a government mid-decision. The short paper sets out the views held in Caracas that spring.
cia-0000135658: The catalog dates this Spanish-language 2506 Brigade document to 1 January 1961 and flags that date as estimated. Brigade 2506 was the CIA's exile army, then training for the Bay of Pigs landing. A New Year's Day date on an estimated record suggests paperwork logged at the start of the year rather than a known event. No subject is recorded for the item. It survives in Spanish in the declassified release, one of many similar records from the brigade's final winter.
cia-0000135858: A declassified CIA cable dated 6 February 1952 turns to a proposed meeting with Castillo, raised years before he led the force that invaded Guatemala. The record comes from the run-up to the June 1954 coup that removed President Arbenz, the goal of the CIA plan called PBSUCCESS. Small as it is, the sheet documents one task, one report, or one order inside a much larger secret effort.
cia-0000136258: 6 May 1954 is the date on a declassified CIA situation report about daily operations situation report number 5, the daily count rising in the final weeks. The record comes from the run-up to the June 1954 coup that removed President Arbenz, the goal of the CIA plan called PBSUCCESS. Students of the 1954 coup use such records to check later accounts against what was written at the time.
cia-0000136858: Was a man a government plant? This cable to LINCOLN asks the station to check. A trusted source calls him a ringleader of the Salama uprising. The uprising failed on 28-29 March 1953. Papers said four leaders were shot escaping jail. Three others found asylum in the Mexican embassy. The source suspects a setup. The ringleaders may have been government agents in a fake uprising. They now enjoy a paid vacation in Mexico, he says. Verify before any request goes on.
cia-0000141158:
Word reached the CIA in November 1961 that B-26 number 933, painted with Cuban markings, lay deep in jungle a few miles from the Bocay River in Nicaragua. The wreck held the remains of two men. General Somoza's forces were heading to the crash site by helicopter to inspect it, and word came back asking what should be done with the remains and the men's effects.

Headquarters replied that 933 had left Boca Chica on 16 April for the base called Tide and never arrived. A small team was to fly to Managua, reach the site, and gather charts, maps, notebooks, and other gear, once local approval came through.
cia-03155958:
A Weekly Summary from the Office of Current Intelligence, dated 4 December 1970, surveys the week to Thursday noon across five regions. Cambodia's battle of the roads leads the Far East section. Laos, and fallout from the Son Tay raid in Vietnam, follow. Thailand's Praphat looms nearer power. Malaysia and Singapore appear as nettlesome neighbours.

Europe takes up the German problem again, Italy's coalition clearing a hurdle, and Hungary's party congress advancing Kadar's reform goals. A long piece weighs Solzhenitsyn: his Nobel prize is a dilemma for a leadership slowly rehabilitating Stalin. Guinea repels a second incursion. Jordan's Husayn mends fences abroad. One month of Allende's Chile, Mexican cabinet appointments, and Guatemalan anti-Communist gains fill the hemisphere section. Short notes close on Turkey and Uruguay.
cia-03179158:
Hungary opens the Current Intelligence Bulletin dated 24 October 1956, in crisis. Students, workers, and off-duty soldiers demonstrated on 23 October for a Nagy government and Soviet troop withdrawal. Police fired on crowds seizing the radio station and toppling a Stalin monument. At least one person was killed. Telephone links westward were cut, and music replaced normal broadcasts.

Party leader Gero's hard speech, fresh from Belgrade, may have sparked the violence. An emergency central committee meeting is called. In Poland, a Gomulka man becomes the army's political commissar. The USSR is building a new type of submarine. Turkey and Iran study a joint oil pipeline. Karamanlis will head Greece's delegation to the UN. Singapore's antisubversion drive antagonises its Chinese community. Afghanistan proposes a railroad built with American aid.
cia-06190258:
Modification Ten, effective 16 September 2008, amends a contract held by General Dynamics Information Technology. The contractor address is given as 3211 Jermantown Road, Suite 120, Fairfax, VA 22030. The underlying contract is dated 18 September 2007 in the form. Its accounting line states that contract funding rises by $418,556.

The file runs to 56 pages of contract terms carried with the change. Standard amendment language on acknowledging receipt fills the first page. Later clauses cover travel, including cases that need approval from the contracting officer before a trip is taken. Foreign travel and travel above a set allocation are named. Training and education costs are also covered, where the contracting officer finds them applicable to the contract.
cia-06235358:
Agency Regulation 9-3, dated 22 December 1999, sets out the CIA employment discrimination complaint system. The regulation was new when issued and took in parts of an older complaint section from AR 9-1. It sits in Category 9, Equal Opportunity, with the Office of Equal Employment Opportunity as the responsible office.

The synopsis covers complaints based on race, color, religion, sex, national origin, disability, and age at 40 and over. Reprisal for opposing discrimination or taking part in the equal opportunity process is also covered. Other classes protected by written Agency policy are included. Middle text requires anyone who directs another person's Agency work to act in a lawful, fair manner. Supervisors must refer a person with an allegation to the equal opportunity office, which also reviews corrective actions.
cia-06776858:
Intelligence assessment dated 23 January 2013, numbered CIA-DI-13-00118 and marked Confidential, covers delayed population counts. It was prepared by the Office of Africa, Latin America, and Global Issues. Its title states that delayed counts in key countries are hindering national development plans.

Key findings state twelve countries had gone more than ten years since last holding a census. The twelve named are Afghanistan, Angola, Burma, Cote d'Ivoire, and the Democratic Republic of Congo. Eritrea, Guinea, Iraq, Lebanon, Pakistan, Somalia, and Uzbekistan complete the list. Half had incomplete systems for recording births, deaths, and population moves. The assessment attributes delays in ten of the twelve to instability or lack of resources. Census figures, it notes, help target funding and plan education, health care, and infrastructure.
comte-catechism-1858:
Auguste Comte recast his positivist system as a catechism in 1852, and Richard Congreve Englished it in 1858. Positivism, Comte's philosophy, trusted science as the guide for modern society. Late in life he shaped it into a Religion of Humanity. The catechism form sets the teaching out as questions and answers.

A priest of the new faith instructs a woman who asks what positivism requires. Their talk covers worship, morals, family, and the order of society. Humanity itself, not God, stands as the object of devotion. The book shows Comte's system in its most personal form. It puzzled some followers and bound others closer.
dictionnaire-mytho-hermetique-dans-leque:
A dictionary of the hermetic tongue fills this Paris book of 1758, printed by Bauche at Sainte Geneviève. The title promises the fabled allegories of the poets, the metaphors, the riddles, and the barbarous terms of the hermetic philosophers, all explained. Its date reads M.DCC.LVIII, with approbation and privilege.

Pernety opens by saying no science ever needed a dictionary more. Readers, he says, cannot hold out half an hour in such books: the names seem empty, and the terms are set double on purpose. The authors warn that they are not to be read at the letter, and give one thing a thousand names. Entries then decode the myths, as with Vulcan's net for Mars and Venus. The book is a key to alchemy's fable code.
dreams-waking-thoughts-and-incidents-pg7:
William Beckford's Dreams, Waking Thoughts, and Incidents gathers his letters from various parts of Europe, opening on 19 June 1780. Beckford presents himself as an ideal being, with a frequent mist before his eyes that makes colours and forms faint and hazy.

He confesses frankly that he has no vanity about making remarks on his journey, and asks readers to accept his visionary way of gazing. The letters that follow mix dreams, waking thoughts and incidents from the road, in the voice of a young traveller of strong feeling. Readers of eighteenth-century travel writing will find Beckford dreamy, self-aware and unlike any ordinary tourist.
europmc-pmc10007858:
Yuan and co-workers review how the matrix around a tumor changes as cancer grows and learns to hide from the immune system, in a 2023 paper. A tumor is not just cancer cells. It sits in a scaffold of proteins and support cells that it reshapes to feed its own spread.

The authors trace how that reshaping helps tumors grow and escape immune attack. They then survey treatments that target the scaffold itself. The review connects basic cell science to drug ideas now in testing, in terms a general reader can follow.
europmc-pmc10390758:
Chen and co-authors gave a 2023 guide to multi-omics, a way to study disease with many data types at once. Each omics layer reads one part of the cell, such as genes, RNA, proteins, or small chemicals. Joining the layers can show how a disease works as a whole system. The guide is aimed at newcomers to the field.

Chen lays out the main tech types and warns on how to design a sound study. Machine learning and deep learning help merge the layers into one picture. Uses span cancer, brain disease, ageing, and the hunt for drug targets. Newer forms read single cells or keep each cell's place in tissue. The guide lists free tools and data banks for the work.
europmc-pmc10393958:
Choi and Park reviewed a stress protein called TXNIP in 2023 and its role in disease. TXNIP binds a guard protein, thioredoxin, that shields cells from damage. By gripping that guard, TXNIP weakens the shield and raises cell stress. New work shows the protein does far more than that.

Choi reports that TXNIP can switch on a danger complex that sparks swelling inside cells. It can also push cells toward death under stress from their inner stores. These acts link TXNIP to diabetes, kidney disease, and brain disorders. Drugs that block TXNIP are thus of keen interest. The review weighs how such drugs might treat these diseases.
europmc-pmc10497558:
Ling and co-authors reviewed amino acid metabolism in health and disease in 2023. Amino acids are the building blocks of proteins. Cells also burn them for energy and use them to grow and split. When their handling goes wrong, illness can follow across many organs.

Tumours lean hard on amino acids taken in from food and blood. Ling reports that blocking select paths can starve tumour cells while sparing normal ones. Immune cells also hinge on these paths, from killer T cells to calming Treg cells. The review spans cancer first, then metabolic, heart, and immune diseases. Each path offers fresh points where a drug might act.
europmc-pmc11256658:
Zheng and colleagues report national cancer statistics for China in 2016 in this 2022 paper. China's National Cancer Center publishes such figures yearly from population registries. For 2016, a total of 487 registries supplied high-quality data on new cases and deaths. Nationwide totals were estimated by scaling registry data to the national population.

China saw about 4.06 million new cancer cases in 2016, and about 2.41 million cancer deaths, they estimate. Lung, colorectal, stomach, liver, and female breast cancers were the five most common, at 57.4 percent of new cases. Lung, liver, stomach, colorectal, and oesophageal cancers led deaths, at 69.3 percent of the total. Rates were split by urban and rural area, sex, and fine age groups. Age-standardised rates used the world Segi population as the reference.
europmc-pmc11298558:
He, Zhou, and Wang review glycosylation, a sugar-tagging of proteins, in this 2024 paper. After a protein is built, cells often modify it by adding or removing chemical groups. Glycosylation transfers sugar chains onto specific amino acid sites using enzymes called glycosyltransferases. It ranks among the most common such modifications.

The tagging is essential for protein function, cell adhesion, and immune escape, the authors note. Faulty patterns are closely linked to cancer, inflammation, and autoimmune disorders. Yet the exact composition and structure of the sugar tags remain undetermined in many cases. The review argues for deeper mapping of tag structures and their varying levels across tissues. It also urges pairing that mapping with advanced detection technologies. Clinical implications run through the paper's closing sections.
europmc-pmc1175958:
Smith and colleagues propose strict definitions for the relations used in biomedical ontologies in this 2005 paper. An ontology is a controlled vocabulary: a fixed list of terms for a field, with definitions. Many biomedical lists use relations such as part-of and located-in loosely. The paper is part of a reform effort by the Open Biomedical Ontologies group.

The authors advance a method for giving each relational term a consistent, unambiguous formal definition. The goal is to help developers and users avoid errors in coding and annotation. The Gene Ontology shows the stakes: it holds three vocabularies, for cell components, molecular function, and biological process, and is reused by databases worldwide. A sloppy relation, copied everywhere, spreads silent errors. The method is offered for ontology building across the life sciences.
europmc-pmc1241758:
O'Neill and a workshop group tackled how wealth shapes pollution harm in 2003. Air pollution and social position each affect health on their own. Poor and working-class areas often face higher pollution too. Early studies hinted social position changes pollution effects themselves.

The authors propose theories for how the two forces interact. They draw on studies from around the world. Methods from air pollution science and social epidemiology are introduced side by side. Gaps in study design get direct attention. O'Neill calls for joint research that treats exposure and inequality together.
europmc-pmc1274258:
Larionov, Krause, and Miller described a standard-curve method for PCR data in 2005. Real-time PCR is the most precise way to measure gene activity. Raw output is a mass of glow numbers. Processing choices can shift final results a lot.

Their procedure skips efficiency estimation entirely. Noise is filtered by smoothing, baseline removal, and scaling. The reading threshold is picked on its own from the standard curve. Crossing points come straight from curve coordinates. Variation within each run gets a statistical estimate. Larionov cuts operator handling to a minimum. It appeared in BMC Bioinformatics in 2005. It ran in BMC Bioinformatics in 2005.
europmc-pmc1403158:
Ocean water teems with archaea, microbes akin to bacteria but with their own branch of life. Hallam and co-authors read genes from one such microbe in 2006, a sea form that lives with a sponge host. They rebuilt its likely routes for taking in carbon and gaining energy from those gene clues.

The genes point to a changed three-step cycle that fixes carbon dioxide into food. Other genes suggest the microbe can also eat organic carbon. Hallam also found genes for using ammonia as fuel. Matching genes turned up in seas worldwide. The work hints these tiny microbes help run ocean carbon and nitrogen cycles.
europmc-pmc1601958:
Drug hunters need to know where a drug can lodge on a protein. Huang and Schroeder improved a site-finding algorithm in 2006, LIGSITEcsc. It scans a protein surface for pockets, using geometry based on the Connolly surface, a smooth skin over the molecule.

The upgrade re-ranks candidate pockets by how conserved their surface residues are across species. Conserved spots tend to matter, so ranking by them greatly improved accuracy. On 48 paired and 210 bound structures, the tool hit success rates of 71 and 75 percent. Huang offers a web server and free source code.
europmc-pmc1634758:
Repetitive DNA clutters every complex genome, and curating it needs tools. Kohany and co-authors presented two in 2006 for Repbase, the reference database of repeats. RepbaseSubmitter formats and annotates new entries through a Java interface.

It auto-computes sequence length and composition, cutting common formatting errors. It can also predict protein-coding regions and pull in PubMed references and species data. The second tool, Censor, scans a new sequence against known repeats at speed. Its output maps the repeats found and can mask them. Both tools run as web services or downloads, Kohany reports.
europmc-pmc1635058:
Putting research into practice in veterans' hospitals needs more than memos. Stetler and co-authors evaluated external facilitation in 2006 within QUERI, a quality program of the Veterans Health Administration. Facilitators are helpers sent from outside a site to ease change.

Through interviews across several multi-site projects, the team found facilitation to be a deliberate, valued process. It joined interactive problem solving with support, tailored to each site's snags. Facilitators differed from other change agents by working problems live with local teams. Stetler argues the role deserves a clear definition, since studies had used the term loosely.
europmc-pmc1635558:
Back pain scales abound, but which detects change best? Lauridsen and co-authors compared five instruments head to head in 2006, in 191 Danish patients from primary and hospital care. They included two disability surveys, parts of a general health survey, a back pain rating scale, and a simple pain number scale.

The Roland Morris questionnaire was most responsive in patients with back pain only. In leg pain patients, it tied with the Oswestry index. Among patients who improved, the Roland Morris again led for back-only cases. Lauridsen gives clinics subpopulation-specific guidance instead of one verdict for all.
europmc-pmc1638158:
Children meet contaminants through air, skin, and mouth, and their habits set the dose. Cohen Hubal and co-authors reviewed in 2000 what is known about children's exposure and what data are missing. Regulators lean on default assumptions because child-specific data are scarce.

Assessing exposure needs activity patterns: where children play, what they touch, what they swallow. Such data are thinnest for the youngest children. The team calls for better age groupings for assessments, better monitoring methods, and data on contaminant levels and transfer rates. Cohen Hubal argues these gaps must close before rules can be trusted to protect children.
europmc-pmc1781458:
Provenzano and colleagues imaged in 2006 how collagen, the main support protein in tissue, is arranged around breast tumors. Dense collagen in breast tissue raises cancer risk, yet how its layout affects tumor growth and spread was unclear. The team studied the border where tumor cells meet surrounding stroma, the supporting tissue.

They used multiphoton laser microscopy and second harmonic imaging, methods that light up collagen in intact, unfixed tissue. The images gave three-dimensional views that normal slicing could not show, such as fibers radiating out from tumors. They defined three tumor-linked collagen patterns, named TACS, that mark where tumors sit and how they behave. Local invasion ran mostly along those altered fibers, suggesting the reshaped collagen helps cancer cells move outward.
europmc-pmc1885958:
Hladik, McElrath and co-authors recreated in 2007 the first hours of vaginal HIV infection in human tissue kept alive in the lab. Most HIV infections worldwide start through sexual contact in women, yet the opening steps were poorly observed for lack of a good model. Their organ culture system kept real vaginal tissue working outside the body.

On contact, HIV-1 rapidly entered two cell types: Langerhans cells inside the surface layer and CD4 T cells beneath it. Entry into T cells happened almost only by direct fusion through the CD4 and CCR5 receptors, and full productive infection followed. Langerhans cells instead swallowed the virus through several receptors, and intact virus lingered inside them for days without clear production. The split behavior may guide designs that block local spread.
europmc-pmc2124758:
J. C. Meakins, resident pathologist at the Presbyterian Hospital of New York, tested vaccine treatment against Staphylococcus aureus in 1910. The angle is opsonic immunity: serum factors that prepare germs to be eaten by white cells. Giving rabbits the germ killed by heat, he found, raises a high degree of that immunity.

Protection then tracks the serum's opsonic power. With opsonins high, animals could recover fully after a dose of living, virulent staphylococcus. Too-frequent vaccine doses, though, could push the opsonic power back down. The immune serum worked best against the very strain used to make it, and only slightly less well against other strains. Human staph infection also raised opsonins sharply, and vaccines could do the same in man. Readers get an early, measured case for vaccine therapy, stated with its limits attached.
europmc-pmc2125958:
A. Garvin, Christen Lundsgaard, and Donald D. Van Slyke measured lung volumes in women with tuberculosis for the third paper of their series, published in the Journal of Experimental Medicine in 1918. They recorded total capacity, middle capacity, and leftover air in twenty adult women, measured each chest, and used X-ray screening to follow how far the diaphragm moved.

Among eight women with early disease, five had near-normal total capacity with slightly raised leftover air and so a somewhat reduced breathing capacity. Three had much smaller totals, and each of those showed a clear added problem, such as widespread miliary disease or a blocked airway. In twelve women with middle or advanced disease, total and breathing capacity had fallen while leftover air stayed near normal, matching the pattern the team had found earlier in men.
europmc-pmc2131058:
Michael Heidelberger, Walther F. Goebel, and Oswald T. Avery isolated the specific substance of Friedländer's bacillus, applying methods proven on the pneumococcus to a second germ. Their paper is the first of a pair, in the Journal of Experimental Medicine in 1925. Toenniessen had earlier reported a nitrogen-free sugar substance from this bacillus's capsule material.

Their method yields a reactive polysaccharide free of nitrogen from the so-called E strain of the bacillus. It is a snow-white, non-reducing sugar chain from the capsule. The pneumococcus work had just tied that germ's specificity to its own sugar substance. Finding the same pattern in Friedländer's bacillus hints that coated germs share a plan. The pair's second paper sets this substance beside the Type II pneumococcus substance directly. A family likeness between germs, written in their capsule sugars, is coming into view.
europmc-pmc2140358:
John Northrop, at The Rockefeller Institute for Medical Research, presented a pepsin measurement method in a 1919 paper, with a study of how pepsin joins its substrate. Enzymes are known to be drawn out of solution by insoluble matter. Northrop followed pepsin digesting egg albumin by the change in the solution's conductivity, a signal that can be read as digestion proceeds.

The conductivity method gives a quantitative measure of pepsin. With it, the amount of pepsin a set weight of substrate pulls from solution was the same whatever the particle size of the substrate. There is a best acidity zone for the joining of enzyme and substrate, and it matches the best zone for digestion. Northrop suggests pepsin joins chiefly the ionized part of the protein.
europmc-pmc2140558:
Jacques Loeb studied selective diffusion through a living membrane in a 1922 paper, using eggs of the fish Fundulus. The egg membrane lets some substances pass and blocks others, and salts in the water change that traffic. Loeb compared common salt with calcium and lanthanum chlorides on acids, alkalies, and potassium chloride crossing the membrane.

Common salt blocked strong acids from diffusing in, like the other salts, but far weaker: it took a much stronger salt solution to match a trace of lanthanum chloride. The salts barely slowed weak, undissociated acids. Both common salt and calcium chloride sped dissociated strong alkali through the membrane, calcium the more. Common salt also sped potassium chloride in moderate strength, while calcium chloride did not.
europmc-pmc2140658:
Crozier, at Rutgers University, studied the temperature law of locomotion in a millipede, a diplopod, in a 1924 paper. Speeds of living processes roughly double or treble for a set rise in temperature, the van't Hoff rule, but that ratio is no constant and jumps near critical temperatures. Crozier uses the critical thermal increment of Arrhenius' equation, a sharper measure, on the millipede's walking speed.

Classifying vital activities by their temperature characteristics gives a way to account for variability in animal conduct, he argues. A process's controlling reaction can change as temperature moves far, bringing a different fundamental reaction into command of the speed. The paper works the millipede data through that scheme and sets out the characteristic value for this locomotion.
europmc-pmc2180258:
A rabbit can look healthy yet carry hidden disease, and Wade H. Brown, Louise Pearce, and Chester M. Van Allen ask whether organ weights give that away. Their 1926 study, the second in a series, weighs the organs of 295 apparently normal rabbits and compares the numbers with lesions found after death.

Even mild hidden disease seems to shift the weights of organs the disease never touches directly. The size of the shift tracks both how far the lesions extend and how active they are. Some evidence points the other way too: an animal's organ balance may shape how disease takes hold and runs its course. For laboratory work, the results warn that normal-looking animals are not all alike inside.
europmc-pmc2186358:
Sherman and colleagues described the DAVID Knowledgebase in 2007, a central database for interpreting large gene lists. Biological knowledge is scattered across many overlapping annotation databases run by separate groups. Analysts must visit many sites to assemble full information on their genes, a bottleneck for high-throughput studies. DAVID groups tens of millions of gene and protein identifiers into single clusters using a method called the DAVID Gene Concept.

Clustering identifiers improves cross-referencing, especially between the NCBI and UniProt systems. It lets more than forty public annotation sources be integrated around those clusters. The knowledgebase is freely downloadable as simple text files. A web interface lets users query varied annotations for large gene lists at once. For one gene, the system enriches the available biological information beyond any single source.
europmc-pmc2211558:
Hopewell and co-authors, with the CONSORT Group, extended reporting standards in 2008 to abstracts of randomised trials. Readers often judge a trial from its abstract alone, so abstracts need clear, complete detail. The team built a draft item list from existing tools and evidence. A three-round Delphi survey, a structured expert consensus process, selected the items, drawing 109 invited participants with a 61 percent response rate.

A January 2007 meeting in Montebello, Canada, finalised the checklist with 26 trialists, statisticians and editors. Recommended items cover objectives, design, participants, interventions, main outcomes and harms. They also cover conclusions, trial registration and funding source. The checklist recommends a structured abstract format. A companion explanation gives examples of good reporting and the reasoning behind each item.
europmc-pmc2216058:
Kern reviewed evidence in 2007 that inflammation drives the early stages of diabetic retinopathy, eye damage from diabetes. The disease was classically seen as purely a blood vessel problem. Diabetic retinas, however, show many inflammation hallmarks: raised inflammatory enzymes and signals, more nitric oxide, vessel leakage and white cells sticking in capillaries. The review focuses mainly on studies in living animals.

Early tissue changes include tiny capillary bulges, loss of supporting pericyte cells, and blocked, degenerating capillaries that cut retinal perfusion. Blocking inflammatory mediators with drugs, or deleting them genetically, significantly slowed those early lesions in many studies. A common thread among successful therapies was suppressing inflammatory mediator production. The hypothesis opens new drug targets for a disease that still lacks early treatments.
europmc-pmc2561058:
Daetwyler, Villanueva, and Woolliams worked out formulae in 2008 for how accurately a person's genetic risk of a complex disease can be predicted from genome-wide data. Predicting risk works well for simple inherited diseases, but complex diseases draw on thousands of genes. The authors derived simple equations that forecast prediction accuracy from study design, without needing each gene's frequency or effect size.

Simulations confirmed the equations were close. Accuracy turned out to hinge mainly on one product: the number of people studied per risk gene, times the disease's heritability. The formulae let researchers size a study to reach a target accuracy before spending on it. They also show how population studies and case-control studies compare, and mark an upper bound that better methods might approach.
europmc-pmc2648658:
Gray and co-authors reviewed in 2009 how a warming climate may change ticks and the diseases they pass to people in Europe. Ticks spread Lyme disease and a brain infection called tick-borne encephalitis. Both illnesses had grown more common over twenty years, and many blamed warmer weather.

For the sheep tick, the main carrier, the range has crept north and uphill, and winter activity has risen as winters softened. Hotter summers may shift the season, pushing most tick activity into the later part of the year. Models suggest eight major tick species could settle farther north as the climate warms. The authors urge care, though: these diseases depend on hosts, habitats, and human habits too. Blaming climate alone, they say, outruns the proof, and better models must fold in living processes.
europmc-pmc2654758:
Van Melderen and Saavedra De Bast reviewed in 2009 a curious paired weapon found across the bacterial world: toxin-antitoxin systems. Each pair joins two genes. One makes a stable poison that can harm the cell. The other makes a fragile antidote that keeps the poison in check.

Some of these pairs act like selfish hitchhikers. They ride on mobile DNA pieces, and if a daughter cell loses the piece, the antidote fades while the poison lasts, killing the cell. That death forces the piece to be kept. Other pairs sit fixed in the main chromosome, and their purpose is far less clear. The review weighs the leading ideas: stress survival, programmed death for the good of the group, and simple self-preservation of the genes themselves.
europmc-pmc2654858:
Haram, Svendsen, and Abildgaard reviewed in 2009 the HELLP syndrome, a dangerous complication of pregnancy. Its name joins three signs: red blood cells breaking apart, raised liver enzymes, and a low count of platelets, the cells that help blood clot. It appears in under one percent of pregnancies, and in up to a fifth of severe preeclampsia cases.

Most cases arise before birth, mainly between weeks 27 and 37 of pregnancy; the rest appear within two days after delivery. The review covers how to spot the syndrome, how to classify its severity by platelet counts, and the risks it carries for mother and baby. Delivery is the core treatment once week 34 passes, or sooner if either patient worsens. Steroid drugs can help the baby's lungs mature before an early birth. Waiting longer is debated and suits only carefully chosen early cases.
europmc-pmc2694358:
Raychaudhuri and colleagues, with the International Schizophrenia Consortium, presented in 2009 GRAIL, a method that finds the real culprit genes hiding in lists of disease-linked genome regions. Genome scans return dozens of regions; the hard part is telling signal from noise. GRAIL scores how related the genes across regions are, mining a quarter million published abstracts for shared biology.

Genes in one true pathway tend to be talked about together in the literature, so relatedness betrays them. Tested on known lipid and height regions, the method picked out the connected subsets cleanly. On 74 borderline Crohn disease signals, it flagged 13; ten of those then confirmed in follow-up typing. On 165 rare deletions from schizophrenia patients, most of them innocent, it found 16 whose genes cluster on brain synapses.
