Gut microbes, blood markers, and past illness may help too. The authors argue that no single test is enough. A combined score could pick the patients most likely to gain.
europmc-pmc6243058:
Duan and co-authors review links between high-fat diets and disease. Eating too much fat is a changeable risk factor. It links to diabetes and some cancers. How it harms health is still poorly understood. The review appeared in Frontiers in Immunology.

The authors focus on inflammation as the bridge. A high-fat diet can trigger lasting inflammation. That inflammation then feeds disease growth. Cancer development is covered as well. The review sets out the main mechanisms involved. Gut changes and immune shifts both feature. The authors argue that grasping these paths matters. The world intake of high-fat food keeps rising. Better knowledge could guide new treatment strategies.
europmc-pmc6271758:
Huang and co-authors review new findings on the chemical makeup of propolis. Their review appeared in Molecules. Propolis is the resinous seal bees make for their hives. It is built from plant resins, wax, oils, and pollen. Bees gather resins from poplars, pines, and many other plants. The mix varies with place, plant source, and bee species.

A database search found 241 compounds reported for the first time between 2000 and 2012. They joined about three hundred compounds known before. Classes span flavonoids, terpenes, and phenolic acids. Folk use covers colds, wounds, and dental care. Lab work supports anti-inflammatory and antimicrobial effects. The authors argue that many compounds act together. That synergy may explain why whole propolis beats single parts. The review maps what is known for future product work.
europmc-pmc6279758:
Bartoschek and co-authors split breast cancer support cells into three distinct subclasses. Their study appeared in Nature Communications. The cells are cancer-associated fibroblasts. They fill much of the tumour surroundings. Their origins and jobs were unclear because the group is mixed. The team read single cell gene activity in a mouse breast cancer model.

Seven hundred sixty-eight cell profiles were gathered after a sorting step. Three subclasses stood out with clear gene signatures. Each sat in a distinct place in the tumour. Origins ranged from blood vessel walls to fat tissue and the tumour lining itself. Human tumours showed the same split. Each subclass gene profile also predicted spread risk on its own. Naming the subclasses opens paths to precise drugs against them.
europmc-pmc6375658:
Gentzke and co-authors present a Vital Signs surveillance report in the Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report. Using National Youth Tobacco Survey data from 2011 to 2018, they tracked tobacco use among US middle and high school students across seven product types.

In 2018, 27.1 percent of high school students and 7.2 percent of middle school students had used a tobacco product in the past month. E-cigarettes were the most common product at both levels. Between 2017 and 2018, e-cigarette use jumped 78 percent among high school students. That surge erased recent progress in cutting overall youth tobacco use. The authors urge full tobacco control measures plus FDA regulation.
europmc-pmc6417258:
Myint and co-authors present a statistics method in BMC Genomics for reporter assays. Massively parallel reporter assays test thousands of DNA switches at once. Analysis methods for them have been ad hoc, with little head-to-head testing.

Their method, mpralm, uses linear models to test each switch's activity. Across several datasets it proved well calibrated and powerful. It beat existing tools in the first broad comparison of its kind. How barcodes are summed also proved to matter, the authors show. Their tool is offered for labs studying non-coding DNA.
europmc-pmc6440158:
Zheng and co-authors report that a circular RNA in colon cancer, circPPP1R12A, encodes a small protein that pushes tumors to grow and spread. Circular RNAs were mainly known as regulators that sponge up microRNAs; evidence that some also make proteins is newer. Screening tumor tissue found this circle sharply elevated in colon cancer.

Patients with higher levels survived significantly less time. The encoded protein, 73 amino acids long, switched on Hippo-YAP signaling, a growth-control pathway, and boosted proliferation, migration, and invasion in cells and tumors in mice. Knocking the circle down weakened those behaviors. A hidden protein product thus joins the list of colon cancer drivers worth targeting.
europmc-pmc6448958:
Uthman and co-authors test whether three diabetes drugs in the SGLT2 inhibitor class share a direct heart effect beyond lowering blood sugar: blocking the sodium-hydrogen exchanger in heart muscle cells. Mouse heart cells received empagliflozin or dapagliflozin at 1 micromole per liter, or canagliflozin at 3, matching the levels patients carry. All three slowed the exchanger and dropped sodium inside the cells from 12.7 to between 10 and 11.

Computer models placed each drug neatly on the exchanger's sodium-binding site. In whole mouse hearts kept beating outside the body, empagliflozin and canagliflozin also widened heart vessels, while energy stores held steady. Cutting heart sodium as a class effect could matter in heart failure and diabetes, where sodium runs high.
europmc-pmc6464058:
Northstone and co-authors update the roster of the Avon Longitudinal Study of Parents and Children, the Bristol birth cohort recruited through pregnancies in 1990 to 1992. The original campaign enrolled 14,541 pregnancies, and the index children have been followed ever since through questionnaires, clinics, samples, and record linkage. Late enrolment matters because cohort studies usually only shrink.

Since age seven, 913 additional index participants joined, 195 of them after turning eighteen, through recruitment drives and opportunistic contact. The baseline now stands at 14,901 index children alive at one year. A three-generation structure, grandparents, parents, and now grandchildren, makes the topped-up sample a continuing resource.
europmc-pmc6477058:
Martin and co-authors review how gut microbes steer the body's chemistry by steering gut hormone release. Hormone-making cells spread through the gut lining secrete CCK, PYY, GLP-1, GIP, and serotonin, which together tune insulin response, blood sugar control, fat storage, and appetite. Bacteria and their products are among the signals those cells listen to.

Bacterial products and cell wall parts reach the sensors in the gut wall and shift hormone output, making the gut flora a chemistry organ by proxy. Diet or drug changes that reshape the flora therefore double as hormone therapy candidates for obesity and metabolic disease. The exact handshakes between certain bacteria and certain cells get the closest reading.
europmc-pmc6513858:
Cravens, Payne and Smolke review ways to make plant natural products in microbes. Their review appeared in Nature Communications. Plant products serve as medicines, flavours and fragrances. Many are hard to make or harvest at scale. Crop supply can fail with pests or bad weather.

Engineers move a plant pathway into a host such as yeast. The work runs in design, build and test cycles. It acts at three levels: host, pathway and enzyme. Hosts must supply enough precursor material. Routes must be planned and missing enzymes found or built. A recent case built a 25-enzyme route to noscapine. The authors also cover making new derivatives and future tools.
europmc-pmc6555258:
Hogan, Chini and Chini review CD38, a surface enzyme that has become a prime drug target, writing in Frontiers in Immunology. CD38 sits on immune cells and breaks down NAD+, a molecule cells need for energy and repair. The authors' own work recast it from a mere cell marker into the body's main NAD+ drain.

Because CD38 faces outward, it also consumes the raw materials cells import to rebuild NAD+. During aging, CD38-carrying immune cells build up in tissues and drag NAD+ levels down, a process tied to the slow burn called inflammaging. In tumors, the same drain can blunt immune attack. The review closes with ways to block CD38 or boost NAD+, from small-molecule blockers to flavonoids, aimed at aging and metabolic disease.
europmc-pmc6602458:
Xu and co-authors present OrthoVenn2, a web server for comparing whole genomes. Their article appears in Nucleic Acids Research. The tool groups orthologous genes across species into clusters. Shared clusters hint at shared function. Diverged clusters hint at distinct roles.

OrthoVenn2 compares up to 12 species at once, up from six. Its species library now spans vertebrates, fungi, plants, and bacteria. An occurrence table shows how clusters overlap between species. An interactive Venn diagram displays the same overlaps. Annotations and summaries attach to each cluster group. A stand-alone version handles larger data sets locally. The server is free to use online.
europmc-pmc6708158:
Zhang and co-authors tested how to make epigenetic clocks more exact. These clocks guess a person's age from chemical marks on DNA. A gap between clock age and real age has been linked to death risk. The team asked whether a sharper clock changes that link.

They trained age predictors on as many as 13,661 DNA samples, mostly from blood. As training data grew, the clock got far more exact. With the best clock, the age gap no longer linked to death in two Scottish birth cohorts. Small training sets, they warn, can be thrown off by the mix of cell types in a sample.
europmc-pmc6800358:
Vázquez-Rodríguez and co-authors mapped how brain structure and function are tethered across the neocortex. White matter wiring promotes synchrony between brain areas, producing patterned activity networks. Whether wiring and activity track each other evenly was unknown. The team tested the relationship region by region across the cortex.

Structure and function aligned closely in primary sensory and motor areas. They diverged in higher-order regions, such as the default mode and salience networks. The decoupling followed the cortex's representational and cellular hierarchies, forming a smooth gradient. A geometry-based model out-predicted a topology-based one in about 70% of nodes. Long connections in higher areas seem less spatially constrained. The gradient reframes how brain organization should be modeled.
europmc-pmc6918658:
Mao and co-authors test a stem-cell signal that may limit heart attack damage. Their study appeared in Stem Cell Research and Therapy. Heart attacks kill heart muscle and carry high rates of death and disability. Tiny vesicles called exosomes, released by stem cells, pass messages between cells after injury.

The team loaded exosomes from human mesenchymal stem cells with a long RNA named KLF3-AS1. In rats and in oxygen-starved heart cells, these exosomes shrank damaged areas. They also cut a fiery form of cell death called pyroptosis. The RNA works by soaking up a small RNA, miR-138-5p, which frees a protective protein, Sirt1. Blocking that protein reversed the benefit.
europmc-pmc6990758:
He and co-authors pool trial evidence on acupuncture and acupressure for cancer pain. Their systematic review and meta-analysis appeared in JAMA Oncology. More than 70 percent of cancer patients suffer pain, and nearly half get inadequate control. Standard pain ladders work, but addiction risk and side effects limit them.

Earlier reviews, more than 20 of them, never reached a firm verdict. Newer, stricter randomised trials had also appeared since. The team updated the synthesis across those trials. Acupuncture and acupressure were associated with reduced pain and lower opioid use in the pooled results. Variation between studies was large, which trimmed the certainty grade. The authors call for trials in specific pain types and treatment phases to pin down where these therapies help most.
europmc-pmc7003858:
Fenwick and co-authors review how T cells wear out during HIV infection. Their review appeared in Immunological Reviews. T cells are the adaptive immune system's killers of infected and cancerous cells. When a virus will not go away, constant exposure to its antigens drives T cells into a broken state called exhaustion.

Exhaustion leaves HIV poorly controlled. It persists even in patients whose virus is suppressed by antiretroviral therapy, shaping how fast the disease advances. The markers of exhaustion also help guard the hidden pool of latently infected cells that blocks a cure. Blocking one marker, PD-1, doubled virus-fighting output from patients' CD8 T cells in the authors' own work. After treatment stops, marker levels predict how soon the virus rebounds. The review ends by weighing how these markers might be exploited in cure strategies.
europmc-pmc7006158:
Ono and co-authors review RANKL, a signal that links bone, immunity, and much more. Their review appeared in Inflammation and Regeneration. RANKL tells precursor cells to become osteoclasts, the cells that eat bone. Its partners, the receptor RANK and the decoy osteoprotegerin, form a system without which bone diseases such as osteopetrosis follow.

RANKL was first found as a T cell product that activates dendritic cells. It also builds lymph nodes and shapes immune cell development, a dual role that founded the field of osteoimmunology. The signal reaches further still: mammary glands, hair follicles, body temperature, muscle metabolism, and tumour growth. In skin, sunlight triggers it in surface cells, expanding regulatory T cells that calm inflammation. The review gathers current knowledge of the trio across all these processes. Few single signals, the authors show, touch so many systems.
europmc-pmc7023758:
Lei and co-authors review circular RNAs in human cancer in the journal Molecular Cancer. Circular RNAs are loops of RNA with no free ends. They were long classed as non-coding by-products of splicing. Newer work shows that some of them are in fact translated into small proteins.

The review first sets out what circular RNAs are and what they do. They can soak up microRNAs, tune gene activity, and bind proteins. The authors then explain two routes that may start protein building without a normal cap. They survey the cancer-linked cases found so far. These hidden proteins, they argue, open a neglected part of the human proteome. That could matter for cancer diagnosis and treatment.
europmc-pmc7054558:
Qiu proposes a change of attitude toward missing data in single-cell sequencing in Nature Communications, writing as sole author. Single-cell RNA sequencing reads only a small fraction of each cell's RNA. The missing entries, called dropouts, plague the method. Nearly every analysis algorithm tries to work around them through gene selection, dimension reduction, or filling the gaps with imputed values.

Qiu argues the dropout pattern itself is a useful signal. By converting counts into a simple present-or-absent binary record, a co-occurrence clustering algorithm can group cells using only which genes dropped out together. Across several published datasets, that binary pattern sorted cells into types as accurately as the expression levels of highly variable genes. Recognising dropouts as information rather than damage, Qiu suggests, opens a different direction for building single-cell analysis tools.
europmc-pmc7056458:
Lin and co-authors assess natural compounds as helpers in cancer therapy in the British Journal of Pharmacology. Standard chemotherapy suffers from toxicity throughout the body. Combining several drugs with different targets already improves efficacy and softens side effects. Plant-based products offer a less toxic source of partners, and interest in them as adjuvants keeps growing.

Laboratory evidence suggests herbal extracts such as Solanum nigrum and Claviceps purpurea can help. Pure compounds including curcumin, resveratrol, and matairesinol can weaken cancer's resistance to drugs and protect healthy tissue when paired with antitumour medicines. Traditional Chinese medicine used alongside chemotherapy has improved quality of life and eased bone marrow suppression in lung and gastric cancer studies. The authors add a caution: plant products carry their own adverse effects and can interact with drugs. More work is needed before such supplements earn a routine place.
europmc-pmc7091858:
Zheng and co-authors report that the virus-fighting lymphocytes of COVID-19 patients showed signs of exhaustion, in Cellular and Molecular Immunology. Natural killer cells and CD8 T cells are needed to control viral infections. The team studied 68 patients at two hospitals linked to Anhui Medical University in China, with 55 mild and 13 severe cases.

Total counts of both cell types dropped sharply in infected patients. A surface marker called NKG2A, linked to cell exhaustion, rose on the remaining cells. In patients recovering after treatment, cell counts returned and NKG2A fell. The pattern suggests the virus weakens antiviral defences early, and that blocking NKG2A might restore them.
europmc-pmc7125958:
Kinoshita reviews how mammals build GPI-anchored proteins and what those proteins do, in Open Biology. At least 150 human proteins are held on the cell surface by a GPI anchor instead of crossing the membrane. The anchor attaches to the protein's end and embeds its fat chains in the membrane's outer layer.

Anchored proteins gather in membrane rafts and often sit on one face of polarised cells. Some ferry cargo across cells; others are cut loose and shed. Kinoshita walks through the assembly pathway step by step and gives examples of anchor-dependent jobs, from enzymes to adhesion molecules. Faults in the pathway cause human GPI deficiency diseases.
europmc-pmc7177758:
Yue and López review how MAPK signaling pathways control apoptosis, the orderly death of cells. Their article appeared in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences. MAPKs are protein kinases that relay signals inside the cell. They guide many processes, from growth to stress response. In cell death, their role is double-sided.

The same pathway can start apoptosis or block it. Which way it acts depends on the cell type and the trigger. The authors lay out the main pro-death and pro-survival routes. They also explain feedback loops that sharpen the response. A simple guide links signal strength and duration to the outcome. Work in frog eggs shows how salt stress uses these pathways. Readers get a framework for predicting cell fate.
europmc-pmc7221158:
Petitprez and co-authors review how the tissue around a tumor shapes response to immune checkpoint therapy. Their article appeared in Frontiers in Immunology. A tumor's neighborhood holds immune cells, blood vessel cells, and fibroblasts. Checkpoint drugs work by freeing immune cells already inside the tumor. Who those neighbors are can make or break the treatment.

Evidence points first to the amount and orientation of T cells present. Other components, from vessel growth to scar-like fibroblasts, also sway outcomes. Such features may help select patients for these expensive drugs. They may also suggest drug combinations that warm up cold tumors. The authors gather a fast-growing body of studies. Their message: treating cancer now means reading its whole ecosystem.
europmc-pmc7244758:
Hu and co-authors show how a protein called IGF2BP2 props up a cancer-promoting RNA in pancreatic cancer. Their study appeared in Cell Death and Differentiation. IGF2BP2 normally manages cell metabolism. Its rise in tumors tracks with poor patient outcomes. Cutting it back slowed cancer cell growth in their tests.

The protein works by reading m6A marks on other RNAs. One target is DANCR, a long noncoding RNA that drives cell growth and stem-like traits. IGF2BP2 binds DANCR and raises its levels. Tests in animals confirmed the partnership matters in living tumors. A specific mark site on DANCR was identified and mutated to prove the link. The authors present this reader-and-RNA pair as a therapeutic lead. Pancreatic cancer badly needs such leads.
europmc-pmc7257158:
Hao, Vadgama and Wang review how a small immune signal helps cancers grow and spread. Their review appeared in Cell Communication and Signaling. The signal is CCL2, and its main receptor is CCR2. CCL2 draws immune cells toward tumors. High levels of both have been linked to worse disease in many cancers.

The authors focus most on prostate cancer. They explain how CCL2 and CCR2 support tumor growth, new blood vessels and spread to bone. They also cover links to relapse and to obesity. Work from their group and others is used to judge the pair as a drug target. Readers get a clear map of one pathway in cancer biology.
europmc-pmc7260058:
Warrington and co-authors present XTRACT, a software package that automatically maps white matter tracts in brain scans. Their methods paper appeared in Neuroimage. Tractography traces the brain's wiring from diffusion imaging data. Doing it by hand is slow, and results vary between laboratories.

XTRACT carries a library of standard protocols for pulling out known tracts in both human and macaque brains. The team tested it on Human Connectome Project and UK Biobank scans, plus macaque data, and built atlases of tracts and their endpoints. The protocols held up across data quality, matched known anatomy, and still preserved real differences between people, including twin similarities. The package is released publicly through FSL, so other groups can run the same standard extractions.
europmc-pmc7296058:
Ge and co-authors review the pentose phosphate pathway and its roles in type 2 diabetes and cancer. Their review appeared in Frontiers in Endocrinology. The pathway branches off from glucose processing. It does not make energy currency for the cell; instead it produces NADPH, a molecule cells use for building and antioxidant defense, and ribose 5-phosphate, a building block for nucleic acids.

Those outputs make the pathway a central regulator of the cell's chemical balance and growth. Its enzymes are reported to matter in many human diseases. Growing cells, including cancer cells, depend on its supplies, while disturbed activity features in diabetes. The authors gather what is known about the pathway's enzymes in both diseases and where intervention might help.
europmc-pmc7332158:
Tangcharoensathien and co-authors report a World Health Organization consultation in the Journal of Medical Internet Research on the COVID-19 infodemic. An infodemic is a flood of mixed true and false information during an outbreak. The online consultation crowdsourced ideas from officials, researchers, media, and platforms.

Participants offered 594 ideas for action. The analysis team condensed them into 50 proposed actions for managing infodemics in health emergencies. Core lessons include basing messages on evidence, turning knowledge into clear steps people can act on, and listening to community concerns. Partnerships with social media firms, universities, and civic groups also matter. Readers get a practical framework for fighting rumor alongside disease.
europmc-pmc7337658:
Dweck and co-authors report a global survey study in European Heart Journal Cardiovascular Imaging. It describes heart scan findings in patients with COVID-19. The survey captured echocardiography done in hospitals in April 2020. It also asked which patients gain most from such scans.

The survey covered 1,216 patients from 69 countries across six continents. The authors report that 55 percent had an abnormal scan. Left and right heart problems were both common. Some patients showed new heart attack, heart muscle inflammation, or stress-related heart failure. Severe disease appeared in 15 percent of patients. Blood test markers and symptom severity helped predict who had problems. Scans changed care for one third of patients. Readers get an early global picture of COVID-19 heart harm.
europmc-pmc7408158:
Rébé and Ghiringhelli review interleukin-1 beta in cancer in Cancers. Inside a tumor, this inflammatory signal is made by immune cells, fibroblasts, and cancer cells themselves. Making it takes two steps: priming switches the gene on, then an inflammasome activates the cutting enzyme that matures it.

Once released, IL-1 beta drives gene programs in target cells and acts on immunity, blood vessel growth, cancer cell growth, migration, and spread. Cancer treatments themselves can provoke its release, with opposite effects on progression. That ambiguity frames the review's core question: should doctors block IL-1 beta in cancer treatment, and when? Gene variants and cell context steer the answer, the authors show.
europmc-pmc7424058:
Jurga and co-authors gather what is known about markers that identify microglia, the resident immune cells of the brain. These cells shift shape and role as brain conditions change. Picking the right marker is key to telling one cell state from another.

The review sorts markers by type: general and specific, on the cell surface or inside it, and some that cells release. It shows how to tell true microglia from macrophages that enter from the blood. It also covers active states, from harmful M1-like cells to healing M2-like cells. Human and rodent markers differ, which adds care to study design. The guide helps labs choose markers for work on brain inflammation and disease.
europmc-pmc7453858:
Wolff and co-authors review risk factors for severe and fatal COVID-19. With no vaccine or drug at the time, shielding high-risk people mattered most. Risk clues also hint at where treatments might act.

The review searched PubMed and a preprint set, then sorted risk factors into groups. It drew on 28 records, eleven of them preprints. High age, obesity, diabetes, and hypertension stood out as risks. Poor general health linked with worse courses again and again. Damage to the heart, liver, and kidneys marked severe cases. Clotting problems may drive much of that harm. Some risks, such as time to hospital entry and tuberculosis, were absent from official lists. The authors say the map can guide later COVID-19 research.
europmc-pmc7734058:
Huang and co-authors trace a circular RNA that drives liver cancer growth. The molecule, hsa_circRNA_104348, was sharply raised in tumor tissue and cells. Patients with high levels had a poor outlook. The team tested its effects in cancer cells and in mice.

Raising this RNA sped cell growth, movement, and invasion, and blocked cell death. It works by sponging a small RNA, miR-187-3p, which frees a target gene, RTKN2. This chain also switches on the Wnt and beta-catenin path. Knocking the circular RNA down slowed tumor growth and lung spread in mice. The authors propose it as a marker and a target.
europmc-pmc7755058:
The CDC COVID-19 Response Team maps how COVID-19 spread unevenly across the United States. It covers February 12 to April 7, 2020. By April 7, the nation had 395,926 cases and 12,757 deaths. The team compared case counts, rates, and growth speed by state and territory.

Rates ranged from 20.6 cases per 100,000 people in Minnesota to 915.3 in New York City. The national doubling time was about 6.5 days. Growth in the last week ranged just as wide between places. The authors blame timing of arrival, density, age mix, testing, and control steps. They urge close tracking at local level to steer the response.
europmc-pmc7759458:
Van Hout and co-authors release exome data for the first wave of UK Biobank participants. The biobank follows 502,543 people with rich health and gene data. Exomes are the gene parts that code for proteins. Reading them in bulk exposes rare variants that array tests miss or must guess at.

The release covers 49,960 people and about 4 million coding variants. Of these, 98.6% occur in less than 1% of people. The set holds 198,269 predicted loss-of-function variants. Over 97% of genes had at least one carrier of such a variant. Tests across 1,730 traits found fresh links, and 2% of people held a medically actionable variant.
europmc-pmc7794558:
Esteva and co-authors survey deep learning for medical computer vision. A decade of fast progress in artificial intelligence opened new uses in medicine. Computer vision systems can now read images and video at high skill.

The authors first sum up ten years of work on convolutional neural networks. They explain the vision tasks these networks enable in health care. Example fields include cardiology, pathology, dermatology, and eye care. Each stands to gain from automated image reading. The survey then turns to medical video. Vision tools could support clinical work as procedures unfold. A final section weighs the hurdles to real clinical use.
europmc-pmc7919858:
Dan and co-authors report a study of immune memory to SARS-CoV-2 over the months after infection. How memory fades or holds shapes vaccine design and the future course of the pandemic. The team measured several arms of memory at once. They studied 254 samples from 188 COVID-19 cases, some taken six months or more after illness began.

Antibodies to the spike protein held fairly steady over six months. Memory B cells for the spike grew more common over time. T cells told a different story. Both CD4+ and CD8+ memory cells faded with a half-life of 3-5 months. Each arm of memory thus followed its own clock. The authors argue that reading only one arm gives a skewed view of protection. Their combined picture helps judge how long defence may last.
europmc-pmc8276758:
Rodríguez-Daza and co-authors assess polyphenols as modulators of the gut microbiota. Plant polyphenols often pass through the gut unabsorbed. Gut microbes hold the enzymes that unlock them.

Those enzymes turn polyphenols into active, available forms. In return, polyphenols reshape the microbe community. Sequencing and metabolome data have charted several action modes. Some effects look like true prebiotic action. The compounds are not yet classed as prebiotics in the strict sense. Certain probiotic strains carry enzymes such as tannase that aid the process. The review maps a two-way exchange. Health benefits to the host are the end goal traced.
europmc-pmc8470858:
Li and co-authors review how probiotics, prebiotics, synbiotics, and postbiotics act on metabolic disease. All four steer the gut microbiota, a key player in these diseases. That makes them hopeful tools for prevention and care.

The narrative review sums up effects on obesity and type 2 diabetes in most depth. Three mechanisms lead. The products reshape microbe mix, tune microbe-made compounds, and strengthen the gut barrier. Trial results in patients are weighed as well. Open points include use in pregnancy diabetes and the best synbiotic blends. Postbiotic gains need more proof. The authors map what is settled and what is still disputed.
europmc-pmc8519958:
Forner and co-authors give a systematic portrait of the 5xFAD mouse model of Alzheimer disease. Mouse models are core tools for probing disease roots and testing new treatments. With so many models on hand, picking the right one and age is a hard first step.

The team profiled the model across its whole lifespan on a clean genetic background. An 18-month point, seldom studied, was included. They measured plaque load, amyloid levels, and tissue damage. Brain function tests and behavior checks joined the set. Glial and neuron changes were tracked too. Gene data from cortex and hippocampus can be browsed online.
europmc-pmc8554658:
Liu and co-authors review how cancers resist chemotherapy and radiotherapy at molecular level. Surgery is the main first treatment for cancer, but spread at diagnosis keeps survival low. Chemo and radiation add key support in combined care. Resistance to them can sink the whole plan.

Radiation resistance grows from DNA repair, cell cycle faults, and stubborn cancer stem cells. Shape change through EMT adds to it. Drug resistance uses many tricks of its own. The review sorts these mechanisms in clear order. It then covers new strategies built to break resistance. Better targets and markers may lift treatment outcomes, the authors argue.
europmc-pmc8568058:
Dyba and co-authors estimate the European cancer burden for the year 2020. Europe holds a large share of world cancer cases, so firm counts matter. Their report covers incidence and deaths for 25 major cancers. It spans 40 countries plus the European Union as a bloc.

The estimates rest on data from 151 population-based cancer registries, plus death records and population counts. They put new cases at about 4 million, with about 2 million cancer deaths. Breast, colorectal, lung, and prostate cancers led the new cases. Those four made up half the total burden. Lung cancer led the deaths, ahead of colorectal and breast cancers.
europmc-pmc8633358:
Fang and co-authors review natural products that may protect the kidneys from the cancer drug cisplatin. Cisplatin treats many cancers well, but it harms the kidneys. Between 20 and 35 percent of patients develop acute kidney injury after treatment. The harm builds with dose and can force doctors to stop the drug.

The review sets out how cisplatin injures kidney tissue. Paths include cell death, oxidative stress, inflammation, and vessel harm. It then sums up studies of natural compounds that fight these paths. Plant groups covered include flavonoids, saponins, and alkaloids. Many show protective effects in cell and animal tests. The authors frame these as leads for future kidney-safe care.
europmc-pmc8753858:
Husereau and co-authors present CHEERS 2022, updated reporting guidance for health economic evaluations. These studies compare the costs and effects of health options. The first CHEERS statement came out in 2013 to make such reports clear and useful. This new version replaces that guidance in full.

The update reflects new methods in the field. It also builds in a larger role for patients and the public. It applies to any health effort, simple or complex, in any setting. A 28-item checklist anchors the statement. The authors explain each item and what good reporting looks like. The aim is reports that readers can trust and use.
europmc-pmc8791758:
Sule, Condon, and Gomes review oxidative stress as a shared feature of pesticide toxicity. Pesticide use keeps rising, since these agents cut pests and raise crop growth. They also carry risks for people and wildlife. Links span heart disease, cancer, and birth defects, and labels urge limited exposure.

Across types, pesticides induce oxidative stress in cells and animals. Both oxygen and nitrogen reactive species take part. These species can switch on at least five signal paths, including one that kills cells via mitochondria. Added antioxidants eased the harm in some lab studies. The review frames oxidative stress as the common thread in pesticide harm.
europmc-pmc8825858:
Zhang and co-authors review lipophagy, a selective way cells digest their own fat stores. In lipophagy, the cell's cleanup system breaks down lipid droplets. This process helps control stored fat, free fatty acids, and energy balance. It matters across many cell types and body states. Yet how lipids themselves steer this cleanup is still unclear.

The review lays out what lipophagy is and how it is regulated. It then asks what faulty lipophagy does in metabolic disease. Fatty liver disease and metabolic syndrome both appear. Cancer gets a careful, open-ended treatment. The authors note that faulty cleanup can leave cells open to death signals. Readers get a full map of a young research field. Open questions are flagged throughout.
europmc-pmc8836058:
Cheng, Chen, and Chen examine osteoporosis driven by hormone imbalance. One form follows estrogen loss after menopause. Bone then breaks down faster than it rebuilds. A second form follows heavy glucocorticoid use. Those drugs thin bone and raise fracture risk. The review compares the two forms side by side.

The authors explain how estrogen normally restrains bone-eating cells. They show how its loss unleashes signals that speed bone loss. They then trace how excess glucocorticoids push stem cells toward fat instead of bone. Those drugs also hasten the death of bone-building cells. Treatment sections contrast the two cases. Estrogen support leads for the first form. Limiting steroid dose leads for the second. Shared drugs, such as bisphosphonates, are also weighed.
europmc-pmc8850458:
Ji and co-authors build a platform that destroys chosen proteins by feeding them to the cell's recycling system. The method is called AUTOTAC. Its molecules have two ends. One end grips the target protein. The other wakes a dormant autophagy receptor, p62. The woken receptor gathers the target into bodies for disposal. The lysosome then degrades the cargo.

The team tested AUTOTACs against several cancer proteins. They also targeted stubborn protein aggregates tied to neurodegeneration. The molecules worked at nanomolar strength in cells and in living animals. Degradation came with a boost to overall autophagic flow. The authors present AUTOTAC as a general tool. It could serve basic research and drug design alike. Proteins once called undruggable are the prize.
europmc-pmc9005658:
Wang and co-authors show that a master immune switch in microglia drives tau spread and harm in mice. Tau clumps define Alzheimer's and kin diseases. Microglia, the brain's immune cells, switch on around them. What that switch-on does was unclear. The switch here is NF-κB, a gene control hub. Tau itself turns it on in microglia. The team forced it on and off in a tau mouse model. Young and aged animals were both tested.

Forcing the switch on worsened tau seeding and spread. Turning it off shrank both. Blocked microglia held onto eaten tau instead of releasing it. Their cleanup system also recovered. In aged mice, blocking the switch rescued learning and memory. Brain gene patterns moved back toward normal. Single-cell reads showed disease states fading in microglia. The authors name this switch a drug target. It links inflammation to tau's march.
europmc-pmc9078458:
Liu and co-authors survey chitosan-based hydrogels used as wound dressings and as drug carriers. Chitosan comes from natural sources and breaks down safely in the body. The gels can kill germs, stop bleeding, and hold moisture at a wound. Such traits help tissue repair move through each stage.

The survey shows how these gels can carry helpful agents to a wound. Those agents include drugs that fight bacteria, growth factors, and stem cells. Makers can also blend chitosan with other polymers to suit burns, cuts, or slow-healing wounds. The authors explain why one gel can serve two jobs at once. Readers gain a clear map of design choices and likely gains for wound care.
europmc-pmc9279158:
Joanito and co-authors use single-cell data to refine how colorectal cancers are grouped. The older consensus grouping rests on bulk tumor profiles, which blur cell types together. The team analyzed 373,058 single-cell profiles from 63 patients. They focused on 49,155 epithelial cells, the layer where these cancers arise.

Two clear epithelial states emerged, named iCMS2 and iCMS3. The split rests on gene activity, DNA copy number, and gene control networks. The team found the same split in bulk data from 3,614 patients. One group covers most unstable tumors and a third of stable ones. Mixing in instability and fibrosis gives a five-part scheme. Cancers with both traits in one subgroup had the worst outlook.
europmc-pmc9321158:
Wenning and co-authors present new diagnostic criteria for multiple system atrophy from the Movement Disorder Society. The disease mixes autonomic failure, parkinsonism, and balance problems, and it worsens over time. Older criteria were the research standard for 14 years but missed early cases. At a first visit they caught as few as 18% of probable cases.

The new set adds a clinically established tier that demands brain MRI markers. A clinically probable tier trades a little certainty for better early reach. A research tier covers possible prodromal cases with the earliest signs. The criteria grew from a literature review, two Delphi rounds, and a member survey. A consensus conference gave the final polish. The authors say prospective testing must now prove the gains.
europmc-pmc9408758:
Sun and co-authors examine the role of NF-kB in Alzheimer's disease. NF-kB is a protein factor that drives inflammation in cells. Brain inflammation is a core feature of the disease, next to amyloid plaques and tau tangles. The disease is the most common cause of nerve cell loss worldwide.

The authors trace how NF-kB acts in neurons and glial cells. They cover its links with reactive microglia and astrocytes. They also cover ties to beta-secretase, APOE, glutamate, and tau. Mouse model work gets attention too. The review then surveys drug work aimed at this path. Blocking NF-kB signals may open new treatment options, they argue. More work on its action by cell type is still needed.
europmc-pmc9499858:
Ianiro and co-authors run a meta-analysis of strain engraftment after fecal microbiota transplantation. The treatment works well for recurrent C. difficile infection. Its promise for other gut linked disorders is less sure. How donor strains settle in the recipient was poorly mapped.

The team pooled stool data from 226 donor-recipient triads. The cases spanned eight different disease types. Strain level profiling tracked which donor strains took hold. Higher engraftment came with higher clinical success across studies. Multi-route dosing raised engraftment rates. So did prior antibiotic use in infectious disease cases. Bacteroidetes and Actinobacteria settled better than most Firmicutes. Machine learning predicted post-treatment species presence at 0.77 average AUROC. The models may help pick donors for targeted protocols.
europmc-pmc9805458:
Gao and co-authors review wearable electrochemical sensors that read health signals from sweat. Sweat carries salts, metabolites, and other telling chemicals. Sensors on the skin can track them without needles. That opens steady, painless health monitoring for daily life.

Electrochemical designs lead the wearable field for good reasons. They are cheap, small, and strong in performance. The review first covers what sweat can reveal about health. Ways to trigger and collect sweat come next in the tour. Soft microfluidic channels move tiny sweat volumes reliably. Parts of a full sensor platform are laid out in turn. Materials and power supply advances get their own sections. Example platforms track salts, sugars, drugs, and metals. The authors close with the field's open challenges. Sample reliability and energy use top that list.
french-constitution-1958:
France adopted the constitution of the Fifth Republic in 1958, presented here in its first, unamended form. The Fourth Republic had collapsed under the strain of the Algerian war, and Charles de Gaulle returned to power on his own terms. Michel Debré drafted the charter under de Gaulle's direction, meaning to cure the ills of shifting parliamentary rule.

The text builds a strong presidency: the president names the prime minister, can dissolve the assembly, and holds wide powers in an emergency. Parliament keeps the laws, but within limits the charter sets. Voters approved the text by a large margin in a referendum. The law that tamed the chaos of the Fourth Republic still rules France today, amended since but unmistakable in its design.
frus-1861-d158:
On 21 October 1861, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote a second letter to William Dayton. It is document 158 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

The paired form appears in the Paris file as in the London one. Each letter owns its point and its answer. Together they show how a single day's French business could fill two files and still leave the desk clear. Two files, two answers: the habit kept replies swift and the record clean. A clear desk at day's end was Seward's small, daily victory over the war.
frus-1861-d258:
News and judgment from James Shepherd Pike reached Seward's desk in a letter dated 9 October 1861. It was printed as Document 258 in the foreign affairs papers sent to the two houses of Congress. It was written in the autumn of the war's first year, while the North worked to block foreign aid to the South.

Such reports fed the facts and rumors together into one desk in Washington, week by week. Letters of this kind are the raw record from which the story of wartime diplomacy is built. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1861-d58:
On 1 July 1861, William H. Seward wrote to Charles Francis Adams at the London legation. The letter is document 58 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

July opened with Congress called to meet and the armies near Manassas. Seward's first of July letter keeps faith with the plan set in spring. It guided Adams through the weeks just before Bull Run, when a quick Union win still seemed within reach. Congress met on 4 July and voted men and money, which backed Seward's bold tone abroad. Men and money voted at home were the facts that gave his words abroad their weight.
frus-1862-d158:
Document 158, dated 10 October 1862, carries a dispatch from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. It sits in the long Great Britain section of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume.

Three days earlier, William Gladstone had said in a speech at Newcastle that the South had made a nation. Words Union men read as a push toward British backing for the Confederacy. Adams had to answer that mood in London. Seward's steady mail, of which this letter is part, armed him with Washington's position week after week. Seward trusted Adams's calm judgment and rarely overruled the man on the spot.
frus-1862-d258:
William L. Dayton reported to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 18 March 1862, in a letter printed as Document 258 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Dayton represented the United States in Paris as its minister.

Mid-March brought the Union's Peninsula campaign toward Richmond just as France was deciding to go it alone in Mexico after its allies pulled back. Dayton reported on a court balancing two American ventures at once. His letters are a chief source for how Napoleon III's government weighed the Confederate cause against its Mexican design that spring. Edouard Thouvenel ran the French foreign ministry for most of 1862 and set Dayton's agenda there.
frus-1862-d358:
William H. Seward, the Secretary of State, addressed Henri Mercier on 20 February 1862 in a letter printed as Document 358 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. It closed a run of three Seward letters to the French minister in two weeks.

Late February 1862 was a bright moment for the Union, with Fort Donelson fallen and Nashville about to follow. Seward negotiated from strength that month, a fact foreign legations registered. His letters to Mercier in this window show a secretary using good news as diplomatic capital while it lasted. Cases in this channel often mixed the war at home with French designs in Mexico.
frus-1862-d458:
On 22 June 1862 John Lothrop Motley sent this report from Vienna to Secretary of State William H. Seward. It stands as Document 458 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, accompanying the President's annual message.

Motley wrote as McClellan stood before Richmond and Europe waited to see if the Confederate capital would fall. Austria, busy with its own Italian and German problems, kept a strict and chilly neutrality. His report told Washington how the war's climax looked from the Danube. Letters like this one, from a minor post in the great question, still mattered. Seward's map of Europe had to be complete. Vienna's silence was itself a fact worth recording.
frus-1862-d558:
On 18 September 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Henry Shelton Sanford in Brussels. The instruction is Document 558 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, printed with the annual message.

Seward wrote the day after Antietam, in the same mid-September round that reached Madrid, Vienna, and The Hague. Sanford's Brussels post gave him a window on French and British thinking through King Leopold's wide family web. Orders to such a post mixed the government's line with requests for what the minister was hearing. The dispatch shows Seward gathering Europe's reaction to the autumn crisis through his most connected small-post minister, even before the battle's result was fully known.
frus-1862-d58:
A dispatch from Secretary of State William H. Seward reached Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London on 5 May 1862. It was printed as Document 58 in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs for 1862. The date falls in the spring of 1862, a year into the war, when the Union fought to keep foreign powers from backing the South.

Readers see the home office side of the exchange, where policy was set before talks began. Its worth grows in context, as one link in a chain of letters that kept the peace with Europe. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1862-d658:
William H. Seward addressed this letter to Robert H. Pruyn on 19 December 1861. Pruyn was the incoming American minister to Japan, named to follow Townsend Harris. The letter appears as document 658 in the Foreign Relations volume printed for 1862.

In the last weeks of 1861 Seward sent Pruyn a run of letters, each adding to the charge the new envoy would carry. They dealt with the work of the legation and the stance the United States meant to keep in Japan. This one is a mid-run piece, useful chiefly as part of the full set that sent Pruyn off with his orders in hand.
frus-1863p1-d158:
Charles Francis Adams wrote this dispatch to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 17 April 1863. Three Adams letters in the volume bear the date. Adams was the American minister in London, and this letter is document 158 in part one of the 1863 volume.

A three-letter day late in April shows the ship question still filling the post's plate. Adams gave the yards, the talks, and the press each a sheet. This one opens the set of 17 April. In the volume's long London run, the day is one more crest in a spring of crests. Each charts Britain's slow turn from the South's hopes.
frus-1863p1-d258: On 25 July 1863, a Mr. Hyland wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward. The letter is document 258 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume, among the papers on relations with Britain during the Civil War. The record gives no first name or office for the writer, so the letter stands simply as one citizen-era note in the wartime mail.
frus-1863p1-d358:
One entry in the running Washington exchange, this note from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington, is dated 10 January 1863. It stands as document 358 of the 1863 diplomatic papers. The document comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States, the government's own published record of Civil War diplomacy.

Washington believed Confederate agents used British ports, ships, and soil too freely. Seward pressed Lyons to have his government tighten its watch. It dates from the month the Emancipation Proclamation took effect, which changed the politics of the war in Britain at once. Alone it settles little; in the run of the volume it helps explain why Britain stayed out of the American war.
frus-1863p1-d458:
Lord Lyons, the British minister in Washington directed a letter to William H. Seward, Secretary of State on 11 April 1863. The letter was later printed in the 1863 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, issued with the President's annual message. Readers meet it in the first part of the 1863 Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the government's own record of its dealings abroad.

For historians, the value lies in the run of the letters. Together they trace, almost day by day, how the Union kept its most dangerous foreign problem from boiling over. Trade ran through the whole exchange. British mills wanted Southern cotton, while Union officials watched every cargo for war goods bound to the South. Alone it is one note among hundreds. In place, it is part of how a war stayed between the two sides that started it.
frus-1863p1-d558:
In the flow of wartime mail, William H. Seward wrote to Lord Lyons on 8 June 1863. Lyons was Britain's minister in Washington, and Seward was the American Secretary of State. Behind the formal phrases stood a live question: would Britain stay neutral, or step into the American war? It forms part of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official printed record of American diplomacy.

The real subject under all the polite wording was British neutrality. Washington wanted it kept strict, and London wanted no quarrel it could avoid. Single letters rarely settle anything here. Their worth is in the chain they form, which lets a reader watch a dispute rise, cool, and fade in real time. Alone it is one note among hundreds. In place, it is part of how a war stayed between the two sides that started it.
frus-1863p1-d58:
Secretary of State William H. Seward resumed the London file with this letter to Charles Francis Adams on 19 January 1863. Adams was the American minister in London. The letter is document 58 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863, set after the Confederate papers.

The volume's order puts the foe's captured letters between two runs of the London mail, and this letter picks the thread back up. Seward wrote to keep Adams aimed at the standing aims: no British aid for the South, no warships out of British yards. It is a hinge piece, joining the winter run to what came before.
frus-1863p1-d658:
The 9 November 1863 mail between Washington and London included a letter from William H. Seward to Charles Francis Adams. Adams was the American minister in London, and Seward was Secretary of State in Washington. Behind the formal phrases stood a live question: would Britain stay neutral, or step into the American war? The exchange belongs to the Civil War years, when Washington's first task abroad was keeping Europe out of the fight.

That autumn the sharpest issue was the pair of ironclad rams built for the Confederacy at Birkenhead. Britain held them back, and this mail ran while that fight played out. Students of the war use this mail to see foreign policy as the men on the spot lived it, page by page. The volume's editors printed it without comment; its meaning comes from the company it keeps in the file.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d158: An editorial note dated May 5, 1943 stands as Document 158 of the Cairo and Tehran volume, far from the volume's opening where its twin note sits. Editorial notes in the Foreign Relations series mark seams where the editors joined bodies of papers, and this one opens the Moscow Conference section that follows. Reading it tells the reader whose files the next papers came from and how the editors handled them.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d258:
The Chinese record of a Cairo conversation between President Roosevelt and Generalissimo Chiang Kai-shek is introduced by an editorial note in the Foreign Relations volume. No official American record of the talk was found, and none appears to have been prepared, so the editors print a Chinese summary instead.

The Chinese government held the record in its own files, had it translated from Chinese, and gave leave for its printing in 1957. The note also flags gaps in the Log. The Log lists the Chiangs, Hopkins, and Colonel Elliott Roosevelt as dinner guests. The colonel's own account gives no sign he attended. Topics his book adds, missing from the Chinese summary, include a coalition government for China, British rights in Shanghai and Canton, and the future of Malaya, Burma, and India.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d358:
Charles Bohlen's minutes record the first meeting between President Roosevelt and Marshal Stalin, at Tehran on 28 November 1943 at three in the afternoon. The two leaders had never met, and Roosevelt opens with pleasure: he has tried for a long time to bring this about.

Stalin blames the delay on military business. Then he gives a frank front report. The Soviets have lost Zhitomir and are about to lose Korosten. They hold the initiative elsewhere, but can attack only in the Ukraine. Roosevelt says he wishes he could pull thirty or forty German divisions off the Eastern front, a question he wants Tehran to address. Talk turns to postwar trade and a surplus merchant fleet for Russia. It turns then to China, whose fighting Stalin faults on its leaders. Last comes Lebanon, which Roosevelt blames wholly on de Gaulle's committee.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d458: Number 458 in the Cairo-Tehran volume is an editorial note. Department historians use the note form to speak in their own voice. They add facts, explain references, and point to other documents. The record here covers the Allied conferences of late 1943. Strategy for Europe and Asia dominated those meetings. So did early arguments about the postwar world. The note gives readers footing before the papers resume.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d558:
A second Churchill message to President Roosevelt is dated March 4, 1944, hard on the heels of the first. The pair continues the dense exchange of that week. The message appears in the State Department's Cairo-Tehran conference volume.

Two messages a day, two days running, tells its own story about March 1944: the invasion was three months off, and every theater's claims collided in the leaders' in-trays. Churchill separated his subjects into single papers, and Roosevelt answered in kind. For readers, this message helps reconstruct a week of alliance management at full stretch, preserved because the State Department printed the conference volumes generously.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d58: Churchill wrote to Roosevelt on October 26, 1943, as the Moscow Conference neared its close. His message is Document 58 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. October 26 was a crowded day in the volume, full of letters between capitals and conference rooms. The record for this one gives the date and the names and nothing narrower. It survives in the Foreign Relations series with the rest of that day's traffic.
frus-1944-quebec-d158:
Admiral Leahy wrote to Hull for the Joint Chiefs on August 29, 1944, giving the military view of French participation in the war against Japan. Indochina, the letter stresses, lies in the China theater and is an area of American strategic responsibility. It quotes the views Chiang Kai-shek expressed at Sextant on how the two theaters should divide Thailand and Indochina.

From a military standpoint, the chiefs concurred with the British proposals. One exception mattered: French participation in planning political warfare should be restricted to the Southeast Asia Command area. The letter also counsels recognizing French desires about Indochina where consistent with American policy, with extent and timing kept under continuing review.
frus-1944-quebec-d258:
Control of the strategic bomber forces in Europe is addressed in C.C.S. 520/4, the United States Chiefs' paper of September 13, 1944. With Allied armies now on the continent, the wartime arrangement under Eisenhower's direction was ending. The Americans agreed in principle with joint control by the RAF's Deputy Chief of the Air Staff and the commander of the United States Strategic Air Forces in Europe.

Those two officers, Bottomley and Spaatz, would act jointly for Portal and Arnold as agents of the Combined Chiefs. The Americans found the British draft directive inadequate in several respects, however, and attached a revised directive of their own. The Combined Chiefs approved it, as amended, the following day.
frus-1944-quebec-d58:
President Roosevelt answered Prime Minister Churchill on September 6, 1944. The reply appears in the State Department's Quebec 1944 volume, among the final pre-conference exchanges.

Roosevelt's answers that week kept the welcome warm and the American positions intact. He faced a guest who would argue hard for Britain's share in the Pacific war and for generous aid terms, and the President's letters prepared his ground. For readers, this message closes the transatlantic preparation: within a week the two men would be talking across a table in Quebec City instead of across an ocean.
frus-1945-50-intel-d158: A memorandum dated 28 June 1946 was prepared for the Secretary of State's Special Assistant for Research and Intelligence (Langer). It is document 158 in the Foreign Relations volume on intelligence for 1945 to 1950. Notes of this kind put a matter before one named man, so work could move at once. His office led the State Department's own research and intelligence work at the time.
frus-1945-50-intel-d258:
A memorandum from Director of Central Intelligence Hillenkoetter reached the Assistant Director for Special Operations (Galloway) on 22 December 1947. It is document 258 in the Foreign Relations of the United States volume on intelligence for 1945 to 1950. The CIA was only weeks old, having replaced the Central Intelligence Group in September 1947 under the National Security Act.

Memos like this one did the quiet work of the system. They carried facts, advice, and requests from one office to the desk that could act on them. Whole policies can be traced through chains of such notes, each one moving the matter a step. Kept with its neighbors in the volume, it shows the new system being built one dated paper at a time.
frus-1945-50-intel-d358:
Dated 1 January 1949, "Report From the Intelligence Survey Group to the National Security Council" comes from the top level of the government. The Office of the Historian kept it as document 358 in the Foreign Relations intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. An outside survey team led by Allen Dulles was then reviewing the CIA, and its findings would drive a round of reform debate.

Reports were the heavy guns of paper work: slower than a memo, but built to end an argument. The replies it drew, kept near it in the files, show how the findings stood up to attack. The report is the Dulles Report. It holds the survey team's full findings and its fixes for the young CIA, sent to the Council in early 1949.
frus-1945-50-intel-d58:
Brownell, an executive officer for the assistant secretary of war for air, wrote to the Lovett Committee members on 17 December 1945. The committee's work was still live at year's end. It is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the retrospective volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

Staff officers keep committees alive: they call the meetings, circulate the drafts, and chase the members' views. Brownell's memorandum shows that machinery turning in December, weeks after the Lovett report. Readers might pass over such a paper, but it marks something real, the refusal of a hard question to die. The intelligence design was still being argued in committee rooms while the secretaries settled its outline above.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d158:
Stalin answered Roosevelt on Poland on 29 December 1944, and the answer closed the door. His message, received in Washington in translation, is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. He had the President's note of the middle of the month in hand.

On the American statement of 18 December, Stalin says he would rather speak in person; in any case, events in Poland have moved well past it. Intercepted radio traffic, he charges, proves that talks with Mikolajczyk screened men who waged criminal terror against Soviet officers and soldiers in Poland. Moscow cannot accept a state of things where émigré agents kill Red Army men. Mikolajczyk's replacement by Arciszewski, he adds, has made matters still worse.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d258:
General Arnold weighed in on the basic paper for planning Russia's entry into the Pacific war. His memorandum of 3 December 1944 is enclosed in a Joint Chiefs paper of 5 December, J. C. S. 1176/1, printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. The covering note comes from the Joint Secretariat in Washington.

The enclosure carries Arnold's approval of J. C. S. 1176, the staff paper on Russian participation in the war against Japan. He approves it with the recognition that it is a basic paper, limited in scope. The secretaries record that the paper has gone to the Joint Staff Planners, working with the Joint Logistics Committee, for necessary action. The distribution list reads like a roll of the American high command, from Admiral Leahy to General Marshall and Admiral King.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d358: Harry Hopkins passed this slip to the President during Stalin's long statement on Poland at the third plenary meeting, February 6, 1945. It reads, in full: why not let this wind up today when Stalin is through, and say we will talk it over again tomorrow. Hopkins added the time: it is 7:15. The note is undated, but the editors place it by its content. It shows the adviser managing the clock and the President's patience in the middle of the conference's hardest debate.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d458:
For the conference's last plenary session, no full minutes exist, and this editorial note explains what survives instead. The Bohlen Collection holds a list of those present and of subjects: the communiqué, reparations, and Japan. Against them stands a blunt notation: no report was written up on this conference.

A later page in the same collection, headed "Report of Last Day's Proceedings," does cover the session's first part. The editors reproduce that paragraph here. Hiss's notes, printed after, supply the detail the official record lacks. The note teaches readers to weigh the famous final day by fragments, not by a full transcript.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d58:
From Moscow on 16 January 1945, Ambassador Averell Harriman reported to President Roosevelt on where the American party would sleep at Yalta. His top secret telegram is printed in the Foreign Relations volume on the Malta and Yalta conferences. It deals with rooms, not strategy.

Harriman says Roosevelt will stay in the Livadia palace, the czar's former summer home. The site has one building of 21 rooms, one of 41, and a third once used by guards. Space for the enlarged military party is still unsure, so he is asking the Soviets for more rooms. The support ship Catoctin, he notes, can only be based at Sevastopol.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d158:
The British Embassy handed the State Department an aide-mémoire on Turkey on June 18, 1945. Only an extract is printed, as document 158 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. The full text appears later in the volume, attached to another document.

The surviving passage says that if the Turkish government has no objection, London hopes Washington will agree to a joint Anglo-American approach to the Soviet government. The approach would be in firm language and made soon. It would concern Soviet demands on Turkey. And it should come before the Big Three meeting, where the whole question might have to be discussed anyway. The note shows the West bracing over Soviet pressure on Turkey, a dispute that fed the later quarrels over the Turkish Straits.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d258:
Assistant Secretary Dunn noted British doubts on the Yalta Declaration in an extract dated July 14, 1945. The extract is document 258 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference, taken from his long talk with Sir Alexander Cadogan at Potsdam.

Cadogan felt the Americans had more faith in the Declaration on Liberated Europe than he did, Dunn reports. Still, the British delegation would come along behind the United States in any effort to secure its carrying out. Cadogan was explaining London's wish for peace treaties with the ex-satellite states. He pointed to a legal snag. Unlike the United States with Italy, Britain cannot resume diplomatic relations with a country it is still at war with. The short passage shows the two Western delegations aligned on Poland and the Balkans, but for different reasons.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d358:
A safeguard on reparations shares is proposed in Pauley's cable from Moscow of June 25, 1945, sent after talks with the British representative, Sir Walter Monckton. It supplements his June 19 wire on the formula for dividing reparations among the Big Three. Pauley now adds a condition to protect the smaller claimants and the three themselves.

The three powers would state publicly that they will give up shares, in proportion, to other nations as justified. But unless all three later agree on the actual amounts for others, and pay them on a 55, 22½, and 22½ percent basis, the whole division among the Big Three would reopen.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d458:
Frontier incidents in northern Greece are enclosed with MacVeagh's despatch No. 1282 from Athens, dated July 4, 1945. Its subject is the north of Greece: frontier incidents, and Anglo-Russian relations. The enclosure is a secret report of July 2. Its author is the embassy's assistant military attaché. He was stationed for a time at Salonika as a special political observer.

His report covers incidents from May 20 to June 20. They occurred along Greece's Yugoslav and Bulgarian borders. Most, it states, were small in themselves. In total, though, they were hard to dismiss, and they weighed on men's minds. The printed list ends with six Greek civilians kidnapped near the Albanian frontier on June 20. They were taken into Albania.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d558:
A top secret briefing paper on Yugoslavia was prepared for Potsdam and dated June 27, 1945. The extract printed here is document 558 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers. Its focus is Venezia Giulia, the disputed land around Trieste claimed by both Italy and Yugoslavia.

The paper notes that Stalin backs the Yugoslavs and blames Field Marshal Alexander. Yugoslavs read the June 9 Belgrade deal to mean their committee rule stays in place under Allied military government. The writers call that a bid to keep control and to sway the final outcome. They urge that no more ground be given and that the deal be enforced in full. The land's final fate, they say, must wait for a peace treaty with Italy.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d58:
Churchill told President Truman on June 14, 1945, that he would bring Labour leader Clement Attlee to the Berlin conference. The telegram, number 88, is document 58 in the Foreign Relations papers on Potsdam. The conference opening on July 15 would still be running when Britain's election results came out.

Bringing the leader of the opposition, Churchill explains, will assure full continuity of British policy, whoever wins the election. He says he has told Stalin of the plan in the same terms. The note proved wise: Churchill lost the election mid-conference, Attlee took his place at the table, and British policy carried on without a break. He closes by saying he looks forward to meeting Truman.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d658:
Ambassador Winant sought orders on U.S. membership in a restored Tangier regime on June 26, 1945. His secret wire is document 658 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. It reports early, informal talks at the Foreign Office in London.

Winant found U.S. and British views on Tangier much alike. London meant to give the French its draft pact for an interim regime the next day. That would let Paris weigh it before the talks opened on July 2. The British proposed a neat shortcut for U.S. entry. A copy of the pact would be sent to Washington with a request to join the zone's administration under its terms. The U.S. reply could carry any conditions it wished, saving the time of separate notes. Winant also asks how a U.S. money share might be funded.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1058:
British Foreign Secretary Ernest Bevin sent Secretary Byrnes a copy of his letter to Molotov on July 31, 1945. The letter answers Soviet claims that German troops in Norway were not being disarmed. Bevin reports the facts as London's authorities gave them, and calls the Soviet allegations groundless.

In all, 365,000 Germans in Norway were gathered into guarded reservations and disarmed. Only officers and two percent of the men kept pistols or rifles, to keep order inside the camps. That comes to about 7,300 armed men in total. The regions Moscow named hold far fewer troops than claimed: under 50,000 near Mo and Trondheim, not 260,000. Bevin also raises how the Germans will be evacuated home.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1158:
London reported to Washington on 18 July 1945, in this dispatch from Ambassador Winant to the Acting Secretary of State. The summit was in its second day. The embassy sent home its read of British official views and press talk at the start of the talks.

Winant's job was to make sure Washington never misread its closest ally. His post heard what the conference room could not: party talk, press mood, and private doubts. This cable is the London listening post at work early in the summit. It set the baseline against which later London reports would be read.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1258:
Prime Minister Suzuki of Japan spoke at a press conference on 28 July 1945. His words gave the world's first public sign of Tokyo's answer to the Potsdam Declaration, issued two days before. The statement reached Washington fast and was read there as a refusal.

Suzuki used a word, often rendered as killing the terms with silent contempt, that hardened Allied views. Whether he meant flat rejection or a wish to wait for Moscow, the effect was the same. The summit's leaders took Japan's answer as no. This statement is that answer in its public form, a hinge on which the war's last weeks turned.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1358:
George Allen wrote to Assistant Secretary James Dunn for a third time in this run on 25 July 1945. Allen's Near Eastern and African affairs office kept a steady file of papers flowing to Dunn during the conference. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official American diplomatic record, prints it in the second volume on the Potsdam Conference.

Dunn sat close to the center of the American effort at Potsdam, so papers addressed to him reached a man who could act. The Allen notes show a regional bureau working its questions into the summit's crowded agenda. For readers tracing Middle East policy in 1945, the Allen papers are a thread worth following. It runs from start to end of the volume's closing section.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-158:
A rapporteur's report dated August 1, 1945 closed a working group's account as the Potsdam Conference ended. Rapporteurs stated what their groups had settled and what they passed upward. On the final day, such reports fed the last drafting. This one was printed in the second Potsdam volume.

A final report reads like a ledger being shut. Most lines are firm; a few stay open for ministers to judge. Readers learn how much of the settlement was built below the top level. The piece honors the conference's least seen workers: the officers who turned talk into text.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-58:
War booty was discussed at a Potsdam meeting whose minutes have never been found. An editorial note in volume two reports the loss. It is the fifty-eighth unnumbered item following document 710. Unlike its neighbors, this note does name the subject that was discussed.

No minutes of this meeting, at which the question of war booty was discussed, have been found, the editors write. They direct the reader to a later summary of the discussion instead. That summary is printed as document 980, at pages 942 to 943 of the volume. War booty was no side issue at Potsdam. The term decided what the Soviet Union could seize in its zone as trophies of war, apart from reparations. The note thus points past its own gap to the nearest surviving account of a contested topic.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d758:
The United States delegation tabled this proposal on July 25, 1945, as document 758. The date falls in the conference's second week. American texts from this stage were aimed at closing gaps. The proposal was printed in the second Potsdam volume of Foreign Relations of the United States.

A proposal written after eight days of talks is a tuned tool. Its writers had heard every objection. Readers can judge how far the American side had moved from its opening drafts. The document also shows the endgame forming early. By July 25 the final protocol's shape was already being sketched, one text at a time.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d858:
Document 858 gathers the texts the Economic Subcommittee considered on July 19, 1945. Rival drafts on Germany's economic future lay before the experts. The bundle was kept as one record in the second Potsdam volume. It dates from the conference's first week.

A set of rival texts is the negotiation in miniature. Readers can lay the drafts side by side and find the fight. Each side's words about production and payment reveal its fears. The document spares readers the hunt through scattered files. It also shows the subcommittee's real work: not deciding, but making the decision possible for those above.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d958: President Harry Truman wrote to General Eisenhower from Berlin on July 30, 1945, about Marshal Zhukov's report to Stalin. Zhukov had charged American and British forces with removing property from the Soviet occupation zone. Truman encloses an informal translation of the report, passed to him during the conference. He asks Eisenhower to investigate the charges and report back to him. The editors note that no reply from Eisenhower arrived during the conference. Stalin raised the matter at the eleventh plenary meeting the next day.
frus-1961-63v11-d158:
A summary record of the Executive Committee's twenty-second meeting tracks the missile pullout from Cuba. About 90 percent of the missile erectors have reached Cuban ports. Six Soviet ships will be photographed with missiles aboard.

President Kennedy directs that surveillance continue until a UN substitute stands. The IL-28 bombers remain the one weapon that must go. A no-invasion pledge waits on full compliance. Plans for a shot-down plane fill the close. The record shows victory managed with care, each claim of Soviet compliance checked by camera before it was believed.
frus-1964-68v01-d258: An editorial note in the Vietnam, 1964 volume records the White House meeting of August 2, 1964, on the Tonkin Gulf attack. President Johnson sat with Rusk, Ball, Vance, Wheeler, and intelligence staff for about 45 minutes. The group judged that a local North Vietnamese commander had likely acted on his own. No strike back was ordered. A protest note would go to Hanoi, and the patrol would sail on. No other record of the meeting has been found. Rusk's book gives the hour as about 10:30.
gadbury-doctrine-nativities-1658:
John Gadbury teaches birth-chart astrology in Genethlialogia, his Doctrine of Nativities, from 1658. The great English manual tells how to cast a horoscope and read a life in it. Gadbury, rival to the famed Lilly, served the Civil War generation with forecasts drawn from the stars at each client's birth.

Rules for houses, aspects, and judgments fill his orderly, confident pages. Health, wealth, marriage, and death all submit to his method here. Judicial astrology stands at its most systematic in this work. Readers meet the heavens treated as a book of lives, open to any reader who learns the signs aright.
gao-gaoreports-b-295958:
Integration Technologies Group protested a Veterans Affairs award for computers for blind veterans in GAO decision B-295958, dated May 13, 2005. The winner was Electronic Vision Access Solutions.
