The firm had been cut from the contest. Its bid used a 107-key keyboard. The rules called for a 104-key board.

GAO denied the protest. The cut was sound because the bid missed a clear spec. GAO also backed the waiver of the Trade Agreements Act for this buy. All bids used parts not from the United States or named partner lands. The case helps readers see how a spec miss and a trade waiver are judged.
gao-gaoreports-b-296158:
Zebra Technologies protested the rejection of its quote as late in GAO decision B-296158, dated June 24, 2005. The Army sought radio frequency gear and services. The firm's quote was for printers in one award group. Blanket purchase deals were on offer to picked vendors.

GAO denied the protest. The record showed the agency act was sound. It also fit the late quote terms in the call. Those terms set a firm cut time for quotes. A late quote could be shut out. Readers can use the ruling for late bid law. The terms in the call rule, and a sound agency act will stand.
gao-gaoreports-b-297758:
United Paradyne protested an Air Force choice on fuels work in GAO decision B-297758, dated March 10, 2006. The site was Wright-Patterson Air Force Base in Ohio. The same fuels call drew an past fight by this firm. This round hit past work marks and the trade-off pick. The method for trust marks was the flaw.

GAO sustained the protest. The method hurt firms with close past work for their far past work. It gave the same weight to close and far work. That mix skewed the trust marks. Close work must count more than far work when the call grades fit. A method that levels fit grades breaks that rule.
gao-gaoreports-b-299058:
OK Produce and Coast Citrus Distributors protested Defense Commissary Agency awards to Coast Produce Company. The contracts covered fresh fruits and vegetables for stores in the west region. Two of the three awards were at stake. GAO ruled in B-299058 and B-299058.2 on February 2, 2007.

The firms attacked the scoring and the picks. Mere dispute with a score does not prove a flawed review. GAO found both sound on the record. The firms also claimed an unfair edge from a hired ex-agency evaluator. That person had no hand in the current terms. No proof showed inside facts were shared. GAO denied the protests.
gao-gaoreports-b-299258:
SourceLink Ohio, LLC protested a Government Printing Office rejection of its bid. The bid buy covered printing and mailing of beneficiary notices. Those notices come from the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services. GAO ruled in B-299258 on March 12, 2007.

The bid lacked a Data Use Agreement sent with it. That pact sets safeguards for CMS data and needs CMS sign-off. The office called the bid nonresponsive for that gap. GAO read the point in a distinct way. The pact goes to a bidder's fitness, not the bid's form. A fitness point can be cured before award. The firm should get a chance to file the pact. GAO sustained the protest.
gao-gaoreports-b-299858:
Computer Cite protested a General Services Administration rejection of its bid. The buy sought basic ordering deals for management and support services. The work aids the Energy Department and a nuclear security office. GAO ruled in B-299858 on August 31, 2007.

The terms set a clear teaming path. A firm could bid as a contract teaming pact, with set rules. Or one firm had to hold all the schedule deals the buy required. The firm's bid fit neither path. It lacked a pact drawn to the stated rules. It also lacked the full set of deals on its own. A bid off both paths can be cast out. GAO denied the protest.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-458:
EPA's power to judge the risks of chemicals is reviewed in GAO report GAO-05-458, dated June 13, 2005. The Toxic Substances Control Act of 1976 lets EPA control chemicals that pose an unreasonable risk. GAO looked at how EPA reviews new chemicals, how it judges chemicals already in use, and how much data from firms it can share.

Reviews of new chemicals give only limited assurance that risks are found in time. Firms need not test new chemicals before sending them in, and most do not. EPA instead uses models that match new chemicals to tested ones with like structures. Those models are not always right. EPA also does not routinely assess chemicals already in commerce. The law puts the costly burden of gathering data on EPA itself. Few rules control existing chemicals as a result. The report sets out options to strengthen the program.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-558:
What airlines truly spent on passenger screening in 2000 is estimated in GAO report GAO-05-558, dated April 18, 2005. Those costs set the base for a security fee the government charges carriers. The security agency had guessed the costs were $750 million. Carriers reported only $319 million on the forms they filed. Lawmakers ordered GAO to make its own independent count of the three main cost parts.

GAO put the true figure at a midpoint of $448 million. Its range, at a 95 percent confidence level, ran from $425 million to $471 million. The gap against the carriers' reports came to $129 million. Private screening firms made up the largest share of costs. Airport costs were the most understated part of the filings. Exact counts were not possible. Five years had passed, airline ledgers were not built to track these costs, and some sums had to be split by assumption. The report shows how GAO built the estimate.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-658:
Polluters who go bankrupt and leave cleanup bills behind are the subject of GAO-05-658 (August 17, 2005). Over 231,000 businesses filed for bankruptcy from fiscal 1998 through 2003. No one tracks how many owed cleanup duties, so the taxpayer risk is unmeasured. The Justice Department chased cleanup claims in just 136 bankruptcy cases for the environment agency in that span.

Firms can lawfully park assets in sister companies away from cleanup debts. Bankruptcy's fresh start also clashes with polluter-pays law. GAO urges the agency to use its financial assurance tools more, requiring proof upfront that firms can pay for cleanup.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-858:
The Navy's business software saga is told in GAO-05-858, a report dated September 29, 2005. Defense business systems have sat on GAO's high-risk list since 1995. The Navy ran four pilot software projects, then merged them into one program. GAO traced the pilots' history and costs. It asked what lessons the Navy drew. And it looked for fresh practices to strengthen oversight.

GAO found the Navy spent about $1 billion on the four pilots. Day-to-day operations barely improved. The pilots were narrow and never built to be fleet-wide answers. Their designs clashed, so the systems could not work together. In short, GAO called the efforts failures. The new program office, by contrast, follows disciplined steps. Its strong grip on requirements stands out, GAO said.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-358:
Small firms can be hurt badly when the Pentagon pays late. GAO ruled on the payment record in GAO-06-358, dated May 19, 2006. Law required GAO to report on how fast the Department of Defense pays small businesses. GAO used data from 9 of 20 vendor pay sites and one contract pay site.

GAO asked whether small firm bills were paid late more often. It looked for system flaws that cause late payment. Case studies showed what late payment did to firms hit often. The report points to wider use of electronic invoicing. Better use of that tool, GAO said, could cut late payments further. Readers get rates, causes, and firm-level effects.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-658:
Defense business systems are reviewed in GAO-06-658, a GAO report dated May 15, 2006. The Department of Defense spends heavily to modernize the computer systems that handle pay, logistics, and other support work. Lawmakers set requirements in law for how the department plans and controls this spending. GAO checked the department's institutional approach, including its business enterprise plan and investment controls.

GAO found that the department was taking steps to meet the law's requirements and improve its approach. It was also putting many of GAO's earlier recommendations into practice. Even so, GAO said further steps were needed to keep thousands of systems aligned and to stop wasteful overlap. The report tracks a slow shift toward managing these systems as one enterprise.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-958:
Health care budgeting at the Department of Veterans Affairs needs work, GAO finds in report GAO-06-958, dated September 20, 2006. The agency expected to serve 5.4 million patients in fiscal year 2006. Congress funds that care each year, based in part on the President's request.

For fiscal years 2005 and 2006, added funds were sought past the first requests. GAO traced how those requests were built. It checked how the agency tracked its spending and told Congress of it. It named the flaws in the budget build that drove the extra asks. The report is a close look at how a big care system plans its money.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1058:
Defense research budget papers sent to Congress lack steady, full, clear facts, GAO finds in report GAO-07-1058, dated September 5, 2007. The Defense Department asked for $73.2 billion in fiscal year 2007 for research, development, testing, and evaluation. Codes and exhibits are meant to tell Congress what that money buys.

A 2006 law told GAO to test those codes and exhibits. GAO read all of the fiscal year 2007 codes and 47 exhibits. It asked if they give exact, steady, full, and clear data. It named what drives the flaws found. The report shows how budget form can hide, or reveal, vast sums.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-58:
Bonus fees for space contractors pay for effort more than results, and GAO-07-58, dated January 17, 2007, calls for a tighter link. Cost-plus-award-fee deals took almost half of the National Aeronautics and Space Administration's (NASA) contract dollars in fiscal years 2002 through 2004. NASA's contract management has been a high-risk area since 1990. Congress asked GAO to test the agency's award fee rules and practice.

GAO read the rules against flaws named in past reviews. It then audited the top 10 award-fee contracts of the period. The rules form a sound frame, the study found. Practice strayed from it. Score sheets leaned on effort inputs and long lists of subfactors, which dilute the fee's pull. NASA had never judged whether its fee use works as a whole. Three recommendations press the agency chief to tie fees to outcomes and to use such contracts only when they pay off.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-658:
Buildings and land inherited from 22 merged agencies fill GAO-07-658, a GAO report issued June 22, 2007. The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) holds a vast, mixed property stock. GAO set out to describe that stock. It then asked what strains the department faces in running it and how it has met a White House property initiative. Headquarters merger in Washington and site security get their own checks.

The strains match those of other big landlords, with a security twist. Surplus and decaying sites drain funds. Property records are weak, so no one can rank the stock with trust. Costly leases fill gaps the owned stock should cover. Funds run short against business logic. GAO credits fresh headway on the initiative's rules. It urges long-range capital planning tied to the asset plan, so the inherited sprawl gets shaped by design rather than drift.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-758:
Staffing at the Department of Homeland Security is analyzed in GAO-07-758, dated July 16, 2007. The department has about 171,000 staff and has faced hiring strain since 2003. GAO surveyed personnel staff across its parts. It read federal personnel data and spoke with top officials. The report covers staff losses, hiring and retention steps, and use of outside workers. It also checks compliance with the Vacancies Reform Act. That law covers acting officials in top posts.

Loss rates for most staff fell from 8.4 percent in 2005 to 7.1 percent in 2006. Both rates topped the roughly 4 percent norm for cabinet agencies. Airport screeners, a third of all staff, drove much of the gap. Without them, the rate was 3.3 percent both years. Senior staff losses also ran high, at 14.5 and 12.8 percent. GAO told the department's lawyers to write clear rules for the Vacancies Reform Act. The department agreed with that call.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-258:
Aviation weather services face change in GAO report GAO-08-258 (January 11, 2008). Weather service meteorologists sit inside each of the aviation agency's en route centers. Their forecasts and briefings warn traffic managers of turbulence, icing, and freezing rain. The weather agency plans to restructure those offices. The aviation agency is rethinking what it needs from them.

GAO checked the status of the restructuring plans. It listed the services the aviation agency requires and its other sources for them. It then judged how well both agencies guard the quality of the products. The title is blunt: both need to do better at ensuring sound forecasts.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-58:
With its report GAO-08-58, dated December 18, 2007, GAO turns to sanctions on Iran. The United States uses sanctions alongside diplomacy and a Gulf military presence to counter Iran's nuclear work and support for terrorism. GAO checked how the sanctions run and what they have achieved since 1987.

Treasury bans U.S. trade and investment with Iran and filed over 94 penalty cases from 2003 to 2007. The State Department has sanctioned foreign parties in 111 instances under proliferation laws. Officials credit the tools with slowing oil investment and cutting access to U.S. finance. Yet Iran has signed energy deals reported at about $20 billion since 2003 and still enriches uranium. No agency tracks the total effect. GAO urged a baseline review led by the National Security Council.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-958:
Undercover tests probe airport security, and GAO-08-958, an August 2008 report, grades the testing program itself. The Transportation Security Administration sends inspectors through checkpoints with test threat items to find weak points and measure screener performance. Congress asked GAO to review tests run from September 2002 to June 2007 and how results get used.

The agency built a risk-based program, choosing airports by threat likelihood and redesigning local tests to measure screening better. But inspectors did not systematically record why tests failed or why some sites passed more often. Failures can have many causes, officials noted, yet without that record the agency cannot target fixes well. GAO recommends logging failure causes, coordinating with other transport testers, and tracking past advice.
gesner-historia-animalium-lib4-1558:
Gesner went down into the waters for the fourth volume of his Historiae animalium in 1558. It treats fishes and water creatures of every kind, the largest survey of sea life yet attempted in print. Rivers, lakes, and oceans all contribute their tenants to his catalogue.

Whales, sharks, and common food fish receive the same careful order. Among them stand the sea serpent and other marine monsters that sailors swore were true. Gesner weighs the reports as best his age allowed. The volume keeps one foot in marvel, and is the more fascinating for it. No earlier book had tried to hold the whole watery world at once.
hansard-admission-of-baron-de-rothschild:
The House of Commons record for July 26, 1858 tells of the day Baron Lionel de Rothschild took his seat at last. Hansard, the verbatim record of Parliament, holds the whole scene in its pages. He had been chosen by the City of London for eleven years, yet kept out by the form of the oath.

The law was changed so a Jew could swear on the Old Testament and sit in the House. Lionel, the head of the London house, thus became the first professing Jew to sit in the Commons. The record is the high point of the long fight for Jewish rights in Britain.
harris-treaty-1858:
Townsend Harris, the first American consul in Japan, negotiated the 1858 treaty of amity and commerce with the Tokugawa shogunate. Four years after Perry's visit, the United States wanted real trade, not just ports for supplies. Harris argued that Japan could gain from open commerce, even as British and French power loomed over Asia.

The terms opened more ports to American ships and let Americans live and trade in set districts of Japanese cities. They also fixed low tariff rates and gave foreigners legal protections outside Japanese courts. Many Japanese saw the deal as unequal and humiliating, and anger at such terms helped fuel the movement that later toppled the shogunate.
herodotus-histories-rawlinson-1858:
Herodotus wrote his Histories in Greek in the fifth century BC, and George Rawlinson gave England its standard version in 1858 to 1860. Rawlinson, an Oxford scholar, added maps and learned notes. His brother Henry, famed for cuneiform work, helped with eastern lore.

Herodotus tells how Greece fought Persia and won against huge odds. Along the way he reports Egypt's customs, Scythian rites, and marvels galore. He mixes inquiry, travel tales, and speeches into one wide survey. Later ages named him the father of history, with cause. His notes draw on fresh finds from Egypt and Persia.
heuvelmans-on-track-of-unknown-animals-1:
Bernard Heuvelmans, a Belgian zoologist, gave the hunt for unknown beasts its first full map in 1958. On the Track of Unknown Animals, in Richard Garnett's English rendering, is the founding book of cryptozoology. Seven parts and nineteen chapters sweep the globe for hidden life.

Heuvelmans weighs reports of the orang-pendek, the yeti, sea serpents, and a mammoth said to live in the far north woods. He sorts strong tales from weak ones and asks what beast each could be. His method treats rumor as a clue to be tested, not a joke. The book shaped every beast hunt that came after.
hocus-pocus-junior-1658:
Hocus Pocus Junior calls itself the anatomy of legerdemain, the art of sleight of hand. First printed in 1634, it appears here in its fifth edition of 1658. It is the first English book of conjuring tricks, and it gave the world the phrase hocus pocus, taken from the patter of stage jugglers.

The book explains cups and balls, card tricks, and feats with string and coin. Its aim is exposure as much as teaching: readers learn how the wonders are done. That honesty made it a landmark in the history of stage magic. Generations of conjurers learned their first tricks from its pages. A working manual and a small delight, it still performs its tricks on readers.
holmes-autocrat-1858:
Oliver Wendell Holmes published The Autocrat of the Breakfast-Table in 1858, gathering essays he had run in The Atlantic Monthly. Holmes, a Harvard doctor and professor, imagines himself as the autocrat of a Boston boarding-house table. His monologues, interrupted by fellow lodgers, made him famous on two continents.

The Autocrat discourses on everything: conversation, poetry, trees, theology, and the young fellow who sits across the table. Poems break up the talk, including The Deacon's Masterpiece, about a carriage built so logically it ran a hundred years. Holmes's wit is learned, warm, and quick with metaphor. The book founded the American familiar essay's reigning style and stayed a favorite for generations.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-aaron-ben-josep:
Aaron ben Joseph ha-Levi, a Talmudist and critic of Spain, is the subject of this Jewish Encyclopedia entry of 1906. He descended from Zerahiah ha-Levi and flourished at the end of the thirteenth century, dying before 1303. He studied under Nahmanides at Gerona, beside Solomon ben Adret. In 1285 he was rabbi in Saragossa, and about 1291 he lived briefly in Toledo.

Aaron's decisions carried such weight that a later rabbi dared not annul one of them, the entry reports. He clashed more than once with Adret, the leading spirit of Spanish Jewry. When Adret published Torat ha-Bayit, Aaron answered with a severe but just criticism. He still treated his opponent with the greatest deference.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abraham-b-isaac:
Abraham b. Isaac of Narbonne, called RABaD II, was a leading Talmudist of Languedoc. Born likely at Montpellier about 1110, he died at Narbonne in 1179. He headed Narbonne's nine man rabbinical board and its academy.

His pupils included Abraham b. David, later his son-in-law, and Zerahiah ha-Levi. Most of his Talmud comments are lost, but his code Ha-Eshkol survives in part. Modeled on Alfasi, it sorted laws by subject and drew more on the Jerusalem Talmud. His responsa show a clear, logical mind. French and Italian codifiers took Ha-Eshkol as their model for years.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-adam-758:
Adam heads the human story in Genesis. In the first chapter he comes at the close of the sixth day of making. He bears the image of God. Rule over the rest of the living world goes to him. Man and woman alike must fill the earth and subdue it.

The second chapter goes deeper. God forms man from dust and breathes life into his nose. A garden in Eden waits for his care. He may eat of all its trees save one. From his rib God builds woman as a fit mate. The third chapter brings the serpent's lure and the eating of the banned fruit. Curse and exile follow. The pair must till hard soil for food. Later Bible books cite Adam's name in a single family list.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-adret-moses-858: Moses Adret was a cabalist of the eighteenth century. He lived and died in Smyrna. He had a rare memory and knew Talmudic and rabbinic books in full. He wrote twelve works in all. Among them were notes on the code of Maimonides and on the laws of Asher ben Jehiel. He wrote legal calls and new notes on most tracts of the Babylonian Talmud. Few of his works saw print. Those few came out at Salonica in 1802, under a title that means Moses Blessed.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-alaman-ashkenaz:
Alaman, also read Ashkenazi or Deutsch, is a wide-spread Jewish family of the Turkish empire. Its founder was Joseph ben Solomon of Ofen, in Hungary. He is said to have led the party that handed the keys of Ofen's citadel to Sultan Solyman I. in 1529. Joseph then settled in Constantinople.

For that act, Joseph and his line won a rare reward. They were freed from all taxes and duties, and from forced service, for all time. A firman confirmed the grant, and each Ottoman ruler ratified it in turn, down to 1901. About four hundred and fifty of his descendants still lived then. They were spread across Constantinople, Adrianople, Brusa, Damascus, Gallipoli, Cairo, and towns in Bulgaria.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-alexander-suuml: Alexander Süsskind ben Samuel Zanwil was a grammarian and a cabalist. He was born at Metz near the end of the seventeenth century. In 1717-18 he published a Hebrew grammar at Köthen, in Anhalt. Its title is "Derek ha-Kodesh," The Sacred Way. A Judaeo-German essay on the Hebrew accents was added. Three more works survive in a Leyden manuscript, on God, grammar, and a translated German book. In 1758 he was living at Leyden. There he wrote a treatise on the Cabala for Professor Philip Puseal.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-allegri-abraham: Abraham Allegri lived at Constantinople about the middle of the seventeenth century. He was a peer of Moses Benveniste. He wrote a defense of Maimonides and his book of laws. In it he fought off the attacks of Nahmanides. The work came out in Constantinople in 1652. Its title means a gladsome heart. The title plays on his own name. A set of his responsa came out at Salonica in 1793.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-amarillo-aaron-: Aaron ben Solomon Amarillo was a Talmudic author. He worked in the eighteenth century. He came from a family of scholars in Turkey. His father Solomon and his brother Moses both wrote books. Aaron kept up that family line of work. In 1796 he brought out his responsa. The book bears a title that means the face of Aaron. It follows the order of the Tur in its plan. The entry says it casts light on much Jewish lore.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-anan-son-of-ana:
Anan, son of Anan, was made high priest in the year 62. Agrippa II gave him the post that year. He held the post for three months in all. As head of the Sanhedrin he took a bold step. The Roman post in Judea stood empty at that time. He called the court and had foes stoned as breakers of law.

The new Roman chief rebuked that high hand. Agrippa then stripped Anan of his post. In the war of 66 Anan still led the city. He built the guards of Jerusalem with care. He stood firm against the Zealot bands. John of Giscala lured in the Idumeans at last. Those men slew Anan at the Temple gates.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-apostole-aposto:
Apostole and Apostoli look alike but mean different things, the entry begins. Apostole named certain moneys or taxes raised for Palestine. Apostoli named the men sent out to collect that money and bring it to the patriarch.

A joint edict of Arcadius and Honorius in the year 399 first records the system, by ordering it stopped. The sums already gathered were to be seized, and the collectors tried as lawbreakers. Five years later Honorius revoked the edict. Jerome and Eusebius both show the apostles still at work in their days, armed with the patriarch's authority. The entry ranks these men among the highest in Jewry and traces the tax through later sources.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-arias-joseph-ze:
Joseph Zemah Arias was a Marano man of letters who flourished in the latter part of the seventeenth century. He belonged to the literary circle of Joseph Penso, the dramatist. He also held a high commission in the Spanish army at Brussels, reaching the rank of captain.

For a time he was adjutant to Colonel Nicolas Oliver y Fullano. He is heard of in Brussels and other Dutch cities beside the poet De Barrios. He is best known for turning Josephus's Contra Apionem into Spanish. It came out at Amsterdam in 1687, dedicated to Isaac Orobio de Castro.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ashkenazi-or-d-:
Behor Ashkenazi, better known by his popular name Behor Effendi, served the Ottoman empire as a government official. Born in 1840, he was schooled at the Institution Camondo. After junior posts, Sultan Aziz named him in 1869 to the council of state, a body of forty members that held two Jews. Under Abdul Hamid II he sat in the Ottoman parliament as a delegate of the Jews.

He then became vice-prefect of Constantinople and held the post for years, making enemies by his strict honesty. He served again and again as president of the central consistory of Constantinople's Jews. His office let him help gather the communal taxes on meat, wine, and brandy. In 1896 the sultan made him state councilor again, and in 1899 he retired after thirty years of service.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-astruc-jean-205:
Jean Astruc was a French physician. He was born at Sauve on March 19, 1684, and died in Paris on May 5, 1766. He taught anatomy at Toulouse, Montpellier, and Paris. His lasting place in Bible study rests on a book he published without his name at Brussels in 1753. Its title, in French, asks what original records Moses used to compose Genesis.

Astruc noticed that some parts of Genesis call God Elohim, and others call him by the name rendered the Lord. He proposed that Moses had worked from older documents and set them side by side. Copyists later mixed them, he said. That would explain the two story lines and the repeats. His scheme named two main sources and about ten smaller ones. The entry calls this the starting point of modern criticism of the Pentateuch.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-aven-2158:
Aven is a name that carries three senses in the prophets. First, it is one of the Egyptian cities threatened with God's wrath in Ezekiel. There the name is a bent form of On, twisted to mean vanity. The Greek version renders it Heliopolis.

Second, in Hosea the high places of Aven most likely point to Beth-el, under a shaming name. Some scholars read the word itself as a term for false worship. Third, the plain of Aven in Amos is the valley between Lebanon and Anti-Libanus. It was famed for sun worship at the temple of Baalbek. Today that valley is called Beka'a.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-baalah-2258: Baalah is one name for three places in the Bible's lists. The first is a border town of Judah. Elsewhere it is called Kirjath-jearim, the town where the Ark rested for a time. The second Baalah is a mount on the border of Judah. The third is a city in the south of Judah. That city passed to the tribe of Simeon. In the Simeonite list it is called Balah, and in the matching list in Chronicles it appears as Bilhah.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bahia-the-bay-o:
Bahia, also called San Salvador, is a city on the eastern coast of Brazil, founded by the Portuguese in 1549. Jews are often said to appear there first in 1624. The entry argues they lived there much earlier, as New Christians who hid their faith. Open practice of Judaism was not allowed. Agents of the Inquisition sent suspects back to Europe for trial.

Secret Jews at Bahia were many and some were rich, worth from 60,000 to 100,000 crusados, the entry says. When the Dutch attacked Brazil, many threw off the mask. They openly returned to their old faith. Later parts cover banished New Christians sent from Portugal. They also trace a slow blending into the Catholic population after the laws of the Marquis de Pombal. The entry ends with the near silence about Jews at Bahia after 1765.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bath-rabbim-265: Bath-Rabbim is a term found only once in the Bible, in the seventh chapter of Canticles. It seems to name a gate at or near Heshbon. The passage is obscure, and the entry lists three proposed fixes by named scholars. One reads Rabbath Ammon, one reads Helbon, and one reads wood of Beth Cerem. The entry closes by saying none of the three is fully satisfying.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-beet-2758:
Beet is a biennial root plant that the Bible never names, the entry states at the start. One scholar dates its farming no earlier than the sixth or fourth century before the common era. Another claims to spot it in an Egyptian picture of a much older dynasty.

Both white and red kinds grow wild in Palestine today. The entry tracks the plant's names in Mishnah, Syriac, and Arabic, and corrects two scholars' errors on those names. Later notes cover its growth, its stems as food, and praise for boiled beet as good for heart and eyes.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ben-temalion-25:
Ben Temalion is a demon named in the Talmud, in a legend tied to Simon ben Yoḥai. When sages went to Rome to seek repeal of edicts against the Jews, the demon offered his help. He would enter a princess of the imperial house and leave only when Simon was called to cure her.

Events follow his plan, the palace glass breaks, and Simon gains entry to the treasure-house. There he finds the edicts and tears them up. The entry compares the tale with Christian saint legends and a Buddhist story from the Panchatantra.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-benjamin-david-:
David Benjamin, a communal worker, was born in London in 1815 and died there on June 25, 1893. In 1835 he went out to Australia and helped found a synagogue in Tasmania. He then settled in Melbourne with his brother Solomon, a founder of that city's Jewish community.

Their firm traded boldly, buying crude gold and holding a large stake in the Bank of New South Wales. Back in England from 1854, Benjamin gave his time to communal work. He served the Bayswater Synagogue, the Board of Guardians, and the Jews' Hospital, and gave freely to charity.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-berezino-3058: Berezino is a village of Russia, in the government of Minsk. Its population in 1898 was 1,900, and almost all of them, 1,824, were Jews. About a quarter of the Jews worked as artisans and laborers, chiefly as loaders. Twenty-four Jewish families took to gardening. The entry paints a hard picture of want. When the state took over the wine trade in 1897, ninety-nine Jewish families lost their living, and many more needed charity for fuel and for Passover food.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-berr-isaac-berr:
Berr Isaac Berr of Turique was a French manufacturer. He was born at Nancy in 1744. He died at Turique on November 5, 1828. He inherited the post of syndic of Nancy's Jews. He had a strong Hebrew education. Jacob Perle, Nancy's chief rabbi, taught him rabbinical literature.

In 1789 the Jews of Alsace chose him as deputy. He pleaded for Jewish emancipation before the Assembly. He also answered the bishop of Nancy in print. Later he served in the Assembly of Notables. He also sat in the Sanhedrin. The entry lists six of his writings. Most defend full rights for French Jews.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bibikov-dmitri-:
Dmitri Gavrilovich Bibikov was a Russian soldier and statesman. He was born in 1792 and died in 1870. In 1837 he became military governor of Kiev. He also governed Volhynia and Podolia. His fifteen years there included harsh measures. Jews caught in Polish unrest felt them most. Berdychev's Jews drew his special animosity.

Yet the entry also credits him with easing some laws. He won relaxations for educated Jews. Jewish merchants gained new rights under him. Jews could elect their own brokers and notaries. In 1852 he became minister of the interior. His later record turned harsher again. One Jitomir restriction bore his name.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-black-death-148:
The Black Death was a violent pestilence in Europe. It raged from March 1348 to spring 1351. It is said to have killed nearly half the population. Sailors brought it to Genoa from south Russia. Jews suffered from the plague as much as Christians. Yet a myth blamed them for it. Jews, the charge ran, poisoned the wells.

Tortured Jews produced false confessions to that charge. Attacks spread from town to town with speed. Pope Clement VI. declared the charge false in July 1348. The massacres continued anyway. The entry lists towns from the Nuremberg Memorbuch. Expulsion later became the towns' chosen policy.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-blaustein-david:
David Blaustein was an educator born at Lida, Russia. His birth fell on May 5, 1866. He studied Hebrew in his native town first. At eighteen he went to Prussia. There Israel Lipkin taught him. He was ordered out of Germany as a Russian subject. In 1886 he settled in Boston. He opened a private school there.

He helped found a Sheltering Home for Immigrants. From 1892 to 1896 he served as rabbi at Providence. Brown University made him a Semitic lecturer in 1896. In 1898 he joined New York's Educational Alliance. He served it as superintendent. In 1900 he studied Rumanian Jews' conditions.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bodek-jacob-of-:
Jacob Bodek of Lemberg was a Galician Hebraist who died at Lemberg in 1856. With his brother-in-law A. M. Mohr, he wrote sharp reviews of new Hebrew books. Their targets included Rapoport, Luzzatto, and Reggio.

Bodek and Mohr later issued a journal called Jerusalem at uneven gaps. He also reprinted the chronicles of Abraham Trebitsch with notes. Those chronicles run from 1741 to 1801. His added part brings the record to 1850. A life of his friend Zebi Hirsch Chajes also came from his pen. The reviews ran in two parts, printed in 1837 and 1839. His life of Chajes ran through four issues of Ha-Maggid in its first volume.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bray-sur-seine-:
Bray-sur-Seine is a small town between Provins and Montereau, in Seine-et-Marne. It belonged formerly to Champagne. In the twelfth century it held a large Jewish community, with rabbis such as Jacob the Tosafist and Isaac.

In 1191 a Jew of Bray was murdered by a subject of the French king. The countess Blanche let the Jews hang the murderer on Purim. Christian reports describe a mocking procession before the hanging. Philip Augustus then invaded, seized the town's Jews, and burned more than eighty at the stake. Only children under thirteen escaped that attack. Jews still lived at Bray later, but all traces vanish after the fourteenth century.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bruck-moses-375: Moses Bruck was a Hungarian theological writer born about 1812 in Prerau, Moravia. He studied at Prague and moved to Hungary when no tutor post opened in Moravia. When the Revolution of 1848 broke out, he enlisted for Hungarian independence. He became a Honvéd officer, died in 1849, and was buried with full military honors in a Jewish cemetery. Bruck backed the Reform movement strongly. The entry calls him a pioneer of modern Jewish theological writing. His works on rabbinic ceremony and Pharisaic customs won praise from Geiger and Fürst.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cabala-10258:
Cabala is the specific term for a mystic teaching about God and the universe. The entry says adepts claimed it came down as a revelation to chosen saints of a remote past. At first it held practical lore. Under Neoplatonic and Neopythagorean influence, it took a more speculative shape. In the geonic period it joined itself to the Sefer Yetzirah.

From the thirteenth century the Cabala spread into a wide literature beside the Talmud. Its holy book was the Zohar, written in a special Aramaic dialect. The entry divides the system into a theoretical branch and a practical, wonder working branch. It notes that the name Cabala appears in print only in the eleventh century. Most modern scholars, it reports, stress the forged ascription of the Zohar and kindred works.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-canaim-of-cagli: Canaim of Cagliari was an Italian archaeologist of the eighth century about whom almost nothing is known. The entry says that plainly. Like his townsman Abraham of Cagliari, he worked at copying and reading old inscriptions. Those inscriptions were Phoenician and Greek. No book, post, or date beyond his century is given for him. His whole record here rests on that shared work with inscriptions in Sardinia.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-caro-abraham-b-: Abraham b. Raphael Caro was a Turkish rabbi active at Adrianople in the first half of the eighteenth century. He descended from Joseph Caro and was stepson and pupil of Eliezer b. Jacob Naḥum, author of Ḥazon Naḥum. He probably succeeded his stepfather as rabbi of Adrianople. None of Abraham Caro's own treatises was printed on its own. Several of them, and quotes from others, survive inside his stepfather's book. The short entry adds that he died young.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-castro-tartas-d: David b. Abraham de Castro Tartas worked as a printer at Amsterdam from 1663 to 1695. He published many rabbinical writings. Among them were prayer books and works on ritual, in Hebrew, Spanish, and Portuguese. His brother, Jacob de Castro Tartas, shared in running the printing office. The hosted entry is short. It gives the dates of his activity, the kinds of books he issued, the three languages he used, and his brother's part in the business, and nothing further.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-caution-4158:
Caution is the warning given to witnesses before they testify. Neither Bible law nor rabbinical law asks a witness to confirm testimony by oath. Jewish jurists held that a man who would lie without an oath would also lie with one. So an oath adds nothing, and a warning takes its place.

In criminal cases, witnesses are first told to speak only of what they saw themselves. They are warned against guesswork and hearsay, and told to expect close questioning. The Mishnah's formal warning then stresses the weight of the act. In civil suits, falsehood costs money, which can be repaid. In criminal cases, the blood of the victim and of his unborn offspring falls on the false witness. Yet honest witnesses must still speak, since letting the guilty escape harms the innocent.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-chaseisch-moses: Moses Chaseisch was a German Talmudist who died at Halberstadt in 1793. Fellow scholars honored him for his learning and loved him for his modesty. Though fit for the post of rabbinical assessor, he chose instead to teach the young in Talmudic science. Poor as he was, he often refused fees for his lessons. He taught for love of the Torah, not for profit, the entry stresses. Most Jewish scholars who lived at Halberstadt between 1780 and 1840 owed their Talmudic training to him.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-chovevei-zion-l:
Chovevei Zion, or Lovers of Zion, were associations across Europe and the United States backing farm settlement by Jews in Palestine. The entry calls the movement the forerunner of political Zionism. Its stated aims joined settlement aid with fostering a national idea, spreading Hebrew as a living language, and raising the standing of Jews at home.

Persecution in Rumania and Russia gave the cause its push, and named advocates in several countries took it up from 1879 on. An Odessa committee led much of the work, with support linked to Rothschild in Paris. The entry tracks the peak in 1893, a Turkish ban on immigration in December, 1892, and hard years for the colonies after that.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cohen-abraham-4: Abraham Cohen was an assistant rabbi in Tunis who died in 1840 at Safed. He had gone there on pilgrimage in his old age. He was a grandson of one of the earliest rabbis in Tunis. His one book, Abraham Yagel, came out at Leghorn in 1843, after his death. The entry calls it loosely arranged in both form and contents. It holds commentaries on several Talmud treatises. Notes on parts of the Bible and on Maimonides and other law codes fill out the volume.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-colorado-4558:
Colorado, admitted to the Union in 1876, drew its first settlers in the rush after gold was found at Pike's Peak in 1858. Pioneers crossed plains and mountains by wagon, facing wild animals and attacks. Named Jewish survivors of that road include Isidor Deitsch, Leopold Mayer, and F. Z. Salomon.

Denver, settled in 1858-59, became the center of Colorado Jewish life. A cemetery association came first, then worship in 1873 and Temple Emanuel in 1874. Fire destroyed its second building in 1897; a new one opened on Jan. 29, 1899. The National Jewish Hospital for Consumptives was dedicated on Dec. 10, 1899, with room for ninety poor patients. Pueblo and Trinidad close the survey, and the state total comes to about 5,800 Jews.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-coriander-4658: Coriander is a plant with white blossoms, native to the Mediterranean district. It is grown widely in the East. It grows wild in Egypt and Palestine, above all in the Jordan valley. Its seeds have a strong, pleasant flavor. They sweeten confectionery and season cooking. They also serve as a medicine that stimulates and eases gas. The Bible names the plant only twice, in Exodus and Numbers. Both times its seeds are compared to manna. The entry then traces its Hebrew, Aramaic, and Greek names.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-crescenzi-alexa: Alexander Crescenzi was a Jewish convert to Christianity who lived at Rome in the seventeenth century. In 1666 he translated a Spanish treatise on chocolate into Italian. The translation was printed at Rome in 1667, with notes by Alexander Vitrioli. Mandosius also speaks of Crescenzi as a mathematician. He won fame for a report on the eruption of Vesuvius in 1660. Crescenzi edited that report with mathematical notes of his own. Three sources are cited at the close of the brief entry.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-daly-charles-p-: Charles P. Daly was a historian and jurist, born in New York city in 1816. He died in 1899, of Roman Catholic parentage. He joined the bar at twenty-three. In 1844 he became a judge of the court of common pleas. He held judicial office for forty-two years, twenty-seven as chief justice, retiring in 1886. He took a deep interest in Jewish affairs and history. He often spoke at Jewish functions against anti-Semitism. His history of the Jews in North America, issued in 1893, stayed authoritative.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-dauphine-10958:
Dauphiné was a former province of France, now absorbed into the departments of Isère, Hautes-Alpes, and La Drôme. Jews are thought to have settled there in the first centuries of the common era, though nothing is known of their history before the thirteenth century. The entry then follows the community through repeated charges, taxes, and expulsions.

Six Jews of Valréas were tortured and burned in 1247 after a ritual-murder charge that was never proved. Pope Innocent IV defended the Jews, yet later allowed their expulsion in 1253. During the Black Death, Jews at places like Veyne were massacred after well-poisoning charges. Later rulers taxed them heavily and annulled their privileges.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-david-kalonymus: Kalonymus David of Naples was an Italian scholar who lived in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries. He is known for one act of preservation. A letter of 1286 from Jesse ben Hezekiah, exilarch of Damascus, had condemned those who slandered Maimonides. Fearing the original might be lost during persecutions in Portugal and western Castile, David copied it three or four times to give the ban wider publicity. His copy is dated at Naples on July 21, 1506. Steinschneider thought he may have been a son of Ḥayyim Kalonymus.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-delgado-joseph-: Joseph Delgado farmed the revenue of Lumbrales, in Castile, and the whole entry is four lines long. On July 26, 1723, he, his wife Antonia de Cardenas, and his brother Gabriel Delgado were sentenced by the Inquisition at Llerena. They had refused to renounce their faith, and the sentence was imprisonment for life. On the same day, Joseph Delgado's mother-in-law was burned at the stake for the same reason. The entry gives no other facts about his life or family.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-deza-diego-de-5: Diego de Deza was the second inquisitor-general of Spain, and this short entry gives his career in outline. He was bishop of Salamanca and professor of theology there, then archbishop of Seville, where he died in 1506. He was a friend and protector of Christopher Columbus. After Torquemada's death he was named inquisitor-general on September 1, 1499. Under him, 1,664 persons were burned alive and 52,456 received lesser punishments. Though of Jewish descent, he persecuted the Maranos harshly, yet was accused of being a Jew at heart.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-dolan-bellan-52: Dolan Bellan was a French physician who lived at Carcassonne in the fourteenth century. The entry makes him a contemporary of Jacob de Lunel, who left Carcassonne for Tarascon. It suggests he may be the Maystre Bellant, a surgeon called to attend King Louis XI in 1419-20. Two other Jewish doctors were summoned with him. A Jew named Bellan was also known at Carpentras in 1357, though the entry does not merge the two men.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-dormido-david-a:
David Abravanel Dormido, also Manuel Martinez Dormido, was a warden of the Jewish communities at Amsterdam and London. He came from a leading city of Andalusia, where he held high revenue posts. The Inquisition held him for five years, from 1627 to 1632, and tortured him.

Freed, Dormido lived eight years at Bordeaux, then moved to Amsterdam in 1640 for the Brazil trade. Ruin came in 1654 when the Portuguese retook Pernambuco. Manasseh ben Israel sent him to London to press for Jewish readmission to England. On Nov. 3, 1654, he petitioned Cromwell. He settled in London in 1663 and led its first synagogue.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-dvinsk-formerly:
Dvinsk, once Dünaburg, is a city in the government of Vitebsk, Russia. It stands on the Düna where two railroads cross. Knights of the Livonian Order founded it in 1278, and Poland annexed it in 1561. The census of 1897 counted 72,231 people, 32,369 of them Jews.

Trade in Dvinsk lies wholly in Jewish hands, chiefly flax, flaxseed, and timber. Yearly business near century's end ran to ten million rubles. Industry is also mostly Jewish, with 330 Jewish-owned works against 99 others. A private count found 4,862 Jewish artisans in 1898. Tailoring leads the trades, and 658 Jews labor by the day.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-elijah-b-judah-: Elijah ben Judah Loeb of Wischnitz was a Polish rabbi. He died in the year 1715. As a young man he left Poland for Germany. At Fulda he took up the post of rabbi. His books gloss the Jerusalem Talmud tract by tract. One treats Shekalim and came out in 1710. A second treats Berakot and part of Zera'im. Two more treat tracts on damages in civil law. Those works were reprinted more than once in his century.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-engedi-5758: Engedi was a town in the wilds of Judah. It stood on the west shore of the Dead Sea. David hid there when he fled from King Saul. Its vineyards had a wide name in old song. Its balsam and its palms drew praise as well. Men called it Hazazon-tamar for its palm trees in one text. Under Rome it stood as the heart of a district. The Essenes made it a chief seat of their order. In the fourth century it was still a large village.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-eskeles-issacha:
Issachar Berush Eskeles was an Austrian rabbi and financier born in 1692. He died at Vienna on March 2, 1753. He was son of Gabriel Eskeles and son-in-law of Samson Wertheimer. At eighteen he was named rabbi of Kremsir, though business often took him away. In 1718 he followed his father at Nikolsburg while living in Vienna.

Emperor Charles VI made him chief rabbi of Hungary in 1725, and he presided over its rabbinical court at Vienna. From Vienna he could act for Jews more freely. In 1742 his work with Baron d'Aguilar won repeal of a heavy Moravian tax. Their pleas also reversed the winter banishment of Bohemian and Moravian Jews in 1744-45. His notes on Berakot stayed unpublished.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ezekiel-moses-j:
Moses Jacob Ezekiel was an American sculptor born in Richmond, Virginia, on October 28, 1844. He studied at the Virginia Military Institute and served as a Confederate soldier before graduating. He tried painting first, then turned to sculpture. In 1868 he moved to Cincinnati and modeled a statue of Industry. With no art school there, he went on to Berlin.

War reporting for the New York Herald got him jailed eight days as a suspected French spy. His marble Religious Liberty, a B'nai B'rith gift for the centennial, was unveiled at Philadelphia in 1876. In Rome he filled the Corcoran Gallery niches with heroic statues of great artists, from Phidias to Rembrandt. The German emperor knighted him.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-feiwel-phoebus-: Phoebus Uri Shraga Feiwel was rabbi of Dubrovno, in the Mohilev government of Russia, around the year 1800. He married a daughter of Elijah Wilna. He is known only for two works, the entry says. Minhat Shelomoh adds notes on the Pentateuch, filling gaps left by Norzi's Minhat Shai. Menorat Shelomoh treats the Masorah, the notes fixing the Bible's exact text. Both were printed with Elijah Wilna's own Pentateuch comment at Dubrovno in 1804. No birth or death dates are given for him.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-fish-and-fishin:
Fish and fishing are covered from Bible times to the Talmud. The Bible names no single kind of fish. Its words are general terms for fish of all kinds. Large sea fish fall under another broad term. By the dietary laws, fish split into clean and unclean. Most fish, having scales and fins, are clean. Eels are counted unclean, the entry notes.

Fish, fresh or salted, was a favorite food among the Hebrews. The Talmud praises it and gives health rules about eating it. Fish oil served as fuel, and skin and bone had their uses. Fishing itself used drag nets, smaller nets, hooks, and a harpoon. The Lake of Gennesaret was a noted fishing ground. A fish market at Jerusalem is also named.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-gadarenes-6458: Gadarenes are the people of Gadara, known from a tale in Matthew, Mark, and Luke. In that tale Jesus moves demons from a tormented man into a herd of swine. The herd rushes down a steep hill and dies. Close study of the texts and the ground points to Gerasenes as the better reading. The place is then Karsa, by the Sea of Galilee. A public debate in 1892 weighed the morals of the act and whether Jews there could lawfully keep swine.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-gehenna-hebr-gr:
Gehenna began as the valley of the son of Hinnom, south of Jerusalem. Children were offered there to the god Moloch. For that reason the valley was held cursed. The name soon came to stand for hell itself. Views differ on when hell was made. Some say the second day, some say before the world, with its fire made on the second day.

Hell is drawn as huge and deep, split into seven parts. Its fire never goes out and burns sixty times hotter than earthly fire. A gate is said to lie in the valley between two palm trees, with smoke always rising. The sun at setting passes by Gehenna and takes fire from it. Warm springs at Tiberias are heated as they flow past it.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-giants-6658:
Giants renders three Hebrew words in English Bibles. Nefilim names a half-human race said to live on earth before the Flood. They were the offspring of the Bene Elohim and the daughters of men. Gibborim means mighty men. Refaim names the old folk of Palestine, east and west of the Jordan, famed for huge height. Og of Bashan is called their last survivor.

Under David the giants link to Gath. Goliath came from there, as did Ishbi-benob, Saph, and a man with twenty-four fingers and toes. A critical view holds that refaim is a class word, not a race name. On that view giants were a breed of tall men found among many peoples, not one nation by itself.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-goldschmidt-laz:
Lazarus Goldschmidt was a German writer on Ethiopic subjects. He was born at Plungiany, Lithuania, on Dec. 17, 1871. Slobodki's Talmudic school gave him his early training. He reached Germany in 1888 and entered Berlin University in 1890. There he studied Oriental languages, above all Ethiopic.

His first book re-rendered the Book of Enoch from Ethiopic into Hebrew (1892). A catalogue of all known Ethiopic prints followed. He edited the Book of Creation and an Ethiopic life of Abba Daniel. In 1896 he began a bold project: the Babylonian Talmud from its first edition. It carried a German translation, variants, and notes. David Hoffmann attacked the edition sharply. Goldschmidt answered him in a pamphlet of his own.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-guterbock-ludwi:
Ludwig Güterbock was a German physician. He was born at Berlin on Oct. 23, 1814. He took his medical degree at the University of Berlin in 1837. He settled in his home city and practiced there until his death on Feb. 28, 1895.

He wrote essays for medical journals. He helped compile the annual reports on progress in medicine across all lands. His books present Schönlein's clinical lectures at the Charité hospital. Another work treats Schönlein as doctor and clinical teacher. The entry is short and gives no facts beyond his career and writings.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hail-7058:
Hail is frozen rain that falls in pellets of many sizes and shapes. The entry gathers what the Bible says about it. Hebrew has several words for hail, one of them only guessed at. Hailstones count as proofs of God's might, kept in His storehouses. The best known storm is the seventh plague on Egypt before the Exodus.

Hail also serves as God's weapon: at one battle more men died by hailstones than by Israel's sword. For that cause hail stands often as a figure of punishment in Isaiah and Ezekiel. It is paired again and again with fire, and named with thunder. The short article works wholly from Bible verses and their plain sense.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hamor-7158: Hamor was a Hivite prince, the father of Shechem. His son's defilement of Dinah brought the destruction of a whole city. Hamor's own family was among the dead. Hamor held great sway over the Shechemites. On his advice they circumcised all their males. The people are called "the sons of Hamor" and "the men of Hamor." From that the entry infers that Hamor founded Shechem. It takes "the father of Shechem" as his title as founder. The same form appears in "the father of Bethlehem" and "the father of Tekoa."
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hayyim-lit-life:
Hayyim, a word meaning life, was a common Jewish first name, above all in the Middle Ages. It appears in Latin as Vita on a mosaic at Kafr Kenna. It also shows in the Jewish burial caves of Venosa. Forms of the name shift from land to land and age to age.

In Spain it became Aim or Haym, in Germany Hayum or Chajim, in France Hagin. The Latin line runs through Vitalis and Vital to Vida and Veitel. The entry notes one special use. People who got well after sickness sometimes took the name. Modern family names such as Hyam and Hayem grow out of it.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hebrew-review-t: The Hebrew Review was a literary magazine published at Cincinnati, Ohio. The Rabbinical Literary Association of America put it out. Two volumes appeared, in the years given as 1881 and 1892. Max Lilienthal, the association's president, edited the magazine first. After his death the vice-president, K. Kohler, took over the editing. The entry is brief and adds nothing about its contents or its readers. It stands as a record of a rabbinic group's try at a learned journal.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-henikstein-alfr:
Alfred, Freiherr von Henikstein, born at Ober-Döbling on Aug. 11, 1810, rose to high rank in the Austrian army. He was the son of banker Joseph von Henikstein. After baptism he joined an engineers regiment in 1828.

Henikstein became major in 1848, colonel the next year, and major-general in 1854. He fought in the Austro-Italian war of 1859 and was made a baron. He later led the fifth army corps at Verona. As chief of staff in the Austro-Prussian war, he faced a court martial after defeat. The court was dismissed without judgment. He then retired in Vienna, where he died on Jan. 29, 1882.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hevesi-ludwig-7:
Ludwig Hevesi, born at Heves, Hungary, on Dec. 20, 1843, began studies in medicine and classical languages at Budapest and Vienna. He soon turned to writing. From 1865 he worked as a journalist and author. In 1875 he settled in Vienna.

Hevesi wrote humor pieces for papers, edited art coverage, and reviewed drama at the Hofburgtheater. He helped found a Hungarian humor paper that became popular. His books include travel sketches, tales, and a comic work popular in Finland. The entry rates him among the most original humorists of his time. It also credits his art writing with shaping public taste.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hirschfeld-otto:
Otto Hirschfeld, born March 16, 1843, at Königsberg, Prussia, was a German historian, inscription scholar, and archeologist. He studied at Königsberg and Bonn, taking his doctorate in 1863. He then spent two years in Italy. He gained a lectureship at Göttingen in 1869.

Hirschfeld taught ancient history at Prague from 1872, then at Vienna from 1875. There he built a famed archeology and epigraphy seminary with Alexander Conze. His work on Roman inscriptions found in Austria was key. From 1885 he held the ancient history chair at Berlin. Major works cover Roman rule, Lyon, Latin law, and Gaulish inscriptions in two large corpus volumes.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hor-7858:
Hor is the name of two different mountains in the Bible. The first stood on the border of Idumaea and was the next stop after Kadesh on the wilderness journey. It is famous as the place where Aaron died. The entry links it to Jabal Harun, a two-peaked mountain east of Wadi al-'Arabah.

The second Mount Hor marked the northern limit of Israel's inheritance in Canaan. The article reviews how Josephus, Eusebius, the Targums, and the Talmud placed these peaks. Later writers disagreed, and several rival identifications are weighed before the entry closes.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-huth-georg-7958:
Georg Huth was a German Orientalist and explorer born on February 25, 1867, at Krotoschin in Prussia. He entered Berlin University in 1885 and took his doctorate at Leipsic in 1889. In 1891 he began lecturing at Berlin on Central Asiatic languages and Buddhism.

In 1897 Huth traveled to Siberia to study Tungusic, backed by the St. Petersburg Academy of Sciences. In 1902 he joined the Turfan expedition to eastern Turkestan. The next year he studied Turkish speech and folk tales in the west. His books include a history of Buddhism in Mongolia from a Tibetan source. He also edited Mongolian inscriptions and Tungusic folk literature.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-idit-8058: Idit is the name of a teacher known from a single passage kept by Nahman. The passage is part of a dispute between Idit and a heretic. The entry says the name should be read Idi. This teacher is the same as the Palestinian Idi. Nothing else is told of him here. The notice runs to a few lines and rests on tractate Sanhedrin and one named modern work on the Palestinian teachers.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ikriti-shemaria:
Shemariah ben Elijah Ikriti of Negropont was an Italian philosopher and Bible exegete, a contemporary of Dante. Born probably at Rome about 1275, he came of a long line of Roman Jews. His father served as rabbi in Crete, which gave the family its Greek name. Shemariah knew Italian, Latin, and Greek and thought with a critical edge.

Until 1305 he studied Bible alone, then added rabbinic lore and philosophy. King Robert of Naples called him to court. By 1328 he had finished philosophic notes on the Pentateuch, Job, and Canticles. He worked to unite Karaites and Rabbinites, and the Karaites honored him. In 1352 he traveled to Spain to win Karaites over. The tale says he posed as Messiah. He was jailed and died in prison.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-izates-8358:
Izates was a king of Adiabene who became a proselyte to Judaism. He was a son of Queen Helena and Monobaz I, born in the year 1 and dead in 55. Sent to Charax Spasinu, he met a Jewish merchant, Ananias, who taught him the faith. He did not know his mother had already been won to Judaism. On taking the throne he found out, and he meant to follow her, even to circumcision.

Ananias and his mother both argued against that step; another Jew, Eleazar, at last persuaded him to it. Peace followed, and Izates was so respected that Parthia's king Artaban III chose him to settle a quarrel with rebel nobles. When his kin openly converted, Adiabene's nobles bought a war from Abia of Arabia; Izates beat him, and Abia killed himself. A plot with Parthia's king then failed at the last hour.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-jacob-ben-solom: Jacob ben Solomon, called Jacob of Courson, was a French tosafist born at Courson, in the Yonne, who worked between 1180 and 1250. He studied under Samson of Sens and apparently taught Meir of Rothenburg. His tosafot are quoted in the "Shittah Mekubbezet" under his town's name, once miswritten as Kurso. A work of his called "Nimukim" held comments on the Talmud. Another, the "Matbea'," may also be his; it held Talmudic decisions. He exchanged letters with the poet Judah b. Sheneor.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-jehoahaz-8558:
Jehoahaz names more than one king in the Bible, and the entry treats them in turn. The first was a son of Jehu who ruled northern Israel from 814 to 797 B.C. Under him Syria pressed Israel hard and cut its army to a handful. His humble prayer, the entry says, brought a savior whose name is not fixed.

The second Jehoahaz, also called Shallum, was a son of Josiah of Judah. The people made him king in 608 B.C., but Pharaoh Necho seized him and carried him to Egypt, where he died. A third use of the name is a form of Ahaziah, king of Judah.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-jewish-spectato: Jewish Spectator holds a first in the entry's telling: it was the first Jewish weekly journal in the southern United States. M. Samfield founded it in Memphis, Tennessee, on Oct. 19, 1885, and he edited and published it until 1904. In 1892 his son Joseph M. Samfield took charge of the business side. The short entry gives one mark of its character: its tendency runs toward moderate Reform. Nothing is said of its readers or its end.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-jonas-emile-875: Emile Jonas was a French musician born at Paris on March 5, 1827. He entered the Conservatoire in 1841, took the first prize in harmony in 1847, and won the Grand Prix de Rome in 1848. After early overtures he gave himself chiefly to comic operettas in Offenbach's style. Named hits run from The Duel of Benjamin in 1855 to Javotte in 1871, later staged in London as Cinderella. He taught singing by note at the Conservatoire and led music at the Portuguese synagogue of Paris, issuing a book of Hebrew chants in 1854.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-judah-jewish-pr: Judah the Jewish prince was a son of Simeon Tharsi. When Antiochus VII sent his general Cendebaeus against Simeon, the old man gave his army to his sons Judah and John. From Modin they met the Syrian force in the plain of Jabneh and beat it. They chased it as far as Azotus, with a loss of 2,000 men. Judah was wounded in the fight. In the year 135 before the common era, when Simeon was murdered by his son-in-law Ptolemy, Judah was killed as well.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-kalischer-solom:
Solomon Kalischer was a German composer, pianist, and physicist. He was born on Oct. 8, 1845, at Thorn, in West Prussia. He studied at Breslau and at Berlin. His prize thesis of 1868 dealt with Aristotle. After a year as a tutor at Amsterdam, he went back to Berlin. There he turned to physics and chemistry.

From 1876 Kalischer taught at the Bauakademie in Berlin. He later joined the Technische Hochschule at Charlottenburg. He became a lecturer there in 1894 and a professor in 1896. The entry lists his mixed output. He edited Goethe's works on science. He turned Faraday's studies on electricity into German. He also wrote on color blindness and on Darwin's theory, plus many papers on physics.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-kitzinger-jacob: Jacob ben Joseph Kitzinger was an author and poet. He lived in the second half of the sixteenth century and at the beginning of the seventeenth. He wrote "Ḥag ha-Pesaḥ," printed at Cracow in 1597. It is a commentary on the Passover Haggadah. The work carries glosses by his father. It also holds a poem on the Passover ritual and a long introduction. Added to it is "Ḳeẓ ha-Pela'ot." That piece treats the end of the Exile and the coming of the Messiah.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-laszlo-philip-9: Philip László, a Hungarian portrait painter born on June 1, 1869, at Budapest, drew notice as a student at the Model Drawing School there. A state grant paid for five years of study at Munich and Paris. His 1891 painting of a storytelling old woman first drew attention. His sitters include the Prince of Bulgaria's family, King Francis Joseph I, Prince Alexander Hohenlohe-Schillingsfürst, and Pope Leo XIII. The entry closes by noting that László has embraced Christianity.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-levinthal-bernh: Bernhard Louis Levinthal, a Russian-American rabbi, was born at Kovno, Russia, on May 12, 1864. He studied at rabbinical schools in Kovno, Wilna, and Byelostok. In 1888 he won rabbinical diplomas from two noted rabbis. He came to the United States in 1891. Soon after, he became minister of six Russian congregations in Philadelphia. He helped found communal bodies in that city. He serves as vice-president of the Union of Orthodox Rabbis of America.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lichtschein-lud: Ludwig Lichtschein, a Hungarian rabbi, was born in Komorn and died at Ofen in 1886. He studied at Papa. He served as rabbinical assessor at Austerlitz, Gross Kanizsa, and Esztergom. From 1876 until his death he was rabbi at Somogy-Csurgó. His first book, from 1866, treats the state of the Jews in medieval and modern times. Later pieces treat the thirteen articles of faith, the Targum to the Prophets, and the Talmud and socialism. One essay treats Kossuth and a Hungarian rabbi.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lob-b-joseph-re:
Löb b. Joseph, known as Reb Löb Sarah's, was an early Hasidic rabbi who died in Yaltushkov, Podolia, about 1797. The entry calls him the strangest of the miracle-working rabbis of his time. He traveled from town to town, spent money freely, and took nothing from his followers.

Most tales about him link him to kings and princes and to help for Jews with rulers. One tale says he slipped past guards into the Warsaw palace in 1764. Another tells of a seven-year struggle with Emperor Joseph II. A letter cited here says he did real services for Jews that could not be put in writing.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lowinsohn-jacob:
Jacob Mordecai ben Judah Löb Löwinsohn (1832–1878) was a Russo-Polish scholar and journalist born in Grodno, and a Jewish Encyclopedia entry from 1906 by Herman Rosenthal and Isidor S. Beaumache profiles him. A rabbi’s son trained in Talmud, he quickly mastered Russian, German, Polish, and French. That training launched his career in the press.

Löwinsohn wrote for Russian papers and, from 1862, for the journal “Jutrzenka,” where he defended the interests of his fellow Jews. The article recalls his heated debates with Hirsch Kalischer and with L. J. Shapiro, and notes that he was ordained at Wilna about 1868 yet never took a rabbinate. It also lists his early book of 1855, printed in a small run for friends. Readers get a portrait of a multilingual writer who argued for Jewish rights in several languages at once.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mandl-moritz-10:
Moritz Mandl, an Austrian dramatist and journalist, receives an entry in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born in Presburg on May 13, 1840, he went to Vienna for newspaper work. He joined the staff of the Wanderer in 1862. Later he moved to the Neue Freie Presse. Since 1877 he had been assistant editor of the Fremdenblatt.

The article lists his writings beyond the newsroom. A pamphlet, Germany and the Moment, printed at Leipsic in 1861, won some attention. His German epic Kathchen von Heilbronn appeared at Vienna in 1873. He wrote a dramatic prologue for the Vienna Kleist celebration of 1876. Several plays of his are also noted, though not named. The brief entry preserves a journalist whose bylines reached the stage as well as the press.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-masarjawaih-or-:
Masarjawaih, who lived at Bassora about the year 883, is remembered in a Jewish Encyclopedia entry from 1906 by Richard Gottheil and Max Schloessinger. He ranks among the oldest Arabic-writing Jewish physicians and as the oldest translator from the Syriac. Even his name is a puzzle: scholars quoted here debate whether its ending marks it as Persian and what the original name really was.

His main work was translating the medical pandects of the presbyter Aaron from Syriac into Arabic, adding two chapters of his own to Aaron's thirty. He also wrote Arabic treatises on the virtues and dangers of foods and of medicinal plants. None of his three writings survives whole; the entry notes that their contents are known only through quotations and fragments preserved by later authors.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mendel-hermann-:
Hermann Mendel was a Berlin music publisher and writer. Isidore Singer and Joseph Sohn profile him in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Halle in 1834. He trained in music there and at Leipzig and Berlin. He worked for the publishers Schlesinger and then Bote and Bock. He kept his own firm from 1862 to 1868. He wrote steadily for the musical press. From its founding in 1870 until his death, he conducted the "Deutsche Musikerzeitung."

His monument is the "Musikalisches Konversations-Lexikon." It is a dictionary of music. He launched it in 1870 with a large and distinguished staff. Mendel died at Berlin on October 26, 1876. By then the work had reached only the letter M. August Reissmann carried it to eleven volumes. They rank among the most comprehensive of their kind. The entry also credits his biographies of Nicolai and Meyerbeer. It credits his edition of some ninety opera libretti too.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-meyer-ludwig-be:
Ludwig Beatus Meyer, born in Gandersheim, Brunswick, on January 3, 1780, was a Danish author best known for a dictionary that still carried his name in 1906. Isidore Singer and Frank Cramer wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry. He came to Copenhagen as a young private teacher and tutored in the family of Count Schimmelmann.

Naturalized as a Danish citizen in 1810, Meyer headed the bureau of the national debt before resigning in 1821 with the title of professor. He then wrote full time, starting with a handbook of German poetic literature in 1828. His lasting work was an 1837 glossary of foreign words and phrases in Danish, Meyer's Fremmedordbog, which passed through several editions as a standard authority.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-minnesota-10858:
Minnesota's thirteen thousand Jews are surveyed by Cyrus Adler and S. N. Deinard in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906: six thousand in Minneapolis, five thousand in St. Paul, a thousand in Duluth, and the rest scattered five to twenty families to a town. The first settlers seem to have been three English brothers named Samuels.

The Samuels brothers kept an Indian trading-post at Taylor Falls on the St. Croix as early as 1852, and Morris Samuels became a Union captain in the Civil War. Isaac Marks traded with the Indians from Mankato on the same frontier terms. St. Paul's Jews organized the state's first congregation, Mt. Zion, only in 1871 — Minneapolis then still had hardly any Jews at all.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-moses-ben-abrah:
Moses ben Abraham Provençal was rabbi of Mantua in the middle of the sixteenth century. Joseph Jacobs and Alexander Kisch wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry. His fame rests on one decision: he approved the first printed edition of the Zohar. The book appeared at Mantua in 1558, with the Inquisition's approval as well.

Not all agreed with him: Meir Katzenellenbogen of Padua and others had opposed printing the Zohar. Provençal also wrote a treatise on two lines that approach but never meet, printed in Hebrew in 1548 and in Italian in 1550. A responsum of his on a divorce case appeared at Padua in 1566. The entry catches a rabbi at the meeting point of print, Cabala, and censorship.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-moses-ben-todro:
Moses ben Todros was a Spanish rabbi who lived about 1150 and served for many years as nasi of Narbonne. Wilhelm Bacher and J. S. Raisin wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry. He was known both as a scholar and for his charity. His modest temper earned him the standing nickname he-anaw, the modest one.

His name appears among the signers of a famous appeal about Torah reading. The appeal asked leave to use an ordinary Torah manuscript in public worship when no regulation scroll could be had. His son Levi is praised by the poet Al-Harizi as a philanthropist. The short entry preserves a communal leader remembered for humility as much as rank.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nabal-lit-fool-:
Nabal, whose name means fool, was a rich Calebite sheep master in the story of David's wanderings. Emil G. Hirsch and M. Seligsohn tell his tale in the Jewish Encyclopedia, from First Samuel. His flocks fed at Carmel while he lived at Maon. The text calls him churlish and a man of Belial, and his wife was Abigail.

David's men had guarded Nabal's shepherds, and at shearing time David asked for provisions in return. Nabal answered with insults, calling David a runaway slave, and David set out to kill him. Abigail rode out with gifts and talked David down. When she told her drunken husband next morning, he fell into a fit and died ten days later.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nathan-jedidiah:
Nathan Jedidiah ben Eliezer was an Italian Hebrew poet. His entry was written by the Editorial Board's Executive Committee and M. Seligsohn for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Orvieto in 1607. At Sienna in 1625 he turned to verse. His models came in part through his own family.

Jedidiah put three confessional prayers into Hebrew verse. He used the Italian three-line form called terza rima. One prayer came from Bahya and one from R. Nissim. A third was by an unknown writer. He followed an Italian verse version by his grandfather Alatrini. He also wrote sonnets in Hebrew and Italian, plus a dirge.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-neuburger-ferdi:
Ferdinand Neuburger was a German dramatist of Frankfort. Isidore Singer and Franklin S. Wilson wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Düsseldorf on Aug. 28, 1839. He died at Frankfort on Oct. 27, 1895. He began as a tutor at the Philanthropin.

Neuburger soon left teaching to write for the stage alone. His first play, Markgräfin von Pommeraye, succeeded at Stuttgart in 1876. Laroche followed, a heroic drama built on Lassalle's career. Politics forced its withdrawal after one performance in 1882. A youthful piece, Das Gastmahl des Ponteus, also survives in mention. His record is short, but it marks a bold attempt. Lassalle on stage was a daring choice for the time.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nissim-benvenis: Don Nissim Benveniste was a Spanish scholar of the fifteenth century. Joseph Jacobs and Isaac Broydé wrote his brief entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Little of his life is recorded in these lines. His fame rests on legal consultations with Isaac Aboab. Those exchanges of question and answer were printed long after. Abraham Meldola published them at Leghorn in 1745. They appear in his work called Shib'ah 'Enayim, under one title. The title is simply She'elah u-Teshubah, question and answer.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-odeka-11658:
Odeka is the first word of a verse in Psalm 118. Cyrus Adler and Francis L. Cohen wrote the entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The psalm forms part of the Hallel, a set of praise psalms. Odeka marks the point where two choirs end their turn and turn singing. From there, the last verses are sung twice.

The way this is done shifts from rite to rite. In the Polish rite each man doubles the verses himself. Parts of one verse may thus be sung four times. The entry gives the tunes used for this verse. One tune comes from the Sephardic rite of Spain. One comes from the Ashkenazic rite of Germany. Both tunes are old and well loved by their groups.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-oren-11758:
Oren is a word used by German Jews for prayer. Cyrus Adler and Francis L. Cohen wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. It comes from the Latin word ora, which means pray. A German verb end was tacked on to that root. The word was known to all in the Middle Ages.

Oren does not mean just to pray in broad terms. It means to say one's set prayers, line by line. A man may do this with the flock in prayer. He may do it at home, in private, as well. Jews in Slav lands use a word dawenen in its place. In England and America, men say daven for the same act. The piece weighs where that word daven first came from.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-palaggi-falaji-:
Abraham Palaggi was a Turkish author and chief rabbi. Isidore Singer and M. Franco wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Smyrna in the year 1809. He died there in the year 1899. His father was Hayyim Palaggi, chief rabbi of Smyrna.

When his father died in 1869, Abraham took his post. An imperial decree gave him the chief rabbi's chair. He held that chair for a full thirty years in all. He oft stood up for Jews against a dire charge. That charge was the false claim of rite based murder. He wrote sixteen works in the Hebrew tongue in his life. He wrote one work in the Spanish tongue of Jews. Each Hebrew work held his name, Abraham, in its title.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pavia-julius-lu:
Julius da Pavia was an Italian Jewish scholar of the eighth century. He is one of the first European Jews known by name. Isidore Singer and Umberto Cassuto wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The record of him comes from Alcuin.
