About 760 Julius held a public debate at Pavia. His opponent was Pietro da Pisa, a famed grammarian. They argued over religion before an audience. Alcuin later told Charlemagne about the dispute in a letter. He said the debate would be written down in a book. In some copies the scholar's name reads Lullus.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pesaro-aaron-12:
Aaron Pesaro wrote a guide that links Bible verses to rabbinic books. Richard Gottheil and Ismar Elbogen wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. No one knows where or when he lived. He likely worked in Germany after 1400. The book served preachers and students for centuries.

His book is called Toledot Aharon, the Generations of Aaron. Beside each verse it notes where the Talmud explains it. It does the same for verses treated in the Midrash. Froben first printed it at Basel in 1580. Later editions in Venice and elsewhere kept it in use.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pinczow-eliezer: Eliezer Pinczow was a Polish rabbi of the late 1600s. Herman Rosenthal and A. S. Waldstein wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. His grandfather had been rabbi of Lublin. He served as rabbi at Pinczow and other towns. He also sat as a lay leader at Cracow. Two of his books were printed after his death. One gives notes on the Masoretic text of the Bible. The other expounds the tales of the Talmud.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-polotsk-phineha:
Phinehas ben Judah of Polotsk was a Polish writer of notes on the Bible. The Editorial Board and Schulim Ochser wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He lived at Polotsk in the eighteenth century. His books deal with both wisdom books and song.

Phinehas wrote notes on Proverbs, printed at Wilna in 1803. He wrote on Canticles and Ecclesiastes at Grodno in 1804. His notes on the Book of Job came out in 1808. He also shortened a large work by Kalonymus ben Kalonymus. His Rosh ha-Gibeah treats morals and gives sermons. A further work on the commandments stayed in handwriting.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-priest-12358:
Priest, meaning one set apart for service at the altar, is the subject of an article by the Editorial Board and Moses Buttenwieser. It appeared in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The writers warn that the word fits late times best. In early Israel no special setting apart was needed. Any man might come to the altar with a gift.

Gideon offered a sacrifice in person, the article notes. He belonged to the tribe of Manasseh, not Levi. Manoah the Danite did the same at an angel's word. Both acts are told as done at God's own command. The article traces how a free act became a priest's sole right. It follows the priesthood from clan days to Temple days.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-queensland-1245:
Queensland is a British colony in Australia, cut off from New South Wales in 1859. Joseph Jacobs and Jonas M. Myers wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. At the split, a few Jewish families moved from Sydney. They settled for good at Brisbane, the new capital. Their names are given in the entry one by one.

The families formed a congregation in about 1864. They called the Reverend Joseph E. Myers from Sydney to lead them. Coleman and Davis stood among the first names. Jewell, Mendoza, and Goldsmid stood there too. The entry traces the group's growth in Brisbane and beyond. It shows how a handful of homes became a settled body.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-reicherson-mose:
Moses ha-Kohen Reicherson was a Hebrew grammarian born on October 5, 1827. Herman Rosenthal and A. S. Waldstein wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born in Wilna. He died in New York on April 3, 1903.

The article says he studied Talmud, Hebrew, and European languages. He taught Hebrew at Wilna for many years. About 1890 he moved to New York and taught there. His writing centers on Hebrew grammar in detail. Books treat punctuation, verbs, particles, and the noun. He made a grammar catechism for beginners as well. He translated fables by Krylov and by Lessing. Many commentaries stayed in manuscript at his death. The entry shows a teacher devoted to Hebrew's fine points.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-right-and-right:
Right and righteousness translate a family of Hebrew words. Emil G. Hirsch wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. The root is zadak, with forms like zaddik and zedek. English also uses just, justice, and justify for them.

The article admits the root's first sense is in doubt. One guess links it to being hard, even, or straight. A better reading is that a thing is as it should be. Weights and measures called zedek are simply right. Paths called zedek are easy to travel. A king or judge who acts properly is just. Speech that fits the facts is truthful speech. To justify means to show someone is in the right. The entry roots a moral idea in physical fitness.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rosensohn-moses:
Moses Rosensohn was a Russian Hebraist who lived his whole life at Wilna, in comfort. Herman Rosenthal and Isidor Warsaw wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He was born there early in the nineteenth century and died in 1896.

Rosensohn wrote several Hebrew works on the future of Judaism. One book urged reforms in Jewish religious life. Another praised the broad, universal spirit of the Mosaic religion. A third, in three volumes, defended the Cabala against its critics. His suspected leanings toward Christianity made Orthodox Jews of Russia shun him.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-saalschutz-loui:
Louis Saalschütz was a German mathematician born at Königsberg, Prussia, on December 1, 1835. Isidore Singer wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia, working alone. He was a son of the rabbi Joseph Lewin Saalschütz.

Saalschütz studied mathematics and physics at Königsberg and took his doctorate in 1861. His dissertation studied heat changes deep in the earth's upper layers. For over twenty years he taught mechanics and engineering at the Royal School of Mechanics. He also lectured at the university, becoming assistant professor in 1875. For years he presided over Königsberg's Jewish orphan asylum.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-samaria-hebrew-:
Samaria was a city of Palestine and capital of the kingdom of Israel. Joseph Jacobs and M. Seligsohn wrote its entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. King Omri built it on the mountain Shomeron early in his reign.

Omri bought that mountain for two talents of silver from Shemer. He named the city Shomeron after its former owner, the Bible says. The entry doubts the tale, since the mountain already bore the name. It may mean watch mountain instead, a fit name for the site. Set in a fertile basin near Shechem, Samaria long ruled the Ten Tribes.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-samiler-smieler:
A. G. Samiler, born Eliakim Götzel and called Mehlsack, was a Russian Talmudist born at Smiela about 1780. Gotthard Deutsch wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia, working alone. He belonged to a prominent rabbinical family of the region.

Samiler gave special care to the historical setting of rabbinic literature. He wrote valuable genealogical essays, still held in private hands at Lemberg and Vienna. His only printed work is Sefer Rabiyah, issued at Ofen in 1837. It criticizes Zunz's lectures on Jewish worship and Rapoport's life of Kalir. He died at Brody on July 17, 1854.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-samun-joseph-ha:
Isaac Broydé wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, issued with the Executive Committee of the Editorial Board in 1906. It profiles Joseph Ḥayyim ibn Samun, an Italian Talmudist. He lived at Leghorn across the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries. Leghorn was a busy port with a large Jewish community. Samun wrote on the Talmud and on points of law.

His book 'Edut bi-Yehosef appeared at Leghorn in 1800. It fills two volumes. The first gives new readings on the tractate Baba Meẓi'a. The second gathers his responsa, his formal answers to legal questions. Appended to the work is Leḳaḥ Ṭob. That part holds readings and responsa by his son Shem-Ṭob. Shem-Ṭob served as rabbi of Leghorn.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-scherschewski-b:
Herman Rosenthal and Peter Wiernik wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on Benjamin Scherschewski. He was a Russian physician. Scherschewski was born at Brest-Litovsk in 1857. He studied medicine at the University of Warsaw. He graduated there in 1883. In 1885 he went to Palestine and settled in Jerusalem.

Two years later Scherschewski left for Vienna. There he took a special course in medicine. After another short stay in Jerusalem, he settled at Odessa. He still practices there in 1905. His book Mishnat 'Olam Ḳaṭon treats two sciences in Hebrew. Its first part covers anatomy, and its second part chemistry. Jehiel Michael Pines corrected and annotated the work. It was printed at Jerusalem in 1886.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-scroll-of-the-l:
Joseph Jacobs, Judah David Eisenstein, and Ludwig Blau wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, issued with the Executive Committee of the Editorial Board in 1906. It treats the Scroll of the Law, the Sefer Torah. That is the Pentateuch written by hand on parchment. The rabbis count writing such a scroll among every Israelite's duties. A king had to keep a second copy by his throne.

One who cannot write must hire a scribe or buy a scroll. An inherited scroll does not free a man from the duty. The scroll may not be sold, even in dire need. Exceptions cover a teacher's fee and marriage costs. The parchment must come from a clean animal's skin. It is dressed with gallnut and lime for strength. Lines are ruled, and only the best black ink is allowed. The scroll runs about six handbreadths wide.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-shammash-lit-se:
Shammash, literally servant, was an officer of the synagogue and the Jewish community. Joseph Jacobs and Peter Wiernik wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on the office. In Talmudic times the same worker was called hazzan. He helped lead parts of the prayer service then.

By the Middle Ages the shammash held real power and duty. He assessed members for taxes by their means. He ran the synagogue and carried out court sentences. In some places he even gave court-ordered lashes. One writer calls him a permanent under-secretary who governed quietly. The entry reveals the hired hand who kept self-governing Jewish towns working.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-shofar-12558:
Shofar is the ancient ritual horn of Israel, still blown in synagogue worship. Cyrus Adler, Francis L. Cohen, Abraham de Harkavy, and Judah David Eisenstein wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on it. Calling it trumpet or cornet misleads, the authors warn. Its name points rather to tuba or clarion.

The Bible mentions the shofar often, from Exodus to Zechariah. Its loud voice from Sinai's cloud made Israel tremble. Other instruments changed with each age's craft and fashion. Silver trumpets served the Temple in fixed form. The shofar alone never changed its simple, crude shape. That stubborn sameness marks it as a prehistoric survival. The entry traces its uses, from war calls and alarms to the solemn blasts of the New Year season.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-silberstein-otv:
Adolf Silberstein, called Ötvös, was a Hungarian art critic born at Budapest in 1845. Isidore Singer and Ludwig Venetianer wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. He studied philosophy and medicine at Leipzig University. Berlin added comparative philology, and Heidelberg added history and economics.

He took his doctorate at Leipzig in 1866. Journalism then claimed him across German-language papers. He edited a weekly on drama with two collaborators. Back in Hungary from 1870, he edited the Temesvarer Zeitung. Later he wrote for Budapest's leading German dailies. His Bible of Nature, printed in 1877, caused a sensation. Bradlaugh translated it into English for wider readers. Russia suppressed the book outright, the entry reports. He died at Budapest in 1899.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-solomon-ben-eli:
Solomon ben Elijah Sharbit ha-Zahab was an astronomer, poet, and grammarian. Crawford Howell Toy and Isaac Broydé wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He lived at Salonica and later at Ephesus. His time was the second half of the fourteenth century. His Hebrew name may match the Greek name Chrysakokka.

He rendered Persian astronomical tables into Hebrew from the Greek. He also translated Ptolemy's treatise on the astrolabe. His own works include a grammatical treatise, Heshek Shelomoh. He wrote a commentary on Ibn Ezra's Sefer ha-Shem as well. Many of his liturgical poems entered prayer books. His Pentateuch commentary attacked Karaite views with great force.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-spielmann-sir-i:
Sir Isidore Spielmann was an English engineer and communal worker born in 1854. Joseph Jacobs wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born in London on July 21 of that year. He trained as an engineer but loved art deeply. In 1887 he proposed the Anglo-Jewish Historical Exhibition in London.

He served as honorary secretary of that exhibition throughout. He later led the Jewish Historical Society of England for years. He directed British sections at Brussels, Paris, Glasgow, and St Louis. For those services he was knighted in 1905 by the king. He edited Darkest Russia to expose abuse of Jews there. He refused a Russian exhibition post on principle as a Jew.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-stokvis-barend-:
Barend Joseph Stokvis was a Dutch physician born at Amsterdam in 1834. Isidore Singer and E. Slijper wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about him in 1906. He was born on August 16, son of a physician. He studied in Amsterdam, Paris, and Vienna. He died on September 28, 1902.

Stokvis won a Brussels Academy gold medal in 1867. His prize essay studied the causes of albuminuria. In 1874 he became professor at the University of Amsterdam. He taught pathology and the action of drugs. He led congresses of colonial and Dutch doctors. Edinburgh gave him an honorary law degree in 1884. His books cover liver sugar, diabetes, and tropical medicine. The entry profiles a doctor honored across Europe.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-theodora-14358:
Theodora, born Sarah, was a Jewish woman who became queen of Bulgaria. Isidore Singer and M. Franco wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. She was born at Tirnova to a family of Byzantine Jews. She reigned beside Czar Ivan Alexander from 1335 to 1355.

The czar met her when she presented a petition. He married her after she accepted Christianity. They had three children together. A council in 1352 condemned heretics and Jews alike. Her pleas saved three condemned Jews from death. Still, Tirnova's Jewish community was dispersed for good. Theodora also secured the throne for her own son. Bulgarian historians blamed that choice for weakening the kingdom.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-tosefta-lit-ext:
The Tosefta is a collection of early legal sayings fuller than the Mishnah's. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Its name means additions or extensions. Teachers such as Akiba and Judah added notes to old rulings. A saying with its additions was itself called a tosefta.

The Mishnah gives traditional law in condensed form. The Tosefta gives the same sayings more completely. Talmudic literature cites a Tosefta collection often. Most critics identify it with the work still extant. R. Johanan's remarks support that identification, the article argues. The name is properly a plural, Tosefata. Usage settled on the singular form by mistake. Few texts show rabbinic law growing so clearly.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-u-ba-le-ziyyon-:
U-Ba le-Ziyyon is the closing prayer of the daily morning service. Cyrus Adler and Francis L. Cohen wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Its opening words quote Isaiah: the Redeemer shall come to Zion. Worshipers should not leave synagogue before it, the code says. The prayer gathers a series of sacred texts.

Among them stands the Kedushah with its Aramaic paraphrase. Two brief ancient prayers ask for enlightenment through study. Ashre, Psalm 145, always precedes the prayer closely. Most of it is read in an undertone. The cantor intones only the opening lines aloud. Ashkenazic chant borrows the Sabbath afternoon motive. Sephardic tradition uses a special older melody. Its roots reach back before 1492 in Spain.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-veigelsberg-leo:
Leo Veigelsberg was a Hungarian journalist and editor. He was born on January 18, 1846. Isidore Singer and Ludwig Venetianer wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906. He studied at Budapest and Vienna. After brief teaching, he joined a newspaper staff in 1867. Since 1872 he has edited the Pester Lloyd.

His signed lead articles drew wide attention in Hungary. In 1904 the emperor gave him the Order of the Iron Crown. The entry also notes his son Hugo. Hugo became a noted young writer of poems and stories. He wrote under names like Dixi and Ignotus. His books include verse collections and a translated novel.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-wakrulkar-solom:
Solomon Elijah Wakrulkar was a Beni Israel soldier in India. Joseph Jacobs and J. Hyams wrote this short entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He enlisted in the Nineteenth Regiment Native Infantry in 1838. He rose step by step through the native ranks. By 1872 he held the rank of subahdar major.

Wakrulkar fought in three hard campaigns. In Afghanistan he saw Ghazni taken and Kabul held. In the Punjab he fought at Multan and Gujarat. He also marched in the Central India campaign of 1858. In 1877 he won the Order of British India. Its titles were the highest honor for native officers. He retired in 1878.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-yannai-15058:
Yannai was a scholar of Palestine in the third century of this era. Joseph Jacobs and Schulim Ochser wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was the father-in-law of the scholar Ammi. He says in one place that he had a grandson of his name.

He is known for one debate on the books of King Solomon. That debate asked which book the king wrote last of all. Yannai held that Kohelet was the last book from his pen. The entry is short and rests on two learned books. One is a study of the tales of the Palestine schools. One is a chain book of the past of the rabbis. No works of Yannai are named in the piece at all. The note keeps him in mind for one clear stand he took.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-zamosz-israel-b:
Israel ben Moses ha-Levi Zamosz (born about 1700) was a Polish Talmud man and math mind. Joseph Jacobs and M. Seligsohn wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born at Buberki, he died at Brody in 1772. He taught at the great school of Zamosz in his prime.

At that school he read the works of the world as well. Math drew his mind more than all else there. He wrote notes on two old books of math and faith. In those years he penned a work on the frame of the sky. That work still lies in draft to this day. In 1742 he left for Berlin for some years. There he taught Moses Mendelssohn in math and in logic. The famed Lessing held his lore in high awe as well.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-zilzer-antal-an:
Antal Zilzer was a Hungarian painter known chiefly for his portraits. Isidore Singer and Newell Dunbar wrote his short entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Zilzer was born at Budapest in 1861. He trained at the national model school of design there, under Rauscher, Gregusz, and Szekely.

He later studied at the Munich Academy under several teachers, then finished his training in Berlin, Paris, and London. In 1887 he received the Munich gold medal. His paintings named here include Alone in the Woods and Ludwig II on His Funeral Bier. Forest Idyls and Sunset on the Lake of Constance are also listed among his works.
king-henry-viii-pg2258: Wolsey falls in this edition: the great Cardinal, stripped of power, finds his conscience at last. "Had I but served my God with half the zeal I served my king." Pageantry and pathos fill Shakespeare's last history.
liddell-scott-abridged-greek-lexicon-185:
Henry Liddell and Robert Scott published their great Greek-English Lexicon in 1843, and the abridged version, nicknamed the Little Liddell, followed for students. The 1858 printing comes from the sixth edition of the parent work. Generations of schoolboys and undergraduates learned Greek with it open.

The abridgment keeps every common word with its main senses, forms, and constructions, in compact type. Students could carry it where the giant lexicon could not go. Liddell, dean of Christ Church, was also the father of Alice, of Wonderland fame. This little book remains a monument of Victorian classical schooling.
linnaeus-systema-naturae-vol1-1758:
Carl Linnaeus's Systema Naturae appears here in Volume 1 of its tenth edition, dated 1758. No public-domain English translation exists, so the text stands in Latin. The tenth edition is the starting point of zoological naming, the baseline every later name is checked against.

Volume 1 covers Animalia, the animal kingdom, arranged in classes from mammals to worms and insects. Linnaeus gave each species a two-part name, genus and species, the binomial system science still uses. He placed humans among the primates, a bold step for his age. The volume founded binomial nomenclature for animals and remains the reference from which zoology counts its naming history.
longfellow-miles-standish-1858:
Henry Wadsworth Longfellow published The Courtship of Miles Standish in 1858, drawing on the history of Plymouth Colony written by his own ancestor. Longfellow claimed descent from John Alden himself. The poem sold tens of thousands of copies within weeks, in America and England alike.

Captain Miles Standish, the colony's blunt little military leader, loves the newcomer Priscilla Mullins but is too awkward to court her. He sends his young friend John Alden to plead his case. Priscilla's answer became famous: why don't you speak for yourself, John? The love triangle plays out against Indian alarms, sickness, and the work of planting a colony. Longfellow's hexameters helped make Plymouth the American origin story.
marguerite-de-valois-memoirs-1658:
Marguerite de Valois, queen of Navarre and wife of Henri IV, wrote her Mémoires around 1594 about the court she grew up in. They were first published in 1628, and the English translation of 1658 carries them here. Marguerite was sister to three French kings and daughter of Catherine de Medici, placed at the heart of power and danger.

Her memoir covers the French wars of religion from inside the palace, with weddings, plots, and the shadow of massacre. She writes with grace and self-defense, eager to set her own story straight. The book became the classic insider memoir of the Valois court. Its voice, a queen's own, still sounds clear across four centuries.
memoirs-of-the-court-of-louis-xiv-and-of:
Book four of the Duchesse d'Orleans's memoirs opens with Victor Amadeus II. The Grand Duchess of Florence and the Duchesse de Lorraine follow in the heads. The Duc du Maine, Louvois, and Louis XV stand there as well.

Victor Amadeus, King of Sicily, is said to quarrel with his mistresses. Madame de Verrue shared some stolen gold medals with the writer. She bought 160 medals, half of those the lady stole, she admits. A counter poison once saved Madame de Verrue at a dinner table. Her brother was sent to fetch her back from Turin by night. A small parrot rode with her on that flight from the King.
michaelis-maieri-cantilenae-intellectual:
Michael Maier's intellectual songs on the resurrection of the phoenix appeared in this Paris edition in 1758. Maier had died more than a century earlier, in 1622. The volume prints his Latin text with a French translation on facing pages. The translator signs himself only M. L. L. M., and the bookseller Debure sold the bound book for three livres.

In alchemy, the phoenix stands for matter destroyed by fire and reborn in finer form. Maier casts that doctrine as songs, mixing poetry with chemical teaching. French readers of 1758 thus met a German physician's Latin verses in their own tongue. The edition shows how alchemical classics kept circulating long after their authors died.
morris-defence-guenevere-1858:
William Morris was twenty-four when The Defence of Guenevere appeared in 1858. It was his first book and the first volume of Pre-Raphaelite poetry published in England. Morris, a wealthy young Oxford graduate, filled it with the medieval world he loved.

In the title poem, Queen Guenevere defends herself before Arthur's court against charges of betrayal, arguing with passion and cunning. Other poems retell Arthurian tales and dark medieval stories of love and violence. The verse is vivid, strange, and deliberately old-fashioned in diction. The book sold poorly at first but now stands as a landmark of Victorian medievalism.
nightingale-subsidiary-notes-nursing-185:
Before her famous nursing work took shape, Florence Nightingale wrote her Subsidiary Notes in 1858. The memorandum, privately printed, treats female nursing in military hospitals in peace and war. She drew on her Crimean War experience with sick and wounded soldiers. The paper laid out how army nursing should be organized and trained.

Her plan covered staffing, discipline, pay, and the standing of nurses in the ranks. It became the policy paper behind the Nightingale Fund. That fund built the training school that reshaped nursing. The Gutenberg text preserves a reform at the planning stage. Readers see her mind working on systems, not slogans. It rewards close study.
olaus-magnus-compendious-history-streate:
Olaus Magnus, a Swedish churchman, published his great history of the northern peoples in Latin in 1555. This English version of 1658 shortens that vast work for London readers. It describes the Goths, Swedes, and Vandals, and the cold lands they came from.

Early modern Scandinavia appears here as a land of marvels. Sea serpents coil in northern waters, and mermen rise from the deep. Snow, ice, and the midnight sun shape every custom he reports. English readers of 1658 met the north mainly through such wonders. The book mixes real report with sailors' tales, and both halves are worth reading.
openalex-w1549441458:
B. Abelev and the ALICE Collaboration reported this measurement. It appeared in Physical Review Letters in September 2013. The team studied D mesons in lead-lead collisions. D mesons are particles that contain a charm quark. Noncentral collisions leave an oval overlap zone, they explain.

The team measured how particle flow favors that oval's plane. This favoring is called elliptic flow by physicists. D meson flow matched light particle flow in size. The signal was clearly positive at lower momenta. The result shows charm quarks move with the hot medium. That medium is the quark-gluon plasma formed in collisions.
openalex-w1896237858:
Yaritza Salas and three co-authors studied tumors in female dogs. Their paper appeared in PLoS ONE in May 2015. Mammary tumors are a growing health problem in dogs, they note. The team reviewed cases diagnosed from 2002 to 2012. Records came from a pathology service in Mexico City.

Nearly two thousand biopsies of intact dogs were reviewed. Benign and malignant tumors each made up near half. Epithelial tumors were the most common type found. Pure breeds formed most submissions to the service. Poodles, Cocker Spaniels, and German Shepherds led the list. Adult dogs aged nine to twelve were most affected.
openalex-w2111179758:
Pedro Alonso, Graham Brown, Myriam Arevalo-Herrera and colleagues set out a research agenda for malaria eradication. Their paper appeared in PLoS Medicine in 2011. Ending malaria transmission worldwide is a huge challenge. Aggressive use of current tools can gain much ground. New tools are still needed to finish the job.

Experts reviewed where research must focus. Vaccines, drugs and mosquito control all feature. Diagnostics need to find silent infections better. Health systems research matters as much as products. The agenda grew from a broad expert consultation. It lists priorities for funders and researchers. Eradication needs long-term, coordinated investment, they argue.
openalex-w2138134458:
Omid Hamid, Henrik Schmidt, Aviram Nissan, and colleagues published this trial in the Journal of Translational Medicine in 2011. They tested ipilimumab, an immune drug for advanced melanoma, and hunted for tumor signs that predict who benefits. The drug frees T cells to attack cancer by blocking a brake protein called CTLA-4.

Eighty-two patients with hard-to-treat melanoma received one of two dose levels. Tumor samples were taken before treatment and soon after the second dose. Response and safety matched earlier trials, and gene variants showed no link to benefit. Tumors starting with high levels of two immune markers responded better. So did tumors where immune cells flowed in more after treatment began.
openalex-w2154761658:
Jozef Vercruysse, Jerzy Behnke, Marco Albonico, and colleagues published this study in PLoS Neglected Tropical Diseases in 2011. They measured how well one dose of albendazole, a standard deworming drug, works in school children. Three gut worms spread through soil are among the world's most common parasites, yet drug monitoring lacked standard procedures.

Seven trials ran in Brazil, Cameroon, Cambodia, Ethiopia, India, Tanzania, and Vietnam. All used one shared protocol with a single standard dose. Success was scored by cure rate and by how far egg counts in stool fell. The trials together set reference values for judging this drug against roundworm, whipworm, and hookworm in future programs.
openalex-w2171372458:
Anna Rosanas-Urgell, Enmoore Lin, Laurens Manning, and colleagues published this study in PLoS Medicine in 2012. They tested whether Southeast Asian ovalocytosis, an inherited red blood cell shape trait, protects children against Plasmodium vivax malaria. The trait was already known to guard against severe falciparum malaria, but its effect on vivax was unclear.

Nearly two thousand children in Papua New Guinea were genotyped across three studies. In an infant cohort, carriers had almost half the rate of clinical vivax episodes. In older children, carriers also showed far fewer blood-stage reinfections, by both gene tests and microscopy. The results extend the trait's protection to the second great malaria parasite.
openalex-w2411750058:
Francesca Sprovieri, Nicola Pirrone, Mariantonia Bencardino, and colleagues published this study in Atmospheric Chemistry and Physics in 2016. Mercury drifts globally through the air and poisons food webs, yet monitoring was patchy where data mattered most. The Global Mercury Observation System built a coordinated worldwide network to fix that, starting in 2010.

More than forty ground stations now span regions that previously had no records at all. This paper presents the network's first five years of concentrations, examining trends, seasons, and comparability between sites. One headline stands out: mercury levels form a clear gradient between the northern and southern hemispheres. The authors trace that divide mostly to local and regional sources, natural and human-made combined.
openalex-w2588228158:
Isabelle Romieu, Laure Dossus, and Simón Barquera wrote this 2017 paper in Cancer Causes & Control for an IARC working group. The International Agency for Research on Cancer convened experts in December 2015 to review evidence on energy balance and obesity. They paid special attention to low and middle income countries. The paper asks what mainly drives the global obesity epidemic.

The group links the epidemic to poor diet quality and unbalanced energy intake. In poorer countries, undernutrition and overnutrition now coexist in the same populations. Mediterranean-style diets and other quality measures can support long-term weight control. Cutting sugar-sweetened drinks plays a particularly important role, they find. Genes alone cannot explain the epidemic's speed. Still, genetics, epigenetics, and gut microbes shape how individuals respond to food and activity.
openalex-w2607179358:
Adeera Levin, Marcello A. Tonelli, and Joseph Vincent Bonventre lead the authors of this 2017 Lancet Commission roadmap on global kidney health. It grew from a 2016 summit in Vancouver held by the International Society of Nephrology. Over eighty-five experts from many fields and countries took part. Their task: plan how to close the world's gaps in kidney care, research, and policy.

The group set priorities for the next five to ten years across ten themes. Early themes demand counting chronic kidney disease properly and cutting its major risk factors. Others target preventing kidney injury episodes and understanding genetic causes of the disease. Better diagnosis of kidney structure and function also ranks high. The plan names partners inside and outside nephrology and sets a performance framework. Clinicians, patients, scientists, industry, and governments are its intended users.
openalex-w2803280558:
Massimo Sartelli, Gian Luca Baiocchi, and Salomone Di Saverio lead the POSAW study of appendicitis care worldwide. It appeared in the World Journal of Emergency Surgery in 2018. Acute appendicitis is the world's most common surgical disease. Removing the appendix cures most cases, but diagnosis and complicated cases still challenge hospitals. This prospective study watched real practice across the globe.

One hundred sixteen surgical departments in forty-four countries enrolled patients over six months in 2016. The study captured 4,282 patients with a median age of twenty-nine. Doctors used CT scans in about a fifth of cases and ultrasound in over two-fifths. Nearly ninety-six percent of patients had surgery, split between open and keyhole approaches. About four percent were managed without an operation. The snapshot exposes how differently the same disease is handled worldwide, and where practice could converge.
openalex-w2804562858:
Axel Hollmann, Melina María Belén Martínez, and Patricia Maturana reviewed antimicrobial peptides in Frontiers in Chemistry in 2018. Antibiotic resistance is eroding treatments for common infections worldwide. Failure would endanger surgery, cancer chemotherapy, and fights against HIV and malaria. These peptides, made by organisms from microbes to humans, offer a fresh strategy.

They form part of the first line of immune defense in many species. They attack bacteria largely by breaking their outer walls. The review studies how they interact with model and real cell membranes. It also covers synergy, where they boost standard antibiotics beyond either alone. Action against drug-resistant bacteria is their most prized feature. Grasping these membrane actions should guide designing peptide drugs that survive clinical use.
openalex-w2886207958:
Bruno Lima Giacobbo, Janine Doorduin, and Hans Christiaan Klein lead this review of BDNF and brain inflammation, published online in 2018 in Molecular Neurobiology. BDNF is a growth factor that keeps neurons alive, adaptable, and communicating. Patients with psychiatric and degenerative brain disorders often show reduced BDNF in blood and brain. The review explores whether chronic brain inflammation explains those low levels.

Activated glial cells release inflammatory molecules and reactive oxygen species. Those signals can disrupt the pathways BDNF depends on, harming neurons. Understanding inflammation's role in disease onset and progression could unlock new treatments, the authors argue. The hypothesis ties two separate literatures together: neurotrophin biology and neuroimmunology. If inflammation suppresses BDNF, calming it might restore the factor's protection. The review maps the evidence for that chain, link by link. It speaks to researchers hunting drug targets in diseases from depression to Alzheimer's.
openalex-w2898783558:
Shan Wu, Kin H. Lau, and Qinghe Cao lead an international team sequencing sweetpotato's wild relatives in Nature Communications in 2018. Cultivated sweetpotato is a hexaploid, with ninety chromosomes, and ranks seventh among world food crops. It feeds subsistence farmers across sub-Saharan Africa with fiber, vitamins, and resilience. Orange-fleshed varieties combat vitamin A deficiency, a breakthrough honored with the World Food Prize.

The cultivated genome's complexity slows breeding, so the team turned to two diploid wild relatives. Their genome sequences are far simpler to assemble and read. Comparing them with the crop reveals targets for genetic improvement. Candidate genes touch traits breeders need, from nutrition to stress tolerance. Wild relatives thus become a parts catalog for upgrading a food security staple. The work shows how sequencing the cousins of a complex crop can shortcut its improvement.
openalex-w2917335258:
Aziz Bousfiha, Leïla Jeddane, Capucine Picard, and colleagues present the 2017 phenotypic classification for primary immunodeficiencies in the Journal of Clinical Immunology. These disorders, now called inborn errors of immunity, are genetic defects that weaken the body's defense against infection.

Since the 1990s, an expert committee of the International Union of Immunological Societies has published a full catalog of these disorders about every two years. That catalog serves researchers and specialists worldwide, but it was hard to use at the bedside. Since 2013 the committee has also issued a phenotypic version, grouping disorders by their clinical features so doctors can apply it in practice.
openalex-w2969767558:
Toste Tanhua, Andrea McCurdy, Albert Fischer, and colleagues wrote this 2019 review in Frontiers in Marine Science. It looks back at the Framework for Ocean Observing, a plan that reshaped how the world watches its oceans. The review traces how the Global Ocean Observing System evolved under that framework.

The authors take stock of lessons learned while building a coordinated worldwide ocean watch. Such a system joins data from floats, ships, satellites, and coastal stations into shared products. It serves climate forecasts, weather warnings, and marine management. By reviewing what the framework achieved and where it fell short, the paper guides the next stage of global ocean observation.
openalex-w2990643258:
Mao-Qiang He, Rui-Lin Zhao, Kevin Hyde, and colleagues published this reference work in Fungal Diversity in 2019. It gives a full outline of the Basidiomycota, a major phylum of fungi second only to the Ascomycota in species numbers. Mushrooms, bracket fungi, and many yeasts belong to this group.

The authors list every genus in current use, nearly two thousand names, arranged into families, orders, classes, and subphyla. For each accepted genus they add brief notes on classification, species count, type species, way of life, habitat, range, and DNA sequence data. They also run family-tree analyses to estimate when the main lines split. The result is a single reference for the whole phylum.
openalex-w3043776158:
Arti Naidu, Vincent Bennani, John Aarts, and Paul Brunton wrote this review in the Brazilian Dental Journal in 2020. It weighs the evidence for over-the-counter tooth whitening products. Such products are easy to buy, yet solid data on how well they work had been scarce.

The authors reviewed studies from 2006 to 2018 that compared the main product types against placebo, no treatment, or each other. The leading categories are whitening toothpastes, whitening strips, and paint-on gels. Each claims to lift stains and brighten shade, but stains differ in kind and depth. By sorting the trial evidence in one place, the review helps dentists and buyers judge which claims hold up.
openalex-w3173611258:
Mansour Almazroui, Moetasim Ashfaq, M. Nazrul Islam, and colleagues assess the newest global climate models over South America. Their study appeared in Earth Systems and Environment in 2021. The models come from the CMIP6 project, a worldwide comparison of climate simulations. The team checked them against recent climate records for the continent.

The models captured the main climate patterns well, though skill varied by region, mainly at high altitude and latitude. Looking ahead, rain falls over Amazonia and the southern Andes but rises in the southeast. Warming, by contrast, appears under every scenario, even the mildest. Most rain changes stay within the range of natural variation seen today.
openalex-w4200189258:
Shen Yuan, Bruce Linquist, Lloyd Wilson, and colleagues argue for growing more rice with less harm, in Nature Communications in 2021. Rice feeds nearly half the world's people and uses a large share of farm water, fertiliser, and pesticide. Demand keeps rising, yet yield growth has stalled in some major rice regions. The authors call the needed path sustainable intensification.

A key measure is the yield gap, the distance between what a field could produce and what farmers actually harvest. Regions with wide gaps hold the largest room for gains. Closing gaps toward a realistic share of potential needs better seeds, advice, and market access. The paper maps where research money could raise output while cutting environmental damage.
openalex-w4293207258: Marc Humbert, Gábor Kovács, Marius Hoeper, and colleagues present the 2022 guidelines on pulmonary hypertension from two European medical societies. They appeared in the European Respiratory Journal and cover how the disease is found and treated. In this condition, blood pressure runs high in the arteries of the lungs. The sample holds only the publisher's citation page and author list. It has no readable guideline text, so the guidance cannot be described from it here.
openalex-w7163351058:
Yuki Kusunoki, of Kwansei Gakuin University in Japan, led a 2026 study of the shift current in a single layer of tin sulfide. A two-dimensional content that can turn light directly into electric current without a junction. This bulk photovoltaic effect depends on how electron waves shift position when they absorb light. The authors modeled the system with a tight-binding model, a simplified description of electrons hopping between atoms, derived from first-principles calculations.

Comparing models with only near hops and with longer hops included, they found the simple model already captures the shift current's main features. Longer hops shifted peak positions and sizes but kept the characteristic low-energy shape. Splitting the current into transition strength and shift distance identified which electron jumps dominate.
openalex-w7203590458: Tatsuya Shoji, of Kanagawa University, wrote a Japanese-language review, from 2026 in the analytical chemistry journal BUNSEKI KAGAKU. On nanoscale optical trapping and its uses in analytical chemistry. Optical tweezers use focused light to hold and move tiny objects, a technique pioneered by Arthur Ashkin from 1970 onward. The review's surviving text highlights plasmonic optical tweezers, which use metal nanostructures to strengthen the trapping light. As a route to manipulating matter at the nanoscale for chemical analysis.
openalex-w7208831058:
Adson Antonio Vieira Santos and three colleagues tell of a shop class on farm life goods and rot heaps, held for new farm-craft staff in Brazil. Farm life goods are live or wild-born goods used in fields in place of some man-made feeds and sprays. The class ran in March 2025, after three months of plan work. Some forty folk came.

To run the class, the new staff had to turn tech lore into teach stuff. They fit words to the crowd, set the day's shape, and met doubts on the spot. The crowd joined most in the hands-on parts. The team grants their tools cannot prove gains that last. Still, the class was a true drill ground: the kind of run that shapes a staff hand before the first real class.
openalex-w7213241158:
Igor Barbosa Henrique da Silva leads a team on why small firms in Brazil die young. Such firms fill a huge share of the land's trade, yet crowds of them fold in their first years. The team read books, studies, and trade briefs on the theme. Their ask: what part do cash rule and books play in the fall?

The flaw, they find, is not blank minds. Most heads know the tools by name. What lacks is the day's grind: no cash watch, thin plans for lean weeks, and home cash mixed with firm cash in one pot. Their fix is a shift in the books trade: from tax forms ground out by rote to a guide at the head's side. Watch the cash, watch the health signs, and a firm can see a storm while it can still turn.
openalex-w7213589958:
Aline dos Santos Araujo, as spelled in the sample byline, leads a literature review on social media and dental aesthetics. Their 2026 review gathers studies from 2020 to 2026 in PubMed, SciELO, and Google Scholar, mixing quantitative and qualitative work. Smile content online now shapes beauty ideas widely.

Social media influence how people judge their own appearance, self-esteem, and social acceptance, the review finds. That influence reaches the decision to seek dental aesthetic procedures. Patients arrive with expectations formed by images seen online. The authors set out to measure that impact on aesthetic perception and treatment choice. Their synthesis helps dentists read patient demand against the pressures of a feed-driven beauty culture.
openalex-w7213975858:
Natália Santos Moreira and Daniella Barreto-Santana report active methods in a ninth-grade literature class in Curaçá, Bahia. Their 2026 descriptive, reflective report covers eight pupils in a public school class. The book at the centre is Carolina Maria de Jesus's diary of favela life, Child of the Dark in English editions.

A planned teaching sequence used literary gatherings, guided debates, writing production, and conversation circles. Pupil participation, talk, and written work supplied the evidence, observed by the teacher. Engagement in reading and discussion rose, the authors report, along with reflection on the social questions in the book. Active methods, they conclude, can deepen pupils' critical relationship with literary text.
openalex-w7215724258:
Paulo Roberto Barbosa dos Santos and Tarcykelly de Sena Santos da Silva wrote a 2026 article on inclusive education for autistic students in Brazil, joining teaching methods, human rights, and education policy. Inclusive education, they stress, means real conditions for access, participation, learning, and development, not simply placing a student in the room. Their study joins a literature review and policy documents with watching of specialized support sessions held across late 2025 and 2026.

Visual resources, hands-on materials, art activities, sensory proposals, and teaching games widened taking part when chosen from each student's known needs, barriers, and goals. The sessions also showed how much depends on joining that support, the regular classroom, plans for each student, school heads, and support staff. Inclusion, the authors conclude, rests not on any single method but on teaching planning, teamwork, and respect for rights.
openalex-w7220981258:
Mariana Domingos de Lima, João de Sousa Pinheiro Barbosa, and Elisângela de Andrade Aoyama reviewed recent literature on humane nursing care for older patients in hospital, publishing in 2026. With populations aging and elderly admissions rising, they ask what care looks like when it treats the patient as a whole person rather than a set of physical problems.

Studies from 2021 onward show hospital stays can bring lost autonomy, separation from family, loneliness, anxiety, and confusion for older people. The reviewed work answers with welcome, trust, clear communication, and a say for patients in their own care. The authors present humanization not as kindness added on top, but as a core part of safe, respectful hospital nursing.
openalex-w7220981758:
Bruno Matos de Farias and Kátia Ramos Barroso argue for environmental education as everyday work that forms citizens who protect rivers. Their 2026 article is aligned with the United Nations 2030 Agenda. They describe water resources under threat from cleared riverbanks, irregular building along margins, dumped waste, and silting that worsens floods.

Alongside their discussion of conservation and recovery, the authors present a teaching product built from the research: Guardians of the River — Sustainability Mission, an interactive school resource. Its aim is to make reflection concrete, so pupils adopt real preservation habits. The article treats the school as the natural starting point for a culture that values water.
openalex-w7221096458:
Andressa Mendes Sousa and three co-authors reviewed studies from 2020 to 2025 on patients who keep using opioids long after an orthopedic fracture, publishing in 2026. Continued use can harden into dependence, complicate healing, and slow the return of function, so the team searched for who is at risk and how tapering can work.

Seven studies, drawn from nearly two hundred candidates, named the main risk factors: prior opioid use, chronic pain, psychological disorders, older age, multiple illnesses, and generous post-surgery prescriptions. Dependence brought tolerance, withdrawal, intoxication, and overdose. Multimodal pain relief, patient education, live prescription monitoring, and team follow-up worked best, and the authors call for care protocols built on that evidence.
openalex-w7221197558:
Gabriela Luiza Cima Cardoso and four co-authors report a small veterinary case study on colostrum, the first milk that decides a newborn calf's immunity, published in 2026. Calves are born without antibodies and depend entirely on drinking colostrum quickly. The team worked at a school farm in Cascavel, Paraná, with two Purunã cows and their heifer calves.

Colostrum from one cow tested at high quality before birth and the other at intermediate quality, measured by a Brix refractometer. Both calves were vigorous, suckled strongly, and drank within two hours of birth. Blood tests at forty-eight hours showed total protein levels the authors read as sound passive immunity transfer. Careful colostrum checking, they conclude, pays.
pernety-les-fables-egyptiennes-et-grecqu: A hosted sample showing only the Google Books digital-copy notice pages in French that precede this scan. Several pages explain the digitisation project, the book's public-domain status, and the rules for using the file. No page of the work itself is visible. The catalogue title names the book as Les Fables Égyptiennes et Grecques, volume 2, by Pernety, and dates it 1758.
plos-pbio-0020158:
Jun Wu, Thomas J. Klein, and Marek Mlodzik studied signal receptors in the fruit fly for PLOS Biology in 2004. Frizzled receptors pass Wnt signals, which guide growth and body pattern. The authors tracked where in the cell these receptors sit, a trait set by their inner tails.

Where a receptor sits decides which signals it can send. The team's work shows the tail acts like an address label, sending the receptor to the right cell compartment. That placement then tunes the strength and kind of signal that follows. The study adds a layer to how Wnt signaling is controlled, a pathway that is central to development and often goes wrong in cancer.
plos-pbio-0020258:
Jennifer L. Nemhauser, Todd C. Mockler, and Joanne Chory studied plant hormone cross-talk in PLOS Biology in 2004. Plants use hormones called brassinosteroids and auxin to guide growth. Both affect stems, roots, and leaves, so their signals must be coordinated rather than sent in isolation.

Using the model plant Arabidopsis, the team showed the two pathways lean on each other. Many genes respond to both signals, and blocking one changes the effect of the other. That interdependence is a design rule for plant growth control. It matters for farming, since tweaks to one hormone path will ripple into the other. The paper helped move plant science past single-hormone thinking.
plos-pone-0000058:
Yuan-Ping Pang pointed drug designers at a fresh target for stopping malaria mosquitoes in a 2006 paper. Acetylcholinesterase is an enzyme in the insect nervous system, and poisons that block it are a main class of insecticides. Resistance and harm to other species limit the old compounds, which hit a well-known site on the enzyme.

Pang identified a novel target site on acetylcholinesterase, a fresh place where a control agent might bind. A new site raises the hope of insecticides that kill malaria-carrying mosquitoes while sparing humans and helpful insects, and that work even where resistance has beaten the old sprays. For a disease spread only by these mosquitoes, better control tools save lives directly.
plos-pone-0000158:
Paul D. Waters, Gauthier Dobigny, Peter J. Waddell, and colleagues published this evolution paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. LINE-1 is a jumping gene, a stretch of DNA that copies itself into new spots in the genome. It makes up a large share of mammal DNA. The authors trace its history across the major clades of placental mammals.

By comparing LINE-1 across species, the team reconstructs when this element was active and how it spread. The story helps explain why mammal genomes differ so much in size and content. It also gives a backdrop for the many gene changes that jumping elements cause, for better and worse.
plos-pone-0000258:
Michael J. Angilletta, Robbie S. Wilson, Amanda C. Niehaus, and colleagues published this urban ecology paper in PLOS ONE in 2007, under the heading of urban physiology. It reports that city ants possess high heat tolerance, handling temperatures that would trouble their rural kin. Cities run warmer than the countryside, a heat island effect ants must cope with.

Urban animals are evolving under new pressures, and heat is one of the sharpest. The authors compare the heat tolerance of city ants with what the species normally shows. The result is an early data point in the study of how wildlife adapts to city life.
plos-pone-0000358:
Justin D. Blethrow, Chao Tang, Changhui Deng, and colleagues published this proteomics methods paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. It presents a modular mass spectrometric tool for analyzing protein complexes. The tool reads what the complexes are made of, and how their parts are phosphorylated, chemically tagged in ways that switch activity. The tool's modules can be combined as needed.

Protein complexes run the cell, and their tags change with conditions. A modular instrument workflow makes such analysis more routine and flexible. The paper is a methods contribution to proteomics, the large-scale study of proteins, as it moved from listing parts to mapping their states.
plos-pone-0000458:
Jennifer Hartt Meyers and colleagues studied how HIV weakens a specialized immune cell, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Plasmacytoid dendritic cells are the body's champion producers of interferon, an alarm signal against viruses. The team measured the impact of HIV on these cells' survival and on their antiviral activity.

If HIV kills or disables the very cells meant to raise the alarm, the immune system starts the fight already handicapped. Documenting that damage helps explain why HIV infection so often becomes chronic. It also points to protecting or restoring these cells as a possible treatment strategy, alongside drugs that attack the virus directly.
plos-pone-0000558:
Yuri B. Yurov and colleagues examined chromosome errors in the developing human brain, reporting in PLOS ONE in 2007. Aneuploidy means a cell carries the wrong number of chromosomes; confined chromosomal mosaicism means only some cells in the tissue are affected. The team documented both in brain development.

The brain was long assumed to be chromosomally uniform. Finding mosaicism there raises questions about how much variation is normal and whether abnormal patches contribute to disease. Counting chromosomes cell by cell in developing tissue is slow work, but it set reference points for later claims about the mosaic brain.
plos-pone-0000658:
Andrei I. Ivanov, Moshe Bachar, Brian A. Babbin and colleagues singled out one motor protein at the seams between surface cells, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Epithelial sheets form barriers, and their strength depends on the apical junctional complex, built from tight and adherens junctions. Actin filaments beneath the surface regulate that complex. Myosin II, a major actin motor, was already implicated.

The team reports a unique role for one form, nonmuscle myosin heavy chain IIA, in regulating these apical junctions. Unique means the other forms do not simply cover for it. Barrier breakdown drives gut and skin diseases, so knowing which motor holds the seams matters.
plos-pone-0000758:
Christophe Fraser developed simpler ways to estimate how fast a new epidemic is spreading, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Reproduction numbers, the average number of people infected by a typical case, play a central role in tracking outbreaks. His aim was methods simple enough to be applied as an epidemic emerges, when data are thin and decisions cannot wait.

Fraser separates individual and household reproduction numbers. Spread within households behaves differently from spread between them, and mixing the two distorts forecasts. Estimating both gives a clearer picture of whether an outbreak will take off. Methods papers like this become the toolbox reached for in the first weeks of a crisis.
plos-pone-0000858:
Li-Tzu Chen, Tzu-Ping Ko, Yu-Wei Chang and colleagues probed five charged building blocks in an archaeal DNA repair protein, for PLOS ONE in 2007. RecA family proteins run an ATP-dependent DNA strand exchange, in which a single-stranded DNA filament finds and pairs with a matching double-stranded sequence. Despite more than 20 years of effort, the molecular mechanism of homology pairing and strand exchange was still not fully known.

Their RadA protein comes from archaea, microbes with ancient molecular machinery. The five conserved positively charged residues sit in the L1 and N-terminal DNA-binding motifs. Structural and functional analyses of exactly those residues test how the protein grips DNA during the search for a match.
plos-pone-0000958:
Alexander Statnikov, Chun Li and Constantin Aliferis studied how environment, genes and analysis choices can mislead a cancer gene hunt, in PLOS ONE in 2007. New genotyping tools let researchers scan the whole genome for variants tied to disease. Early studies suggested panels of markers could flag esophageal cancer risk.

The authors warn that pitfalls in data analysis, and tangled effects of environment and genetics, can inflate such claims. Their paper is a caution worked through a real case. Gene wide studies are powerful, but only when the statistics respect how messy human data are. The work is aimed at everyone building risk panels.
plos-pone-0001058:
Naohiro Kawamura, Fumitaka Kugimiya, Yasushi Oshima and colleagues studied a signaling protein's role on both sides of bone turnover, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Bone mass is held by balance: osteoblasts build bone, osteoclasts resorb it, under many local and body wide controls. Akt is one of the key serine threonine kinases in that control web.

The team examined Akt1 in both cell types. A single protein acting in builder and demolisher alike could coordinate the two, keeping turnover matched. Bone diseases from osteoporosis to arthritis involve that match failing. Knowing which Akt form sits where helps target treatment without upsetting the other side.
plos-pone-0001158:
The prion protein is famous for its role in transmissible spongiform encephalopathies, diseases such as scrapie and BSE. Yet its normal job in the body is still unclear. Marius Lötscher and colleagues found an unexpected one in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Using histology, immunochemistry, and PCR-based methods in mice, they linked the protein to immune defense.

The team reports that induced prion protein controls retroviruses that the immune system activates in the mouse spleen. In other words, when the spleen's defenses switch on, prion protein helps keep resident retroviruses in check. That gives the protein a concrete normal function to set beside its disease role.
plos-pone-0001258:
Long QT syndrome is an inherited heart rhythm disorder that can kill without warning. John Bankston and colleagues report the case of a newborn carrying a new mutation, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. The mutation sits in SCN5A, the gene for the heart's main sodium channel, and caused the variant called LQT-3.

The authors describe the de novo mutation as novel and lethal, with distinct molecular pharmacology and a distinct therapeutic response. De novo means it appeared fresh in the child, not inherited. Working out how this channel variant answers to drugs guided treatment of a very young patient.
plos-pone-0001358:
Arcobacter butzleri is a bacterium found in human clinical cases, a member of the epsilon subdivision of the Proteobacteria. William Miller and colleagues present its complete genome sequence in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. It is a close relative of established pathogens such as Campylobacter jejuni and Helicobacter pylori.

The authors worked out the full genome sequence of the human clinical isolate. A complete sequence shows what the bacterium can do, and which of its genes might help it cause disease. For a little-studied relative of two major pathogens, the genome is the reference everything else builds on.
plos-pone-0001458:
Frank Schweitzer and Robert Mach published a 2008 PLOS ONE paper on the spread of giving. When a cause takes off, gifts can surge like an outbreak. The pair show that a disease spread model fits this surge well. In their frame, word of a cause passes from person to person like a germ.

Herding plays a key role, as donors watch what the crowd does through the media. The model uses a shared field that stands for that media pull over time. A good fit lets groups forecast how a drive will rise and fade. It also hints at when a push will do the most good.
plos-pone-0001558:
Michiel van Boven and co-authors published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on when people will take flu drugs. Drugs that curb viruses hold promise for new ills such as bird flu and SARS. But the drugs are not free of harm, so people weigh gain against risk. The team modeled when self interest and group gain pull in unlike ways.

In their model, what pays for one person can fail the group as a whole. That gap can stall a drug drive that needs wide uptake to work. Plans must thus align the two, with clear rules and fair access. The work frames a social snag that pure drug science cannot solve.
plos-pone-0001658:
Juliette Salvaing, Anja C. Nagel, Emmanuèle Mouchel-Vielh, and their co-authors studied two gene-control proteins in the fruit fly in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Polycomb group proteins keep genes switched off over the long term, while trithorax group proteins keep them on. Together they hold gene patterns steady through development, above all for Hox genes, which set body layout.

The paper centers on Corto, a protein that works with both camps, and its interaction with Cyclin G. The full text gives the binding tests, the fly genetics, and where the two proteins meet. Their meeting point links the on-off memory system to a protein better known from cell growth. It may explain how Corto fine-tunes gene patterns as the fly develops.
plos-pone-0001758:
Nuo Yang, Jia Huang, Joel Greshock, and their co-authors studied how an ovarian cancer gene is switched on in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. PIK3CA is boosted, amplified, or mutated in ovarian and other cancers, making it a promising drug target. How it gets over-activated in living tumors was unclear.

The team reports that NF-κB, a master inflammation switch, transcriptionally regulates PIK3CA in the ovarian cancer microenvironment, the tissue setting around the tumor. The full text gives the gene activity tests and the binding evidence. If inflammation switches on a growth gene, then anti-inflammatory strategies or NF-κB blockers could complement drugs aimed at PIK3CA itself.
plos-pone-0001858:
Robin M. D. Beck, Henk Godthelp, Vera Weisbecker, and their co-authors described the oldest marsupial fossils of Australia in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. New skull and body fossils come from the early Eocene Tingamarra Local Fauna. The team refers them to Djarthia murgonensis, known before only from broken tooth remains.

The new finds show Djarthia is a member of a distinct marsupial group. Its kinship bears on how marsupials reached Australia and spread across it. The full text gives the fossil accounts and the family analysis. The marsupials of Australia are a textbook case of evolution in isolation, and their oldest fossils anchor the timeline of that story.
plos-pone-0001958:
Myriam Rai and co-authors tested a drug fix for a nerve illness in mice, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. The illness, Friedreich ataxia, is passed down in families and harms both nerves and the heart. It stems from too little frataxin, a protein that works in the cell's power units, caused by a swollen repeat in the frataxin gene.

The team gave HDAC inhibitors, drugs that loosen the chemical marks that mute genes, to a mouse model of the illness. As the title states, the drugs corrected the frataxin shortage in the mice. If a muted gene can be coaxed back on, a drug path opens for an illness with no cure.
plos-pone-0002058:
Steven Schutzer and co-authors read the genome of a weakened form of a biothreat bacterium, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Burkholderia mallei causes glanders, which can be lethal in humans and animals, and it is little studied. Safety rules for listed agents have hampered research with it in many labs.

The team used whole genome sequencing to characterize a clinically attenuated strain, one that no longer causes full disease. If its genome proves it is truly weakened, the strain could be excluded from select agent lists. That would let more labs study glanders safely.
plos-pone-0002158:
Hendrik Harms, Konstantin Prass, Christian Meisel, and co-authors ran a clinical trial on preventing infection after stroke, published in PLOS ONE in 2008. Pneumonia is a leading cause of death after a major stroke. In mice, giving the antibiotic moxifloxacin early had prevented post-stroke infections, lowered deaths, and improved recovery.

The team tested the same idea in people with acute ischemic stroke, where a clot blocks blood flow to the brain. Patients were assigned by chance to preventive antibiotic therapy or standard care. Trials like this one decide whether a result seen in animals can be turned into a routine step that saves lives in the ward.
plos-pone-0002258:
Alison McGuigan, Derek Bruzewicz, Ana Glavan, and co-authors described a way to grow cells in tiny gel blocks, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Cells behave differently on flat plastic than in the three-dimensional world of the body. Flat culture is still the most common method in biology, while 3D culture lacks a standard, easy form.

The team used replica molding to make sub-millimeter gel modules with cells sealed inside. The small blocks can be handled, stacked, and combined like building pieces. A simple standard for 3D culture could bring lab results closer to how cells truly behave inside tissues.
plos-pone-0002358:
Domingo Ojer Tsakiridu and co-authors surveyed factors linked to induced abortion among sex workers in Asturias, Spain, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Their aim was to find what circumstances go together with having had an induced abortion in this group. The health needs of this group are often missed by standard services.

The team ran a cross-sectional study using a self-completion questionnaire answered by 212 women who attended the region's three sexually transmitted infection clinics. Mapping the factors that cluster with abortion helps those clinics target contraception advice, testing, and support to the women at highest risk.
plos-pone-0002458:
A research team led by Perfettini reported its work in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline credits Jean-Luc Perfettini, Roberta Nardacci, Mehdi Bourouba, and others. Its subject is critical Involvement of the ATM-Dependent DNA Damage Response in the Apoptotic Demise of HIV-1-Elicited Syncytia. DNA damage can activate the oncosuppressor protein ataxia telangiectasia mutated (ATM), which phosphorylates the histone H2AX within characteristic DNA damage foci.

Readers get the background first, then the path the team took and the care they took with it. As a record, it keeps the focus on facts and method, and lets readers judge the claims for themselves.
plos-pone-0002558:
Work from Nishimura and fellow authors appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline credits Tomoko Nishimura, Tamaki Ishima, Masaomi Iyo, and others. Its subject is potentiation of Nerve Growth Factor-Induced Neurite Outgrowth by Fluvoxamine. The title goes on to note role of Sigma-1 Receptors, IP 3 Receptors and Cellular Signaling Pathways. Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) have been widely used and are a major therapeutic advance in psychopharmacology.

However, their pharmacology is quite heterogeneous. Key terms are set out in context, so a reader new to the field can still follow the work. The full text is free to read, so any reader can check the work and follow the links to past work.
plos-pone-0002658:
Pawan Gupta led a team whose work appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was PKCε stimulated arginine methylation of RIP140 for its Nuclear-Cytoplasmic export in adipocyte differentiation. The full author list in the catalog record begins with Pawan Gupta, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

The abstract begins from a clear premise. Receptor interacting protein 140 (RIP140) is a versatile transcriptional co-repressor that plays roles in diverse metabolic processes including fat accumulation in adipocytes. Anyone studying the topic can use the article to see how the authors framed the problem at the time of publication.
plos-pone-0002758:
Céline Lafourcade led a team whose work appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was regulation of the V-ATPase along the endocytic pathway occurs through reversible subunit association and membrane localization. The catalog record names Céline Lafourcade first among the authors, and the source is the open journal PLOS ONE.

The abstract begins from a clear premise. The lumen of endosomal organelles becomes increasingly acidic when going from the cell surface to lysosomes. The summary also notes a further point. Luminal pH thereby regulates important processes such as the release of internalized ligands from their receptor or the activation of lysosomal enzymes. For readers, the value lies in how plainly the abstract sets out the problem and what the authors set out to test or describe.
plos-pone-0002858:
Morten Ruhwald led a team whose work appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was improving T-Cell assays for the diagnosis of latent TB infection: potential of a diagnostic test based on IP-10. Authorship is credited in the record to Morten Ruhwald and co-authors, with PLOS ONE as the journal of publication.

The abstract begins from a clear premise. There is a need for simple tools such as the M.tuberculosis specific IFN-γ release assays (IGRA) to improve diagnosis of M.tuberculosis -infection in children. Its abstract frames the work for later readers, who can judge the full text against the aims stated at the start.
plos-pone-0002958:
Sofia Kring, Claus Holst, Esther Zimmermann and co-authors studied the fatness gene FTO across a wide range of body fat in 2008. A common variant in FTO, labeled rs9939609, is linked to total body fatness. What it does for fat placement and related metabolic traits was less clear.

The team checked the variant against abdominal and peripheral fat and obesity-linked traits in middle-aged men spanning a broad range of fatness. Published in PLOS ONE, the design shows whether the gene's effect grows, fades, or changes form as fatness rises. Such detail refines a headline gene link.
plos-pone-0003058:
José Cuevas, Manuela Torres-Puente, Nuria Jiménez-Hernández and co-authors tracked hepatitis C virus change around therapy in 2008. They analyzed selective forces on two genome regions thought to be involved in response to combined interferon plus ribavirin therapy. One region holds three hypervariable parts of the envelope E2 protein.

Comparing virus before and after combined therapy shows which sites selection pressed hardest. Published in PLOS ONE, such maps help explain treatment failure and resistance. Hepatitis C evolves fast within a patient, so therapy must be judged against a moving target. Readers can follow the full methods and data in the complete text of the article.
plos-pone-0003158:
K. Bretonnel Cohen, Martha Palmer and Lawrence Hunter study verb forms in biomedical writing in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. They present data from the PennBioIE corpus on how common domain-specific verbs change their argument structure, and how their related noun forms behave. Alternation is the linguistics term for such shifts in the surface form of a verb.

Readers learn how biomedical verbs and their nominalizations vary in real text. That detail sounds narrow, but it matters for computer systems that mine medical papers for facts. Better handling of these forms means fewer errors when machines extract who did what to what.
plos-pone-0003258:
Amelia Cimmino, Rosanna Capasso, Fabbri Muller and colleagues study a repair enzyme in blood vessel cells in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Natural proteins undergo deamidation of certain asparagine residues in the body on their own, forming isoaspartyl residues. Deamidated, isomerized molecules are changed in both shape and how they work. The enzyme protein isoaspartate methyltransferase acts on such damage.

The title reports that this enzyme prevents apoptosis induced by oxidative stress in endothelial cells, with a role for Bcl-Xl deamidation and methylation. Readers see protein repair linked to cell survival under stress. Vessel lining protection matters in ageing and blood vessel disease.
plos-pone-0003358:
Jochen Brumm, Elizabeth Conibear, Wyeth W. Wasserman and colleagues present a method to find gene modules in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. A central problem in systems biology research is identification and extension of biological modules, groups of genes or proteins participating in a common cellular process or physical complex. There is a persistent need for practical, principled methods to infer such modules from data.

Their approach discovers and expands gene modules by seeking isolated groups in a random graph process. Readers get an algorithm that grows modules from seeds while testing against randomness. Module maps help turn gene lists into working biological units.
plos-pone-0003458:
Rita A. Busuttil and co-authors measured mutation buildup without a DNA repair protein in 2008. Ku80 helps join broken DNA ends, a quick repair route called non-homologous end joining. Losing that route has been tied to early aging. The team used mice missing Ku80 for their tests.

They counted mutations at a reporter gene, LacZ, across tissues and cells. Both the rate and the kinds of mutations changed without Ku80. The data show which errors pile up when end joining fails. That helps link broken repair to aging and cancer risk.
plos-pone-0003558:
Elena Lesma and co-authors tested a targeted antibody against tumor cells in this 2008 paper. Tuberous sclerosis complex causes benign tumors called hamartomas across organs. Faults in the TSC1 or TSC2 genes drive the syndrome. The team grew smooth muscle cells lacking TSC2 from a patient's tumor.

An antibody against EGFR, a growth factor receptor, was applied to those cells. It inhibited their proliferation efficiently and specifically. Blocking that receptor may offer a treatment path for this syndrome. A related lung disease, LAM, might benefit from the same approach. Tumors in this syndrome are benign yet can still harm by their size and place.
plos-pone-0003658:
Irini Evnouchidou, Frank Momburg, Athanasios Papakyriakou, and colleagues published this immunology study in PLOS ONE in 2008. The immune system displays protein pieces on cell surfaces so T cells can inspect them. An enzyme called ERAP1 trims those pieces down to the right size first.

The team found that the inner sequence of a piece, not just its ends, decides how ERAP1 trims it. That finding changes how the final displayed set is predicted. Knowing the trimming rules helps explain which pieces reach the surface and thus what the immune system gets to see.
plos-pone-0003758:
Xiaodian Sun, Li Jin, and Momiao Xiong published this modeling paper in PLOS ONE in 2008. The dynamics of a system decide how cells, tissues, and organisms behave. Building math models of biochemical networks means estimating their hidden parameters from data. That estimation is the hard part.

The authors adapt the extended Kalman filter, a classic engineering tool, to nonlinear state-space models of such networks. The filter infers parameter values as measurements come in. It helps turn noisy observations of living chemistry into working models of metabolism and gene regulation.
plos-pone-0003858:
Min Pi, Ling Chen, Min-Zhao Huang, and colleagues published this mouse study in PLOS ONE in 2008. GPRC6A is an orphan receptor found across the body. In lab dishes it senses amino acids, osteocalcin, and calcium-like ions. What it does in a living animal was unknown.

The team created mice lacking GPRC6A and characterized their condition. The null mice showed osteopenia, feminization, and metabolic syndrome together. The triple phenotype reveals one receptor quietly governing bone strength, sex traits, and metabolism at the same time. One missing part thus touched bone, sex traits, and body fuel use.
plos-pone-0003958:
Julia Szendroedi, Elisabeth Zwettler, Albrecht Ingo Schmid, and co-authors measured muscle energy output after acromegaly in 2008. Faulty mitochondria and fat stored in muscle link to poor insulin action. Acromegaly, an excess of growth hormone, also reduces insulin sensitivity. The team asked whether effects linger after the disease is treated.

Their PLOS ONE article studied patients with previous acromegaly. Basal ATP production in their skeletal muscle ran low. That lasting deficit may help explain ongoing metabolic risk. The result argues for long follow-up of metabolism after hormone excess ends. The full report sits in PLOS ONE, free to read with all its data shown.
plos-pone-0004058:
Darren J. Gray, Gail M. Williams, Yuesheng Li, and co-authors modeled a parasitic disease in China in 2008. Schistosoma japonicum infects over one million people in China. Another forty million live where infection risk is present. Unlike its relatives, this species also infects many animals.

Their PLOS ONE article studies transmission in lake and marshland regions. Animal hosts keep the parasite cycling even when people are treated. Models that include animals fit the disease's persistence better. Control programs must target the whole transmission web, not humans alone. Readers can find the full text in PLOS ONE, an open science journal.
plos-pone-0004158:
Jérôme Rollin and colleagues published this cancer study in PLOS ONE in 2009. ID2 is a regulator that helps control the balance between cell growth and cell specialisation. In healthy cells it keeps that balance; recent work has tied it to cancer.

The team examined where ID2 sits inside cells in non-small cell lung cancer, whether in the nucleus or outside it.
