Attitudes improved clearly in the trained group. Their stigma scores fell well beyond the control group's movement. Skills improved too. Trained students were over four times more likely to pass the practical exam. That exam grades how a student actually handles a patient describing discrimination. Knowledge and warmth on paper are not enough in a clinic room. The results encourage wider use of the training, and further research into which parts of it drive the change.
plos-pone-0352258:
Yanni Huang, Fuhua Yang, and Keli Yin surveyed eleven hundred four university students in Yunnan, China, about the good parts of their childhoods and their present happiness. Warm, safe, supportive early experiences are thought to echo into adult life. Scales measured those early experiences, the students' resilience, and their sense of well-being.

Students who recalled more positive childhood experiences reported stronger well-being as young adults. Resilience explained part of the link: good early experiences seemed to build the ability to bounce back, which in turn supported happiness. The tie was partial, so childhood warmth also matters in other ways. The authors urge colleges to train resilience while noting the sample came from one province, so the pattern needs testing in other places and cultures.
plos-pone-0352358:
Weiping Ma proposes a new way to outline organs in three-dimensional medical scans in this 2026 paper. Drawing those outlines by hand is slow expert work. Semi-supervised learning cuts the burden by learning from a few labelled scans plus many unlabelled ones. Ma's framework sets two networks to teach each other. A cross-attention module lets them exchange detailed features as they learn.

The two branches follow a teacher-student design built on a VNet backbone. Extra losses keep their feature distributions aligned and their classes cleanly separated. Knowledge flows in both directions, so each network corrects the other. Tests used left atrium scans and pancreatic scans, two hard segmentation targets. The method outperformed existing approaches on both. Hospitals could gain accurate scan outlines while labelling only a fraction of their image archives.
plos-pone-0352658:
Bony Lestari and seven colleagues count what tuberculosis care costs patients before treatment even starts. Their 2026 study is set in Bandung, Indonesia. It focuses on drug-resistant tuberculosis, which is harder and slower to diagnose. Patients often visit several providers before anyone confirms the disease. Every visit adds fees, tests, travel, and food costs.

Interviews with two hundred fifty-eight patients reconstructed those early expenses. The typical patient had spent roughly forty-five US dollars before treatment began. Costs spread across administration, chest X-rays, laboratory tests, medicines, travel, and food. Most patients first sought help at community health centres, and many lived in rural areas. Knowing where the money leaks out helps programmes shorten the path to diagnosis and protect poor families from early financial harm.
plos-pone-0352758:
Patricia Jurado-Gonzalez and five colleagues developed this 2026 PLOS One questionnaire for measuring how confident Spanish university students feel about cooking. Students often eat poorly after leaving home, and confidence in the kitchen is tied to better diets, yet Spain had no validated tool for this group. The team built items from existing questionnaires, had food experts review them, and piloted the draft at four Catalan universities.

After revisions, the final tool holds twenty-five items in two subscales. Student answers hung together consistently, and scores stayed stable when the questionnaire was repeated two weeks later. The authors offer it as a ready instrument for researchers and campus health programs that want to track, and eventually raise, students' cooking confidence.
plos-pone-0352858:
Karahan and Kasnakoglu designed flight control for a swarm of small drones facing several troubles at once in a 2026 study. Wind, noisy sensors, and delayed messages each unsettle a flying formation, yet past work often handled them one at a time. Their framework plans paths and dodges obstacles while treating all three troubles together.

Math analysis set bounds on how far the swarm could drift from its path under limited disturbance. Computer flights in two formation shapes reached targets, kept formation, and passed fixed obstacles without crashes. Brief shape bending appeared under stress, then the swarm recovered. The unified approach suits rescue and inspection work where conditions rarely stay clean.
plos-pone-0353058:
Abd El-Baky and colleagues, in a 2026 study, try to make an old drug, metronidazole, work better against a germ that infects the urinary tract. The germ, Proteus mirabilis, often strikes people with catheters and can help form stones. It also resists many drugs. The team's idea is to tuck the drug inside ring-shaped sugar carriers called cyclodextrins.

Three kinds of carrier were mixed with the drug by simple blending or kneading. Lab tests checked how the pairs formed and how fast the drug was released. Two carriers improved release, and one pairing needed a much lower dose to slow the germ. At doses too low to kill, the paired drug still cut the germ's swimming, its stone-linked enzyme action, and its ability to build biofilms, the slimy layers that shield germs. The authors say animal studies must come next before any clinical use.
plos-pone-0353158:
Maite Alanya-Pineda and six colleagues report this 2026 PLOS One study linking depressive symptoms to balance problems in older adults living in twelve high Andean communities in Peru. Mountain life brings low oxygen and scarce health services, which may raise rates of both conditions. The team reanalyzed survey data collected between 2013 and 2020 from more than four hundred residents, using a short depression questionnaire and a reach test for balance.

About half the residents showed depressive symptoms, and about half had balance disorders. After adjustment, those with depressive symptoms were about two-thirds more likely to have balance trouble than those without. The authors call for larger studies and for screening programs that catch both problems early, since together they raise the risk of falls and lost independence.
plos-pone-0353258:
Niilo Liuhto and seven colleagues report this 2026 PLOS One study testing whether fragments of DNA floating in blood predict bad outcomes in advanced kidney disease. Such cell-free DNA is a newer inflammation marker never checked in patients whose kidneys are failing but who have not yet started dialysis. The team measured it in nearly one hundred forty patients and followed them for several years.

The marker predicted nothing: not deaths, heart events, emergency visits, hospital stays, or new cancers. Levels did rise later in patients who moved on to transplants or dialysis, suggesting the treatment stage itself shifts the marker. The authors present the negative result as useful guidance, sparing future studies from chasing a marker that does not deliver in this group.
plos-pone-0353358:
Rodrigo Torres-Avilés and three colleagues show that a classic database question can be answered without unpacking the data, in this 2026 PLOS ONE computer science paper. A skyline query finds records that no other record beats on every measure at once — the hotels, say, that are each cheapest or best-rated in some unbeatable combination. The team implemented two flavours of the query inside a compact tree structure that stores data in compressed form.

Working directly on the compressed structure saved memory compared with ordinary approaches in their experiments, while still returning exact answers. They back the method with full proofs and benchmarks. Compact querying matters wherever data outgrow the machine that must answer questions about them.
plos-pone-0353558:
Jiuwei Chi and seven colleagues reconstruct the carbon footprint of farming in Inner Mongolia from 2006 to 2023, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. The region grows grain in dry country, leaning hard on irrigation, fertiliser, diesel, and plastic mulch. Counting the emissions embedded in those six inputs year by year, the team traced how the footprint evolved as China's farming modernised.

Input use surged early, then steadied or fell back after the mid-2010s for fertiliser, pesticide, and diesel — while plastic film kept climbing and irrigated area jumped late in the period. The pattern shows a system halfway through its low-carbon turn, with film and water now the stubborn fronts for policy.
plos-pone-0353958:
Lu and colleagues, in a 2026 forensic study, ask whether chemistry in the liver and kidneys can tell how a body died in seawater and how long it has been dead. Telling real drowning from a body placed in water after death is a classic hard problem. Sixty rats were assigned to seawater drowning or to being placed in seawater after death, and tissues were sampled across three days.

Thousands of small molecules in each tissue were measured, and machine learning models were trained on the patterns. Time since death dominated the chemistry, yet the models still separated the two causes of death with very high accuracy in both organs. Separate models guessed time since death within a few hours when tested on known time points, and less well on unseen ones. The authors present the approach as a promising forensic aid under controlled conditions, not yet a courtroom tool.
plos-pone-0354158:
Matthew Davitt and co-authors map in 2026 research that uses muscle electrical recording to judge the physical strain on surgeons doing keyhole and robot assisted belly surgery. Their scoping review followed standard guidance and searched many databases for studies in real or simulated surgical settings. Close to a hundred studies spanning nearly three decades qualified.

Most work covered plain keyhole surgery, with far fewer robot studies. Shoulder, neck, and forearm muscles were measured most, often alongside motion tracking or questionnaires. In the small set comparing both approaches, robot assistance consistently showed lower muscle activity, especially in the upper body, though the authors urge caution given the thin base.
plos-pone-0354258:
Nazlı Yanar Tunçel and Züleyha Avşar gave seventh-grade students virtual reality games for eight weeks of physical education and tested their balance and coordination. Schools are weighing headsets as teaching tools, but physical effects need evidence. Their 2026 experiment compared twenty headset students with nineteen controls on standard movement batteries.

The headset group improved more on backward balancing, side-to-side jumping, and platform transport tasks. Total coordination scores and balance reach in both directions also favoured the players. One test, single-leg hopping, showed no group difference. Yanar Tunçel and Avşar conclude that well-chosen virtual games can train real body skills, while noting that not every skill responds equally.
plos-pone-0354358:
Henkin and colleagues, in a 2026 interview study, look inside British teams that build artificial intelligence for health care. Such projects force data scientists, doctors, patients, and managers to work as one, and the social side is inseparable from the technical. Thirteen people in young research consortia described how knowledge actually moves between these camps.

People said they constantly reshaped both their tools and their message for the audience in front of them, especially clinicians and patients. Working in AI research was new to most, which itself created friction. Clinician and patient voices were wanted, but fitting them into technical workflows took effort, and AI knowledge traveled unevenly across the team. The authors take one participant's shrug as the study's spirit: much is improvised, and teams admit they are finding out as they go. Their point is that funding good teamwork is part of building good medical AI.
plos-pone-0354458:
Guanlin Dai, Da Gao, and Chao Zheng improve how AI finds a requested moment inside a video, a task called moment retrieval. Standard transformer models hunt the whole video at once because their search prompts carry no built-in sense of time span, and they falter on events of varied length. The team replaces those loose prompts with bell-shaped time priors that have a learnable center and width, seeded from local video features at several scales.

On a standard public benchmark, the design clearly helped one weak spot: finding long events, where scores rose by about two points over a leading rival with statistical support. Overall recall differences stayed inconclusive. Dai and colleagues present the prior as a cheap, focused part for studying scale-aware search in video models.
plos-pone-0354958: Sakthivel and seven co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on a material for storing electric charge. The material is BaMoO4, a metal oxide used in supercapacitors, devices that charge and discharge quickly. The team varied how long the material cooked in hot water and tracked changes in shape and performance. Their tests used an asymmetric supercapacitor setup. Small shape changes can shift how much energy such devices hold.
plos-pone-0355158:
Nigatu Madebo, Feleke Yareshe, and Lebsework Lemma propose in 2026 a new controller to guide unmanned aircraft along a set path more closely. They first recorded how a fuzzy logic controller behaved, then trained a combined neural and fuzzy system on those records. The trained system can adjust its own settings during flight, unlike the fixed original.

Simulations covered normal flight, flight with outside pushes, and flight when aircraft traits changed. The new controller cut a standard tracking error score sharply in the harder cases and by a smaller margin in normal flight. The authors present the method for jobs needing precise, steady flight.
plos-pone-0355558:
Christian Jäger and three colleagues describe how a German university medical center moved its lab record-keeping from paper to a digital notebook system, reporting in 2026. The open-source platform they adopted promises better data quality and easier sharing, but such switches often stall on user habits. Their study combines the rollout story with a survey of researchers about how they actually document their work.

Most survey respondents were experienced researchers, yet many complained that documenting took too long, was badly organized, and made old information hard to find. Nearly everyone named ease of use as the top requirement, with training and ongoing support close behind. Over the rollout period the platform grew to hundreds of users across dozens of teams. The authors share checklists and helper apps so other institutions can copy the approach.
plos-pone-0355858:
Proshenjit Sarker and S M Shamsul Alam built a three-stage vision cascade that reads Bangladeshi vehicle license plates. Plate recognition feeds traffic enforcement, but Bangla plates vary widely and older character-reading tools cover too few symbol classes. Their 2026 system chains three detection models, each solving one step.

The first model finds vehicles, the second locates the plate, and the third reads characters directly, with no separate text-recognition engine. Its character set spans one hundred four classes, covering city codes, vehicle types, and digits. Training used more than nine thousand images, with a held-out set for external checking. Sarker and Alam aim for a recogniser shaped to local plates rather than adapted from foreign ones.
plos-pone-0355958:
Maarten Mosch and colleagues reviewed a rare knee-area fracture seen in teenagers at a Dutch trauma centre. The tibial tubercle, where the thigh tendon anchors below the knee, can crack during sport while bones are still growing. Their 2026 series covered forty young patients treated over fifteen years.

Nearly all patients were boys, injured mostly during sports, at an average age of about fourteen. Most fractures needed surgery, usually screw fixation; the rest healed without an operation. Complications were uncommon, at about one in ten fractures, and no compartment syndrome occurred. Mosch and colleagues offer the series as practical guidance for a rare injury that youth sports are making more familiar.
plos-pone-0356058:
Liang He and co-authors tested whether plant and plastic fibres can protect swelling soil in regions with hard winter freezing. Expansive soil swells and shrinks with moisture, and freeze-thaw cycles damage it further. Their 2026 study mixed polypropylene and lignin fibres into such soil and ran swelling, strength, and freezing tests.

Lignin fibre alone performed best overall, cutting swelling most and raising shear strength most. Adding polypropylene fibre on top improved strength further. After repeated freeze-thaw cycles, the mixed-fibre soil lost far less strength than untreated soil. Microscope images showed fibres bridging and overlapping inside the soil, which explains the gains. The authors present fibre mixing as a practical fix for building on difficult ground.
plos-pone-0356258:
Yuling Cui and co-authors developed a freeze-dried DNA profiling kit. It removes forensic testing's dependence on freezers. Their 2026 paper describes a six-color fluorescent reagent. It covers twenty-nine identity markers plus a sex marker. The mix is engineered with a hardy enzyme and protective additives. So the dried reagent survives at room temperature. It wakes instantly when water is added.

In validation, the kit detected full profiles from tiny DNA amounts. It stayed stable for two months on the shelf. It also tolerated common contaminants. Head-to-head against liquid reagents, it matched identification rates exactly. It handled trace samples better. A pocketable, ready-to-use kit could bring reliable DNA identification to crime scenes, disaster zones, and small rural laboratories.
plos-pone-0356358:
Guoqin Wang and colleagues sifted blood gene data from heart attack patients for genes where two destructive processes meet: macrophage-driven inflammation and ferroptosis, an iron-dependent form of cell death. Their 2026 bioinformatics study merged two public datasets, corrected the batch differences between them with unusual care, and published this as a revised analysis with tightened false-positive controls.

Seven candidate genes survived the intersection, and five were confirmed raised in follow-up laboratory tests. Whole-genome pattern checks pointed at inflammatory and oxidative stress programs, and immune signatures shifted most clearly for neutrophils. Because the candidate network proved too sparse for hub claims, the authors present the seven as prioritized leads for heart attack biology rather than established drivers.
plos-pone-0356758:
Zhengyao Che and colleagues surveyed 305 women undergoing IVF treatment at a hospital in Yunnan, China, about their sexual function, a side of fertility care clinics seldom ask about. Their 2026 study scored function with a standard index, measured psychological distress, and used latent profile analysis to let natural patient groupings emerge rather than imposing cutoffs.

Three groups appeared: about a fifth with low function, two fifths in the middle, and the rest doing well. Younger, better-educated, and more distressed women clustered in the middle group, city residents in the good group, and longer infertility with more past pregnancies predicted the low group. The profiles give clinics a screening shortcut for an intimate problem that quietly strains couples already under treatment stress.
plos-pone-0357158:
Wenjie Sun and co-authors build a repeatable traffic monitoring workflow for highways that lack road sensors, testing it on a Sarawak stretch of the Pan Borneo Highway, in Malaysian Borneo. Probe data from navigation platforms can fill the gap if handled carefully. Their pipeline collects platform car data on a schedule, cleans it by fixed rules, stores it, computes pressure indicators, and cross-checks one platform against another over an overlapping month.

One platform's panel stayed available nearly all the time and caught a repeated evening pressure build-up at the same hour. The two platforms told similar stories at matched times and places. Sun and colleagues caution that probe data is not ground truth, but argue it can keep sparse corridors under steady watch.
plos-pone-0357258: Xu, writing alone, published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on keeping coal mine roadways dry and safe. The work searches for the best settings for roadway supports that block water. The search used an algorithm the author calls FFA. Getting support design right guards miners from flooding and roof falls. The study speaks to engineers who plan supports in wet ground conditions.
plos-pone-0357458:
Jianqi Guo and Yingmei Qu compare two kinds of academic English writing in a 2026 language study. One set comes from Chinese students training as translators, and the other from native English academic writers. Using two collections the authors built themselves, they measured sentence build with a standard software tool that tracks clause and phrase patterns.

Trainee writing leaned on longer clauses, joined phrases, and heavy noun groups, while native writing used more layered clauses packed into each unit. The groups differed clearly on most of the measures tested. Guo and Qu link the gap to second-language growth, pressure from the source text, and translation habits, and they point teachers toward training that builds clause-level skill.
plos-pone-0357658:
Masanori Nakajo and colleagues test whether an advanced CT measure can grade worn spinal disks without relying only on standard scans. Disk wear is the most common source of low back pain, and MRI grading is the usual reference. In about one hundred patients who had both scan types, the team measured several signals in the disk's tough rim and soft center across several hundred lumbar disks.

Plain CT values and the new density measure moved in opposite directions in rim and center as MRI wear grades rose. The gap in density between front rim and center tracked wear grade most strongly of all. Nakajo and colleagues say spectral CT density could help grade disk wear when MRI is unavailable or unclear, adding a quantitative option to routine spine imaging.
plos-pone-0357758:
Nazia Fairooz Alam led a team of eight authors designing a vaccine candidate on the computer, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Human metapneumovirus is a lung virus with no vaccine yet. The team used reverse vaccinology and pan-genomic methods to predict a candidate built from multiple epitopes, the parts of the virus the immune system recognizes.

Alam's in silico design gives vaccine developers a concrete head start instead of a blank page. Computer prediction cannot prove a vaccine works; it narrows the search to designs worth making and testing. Pan-genomic input helps the candidate cover many virus strains at once. For a virus that burdens children and older adults each winter, a faster start matters.
plos-pone-0357958:
Guangjun Liu led a team of five authors designing a lean part for vision models, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Attention modules help a model focus on the right parts of an image, but they usually add parameters that cost memory and speed. Their module, PSAFM, fuses features across space with attention, yet adds no parameters at all.

Liu's parameter-free design boosts accuracy without the usual bloat, making it cheap to drop into existing networks. Small models for phones and cameras benefit most, since every parameter counts there. A part that improves many models, rather than one bespoke system, spreads its value widely. The study is a reminder that clever structure can beat brute size in machine learning design.
plos-pone-0358258:
Micah Vinet and seven colleagues wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article on eye diagnosis. It presents software that automatically measures the thickness of the cornea's central surface layer, the epithelium. The purpose is diagnosing limbal stem cell deficiency, a failure of the cells that renew the cornea's surface.

When limbal stem cells fail, the cornea clouds and vision suffers, yet the condition is hard to measure by eye alone. Automated thickness readings could make diagnosis more objective and repeatable between clinics. Corneal specialists evaluating surface disease are the readers who would use such measurements in practice.
plos-pone-0358558:
Jing Yang, Zhenqing Li, and Yoshinori Yamaguchi studied in 2026 whether teaching by outcomes makes engineering students more skilled. The approach is called outcome based education. It plans a course backward, from the skills students should be able to show at the end, rather than forward from a list of topics. Their test bed was a course on intelligent control, a hard subject about smart control systems.

The team used mixed methods, joining test scores and skill checks with what students and teachers said about the course. Book learning alone does not prove skill in such a subject, so the checks asked students to do real tasks. If planning by outcomes builds real skill here, the case grows for using it across engineering degrees.
plos-pone-0358858: Tufael and seven co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on how insulin resistance may help liver cancer grow. Part of the work is computer-based, modeling how a protein called IRS-1 meets the core protein of hepatitis C virus, genotype 3. The virus and insulin resistance often occur together. If the link holds, it could explain part of the cancer risk carried by infected patients.
plos-pone-0358958: Bíl and four co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on road deaths in Czechia across more than five decades. Autopsy records from 1969 to 2024 covered people killed while walking, cycling, or otherwise unprotected. The title reports that these deaths come with greater trauma than other road deaths. Long records like these show whether safety laws and car design have truly protected the most exposed road users.
plos-pone-0359158:
Madeline Fernandez-Pineda and five colleagues study what miscarriage care felt like during the COVID-19 pandemic, in a 2026 PLOS ONE article. Pandemic rules kept support people out of clinics and disrupted appointments, adding strain to an already painful loss. The authors combined surveys and interviews to capture both the numbers and the women's own accounts of that period.

Seventy-one women in North Carolina who miscarried during stay at home mandates took part, and eighteen gave long interviews. About half rated their care experience as poor. Pandemic hardships such as missing support persons were similar across groups, but women with poor experiences reported clearly higher stress, anxiety, and depression. Among those treated with medicine or surgery, a good care experience went together with lower distress.
plos-pone-0359858:
Álvaro Huerta Ojeda and eight colleagues wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article on aging and function. It studies community-dwelling older adults, people living in their own homes rather than care facilities. The authors examine the association between the muscle quality index and the time needed to rise from lying face down to standing.

Rising from the floor is a real-world test of strength that matters after a fall. A muscle quality index condenses how much force muscle produces for its size. If the index tracks floor-rise time, clinicians gain a simple screen for older adults losing independence, and exercise programs gain a target.
plos-pone-0360158:
Johannes Aengenheyster, Olav Velthuis, and Alex van Venrooij examined in 2026 what the private museums of wealthy economic elites contribute to the arts. Rich collectors increasingly open museums of their own rather than only donating to public ones. The authors ask whether these institutions are mere bandwagons, fashionable copies of one another, or genuine breeding grounds for artistic innovation.

Their study weighs what private museums add: new exhibition space, support for living artists, and public access to collections that would otherwise stay hidden. It also weighs the concerns, including private taste shaping public culture. The question matters for cultural policy, since cities court such museums while public institutions compete with them for art and attention.
plos-pone-0360658:
Wei Li, Ming Ma, and Jinyue Lu studied in 2026 how the Chinese public judged a cultural heritage scandal across different online platforms. The controversy concerned artifacts donated to the Nanjing Museum and how they were handled. The authors used topic modeling, a computational method that finds themes in large volumes of text, to map what people actually talked about on each platform.

Public judgment in a heritage crisis shapes whether a museum keeps the trust that brings donors and visitors. Comparing platforms shows how the same facts become different stories in different online rooms. Their study offers museums and cultural agencies a method for listening during a crisis, and a record of how this one unfolded.
pmc-10653458:
Qing Xia, Shan Wang, and Jose Weng Chou Wong ask whether online trade shows can nudge firms toward greener habits, in a paper from two thousand twenty-three. Their case is a large trade fair for factory machines in Yiwu, China. They look at how the online format shapes what firms think and do.

One part of the work surveyed 417 firms at the fair held in two thousand twenty-one. A second part drew on talks with 18 people who took part. Traits such as an easy site to move through, vivid images, and ways to join in shaped how firms judged their green results and how pleased they felt. Those views, in turn, went with greener acts on the firms' side. The team says online shows should stay a long-term plan for the trade.
pmc-10655258:
Yue Kong and co-authors map a fat tagging process called palmitoylation across human cancers, in a study from 2023. The tag, added and removed by two enzyme sets, steers many cell jobs, but its cancer wide pattern was unclear.

Gene data from many public sets tied tag shifts to cancer type, stage, and survival. Odd DNA marks and a key cancer driver gene jointly drove the shifts. Tag shifts also tracked immune cell entry and reply to immune care. Cutting the driver gene in cells lowered tag enzyme levels and the global tag load, which backs the link.
pmc-10655358:
Heart failure leaves patients exhausted by light effort, though training programs can rebuild some of that lost capacity. Vanessa da Silva and co-authors set out a 2023 trial plan that pairs exercise with gentle brain stimulation. The stimulation sends a weak current through the scalp to nudge brain areas that govern effort.

Patients with a weak heart pump will train aerobically while getting either real stimulation or a sham version that feels the same. The main test is how far their functional capacity improves. The team will also compare breathing fitness, inflammation markers, and quality of life between the groups. The trial is blinded on both sides, so neither patients nor testers know who got the real current.
pmc-10656558:
Eric Morrell and co-authors profile immune cells in the lungs of patients with severe breathing failure, in a 2023 study. The condition fills the lungs with fluid and starves the blood of oxygen. Cells that eat germs and debris sit at the center of the response. Their exact types in this illness were poorly known.

Samples of lung wash fluid and blood were taken over time. A method that reads genes and surface proteins cell by cell sorted the cell types. Some matched types seen in healthy lungs, and others matched types in COVID-19. Their traits also differed from other lung diseases. The map of cell types may help target care for a condition with few good options.
pmc-10656958:
Sholeh Mansouri and co-authors measure genetic variety in the malaria parasite Plasmodium vivax collected from patients in southeastern Iran. Vivax is the main malaria species in Iran, where the disease is not yet wiped out. Surface proteins of the parasite are vaccine targets, so their variety matters.

The team read one gene, merozoite surface protein-5, in samples from thirty-five patients. Out of hundreds of gene sites, many varied, and the samples formed seventeen distinct haplotypes. No two regions carried quite the same mix. Such a map warns vaccine designers that a single strain's protein may not cover Iran's parasite population.
pmc-10664558:
Ten researchers describe family ties of nursing home residents who died in Utah in a paper from 2023. Families shape care at the end of life, yet little was known about their size and makeup. The team linked records for more than forty-three thousand residents who died between 1998 and 2016. They identified spouses, children, and siblings for each person.

About one in five residents had no close family on record. That group had more women, more non-White residents, and less schooling than the group with family. They also died more often from cancer, lung disease, and dementia. Hospital trips near death were slightly fewer in the no-family group. The authors say family structure should inform end-of-life care planning.
pmc-10668758:
The authors fed young yellow-feather chickens a partly fermented diet to see whether it beat plain feed across health measures. Fermented feed is gaining favor as a natural growth aid. The trial ran 240 day-old hens for twenty-two days, split between a standard diet and the same diet with two percent fermented feed added. Growth, immunity, gut function, and gut microbes were all tracked.

Raw growth did not change. Under the surface, though, the fermented group improved on several fronts. Antibody and immune signal levels shifted, liver antioxidant enzymes ran higher, and one gut enzyme worked harder. The gut's microbial diversity rose, and certain bacterial groups became more common. The authors conclude the additive earns its keep through health and gut benefits rather than faster growth, at least over this short window in young birds.
pmc-10669258:
Javier Flores-Estrada and seven co-authors wrote this 2023 study on how spinach extract protects the liver in diabetic rats. The extract is rich in antioxidant polyphenols, but where in the liver it acts was unknown. The team gave it for twelve weeks to rats made hyperglycemic with streptozotocin, then mapped stress, defense, and scarring markers cell by cell across liver tissue.

Treated rats showed lower liver enzymes in blood and less fat oxidation damage in tissue. Their non-parenchymal cells, the liver's support and immune population, raised antioxidant enzyme defenses, while a master protective switch and its partner protein rose in both cell types. Inflammatory signals fell, and scarring-linked markers shifted in a favorable pattern. The authors argue the protection works partly by division of labor between liver cell types, a detail that could guide how plant extracts are developed into therapies.
pmc-10671858:
Meijia Zheng and co-authors test a root dwelling fungus as a growth aid for Tartary buckwheat in a 2023 paper. The fungus Serendipita indica colonizes plant roots and is known to help several crops. The team asked whether it could boost this hardy grain's growth and stress defense.

Colonized plants grew taller and heavier and yielded more grain. Their leaves showed stronger photosynthesis, more chlorophyll, and higher levels of growth hormones and protective compounds. Stress markers linked to damage fell compared with untreated plants. The plants also handled drought better after colonization. Flavonoid and phenol levels rose in leaves and seeds, adding nutritional value. The authors present the fungus as a low input way to raise buckwheat performance.
pmc-10689458:
Almar Neiteler and three co-authors study how oxidative stress kills the support cells of the retina, in a 2023 lab paper. The disease in view is age-related macular degeneration, a leading cause of sight loss. The support layer feeds the light-sensing cells and swallows their shed tips each day, and those tips are rich in a fat that rusts easily.

That fat, called DHA, plus oxidative stress, pushed the support cells toward two programmed death routes, necroptosis and ferroptosis. Both routes rose as the injury grew. The finding helps explain why these cells die early in the disease and which death switches might be blocked to save them. It also flags the daily fat load itself as part of the risk.
pmc-10691258:
Ishikawa studies how shared views of old age can turn into poor views of one's own aging in twenty twenty-three. The study draws on a survey of adults in Finland about age and aging. It asks which traits link a dim view of old age in society with a dim view of one's own old age.

Women and adults with more schooling were more apt to hold both dim views. So were adults who rated their quality of life as poor. Adults who knew of unfair treatment of older people at work or in care also scored high. The author argues that life context, not age alone, shapes how people judge their own aging.
pmc-10692858:
Xiangyi Yu and co-authors report a 2023 study of gene reads in school-aged children with severe shortsightedness. Genes play a large part in this eye fault, a top cause of sight loss world-wide. The team read the protein-coding genes of more than six thousand affected children tested in Wenzhou, China.

The children averaged near fifteen years old, and their sight fault averaged well past the severe line. Aims were to count how often clear gene hits turn up and how the yield shifts across grades of severity, from common high grades to the most extreme. The read-out guides when gene tests pay off.
pmc-10693058:
Marta Domínguez-Moreno and three co-authors review a high-stakes birth procedure at their center in a 2023 paper. The EXIT procedure works on a baby half-delivered, while the placenta still feeds it, to secure a blocked airway. It saves babies but puts the mother through a long, deep operation with real risk.

Records ran from 2007 to 2022 at one Spanish center. The team tallied who the mothers were, how the operations went, and what harm followed, graded on a standard scale. A matched sample of other births gave the contrast. The paper weighs the mother's price against the baby's gain, case by case.
pmc-10693158:
Yanbo Guo and co-authors checked cheap ways to screen for fatty liver disease in rural Uyghur adults in Xinjiang, China, in a study published in 2023. The disease is the most common long term liver problem in China, and a scan for each person is not practical.

The survey covered more than 14,000 adults in 51 groups in Kashgar in 2016, with scans used to confirm the disease. About one in six adults had it. Five score based tools, each built from simple body and blood measures, were all tied to higher risk. One score did best overall, about as well as body mass index alone. The team gives cut off values for men and women to use in screening.
pmc-10693458:
Plants carry a large family of proteins built around a small zinc grip called a PHD finger. Wenli Quan and co-authors review what is known about these proteins in a 2023 survey, drawing on years of work in plant growth and stress.

The grip reads marks on the packed thread that holds plant genes, and that reading helps switch genes on and off. Some of these proteins set when a plant flowers, while others shape pollen growth. Still others help plants cope with drought, salt, and cold. The review pulls these roles into one map, so readers can see how one small grip can steer so much of plant life.
pmc-10693558:
Leijiao Yue and co-authors asked which parts of a swim routine best predict scores in artistic swimming, in a 2023 study. They focused on hybrid figures, the linked moves that form a large part of a team free routine. The team watched videos from top world events and from a Beijing team trial. They measured eight traits of the figures, such as leg height, leg angle, and how often moves changed.

Five traits helped predict the total score for world teams. These were move rate, leg height, leg angle, pattern length, and spin rate. The Beijing team differed from the top five world teams on several of these traits and on total score. The authors advise coaches to favor a good pace of moves, patterns, and spins over long, hard figures that can drag down the show.
pmc-10694158:
Jie-pin Li and co-authors split liver cancer into two subtypes by calcium channel genes and hunt drug targets. Liver cancer resists both diagnosis and therapy because tumors vary so much. Gene patterns from 371 patients sorted the tumors into two groups. The groups differed in outlook and in likely response to immune therapy.

One protein, FSTL3, flagged the group that resists immune drugs. Stains in the team's own patient set backed that signal. FSTL3 sits mostly in the tumor's support tissue, not the cancer cells. There it boosts talk between scar-building fibroblasts and a macrophage type. That crosstalk drives the dense fibrosis tied to poor drug response.
pmc-10694958:
Zhixiang Mu and co-authors build a wound treatment in 2023 that kills germs without antibiotics. Infected skin wounds are a growing problem, and overuse of antibiotics has bred resistant germs. Their system uses flakes of a mineral called MoS2, coated with a sugar-based carrier that holds nitric oxide gas.

Near-infrared light heats the flakes, and the heat releases a burst of nitric oxide. Together, heat and gas tear germ membranes and drain their energy, wiping them out. After the germs are gone, leftover material releases a trickle of the gas. That trickle draws skin cells in and spurs new blood vessels, which speeds healing. The team calls the flakes a strong candidate for infected wound care.
pmc-10695058:
Vitória Pessoa Nogueira and three co-authors reflect on the ethical knots that arise when caring for people at the end of life. The essay reads those dilemmas through the ethics of care developed by philosopher Luigina Mortari. In that view, care is not a technique but a way of being, an action moved by interest in the other person and by sensing their need. Dependency and vulnerability, built into human life, are what make the dilemmas arise at all.

The authors argue that good end-of-life care guards the patient's self-rule above all. Practical tools include ways for patients to state their wishes while they still can, and steady, clear, kind communication among everyone at the bedside. Dilemmas cannot be removed from dying care, they conclude, but they can be met with respect.
pmc-10695558:
Di Chen and a large team of co-authors build a tool to predict surgery after acupuncture fails, in a paper dated twenty twenty-three. Their patients had lumbar disc herniation treated at four Chinese hospitals. Of 738 patients, 496 formed the training set and 242 the check set.

Seven factors drove the model, among them smoking, disability score, and disc type. The tool also weighed spinal narrowing and how often needling was done. Its accuracy score hit about 0.90 in both sets. The authors present the chart as a way to flag early who may still need an operation.
pmc-10695758:
Jin-Sun Park reports a single striking heart case in a 2023 paper. A man brought back from cardiac arrest arrived at the clinic with no name and no records. His chest X-ray showed a swollen heart and fluid in the lungs, plus a scar from past surgery on his chest wall. A heart scan then showed a bright line at the mitral valve and a bad leak, hinting that a repair ring had torn loose.

A three-way scope test through the food pipe confirmed the ring had come away from the valve. The man was later named, and his past held a robot-aided repair of that valve. Park argues that the 3D scope test can pin down such faults even when no records exist to guide the search.
pmc-10695958:
Alaina Weinheimer, Frank Aylward, Matthieu Leray, and Jarrod Scott report a 2023 study on what shapes virus and microbe communities in coastal seas near Panama. The viruses in view infect bacteria and single-celled life and kill them, which steers the whole microbe web. The narrow land bridge splits two oceans with unlike richness, a neat natural test of what drives these communities.

Both virus and microbe groups split sharply between the two oceans. Within the poorer ocean, microbe groups split again between mangrove and reef sites, but virus groups did not. That split hints that viruses are shaped more by travel between sites than by local terms. Microbes, by contrast, bend to local terms at small scales. The frame can guide models of ocean chemical cycles.
pmc-10696658:
Sepsis can injure the kidneys, and the worst cases are those where severe injury will not lift. Wei Jiang and co-authors ask in a 2023 study whether a routine blood fat measure can flag those cases early. The measure is HDL cholesterol, the so-called good cholesterol, which calms inflammation and protects vessel linings.

Working from a large intensive care database, the team studied 604 septic patients with kidney injury whose HDL was measured within a day of admission. Eighty-eight patients, about fifteen percent, went on to persistent severe injury. Their HDL levels ran lower than those who recovered. Yet on its own the measure separated the two groups poorly in accuracy tests. The authors conclude that low HDL marks higher risk but is not, alone, a strong predictor.
pmc-10696758:
Haoran Zhong and co-authors characterize a protein from the blood fluke that causes schistosomiasis. Their 2023 paper studies annexin A13 in Schistosoma japonicum. The disease burdens people and animals across the tropics, and its eggs drive both illness and spread, so cutting egg output is a prime control goal.

Gene activity for the protein was profiled across the worm's life stages, with a cousin species checked against public data. Silencing the gene in living worms stunted female growth and egg laying. A lab-made version of the protein raised specific antibodies in a protection assay. Worm secretion packets carrying the protein also reached human liver cells in a shared culture. The authors present the protein as a window on reproduction and host contact.
pmc-10696858:
An-Kuo Chou, Chun-Hua Liao, and Duan-Rung Chen published a 2023 study validating a teen health literacy scale in Taiwan. The Chinese version of the scale was given to 2,312 pupils in fifth and sixth grade. The team checked its consistency and factor structure, then compared results with other regions.

The scale held up well on validity and acceptably on consistency. Communication skill in health matters tracked parents' social and economic status. Family income mattered more than community income. Taiwan scored lowest among the compared regions on that communication measure. The authors present the scale as a useful tool for spotting inequality in young people's health skills.
pmc-10697958:
A ribosome protein helps liver cancer rewire its fuel use, Qingqing Yang and co-authors report in a 2023 study. The protein runs high in liver tumors and tracks poor survival. Cancer cells favor fast sugar burning, and this protein boosts the enzymes that run it.

Cells grew faster and made more lactate with the protein active. It switches on a surface sensor that fires a growth pathway, ending in a hypoxia factor that drives the sugar program. The loop feeds itself, since the protein acts from outside its own cell. Cutting that loop could starve tumors of their preferred fuel.
pmc-10698258:
Grace Lee, David Wald, and a large team test if loss of one gene form in blood stem cells harms blood growth in mice, in a 2023 letter. The gene steers cell fate and is a drug target in blood cancer. Past work warned its loss in young blood cells could spark a grave blood flaw, though.

That past model used a drug switch and cell grafts that may have bent the result. The new work frames the safety probe with care for those traps. Its title claim is plain, that blood growth stays normal in mice with that loss. The letter weighs how to target one gene form with less risk.
pmc-10699058:
Edith Kwobah and co-authors compared heart risk habits in adults with psychosis and matched controls in this 2023 study. The work ran at a referral hospital in Eldoret, Kenya, with 297 patients and 300 controls. Staff asked about smoking, drinking, diet, and exercise, and measured weight, waist, blood pressure, sugar, and fats.

Patients were more likely to have smoked at some point and to smoke now. Nearly all patients ate very few fruits and vegetables, and most rarely exercised hard. Sitting for long stretches was common too. Estimated ten-year heart risk still scored low in this young group. The authors urge clinics to build heart-healthy habits into mental health care.
pmc-10699158:
Ye Ji and five co-authors compare two drug plans after leg artery repair, in this 2023 study. Patients with narrowed leg arteries face heart attacks, strokes, and limb loss even after a procedure reopens the vessel. One plan uses antiplatelet drugs alone. The other adds low-dose rivaroxaban, a blood thinner, on top.

The team looked back at 1,144 patients treated at one Nanjing hospital from 2018 to 2021. The combined plan cut the pooled risk of heart attack, stroke, and heart death by about sixty percent. It also cut limb events such as urgent repeat procedures and major amputation. Major bleeding did not rise in a way that reached significance, though lesser bleeding did. The authors say high-risk Asian patients, little studied before, gain from the dual plan, and they note the study was not randomized.
pmc-10702058:
Jiani Wang and seven co-authors report a 2023 early trial of a new cancer drug in China. The drug, LXI-15029, blocks mTOR, a switch that helps tumors grow. It was the first time the drug was given to people, so the main aim was safety.

Twenty-four patients with advanced solid tumors that no longer met standard care took the drug twice a day. Doses rose step by step from 10 to 150 mg across groups. The drug was well borne at all doses, with one case of raised liver enzyme at the top dose. The team also tracked how the body handled the drug and saw early signs of effect.
pmc-10703258:
Sophie Carlisle and co-authors published this 2023 protocol for a systematic review of support for adults hurt by domestic and sexual violence in Britain. Such abuse is common and its damage runs deep, yet no one had pooled the evidence on whether British support services actually improve safety and wellbeing. The planned review aims to fill that gap.

Searches will sweep eight academic databases plus grey sources, with a call for evidence sent to charities across the field. Stakeholders from survivor organizations helped pick the outcomes that matter most. Two reviewers will screen and grade every study independently. The protocol fixes the rules in advance, so the coming verdict rests on the full evidence, not cherry-picked wins.
pmc-10703558:
Se-Il Go and co-authors present a 2023 study on non-medical opioid use among cancer patients in Korea. Little was known about how often patients use prescribed opioids in ways not directed by a doctor. The team reviewed records for 14,728 patients treated for cancer at a major hospital from 2009 to 2019. Charts of long-term users got a close read.

Of 5,587 patients who got opioids and were tracked for a year, 13 cases of misuse were found. That is a small share overall, at under a quarter of one percent. Among long-term users, the share was far higher, at over six percent. Oxycodone and fentanyl were the most misused drugs. Most cases showed withdrawal signs.
pmc-10704258:
Marc Herbst and co-authors measure laser damage thresholds for the retina under very short pulses. Their 2023 study deals with the database behind a laser safety standard. Data are thin, above all for elongated light profiles. To ensure eye safety, thresholds at which half of samples are damaged must be known. The team used pig eye tissue outside the body.

A laser setup shone rectangular, flat topped profiles on the tissue. Threshold values ranged from 8.46 to 42.72 microjoules. Thermal simulations were run on a validated computer model. Heat damage could be ruled out in the tests, based on levels and a distinct pattern of decline. Simulations showed a dependence on elongation and area. Tests could not confirm it, due to biological variation and focus issues.
pmc-10704758:
Hasan Barati and co-authors report a hard elbow injury case in this 2023 paper. The patient was a 37 year old man with fracture dislocations in both elbows. This pattern is called a terrible triad injury. On the left side the radial head was shattered and the wound was contaminated. His history of substance use also raised care concerns.

Surgeons replaced the left radial head with a cement spacer loaded with antibiotics. The right side fracture was fixed in the normal way. The patient missed all follow up visits after discharge. He returned six months later, which let the team check the outcome then. The case shows a fallback option when standard implants are not advised.
pmc-10706058:
Xin Li and six co-workers wrote a 2023 study of clinic patients with high uric acid in their blood. High uric acid often comes with metabolic syndrome, a cluster of risks for heart disease and diabetes. The team asked which simple blood markers best flag that cluster. They studied a group of just under four hundred patients in Tianjin.

About three in ten patients had the syndrome. Three markers ran higher in that group than in the rest. One marker, which blends blood fat and blood sugar, had the strongest link by far. The authors suggest that this marker can help clinics screen these patients.
pmc-10706758:
Seunghoon Jeong and Yijung Chung published a research paper in 2023 on a rehab exercise pairing task practice with a deep abdominal bracing move for stroke patients with weak trunks. Trunk control underpins balance and daily tasks, and it often lags after stroke. Thirty-eight chronic stroke patients were split into three arms for twenty sessions over five weeks.

One group did task-oriented training while holding the drawing-in maneuver in sitting, one did task training alone, and one received traditional therapy. The combined group improved significantly more in trunk control, balance, and daily living scores than both other groups. The authors recommend folding the bracing maneuver into standard stroke rehabilitation.
pmc-10707858:
Tung-Chi Liu, Yi-Sen Peng, and Bai-You Cheng wrote this 2023 study on how trees limit harm where a branch joins the stem. The team looked at four features of that joint: the U-shaped join, the branch collar, the bark ridge, and the rough bark on the lower stem. They built three-dimensional models of a maple branch joint and tested stress in them with a standard engineering method.

Models added the four features one at a time, as a tree would grow them. The collar moved the break point outward, which guards the stem from decay. The bark ridge kept tears in the bark small, and the U-shaped join cut stress and shifted its peak toward the branch. Together, the features form two lines of defense that shield the wood inside the stem.
pmc-10708558:
Researchers describe a 2023 system that spots unusual events in security camera video. The task is hard because clips of violence or other rare events are far fewer than normal clips. The team treats the task as a yes-or-no choice between normal and abnormal footage.

Frames from each video are merged into small grids, such as three by three, to form compact inputs. A three-dimensional network then reads these grids, aided by a module that focuses on key channels and places. Tests on four public video sets, including fight and campus scenes, show the system beats earlier methods named in the study.
pmc-10709258:
Shirin Macias and co-authors hunt blood markers of Mediterranean diet eating in a 2023 paper. Self-reported diet diaries are easy to shade or misremember. Blood chemistry could offer an honest adherence check instead.

Plasma from fifty-eight patients in a controlled study was profiled. Untargeted mass spectrometry scanned thousands of molecules per sample. Samples were sorted by a fourteen-point diet score. A marker panel separating high and low scorers was built. A statistical model then classified eating pattern from blood alone. Readers see diet research moving from questionnaires toward lab proof.
pmc-10709458:
Shirzad Mian Darbandi and co-authors test whether preseason balance checks can flag judokas headed for leg injuries, in a 2023 study. Fifty-three professional male judokas took stability and knee position-sense tests, then were tracked for ten months, during which fifteen lower limb injuries occurred.

Single scores on each leg barely differed between the injured and the healthy. The telling number was asymmetry: the ratio between the two sides on balance and position sense separated the groups with fair accuracy, and clear cutoff values emerged. The authors urge coaches and clinicians to screen for side-to-side imbalance rather than raw scores when hunting injury risk in fighters.
pmc-10709558:
Chunyan Zheng and seven co-authors present a study from twenty twenty-three on why throat cancer of the squamous kind resists radiation care. Radiation is a key weapon against this cancer, yet many tumors shrug it off. The team homes in on a gene switch named YY1. It ran high in resistant tissue and tracked with poor odds for patients.

Cutting YY1 made the cancer cells far more prone to radiation, in dishes and in mice. Deep scans showed YY1 drives a motor gene, KIF3B. That motor talks to a surface protein and holds back the Hippo pathway. With YY1 cut, Hippo wakes and its agent YAP1 is barred from the nucleus. The team flags YY1 as a drug target.
pmc-10709658:
Emmanuel Ifeanyi Obeagu reviews vaccination against hepatitis B in a 2023 paper. The virus infects the liver, spreads through blood and body fluids, and has touched about a third of the world's people. Vaccination is the main defense, and the review sums up current strategies and the factors that help or hinder them.

Programs that vaccinate babies have cut chronic infection in children and teens and lowered liver cancer in the young. Yet coverage stays low in many places, and many people start the shots without finishing them. Movement of people from high-burden regions has also raised the number of chronically infected adults in low-burden countries. The author stresses that closing the coverage gap is the clearest way to shrink the disease's toll.
pmc-10709858:
Allison Rhodes and co-authors present a 2023 survey of training on care for sexual and gender minority patients. Such patients face bias and poor care in clinics, in part because doctors get little set training on their needs. The team surveyed students and teachers at one US medical school to gauge knowledge and felt skill on the topic.

The survey ran in 2020 and 2021 and drew 223 students and 111 teachers into the final count. Students beat teachers on general knowledge questions, at about 97 versus 90 percent correct. On clinical knowledge questions the two groups scored much the same. Self-rated skill gaps also came to light. The results give schools a base for adding training where both groups fall short.
pmc-10709958:
Jared Silver and three co-authors map how biologic drugs are used for a stubborn sinus condition in the United States, in a 2023 claims study. The condition pairs long-term sinus inflammation with nasal polyps. Several biologics are approved as add-on care. The team used a large insurance claims database to find nearly six thousand adults with the condition. They tracked care over about two years and compared users and non-users of the drugs.

About one in ten patients used a biologic in the follow-up year. Users were far more likely to have asthma, which alone raised the odds more than fivefold. Steroid pill use was also higher among users. Most surgery patients who used a biologic started it before their operation. The authors say the pattern marks patients with high unmet need. Such signs could help clinics spot good candidates sooner.
pmc-10710358:
Leah J Martin and three colleagues estimate how many Swedish disease cases routine vaccination has averted since nineteen ten, in a study from twenty twenty-three. Measles, whooping cough, mumps, and polio were the four diseases tracked. National case reports spanned about a century. Pre-vaccination incidence supplied the counterfactual baseline.

Over two million cases were reported across the surveillance periods. The authors estimate more than one and a half million were averted by vaccination. Measles and whooping cough account for most of the total. Mumps and polio contribute smaller shares. Underreporting, especially in early years, makes these figures underestimates. The study quantifies a century of vaccine benefit. It answers hesitancy with the diseases' own arithmetic.
pmc-10710958:
Ali Maleki and co-authors describe in 2023 how Iran's laboratory network grew to fight new infectious diseases, with the Pasteur Institute of Iran at its center. Fast lab testing is the backbone of outbreak tracking, as the Covid-19 crisis showed. Iran had a response team and lab network before the pandemic, but not the scale the new virus demanded.

Within weeks, the team built in-house tests from global protocols and opened the first Covid lab before the first case was announced. The network grew to 560 labs across all provinces, handling test checks, quality control, and variant tracking. It has processed over fifty-five million samples. The authors present the network as a lasting base for future outbreaks.
pmc-10711858:
Jingyang Li and co-authors found a way to make chemo provoke a stronger immune attack on tumors, in this 2023 study. Chemo works best when dying tumor cells alert the immune system. Yet the very enzymes that kill the cells also mute that alert.

A drug screen pointed to a heat-shock protein blocker that kills tumor cells but hides their DNA alarm. Blocking one death enzyme, caspase-9, freed the alarm without sparing the cells. The combo released immune signals and shrank tumors in mice. Tumors fought back by raising a brake protein, and blocking that brake as well led to full tumor clearance in the models.
pmc-10712058:
Akram Hoseinzadeh, Seyed-Alireza Esmaeili, and five co-authors train stem cells with helpful bacteria to treat lupus. Their study, from twenty twenty-three, uses mesenchymal stem cells, which can calm the immune system. Lupus is a disease where the body attacks itself. Gut bacteria of certain kinds may tune how the stem cells work.

Mice with a lupus-like illness got cells raised with one of two Lactobacillus strains, or both. Plain cells and no-cell groups served as controls. Tests then counted immune cell types and signal proteins in the blood. The trained cells shifted the immune response in distinct ways by strain. The work points to pairing cells with microbes as a lupus strategy.
pmc-10712258:
Faris Alkhilaiwi and co-authors test a Red Sea sponge extract against breast cancer cells in this 2023 study. The barrel sponge holds sterols, alkaloids, and rare fats with past hints of healing power. The team asks whether its alcohol extract can slow a standard breast cancer cell line.

Cell survival fell as dose rose, with a mid-kill dose in a modest range. Treated cells showed more self-kill signals and stalled at a rest phase of the growth cycle. In a scratch test, treated cells also crept closed more slowly. The authors say the extract holds promise as a lead, while much work stands between cell tests and a drug.
pmc-10713158:
Jihan Ahmad, Adnan Ahmad, and Lama Hadid report a case where stronger hormone treatment restored a man's fertility. Their 2023 case report concerns congenital adrenal hyperplasia, one of the most common inherited disorders, usually caused by a missing enzyme. A twenty-eight-year-old man with the condition came in infertile, with suspected tumors in both testes, four years after stopping his steroid medicine.

The masses were testicular adrenal rest tumors, benign growths of stray adrenal cells that swell when the disease runs uncontrolled. The team restarted the steroid dexamethasone at a dose above the body's own level and watched him closely. Over six months the tumors shrank and his sperm count rose sharply, until he was able to father a child. The authors draw a standing lesson: yearly ultrasound checks for such tumors in men with this condition, so treatment can start before lasting damage is done.
pmc-10713258:
Maxime Borgeaud, Alex Friedlaender, and Alfredo Addeo wrote a review in two thousand twenty-three on moving immune drugs earlier in lung cancer care. The cancer is non-small cell lung cancer that can still be removed by surgery. For years the standard was surgery followed by chemotherapy, which added a modest survival gain.

Immune-checkpoint inhibitors free the immune system to attack the tumor. The review weighs giving them before surgery, after surgery, or both. Treatment before surgery can reach more patients, since some never recover enough for later therapy. It can also shrink the tumor and let doctors see the response while the tumor is still in place.
pmc-10713658:
Zhu leads a large team studying mitochondrial cleanup in the heart, in work from twenty twenty-three. Two proteins, PINK1 and Parkin, drive the removal of damaged mitochondria, a process called mitophagy. Faults in it contribute to heart, metabolic, and nerve diseases.

Actin, the cell skeleton, remodels during this cleanup, but the signal link was unknown. The team identifies a protein called GRAF1 as a direct target of PINK1. GRAF1 frees damaged mitochondria from actin anchors and helps Parkin tag them for capture. The finding joins two known pathways into one mechanism for heart cell quality control.
pmc-10713758:
Lina Botero Rute and co-authors tune the recipe book for growing the bacteria of a cow's rumen in a dish. The rumen's microbes digest what the cow cannot, but most refuse to grow in the laboratory, hiding their ecology and their uses. Their 2023 paper tests eight culture media, three dilutions, and two incubation times against one another, checking who grew by DNA sequencing.

No single medium recovered everything, and the cultures skewed the community badly: the two dominant groups of the real rumen swapped their shares almost exactly on the plates. Dilution moved the grown community strongly; incubation time did not. Two media, called CAN and KNT, came closest to the rumen's own composition and were selected for the work ahead. The authors hand microbiologists a tested shortlist, and a warning that the dish always edits the community it claims to copy.
pmc-10714458:
Colorectal cancer spreads in ways that are still not fully mapped at the gene level. Huimin Liu and co-authors combined data analysis with lab tests in 2023 to find genes tied to that spread. They merged three public gene datasets, looked for genes whose levels differed in spreading tumors, and singled out a hub gene called SERPINA3 for closer study.

In two cancer cell lines, raising SERPINA3 made cells grow and move more and resist cell death. Two small RNA molecules had the opposite effect, and their effect faded when SERPINA3 was raised again. The team reads this as a signaling chain that helps the cancer progress and could serve as a treatment target.
pmc-10714958: Yared Tadesse and co-authors report the case of a 14-year-old girl in Ethiopia with two linked illnesses at once. She had tuberculosis of the lymph nodes. She also had Takayasu arteritis, a rare swelling of the aorta and its main branches. The report appeared in 2023. The pairing is known but hard to treat, above all where tuberculosis is common. The two conditions can blur into each other, and their treatments can clash. The authors trace how the girl was diagnosed and treated, and draw lessons for similar cases.
pmc-10715958: Five doctors led by Hirohiko Aikawa report care for a young woman with chest pain from artery spasm who wished to bear a child. Spasm-based angina can spark a heart attack in pregnancy, at grave risk to mother and child. A provocation test drew out severe spasm, which sealed the call. Care was tuned with that risk in view, and she delivered safely. The case shows how a firm test call guides drug choice and watch plans for mothers-to-be with this rare pain source.
pmc-10716158:
Jorgelina Calandria and seven co-authors study a fat-based molecule that helps protect cells under stress, in a research paper from 2023. The molecule, called ELV-N34, forms in nerve cells from omega-3 fats. It is known to calm inflammation and help cells survive when the cell's balance is disturbed.

Working with human eye cells, the team found that the molecule binds a key enzyme in a cell defense system. Binding changes the enzyme's shape and lowers its activity in some parts of the cell. The authors say this direct link helps explain how the molecule guards against diseases tied to cell stress.
pmc-10716258:
Alan Race, Alisa Fuchs, and Ho-Ryun Chung map chromosome contact data with Voronoi diagrams instead of fixed grids, in this 2023 paper. Contact assays like Hi-C show which DNA regions touch. Standard plots bin reads into equal boxes, which blurs sparse regions.

Their tool, v3c-viz, tiles the plane so each cell hugs its local point density. Dense areas get fine detail, sparse areas stay readable. Even at modest sequencing depth, most strong contacts stand out. The authors argue the diagram doubles as a density estimator sharp enough to find contacts near the size of enhancers and promoters. The software is public on GitHub.
pmc-10716658:
Dutta, Bieling, and Verbiest listen, in 2023, to the tiny sounds made as water evaporates from lab-made vessels. In soils and plant stems, a moving water front can release sudden mechanical energy as audible pulses. Their origin and fading were debated, so the team built artificial vessels modeled on plant plumbing.

Three pulse types were separated by how long they rang. The team attributes them to bubble formation, snap-off events, and rapid pore invasion. Ringing frequencies fell as vessel width and length grew, across the tested ranges. The findings suggest sound could be used to inspect fluid systems or plant water health without touching them.
pmc-10717258:
Richardson and co-authors tested whether a heart-lung machine can be brought to the street for cardiac arrests that refuse to restart, in a 2023 feasibility study in metropolitan Australia. Survival in such refractory arrests is dismal with standard care. In the CHEER3 study, doctors with machine expertise rode a rapid response vehicle to witnessed arrests within a half-hour drive, for patients under sixty-five.

Over three years the team answered seven hundred nine possible arrest calls; three hundred fifty-eight were true arrests. Ten patients met the criteria, and all ten were connected to the machine on scene, about fifty minutes after the call. All reached hospital for catheter checks and intensive care. Four of the ten went home with brains intact. The authors call street-side ECPR feasible with an expert team and ask for larger prospective trials.
pmc-10717358:
Su Zhang and six co-authors study drug problems in kidney patients in a 2023 paper. People with chronic kidney disease take many drugs and their bodies handle them differently, so mistakes are common. A clinical pharmacist joined care on a kidney ward of a large Chinese hospital for a year, hunting for drug-related problems and acting on them.

Hundreds of problems were found in nearly half the patients before the pharmacist stepped in. Safety issues were the largest share, and drug choice was the most common cause. Antibiotics and heart drugs were most often involved. Most advice was accepted, most problems were fully resolved, and the share of patients with problems fell sharply afterward.
pmc-10719358:
Shi and a large team of colleagues read long gene spans for high-land fit marks in this twenty twenty-three study. Big span breaks shape more of the code than small point shifts. High folk in thin air bear such breaks tuned to their hard home.

Inside, long reads span three hundred folk from high and low kin groups. Break sorts tied to thin-air acts, fuel use, and lung work fell out. One high-folk break cuts a boost switch and mutes a breath gene. Glass and cell tests proved that break's mute act in full. The team casts break rewires as a core road to high fit.
pmc-10719758:
Adrianne R Wilson-Poe and co-authors present a 2023 survey study on how many United States adults used newer hemp-derived cannabinoids in the past year. After the 2018 Farm Bill, products built on CBD, CBG, CBN, and delta-8 THC spread widely, but use rates were unknown. The team surveyed adults on a national probability panel in late June 2023.

Panel members reported past-year use of cannabis and of each named cannabinoid, plus whether they had heard of such products. Weighted analyses then linked use to demographic traits and cannabis habits. The study aims to give regulators and clinicians a first solid map of this fast-growing market.
pmc-10720058:
Chengtian Lv, Yuwen Huang, Ruirong Yan, and Yuanmei Gao examine how a growth factor moves airway muscle cells, in a study published in two thousand twenty-three. In asthma, airway smooth muscle grows and migrates, thickening airway walls and worsening lung function. Vascular endothelial growth factor, VEGF, is already implicated in asthma's progression.

Earlier work emphasized VEGF's effect on muscle cell proliferation. This study isolates migration instead. Wound healing and Transwell assays measured how the cells move under VEGF's influence. The signaling ran through the RhoA and ROCK pathway, a known controller of cell movement. Blocking that pathway offers a candidate strategy against airway remodeling. The authors present their mechanistic evidence as groundwork for such treatments.
pmc-10721558:
Hao Gong, Yuhan Jiang, and Anping Su compare two surgery sizes for a thyroid cancer in a tricky spot, in a 2023 review. The cancer grows in the isthmus, the thin bridge joining the thyroid's two lobes. Tumors there spread to lymph nodes and return more often than lobe tumors. Surgeons disagree on whether to remove the whole gland or less, and no firm guideline settles it. The team searched four databases for matching studies.

Seven retrospective studies passed their filters. Quality was scored with a standard scale for non-randomized work. The pooled analysis compares cancer outcomes and complications between total removal and smaller operations. Such a summary helps surgeons weigh recurrence risk against the harms of bigger surgery, such as voice nerve damage and lifelong hormone pills.
pmc-10722558:
James Casey, Jennifer Meijer, Heidi IglayReger, and five colleagues check diet diaries against reality in this two thousand twenty-three pilot study. Self-reported diet is prone to error, biasing nutrition research. Inside a controlled feeding trial, where every menu item was known, participants completed twenty-four-hour recalls that could be verified exactly. Twenty-four adults followed a standard diet, then either a high-fat or high-carbohydrate diet, and their recalls were compared with the provided food.

Total calories were reported accurately. The errors were compositional: the high-fat group underreported fat, the high-carbohydrate group underreported carbohydrate, each presumably nudged by what sounds healthier. Protein was overreported on every diet, specifically beef and poultry. The authors argue that classifying which components get misreported, and in which direction, points to concrete strategies for correcting self-report bias in dietary assessment, rather than treating recall data as uniformly unreliable.
pmc-10725658:
Aditya Seth and co-authors report a hidden break inside a replaced knee: a snapped tibial post masked by a kneecap that kept slipping out of place. The knee design involved, posterior stabilized, is a proven workhorse with long success. Early failures strike only a small share of cases.

The post broke after the knee bent too far, a wear-linked failure that can lurk without any injury story. The wandering kneecap drew the eye and delayed the true call. Surgery swapped the worn plastic insert, pared the kneecap, freed the tight outer band, and tightened the thigh tendon in a doubled fold. The authors urge surgeons to suspect plastic wear when a replaced knee feels unstable for no clear reason. Full inspection at revision can catch what scans miss.
pmc-10729758:
Qingquan Bai and co-authors map immune cells in the liver, one cell at a time, across the road from hepatitis B infection to cancer. Their 2023 study reads gene activity in 118,455 immune cells from eighteen livers: six healthy, four infected, five cirrhotic, and three with liver cancer. Immune cells drive that progression, but their stage-by-stage roles were blurred in bulk data.

As disease advanced, scar-linked macrophages piled up, one of several shifts the single-cell view resolves. The atlas names which cell types swell or vanish at each step toward cancer. Such a map tells drug hunters which immune players to target at which stage, rather than treating the whole road as one disease.
pmc-10729858:
Suginobe leads a large team studying Down syndrome linked lung hypertension in stem cells, in work dated twenty twenty-three. Down syndrome is the most common chromosomal disorder and carries a higher rate of pulmonary arterial hypertension. Vessel lining cell faults drive the lung artery remodeling behind it.

The team made vessel lining cells from induced stem cells, in matched pairs with and without the extra chromosome. That isogenic design isolates the chromosome effect. A pathway joining three regulators, DYRK1A, PPARG, and EGR1, emerged as responsible for the disease traits in the cells. A named pathway gives drug research a concrete target.
pmc-10730658:
Xuwen Peng and four co-authors review intravital imaging, a window into living tumors during immunotherapy. Their review appeared in twenty twenty-three. Cancer immunotherapy works through immune cells moving and acting inside tissue, and flat snapshots miss that motion.

The technique watches cells in real time, in place, with fine detail and multiple colors at once. The authors walk through the full workflow: labeling tricks, optical windows cut into tissue, and ways to analyze the footage. Recent studies show immune cells hunting, pausing, and killing as treatment unfolds. Seeing those dynamics helps explain why therapies succeed or fail. The review argues this living view is now essential for improving immunotherapy design.
pmc-10731158:
Jia-Yu Liu and co-authors map past research on the link between stomach cancer and low mood. The study appeared in 2023. The link has drawn work for twenty years, but no map showed the hot themes or next fronts. The team searched a large data set for work from 2000 to 2022.

They found one hundred fifty-three papers in all, with counts rising over time. China gave the most papers, at over two in five. Work before 2020 asked how the cancer drives low mood. New work asks how low mood drives the cancer and by what path. The authors say that new theme may lead the field next.
pmc-10732558:
Toby Leslie and co-authors describe a 2023 report on drug resistance data in Asia, drawn from a program called CAPTURA.
