Germs that resist drugs are a growing threat, and poorer nations often lack staff and tools to track them well. Good records are needed before health leaders can act on sound facts.

From 2018 through 2022, the program gathered past lab records in seven nations in South and Southeast Asia. Teams also checked lab and clinic quality and reviewed drug use records. Talks with local partners and data sharing deals shaped the work. The report ends with steps to build stronger, shared tracking systems in each nation.
pmc-10733658:
Vennegoor and co-authors survey how fully Dutch schools carry out whole school health promotion programs. Schools are complex systems, so even good programs land unevenly. Their 2023 survey reached about twenty four hundred schools of all types, and staff from 535 schools replied, a response near twenty two percent.

Average implementation sat just above the middle of the scale. Pupil responsiveness and sticking to the plan scored lowest, while blending the program into school life and adapting it scored highest. Schools that called themselves health promoting schools scored higher on most measures. Primary schools outscored other school types on several counts. The authors say most schools still have much room to improve.
pmc-10733758:
Sabba Salebaigi examines the rights of older prisoners during COVID in a solo 2023 paper, whose full head title frames the work as locked up and left behind. The pandemic hit prisons hard, and older inmates faced the worst odds from age and chronic ills. Salebaigi asks whether their treatment broke the national ban on cruel and unusual punishment.

The paper walks through how the virus spread in locked settings, why guard steps were hard to run, and how the strain hit body, mind, and social life for older inmates. It weighs the facts against the Eighth Amendment line. Fixes urged for the next health crisis pair cleaner wards with letting more low risk elders out.
pmc-10735158:
Lizhi Cao and co-authors weigh heart death risk in liver cancer patients, in this 2023 study. Heart disease has grown into a top killer in this group. Records of US patients from 2000 to 2014 were set against the general public.

Heart death ran about eleven times the public rate. The gap yawned widest in patients under 55, at over fifty times, and narrowed with age. Tumor traits, stage, and surgery status each shaped the risk on their own. The authors urge heart screening and care woven into cancer treatment. Long survival, they note, now demands guarding the heart as well.
pmc-10735458:
Joseph Gaugler, Lisa McGuire, and Fayron Epps frame in 2023 a symposium on how social conditions shape dementia and how public health should respond. Social determinants, the settings where people are born, live, work, and age, sway health and life quality broadly. Dementia both grows from those settings and strains them.

Presenters come from national public health centers for dementia infrastructure and brain health programs. Talks cover prevention, early detection, and family caregiving through a social lens. One talk tackles the tangled links among equity, social conditions, and dementia head-on. The session aims to spur local, tribal, state, and federal action. Organizers hope to reframe dementia as a public health duty, not just a clinic concern.
pmc-10735658:
Trends in new cases of multiple chronic conditions among older Americans from two thousand to twenty twenty form the subject here. The study was published in twenty twenty-three. Rising multimorbidity strains patients and the care system alike.

Adults aged fifty and over from a long-running national survey were split into nine overlapping cohorts. Four kinds of multimorbidity were defined from seven physical diseases and two mental conditions: general, physical only, including mental disorders, and heart-metabolic. Adjusted rates of new general multimorbidity rose from seventy-six to about one hundred and twelve per thousand person-years across the period. Mental-inclusive multimorbidity rose too. The authors trace how much of the climb reflects who the patients are.
pmc-10735758:
Edna Darlene Rodrigues and six co-authors measured how much radiotherapy older Portuguese cancer patients actually receive in a 2023 paper. Cancer is Portugal's second killer, and about half of patients should get radiation at some point. The authors mined the 2018 national registry for 14,448 patients aged seventy and over.

They compared real use against estimated optimal use for each cancer site. Actual care reached only 56 percent of optimal for ages 70 to 74, falling to 36 percent for those 85 and older. The authors weigh older patients' complex health and the thin trial evidence behind decisions. They call for trials that include older adults, less ageism, and better access to modern short-course treatment.
pmc-10735858:
Yu-Chih Chen and Sicong Sun study how money skills and habits link to health in later life. They also ask how the links differ for men and women. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-three. They surveyed more than eleven hundred adults aged forty-five and up online. The survey covered money knowledge, access to financial tools, and day-to-day money behavior.

Access and behavior mattered more for health than money knowledge alone. For men, money knowledge tied more to self-rated health and life satisfaction. For women, day-to-day money behavior mattered more. Access to financial tools also eased worry about retirement for women, but not for men. The authors argue that programs to build money skills should take these gender paths into account. One-size programs may miss what each group needs.
pmc-10735958:
Atiqur Rahman and co-authors trace the last five years of care for Swedes who die with dementia, using the country's linked registers. All decedents aged seventy and up in late 2019, over six thousand people, were sorted by whether they used no eldercare, home care, or residential care before death. The study asks who gets what, and which social facts tilt the answer.

Nearly a quarter of people with dementia used no eldercare at all, most often the newly diagnosed and those living with a partner. Three quarters spent their final years in residential care. Age, sex, and living arrangement all shaped the pattern strongly. The authors flag the no-care group for policy attention: diagnosed need without a service attached.
pmc-10736058:
Robert Penfold and co-authors report early results from a trial of online training for dementia caregivers, in a 2023 paper. The STAR-Caregivers program teaches families skills that ease the behavioral symptoms of dementia. The trial tests a six-session, self-paced online version, backed by secure email and short coaching calls, to reach more families.

Caregivers and the person with dementia were paired and randomly assigned to the program or usual care. Baseline surveys measured dementia severity and daily function, plus caregiver anxiety, stress, depression, and sense of mastery. The study enrolled 67 pairs, and sign-ups rose sharply once word spread through care networks. Reporting who joins and where they start helps judge who the online format can serve.
pmc-10736258:
Katy Cao, Dawn Carr, and Rebekah Carpenter ask whether complex jobs protect the aging mind equally across racial groups, in a 2023 conference abstract. Stimulating work is known to guard against later cognitive decline. Black and Hispanic workers, though, get less access to such jobs than white workers.

The team linked national occupation data to a retirement study's life histories for 1,080 people. They summed each person's exposure to cognitively complex work between ages twenty-five and fifty-five, then compared thinking scores at seventy, adjusting for scores at fifty-five and background factors. Moderate complexity added about three quarters of a point, and high complexity about one and a quarter points. Among moderately complex job holders, Black workers gained less than white counterparts. The authors point to job access as a lever against unequal cognitive aging.
pmc-10736658:
Joseph Gaugler and co-authors describe a 2023 special interest group that builds team links in Alzheimer's disease research at the University of Minnesota. Federal funds for dementia science have surged since a national act, which opens room for new team work. Yet finding shared interests across fields is hard when people sit in unlike units.

The group, housed in a centre for healthy ageing, joins faculty, postdoctoral fellows, and graduate students across the university and beyond. Its tools span a crosswalk matrix that maps members' interests, skills, and data sets against each other. A member-led journal club and a dashboard that tracks joint work add to the push. Though young, the group aims for joint papers first and full team science projects in time.
pmc-10736758:
Erin Ballard and her five co-authors, publishing in 2023, study the long shadow of Hurricane Maria on older Puerto Ricans. The data come from a long-running health study of the island's elders. The 617 participants were all 78 or older. They were interviewed in 2021 and 2022, years after the storm. The team asked about fright during the hurricane and about later worries, over home damage, family and friends, and work and health.

About 41 percent said they had been somewhat or very frightened right after the storm. Over half faced home repairs, neighborhood damage, or trouble paying bills. Fright at the time was tied to higher stress years later. So were all three kinds of later worry. Women reported higher stress in every model. The authors argue a disaster's mental toll does not fade when the skies clear, and support should plan for years, not months.
pmc-10736858:
Shannon Freeman and co-authors wrote a survey study from 2023 on what geriatric nurses know and think about artificial intelligence in their decisions. Nurses remain accountable for choices they make for older patients, even when a tool suggests the path. With chatbots in the news, the team asked community nurses who serve older adults how AI already touches their work. The survey ran online over four months.

Knowledge of machine learning in elder care was thinner still. What they knew came mostly from media, social feeds, and family, not from formal training. pmc-10736958:
Gizem Hueluer and co-authors introduce a symposium on how surroundings shape adult development and aging, in this 2023 paper. Lives unfold inside layered contexts, from culture and history down to home, family, and partners. The session gathers studies that test those layers against health, thinking, and feelings.

One study compares how good mood and loneliness predict lifespan in the United States and Japan. Another uses thirty-five years of Seattle data to link neighborhood views with thinking decline. Further talks cover social contact paths in Japan and daily emotion tuning between younger and older couples. The set argues context is not background but an active force.
pmc-10737058:
Rashmi Devkota, Colleen Maxwell, and their co-authors asked whether how assisted living homes handled the COVID-19 pandemic affected how lonely their residents felt. Their 2023 study notes that loneliness was already common in such homes and grew worse in the pandemic. Loneliness is tied to illness, memory decline, and early death in older adults.

They tested whether traits of the residents, their social ties, and each home's readiness and response tracked with loneliness. pmc-10737158:
Meki Singleton and Susan Enguidanos study advance care planning among older lesbian and gay adults. Their paper, from twenty twenty-three, asks which traits link to planning for future medical care. Such planning can include a living will. It can also name a person to make health choices if one cannot.

The study uses an online survey of one hundred thirty-nine adults. White, older, and working adults felt more at ease with medical choices. Higher income and a health problem linked to having a living will. The authors say income and work shape planning in this group, not just age or schooling.
pmc-10737258:
Philippe Landreville and three co-authors present this 2023 conference abstract on treating anxious older adults with a self-help manual and a friendly voice, no therapist required. pmc-10737358:
Yuezhong Liu, Chek Hooi Wong, Ringo Ho, and Yin-Leng Theng study how city surroundings shape walking in older adults in Singapore in a 2023 paper. They track a small group of older adults over many days as they move through their neighborhoods, logging vast numbers of steps. Both groups walked slower outdoors where building density was high. Those with impairment walked slower overall, with the largest gap in business areas, and leaned more on vehicles. The authors suggest that surroundings that demand less attention could help impaired walkers stay safe and active.
pmc-10737558:
Erin Robinson, Geunhye Park, and Getrude Nyang'au surveyed older adults about HIV talks with their doctors, in a 2023 study. Older adults make up half of people living with HIV in the United States. Yet many say doctors spoke with them about HIV mostly when they were young, not in later life.

Most of the group also said they would raise condom use with a new partner. The authors urge doctors to keep these talks going.
pmc-10737758:
Gwen Windham and seven co-authors published this study in 2023. It tracks how physical ability changes with age in Black and White older adults across four United States communities. Ability was scored with a standard battery of standing, walking, and chair-rise tests.

The study followed 5,836 adults over sixty-five, with tests repeated over about six years. On average, scores fell more than three times faster in Black participants than in White participants. But place mattered just as much. White adults in Maryland declined far faster than White adults in North Carolina, and gaps between races shrank when the same town was compared. pmc-10737958:
Rajean Moone names a paradox facing LGBTQ older adults in a 2023 paper. Sexual and gender minority elders carry higher rates of chronic illness, mental illness, and disability than peers. They also more often age alone, without family caregivers to lean on.

Yet many hesitate to use formal long-term care services. Fear of bias and poor treatment drives that avoidance, and one study found some trans elders preferred death to a nursing home. Moone calls this a trap: greater need, thinner informal support, and fear of the formal help that remains. Education, awareness, policy change, and further research are offered as ways to ease it.
pmc-10738058:
Karl Pillemer and Matthew Luebke argue in 2023 for wider engagement of older people in climate action. Green volunteering can boost health in older adults and help communities face climate harm. Yet few climate groups actively recruit older people.

Most debate treats older people only as victims of climate effects. The authors review barriers, including lower concern and lack of access to activist roles. A global survey found models that do mobilize older people, notably in lower-resource countries. They offer design tips so groups can include older adults in prevention and response work.
pmc-10738158:
Alisha Thompson and three co-authors published a 2023 account of a summer policy internship with the Gerontological Society of America. Thompson writes in the first person about work tied to a federal health preparedness law. Her past research dealt with how older people get ready for public health emergencies. The internship placed that interest inside the national lawmaking process.

Inside the account, she follows the 2023 renewal of the preparedness law, tracks funds in the federal budget, and sits in on hearings in Congress. She also gave feedback on how the bill touched the interests of her host group and on a draft shared by both parties. Thompson says the work left her better placed to speak up for older people in aging policy.
pmc-10738258:
Pui Cheung, David Curtis, and Ming Wen test how poor neighborhoods wear down physical function, and whether the path differs by gender. Their 2023 study uses a national sample of over two thousand adults aged 55 to 93. Poverty links to functional limits are known; neighborhood paths are not.

County poverty ties to daily living difficulty for both women and men. Two paths carry the effect for women only: feeling unsafe or disordered nearby, and stress eating. For men, neither path mediates the link. The indirect effect for women is significantly larger than for men. Multilevel models test the three candidate paths at once. The authors argue gender-specific mechanisms explain part of the known gender gap in later-life physical function.
pmc-10738358:
Being bullied or threatened at work is linked to later mental illness, but families share both genes and workplaces, tangling cause and effect. Linda Magnusson Hanson and co-authors used twins to cut the tangle. They followed 8,795 Swedish twins for at least twelve years, tracking certified sick leave for depression and anxiety.

In ordinary analysis, exposure doubled the odds of later absence for violence or threats, and raised them by half for harassment. Comparing twins within a pair, where one was exposed and the other not, shrank those numbers and blurred their certainty. Family factors explain part of the link, the authors conclude. Prevention still matters, but honest science must count the confounding.
pmc-10738558:
Shaelyn Ward and six co-authors checked the author rules of leading journals on aging, in a study from twenty twenty-three. Journals can ask authors to follow reporting guides and to register trials before they start. Such rules cut bias and make research easier to trust and check.

The team read the rules of one hundred top journals in the field. Fewer than half pointed authors to the main guide for trial reports. Many journals said nothing about some common guides at all. Nearly half said nothing about trial registration. The authors urge editors to press for clear rules, so reports in the field become more open and complete.
pmc-10738758:
Xiangxiang Jiang and three co-authors wrote a 2023 study estimating the causal effect of anti-dementia drugs on patients' medical costs. Dementia care is expensive, and whether the drugs themselves raise or lower total burden was confounded in past work: sicker patients both get drugs and cost more. The team used double machine learning to strip out that bias.

Data came from a national Medicare beneficiary survey linked to Medicare records, 2015 to 2017. Random forest and penalized regression models handled the confounding. Drug users numbered over 218,000 in the weighted sample, with average total costs near 16,700 dollars. Non-users, the vast majority, averaged about 27,600 dollars. Adjusted models then estimated the drugs' causal contribution to that gap. The approach showcases modern causal inference for health economics.
pmc-10738958:
Mild memory loss can cut people off from pastimes they once shared, and that isolation can speed the very decline they fear. Kara Mumma and co-authors study games as one way back in, in a 2023 report. They spoke with seven pairs, each made of a person with mild memory loss and their care partner, about what playing games together feels like.

Pairs spoke of games as a welcome break from routine, and for some as a calm part of the routine itself. The ease and familiarity of play drew praise. Gains named were social and emotional: shared laughs, closeness, and a lift in mood. The team ties these reports to design choices for games built for such pairs, where simple rules and known formats help both players join in.
pmc-10739158:
Steffen Desch and co-authors argue, in a 2023 article, that a once-hopeful heart support machine is losing its place in heart attack care. When a heart attack triggers shock, four to five of every ten patients die in hospital. Only reopening the blocked artery has proven lifesaving in trials.

The machine, which pumps and oxygenates blood outside the body, spread fast on hope rather than proof. It supports the circulation during the first critical days after the attack. The authors survey where the evidence now stands and find the case collapsing. Their title's verdict is blunt: the era of routine use is ending. The piece warns against adopting costly rescue devices ahead of solid trials.
pmc-10739258:
Melanie Horning wrote a 2023 study of how families talk about the end of life when a loved one is dying of a long illness. An uncertain disease course often delays these talks, which can leave wishes unstated and hospice care late. Horning asked whether a family's general talk style shapes whether the talks happen at all.

She surveyed fifty-six family members of people who died in hospice care, using a standard family communication tool. The largest group of families was open in talk with low pressure to conform, and these families held more end-of-life talks than guarded families. The findings suggest the tool could help guide talks and choices near death.
pmc-10740558:
Kailyn McFarlane and Jason Sanchez test electrode setups for recording early auditory evoked potentials. They are a popular proxy for cochlear synaptopathy, the loss of synapses between inner ear cells and nerve fibers. That loss may explain hearing trouble in noise. Yet human evidence stays mixed, since methods vary widely between labs.

The study records electrocochleography traces in 35 young adults with vertical and horizontal electrode arrays. Standard scores plus peak amplitudes and timings for the first waves are set side by side across arrays. Vertical setups give larger peaks in all cases for the key nerve wave. The authors advise that montage as the standard for peripheral nerve recordings in future synaptopathy work.
pmc-10740858:
Seven authors led by Ermias Balcha read the gene mix of microbes in one of the harshest places on Earth. Microbes there may carry genes that shrug off both drugs and heavy metals, a pairing of keen health note. Samples came from lake water and salt crust at two sites in the zone.

Metal levels, above all mercury, tracked with how many metal genes showed up. Zinc and cadmium tracked with drug genes too, which hints the two sets are picked as one. Web maps link the sets in a tight shared net.
pmc-10741658:
Augustinas Bausys and co-authors study a treatment path for a stomach cancer subgroup in this 2023 paper. Some stomach cancers show cancer cells in belly wash fluid but no other incurable signs. Chemotherapy before surgery, then stomach removal, is a hopeful path, but Western data were scarce.

The cohort covered 43 patients treated at four centers in Lithuania, Estonia, and Ukraine from 2016 to 2020. All had surgery after chemotherapy. About 54 percent cleared the cancer cells from the fluid, and about 23 percent had a major response in the tumor. Median survival was 20 months. Clearing the fluid cells strongly cut the risk of spread in the belly, the authors report.
pmc-10742458:
Charlotte Stubner and co-authors review studies on early-life exposure to PFAS chemicals and children's language development, in work published in 2023. The team searched three databases and found fifteen studies. Most covered general populations with background exposure, and two covered highly exposed groups. Some studies hinted at harm, but the pattern was inconsistent across sex, age at testing, and exposure level. No systematic effect on language and communication was found. The authors note many studies used broad tests with weak validity for language skills. They call for studies over a wider exposure range with sharper language instruments.
pmc-10742558:
Andrey Petrov and colleagues offer a two thousand twenty-three study of gel-like blocking materials for treating benign overgrown blood vessel lesions in the head and neck. These gels flow deep into abnormal vessels yet stay controllable, unlike glue or coils. Two lesion types with intense shunting flow were treated.

Records covered patients treated over eight years at one clinic. Outcomes with the gel were compared against coils, glue, and particles used in other cases. Safety, effectiveness, and technical handling were judged. Such malformations and hormone-active tumours share demanding flow, making agent choice decisive for success.
pmc-10742758:
Longxia Wen and co-authors tested how best to store the fresh roots of a prized herb after harvest, in 2023. The herb, a kind of Codonopsis, is grown at scale for food and drug use. Roots sat at just below freeze, at deep cold, and at two cool levels. Twenty marks of worth were tracked, from looks and taste to active parts and cell stress. The just-below-freeze roots at day forty read near fresh. That level kept the guard enzymes strong and the active parts up. It held back rust-like waste and the enzymes that brown and soften the root. Deep cold and cool rooms let worth slip more.
pmc-10742858:

pmc-10743358:
Pavlos Zitis and co-authors asked whether COVID bent the rules of currency markets in a 2023 study. A weak form efficient market should not let past prices foretell future ones. The shifts held in both rising and falling markets. The authors say the finds can guide investors, fund managers, and policy makers who watch market health.
pmc-10743658:
Wiktoria Kowalska and co-authors compared two stroke guards for heart patients with low platelet counts in a 2023 study. The patients have a fluttering heart rhythm that raises stroke risk. The joint rate of stroke, brain bleed, major bleed, and heart death was lower in the plug group, though the gap fell short of firm proof. Total deaths split more clear, with none in the plug group and a tenth of the drug group lost. The authors back the plug for such patients.
pmc-10743758:
Pseudomonas aeruginosa is a bacterium that resists many antibiotics, partly by pumping them out of the cell. Earlier hints came from a mutant with a disruptive insertion, so the team made a clean deletion of the gene to rule out side effects on neighbors.

pmc-10744058:

pmc-10744158:

pmc-10744258:

They close with their own work making a certified organic oil in southern Italy from three local olive types.
pmc-10744358:

Tasks built for the study also showed gains in sound recognition and sentence understanding. The authors call the uptake and gains very encouraging for such a short program.
pmc-10745358:

Tests showed fine resolution in all three axes, best in pitch and yaw. Short-term readings stayed steady as well. The authors pitch the probe for high-end craft and precision instruments on the ground.
pmc-10745758:

pmc-10745858:

Each person kept close food records and took tests of energy use, blood health, and mouth and throat skill during meals. pmc-10745958:

pmc-10746058:

The team grew two skin species alone and together, both free floating and in biofilms. Biofilms are sticky groups that resist drugs. The hormone plus azithromycin had mixed effects that hinged on surface type, dose, and species. On water hating surfaces it often opposed the drug. On glass it often helped. Cells also clumped more. pmc-10746358:

Immune therapy has flopped here in part because the tumors are cold: few immune cells get in, and many suppressor cells guard the tumor.

pmc-10747058:

The team charted each gene's place, traits, likely cell home, partners, and switches, then compared family trees across plants. In three thousand rice lines, the genes showed sharp splits between subspecies and heavy selection marks from modern breeding. Activity rose under several stresses. The authors say natural variants at most of these spots could lift yield and stress tolerance. They urge breeders to test the favorable versions in the field.
pmc-10747258:

pmc-10747358:

Root-made enzymes showed up in place, and their activity climbed as the soil warmed. Soil right at the root ran richer and livelier than soil a short step away, with more carbon stored under heat. One acid-loving germ group ruled the root soil, and a single genus led the pack. Root leaks fed the microbes, which broke down soil carbon and fed the plant in turn. The authors read the warming loop as a stronger two-way talk between root and soil.
pmc-10747958:
Vasiliki Rapti and co-authors review a dangerous hospital yeast in this 2023 paper. Candida auris, first described in 2009, has caused large outbreaks worldwide. Unusually for a yeast, it invades the body readily, spreads between patients, and lingers for months on people and surfaces.

pmc-10748058:

pmc-10748258:

pmc-10748758:

pmc-10749458:

Scores varied with sex, job, region, hospital level, and department. Training, hands-on bite experience, having antivenom on site, and self-rated skill all lifted scores. The authors call the overall level weak and urge targeted training, especially where snakes are common and antivenom is scarce.
pmc-10749958:

pmc-10753558:

pmc-10754558:

Better-designed trials are needed before strong recommendations.
pmc-10755458:
Zhanguo Gao and co-authors examine in 2023 gene activity in mice whose vessel lining cells lack telomerase, the enzyme that guards chromosome ends, to learn how lining aging drives wider decline. The lining meets every blood borne toxin first, and its senescence, a locked stop in cell division with a fiery secreted mix, is thought to seed age related disease. Yet how that aging spreads harm to vessel walls and organs was unsettled.

In fat and muscle, where tissue renews often, lining cells face heavy copying pressure and may wear their chromosome ends early. The study reads gene shifts in this model to trace how lining aging talks to support cells and tissue. Results aim to ground therapies aimed at vessel aging.
pmc-10755558:
Matthäus Fellinger and Thomas Waldhör lead a team counting involuntary psychiatric admissions across Austria before and during COVID-19 lockdowns. Their country report was published in two thousand twenty-three. Forced admission is psychiatry's last resort, legally and ethically fraught. Whether lockdowns raised or lowered its use was unknown.

Records covered three years and tens of thousands of admissions nationwide. During lockdown weeks, involuntary admissions fell significantly compared with prior years. Those admitted, though, stayed longer on average. Mechanical restraint accompanied about a third of admissions throughout. The lockdown association held after adjustment, while sex and age showed none. The authors read the dip as access and behavior shifting under restrictions, not need vanishing. Longer stays hint at delayed presentation. The report gives policymakers a rare whole-country baseline.
pmc-10756658:
A poison control center in Pavia reviews 15 years of exposures to hydrogen cyanamide, a farm chemical once sold in Italy as Dormex, in a 2023 case series. The growth regulator was pulled from the market in 2008 and is no longer authorized in Europe, yet cases kept arriving. The team pulled every referral from 2007 to 2021 and charted routes, symptoms, severity, and whether alcohol was involved.

Thirty cases were found, nearly four in five after the market withdrawal, and almost all in Sicily. Every exposure was accidental and work related, and about two in five patients had also drunk alcohol, which worsens the reaction. Flushing, redness, and breathlessness were the most common signs.
pmc-10756758:
Chihiro Miura and eleven colleagues wrote a study in twenty twenty-three on how orchid seeds switch on their pact with fungi. Orchid seeds hold almost no food stores, so they must take nutrients from mycorrhizal fungi to sprout. To do so, they borrow the signaling system of a mutual pact that other plants make with such fungi.

The plant hormone gibberellin helps most seeds sprout, yet it blocks fungi from settling in, and orchid seeds barely respond to it. The team found that orchids switch the hormone off as they sprout. That switch turns the pact signaling on by itself, so the fungal partner can move in at once. The work shows how a plant that lives off fungi lines up its sprouting with the arrival of its provider.
pmc-10757558:
Amira Alghazaly and Lamees Al Habib report a 2023 case of a pain flare after root canal work, with a broad review. Flares bring pain or swelling during or soon after the procedure and hit up to 16% of cases, at times far more. They force unplanned visits and can shake patient trust.

Causes span tool strain, chemical irritation, and germs left in the tooth. Repeat treatments on teeth with tip infection, done in one visit, flare most often. The case here flared between visits on a tooth with a shadow at the root tip on X-ray. Steps used to calm the flare are laid out in full. The authors note that no proven standard yet exists to stop flares.
pmc-10758258:
Mohammed Bondagji and co-authors present a 2023 case report on Addison disease. In this disorder the adrenal glands fail, leaving the body short of key hormones. A man of forty who worked indoors came to a skin clinic with slow darkening of the skin over three years.

The dark patches spread over his face, hands, and palms, and he also felt tired and lost weight. Morning blood tests showed very low cortisol with a sky-high signal from the pituitary gland, which fit gland failure. Hormone pills were started at set doses split across the day. Within two weeks his skin and energy improved a great deal. Swelling then led the team to trim one drug dose.
pmc-10758658:
Christie Swaminathan and co-authors compare two wound washes for preventing infection after abdominal surgery in a 2023 meta-analysis. Surgical site infections are a known complication of laparotomy, raising deaths, illness, and costs. Irrigating the wound before closing is a simple preventive step.

The analysis pooled randomized controlled trials of povidone-iodine versus normal saline irrigation in gastrointestinal operations. Pooling trials gives a sharper answer than any single study on whether the antiseptic wash beats plain saline. A cheap change in the operating room routine could prevent many infections if the benefit is real.
pmc-10761758:
Minna Peippo and co-authors interrogate three actin-shaping proteins for roles in HER2-positive breast cancer. Formins build the cell's skeleton, and HER2 signaling needs that skeleton to drive invasion, yet the connection was unmapped. Database mining first flagged the formins FHOD1, INF2, and DAAM1: higher message levels of each tracked with worse outcomes.

Tissue staining added that strong FHOD1 protein marks higher-grade tumors and hormone-receptor-negative ones. In two HER2-positive cell lines, knocking the formins down, singly or together, slowed wound closure and migration while barely touching growth. Silencing HER2 itself disturbed the same signaling pathways and selected formins. The authors present formins as candidate links between HER2 signaling and the cell movement behind metastasis.
pmc-10768558:
Prerna Kulshrestha and co-authors probe an immune pathway's role in eye inflammation, in this 2023 paper. The disease, non-infectious uveitis, swells the eye's middle layer and is a leading cause of blindness in young people. What triggers its flares remains unclear.

The team studied the alternative complement pathway, a branch of immune defense. They measured gene activity in blood cells and protein levels in eye fluid from patients with front or back eye inflammation. Some key genes were turned down in front-eye disease and up in back-eye disease. The split pattern suggests the pathway behaves differently by disease site, a clue for future treatments.
pmc-10772358:
Ahmed Elheet and colleagues examined how heart disease and kidney disease travel together in patients at a Saudi Arabian center. The two conditions share risk factors and worsen each other, yet local data were scarce. Writing in twenty twenty-three, the team reviewed patient files from most of that year. Most patients were men, most were in their sixties and seventies, and smoking, diabetes, and high blood pressure were common. The analysis linked artery disease severity, kidney function, and the heart pumping fraction.

As coronary artery disease grew more severe, kidney function fell. A lower pumping fraction also tracked with worse kidney numbers. Age, smoking, and artery disease tracked with kidney dysfunction, while smoking, prior stroke, limb artery disease, body weight, and pumping fraction tracked with artery severity. The authors call for work on treatments that blunt the combined harm.
pmc-10772458:
Whitney Do and co-authors read viral exposure histories from blood to flag liver cancer risk in a 2023 study. A phage display method screens antibodies against over a thousand virus strains at once. Liver cancers may carry viral fingerprints beyond hepatitis. Thai and other cohorts supply the samples.

Machine learning built viral scores for the two main liver cancer types. Both scores tracked liver function markers in at-risk groups, whatever the hepatitis status. The liver cell cancer score also predicted eight-year death risk, while hepatitis status alone did not. Non-hepatitis viruses may feed liver cancer risk, the team suggest, and blood antibody patterns could help spot patients headed for trouble.
pmc-10776058:
Khongorzul Erdenebaatar, Joon Moh Park, and Jachoon Koo shared a genome note in twenty twenty-three. They report the full chloroplast genome of Spergularia marina. It is a plant that lives on Korean coasts and bears salt well. No chloroplast genome from its genus had come out before. The team used next-generation sequencing and put the whole molecule together, base by base.

The genome runs about one hundred fifty-two thousand letters. It has the standard four-part form of plant chloroplasts. It holds one hundred thirty-one genes in all. Eighty-six of them code for proteins. The rest are the RNA parts the plant needs for photosynthesis. The team compared seventeen kin in the pink family. This species sat closest to Spergula arvensis. The sequence gives staff a reference to name and sort this coastal genus.
pmc-10784758:
Ankita Pathak and co-authors report a dental rescue case in 2023. A front tooth implant had been placed at a bad angle, which spoils the look and bite of the crown. Such rescue cases are hard because makers rarely sell angle fixing parts. The patient was sent to a specialist prosthetics unit for repair.

The team weighed cemented options to rebuild the tooth on the tilted implant. They describe using a castable long connector and a custom made connector shaped for the case. A tailored connector can save an implant that would otherwise be lost. The report gives dentists a path when implants land off line.
pmc-10800358:
Xiufang Kong and eight co-authors survey COVID-19 infection and its impact on patients with Takayasu arteritis in China, in work published in 2023. A web survey in January 2023 covers a large patient cohort and their co-residents. Symptoms, long term after effects, disease activity, treatment, and immune measures are compared between groups.

Infection rates are lower in patients than in co-residents. Patients show more gut symptoms, sleep problems, and multi organ symptoms after infection. Hospitalization is rare and no case turns life threatening, yet long term after effects are more common in patients, above all those with active disease. Active disease after the pandemic is lower in infected than uninfected patients. Multi system symptoms flag higher relapse risk.
pmc-10806158:
Jun Yin and co-authors review how reversible gene-control changes shape breast cancer immunity, in work published in 2023. Breast cancer is the most common non-skin cancer in American women. Tumors grow as genetic and epigenetic changes free cells from normal growth controls.

Unlike mutations, epigenetic changes such as DNA methylation and histone marks can be reversed. That makes them attractive drug targets for waking up immune attack on tumors. The review covers the mechanisms and the clinical implications for immunotherapy response, where many patients still do not benefit from current drugs.
pmc-10808558:
Mathieu Nacher and co-authors sketch the contrasting life paths that shape health in French Guiana, in a review whose text is dated 2023. People there die two to three years younger than in mainland France, and much of that gap is preventable with basic care. Yet averages hide a split: half the population lives in poverty, while better-off residents may match mainland lifespans.

The team gather what is known about exposures — the full set of surroundings, habits, and hardships people meet across life, called the exposome. They outline the typical exposure profiles of the territory's main groups and tie them to known health outcomes. Seeing the split clearly can aim public health money at the group whose deaths are most preventable.
pmc-10827858:
Edward Gibson-Smith and co-authors survey food knowledge in contest climbers in a 2023 paper, per its head. Climbing draws more study of diet, yet senior contest climbers had not been surveyed. Weight loss habits and supplement use were also unknown.

Fifty climbers filled a long survey on food facts, diet habits, and pills. Mean food scores sat at mid level, with wide spread by person. Sex and age did not sway scores, but home land level did for core food facts. Climbers scored well on protein, carbs, alcohol, and pills. Thin spots in the scores point to where diet coaching could help most.
pmc-10831358:
Sukanya Dhar and a large team tie a hold-back immune cell signature to lymphoma care that falls short. Their study from twenty twenty-four tests patients on standard chemotherapy. The R-CHOP drug mix fully cures just about half of patients. Comeback of the cancer and drug resistance drive the shortfalls.

Hold-back cells of the monocyte line were counted in patients. Their signature flagged drug resistance to come on many fronts. It also flagged the cancer coming back after remission. The space around the tumour shelters such hold-back cells. To block them might bring back how well chemotherapy works. A blood signature could flag high-risk patients at the start. Such patients could then get stronger or added care.
pmc-10834758:
Xingmin Zhang and co-authors review a signaling path in worn spinal discs in this paper. Their text is dated 2023, one year earlier than the catalog year shown for the entry. Disc wear is a main cause of low back pain and brings heavy costs to patients and health systems.

The path they review touches nearly every step of disc decay. It feeds swelling, breaks down the disc's support matrix, and drives cell death, aging, and stress harm. Current care mostly eases symptoms rather than halting the decay itself. The authors argue the path is a strong drug target and map what is known about its roles. They close by pointing to gaps that targeted treatment work must fill.
pmc-10836258:
Wanxin Zhang and co-authors survey sleep across China in this 2023 Europe PMC paper. The web-based survey, run in 2022, covered most provinces and gathered nearly nine thousand valid responses. It asked about sleep length, timing, quality and problems, and defined a combined measure of good sleep.

Most people slept under seven hours a night, and only about twelve percent met the full good sleep standard. Nearly half reported insomnia symptoms in the past three months, and a fifth reported snoring. Sleep timing varied by age, sex, job and region: the young, men, students and city dwellers slept later, while northerners woke earlier. Midday napping linked to better sleep in mid-aged adults.
pmc-10839058:
A case report from 2023 describes a fifty-one year old man with liver damage from alcohol who also had failing kidneys and heavy protein loss in his urine. Yusuke Yoshimura and co-authors found that a kidney biopsy showed IgA nephropathy, a disease where an immune protein builds up in the kidney. Standard steroid drugs were risky for this patient.

The team treated him with dapagliflozin, a drug first made for blood sugar, plus strict steps to stop drinking. Within one week his urine protein fell sharply, and no low blood sugar events occurred. The authors say the drug may offer a safer path when steroids are a poor fit. They also stress that one case cannot prove the treatment works for others.
pmc-10844658:
Yunhan Zhao and five colleagues connect chronic gut inflammation to a protective peptide's suppression in children, in a study published in two thousand twenty-four. Children with inflammatory bowel disease often grow poorly and lose bone health. Humanin, a cytoprotective factor found in bone, was their suspect.

Blood from forty patients and forty healthy children was compared. Humanin levels were measured by immunoassay. Growth plate tissue from children's surgeries was cultured with patient serum or with TNF, a key inflammatory signal. Staining tracked humanin and growth-related markers in the tissue. Cell line experiments tested TNF dose effects. The authors report a novel link: inflammation regulates humanin downward. That suppression may help explain stunted growth in pediatric bowel disease.
pmc-10849758:
Schaer and seven colleagues study how bleeding inside tumors helps cancer grow in twenty twenty-four. Small bleeds are common in cancers but are often ignored as a factor. Macrophages clean up red blood cells, so they sit at the centre of this process. The team traced how a red cell product, heme, reshapes these immune cells.

Maps of gene activity showed a cell type clustered near bloody, dead tumor regions. Those cells had a cancer promoting profile driven by a factor called NRF2. Heme switched on NRF2 in macrophages and pushed them toward that profile. The altered cells helped cancer cells invade and spread in lab models. They also resisted reprogramming by immune therapies. Mice with NRF2 locked on in immune cells resisted a key immunotherapy drug.
pmc-10859758:
Benjamin Lantz and co-authors study low oxygen and immune cells in mice in a 2023 paper, per its head. A balance sits between attack ready T cells and calm regulatory T cells. When that balance tips, lung blood pressure can rise.

Mice kept in low oxygen grew more attack cells in the lungs, with no rise in calm cells. Gene reads showed some calm cells had switched sides and joined the attack type. That switch may explain why calm cells fail to stop the lung harm on their own. The work points at cell switching as a step in this form of lung disease.
pmc-10937458:
Fang-Ying Hsu and three co-authors present a study published in 2023, though the catalog lists 2024, building a model that predicts tumor control for a special radiation care. The therapy uses boron loaded cells hit by neutrons, and it is still in trials in Taiwan with no standard dose rule. A model could link dose spread to tumor response.

The team chose a universal survival curve as their base model. They fed it dose maps and tumor responses from the first trial protocol for returning head and neck cancer, run by a Taipei hospital and a university. The model's predictions tracked the real dose and response link well, they report.
pmc-10976658:
Ieva Vanaga and co-authors studied gene variants of the immune system in patients hospitalized with acute COVID-19 in a 2023 paper. Whether these HLA genes shape how severe the disease gets was underexplored. The team also measured two blood markers. One marks dying surface cells, and the other marks tissue matrix build up. One hundred one patients, with an average age of sixty, took part.

Sixty one patients had a non severe course and forty had severe or critical disease. Severity tracked with older age, male sex, higher marker levels, and inflammation signs. No HLA variant tied directly to severity. Yet two variants in one gene linked to lower or higher levels of the matrix marker. One variant in another gene linked to lower levels of the cell death marker and a liver enzyme. The study maps indirect gene effects on organ damage signals rather than on severity itself.
pmc-11001358:
Romaric Larcher and co-authors study kidney harm in grave COVID-19 cases in this 2023 paper. Tube damage in the kidney is the main driver of sudden kidney failure in such patients. Urine marks may warn of failure before blood tests do, so the team grades several marks.

Sixty intensive care patients were tracked over two months of the first wave. About half showed tube function faults, and over half met kidney failure marks. One urine protein gave the best, still modest, warning for both plain and lasting failure. In firm models, illness severity and body weight, not urine marks, tied to failure onset. The authors say urine tests alone cannot carry the forecast.
pmc-11041658:
Andreu Porta-Sanchez and a large team describe animal work from 2023 on Timothy syndrome, a rare condition that causes a long heart rhythm delay and sudden death. The group built a pig model that carries the same gene change found in people with the syndrome. Pigs were chosen because their hearts are close in size and wiring to human hearts.

The pigs showed the long delay and early deaths seen in patients. Mapping of the heart found slow spread of the electric signal, which set up looping rhythms. Cell tests showed too much calcium and a weaker sodium current than expected. The team also used a risk index to test several drugs, showing how the model can screen new treatments.
pmc-11225458:

Their 2023 study covers 1,473 patients; 66, or 4.5 percent, still leaked cerebrospinal fluid five days after non-surgical treatment began, marking them as persistent cases.

Men made up 92.5 percent of the leak group, and the 21-to-30 age band led. The commonest injury pattern combined all three Le Fort levels with nasal, cheek, and jaw fractures, a whole-face breakage. Leakage through the nose alone was the typical sign, in two thirds. Most cases, 84.9 percent, resolved once the facial fractures themselves were treated. The authors tie the leak's fate to the fracture repair, arguing the bone work is the leak work.
pmc-11532458:
Keting He and co-authors hunt in 2024 for stable housekeeping genes in mouse liver for studies of chemical injury and cell aging. Such steady genes are needed as anchors if gene activity measures are to be trusted.

Mice were given a liver harming chemical, and livers were taken at four time points over two days. Twelve candidate genes were ranked by five methods in PCR tests. Four genes tied to the secretions of aging cells served as targets. Two genes, Gapdh and Tbp, came out as sound anchors for this injury model. The paper also tables past picks for other liver disease models, as a guide for future work.
pmc-11535758:
Sarafian, Robinson, Christov, and Tarchini studied in twenty twenty-four health gaps for Bulgarian Roma folks who moved to the United Kingdom. The Covid wave hit small groups in that land with more force than most. They lived and worked with Roma groups in two cities for the study.

Poor jobs and tight homes, plus hid-ing who they are to dodge bias, cut their reach to care. The wave and the split from Europe made those strains worse in their lives. Kin and group aid nets were a key way to cope, yet those nets are thinning. The team calls for health plans that fit such groups.
pmc-11536958:
Rida Jaber and co-authors report a rare cause of seizures in an infant girl in a 2024 case report from Syria. The baby had seizures from her second day of life, and standard drugs failed to stop them. Tests of her metabolism, brain waves, and seizure form pointed to a vitamin linked illness.

Gene tests found a fault in both copies of the ALDH7A1 gene, which blocks a step in processing a brain chemical. Oral pyridoxine, a form of vitamin B6, then stopped the seizures in full. The authors urge doctors to weigh this rare cause early when newborn seizures resist drugs, since swift treatment spares needless drug use.
pmc-11537558:
Yi Chen and three co-authors describe how they repaired a large surgical wound in a rare skin cancer case from 2024. The cancer, an extramammary Paget disease, had spread across the groin, penis, and scrotum of one patient. Wide removal of the diseased skin is the standard treatment, but it leaves a defect that is hard to cover well in that area.

The patient had two rounds of removal surgery. The team then rebuilt the scrotum with a thick sheet of skin taken from elsewhere on the body, a graft thick enough to hold up yet thin enough to take root. They followed the patient for 37 months. No return of the tumor was found, and the team judged the result satisfactory in both function and look.
pmc-11538358:
Colin Greeley, Lawrence Holder, Eric Nilsson, and Michael Skinner teach deep learning to read pathology slides in a 2024 paper. Whole slides are gigantic, with tangled tissue features throughout. Most AI readers are tuned to one narrow problem. Their method aims to train on varied tissues and diseases.

A pyramid tiling scheme keeps spatial context around each patch. That design scales to gigapixel images without losing place. Training covered testis, ovary, prostate, and kidney tissues. The system spots pathologies and classifies whole slides at once. It beat manual reading on speed and accuracy in tests. Results held up on public datasets as well. The authors pitch it as a reproducible lab tool.
pmc-11538558:
Qian Wang, Dehong Gong, Zhongxiao Zhang, and co-authors test a two-phase solvent that captures carbon dioxide and turns it into mineral form in this 2024 study. Carbon capture is held back by the energy it takes to free the gas from normal solvents. Their solvent splits after absorbing the gas, so only the loaded half needs further handling.

The loaded phase was mixed with a calcium source to lock the gas into solid form at normal temperature and pressure. With sound-wave treatment for thirty minutes at fifty degrees, about ninety-six percent of the loaded carbon was mineralized. Over six cycles, the loaded phase kept a steady share of the solvent volume and a high gas load. Tests with heat, X-ray, and magnetic methods confirmed the products. The authors say the cycle can cut the energy cost of capture while recycling the solvent.
pmc-11539258:
Quinn Steiner and colleagues track body makeup and bone strength in college athletes after hip surgery, in this case series from twenty twenty-four. The surgery, hip arthroscopy, fixes a painful clash of bone shapes in the joint, but rest afterward can thin muscle and bone. The team checked whether young athletes bounce back.

Twenty-three Division I athletes had full-body scans before surgery and again over the next two years. Pelvic bone density dipped at three and six months, then returned to its starting level by twelve months. Bone density in the operated leg was higher than at the start by the two-year mark, while leg fat rose over the same span. Total body fat and muscle mass barely moved. The authors advise care teams to watch bone health in the first year after surgery, even in fit young patients.
pmc-11539758:
Lior Seluk and co-authors survey, in a 2024 study, why Israeli doctors return home, or not, after fellowship training abroad. Fellowships abroad are a key career step in high-income countries. They also risk losing trained doctors for good.

The survey, run in early 2024, reached Israeli doctors who trained abroad between 2013 and 2024. Questions covered background, training experience, and professional challenges. Statistical analysis sorted which factors swayed the return decision. Every doctor who stays abroad is a loss to a small health system. Knowing the true levers behind the choice helps Israel design policies that welcome its fellows back.
pmc-11550558:
Far right parties that win votes on anti migrant lines might be thought to drag public views the same way. James Dennison and Alexander Kustov test that thought in a 2023 study of twenty four European states over thirty years. They track party wins against survey views on migrants.

Party success linked, on the whole, to warmer views on migrants, not colder ones. The pair call this a reverse backlash. Voters who dislike such parties may dig in on fair norms, and the split in views may push pro migrant voices to speak up. The find cuts against the plain view that party cues drag all views one way. It also shows how norms can snap back.
pmc-11558858: Berenika Olszewska, Anna Zaryczańska, Roman Nowicki, and Małgorzata Sokołowska-Wojdyło reported in 2024 a case of tumor lysis syndrome. The trigger was the drug brentuximab vedotin, used in a patient with mycosis fungoides, a lymphoma of the skin. Tumor lysis syndrome is a dangerous rush of cell contents into the blood. It occurs when cancer cells break down fast. Reports tying it to this drug in this disease are rare. A documented case is therefore useful for clinicians who use the drug in similar patients.
pmc-11569258:
Piotr Jerzy Skrzypczak and co-authors compare one bar against two in chest-wall repair surgery. Their 2024 study covers 1,238 patients who had the Nuss procedure for a sunken chest at one centre over two decades. Matched groups of 546 patients each balance age, sex, and chest shape.

Both groups ended with the same correction of the chest index. Problems after surgery, though, ran near twice as common with two bars. Air leaks, blood in the chest, fluid build-up, and bar shifts all rose. Statistical models kept two bars as a risk factor on their own. The authors advise weighing the extra bar's cost in harm.
pmc-11570858:
Newborn circumcision is common and safe on the whole, yet rare mishaps can strip the shaft skin and need swift surgery. Randy Casals and co-authors report one such case in work from twenty twenty-four. The harm came after a clamp device was used, one of three standard tools for the task.

Most mishaps in this care are bleeds that settle with plain care. This case ran far past that: wide skin loss that called for urgent repair. The report walks through the repair and the child's course. The authors stress gear checks and clean method as the true guard, since the tools are safe when used with care. The case adds a rare worked example to the record.
pmc-11573558:
Heilmeier and eight colleagues link chronic inflammation to cardiovascular risk in systemic sclerosis in twenty twenty-four. Systemic sclerosis damages blood vessels and raises heart disease risk. About a quarter of patients have persistently raised C-reactive protein, a marker of inflammation. Whether that predicts atherosclerosis in this disease was unclear.

Sixty-five patients were split into inflamed and non inflamed groups by repeated protein measures. The inflamed group had worse cholesterol and triglyceride profiles. Their estimated ten year cardiovascular risk was significantly higher. Within the inflamed group, protein levels tracked with carotid artery wall thickness. Machine learning models found lipid traits best separated the two groups. The authors identify an inflammatory subtype with higher vascular burden.
pmc-11574958:
Yi Lu and co-authors link vaping, smoking, and using both to high blood pressure and death risk, in a 2024 study of United States survey data. Burning cigarettes are known to raise blood pressure, but data on e-cigarettes and dual use were thin. The team draw on a national health survey from 2015 to 2018.

The sample holds 7,696 adults. After adjustment, vaping alone tied to 56 percent higher odds of high blood pressure, smoking to 29 percent higher, and dual use to 83 percent higher. Among people who already had high blood pressure, current vapers died at higher rates over about three years of follow-up, from all causes and from heart causes alike. The authors warn that past smoking may drive part of that link, but they back tighter control of e-cigarette use.
pmc-11577058:
Jakob Ketterer and co-authors test whether training balance with warped vision changes how young adults stay upright. Twenty-two healthy volunteers trained for four weeks. One group did classic balance drills, while the other wore virtual reality gear that twisted their visual input, forcing their senses into conflict.

Standing sway was timed with eyes open, a trained state, and eyes closed, an untrained one. A model of the balance system split out how much each sense contributed and how the feedback loops gained. Across both groups, the visual sense's share in balance grew over the training, and one feedback gain rose too. The results probe how practice rewires the blend of sight, inner ear, and body sense that keeps us standing.
pmc-11579258:
Guro Strom Solli, Oyvind Sandbakk, and Kerry McGawley review sex gaps in winter endurance sports in a 2024 paper. Most past comparisons came from summer sports with matched male and female athletes. Winter events at the Olympics, from cross-country skiing to speed skating, had never received the same full treatment.

Top speeds differ by roughly seven to sixteen percent across the skiing and skating events. Women's races often cover shorter distances, which complicates direct comparison. Technique choices differ too, with women using certain ski gears more often. Skating gaps may reflect a less effective push-off pattern. Two newer Olympic sports lack published comparison data entirely. The review sets a baseline for fairer training and event design.
pmc-11583458:
Sherine Saad, Yousreya Shalaby, and Amir Azer published a dental study in 2024 on a digital method for fitting computer-made crowns. A crown must meet the bite well as the jaw moves, or high spots can cause harm. Copying a patient's jaw motion on a computer is hard. The team tested a method that builds the crown path from the patient's own recorded motion.

Thirteen patients each got two zirconia crowns for the same tooth type, adjusted by two digital routes. One route used more motion records than the other. A pressure sensor then measured the bite. Crowns from the fuller-record route showed lower peak pressure during side jaw moves. The authors say the method helps find and fix high spots before fitting.
pmc-11585558:
Petr Smirnov and co-authors dissect a brain tumor whose chromosomes shattered in a single catastrophe. Chromothripsis, that shattering and chaotic reassembly, is a frequent route to cancer genome chaos. How it varies between clones of one tumor, and shifts under treatment, was largely unknown.

Working with p53-deficient medulloblastoma and neural stem cells, the team profiles single cells' genomes and gene activity together. They rebuild the order of events after the shattering and spot the early changes it likely caused. Multi-omic detail at single-cell scale shows how one bad day in a cell's life seeds a diverse, evolving tumor. The map may reveal weak points that targeted therapy can press.
pmc-11585658:
Yuefeng Zhao and five co-authors build a neural network that sorts land cover from the many colors of hyperspectral images.
