Their network instead pays adaptive attention to the pixels themselves.

Three modules do the work. One enriches the spectral and spatial signal in the input cubes. The core attention step compares pixels by both distance and angle, learning which neighbors matter at several scales. A third module mixes features across layers so telling details are not lost between levels. On four standard data sets the network beat current classification models on accuracy, and it ran faster than rival three-dimensional designs. The authors aim the method at remote sensing tasks where fine spectral detail decides the label.
pmc-11585958:
Lei Cheng and co-authors sort cancer subtypes by fusing many layers of cell data at once. Their 2024 paper notes that single-layer reads miss links between genes, marks, and RNA that mark a subtype. Prior fusion tools also drop the web of ties between patients, which holds useful shape.

Their method builds a patient graph from each data layer, runs graph networks to embed each layer, then lets self-attention weigh which layers matter for each case. A final classifier names the subtype. On three cancer sets it beat rival tools, the authors report. It also flagged key marker genes for breast cancer, which aids lab follow-up.
pmc-11590558:
Parisa Tehranifar and eight co-authors asked whether changes in breast density over time predict breast cancer, in a 2024 study. Dense breast tissue on mammograms is a known risk factor. Less was known about the path density takes. The team used a cohort of women with family history of the disease. Over twelve thousand mammograms were analyzed.

Cases had higher starting density and slower declines than controls. Women whose density stayed stable faced higher risk than women with steep yearly drops. Rising dense area raised risk further, most in women starting with the most dense tissue. Patterns were similar across menopause and family risk groups. Links looked stronger in pre-menopausal and lower-risk women. The authors suggest tracking density paths in risk checks. Women without declines may merit closer monitoring.
pmc-11590858:
Wigham and co-authors set up group consultations in a lower limb musculoskeletal outpatient service. Group consultations have been shown to lift outcomes with greater efficiency. The aim was a faster physiotherapy-led path for common lower limb problems. The new path had to meet rising demand with no loss in patient satisfaction. Three Plan-Do-Study-Act cycles tested the new approach.

Virtual group sessions and face-to-face group sessions were both tried. Four common conditions formed the test set. They were kneecap pain, Achilles tendon pain, sole pain, and knee osteoarthritis. Measures covered patients seen, staff time, patient experience, and outcome scores. One-to-one care took 45 minutes of staff time per patient in the past. Virtual sessions cut that time to 22 minutes per patient. Face-to-face groups cut it further, to 12 minutes per patient.
pmc-11591258:
Samuel Keightley, Ayla Pollmann, Benjamin Gardner, and Myanna Duncan mapped how home-working psychology connects to health and wellbeing, in a 2024 exploratory study. Nearly five hundred home-workers rated ten home-working responses, from the ability to switch off to day planning, alongside ten health behaviors and seven wellbeing measures. Network analysis charted which responses sit at the center of the web.

Four response clusters emerged: home-working independence, the home-work transition, daily work pressure, and work-day forecasting. Within them, a few perceptions carried outsized influence. A manageable workload, the ability to switch off, autonomy, and day planning cascaded into sleep, activity, and wellbeing indicators. The authors caution that the design cannot prove causation. Even so, they argue it tells employers and public health planners where support would bite: protect the off-switch and the plan, and much else follows.
pmc-11592158:
Yu Chuan Ong and co-authors use computer immune modeling to design vaccine pieces shared across many coronaviruses. Their study appeared in 2024. Three coronavirus outbreaks in twenty years, capped by COVID-19, exposed how unready the world was. A universal vaccine would target the parts of the virus that barely change. The team scanned the spike protein for fragments that T cells and B cells recognize, hunting ones conserved across bat, pangolin, and human coronaviruses, including the MERS virus.

They found 132 candidate fragments, most of them widely conserved. Aligning them revealed overlapping stretches, which were assembled into two lead peptide builds with strong immune-stimulating profiles. The authors present these as starting points for a universal coronavirus vaccine. Lab testing is the next step before any clinical promise can be claimed.
pmc-11592458:
Quartuccio and co-authors pool in 2024 results on radioembolization for breast cancer that has spread to the liver. The therapy threads radioactive spheres into liver arteries. Response and disease control rates were the two outcomes of interest across past studies.

Eighteen studies with 650 patients qualified. Overall response rate was 50.71 percent and disease control reached 88.37 percent. Resin spheres scored higher, with response at 60.35 percent in 395 patients, and disease control at ninety-two point seven three percent. Glass spheres in 144 patients gave a 32.38 percent response rate, with disease control at eighty-two point six nine percent. The authors favor the therapy for this patient group on these numbers.
pmc-11592558:
Erick Vargas and co-authors review what makes a replacement jaw joint last. The jaw joint is key to a steady bite and smooth jaw work. Surgery is held for hard or end stage cases, since the joint is more complex than most in the body.

The review weighs both counts and qualities from studies of at least ten patients, with stock or custom made joints. New tech lets a joint fit a patient's shape more closely, with better function and comfort. Lasting power turns on the choice of safe materials that resist rust and wear, the design of the joint, and the right diagnosis at the start.
pmc-11593858:
Röhrs, Rohn, and Pfeifer build a scoring matrix to grade food incident reports for use in AI-supported risk spotting. Foodborne illness still strikes one in ten people worldwide each year. Data and smart tools to fight it keep growing. The hard part is using the flood of reports well. Their scheme uses multi-criteria decision analysis to rate each incident. Ratings can feed an AI database that sorts risks on its own.

A set priority level helps surface new or rising threats early. The matrix weighs harm, spread, and other set factors. The authors frame it as groundwork for autonomous risk sorting. Human judgment sets the weights; the machine applies them at scale.
pmc-11594858:
Aldo Ummarino and co-authors review stress responses inside tumors in a 2024 paper. A growing tumor is a hostile place: food and oxygen run short, waste builds up, and swelling persists. Cancer cells survive by switching on an ancient stress program that rewires how they work.

That program also shapes the normal cells nearby, including the immune cells that enter the tumor. The review maps the main stress pathways in both cancer and immune cells and how they interact. Knowing which pathways fire under stress could reveal new drug targets, since easing or blocking the stress response might slow the disease. The authors present this as a growing frontier in cancer immunotherapy research.
pmc-11595358:
Witkowska and colleagues (2024) examined how aging changes the inner structure of a high-manganese steel. The steel, X85MnAl29-9, can be hardened by aging. The team tracked its microstructure, crystal texture, and hardness after rolling and holding it at 550 degrees for up to 100 hours. They used X-ray analysis, light and electron microscopy, and hardness testing.

Aging produced two carbide types: fine particles inside the grains and a second kind at grain boundaries. Diffraction patterns after long aging suggested nano-sized carbides forming by a gradual decomposition inside the matrix. Short aging, up to a day, raised hardness as the fine particles appeared. At 100 hours the steel overaged: more carbide formed and hardness fell. The authors frame the findings for designers of safety systems who need to know how this steel's structure, and so its strength, evolves with heat and time.
pmc-11598558:
Franz Fuss, Batdelger Doljin, and René Ferdinands sort, in 2024 work, the throws of spin bowlers in cricket with a smart ball. In the lab, motion rigs can tell throw types apart, but the kit is heavy and slow. The team asked if a ball with fast spin sensors could do the job on its own.

They reworked the classic split of throw types, then turned the ball's spin axis into world terms and mapped throws by two angles. Seven bowlers were profiled, and the smart ball agreed with the lab rig within tight bounds. Throws, it turns out, form a smooth range, not sealed boxes. Mixed throws bend the ball's flight most in all planes. The team backs the ball for field profiling.
pmc-11598658:
Camelia Savulescu and co-authors tracked COVID infections and booster vaccine performance among European hospital staff from 2021 to 2023, in work published in 2024. The catalog creator list is cut off mid name, while the head gives the full study group. About three thousand staff in nineteen hospitals gave regular test samples.

Infection rates were far higher during the Omicron period than in earlier waves. A first booster added protection over the basic course, about half in the first three months of the Omicron wave, fading later. During the Delta wave the added benefit was less certain. The authors say such worker cohorts are key for guiding health policy in future waves.
pmc-11599758:
Melinda Katona and three co-authors studied a little-known human virus in a 2024 paper. The virus, human polyomavirus 9, was found only recently, and how it spreads or where it grows in the body was unclear. Past surveys of past infection gave widely varied numbers.

The team tested over a thousand blood samples from people aged under one to ninety-three. Signs of past infection rose with age in the young and reached about thirty-six percent in adults. They also hunted the virus in airway samples, finding it in about five percent of nose and throat samples and rarely in tonsils. Lab tests on cell types showed the virus's switches work best in lung cells, and a viral protein boosted one of them. The results point to the airways as a likely home for this quiet virus.
pmc-11600558:
Ozgür Komurcu and a team of co-authors asked if checks before surgery cut early problems. Their study, from twenty twenty-four, watched patients who had planned surgery. It is not clear if routine checks with the sleep doctor change risk. The team tracked blood flow and breathing problems during surgery and in the first day after. They also tracked how long patients stayed in hospital.

The group held more than one thousand one hundred patients with full data. Care ran from late twenty twenty-three to early twenty twenty-four. Readers who run surgical care learn what the pre check buys in safety. The work helps teams judge if the check earns its time and cost for each patient.
pmc-11600758:
A rare inherited disease called alpha-mannosidosis mimics a better-known group of storage disorders, so patients can be misdiagnosed for years. Maryana Marins and co-authors screen for the look-alike in this 2024 study of 250 Brazilian patients whose tests for the common disorders had stayed inconclusive.

Enzyme testing flagged fifty-three samples, and gene sequencing confirmed three affected families, all carrying the same stop-sign variant that leaves the enzyme dead. The authors urge screening centers to test for this disease alongside the common group, arguing that the shared symptoms hide cases that early treatment might help.
pmc-11600858:
Ke Ni and co-authors test, in a 2024 lab study, whether pretreating chalky white spots on tooth enamel helps a sealing resin soak in and resist acid. White spot lesions are early decay, common after braces. Resin infiltration can arrest them if it penetrates deeply enough.

Enamel blocks from human premolars were artificially demineralized for three days. Four groups of forty compared resin alone against pretreatments with bleach-like solution, a chelating agent, or both. Microscopy measured how much pore space opened up. Infiltration depth and acid resistance followed. Better pretreatment could make a no-drill fix for early lesions more reliable in everyday dentistry.
pmc-11602058:
Yue Yuan reads intended hand movements from forearm muscle signals with a signal cleaning pipeline, aiming at prosthetic control and rehabilitation, in this 2024 paper. Surface electrodes pick up rich movement information but buried in noise. The method first splits each signal into layered components with a variational decomposition, keeping only the most telling layers.

Four features are drawn from those components, and a ranking algorithm prunes the redundant ones. Eight trimmed feature sets were compared, and three standard classifiers did the final recognition. On a public data set of basic hand movements, the pipeline averaged 99.14 percent accuracy, beating prior results the author cites. The paper presents the recipe as a practical front end for clinics and devices that must know what a hand means to do.
pmc-11602858:
Franziska Neemann and co-authors compare, in a 2024 study, two portraits of a rare cancer: a German registry's patients and the reference-center cohort that guidelines rest on. Retroperitoneal sarcomas are uncommon and varied. Treatment advice comes mostly from elite centers, whose patients may differ from the typical case.

The registry cohort covered primary cases from one German state over six years. The working-group cohort came from specialist centers across three continents. Comparing the two tests whether registry data can support real-world conclusions. If reference patients are younger or fitter, published outcomes flatter what ordinary hospitals achieve. Registries, whatever their flaws, count everyone.
pmc-11603058:
Xi Liu and co-authors develop a safer drug lead against pancreatic cancer. Their earlier candidate hit a protein that helps this cancer grow. It stalled because it also gripped a heart channel, risking rhythm harm. The team screened ten thousand compounds for a fresh lead that binds the target but spares the channel.

One compound passed both tests. It killed cancer cells by several death routes at once, wrecking their power plants. A related compound that blocks one death route could undo the effect, confirming the path. In mice, tumors shrank with dose. Tweaked versions of the lead gained strength, and the best few moved on for deeper study.
pmc-11603158:
Chunyan Li and co-authors compare semen collection methods in goats by their molecular fingerprints in this 2024 study. Breeding programs freeze goat semen for artificial insemination. How the semen is collected, by artificial vagina or electric stimulation, may change sperm quality and how well it survives freezing.

The team profiled proteins and small molecules in fresh and frozen samples from both methods. Yunshang black goats supplied the samples, split into four groups. Molecular profiles explain why one method's sperm might thaw better. The results help breeding centers pick collection routines that protect fertility. Goat herds gain from semen that travels and stores well.
pmc-11603458:
Chang Zhang and co-authors flag a fat-burn gene as a mark of ill fate in a 2024 study. The ill is a blood seed cancer whose gene maps read plain, so risk calls there rest on few marks.

In bank sets of the sick, high counts of the gene tied to short spans free of ill and short life. The tie held when all else was weighed. A risk score built on the gene split the sick in a high pack that fared worse by a wide odds mark. In dish cells, hush of the gene curbed growth of the cancer. Gene set reads tied the gene to a burn call path through the cell's growth switch. The authors cast the gene as both mark and aim.
pmc-11603658:
Hyung Jun Park and co-authors test, in a 2024 computer study, a newly designed bone plate for a knee realignment surgery that opens a wedge in the shin bone. The surgery eases arthritis by shifting load, but the plate's screw holes gather stress, and a break of the outer hinge can occur. The team modeled the shin of an older woman in fine detail.

Three plates were compared under load. The new plate cut peak stress around the key hole well below both its older version and a rival plate. It did not win on stress across the whole plate, though. With a hinge break, its peak stress moved to a safer hole, a promising sign for stability.
pmc-11603858:
Shi Zhou and co-authors pool studies on the link between depression and motoric cognitive risk syndrome in older adults, published in 2024. The syndrome combines slow walking with memory complaints and predicts dementia well. Depression is a public health challenge of aging societies, yet its tie to this syndrome had not been gathered.

Ten databases were searched under a standard reporting checklist, and study quality was scored with accepted scales. Thirteen studies qualified, split between one-time surveys and follow-up cohorts. In the survey studies, depression came with well over twice the odds of the syndrome. Cohort results were extracted in parallel. Variation between studies was measured and publication bias checked. The authors present the pooled link as a reason to screen mood and movement together in older patients.
pmc-11604158:
Jonny Crocker and thirteen co-authors offer a reporting guide for water and health work in 2024. Trials of wells, latrines, and hygiene drives often leave out the facts a reader needs to copy or judge them. What was built, where, by whom, at what cost, and with what local fit all shape the results. Patchy reporting has made it hard to repeat wins or learn from flops.

The team built the guide by adapting an older health checklist. They scanned past guides and current practice, drafted candidate items, and refined them through four rounds of expert review. The final list has fourteen items, from the plan's name and logic to dose, faithfulness, cost, and materials. Each item comes with a plain note, an example, and tips for use in any kind of study.
pmc-11604658:
Tamara McErlain and co-authors present a method for growing vessel support cells in a 2024 paper. These cells, called pericytes, control capillary flow and guard vessel walls. Their failure links to many diseases and can aid cancer growth, yet good lab models have been lacking. The team isolated the cells from mouse lung, brain, bone, and liver.

Growing cells at oxygen levels like those in the body helped them keep their true traits, the team found. Marker genes and proteins stayed stable, and the cells joined vessel like tubes in tests. Conditions that limit a plasticity factor stopped unwanted switching. The team could also trigger disease like switching with tumor signals. Readers get a sturdy platform for studying these cells.
pmc-11604958:
Muhammad Aqeel Shahzad and co-authors tested in 2024 a three-part shield for fenugreek growing in lead-poisoned soil: a growth hormone, quantum dot biochar, and root-zone bacteria. Lead stunts plants across their metabolism. Pots received the treatments alone and combined, with and without a heavy lead dose, in six repeats each.

The strongest mix, the higher hormone dose plus biochar and bacteria, lifted shoot and root weights by wide margins over untreated stressed plants. Leaf greenness rose sharply too, with total chlorophyll up about a third. The authors credit the hormone's growth drive, the biochar's soil cleanup, and the bacteria's help with nutrients and defense. They propose the trio as a practical recipe for farming on contaminated land.
pmc-11605058:
Sijun Fang and co-authors give a design method for space telescopes that hunt gravitational waves in a paper from 2024. The telescope is a key payload in a space interferometer. A noise type called tilt-to-length coupling blurs the measurement when beams tilt. Its non-geometric part dominates inside the telescope and tracks tiny optical flaws at the small pupil.

Heat and stress in orbit can warp the structure and worsen those flaws. The team modeled the noise with Zernike polynomials, a standard optics language. An evaluation score then guides the whole structural design phase. Keeping the score low from the first sketch avoids late redesigns. The method serves planned space missions that listen for ripples from merging black holes.
pmc-11605158:
Umar Hayat and a large team of co-authors study in 2024 disparities in COVID-19 outcomes among patients with liver cirrhosis in North America and Europe. Patients with advanced cirrhosis face higher risk of hospital care and death from the virus. How demographics shape those outcomes was unclear.

Using two international registries, they evaluated 718 patients. In North America, Black patients had higher hospital, intensive care, and death rates. In Europe, White patients had higher death rates than non-White patients. After adjusting for other conditions, the gaps lost statistical significance. The authors suggest other illnesses drive much of the disparity.
pmc-11605958:
Marius Takvam and five co-authors present a 2024 study of magnesium control in salmon kidneys as the fish prepare for the sea. Salmon move between fresh water and the ocean, facing huge swings in magnesium around them. The kidney carries much of the balancing work, yet the molecular machinery in salmon was unknown.

The team tracked three transporter families known from mammals during the young salmon's transformation for sea life. All three families were present, and their genes switched on and off in differing patterns as salinity readiness rose. The differing regulation hints at evolved division of labor for salty water. The findings sketch how a migratory fish retunes a basic mineral system.
pmc-11607058:
Alexander Gabri and ten co-authors tracked long-term results of focused radiation for pituitary tumors, in a study from twenty twenty-four. These growths on the pituitary gland often come back or remain partly after surgery. A tightly aimed radiation treatment, given in one session, is a common next step.

The study followed patients treated over two decades in one population. Most stayed free of tumor growth for many years, with strong control rates at five and ten years. One tumor type, those making growth hormone, proved least likely to regrow. The main side effect was loss of pituitary function, which hit about a third of patients. The authors call the treatment effective but not risk-free.
pmc-11607958:
Tears at the root of the inner meniscus in the knee let the cartilage slip outward and speed up joint wear. Zhou and co-authors compare two repairs: root repair alone, and root repair combined with a centralization technique that pulls the meniscus back into place.

The study reviewed 87 patients treated at one hospital between 2020 and 2022, split between the two methods, and followed them for about two years. Both groups improved on knee function scores, but the combined group scored significantly higher. Scans showed the added technique also cut meniscus displacement from 4.6 to 2.6 millimeters, while repair alone barely moved it. The authors conclude that adding centralization gives better clinical results for these tears.
pmc-11608258:
Gong and five co-authors build prognostic models for young cervical cancer patients, in work from twenty twenty-four. Cervical cancer is a top cause of illness and death among young women. Yet no age specific definition of young cervical cancer, nor tailored prognosis models, existed.

Data on cases from twenty to twenty nineteen came from a United States registry database. Age was split into strata based on its curve shaped relation with cancer specific death, found with spline modeling. Prognostic models were then built and validated for the young group. Age tailored forecasts can guide treatment intensity and follow up for younger patients.
pmc-11608358:
Ahmad Hedayatzadeh Razavi and co-authors built a computer model in 2024 that predicts how a broken bone heals in rodents, day by day. Healing blends mechanics, blood supply, and cell behavior, and a model that juggles all three could one day guide human care.

Day one measurements of the fresh break, from fine scans and probe tests of stiffness, seed the model. It then grows the healing callus without preset size limits, moves stem cells through it, and grows new vessels alongside. Run on forty-eight animals over twenty-one days, its predicted tissue patterns and stiffness matched what microscope slides showed. The authors see a path toward simulating patient healing in advance.
pmc-11608458:
R Haridian Sosa Barrios and five co-authors tell of rare germ gut swell in a patient on belly dialysis. Their case study appeared in twenty twenty-four. Such swell is a known hit of this care and can end the care line. Most hits come from gram-plus skin germs, while gram-less kinds fare worse. The germ here, Acinetobacter ursingii, is rare in this set.

It was the third known case of its kind. Germ drugs put straight in the belly cured the ill with a good end. The germ is hard to name and oft drug-proof, so the team urge two drugs, close watch, and tight care drills.
pmc-11608758: Fabian Leo and Christian Grohé report in 2024 a rare nerve syndrome tied to a Mycoplasma pneumoniae infection. The syndrome, Parsonage-Turner syndrome, brings sharp shoulder pain followed by muscle wasting in the shoulder and arm. Nerve harms during chest infection can point clinicians toward this germ as the cause. Reports of the pairing remain rare in the medical literature.
pmc-11610058:
Viviane Cristina de Lima Gusmão and co-authors set research priorities in a 2024 Brazilian study. Nurses play a growing role in antimicrobial stewardship, the effort to use antibiotics wisely and slow resistance. In middle-income countries, though, that nursing role is barely studied.

At a three-day online workshop, nursing professionals proposed ideas in a structured group process. From 68 initial ideas, 45 survived clarification and voting. Top priorities were defining nurses' duties and skills in stewardship, planning how their stewardship work is organised, and using digital tools to support them. Nine broader themes emerged from the ideas. The authors say the agenda fits Brazil and may guide similar countries as well.
pmc-11610258:
Maija Sohlman and co-authors report in 2024 that blood signs of insulin resistance raise the risk of a stiff heart valve. The stiff valve, called aortic stenosis, narrows the heart's main exit and strains the heart. The team drew on a health study of 10,144 Finnish men who had no valve disease at the start.

Staff measured body traits and a wide set of blood markers at the start. They then tracked the men for about 11 years and found 116 new cases of the valve disease in health records. Math models sorted which markers foresaw the disease. A second method grouped linked markers into a few clusters, which also foresaw risk. If blood traits flag risk years ahead, doctors could watch high risk men more closely and act sooner.
pmc-11610458:
Jonas Gustafson and co-authors published a study in 2024 reporting high-coverage nanopore sequencing of samples from the 1000 Genomes Project, to build a full catalog of human genetic variation. Nanopore sequencing reads long stretches of DNA at once. Such long reads capture kinds of variation that short-read methods miss.

Fewer than half of people with a suspected inherited genetic condition receive a precise molecular diagnosis after full clinical testing. Long reads may raise that share, but clinicians lack a clean reference set of well-characterized samples for filtering true variants from noise. The project plans to sequence at least eight hundred of the known reference samples. The study presents the first one hundred, drawn from all five continental population groups of the collection. Each was sequenced to a deep level of coverage. The resulting data set will serve as a baseline of ordinary human variation.
pmc-11610558:
Shen and five co-authors show how a gut germ fans bowel swelling in mice in this twenty twenty-four study. The germ grows more common in folks with sore, swollen bowels, yet its role was dim. The team fed it to mice whose bowels were primed to swell by a salt cure.

Inside, dosed mice showed worse gut harm and a weaker gut wall than primed kin. Their gut germ mix also slid out of fair shape as the ill grew. In gut wall flesh, the germ lit a death path in guard cells by a scent route. Dish tests with guard cells showed the same fire-death and scent spill at work. Blocks on that scent route cut the harm the germ caused.
pmc-11611158:
Miguel Alfaro and co-authors present a 2024 study modeling COVID-19 spread in Santiago de Cali, Colombia. The pandemic strained both science and government in the country. A local model could show how the virus moved through this city and what containment could achieve.

Their biomathematical model uses difference equations fitted to the period from March 2020 to June 2022. Parameters were estimated with a Gauss-Newton method. The results suggest most residents could test positive at some point, yet containment could keep the count of sick cases at a manageable level. Deaths over time were fitted with a Gompertz curve. The authors offer the model as an input for city decision making in future outbreaks.
pmc-11611658:
Jong Woo Hahn and co-authors chart liver deaths across the world in a 2024 study. Liver ill kills more than two million people a year, about four in a hundred of all deaths. The team mined the world health death file for counts in more than a hundred lands.

Rates were set on a fair age scale from 1990 to 2021. The team then cast those lines ahead to 2050. Splits by land and by broad zone show where the load grows and where it eases. Such a long, wide view helps health chiefs plan wards, shots, and drug funds far ahead of need.
pmc-11611958:
David Jovel, Janice Cabrera, and Mitchell Walker test a new tool for electric space thrusters in this 2024 paper. Such thrusters push craft with charged gas, and their flow pulses in waves that are hard to measure. The pulsing makes the thruster act like a changing electric load, not a steady one.

The team sends a tiny test signal through a large thruster and reads how it resists and stores charge. They ran the test at two power levels with a gas called krypton. Values for a known pulsing mode matched checks from a second tool. The authors offer the tool as a fresh way to read thruster health and tune designs.
pmc-11612058:
The GBD 2021 HIV Collaborators map the global burden of HIV and AIDS from nineteen ninety to twenty twenty-one, in a research paper from 2024. The study covers two hundred four countries and territories. It also projects new infections, people living with HIV, and deaths forward to twenty fifty.

New infections fell by about a fifth between twenty ten and twenty twenty-one. Still, the total number of people living with HIV keeps growing, so care must be sustained. The team built the estimates from surveys, clinic data, death records, and program reports to UNAIDS. Two new measures track unsuppressed virus in the population and the lifetime chance of catching HIV.
pmc-11612458:
Jin Yu and co-authors show how scalp arteries pitch in after a new bypass for moyamoya disease. In this disease, brain arteries narrow and surgeons reroute scalp blood inward. Their side to side technique keeps the scalp artery's far branch alive, unlike the standard end to side join. Eighty four patients compared the two.

Overall healing grades matched. But the new join recruited the occipital artery far more often and widened the frontal scalp branch more. Among poor healers the contrast was stark: the preserved branch carried the day. The authors present scalp arteries as a reserve supply worth keeping open.
pmc-11612858:
Davide Ramoni and co-authors argue, in a 2024 letter, that simple inflammation markers could cheaply flag the fatty liver patients most likely to worsen. The condition, now called metabolic dysfunction-associated fatty liver disease, affects about a quarter of the world's people and is the most common chronic liver problem. Finding it early and judging its course usually needs costly scans or biopsies. The authors build on a study that stressed the need for non-invasive tools.

They survey inflammation-linked markers that also tie into heart and metabolic disorders. Such markers might sort patients by risk and show whether treatment is working, at a fraction of imaging costs. Gaps remain: labs lack shared protocols, and the markers need firmer proof in clinic use. The letter calls for research to settle those questions and unlock a low-cost testing path.
pmc-11613358:
Susana Fried and co-authors fault a UN report on prostitution and violence in a 2024 commentary. The piece answers a report by the UN Special Rapporteur on violence against women and girls. The authors say its account of prostitution law, sex worker health, and human rights law rests on errors and wrongly shaped claims.

They set out the fixes on law status, health proof, and the needs of people of all genders in the sex trade. The aim widens past one report: good habits on proof, openness, and self rule in contested rights work. They also place the dispute in a frail moment for global rights and health systems.
pmc-11613758:
Jing Tian, Ke Jin, Haohao Qian, and Hongyang Xu published a 2024 study of the so-called obesity paradox. Their patients were older people with cardiogenic shock, a state where the heart suddenly fails to pump enough blood. In some heart diseases, heavier patients survive better, which seems to defy logic. The team used a large intensive care database and studied 1,827 patients, split by age and by body mass index.

Among patients aged 65 and older, being overweight or obese showed no clear link with death within 28 days. Being underweight, by contrast, more than doubled the risk of death. Simple survival curves did favor heavier patients, but the gap faded once other factors were counted. The authors conclude that low weight, not high weight, is the warning sign in this group.
pmc-11613858:
Huihui Fu and eleven co-authors study how support cells feed energy units to leukemia stem cells in a 2024 paper. Acute myeloid leukemia comes back often due to stem cells that resist drugs. Bone marrow support cells help those stem cells survive. A gap protein called CX43 links the two cell types.

The team grew support cells with extra CX43 next to leukemia cells. More cell power units, called mitochondria, moved from support cells into leukemia cells. The leukemia cells then stuck, grew, and formed colonies more strongly. Gene and chemical tests showed a shift in energy use and growth. Mouse tests backed the lab findings. The authors name CX43 as a drug target worth testing.
pmc-11614858:
Fábio França Vieira e Silva and nine co-authors test whether a cell-death protein in tumor tissue forecasts how mouth cancer patients will fare. Oral squamous cell carcinoma is rising in incidence and mortality, and better prognostic markers could sharpen treatment choices. The protein Smac/DIABLO promotes apoptosis, the process cancers learn to evade.

Staining tumor samples showed that low Smac/DIABLO levels tracked with worse overall, relapse-free, and disease-specific survival over long follow-up. Low expression also came with more lymph node spread. In adjusted analyses the protein stood as an independent prognostic factor, with hazard ratios well above one for each outcome. The authors propose it as a practical immunohistochemistry marker for risk stratification.
pmc-11615358:
Camile Reinert and eight co-authors link, in 2024 work, the shield worth of food to rust marks and body fat in top soccer referees. Hard-trained folk breed more cell rust, so food shields may count double for them. Twenty male referees gave food logs, blood marks, and body reads.

The more shield worth in the diet, the lower one rust mark ran, and the lower the fat share ran too. One shield enzyme's pace also shifted with diet worth, though the pair of links did not point the same way. The team reads food shields as a real lever on rust load and build in such athletes.
pmc-11616358:
When COVID-19 lockdowns hit, clinics turned to the virus and away from teenagers. They spoke with thirty-four providers and stakeholders, and held group discussions with young people in Zambia.

The shift of staff and supplies to the virus response starved services that were already thin. Workers fell ill or isolated, supply chains broke, and HIV testing and counselling lost quality and reach. Teen pregnancy and testing access were the study's focus outcomes. Young people described their own view of closed doors and missing information. The authors map direct and indirect effects of the restrictions, offering lessons for keeping youth services alive in the next emergency.
pmc-11616458:
Alejandro Macchia and co-authors pool in a 2024 meta-analysis the placebo arms of dengue vaccine trials to ask what a past dengue infection does to the next one. Four studies from three large trials met their bar, all with antibody-confirmed prior infection.

Previously infected participants were modestly less likely to catch confirmed dengue again, and no likelier to be hospitalized for it. Yet their odds of severe dengue nearly tripled. No dengue deaths occurred, and overall mortality did not differ clearly. Prior infection, the pooled data say, protects a little against catching dengue while raising the stakes if it turns severe.
pmc-11618658:
Meng and co-authors ask whether a simple blood ratio can warn that a heart stent is likely to narrow again. The ratio divides the monocyte count, a sign of inflammation, by HDL cholesterol, the protective kind. Earlier work tested it for bare-metal stents, not the drug-coated stents now in common use.

The study followed 474 patients with unstable angina who received drug-eluting stents. Those whose stents narrowed again had higher ratios at the start, and the ratio stayed an independent predictor after other factors were counted. A cutoff value separated risk groups fairly well. The authors say this cheap, routine measure could help flag patients who need closer follow-up.
pmc-11619458:
Daichi Umemoto and co-authors report a case where cholesterol embolism came with vessel inflammation in a 2024 paper. Embolism occurs when cholesterol bits break loose and lodge in small vessels, harming skin, kidneys, and gut. Paired inflammation of small vessels is rarely reported beside it.

A man aged eighty-two had lasting fever, high counts of a white cell type, and low immune helper levels. Two months later came a rash and sore thighs. Scans and tissue samples confirmed both embolism and small-vessel inflammation in skin and muscle. Steroids eased the pain fast, but a gut artery block later proved fatal.
pmc-11621358:
Dayane Santos Martins and co-authors present a 2024 study of dropout from online therapy. Quitting therapy early harms patients and raises system costs. During COVID-19, essential workers got brief online care: four weeks of cognitive behavior therapy or interpersonal therapy. Records from 804 workers who attended at least one session feed the analysis. Of them, 138 quit early, about seventeen percent. Predictors were tested in three blocks: personal, clinical, and therapist traits.

Survey scales measured symptoms and burnout at intake. The design is a secondary analysis of a randomized trial, so the data are rich and the arms balanced. Service planners learn who leaves before brief therapy can help. Dropout forecasts let programs add check-ins or switch formats for high-risk starters. Online brief care is scaling fast after the pandemic; knowing its leak points is basic quality control.
pmc-11621858:
Xiuxiu Qiu and co-authors link a new inflammation index to death risk among cancer patients in a national survey. Body-wide inflammation shapes how cancers grow and end. The Inflammatory Burden Index was built to gauge that load.

Data came from a United States health and nutrition survey over two decades. Thousands of cancer patients were followed for many years. Weighted models tied the index to deaths from all causes. Deaths from cancer and heart disease were tracked separately. Survival curves and subgroup checks filled out the picture. Accuracy tests weighed the index as a predictor. The study asks if a cheap blood index can guide care. Its scale gives the answer unusual weight.
pmc-11622158:
Sara Aissati and co-authors tested in 2024 prototype lens designs meant to slow shortsightedness in the young. The three test patterns put clear distance vision in the center and different mixes of extra power, astigmatism, and coma toward the edges. An adaptive optics simulator projected the patterns onto volunteers' eyes, letting the team measure vision through focus and how the eye adjusts its own focusing.

Distance sharpness dipped only slightly against single-vision correction. One design, with off-center positive power in the periphery, clearly improved focusing response in myopic eyes without hurting distance sight. The multifocal patterns also shrank pupil size in myopes at all distances. The authors say the simulator reveals how design and eye physiology interact. That insight can guide custom myopia-control lenses. A two-zone layout emerges as the favored candidate.
pmc-11622458:
Augustus Osborne and Bright Ahinkorah write on fathers and early childhood in Africa in a 2024 commentary. Research long centered on mothers, but evidence now shows fathers shape thinking, emotion, and social growth in their own ways. Stimulating play and rich talk feed mental growth. Warm engagement builds self-esteem and resilience, and fathers model social skills while encouraging exploration.

Fathers' own mental health, income stability, and co-parenting quality also matter. Yet money pressure, cultural norms, and migration keep many fathers at a distance. The authors outline policy steps to support involved fatherhood and argue that removing those barriers is key to child and teen mental health.
pmc-11623458:
Dálete Assíria de Souza Ribeiro and co-authors lay out a plan to review probiotic use in type 2 diabetes, in this 2024 protocol paper. Diabetes keeps blood sugar too high when the body makes or uses insulin poorly. Gut microbes seem to play a part in the disease, which has raised interest in live-microbe supplements. Such supplements might shift gut balance and help with weight and sugar control, though the paths are unclear.

Rather than report new results, the paper states the rules the review will follow. It sets out which studies count, what body measures matter, and how the pooled math will run. The focus is body shape and weight measures in patients who take probiotics. A clear plan set in advance helps readers trust that the later review did not cherry-pick its findings.
pmc-11624258:
Alessandra Moretti, Christian Kupatt, and Eckhard Wolf review a new monkey model of Duchenne muscular dystrophy and what it reveals about the disease's cells, published in 2024. The disorder, caused by losing the dystrophin protein, destroys skeletal and heart muscle. Mouse models are small and mild, limiting translation. The study under review bred rhesus macaques carrying frameshift mutations, producing six dystrophy animals with no dystrophin.

Their muscles showed the classic signs: varied fiber sizes, central nuclei, scarring, and blood markers of muscle damage thirty to one hundred times normal. One-year-old monkeys showed early weakness like young patients, though hearts stayed normal so far. A full single-cell survey of the muscle accompanied the model. The commentators present the primate model as a stronger bridge to human trials of gene repair.
pmc-11624758:
Lee and colleagues reported in twenty twenty-four on muscle loss, air pollution, and thinking skills in older Koreans. Sarcopenia means loss of muscle mass and strength with age. The team drew on a long-running community health study. They studied two thousand two hundred seventy-four adults, with an average age near seventy. Thinking was tested with a standard screening exam.

About nine percent had sarcopenia, and more had possible sarcopenia. Muscle loss was linked to lower test scores and to poor thinking outcomes. In contrast, fine dust exposure over one month to three years showed no link to muscle loss. Dust also did not change the link between muscle loss and thinking. The authors say keeping muscle may help protect the mind.
pmc-11625258:
Abdullah Al-Ansi and three co-authors review in 2024 how artificial intelligence and connected devices could lift electronic government services. Governments worldwide are moving services online, and the question is what smart tools add beyond a website.

The team systematically reviewed a decade of studies, from 2014 to 2024, drawn from many academic databases. They sorted the literature by themes: how the tools are adopted, what they change in service delivery and citizen engagement, and where they stumble. The review gives officials a map of the promise and the pitfalls of AI- and sensor-driven public services.
pmc-11625358:
Evan Smith and four co-authors ask what marks of mind and brain foretell how well older adults learn two kinds of plain video games. Their study is from two thousand twenty-four.

Game-based mind training can lift thought in those past sixty, but how much swings by the way it is done. How one learns the game itself may drive the gain. Thirty-two older adults played an action game and a plan game. The team read their pace of learning in each. A broad mind test and scans of brain bulk were matched to that pace. The aim is to learn which traits count for which kind of game.
pmc-11626158:
Shuting Wang and co-authors build a magnetic soft microrobot to deliver healing cells for erectile dysfunction. Their 2024 paper targets a key weakness of cell therapy: injected stem cells often fail to stay or survive in the target tissue. Their robot is an ultrasoft gel sphere threaded with a chain of magnetic particles.

The sphere is softer than most body tissue, so it can change shape inside narrow blood vessels. Chemical groups on it mop up harmful reactive oxygen species. In rat and beagle models, the robot kept more cells alive in place than plain injections. Treated tissue healed faster and function returned. Gene reads pointed to helpful immune cells aiding nerve and vessel regrowth.
pmc-11627158:
Michail Vavourakis and a team of co-authors study whether a twisted thigh bone after hip fracture surgery hurts recovery. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-four. The twist can occur when a rod is nailed inside the bone to fix a break near the hip.

Seventy-four patients had scans of both hips and knees after surgery. The twist angle was compared with the healthy side. About thirty-one percent had a twist classed as a deformity. The rest had an acceptable angle. Patients were scored on hip function at six months and one year, against their level before the break. Healing, complications, and deaths were also tracked. The study weighs how much the twist matters for daily function after this common operation.
pmc-11627358:
The World Health Organization advises at least eight antenatal care contacts during pregnancy, yet many mothers in poorer countries fall short. Seungwon Lee and co-authors measure the gap in eastern Uganda, surveying 1,104 mothers who had given birth within the past two days at four hospitals. Records showed how many contacts each mother had and when they began.

Only 23.4 percent of the mothers met the eight-contact schedule, and just 23.2 percent had started care in the first trimester. Starting early was the strongest predictor of finishing the schedule, raising the odds more than sixfold. Mothers with insurance were also more likely to comply, while those with two to four children were less likely. The authors urge more health education, above all for mothers with several children, and efforts to bring women into care during the first trimester. They also suggest studying how a partner's support shapes attendance.
pmc-11627558:
Michael Wolfson proposes simple yardsticks for whether Canada's health data can flow where it is needed, in a 2024 paper. Patient records sit in many separate databases that do not talk to each other. That blocks good care and blocks honest grading of the health system. Governments have lately poured money and new law into fixing the split.

Wolfson offers three sharp test signs. Can a patient see their whole record? Can a care provider see a patient's whole record? Can an analyst reach the data needed to grade care quality? He argues these three signs are narrow, valid, and telling. They need not cover every detail to hold governments and vendors to account for real progress.
pmc-11628258:
Martínez-López and colleagues published in twenty twenty-four a case report of a hidden bowel injury after a car crash. A sixty-five-year-old woman suffered multiple injuries in a traffic collision. Ten days later, swelling appeared on the right side of her abdomen. Scans showed trapped air and a large fluid collection behind the abdominal muscles. Emergency surgery found a perforated jejunum, part of the small intestine. Bile-stained fluid had spread into the tissue planes behind the wall.

Surgeons removed the damaged bowel and rejoined the ends. They washed out the cavities and placed drains for recovery. A dissolvable mesh reinforced the weakened abdominal wall. Negative pressure therapy protected the closed wound during healing. Follow-up scans showed steady recovery with no infection. No hernia appeared over twelve months of follow-up. The authors say such hidden perforations should be suspected after blunt trauma.
pmc-11628558:
Lukas Heuplick and co-authors grow extra-large dye molecules directly on metal surfaces, in a 2024 study. Phthalocyanines with wider electron systems absorb redder light, a prize for optoelectronics, but they are hard to make in solution. The team laid two naphthalene-based building blocks on silver and gold and watched with tunneling microscopy and photoelectron spectroscopy.

The larger precursor joined into silver naphthalocyanines on its own, forming one-dimensional ribbons. The smaller one needed co-adsorbed iron to cyclize, then spread into two-dimensional networks, while without iron it formed open chains instead. The authors show surface chemistry can steer the same building blocks toward rings or chains and set how the products organize.
pmc-11628958:
Joma Younis and co-authors measure blood pressure in a 2024 study of health workers in the Gaza Strip. High blood pressure is a leading driver of heart disease worldwide, and health workers face long hours and heavy stress. The team sampled staff at ten hospitals and fifteen clinics in early 2020.

One thousand eight hundred fifty workers took part, most of them nurses. About eight percent had high blood pressure by the study's rules, counting medication use or measured readings. Body weight, smoking, coffee intake, and activity level were the changeable factors tied to the condition. Body measures ran higher in the affected group. The authors call for workplace programs that help health workers guard their own hearts.
pmc-11629258:
Jakub Gubala and co-authors set out a protocol for growing kidney and kidney cancer organoids from patient tissue in 2024. Even with better targeted and immune drugs, many kidney cancer patients do not answer first-line care. Mini-organs grown from a patient's own tumor could test drugs before the patient takes them.

Organoid screening is held back by practical hurdles in getting cultures started and kept alive. The protocol walks through isolating and growing both healthy kidney and cancer organoids from patient samples. Steps cover material handling through to upkeep for drug screening. The aim is a workable bench routine that labs can adopt for precision oncology work.
pmc-11631458:
Alexandra Fernandes, Diego Pol, and Oliver Rauhut name a new flying reptile from Argentina, in this 2024 paper. The fossil, a partial skull with bones, comes from Early Jurassic rocks in Patagonia. It belongs to Monofenestrata, the pterosaur group marked by a single opening in front of the eye socket, which later gave rise to the best-known pterosaurs.

Named Melkamter pateko, it is the oldest member of that group found anywhere. A lone tooth from the same site hints at another pterosaur family. The finds enrich the thin southern record of Jurassic pterosaurs and sharpen ideas about how the group changed early on.
pmc-11631858:
Xiang Gao and five co-authors test a plant-based drug for clearing stone bits left after kidney stone surgery, in a 2024 study. The surgery uses a flexible scope and laser to dust stones in the urinary tract. Dust and small bits often stay behind, and no drug had been shown to clear them. The drug, a flavonoid mix from a Chinese herb, was listed in 2022 for ureter stones. The team compared one hundred sixty-one patients, half given the drug after surgery.

Stone-free rates at follow-up ran near ninety-nine percent with the drug, against about eighty-nine percent without it. Among patients who did have leftover bits, clearance was more than twice as high with the drug. No clear side effects appeared in either group. Cost per unit of benefit was lower with the drug. The authors back the pairing for routine care.
pmc-11632158:
Jens Dietrichson and co-authors set out a 2024 protocol for a review of machine learning in meta-analysis. Meta-analysis pools many studies, and moderator analysis asks which factors change the size of an effect. New machine learning methods claim to help pick those factors, but their use has not been mapped.

The protocol has three aims. First, it will list machine and statistical learning methods built for moderator meta-analysis. Second, it will describe how those methods have been used in health, medical, and social science reviews. Third, it will test the methods on tutoring study data and compare them with standard regression tools. The review follows Campbell Collaboration guidance, and the test uses studies on help for students who struggle in school.
pmc-11632658:
Shahadat Hossain and four co-authors create nanomaterials whose assembly can be switched by a lipid tag that hides or shows itself. Their paper came out in 2024. Proteins are attractive building blocks for nanomaterials, but once a protein is made, its structure is normally fixed and cannot adapt.

They fused a calcium-sensitive switch protein to a stretchy, heat-responsive protein chain. When calcium arrives, the switch exposes its fatty tag, which seeks out membranes and changes how the fusion protein clumps. Light scattering and electron microscopy confirmed that assembly depended on both calcium and the lipid tag being present. The authors call this strategy liposwitching. They propose it for synthetic biology and cell engineering, where controllable assembly is valuable.
pmc-11633058:
Lino Braadt and eleven co-authors lay out the DISCOVER trial, a study protocol for treating depression after stroke by telephone. Their 2024 paper notes that up to one in three stroke survivors develops depression, yet screening and treatment programs remain rare in aftercare. The trial runs at the University Hospital of Augsburg.

Every adult stroke patient admitted over one year is screened with a standard questionnaire; those still showing signs eight weeks later enter the trial. Patients are randomized to behavioral activation therapy or a mindfulness-based program, both delivered by phone. Symptoms are tracked for a year alongside function, quality of life, and major heart events. The team aim for proof that phone-based, need-matched therapy can cut long-term depression after stroke. A positive result would give clinics a cheap, scalable aftercare tool.
pmc-11633458:
Xiaokang Niu and twenty co-authors run a blinded trial of a combined pro- and prebiotic for adults with obesity. Synbiotics pair live helpful bacteria with the fibers that feed them, and past results for weight have been mixed. Their 2024 trial gave eighty adults either the synbiotic or a placebo, with neither side knowing which. The formula used a screened Bifidobacterium strain plus two oligosaccharide feeds. Weight outcomes and gut microbe profiles were tracked through the trial.

A screened, pre-tested formula is the point: random pairings have produced much of the field's noise. If the gut community shifts alongside weight, the mechanism gains support. The authors run the design double-blind, the standard for belief-proof results. Their study is one careful brick in a wall still being built.
pmc-11633758:
Zhenfeng Pang and co-authors developed a way in 2024 to hear the nuclear spins that a response strength-boosting method usually hides. Dynamic nuclear polarization borrows the large polarization of unpaired electrons to amplify nuclear magnetic resonance signals. But the nuclei closest to those electrons are shifted so violently by the coupling that their lines vanish from the normal spectrum. The team worked with the polarizing agent TEMPOL in frozen glycerol and water just above one kelvin.

Their method, spin diffusion enhanced saturation transfer, reveals the hidden spins indirectly through their neighbors, and they also logged proton lines spread across a wide rate range. Models and quantum chemical calculations pinned the signals on protons of the TEMPOL molecule itself. 2D tests then showed polarization flowing from hypershifted nuclei to the bulk across the usual spin diffusion barrier, knowledge that can guide better polarizing agents.
pmc-11634158:
Dhrupad Banerjee and co-authors review fresh approaches in stem cell therapy for cancer and brain disease, in an overview from two thousand twenty-four. Mesenchymal stem cells sit at the center, since they can either feed or fight tumors depending on context. Their released packets, called exosomes, carry signals between cells.

Those packets show both pro-tumor and anti-tumor effects across studies. They also sway how tumors answer chemotherapy. Edited stem cells can ferry therapy straight into the tumor's neighborhood. For brain and immune disorders, the cells can rebuild tissue and calm immunity. Personalized, targeted use is the closing theme.
pmc-11634758:
Hifza Javed and co-authors published this study in 2024. It builds a model of how two people feel about each other during a conversation, not just how each feels alone. The goal is social robots that can mediate between people in real settings. Past affect tools read one person at a time, missing the shared mood. The team recorded conversations in uncontrolled settings and pulled features from sound and video.

The model weighs both partners' views to predict the pair's relational affect. Early tests show it can track how the shared mood evolves live. That skill could let a robot step into a souring exchange, lift a flat one, and leave a warm one alone. The authors discuss limits frankly: human ratings are subjective, and real scenes are messy. Still, they frame the model as a step toward robots that truly mediate.
pmc-11634958:
Jose Agudelo and co-authors report in 2024 direct evidence that kidneys hold their own microbes, and that a common surgical antibiotic shifts them. Past signs of kidney bacteria came from indirect sources. In mice, the team found bacteria in small niches inside kidney tubules, then gave an antibiotic used around surgery and watched the mix change.

Helpful lactobacillus types fell, while a family that includes many urinary pathogens grew. The effect depended on how long treatment lasted and reversed after it stopped. Two microbe types also pushed kidney stone crystal growth in opposite ways. Human kidney samples showed distinct microbe signs in two zones, with age related patterns.
pmc-11635458:
Amit Narawane and co-authors use a food dye to see deeper into the eye in this 2024 study. Optical coherence tomography pictures tissue layers with light, but the eye's white outer coat scatters too much for deep views. Hidden spaces behind it matter for drug delivery research.

The team built a custom handheld scanner for the eye's front and the space above the choroid. They tested tartrazine, the dye called Yellow 5, which can clear tissue for visible light. Eyes studied outside the body served as models. Clearing the coat let the scanner reach the target space. The method may open a window for testing eye drug routes.
pmc-11635658:
Bruno Vincenzi, Paolo Casali, and eight co-authors report real-world use of a cancer drug in Italy. Their study, from twenty twenty-four, covers pazopanib for soft tissue sarcomas. These are cancers of muscle, fat, and other soft parts. The drug is used after prior chemo in advanced cases that are not mostly fat-based.

A national registry run by the Italian drug agency tracked all users. Data span from twenty thirteen to twenty nineteen. Near two thousand patients took part, a very large group for a rare cancer. The main measure was how long patients stayed on the drug. Dose cuts and their timing were also logged. The registry shows how the drug performs outside strict trials.
pmc-11636558:
Caterina Matucci-Cerinic and co-authors tested the child form of the rule set for Behçet's disease, a rare ill of swelling in blood vessels. The catalog lists it under 2023, but the head of the text gives 2024, the year used here. Kids with the ill can be hard to sort from kids with like fever ills. Three rule sets are in use, and their worth in kids needs hard proof.

The team drew two hundred ten young patients from a Europe-wide fever roll. A panel of eleven experts, blind to the first calls, judged each case. Mouth and groin sores, skin bumps, a skin-prick flare, and back-of-eye swelling marked the true cases. The child rule set missed about half the true cases but was near never wrong on the rest. A broader set caught more true cases at a small cost in false calls.
pmc-11637358:
Adrian Amil, Albert Albesa-Gonzalez, and Paul Verschure ask why the brain's memory rhythm sits where it does in a 2024 paper. The hippocampus, a memory hub, pulses at theta rhythm, about three to eight beats per second. Neurons stamp information by firing at set phases of that pulse. Faster pulses could sample the world more finely, so the slow choice needs a reason.

Their theory weighs sampling speed against coding precision under realistic neural noise. Faster sampling blurs each stamp, so total information flow peaks inside the theta band, near one to two bits per second. The same frame explains why theta holds steady along the hippocampus despite changing anatomy, and why it speeds up as an animal runs faster. The authors extend the logic to vision and smell regions.
pmc-11637758:
Dechang Cao wrote a 2024 commentary on how plants tell spring from autumn, and on a gene that may blur that signal. Plants use vernalization, a long spell of cold, to time flowering for spring. Without it, they avoid flowering in autumn, when winter cold would kill the blooms. Warming winters make this timing system more important for crops.

The piece centers on the gene VRT2 and asks whether it drives vernalization or its undoing, called devernalization. Cao notes that some genes link seed dormancy and flowering, so cold sensing in seeds and buds may share parts. The commentary frames open questions about how plants keep the memory of winter. Answers could help breeders steady flowering as winters grow erratic.
pmc-11637858:
Zijian Ye and ten co-authors test radioactive antibodies against staph infections that coat artificial joints, in a 2024 lab study. Such infections form biofilms, slimy shields that blunt normal drugs. The team armed an antibody that locks onto a wall sugar of Staphylococcus aureus with one of two radioactive tags. They then dosed free bacteria and biofilms in dishes and counted survivors over four days.

Both armed antibodies killed in step with dose. At set doses they cut free bacteria ten-thousand-fold. Biofilms fell a hundred-fold under one tag and ten-thousand-fold under the other. Plain antibodies without the tags did not match the effect. The authors call the approach a promising targeted strike for joint infections. Animal and safety work would be the next steps.
pmc-11638358: Aba Folson, Philip Eghan and Daniel Amenu present a case on left ventricular noncompaction, a genetic heart muscle disease common in people of African ancestry. It can appear in adulthood and is hard to spot once heart failure is advanced. Diagnosis rests mostly on echocardiography or magnetic resonance imaging, yet both tools are scarce in low and middle income countries. The case turns on what echocardiography can still offer in such a setting, where the scan may be the only imaging route at hand.
pmc-11638858:
Von Hippel-Lindau disease is a rare inherited condition, affecting about one in 36,000 births, in which tumors grow in many organs. Few patients are seen at any one center. Hochberg and a twelve-author team asked whether TriNetX, a database covering over a hundred million patients, could give a fuller picture of how the disease is managed in real practice. They pulled every patient with the diagnosis and counted how many had each linked condition.

The search found 1,232 patients. Kidney cancer appeared in about twenty-nine percent, adrenal tumors in twenty percent, and brain tumors of one type in about fourteen percent. Several rarer features showed in only a handful of patients. Compared with published studies, these shares ran low, suggesting the disease and its features are under-recorded in the database. The authors conclude that TriNetX gives a blurred picture of this rare disease.
pmc-11639758:
Five Korean researchers test plant compounds against leukemia cells. From the roots of Peucedanum japonicum, a traditional East Asian medicine plant, they extracted the mixture with solvents and sorted it by activity. Two coumarins came out of the screen. Both were checked against three cancer lines, including the HL-60 leukemia line, and their structures were confirmed by magnetic resonance readings.

The second compound drove the leukemia cells into programmed death. Treated cells piled up in the death-marked phase of the cycle, showed early and late death signals, and lost voltage across their mitochondria, the cell's power plants. The executioner proteins of cell death were cut into their active forms. The authors present the compound as a candidate worth developing for leukemia, an example of a natural product that triggers the mitochondria-led death route.
pmc-11640258:
He Ma and co-authors test whether a mushroom sugar's benefits travel with gut microbes, in this 2024 mouse study. The sugar comes from Floccularia luteovirens, a mushroom whose polysaccharides earlier eased gut immunity problems. The drug cyclophosphamide, used in chemotherapy, suppresses immunity and injures the gut lining.

Mice harmed by the drug received stool transplants from sugar-fed donors. The transplant raised protective gut antibodies and immune signals, switched on defense pathways, and lowered oxidative stress through a known protective switch. Barrier proteins that seal the gut wall rose, and the microbe mix partly healed, with several healthy groups rebounding. Metabolite patterns in the stool shifted too. The authors conclude the sugar protects mainly by reshaping the gut community, and they propose it as a natural guard against chemotherapy's gut damage.
pmc-11640458:
Hideto Ueki and nine co-authors test machine learning models to forecast lymph node spread in prostate cancer, in a 2024 study of Japanese patients. Wide node removal helps staging but adds harm when nodes are clean. A sound forecast could spare needless removal. Records covered 625 men who had robot-assisted prostate surgery over more than a decade.

Node spread showed in thirty-four men, about five percent. A gradient boosting model sorted best, with a top curve score, and a forest model came second. Both beat classic paper nomograms in the check set. Gains were largest at low risk thresholds, where calls to skip removal matter most. The authors back model use in surgical planning.
pmc-11640658:
Zishen Zhang and co-authors use light beyond the visible range, plus machine learning, to grade pears without cutting them open. Their 2024 study serves farms and food firms that must sort fruit fast and gently. Six kinds of pear went under the camera, which reads how each fruit reflects light across a wide band.

The team tried ways to clean the light data and to pick the wavelengths that carry the most signal. One pairing won: a fast detrend clean-up plus a sampling method that keeps the keenest bands. With those, their model guessed firmness, sweetness, acidity, color, and ripeness well. A joint model across all six kinds also held up, which points to one tool for mixed fruit lines.
pmc-11640958:
Jianyu Shan and co-authors published this photosynthesis study in 2024. Photosystem II is the molecular machine that splits water and releases oxygen on Earth. In plants it docks with light-harvesting antennae to form huge megacomplexes. The team mapped one such assembly from a common plant, using electron microscopy, structural mass spectrometry, and ultrafast fluorescence measurements, and compared it with a mutant missing a small protein called PsbR.

Their structure shows PsbR gripping the complex from the inner side with three contact domains. It touches the core proteins, associates with a redox-active component, and braces an outer protein needed for oxygen release. With PsbR and a partner protein centered between two photosystem cores, the assembly gains a basis for regulating electron flow, energy transfer, and oxygen output. The mutant comparison shows how the megacomplex reorganizes without PsbR.
pmc-11641758:
Gaurav Baranwal and co-authors review stem cell therapy to keep dialysis access open in a 2024 paper. Kidney disease affects more than a tenth of the world. For dialysis, a fistula joins an artery and vein, but many fistulas fail within the first year.

Mesenchymal stem cells are studied as a way to heal and protect these access points. The review covers cell sources, from fetal to adult tissue, and past work on markers, immune cells, and low oxygen. It weighs how cell therapy might cut repeat procedures for patients. The field is still young, so the review maps both promise and gaps.
pmc-11641958:
Christian Than and a large team review whether wearing tape between exercise sessions helps adults with kneecap pain, in a 2024 systematic review. Patellofemoral pain is common, and taping is often added to exercise therapy, but most studies only tape during workouts. The team gathered studies where tape stayed on outside exercise and combined 17 of them covering 348 patients.

Both Kinesio and McConnell taping showed clear gains. Pain scores fell from around five to near two on the scales used, and function scores rose into the mid-eighties. Benefits crossed the threshold patients can feel by six weeks. The authors conclude that prolonged taping looks helpful alongside exercise, though the studies varied a lot.
pmc-11642058:
Pietro Pugliatti and twelve co-authors review, in 2024 work, how exercise testing can guide care for a heart illness caused by protein buildup. The illness stiffens the heart and grows worse over time, in two main forms. Judging how far it has gone, and whether drugs help, is hard by symptoms alone.

A test that tracks breath and heart work during exercise gives hard numbers: peak oxygen use, breath flow, and how much a patient can do. Those numbers help staff stage the illness and judge its likely course. They also let teams tune care to each patient and check if new drugs are working. The reviewers call the test a core tool for personal care in this illness.
pmc-11642258:
Eight authors, led by Catarina Marreiros, test in 2024 whether a protein that blocks vessel hardening can serve as a warning marker in dialysis patients. Hardened vessels drive heart disease, the top killer in kidney failure. The protein also calms swelling, which makes it a promising sign to track.

The study drew on just over one hundred patients on home based dialysis. Blood levels of the protein tracked against a vessel hardening score and mineral and swelling markers. Higher hardening came with lower protein levels. Over a third of patients showed wide vessel hardening. The team weighs the protein's worth for risk care.
pmc-11642358:
Giorgio Frega and co-authors published this study in 2024. It reviews treatment sequences for biliary tract cancer, a rare and aggressive cancer of the bile ducts and gallbladder, at one Italian referral hospital. The series covers the years before immunotherapy arrived, when chemotherapy order was the main strategic choice.

Fifty-six patients who received at least three rounds of therapy were analyzed. The standard sequence, a gemcitabine-cisplatin doublet first and a fluorouracil regimen second, was compared with every other combination doctors had chosen. Survival did not differ significantly between the standard path and the alternatives, in either line. The authors note their filter, patients fit enough for three lines, selects long survivors by construction. Even so, the series is among the first to test sequencing itself in this cancer. It suggests flexibility in regimen choice costs little, leaving room to tailor by tolerance and patient preference.
pmc-11642558:
Alma Nurtazina and co-authors present a 2024 case-control study on B vitamins and metabolic syndrome in Kazakhstan. The syndrome bundles insulin resistance, belly fat, abnormal blood fats, and high blood pressure, and it affects a fifth to a third of adults worldwide. B vitamins keep mitochondria, the cell's power units, working well, and weak mitochondria feed the syndrome.

The study enrolled 190 Kazakh adults aged thirty-five to sixty-five at a clinic in Semey. One hundred four had metabolic syndrome and eighty-six did not. Blood tests covered sugar, long-term glucose, kidney function, and fats, alongside B vitamin levels. The team compared vitamin levels with standard reference ranges to look for links with the syndrome.
pmc-11642658:
Robert Zablotni, Grzegorz Zając, and Rafał Rusinek probe, in a 2024 study, the mechanics of middle ear implants and find a hidden fork in their behavior. These implants pass sound energy to the stapes and the inner ear, and their reliability rests on predictable vibration. The team built a lumped model with five degrees of freedom and checked its output against the global ASTM standard and against experiments on human temporal bones.

The simulations uncovered bistability: under the same conditions, the implant's periodic response can settle into either of two distinct patterns. The authors map which starting states fall into which pattern, drawing the basins of attraction for the pair. Finding the second solution matters, they argue, because a device that can jump tracks may not behave as its designers expect. The work speaks to both the theory of such implants and their practical tuning.
pmc-11643258:
Dai Pu and co-authors set out a test of a plain hunch: proof lands best where it was born, in a protocol from 2024. Ward folk trust home rules and home word more than far press. If a ward helped make a find, will it take the find up with more will?

One find, on move alarms that bar falls, will go out to 36 wards in Victoria, Australia. Half bore the find; half did not. Take-up will be read at three points, by counts and by talks. No scores are in; the worth is the clean test of a lore all crews feel. If birth place moves take-up, the way finds are made and spread must change hands.
pmc-11643458:
Chen and co-authors present a 2024 study on a live ultrasound system that watches hydrogen damage build inside pipeline steel. Hydrogen embrittles the X80 steel used in energy lines, yet damage is hard to spot without cutting samples out. Their rig charges steel with hydrogen in a temperature-held bath while ultrasound probes it. Smarter signal math sharpens both timing and strength readings.

Under steady charging, the steel saturated with hydrogen after about eight hundred minutes. Sound loss grew in a straight line with charging time until that point, then flattened and turned erratic. Microscopy blamed hydrogen-driven cracks for the shift. The team maps how a hidden damage layer forms as charging proceeds.
pmc-11643558:
Małgorzata Matusiak and co-authors test in 2024 how liquid sweat moves through firefighter clothing layers paired with underwear. A firefighter's outfit blocks heat and hazards, but those same layers trap sweat, which can condense on the skin and sap comfort and focus. The study asks which fabric pairings carry that liquid best.

Sixteen assemblies combined four underwear knits with four protective multilayer sets. A moisture management tester tracked liquid spread through each stack. The knits moved liquid well on their own. In the protective sets, sweat travel stayed mostly in the inner layer next to the skin, barely crossing the outer barriers. Pairing the right knit with the right inner layer lifted total transport. The findings give gear makers a practical way to tune comfort without giving up protection.
pmc-11643658:
Carlos Barba-Ostria and co-authors published a 2024 study of plant pigments packed in tiny capsules, drawn from two old food crops of the high Andes: a purple corn and a purple potato. The pigments, anthocyanins, are known foes of microbes and of rust-like damage. Packed well, they last and work in food and care products. The team studied what the packed pigments can do.

The pigments were packed in a starch-sugar carrier coat. Beam and spectroscopy readings showed the pigments held in the coat in sound shape. The potato pigment led on antioxidant fight, and it hit two cancer cell lines hard. The corn pigment led on antimicrobial fight, even against drug-resistant microbes and film-forming kinds. The conclusion presents the packed pigments as versatile goods for both food and care use.
pmc-11643758:
Wenyuan Zhang and co-authors review plant sugars for use in infant formula in a 2024 article. Human milk is rich in special sugars that feed good gut bacteria and build infant immunity. Formula lacks much of that profile, and formula fed infants often have poorer gut health as a result.

The review covers using dietary polysaccharides as prebiotics, and as partners or products of good bacteria, called synbiotics and postbiotics. Prior studies show effects on gut microbes, gut acid production, and immune development. The combined and product forms looked stronger for shaping microbes and blocking infections. The authors note safety testing in large, long trials is still needed, and they compare milk like options such as pectin and inulin.
pmc-11643858:
Zixuan Jin and co-authors enrich a rare ginseng compound and test its heart protection. Their 2024 study works on 25-OH-PPT, a scarce sapogenin from ginseng stems and leaves. The compound is known for sugar, antioxidant, and anti-inflammatory effects.
