Acid treatment of the plant extract raised the compound's share to about 12 percent with strong acid. A food-safe acid reached only about 2 percent but with a cleaner safety profile. In heart cells stressed by a drug, the compound cut damage markers and restored defence enzymes. Scar-related proteins in the heart shifted toward normal. The authors map a possible route against heart fibrosis.
pmc-11643958:
Jan-Olof Drangert and co-authors argue that city eaters hold the key to world food security in this 2024 paper. New global data let them trace how food choices ripple into land use, emissions, and health. Cities now house most people, so urban demand shapes what farms grow across half the world's habitable land.

The review finds that eating less meat and more plant and soilless food, wasting less, and recycling city nutrients as fertilizer could halve farm land needs. Freed land would let nature regrow and store carbon. Poor diets now kill far more people each year than the pandemic did. A shift in city diets could cut diet-linked diseases by up to a fifth.
pmc-11644058:
Isyaku Abubakar and co-authors model where a rare salt loving moss may live in Serbia as the climate shifts. Their paper from 2024 deals with Entosthodon hungaricus, a red listed moss of salty grasslands. Its home is being lost, and it has no easy way to move.

Several distribution models were run under climate paths for the next eight decades. Every model showed the range shrinking, to unlike degrees. The moss needs a set salty soil type, so shifting ground is not an option even where climate might fit. The authors call for special care and management for the species in Serbia, since loss of its few sites could end it there.
pmc-11644158:
Yuan Fan and co-authors report a green way to make chiral gold nanoparticles that are compatible with living tissue. Their 2024 paper deals with particles that show promise for biosensing, fighting bacterial infections, and tissue regeneration.

Some agents used to make such particles can be toxic, so a safer route matters. Their method reduces a gold salt in place with alginates, which act as reducing agent, chiral inducer, and stabilizer at once. Several analyses confirmed the particles had formed, with a mean size near fifty-four nanometers. Cell viability stayed high even at a strong dose, showing good biocompatibility.
pmc-11644258:
Albert Tucci, Miguel Flores-Vergara, Robert Franks, and Stefan de Folter infer gene networks in developing monkeyflower seeds. Their study from twenty twenty-four uses machine learning on time-series gene data. Seeds helped flowering plants spread and diversify widely. Hybrid seed failure also locks species apart permanently.

The team crossed two Mimulus species that produce viable seeds. Gene activity was tracked across seed development stages. Network inference highlighted which genes regulate which others. Active control links in hybrid seeds emerged from the analysis. The results form a reference set for later experiments. Understanding these networks may explain why some hybrid seeds fail. Plant biologists gain targets for testing speciation mechanisms directly.
pmc-11644358:
Kalavathy Rajan, Paula Berton, Robin Rogers, and Julia Shamshina ask if kraft pulping should anchor future plants that turn plants into products, in work from twenty twenty-four. Kraft pulping makes most paper pulp today from wood. It also brings sulfur waste and high water and energy use.

The authors trace the rise of chemical pulping since the factory age began. Gains in yield and cost have not solved waste or full use of wood parts such as lignin. They weigh the bottlenecks that keep plant based goods from being truly green. Other routes to break down wood get a look as well. The piece urges a hard check of old methods before new plants copy them.
pmc-11644458:
People with Parkinson's disease often lose balance and fall when pushed or jostled. Chi-Shiuan Lee and co-authors develop a hip-worn exoskeleton robot to help them recover a standing balance. The robot senses the body's balance point and plans a hip motion that brings it back over the feet.

A smart controller then drives the robot through that motion, adjusting without a detailed body model. The team tested healthy volunteers and Parkinson's patients, with and without the robot's help. Trials used real pushes to disturb standing. Results showed the robot and its controller could support recovery in the patient group. The authors present the system as a step toward wearable aids that cut fall risk in daily life.
pmc-11644558:
Film coats that fight biofilm on water filters are built by Mario Castillo-Ruiz and co-authors in work dated 2024. Biofilm growth chokes filter flow in water plants. The team stacked thin charged layers on a tough base film, with one mix holding graphene oxide flakes. Layer counts and surface traits were checked with scans and charge reads.

The graphene form came out smoother and passed salts at split rates by type. Both changed films cut biofilm growth by around four fifths for two germ types. Germ life on the films fell hard as well. First sticking was not fully stopped, but spread and slime build were blocked.
pmc-11644658:
The authors model where a wetland herb can grow in China now and under future climates, in a study from 2024. Sweet flag is prized for looks, water cleaning, and medicine, but wild stocks are shrinking as demand rises. Using 266 known sites and eighteen climate and land factors, they built a tuned distribution model.

Rain in the wettest month, human footprint, yearly rain, and daily temperature range drove the map most. Good habitat now sits east of the line where yearly rain reaches about four hundred millimeters. Forecasts under three climate paths for mid and late century shift that range, guiding planting and wild protection.
pmc-11644758:
Veronika Zemanová and co-authors dosed spinach with rising zinc to map where help turns to harm in a 2024 paper. Zinc is a plant nutrient, but too much poisons growth. Pots held substrate with zero to 300 milligrams of zinc per kilogram, and the team tracked yield and nutrient content.

Water-soluble zinc rose with dose. Up to 150 milligrams, plants held up well, with tolerance scores backing a mild benefit. At 300, above-ground yield fell by a third, and calcium, copper, and iron in the leaves dropped. Pigments and photosynthesis suffered too, likely under oxidative stress, and oxalic acid output signaled strain. The study pins down the dose where a nutrient becomes a toxin for spinach.
pmc-11644858:
Hoejun Jeong and colleagues combine deep learning with dynamic time warping to diagnose a hidden degradation inside nuclear reactors. The core support barrel, an internal structure, is held by clamping force whose degradation can significantly affect plant safety and reliability. Earlier studies could detect that degradation occurred but not pinpoint its size and position.

The method applies time warping to the magnitude of ex-core neutron noise signals in the frequency domain, letting the model learn how sensor values change with damage state. Autoencoder-based representation learning extracts features while preventing overfitting, improving robustness. Experiments show the size and position of clamping force degradation can be accurately predicted. Internal structures cannot be inspected directly while a plant runs. The approach turns vibrations a reactor already emits into a map of its own wear.
pmc-11644958:
The authors study drilling signals from a diamond drill bit in a 2024 experiment on rock strength. Knowing when a bit passes from strong rock into a weak layer could warn of roof collapse in mines. The team drilled media of different strengths in the lab and recorded thrust and torque.

In the weakest material, drilling was fastest and forces were smallest. Some simple signal measures failed to separate the media well. Time and frequency analysis, plus a decomposition method, showed clear shifts at layer boundaries. The authors argue those signals can serve as extra criteria for spotting weak layers during drilling.
pmc-11645058:
Davide Lillini and co-authors present a system to spot sleep apnea from a throat microphone in a 2024 paper. Sleep apnea, where breathing pauses in sleep, affects a share of the world population and often goes unfound. The standard test is intrusive and relies on expert judgment, so a simpler aid could widen screening.

Their system turns sound into a frequency image and processes it with a paired network design that mixes image and sequence layers. An unsupervised grouping step then marks apnea events. Tests on overnight records from eight patients reached a high recall for apnea events. The authors compare their system with a recent fully image based method and discuss the best input settings.
pmc-11645458:
Brain waves tied to the heartbeat can reveal whether a silent patient is following commands inside, and Emilia Fló and co-authors tested that signal in work from twenty twenty-four. Healthy people first did a task: attend to their own hearts, then to sounds. Brain shape shifts split the two states cleanly.

Classifiers read the heartbeat signal and sorted most healthy minds right. Other brain marks scored as high, and one hit full marks. Five brain-injured patients then did a changed task. Two, one in a waking coma and one locked in, willed the heartbeat signal to shift, which hints at hidden awareness. The test may reach patients that exams miss.
pmc-11645758:
Vahideh Hamidi Sofiani and co-authors test whether two viruses travel with a cancer mutation in a 2024 study. A change in the KRAS gene, known as G12D, drives many gut cancers. Separately, papillomavirus and Epstein-Barr virus turn up in tumor tissue often enough to raise suspicion of teamwork.

The team screened ninety-two patients with stomach or bowel cancer and one hundred healthy controls. Sensitive DNA tests looked for the mutation and for both viruses in each sample. Epstein-Barr appeared in about half the tumors of both types, papillomavirus in a small share. Mapping how often they coincide with the mutation sharpens, or weakens, the case for viral help in cancer growth.
pmc-11645958:
Tim Lambert and colleagues studied sugary drink intake in severe mental illness in 2024. People with severe mental illness die early more often. Poor physical health drives much of that gap. The team measured added sugar from sweetened drinks. They used data from routine community mental health care.

Intake of added sugar was four times the general population level. That figure also misses sugar from other snack foods. So true intake was likely higher still. Several poor health factors tracked with higher intake. The authors suggest a simple drink measure. It could flag diet risk when no dietitian is available.
pmc-11646658:
Alba Gracia-Sánchez and co-authors ask in a 2024 study whether wet skin on the foot makes hikers more likely to blister. They read skin moisture with a probe on eighty-six long-distance hikers, in zones from toes to heel, and logged who had blisters. Moister zones were the toes, forefoot, and heel.

The blister group was moister overall, and the link was firm on the left foot. Women ran moister than men, and moisture fell with age. Cutoff values on each foot flagged blister risk with good sensitivity. Dry-sock habits may be a cheap shield, the team hints.
pmc-11647058:
Nora Hamdiui and co-authors report how they reached Turkish and Moroccan immigrant women in the Netherlands for a study on cervical cancer screening. Uptake of the national screening program is very low in these groups. The team made a teaching video in the women's own cultural frame, then tested it with a survey.

Six routes were used to find women for the survey, and nearly fifteen hundred took part. Peer-to-peer chains, where each woman recruited others, reached more older, less schooled, first-generation women with low screening knowledge. Social media reached younger, highly schooled, second-generation women instead. The authors show that mixing routes is what brings the hardest to reach into a study.
pmc-11647258:
Luyao Kang and co-authors build a prediction chart for a mixed womb cancer in work dated 2024 in the text. The mixed form blends two or more tumor types and makes up a small share of womb cancers, and its drivers and best care stay unclear.

Using a large United States cancer database, the team screened near thirteen thousand patients who had the womb removed. Factor hunts yielded a chart that split patients by risk with strong accuracy. Drug therapy lifted survival in the high risk group and in those with more spread to glands. Beam therapy helped set groups as well. The chart aims to match care to risk.
pmc-11647358:
Dafne Capelusnik and co-authors published a 2024 study comparing questionnaires for pain and morning stiffness in a spinal arthritis condition. The condition, axial spondyloarthritis, stiffens the spine and causes chronic back pain. Trials and clinics measure these symptoms with several rival scales, all scored from zero to ten. The team asked which scales measure what they claim, and which best separate patients into known groups.

They used data from a long-running international cohort of patients with the X-ray form of the disease. Eighty-five patients with eight years of records were assessed. Three pain scales and three stiffness scales were tested against set predictions about how they should relate to other measures. All six passed most of the tests. One pain question, covering neck, back, or hip pain, separated groups slightly better than the rest. Night back pain performed worst. Background factors had little effect on the comparisons.
pmc-11647758:
Muscle weakness in many diseases comes with swelling, lost fibers, fat creeping in, and scarring. Kai Yin led a team that reviews the muscle's inner neighborhood and the cells that keep it in balance. At the center sit FAPs, flexible starter cells that never become muscle themselves. Instead they can turn into fat, bone, cartilage, or scar-forming cells, build the tissue scaffold, aid repair, and tend the nerve-muscle link.

When injury or disease upsets the neighborhood, these same cells misbehave and drive the damage patterns doctors see. The review maps the signals that steer the cells, for good or ill. It picks out drug targets on those paths that might restore balance and help muscle heal.
pmc-11647858:
Ryuichi Maekawa and a team of co-authors found a new fluid to peel graphite into thin sheets. Their study, from twenty twenty-four, used a water mix with ammonium hydrogen carbonate as the bath. An electric charge drives the peeling from the top layer down. Such thin carbon sheets draw wide use, and makers want better ways to mass produce them with fresh traits.

The peeled product has a porous two layer shape and stays spread in water for years. Its worn, holed face makes a fine base for metal based catalyst parts. Those parts went on to drive hydrogen making as stand in catalysts. Readers who make carbon sheets get a bath that yields a long lived, catalyst ready product.
pmc-11648058:
Patrícia Coelho de Soárez and six co-authors tally what measles outbreaks cost Brazil's public health system after the country had eliminated the disease, in this 2024 study. Over thirty-six thousand cases were confirmed between 2018 and 2020. The team costed hospital and clinic care, laboratory testing, and the vaccines and lab work spent on outbreak control.

The outbreaks cost about one hundred and eight million dollars in total. Each case ran between roughly twenty-six hundred and thirty-seven hundred dollars, averaging near three thousand. Sensitivity checks bracketed the uncertainty without changing the story. The authors argue that the bill itself is a policy argument: prevention and rapid control are cheap next to resurgence. Budgets should be planned so the next importation never becomes an outbreak.
pmc-11648558:
Larissa Becker and co-authors fed a plant-based vitamin D form to young pigs in a 2024 farm study. The additive is a glycoside form of the active vitamin D hormone, drawn from a plant extract, and pig raisers want to know if it beats the standard supplement.

A total of 2,268 weaned pigs ate one of three diets for 42 days: the standard feed alone, or the feed plus a low or higher dose of the additive. The team tracked growth, blood markers of immunity, and bone measures from sampled pigs at the end. The trial gives hog producers data on whether this plant form supports healthy, fast-growing nursery pigs.
pmc-11648658:
Yali Wu and nineteen co-authors study a natural compound that blocks cell recycling in this 2024 paper. The compound, hapalindole Q, comes from a family of plant like indole molecules. Cells normally fuse their waste bags with digestive sacs to finish autophagy, the recycling process. This compound stops that fusion. It does so by an unusual route: it tags a growth protein, YAP1, for destruction by a side channel of the same recycling system. With YAP1 gone, a trafficking protein scatters and fusion fails.

Binding tests confirmed the compound grips YAP1 directly. A structure study showed the core scaffold, not its sulfur bearing tip, does the work. Blocking autophagy is a live strategy in cancer and other diseases. A molecule that does it by removing one named protein offers a clean tool. The authors also see a drug scaffold against YAP1 driven disease.
pmc-11649058:
Bhavya Balaji and four co-authors describe clearing a blocked windpipe in a child in this two thousand twenty-four case report. Long ventilation and a tracheostomy can leave scar tissue, called granulation, inside the trachea. Large growths are usually cut out by surgery or treated through a scope. Their patient was a six-year-old boy whose windpipe had closed completely. The block followed a tube cuff injury and a long tracheostomy.

The team avoided open surgery. Across several sessions, they widened the passage with a rigid scope and froze the excess tissue with cryotherapy. The airway reopened by this unconventional route. The case offers an option when surgery is risky. Pediatric airway specialists are the readers.
pmc-11650358:
Shang Gao and Renli Tian use genetics to test whether neuroticism causes upper urinary tract stones in this 2024 paper. Stone patients often suffer depression and anxiety, and neurotic traits had been linked to urinary disorders. Direct evidence on cause was missing.

Their Mendelian randomization used genetic variants as instruments for neuroticism and its component traits. Two methods found neuroticism raised stone risk modestly, and a verification set confirmed the score as a risk factor. Among traits, mood swings, loneliness, and worry each associated with stones; mood swings stayed an independent factor after joint adjustment. Bias checks found no pleiotropy or heterogeneity. The authors frame the result as a brain-kidney link worth watching in clinic.
pmc-11651158:
Paulina Sudnik and four co-authors report two fatal lung infections tied to bat droppings in a 2024 case paper. A fungus that lives in soil and droppings causes the disease when its spores are breathed in. Both patients had used bat guano as fertilizer while growing cannabis, one from a store-bought bag.

The fungus was once tied to two river valleys, but cases now show up across the United States. Single-person exposures, like these in Rochester, New York, now outnumber workplace outbreaks. The authors warn growers that a natural fertilizer can carry a lethal load, and urge care when handling it.
pmc-11651458:
Eight researchers test a bone signal system for a link to scoliosis in a 2024 paper. Scoliosis is a sideways curve of the spine, and past work ties it to low bone mass. The signal system helps control how bone is broken down and rebuilt.

The team used gene data from large banks in a method that mimics a trial, testing the link both ways. Two parts of the system showed no clear causal tie to the curve. The third part, a guard protein, looked protective, with higher levels tied to lower risk. Checks run the other way found no sign that the curve itself drives the system.
pmc-11653158:
Chirawadee Sathitruangsak and co-authors present a 2024 study of bile duct cancer outcomes in southern Thailand. The cancer is famed in the northeast of the country, where liver flukes drive it. Whether southern cases look the same was unknown. The team reviewed 223 patients treated at a large center from 2018 to 2021 and split them by where in the duct tree the tumor sat.

The in-liver form was most common, at about half of cases. Most patients arrived at a late stage, and no fluke signs were found. Only about 15 percent could have surgery. Median survival ran from about 19 to 27 weeks by subtype. One-year survival split hard by surgery access: about 85 percent with surgery against 21 percent without. Late arrival, the study shows, is the core enemy.
pmc-11653558:
Lihong Zhu and Juan Lin write a letter to the editor questioning a study that linked generous oxygen targets with better survival in sepsis. The study they discuss matched 2,422 intensive care patients into liberal and conservative oxygen groups and found lower 28-day death rates with higher oxygen in the first three days. Their 2024 letter welcomes the work, then presses on its weak points.

The letter notes that most of the survival gap opened by day seven and then stayed flat, which hints at an early effect or at sicker patients dying first for other reasons. The matching method dropped nearly half the patients, which can skew who the results speak for, and it cannot adjust for things that were never measured. The writers ask for deeper analysis of when the benefit arises and what drives it. Their aim is care in judging oxygen targets for sepsis.
pmc-11653658:
Guangju Mo and co-authors checked what changed when a large hospital in Anhui Province, China, switched to a new pay system in 2022. Under the system, the hospital is paid a set sum per illness group rather than per service. The 2024 study used monthly data from April 2020 to September 2023 and tracked nine signs of how the hospital ran.

After the switch, more patients were sent home and beds turned over faster. Deaths among low-risk patients fell, and the cost per stay dropped. Stay length and clinic visits did not change in a clear way. The authors read the shift as a net gain in safety, speed, and cost control.
pmc-11653858:
Yaqin Song and co-authors build a chart-based tool to predict severe complications during hospital care for heart attack patients. Such models are lacking for patients admitted through emergency departments. The study covers 1,024 patients treated at one hospital in Changsha between 2020 and 2023. About 717 patients form the group used to build the model, and 307 form the test group.

Analysis of admission data finds seven factors that independently predict severe complications. They are age, heart rate, mean arterial pressure, diabetes, hypertension, triglycerides, and white blood cell count. The team builds a nomogram, a scoring chart, from these seven factors. The chart predicts well in both groups. Calibration checks show predicted and observed rates agree closely, and a curve analysis shows the tool helps decisions across a wide range of risk thresholds. The authors offer it as practical support for emergency clinicians.
pmc-11654058:
Azadeh Dehghani and four co-authors examined how iron deficiency anemia reached Iran's policy agenda, in a study published in 2024. The condition is a moderate-level problem in the country, worst among pregnant women, children, and teenagers. The team used a well-known three-stream framework: the illness as one stream, solutions as a second, and the political mood at home and abroad as a third. Twelve policy documents and 33 in-depth interviews fed the analysis.

The solutions stream stressed staffing in health centers, blocking parasites and chronic illness, and the trio of supplements, education, and food fortification. National and international backing gave the topic favorable conditions. Barriers stood in the way: a treatment-first mindset, tight money, and limited reach of services, hit by sanctions and the pandemic years. The authors urge more spending on prevention before deficiency occurs, not only cures afterward.
pmc-11654158:
A virus that causes leukemia in chickens meets a strong defense in one genetic line of birds, and the exact targets of that defense were unknown. Xueqing Li and co-authors pinned them down in this 2024 study. The birds carry the B2 immune type, known for resisting many poultry pathogens. Infection raised the share of killer T cells and switched on their weapon genes.

From the virus's binding patterns, thirty-two candidate fragments were shortlisted. Three fragments proved to be true targets, spread across two of the virus's main proteins. Cells from infected birds answered those fragments with strong defensive signals. Shared, stable targets like these are what vaccines aim at. The findings guide vaccine design for a costly poultry disease.
pmc-11654258:
Yuyao Qu and co-authors map blood vessel volume in the choroid, the layer feeding the outer retina, in a 2024 imaging study. They use ultra-widefield swept-source optical coherence tomography angiography to measure two deep vessel layers in adults and ask how the measures relate to age, eye length, and body mass index.

Scans were split into a grid of nine regions, and three-dimensional vascularity indices were computed for each eye. Values in the left and right eyes of the same person matched strongly. The study also reports where imaging artifacts cluster in the lower grids, a practical warning for anyone reading these wide scans.
pmc-11654658:
Sumira Kiran and co-authors count spinal fluid leaks after pituitary surgery in Lahore in a 2024 study. The surgery goes through the nose to reach tumors at the brain's base. Rebuilding the skull floor is standard in many centers; this team skipped it.

Records covered 316 patients from 2018 to 2022 at a neuroscience institute. Most tumors were large, and two thirds of patients were women with a mean age near forty-one. Leaks after surgery hit just 2.8 percent overall. Rates did not differ by sex or tumor size in any clear way. The authors conclude the floor rebuild can be safely omitted when no leak appears during surgery. The setting is a low-middle-income country, where saved steps matter.
pmc-11655458:
Fulvio Riondato, Alberto Alvarez-Barrientos, and Francesco Grandoni introduce a research collection on flow cytometry in animal science in a 2024 editorial. The technique, which reads traits of single cells as they stream past a laser, has drawn veterinary interest since the late nineteen seventies. Yet the field still trails its medical counterpart by a wide margin.

The editors count thousands of veterinary papers using the technique, spread across more than a hundred journals. Growth has been steady and sped up in recent years. They note there is no dedicated journal home for this work. Their collection aims to take the pulse of the field today and showcase recent studies in key areas.
pmc-11655558:
Zhuoshi Li and co-authors show how a gene called MACC1 lets ordinary lung cancer cells turn back into stem-like cells. Tumors hold a mix: stem-like cells that seed growth, and regular cells that can dedifferentiate into them. MACC1 was already tied to lung cancer spread, but its role in this switch was unclear.

Cells rich in stem traits carried extra MACC1, and adding it pushed regular cells toward the stem state, while silencing it blocked the shift. The chain runs through a small RNA: MACC1 suppresses microRNA-25, which normally hastens the decay of a brake gene's message, KLF4. With the brake kept longer, the switch is eased. The authors say the finding may guide precision drugs aimed at cancer stem cells.
pmc-11655658:
One gene in cancer cells can be spliced into two proteins with opposite jobs, and a 2024 review by Mariusz Hartman explains why the short one matters. The long form of MCL-1 keeps cells alive and runs high in many cancers. The short form pushes cells toward death.

Cancer cells keep the ratio tilted toward survival. Drugs that block splicing regulators, tools that act on the gene's message directly, and several less understood compounds can all raise the short form. Hartman also notes the short protein may shape how mitochondria split and fuse, a role still unsettled. Shifting the balance, he argues, could break drug resistance.
pmc-11655858:
Hao Chen and co-authors report a 2024 study of electricity use in big-area 3D printing of fiber-filled plastics. Large-format printing cuts waste and frees shape design, but its green claims rest on thin energy data. Most past data came from desktop printers, which do not scale to plant-size machines.

The team metered fifteen print jobs over two months in a real plant. The jobs used fiber-filled pellets, the usual feed for this method. The dataset fills the gap for plant-scale printing and can feed later life-cycle and cost work by other teams.
pmc-11656058:
Ju-Hee Park and seven co-authors test a cannabis compound in lab dishes in this twenty twenty-four study. The compound, called cannabigerol, was given to two lines of human bowel cancer cells. The team wanted to see if it slowed growth or killed the cells, and by what route.

Growth tests showed the compound held back both cell lines, with the dose that halves growth differing by line. Staining tests showed many more cells dying in a neat, programmed way after treatment. Checks on cell cycle and on death-linked proteins backed that finding. The work is early lab proof only, but it marks the compound as a lead for more study on bowel cancer.
pmc-11656258:
Trace water in a solvent can ruin chemistry, and Malee Sinchow and co-authors build a glowing test for it from lanthanide metals. They synthesize a family of ten complexes pairing lanthanides with a dimethoxybenzoic acid partner, and map their crystal structures, heat resistance, and chemical sturdiness. Their glow responds to drying and wetting in a way they trace to weak links between molecules.

The europium member shows the trick best: drying switches its red glow off, and water switches it on. Filming that change with a phone camera and a free app lets them measure water in ethanol, acetonitrile, and acetone. Readings tracked water content linearly from zero to three to five percent, with detection possible below half a percent and recoveries between ninety-two and one hundred ten percent. The authors present the crystals as a cheap, visual route to water sensing.
pmc-11656358:
Stephanie Enríquez and co-authors (2024) make a bone-like material glow, then check it does not poison nerve cells. The base is hydroxyapatite, the mineral of bone, shrunk to nanoparticles and doped with samarium, a rare earth that emits light. Such particles could one day image tissue and help nerves regrow. The team synthesized the material with a range of samarium content, heated samples between 200 and 800 degrees, and characterized them with a battery of microscopy and spectroscopy tools.

The samarium entered the crystal. Emission was strongest at a samarium fraction of 0.05 after heating to 800 degrees, a recipe for the brightest particles. The team then exposed SH-SY5Y neuroblastoma cells, a nerve cell model, to the particles to gauge toxicity. A glowing bone mineral is only useful in medicine if cells can live with it, and this study takes both halves of that question in one pass.
pmc-11656558:
Graham Danzer and co-authors ask, in a 2024 study, whether a psychiatrist's judgment that a patient is not taking medication predicts how that patient's hospital stay turns out. In psychotic illness, stopping medication is a well known road to relapse. Most research on it uses tightly controlled designs that real wards cannot match.

The team deliberately chose a practice like design. Their sample was 182 inpatients with psychotic spectrum disorders and heavy risk factors. Non adherence was taken from the treating psychiatrist's own diagnostic coding. Outcomes included symptom severity on a standard rating scale, recent hospitalizations, and length of stay, modeled together in regression analyses. The headline results were null, the segment shown begins. A null from a real ward is useful: it warns that a clinician's adherence label, however confident, may carry less signal than the field assumes.
pmc-11656658:
Mincheva and co-authors test a cell-free treatment for the thinking problems that come with mild liver damage, in this 2024 study. Rats with such damage show brain inflammation that disturbs signaling in the hippocampus, a memory region. The treatment uses tiny vesicles released by mesenchymal stem cells.

Rats given normal vesicles showed calmer immune cells in the brain, lower levels of an inflammatory signal, and restored receptor parts tied to memory. Their performance on a location memory task improved. Vesicles from cells with a key growth factor silenced lost most of these gains. The contrast points to that factor as a main driver of the benefit. The work supports vesicle therapy as a candidate for this condition.
pmc-11656958:
Dan-Hui Wu and co-authors study how a cell defense protein fights viruses, in a 2024 paper. The protein, called STING, is part of the body's first line of defense. Its link to sugar use in cells was less clear. The team asked whether STING turns on a sugar path that helps fight infection.

Using mouse tissue and cells with or without the protein, they tracked changes in cell chemistry. A virus switched on the sugar path in host cells. The protein helped drive that switch and raised the action of two enzymes in the path. The results tie a known defense protein to a cell fuel path, and they suggest the fuel shift is part of how cells resist the virus.
pmc-11657358:
Nobuhiro Kanaji and co-authors study lung scarring in people with psoriasis in this 2024 paper. Psoriasis is an immune-driven skin disease, but its link with scarring of the lung tissue had been little explored. The team reviewed records for 117 patients with psoriasis, leaving out cases whose lung disease could stem from other causes.

Lung scarring was found in 12 patients, about ten percent. Cases split evenly between the common skin form and the joint form of psoriasis. A blood marker tied to lung disease was higher in those with scarring. Over a follow-up of about nine years, the scarring progressed in only five patients, and none died from it. The authors propose a named form for this link.
pmc-11657558:
Saber Gharagozlou and co-authors surveyed this 2024 question of why parents accept or resist COVID-19 shots for their children. The team questioned families of 226 children, aged five to eighteen, at a Tehran children's hospital over the summer of 2023. Only about twenty-two percent of the children had been vaccinated.

Children of vaccinated parents were vaccinated more often, and age, parental schooling, and past COVID hospital stays all mattered. Parents who accepted shots mostly wanted safety and protection from severe illness. Those who hesitated feared side effects most. The survey gives health planners a local map of trust and worry, useful for designing outreach that answers the actual concerns families voice rather than imagined ones.
pmc-11657658:
Gautam, Parajuli, and Pandey gauge gut worm load in a native group in Nepal. Years of state deworm work have not cleared worms in all groups. The Badi group has a way of life unlike most of the state. Few past studies probe worm risk in that group.

The team took stool samples from 205 adults aged 18 to 70. Each person also gave facts on home, work, and habits. Three lab methods checked each sample for worm eggs. The team weighed which habits and home traits tracked with infection. Their aim is care that fits the group real risks.
pmc-11657758:
Julie Rodriguez and co-authors examined consumer microbiome testing in Europe in a 2024 paper. Gut testing firms now sell straight to the public online. Quality and rules vary widely between sellers. To see what buyers get, one stool sample was sent to six firms.

Five firms sat in Europe and one in the United States. Reports came back with unlike depth and advice. The team weighed lab accuracy, ethics, and regulation together. Gaps between firms were wide enough to worry regulators. The paper calls for shared standards in this fast market.
pmc-11658258:
Michael Eichinger and co-authors checked what gear Austrian doctor response units carry for severe bleeding, in a 2024 survey. Heavy blood loss after injury is a top cause of deaths that could be stopped before hospital. The team sent a digital survey to all one hundred thirty-nine physician response units in the country and compared the replies with current care guidelines.

Nearly every unit replied. Some items were universal: pelvic binders and a clot-aiding drug sat in every unit, and tourniquets in nearly all. Advanced tools were rare, such as kits for blocking the main artery from inside or opening the chest. Four in five staff said their gear was good enough. Still, the gaps led the authors to call for one shared kit list, steady updates, and training that keeps pace with the guidelines.
pmc-11658358:
Chu Pan and Yanlin Chen present a software package for measuring nonlinear links between variables in biological networks, in a paper from 2024. Gene and protein networks often bend in ways that straight-line statistics miss. Information theory offers measures for such links, but they are heavy to compute and lacked a handy tool.

Their package, called Informeasure, runs inside the R language and its biology software collection. It bundles five measures. One handles pairs of variables for network inference. The other four handle triples, splitting shared and unique information between sources. The package is ready to use on install, with no extra setup. It is shared freely through the Bioconductor platform, with a public page for download.
pmc-11658458:
Xiao and three co-authors traced teen sleep problems to exercise and phones in this study from twenty twenty-four. Nearly five hundred adolescents, average age about thirteen, filled out surveys in twenty twenty-four. The team measured activity, sleep trouble, anxiety, and phone dependence. Statistical links were then arranged into a chain model.

More activity went with less anxiety, less phone dependence, and fewer sleep disorders. Anxiety and phone dependence together fully carried the link from activity to sleep. In other words, exercise seems to help sleep by calming worry and loosening the phone's grip. The chain order matters: anxiety first, then phone habits. The authors urge families and schools to push activity for better sleep.
pmc-11658958:
Ziyao Zheng and co-authors review a plant compound called cryptotanshinone in a 2024 paper. The compound comes from a red sage root long used in Chinese medicine. Interest has grown as lab studies link it to benefits in heart disease, cancer, and brain disorders.

The review screened 915 papers and kept 184 for close reading. In heart disease, the compound acts mainly through two signalling pathways tied to inflammation and growth. In cancer, it works through pathways that control cell survival. In brain disease, it counters damage through a protective stress pathway. Computer analysis predicted five key target proteins, and docking tests checked how tightly the compound might bind them. The authors call for direct tests of those targets.
pmc-11659258:
Jinglin Zhao and co-authors review a gut bacterium, Clostridium butyricum, as a possible treatment for sepsis. Sepsis is a runaway body response to infection that can fail many organs and kill the critically ill. Gut microbes guard the gut wall and tune immunity, and their upset worsens sepsis, the review argues.

The bacterium has long served as a probiotic in poultry feed. Recent work links it to protection in gut infections, bowel inflammation, and colorectal cancer. Their 2024 review gathers the mechanisms behind those effects, from barrier support to immune calming. It then weighs the early evidence for sepsis care and hunts for new treatment targets.
pmc-11659358:
Turn-by-turn navigation apps get people there, but they leave the mental map of a place thin and patchy. Frank Dickmann and co-authors argue that map design should work with the brain's own navigation machinery. Brain cells called grid cells fire in patterns that track metric space, and their activity steadies around walls and boundaries. The authors propose arranging cardinal lines and landmarks on maps to stabilize that firing while people read.

Because the same cells activate when we merely imagine moving through a space, a well-designed map could train orientation rather than replace it. The framework marries neuroscience findings with classic cartography research.
pmc-11659758:
Kei Shing Ng, Jie Lian, Fan Huang, Yan Yu, and Varut Vardhanabhuti wrote this research paper, published in 2024. It uses wrist-worn motion trackers from the UK Biobank to link how much brisk activity adults do with their later risk of chronic disease.

The study followed nearly sixty thousand adults who were free of chronic disease at the start. Their weekly minutes of moderate to strong activity were split into low, middle, and high thirds. People in the lowest third faced clearly higher risks, from about a quarter more to double, across a range of diseases. In men, low activity tracked most strongly with type 2 diabetes and with brain-degenerating disease. The risk rose step by step as activity fell, a dose pattern that strengthens the case for cause and effect.
pmc-11660158:
Martina Cotti and co-authors trace how a copper sulfate salt takes up water step by step. The salt can hold one, three, or five water units per formula. Their 2024 study starts with the one-water form and watches it head toward the five-water form. The three-water form may act as a stop along the way.

That stop proved to be the real path. The five-water form never sprang straight from the one-water form. The same birth-and-growth pattern ran twice, once for each step. The last step grew fast, as if the middle form lost its usual hold. A simple one-front spread model could not match the pace in pressed tablets. The work warns that such salts may act in layered ways in storage and heat use.
pmc-11660658:
Dalia Caleffi and four co-authors review what is known about getting patients up and moving after a heart device implant. Their twenty twenty-four scoping review deals with pacemakers and kindred devices, now given to older, sicker patients. Long bed rest after implant is customary, but no consensus backs one schedule.

The team searched six databases and kept eight studies, most of them randomized trials. Three themes emerged: how patients were mobilized, what complications arose, and which device was used. Early movement looked safe and did not raise complications. The chief barrier is the lack of an agreed time and method, though an arm support seems to help. More rigorous work is called for.
pmc-11662258:
Raising the legal age to buy tobacco to twenty-one cuts smoking, but the lives saved differ by state. Jamie Tam and co-authors estimated those savings state by state in this 2024 study. States differ in how much people smoke, how often smoking kills, and how widely the age rule was adopted. A national average hides those gaps.

The team used a long-running simulation model of smoking in the United States. It drew on state-level data for how people start and quit smoking and for death rates by age, sex, and birth group. They added records of where the age rule applied, from towns to states, between 2005 and 2024. The model then projected deaths tied to smoking under the rule. State maps like this help lawmakers see the local payoff of the policy.
pmc-11662658:
Karen Kanke and co-authors present a 2024 study of a better way to insert new gene code into primary cells. Gene editing can knock in a wanted sequence, but success rates are often low. The team used single strands of DNA as the template for the insert. They changed a share of the bases inside those strands with chemical tweaks. The tweaked strands were tested in several kinds of human cell.

The new strands raised the insert rate two to three times over older forms. In some cell types, more than half of the copies of key genes took the insert. One gene linked to blood disease reached a still higher rate with a helper drug. It did not help in lab-grown stem cells, for a reason traced to a missing enzyme. The work targets short stretches of code, fit for therapy and for lab models.
pmc-11664458:
Min Tian and nine co-authors examine whether drinking alcohol worsens the course of a rare brain disorder, in a 2024 study. Progressive supranuclear palsy robs patients of balance, eye movement, and thinking. The team recruited 128 patients at a Shandong hospital, confirmed by current diagnostic criteria, and interviewed them about drinking.

About forty-five percent drank. Drinkers, especially men, showed more severe symptoms than abstainers. Movement scores were worse, and thinking suffered across visuospatial skill, executive function, memory, and language. Sorting by weekly intake sharpened the pattern: heavy drinkers scored significantly worse on both disease rating scales and both cognitive screens than non-drinkers. The design is a snapshot, so cause cannot be proven. Still, the authors raise the possibility that alcohol shapes how this disease unfolds, and suggest patients be counseled accordingly.
pmc-11665258:
Kenta Torigoe and ten co-authors report a rare germ behind an infection of home dialysis, in a 2024 case report. A 46-year-old woman on peritoneal dialysis, where fluid is exchanged through the belly, came in with cloudy drainage fluid that had stayed cloudy for ten days. Its white cell count was very high, confirming infection of the abdominal lining.

Two antibiotics cleared the fluid within two days, and its cell count fell to zero by day six. Cultures then grew Moraxella osloensis, a skin germ almost never blamed for this infection. Treatment narrowed to one drug, and 21 days of therapy cured her fully. The authors note that modern identification tools are surfacing such rare culprits more often, and that naming the germ early lets therapy be trimmed safely.
pmc-11665458:
Abolfazl Shokri, Mohammad Amin Larki, and Ahad Ghaemi model hydrothermal carbonization of poultry litter. Their twenty twenty-four study aims to recover carbon and inorganic phosphorus. Heat and water turn the litter into higher value materials. Temperature and reaction time are the main settings under study.

One modeling approach mapped how the settings affect recovery. Two neural network models then competed to fit the data better. The multilayer perceptron model won on both accuracy and simplicity. It needed fewer neurons and gave lower error for both products. Its fit scores were near perfect in the tests reported. The results point to better nutrient recycling from farm waste streams.
pmc-11666358:
Yuan Wang and co-authors improve a key nitrogen gauge for rice in a 2024 study. The gauge tells how well fed a rice crop is, and getting it right helps farmers use fertilizer with care.

The team took leaf color readings from the first five leaves of plants across five sites and fifteen rice types. They fed those readings to machine learning models. Two tree based models did best at guessing leaf nitrogen and the nutrition index. The second leaf from the top mattered most for leaf nitrogen, and the third leaf for the index. Adding summary stats of the readings helped as well. The method points to sharper, greener fertilizer use.
pmc-11668458:
Bowel irritation and womb-lining overgrowth share pain, bloating, and hard-to-tell symptoms. Nashwa Aldardier and co-authors count their overlap in a 2024 Saudi study. The survey covers women with endometriosis at one Jeddah hospital.

Nearly half, 47.8 percent, already carried a bowel syndrome diagnosis. Saudi patients showed the overlap more than non-Saudi ones. Other traits of the women or their disease did not split the rate. Food intolerance, reflux, and colon inflammation did raise the odds. The team urges doctors to screen for both at once. Joint care could spare years of split treatment.
pmc-11669058:
Amankeldi Salybekov, Aiman Kinzhebay, and Shuzo Kobayashi review cell therapy as a route to kidney repair, in an overview from two thousand twenty-four. Kidney injury and chronic disease are rising with diabetes and high blood pressure, and current care often falls short. Transplanted cells may protect the kidney through signals they release, immune calming, and direct tissue joining.

The review follows the field from animal work to human trials. Gains appear in both sudden injury and chronic disease settings. Open problems include where cells come from, how to deliver them, and how long benefits last. Tuning dose and cell power is the next frontier, they say.
pmc-11669958:
Ming-Qi Chen and Qi-Sheng Zhang comment on sedation practice for outpatient gut procedures in a 2024 article. Scopes through the bowel or stomach are now routine day procedures, and sedation keeps patients comfortable. The risk sits in giving deep sedation to the wrong patient in a lightly staffed setting.

The piece discusses a study showing that a strict triage tool cut sedation problems and drug reversals. Sorting patients by risk upfront lets clinics match the sedation level to the person, and even complex procedures can run under lighter sedation for the right patients. In stretched health systems, that sorting protects patients and frees scarce anesthesia staff at once.
pmc-11671958:
Robert Staruch and four co-authors wrote an article in two thousand twenty-four on tissue loss in combat casualties. Progressive tissue loss has complicated limb wounds in recent conflicts. It can leave a shorter residual limb and can change how rehabilitation goes.

The authors say the burden of wounds in combat is hard to measure. Data sets are of poor quality and lack the detail needed for close analysis. Their article sets out the main hurdles in counting that burden. It also proposes simple steps to improve how data are captured in future. Better records, they argue, would help plan care and support for the war-wounded. The piece is a review and call for better data, not a trial.
pmc-11672058:
Amar Taha and co-authors study stroke risk in the year after heart bypass surgery when a new irregular heartbeat appears, in a 2024 paper. Swedish registry data covered more than ten thousand patients who developed the rhythm problem after surgery between 2007 and 2020.

Among patients sent home without blood thinners, about three percent had a stroke within a year. Prior stroke was the strongest warning sign, with age, heart failure, and past heart attack also raising risk. Two standard risk scores predicted stroke about equally well. Strikingly, most patients whose scores called for thinners were not discharged on them. The authors flag a treatment gap worth closing.
pmc-11672158:
Kevin Saulnier and five co-authors ask whether proven talk therapies for posttraumatic stress disorder also lower suicide risk in veterans, in this 2024 study. Suicide rates run high among veterans with the disorder, and the Veterans Health Administration wanted to know if its recommended therapies change that risk. The team followed veterans who received a first PTSD diagnosis between 2016 and 2019.

The cohort held eight hundred forty-seven thousand veterans, and one thousand five hundred fifty-two died by suicide through 2020. Veterans who started one of the two recommended therapies, cognitive processing therapy or prolonged exposure, faced about twenty-three percent lower suicide risk than those who never started. Completing eight or more sessions showed no added link either way. The pattern held when the comparison was limited to veterans who got some therapy. The authors read starting therapy as the step that matters most in these data.
pmc-11672458:
Wang and colleagues reported in twenty twenty-four on feeding bile acids to older laying hens. As hens age past their peak, laying can fall and fat can build up in the liver. Bile acids help break down fat during digestion. The team fed one hundred forty-four hens, aged seventy weeks, for five weeks. Birds got a plain diet or diets with a low or high dose added.

The added acids did not clearly change laying output during the trial. Treated hens had more follicles, and their eggs had heavier shells and deeper yolk color. Liver fat fell, and liver cells showed smaller fat spaces. The low dose also shifted gene activity away from making fat and toward breaking it down.
pmc-11672558:
Adriana Rodríguez-Forero and co-authors study heat needs of a tropical sea cucumber in a 2024 paper. The species is Isostichopus isabellae, a sea cucumber that may be farmed. The team kept 60 animals in tanks to learn what heat range suits them best. They tested growth, survival, and heat choice over 30 days.

Animals were held at 23 and 26 degrees, and their choice was tracked across a 20 to 29 degree range. They chose the heat they were used to, and the best survival, at 86 percent, was at 23 degrees. Weight loss did not differ between the two tank heats. The team found the top heat limit near 36.5 degrees and the low limit near 8 degrees. They advise farms to hold tanks near 23 degrees.
pmc-11672658: Huayan Chen and co-authors present a 2024 case study from the Xisha Islands. The site lies in the South China Sea. DNA barcoding maps the diversity of Dryinidae wasps there. It also maps the hosts they use. Dryinidae is a wasp family found all over the world. It holds more than nineteen hundred known species.
pmc-11672858:
Blain Thayer, Jonathan Edwards, Madeline Belk and Spencer Durham assess a protocol that lets pharmacists order a nasal PCR test for MRSA in hospital patients with pneumonia. A negative nasal test is a strong sign that MRSA is not the cause, so drugs aimed at it can be stopped. Charts were compared before and after the protocol began.

The before group held a random sample of one hundred patients, and the after group held 625. Vancomycin days of therapy fell where pharmacists ordered the tests. Average hospital stay and thirty-day readmission rates were also lower after the protocol, while death rates showed no clear change. The authors credit pharmacist-led testing with better drug use.
pmc-11673058:
Claudio Lavín, Roberto García, and Miguel Fuentes study, in a 2024 paper, how mood and confidence shape choices made under uncertainty. People update what they know from past choices and outcomes, and feelings color that process. Mood and confidence do not always move together, since they change on different time scales.

The authors propose that mood lifts or lowers confidence, and confidence in turn steers how flexibly a person switches between exploring new options and using known ones. Their results back that chain. Confidence changed learning rates and switching choices, while mood shaped how rewards felt and how confident people were. The work frames self-knowledge as a balance between feeling and judgment.
pmc-11673158:
Lu Hai and co-authors test a theory of working lives on the students it usually forgets: rural Chinese undergraduates facing a hard job market. Psychology of Working Theory holds that context shapes whether people feel free to choose work, adapt to it, and expect decency from it. Their 2024 study surveys 946 rural students, most of them women around twenty, on family atmosphere, school climate, and those work beliefs.

Both home warmth and a supportive campus predicted stronger work volition, the sense of choice despite constraints, along with career adaptability and hopes of decent work. Volition itself predicted the other two outcomes, and it carried part of the contexts' effect: good homes and schools raised adaptability and expectations by first raising the feeling of agency. The authors argue that for rural students, the road to decent work runs through the climates that raised them.
pmc-11673258:
Mikko Lammi and co-authors survey three spatial omics toolkits and what they can do for tissue engineering, in this 2024 review. The methods read gene activity, proteins, and gene-control marks while keeping each cell's place in the tissue. That lets researchers spot rare cell types and see how engineered tissues are really organized.

The review is candid about limits. Single-cell reads suffer noise and dropouts, joining the data layers is hard, and the spatial protein and epigenetic methods are slow and costly. Still, the authors expect the combined view to sharpen how builders steer cells inside constructs. Better maps of real tissue, they argue, should raise the quality of lab-grown replacements.
pmc-11673558:
Jiayin Li, Xiaomeng Liu, Deqi Zhu, Haozhe Jiang, and Gengfeng Niu wrote this research paper, published in 2024. It studies how parents' help with homework shapes Chinese students' negative emotions, and what softens or carries that effect.

Homework help is a hot topic in China, praised for lifting learning but blamed for stress at home. The team drew on a national family survey run by Peking University, ending with 494 clean cases. Analysis showed that parent involvement did sway students' bad feelings. A sense of family responsibility carried part of that effect, passing the influence along. Warm, open talk between parent and child changed the strength of the links. The authors read the results through family systems theory and suggest the findings can guide efforts to protect children's mental health.
pmc-11673858:
Cătălina Elena Bistriceanu and co-authors compare brain rhythms and network links across epilepsy types in this 2024 study. In generalized epilepsy the whole brain seizes at once, and the default mode network, active at rest, behaves oddly. The team asked whether drug-resistant cases stand apart.

They recorded brain waves from thirty-nine patients across three generalized syndromes plus twelve drug-resistant patients, with healthy controls matched for age. Two analyses ran on the same recordings: power by rhythm band, and connection strength inside the resting network. Rhythm power differed little, showing up only in one band for one syndrome. Connections told a sharper story. The three standard syndromes showed stronger links than controls, while drug-resistant patients showed weaker links. The authors suggest network measures, not rhythm power, may yield markers of who will resist drugs.
pmc-11673958:
Bojana Nedić Vasiljević and co-authors review a double life for zeolites, the sponge-like minerals with orderly pores, in a 2024 paper. Loaded with plant phenolics, zeolites can ferry these antioxidants and anticancer compounds through the body, releasing them where needed and shielding them on the way. The same pores can also strip phenolic pollutants out of wastewater.

The review weighs both roles and gives theory a guiding part, since computing can predict which pairing of guest and pore will work before lab trials. The authors sketch multipurpose materials that heal patients and clean water with one chemistry. Both uses lean on the same trait: pores sized to hold small molecules.
pmc-11674058:
Aleksandra Zienkiewicz and co-authors estimate blood pressure continuously from chest vibrations, in a study published in 2024. A cuff-free, always-on pressure tracker remains an open goal in medicine. Their signal is the seismocardiogram, the tiny chest motion from each heartbeat, timed against the electrical ECG trace. The key interval ends at a heart moment they can read from the vibration itself, rather than at the aortic valve opening used traditionally.

Data came from nine anesthetized patients across eighteen sessions, checked beat by beat against an arterial line. The new interval tracked systolic, diastolic, and mean pressure slightly better than the traditional one. A refined model using it estimated mean pressure with errors near nine to eleven millimeters of mercury. Follow-up tests held accuracy without recalibration. The authors see promise in measuring both pulses close to the heart.
pmc-11674258:
Andrea Sonaglioni and co-authors pool heart scans of babies born to mothers with pregnancy diabetes in a 2024 review. Diabetes in pregnancy is the most common such complication and can strain the fetal heart. Small past studies used speckle tracking scans to gauge heart squeeze in these babies, with mixed verdicts.

The pool held 18 studies with more than a thousand exposed babies and even more controls. Strain gauges for both heart sides ran lower in babies of diabetic mothers, in the womb and after birth. The pooled gap was firm across the set. Such strain reads may flag at risk hearts sooner than plain scans.
pmc-11674558:
Nin-Chieh Hsu and four co-authors answer ten practical questions on lung ultrasound for pneumonia care at home, in a 2024 article. Hospital-at-home programs treat acute illness in patients' houses. Ultrasound often replaces big imaging machines there. Standard and handheld scanners both serve. Probe choice and patient position follow set protocols.

A ten-point scan protocol is recommended for sensitivity. Five core patterns anchor diagnosis, from healthy air lines to solid-looking lung. Fluid around the lung is common in these patients. Its appearance hints at severity and drainage needs. Evidence is thinner for specific pneumonia causes. Atypical, tuberculosis, and ventilator-linked cases still show good detection in studies. More research inside home programs is needed. This first part covers technique and patterns; management follows in part two.
pmc-11675358:
Rajech Sharkia and co-authors update the known picture of IMNEPD, a rare inherited disease of infancy that strikes the nervous system, hormone organs, and pancreas together. The disease comes from faults in both copies of a gene called PTRH2. The paper adds a new case with a known mutation, re-tallies symptoms across all published cases, and analyzes new gene variants with structural bioinformatics.

Across cases, the most common features are motor delay, nerve damage, intellectual disability, weakness in the hands and feet, hearing loss, and poor coordination. Computer modeling showed one protein position is highly conserved, and swapping it badly destabilized the protein, which hints at why such mutations cause disease. The update gives clinicians a clearer symptom map for spotting this rare condition.
pmc-11675558:
Susan Ka Yee Chow and co-authors survey hospital nurses in Macau on how they spot and handle delirium. Published in 2024, the cross-sectional study gathered 342 nurses across hospitals, asking about knowledge, daily care behavior, and what blocks good assessment. Delirium is sudden, often reversible confusion, common in older and post surgery patients, and costly when missed.

Nurses scored in the middle range on delirium knowledge, and knowledge tracked behavior moderately. Patient related factors outweighed personal and organizational ones as barriers to assessment. Experience, longer training courses, and knowledge itself predicted stronger care behavior, while personal barrier scores pulled it down. The authors call for structured protocols and formal training to lift practice.
pmc-11675658:
Hung-Hsiang Fang and co-authors present three cases of a rare inherited disorder in a 2024 paper. Lesch-Nyhan syndrome stems from faults in a gene on the X chromosome and blocks the body's recycling of a key building block. Finding it early shapes care, yet its first signs can look vague, so whole-exome sequencing can speed the call.

All three Taiwanese boys showed high uric acid, low muscle tone, stiffness, and slow motor growth. Gene faults were found in two, and lab chemistry confirmed the third. Two had orange crystals in their diapers, a classic clue. Self-harm, the syndrome's grim hallmark, had not yet appeared in the youngest. The authors urge early gene testing when the early pattern fits.
pmc-11676158:
Hee Jin You and co-authors scan the soybean genome for defense against a root rot pathogen in a 2024 study. The water mold Phytophthora sojae menaces soybean fields worldwide, and resistant varieties are the cleanest defense.

The team tested close to a thousand soybean lines from germplasm banks against one strain of the mold. Three statistical models, run in parallel, all pointed to the same stretch of chromosome 3, a known resistance cluster. Eighteen markers inside it scored high in every model. Sorting lines by the pattern at one block split them cleanly: two patterns mostly resisted, three mostly fell ill. Breeders can now track that block when building resistant seed.
pmc-11676358:
Decsi and four co-authors test plant conditioners on maize in a paper from twenty twenty-four. They used humic acid alone and humic acid mixed with amino acids. Both are sold to boost plant health, but exact gene effects were not well known.

Field tests measured plant traits and yield after two priming treatments. Yield rose clearly in treated plants. A full gene activity scan then showed which genes switched on. Photosynthesis, cell breathing, and protein making paths were all more active. Those shifts help explain the yield gain, even in a year with extreme rain. The work links a farm input to clear changes inside the plant.
pmc-11676458:
Mariona Pont and co-authors survey treatments in 2024 for triple-negative breast cancer, an aggressive form that lacks the usual drug targets. It makes up about a sixth of breast cancer cases yet drives a far larger share of deaths. Its variety and quick drug resistance strain care.

The review lists current therapies and the trials now testing new ones. Lab-stage ideas get special attention: gene-editing tools, tiny proteins, radioactive conjugates, vaccines, and drugs that destroy target proteins. The authors also map what blocks progress, from tumor variety to delivery hurdles. New directions that may reshape care close the survey.
pmc-11676658:
Xiaoqiang Zhu and co-authors build a whole-body computer model to predict how a stroke drug candidate travels through rats, dogs, and people. SPT-07A, a form of D-borneol, is in development in China for ischemic stroke. Physiologically based models can forecast blood levels in humans before any volunteer is dosed.

Test-tube studies with liver, kidney, and gut tissue showed the drug is mainly cleared by glucuronidation, a tagging step for excretion. The model, fed those data, first reproduced rat measurements, then scaled to dog and human. A validated ladder like this de-risks first-in-human dosing and can trim animal testing along the way.
pmc-11676758:
How a droplet dries on a surface depends on whether its edge stays pinned or slides inward. Hoang Huy Vu, Nam-Trung Nguyen, and Navid Kashaninejad study this in 2024 on surfaces carved with tiny mushroom-like posts that overhang, trapping air under the drop. They compare two base materials with unlike surface energy, and posts spaced at unlike gaps.

On the lower-energy material, drops let go of the edge sooner and spent less of their drying time in the pinned mode. Narrower gaps, which raise the share of solid under the drop, held drops in place longer in both modes. The results show how surface chemistry and post layout together steer drying, which matters for cooling, printing, and self-cleaning designs.
pmc-11677158:
Qinglong Wei and five colleagues review recent progress in triboelectric nanogenerators built from electrospun nanofibers. These small devices turn touch and motion into electric power. They promise energy harvesting and self-powered sensors that need no battery.

The review first explains electrospinning and triboelectric charging in plain terms. It then surveys fiber materials, including PVDF, polyamide, polyurethane, and polyacrylonitrile, and compares how each performs. Designs range from plain fiber mats to layered and nature-inspired structures. Uses include wearables and ambient energy capture. The authors end with open problems and likely next steps for engineers in the field.
pmc-11677258:
Abdul Ghafar and co-authors present a method from two thousand twenty-four for detecting plant diseases with a real-time vision model. Early spotting of crop disease limits losses, but field checks are slow and expert eyes are scarce. The team trained a custom version of the YOLOv8 object detector to find and classify plant conditions in images.

They evaluated the model first on a held-out test subset from their data. To probe real-world strength, they then ran it on fresh images pulled from web search, which the model had never seen. Results were promising, with high accuracy across plant conditions. The authors stress the model's speed and precision, which suit live monitoring in the field, and its promise for wider farm use.
pmc-11677358:
Jing-Hua Fu and co-authors reinforce concrete beams with basalt fiber bars and steel fibers rescued from old tires. Their study appeared in 2024. Six beams were built, mixing three fiber doses with three bar ratios, then bent to failure while cameras tracked surface strain in three dimensions. The tire fibers slowed cracking, cut bending, and raised both the first-crack load and the final strength. At equal bar ratios, cracking loads rose by up to about forty-three percent and ultimate strength by up to about thirteen.

The team also adjusted the standard strength formula to credit the fibers' pull, and predictions matched the tests well. The authors pitch the pairing as a greener reinforcement: basalt bars do not rust, and the fibers turn waste tires into structure.
pmc-11677958:
Leônidas dos Santos and co-authors feed wheat a trace of selenium and watch it shrug off drought. Much of humanity runs short of selenium, and wheat is a natural delivery vehicle. In a factorial trial, five soil doses met two watering regimes, hard drought or none, with the selenium applied as sodium selenate.

Grains loaded with selenium as hoped. Low doses also enriched sulfur, iron, copper, and zinc, raised amino acids and soluble proteins, and trimmed yield losses under drought. Higher doses cut oxidative damage markers, boosted a protective enzyme, and improved water use efficiency. The authors settle on the lowest dose as the sweet spot for biofortification: better grain, less drought damage, no excess.
pmc-11678258:
Plant medicines and cannabis extracts are both used against pain, and combining them might do more than either alone. A research team tested annatto seed formulations together with a cannabidiol-rich cannabis extract in rats, in a 2024 study. They used four standard pain tests, covering chemical irritation, heat, and cold, and checked the oils' chemistry first.

The annatto oil was rich in a vitamin-E-like compound, and the cannabis oil carried much cannabidiol. Combined doses cut pain responses far more strongly than the annatto products alone. The authors describe the pairing as synergistic and suggest it deserves study as a plant-based pain strategy.
pmc-11678458:
Una-Jovana Vajic and co-authors test whether nettle leaf extract can protect the kidneys of rats bred for high blood pressure. Their study appeared in 2024. Earlier work showed the extract lowers blood pressure and fights oxidative stress across the body. Here the team asked whether it guards the kidney itself, and by what route. Rats received water, a standard pressure drug, or one of three extract doses for four weeks.

The standard drug and the middle extract dose both lowered pressure, protein leakage in urine, and signs of stress and scarring in the kidney. The effects matched those of the drug losartan. Notably, the benefit did not run through a master stress switch called NRF-2; some signals tied to that switch even fell. The authors say the extract guards the kidney by a different path.
pmc-11678658:
Storage ills that clog cells share gene misreads, yet only some burn the brain, and Karolina Wiśniewska and co-authors compared the two kinds cell by cell, in work from twenty twenty-four. Patient cell cultures from many types of the ill were read by full gene sequencing. Shared and split misreads were sorted.

A few genes misread in nearly all types, which marks them as core to the disease. A second set misread only in the brain-burning types, which makes them candidate flags for early brain risk. No easy blood test exists today for that call. These lists give the hunt a start.
pmc-11678758:
Alexios Tsikopoulos and co-authors systematically review how biofilms grow on cochlear implants, and how that growth might be stopped. A biofilm is a slimy shield of bacteria; on an implant it drives infections that often force removal and repeat surgery. Preventing it would spare patients and budgets alike.

Searching three databases through mid-2024, the team gathered lab and animal studies on biofilm formation on these hearing devices. They review how the films develop and grade experimental defenses, from surface treatments to antimicrobial strategies. Quality tools suited to each study type check the evidence. The synthesis maps what is proven, what is promising, and what remains untested.
pmc-11678858:
Hua Xu and co-authors find a gene that helps maize roots push through hard soil in a 2024 paper. Compacted soil squeezes roots and stunts crops across modern farms. A corn gene in the SPL family, switched on by the gas ethylene, stood out in their screens. Plants with extra copies of the gene kept growing roots under pressure that stalled normal plants.

Tissue slices showed the root cap, the root's battering tip, lies at the heart of the effect. The gene tunes the ethylene signal path that steers growth under squeeze. Field soils keep compacting under heavy machines, so inborn push power matters. Breeders can now look for this gene's strong forms in seed lines.
pmc-11679058:
A research team built a laser listening device that sniffs out traces of sulfur dioxide gas at parts-per-billion levels, in this 2024 paper. The gas appears when sulfur hexafluoride, an insulating gas in power gear, breaks down, so spotting it early flags failing equipment. Their sensor shines an ultraviolet laser pulse into the gas and hears the tiny sound the warmed gas makes.

The laser is a low-cost solid-state design with strong output, and the sound chamber is shaped to ring loudly while muting flow noise. Because the laser's power wobbles, each reading is scaled to the measured power. The finished sensor detected the gas down to about two parts per billion in one second. The authors present it as a sensitive guard for power systems.
pmc-11679458:
Matheus Almeida Ferreira, Cristina Celia Silveira Brandão, and Yovanka Pérez Ginoris report a 2024 bench test on cleaning lake water. Blooms of blue-green algae are on the rise, and plain water treatment does not remove the toxins they release well. One toxin is hard to break down and poses a real risk to health.

The team spiked water from Paranoá Lake in Brazil with the toxin and treated it with the Fenton process, which uses iron and peroxide. At the best mix, the process broke down nearly all of the toxin. Low pH helped a great deal, while plant matter in the water hurt the result only a little.
pmc-11679558:
Vladislav Deigin leads a team on a new peptide that boosts blood cells. Their study from twenty twenty-four deals with a ring shaped mimic. Blood cell peptides tend to break down fast in the body.

The lead ring was weighed against a known drug in mice. It raised young blood cell counts in blood and marrow. It worked when given by shot and by mouth alike. That mouth use sets it apart from most such peptides. Tests used both plain and irradiated mice for the checks. Early stage proof is set out in full.
pmc-11679758:
Lucas Muzi, Marina Antonio, and Rubén Maggio apply quality-by-design thinking to tablets of a parasite drug, in a study from 2024. Triclabendazole treats fascioliasis, a neglected tropical disease, but the drug crystallizes in more than one form, and the form can change how a tablet dissolves. The team screened crystal purity, filler choices, and compression force with a compact experimental design.

Crystal purity and cornstarch content emerged as the levers that matter. A regression model linked those settings to dissolution curves. In parallel, a near-infrared method learned to read the key settings straight off finished tablets, hitting near-quantitative accuracy on fresh samples. Its dissolution forecasts matched the real curves closely. The authors offer the paired model as a control tool from crystal to shelf.
pmc-11679858:
Celia María Curieses Andrés and four co-authors survey synthetic cathinones, stimulant drugs related to the khat plant, from two directions at once. Since the 2000s these compounds have spread through the illegal drug market as stand-ins for amphetamines and cocaine. Their many chemical forms make them hard to detect and regulate, and they are tied to poisoning, addiction, and death. The review covers their chemistry, how the body handles them, and their toxic effects.

The second direction is newer: cathinone and extracts of the khat plant can kill bacteria, including drug-resistant strains of common pathogens. That activity hints at a role in the fight against antibiotic resistance. The authors call the idea an exciting frontier for drug design, while warning that any medical use must be weighed against the strong psychoactive risks.
pmc-11680158:
Elizabeth Zumbrun and co-authors run a randomized, blinded dose-ranging study of the antiviral drug remdesivir against Ebola virus in rhesus monkeys, published in 2024. The virus kills up to ninety percent of human patients, and the drug had already shown a survival benefit in exposed monkeys. The trial pinned down how much drug, and on what schedule, works best.

Thirty monkeys were implanted with telemetry devices and central lines for monitoring and dosing. Treatment began four days after exposure, once all animals showed early disease signs and measurable virus in blood. A loading dose was followed by daily maintenance doses for eleven days, at three dose levels, against a vehicle control. Survival was tracked for six weeks after exposure. The large author team spans the collaborating institutes.
pmc-11681558:
Yun-Ting Wang and nine co-authors study tiny heart vessels that fail early under high cholesterol, in a 2024 mouse study. Before any heart damage shows, the small vessels that feed the heart can lose their flow reserve. The team fed mice a rich diet for eight weeks and tracked heart flow with sound scans, then probed the vessel lining in tissue and in lab cells.

The diet cut flow reserve while leaving heart shape and pumping untouched. Vessel linings fired up a cleanup system inside cells, run by a switch called TFEB, and swelling cells crept into the heart wall. A cholesterol-lowering drug eased all of it. In lab cells, blocking the cleanup made a harsh cholesterol by-product worse, so the authors read the cleanup as a shield.
pmc-11681858:
Tadele Gerasu and co-authors grade climate models over one Ethiopian catchment in a paper published in 2024. Regional models in the Africa-CORDEX set simulate rain and heat, but their local skill varies. The team tested single models and grouped averages against records for the Melka-Wakena catchment in the southeast.

Rankings combined many measures at daily, monthly, seasonal, and yearly scales.
