Small groups of top models often beat the full set, and a hybrid of the best single model with the group average did best for daily values. Two model families stood out for matching local heat and rain. Single best models could still serve well for long spans. The authors say such checks should guide local planning for climate change.
pmc-11681958:
Shivashankar Ajur and co-authors report the unusual case of two different congenital neck cysts appearing in one adult man. Their 2024 case report describes a patient in his early thirties with a large painless swelling on the right of his neck. Careful examination found a second, smaller swelling near the midline that moved when he swallowed or stuck out his tongue.

Those movement clues pointed to a thyroglossal cyst, while scans confirmed a branchial cyst on the right side. Each cyst type is common alone, left over from development before birth, but together they are rare. Surgeons removed the branchial cyst and performed the standard Sistrunk operation for the other in one session. The authors stress that knowing the embryology of the neck helps surgeons expect the unexpected. The case adds one more documented pairing to the literature.
pmc-11682758:
Jiashi Feng and colleagues report eye and perineal skin cancers in an aged dairy cow, in a case from 2024. Squamous cell carcinoma is a costly cattle cancer tied to sun exposure and pale skin. Eye and rear sites dominate, with slow local growth and rare spread to distant parts.

A seventeen year old Holstein arrived with a swollen shut eye and perineal lumps. Surgeons removed the eye and the largest rear mass after drugs failed to help. A year later, pus from the nose and hard breathing led to euthanasia. Postmortem work found tumour invading the sinus, plus a bacterial infection there. Lymph nodes showed reaction only, with no tumour spread inside them.
pmc-11683458:
Moyang Liu and co-authors ask how extra sets of chromosomes reshaped one of the cell's housekeeping systems in plants, in a study published in 2024. Autophagy recycles worn cell parts, and in plants it has taken on extra jobs such as splitting chloroplasts and timing flowering. Whole-genome duplication, or polyploidy, copies every gene at once, giving such systems new material to specialize.

The team catalogued nearly ninety-three thousand autophagy-associated genes across seventy-seven plant species, including Arabidopsis, tomato, and oil tea. About 46 percent of those genes traced back to polyploid events. The pattern suggests that chromosome doubling repeatedly expanded the autophagy toolkit, letting it branch into plant-specific tasks. The work links genome history to the division of labor inside plant cells.
pmc-11683658:
Jonas Roos, Ron Martin, and Robert Kaczmarczyk compare AI chatbots with students on medical image questions in a 2024 study. The test held over one thousand image based exam questions in English and German. Each model had to read the image and pick the most likely diagnosis. Student scores came from the same learning platform.

One model answered about fifty-seven percent correctly, ahead of its rival at about forty-five percent. It also skipped far more questions than the rival did. On answered items alone, it beat the average student pass rate. A student majority vote still won by a wide margin, near ninety-five percent. Both models scored better in German than in English.
pmc-11684458:
Yuancai Zhang leads a team of seven authors reviewing why teens quit organized sport. They pull the research together through an ecological lens. Youth sport helps body and mind, yet late adolescence loses many players. Their search found five hundred twelve papers. Just eleven of them fit, as peer-reviewed studies of athletes under twenty-five with real data.

Gender gaps got the most study time and did play a real part in dropout rates. By contrast, social, cultural, and ethnic roots got scant note in most studies. Factors in the mind, such as how able a teen feels and how much fun sport brings, also stood out. The team sort the causes by the levels of the Bronfenbrenner model, from the self to the wider culture. They close by naming the blind spots that future dropout research should fill first.
pmc-11685058:
Parent, Stryhn, Hammell, Fast, and Vanderstichel build a forecast model for sea lice on salmon farms in twenty twenty-four. The lice harm farmed Atlantic salmon in the Bay of Fundy in New Brunswick. Farms count lice often, and those counts go into a shared database. The team used counts from twenty sixteen to twenty twenty-one.

Their model tracks adult female lice over time at each farm. It includes treatments, water temperature, and pressure from lice at the same site and nearby sites. Pressure from nearby sites raised lice counts, and the effect fell with distance. Checks within the sample showed good accuracy for short term forecasts. The authors say farm managers can use the model to plan lice control steps.
pmc-11685158:
Atit Kumar and four co-authors compare two tools for placing breathing tubes in neck surgery patients. Their 2024 study enrolls sixty adults having planned cervical spine surgery. A stiff, unstable neck makes tube placement risky and hard. The rivals are a McCoy blade scope and a video scope from BPL.

Thirty patients were assigned to each tool by chance. The video scope took longer on average to place the tube. Yet it gave a clearer view of the voice box in far more patients. The team also logged difficulty scores, ease ratings, and body responses over time. The trade-off between speed and view can guide airway choices for fragile necks.
pmc-11687358:
Nathan Jones and a team of co-authors tested a new way to repair early tooth decay in two thousand twenty-four. Most noninvasive treatments work on the tooth surface, which may limit how well they heal a lesion below it. Their idea uses starch particles loaded with minerals, made to reach the subsurface of early lesions.

The team made particles with calcium, phosphate, and fluoride, plus a fluoride-free version. They treated natural smooth-surface lesions for twenty days, with acid challenge and artificial saliva. Scans showed the particles restored far more mineral than fluoride or water controls. The gain was strongest below the surface, and treated teeth looked less white and chalky. The work is an early lab proof of concept.
pmc-11688058:
Leiomyosarcoma is a rare cancer of smooth muscle, and its causes are poorly mapped. Jin and co-authors use Mendelian randomization, a genetics-based method that mimics a natural trial, to test whether blood lipids help cause the disease. They scan 179 lipid types against case and control data, then ask whether immune cells carry part of any effect.

Genetically higher triglycerides more than doubled the odds of the cancer, while the cancer itself showed no effect back on triglycerides. One immune cell type, CD8 positive natural killer T cells, carried about six percent of the path between the fats and the tumor. The authors present the chain as a lead for prevention research.
pmc-11688758:
Jennifer Ailshire sums lessons from a minority ageing research center in a 2024 paper. The national institute on aging renewed the University of Southern California center for five years with a 3.6 million dollar grant. The center backs junior scientists who study dementia disparities. Its home is a policy and economics institute, which shapes its angle.

The work follows how social, money, and policy paths drive gaps in dementia risk and in life with the disease. Three leaders from mixed fields run the center. Training minority ageing researchers is itself part of the remedy, since who asks the questions steers what gets asked. The paper shares what the center has learned for peers building like programs.
pmc-11688858:
Tingzhong Xue and co-authors describe co-designing a phone-based brain training program with older Chinese Americans and their adult children, in this 2024 paper. This group faces high dementia risk yet often misses prevention services due to language and travel barriers. A proven training app, BrainHQ, could reach them at home if it fit their language and customs. More than thirty training exercises were translated and adapted with the app's maker.

Focus groups with older adults explored what they saw as gains and hurdles in training. Their adult children, who often carry care duties, were interviewed apart. A hands-on workshop then brought both generations together with community partners. Participants mapped pain points and built sample fixes, shaping a program the community can trust.
pmc-11689158:
Erick Carranza and four co-authors probe how relationships, pain, and resilience intertwine in older adults, in a 2024 study. Feeling well cared for by a partner seems to ease distress in chronic illness. Yet good relationships have also been linked with reporting more pain, a puzzle worth untangling.

The team frames pain as the middle step: relationship quality may shape how much pain a person feels, which in turn sets resilience. Their analysis draws on survey data gathered during the COVID-19 years, when support was strained. A health model that splits inborn capacity from acquired resources guides the test. The work aims to show whether easing pain is the lever through which strong relationships protect well-being in later life.
pmc-11689658:
Ting Lan, Qilong Liu, Jinying Ge, and Yong Wang build a virus system that can carry and express two foreign genes at once, in work from 2024. Newcastle disease virus is a handy vector for vaccines and for cancer therapy research. Making it express two added genes together is key for multi part vaccines.

The team built a reverse genetic system for one strain, driven by a cell promoter. A glow marker gene was placed between two viral genes as its own unit. The rescued virus passed through ten rounds in eggs and kept expressing the marker. Building on that base, they add a route for a second gene. Stability tests guide the design.
pmc-11689758:
Patricia Heyn describes how remote coaching helped her father, a nursing home resident in Brazil with dementia, walk again, in a 2024 case study. As an Alzheimer's researcher turned caregiver, she pushed against care models that park older adults in wheelchairs. She applied the Age-Friendly 4Ms framework, which centers medication, mobility, mentation, and what matters most to the person.

Working through WhatsApp, she trained a local caregiver to deliver tailored physical and cognitive exercises. Within a year her father moved from wheelchair to walker, then to a cane, and finally to walking unaided, with better strength and speed. Heyn argues the case shows technology can keep families involved in care from far away.
pmc-11689858:
Lena Rebecca Richardson and five co-authors study older adults who fled abuse and now live in a shelter in western Canada. Their work, from two thousand twenty-four, asks what helps these people feel they belong.

The team re-read talks with ten clients and five staff, through a lens that puts care at the center. Three themes stood out. First, trust grew when staff gave care that bent to each person's needs. Next, clients who cared for each other felt more at home. Last, a sense that care was lacking broke trust and blocked belonging. The authors show how house rules and daily acts shape whether a shelter feels safe.
pmc-11690258:
Dakota Witzel and co-authors link daily good events to thinking skill in over one thousand adults, in a study from two thousand twenty-four. Participants kept an eight-day diary and took phone tests of planning and memory. Counts of good days, counts of good events, and mood swings around them were scored per person.

More good days and more good events tied to better planning and better memory. Stronger drops in bad mood after good events also tied to better planning. Stronger lifts in good mood tied to worse memory alone. Stress exposure and schooling were weighed in the math. Readers see good days help thought, but mood response cuts both ways.
pmc-11690358:
Eileen Graham, Rachel O'Conor, and Michael Wolf introduce a symposium on how older adults juggle several chronic diseases at once, in a 2024 paper. Carrying many conditions at once, called multimorbidity, complicates care and erodes quality of life. The symposium gathers work from three of the fifteen national Pepper Centers, a United States network devoted to keeping older adults independent. The summary previews each talk in turn.

Graham opens with findings on how a growing pile of conditions tracks with physical and mental quality of life over time, and what drives those paths. The following three talks turn to caregivers: the family and friends who keep complex care running at home. Their role in supporting health and daily life for people with many conditions is the thread. The piece maps a research agenda for ageing with multiple illnesses.
pmc-11690458:
Six authors present a study from two thousand twenty-four on partners who care for a spouse or partner living with dementia. Dementia care brings heavy stress, and it can harm the caregiver's own body and mind. The authors focus on the strengths and habits that help caregivers cope, which they call positive adaptive factors.

The study centers on Black and African American caregivers, a group past research has often missed. The authors used personal stories, gathered through narrative inquiry, to explore how culture shapes resilience in this role. A resilience framework, adapted for the study, guided how they read and sorted what caregivers told them.
pmc-11690558:
Claire Cleland and Ruth Hunter present a 2024 map of all review-level proof on city life and brain health. Cities shape minds through air, noise, design, and social life, yet the proof is scattered across many reviews. The pair gathered 57 reviews with 257 outcomes into an interactive gap map. Most reviews rated mid quality, a few high, and some low.

Proof clusters on smog and schooling, tied to dementia and general brain decline. Whole areas sit thin: traffic habits against any brain outcome, and all exposures against child brain growth. The map shows funders where the next reviews would pay off most. A living map keeps the picture fresh as new reviews land. City design choices gain an evidence compass.
pmc-11690758:
Shakshi Sharma and three co-authors study variant forms of a gene switch and their effect on cell powerhouses and aging, in a 2024 study. The switch, called SRF, turns on many muscle genes in heart and skeletal muscle. Cutting and rejoining its message yields several protein forms, and some forms rise in the human heart with age.

The team cloned two new forms found in human tissue, missing one or three segments of the full switch. They placed each form into a mouse muscle cell line and measured gene output and protein levels. A bench analyzer then tracked how well the powerhouses breathed under each form. The forms did not act alike, which suggests that the age-linked shift in forms may itself shape how aging muscle cells make energy.
pmc-11690858:
Ignacia Arteaga and four co-authors study why Latinx people in the United States face more risk of Alzheimer disease and kin forms of dementia. Their work, from two thousand twenty-four, uses close field study of daily life.

The team drew on eighty-four deep talks with older adults and family carers, plus three years of time spent in town centers in two states. They show how strong trust in kin can clash with low pay, poor care access, and ill health in the family. When care work brings in cash the home needs, strain and fights can grow. The paper links these home facts to wider bars to health.
pmc-11690958:
Losing a spouse is one of the hardest events for mental health, and friends, family, and money can soften the blow. Shekhar Chauhan, Dawn Carr, Miles Taylor, and Amanda Sonnega compared recent widows and widowers in the United States and India in 2024, using matched survey data from over seventeen hundred people. They measured depressive symptoms and asked which resources protected against them in each country.

Symptoms were lower on average in the United States sample. Having children, higher social standing, and better self-rated health protected people in both countries. Having friends and living in a rural area helped only in the United States, while rural life in India came with more symptoms. Gender mattered in neither sample.
pmc-11691158:
Daejin Kim argues that smart home technology can help older adults live safely at home longer, in this 2024 paper. Populations are aging worldwide, and most older people prefer to stay in their own homes. Standard homes, though, are not built for frailty, memory loss, or chronic disease. Kim reviews how connected sensors and devices, guided by machine learning, can fill those gaps.

The systems described adjust lights and heat on their own, watch health signs, and track daily routines for early warnings. Learning algorithms spot shifts that may signal a fall risk or a new illness. The promise is more independence with a safety net that does not feel like a hospital. Kim frames this as a new era for home health care, with design that must fit real older lives.
pmc-11691358:
Heatwaves, storms, and floods hit older adults hardest, and climate change is making all three worse. Alexandra Holland and Sadaf Milani scan the research for ways older people can adapt. Their scoping review searched the medical literature and kept 133 studies that fit the topic.

Most work dealt with extreme heat, then with natural disasters. Recurring themes were how older adults judge their own risk, and the personal steps they take, such as cooling and checking on neighbors. System-level action was thin on the ground, apart from national heat plans and changes to buildings and streets. The authors say the review can guide stronger shared defenses. They call for research that tests community and policy measures, not only personal ones.
pmc-11691658:
Cathy Maxwell and six co-authors report in twenty twenty-four on how to draw long-term care homes into research. Older adults in care homes can gain from studies on health and daily life, yet homes are hard to sign up. The work grew out of three long studies in two state areas with more than three hundred care homes.

Trust sits at the core of their method. Staff used long ties in the area, reached out to health groups, and made calls more than once. They also gave health checks and fun tasks for the people who live in the homes. Of the homes that first replied, close to half joined. The authors say steady, kind contact works best.
pmc-11691758:
Avani Shah and McKenzie Brown published a 2024 scoping review on how well pain treatment research in older adults includes minority populations. Psychological treatments for pain are a mainstay for older patients, yet evidence in minority groups is thin. The review asked three questions: were treatments tested in minorities, were minorities included enough in trials, and did any trials target minority groups specifically.

The search spanned three databases and screened fourteen thousand records down to hundreds of full texts. Eligible studies were randomized trials of psychological pain treatment with pain as the main outcome, in adults over fifty. Trials with at least ninety percent minority samples counted as minority specific. The authors close with recommendations for building research that serves the patients most often left out.
pmc-11691958:
Natalie Turner studies how easily older adults can get self-directed services through Medicaid home and community-based service waivers. Self-direction lets people control their own long-term services and supports. It rests on choice and on power over one's own care. The model lifts health results and care satisfaction. It can also give care in a way that fits a person's culture, yet it stays little used.

Each state picks which services can be self-directed and how many people may do so. So state policy shapes access. Turner used framework analysis and counts on the section 1915(c) waivers that serve older adults. Of 60 such waivers, 35 allowed self-direction. They covered 26 states and the District of Columbia. Most waivers set very low goals for uptake.
pmc-11692058:
Sinwoo Hwang and Eunhee Cho test a wearable walking robot for older adults living at home, in this 2024 study. Two-thirds of people over sixty-five need help with daily tasks, and keeping legs strong guards independence. The program ran twelve sessions over six weeks, mixing robot help with robot resistance, across varied ground rather than a flat lab floor.

Twenty-three older adults finished the program. Walking speed over ten meters, a stand-and-turn test, and a stepping test all improved clearly by the end. Leg muscle strength rose as well. The gains came in real community settings, a step past earlier controlled trials in patients. The authors present the robot program as a preventive service that could slow frailty and support independent living.
pmc-11692158:
Magdalena Delaporte and Jere Behrman link midlife work paths in Chile to how minds age later, in work from 2024. As populations age, knowing what protects late life thinking grows urgent. Work fills most of midlife, so its shape may leave a mark.

A long running Chilean survey let the team reconstruct job paths from 1980 to 2016. A trajectory model sorted men and women into four work patterns each. Those paths were then tied to later thinking scores. Men who stayed employed with high probability scored better on orientation, memory, attention, and executive tasks. For women the pattern differed by domain. The study ties labor history to cognitive aging.
pmc-11692258:
Keiko Ono published this program assessment in 2024. In May 2024, seven undergraduate nursing students from the United States joined a short exchange at a university in Japan. One day of the program focused on services for older adults, with lectures on Japan's long-term care insurance and visits to care facilities. Ono evaluated that day's impact using a qualitative design: students answered questions before and after, with group discussion in between.

Before the program, none of the students knew anything about elder services in Japan. Afterward, the share interested in such services rose from about 57 percent to about 71 percent. Their image of older adults brightened as well. Students described them as sociable, active, happy, and well cared for. Ono concludes that even a single focused day can shift how visiting students see aging in another country.
pmc-11692358:
Trials often miss their sign-up goals, and the gap widens for older, low-income, and minority volunteers. Carla Leinbach, Abigail Tice, and Janet Lopez report a recruitment fix tried in Orlando in a 2024 paper. Their team joined a university with city partners to reach diverse seniors for a funded trial. Data were gathered from May to August 2024, before and after the new plan.

Before the change, sites drew fewer than ten people each and took months to set up. Four moves changed that: city partnerships opened seventeen new senior programs, untapped places were tried, marketing ran in several languages, and inquiries were captured fast. Sites had also seen researchers as vendors, not partners. The new ties rebuilt that trust.
pmc-11692458:
Noah Brenman, Mengyuan Cheng, and Nasim Ferdows study dementia deaths in rural and urban areas in a 2024 paper. Older people form a fast-growing share of rural towns. They also face more risk factors and less access to care. The team asks whether death rates from dementia run higher in the countryside.

The authors used county data on age-adjusted death rates for the years 2018 to 2020. They sorted counties by how rural they were, from urban to far rural. Rural areas had higher dementia death rates than urban areas. The gap held even after the team took county traits into account. Rural rates ran about seven to ten percent higher. The gap also grew wider across the three years studied.
pmc-11692558:
Yalu Zhang and Ziyan Chen ask how the timing of disability shapes how older adults in China feel about their own aging, in a 2024 study. Some live with disability from youth, building years of adaptation. Others meet it late, often with more money saved but less time to adjust. Survey data from 2018 let the team weigh the two paths.

Most impaired elders in the data gained their disability after age 65. That late group felt worse about their aging, skills, and social worth than the early group. The gap yawned far wider among those who had faced elder abuse in the past year. Their odds of a bleak self-view ran many times higher. The authors say onset timing, and abuse above all, should steer how support for disabled elders is built.
pmc-11692658:
Lisa Bradley explores what turning fifty means for African American women in this 2024 qualitative study. Adult development research has largely skipped this group, so she interviewed eleven women aged fifty to fifty-five about the milestone. The study builds on ideas about overlapping identities and aging.

Across repeated interviews and several rounds of coding, three processes emerged: reflection, realization, and resolution. Together they form what Bradley names shemancipation, a freeing self-redefinition at midlife. The pattern partly matches older stage theories of midlife review and liberation. Direct quotes carry the women's voices throughout. She recommends follow-up work with new cohorts, including how the pandemic shaped this inner turn.
pmc-11692758:
Yeongin Jung and co-authors weigh in 2024 the cost value of screening for early Alzheimer disease with a blood marker. New drugs and blood tests make early finds more feasible than before. Two plans face off for adults aged sixty five and up with early brain changes.

One plan uses the blood test alone, while the other adds a brain scan to confirm positives. A hybrid model tracks costs, health gains, and disease stages over thirty five years for a thousand-person cohort. The blood-only plan wins on both axes in the runs. It adds near nine hundred quality life years in the model at lower added cost.
pmc-11692858:
Sehyun Baek and Sungkyu Lee (2024) examined how living alone changes the link between social activity and depression in older Koreans. Social participation is tied to health and life satisfaction, yet activity shrinks with age and depression rises. Using a 2022 national aging study of 6,055 people, the team ran a moderated regression to test household type as the moderator.

Social participation was linked to lower depression, as expected. The household effect was significant too: the protective link was stronger for older adults who live alone than for those who live with others. In other words, the loneliest group gained the most from taking part. The authors urge policy that raises social participation among older adults, with priority for the growing share who live alone, as a direct lever on late-life depression.
pmc-11693058:
Haruno Suzuki and Margaret Wallhagen test an old disable path model for late life sight loss, in a 2024 study. The model traces how a long ill leads to lost acts in steps. Its fit for old folks with sight loss had scant checks till this read.

Set marks grade the model on tale form and deep thought tests. Its step path from ill to lost acts reads clear and wide in scope. Step force sizes stay dim, though, a gap for health call use. The model leans on a cure lens and skips strength views. A tweak to add strength and town aids is urged.
pmc-11693158:
Lisa LaRowe and three co-authors ask older adults on opioid painkillers what might push them toward other substances if their opioids are reduced. Their qualitative study came out in 2024. Doctors are urged to taper opioids in this group, but patients may self-medicate the pain that returns.

Three focus groups with ten patients aged sixty-five to ninety-two identified the risks. Intolerable pain, no access to other treatments, distress, and a history of substance use could all drive substitution. Access to alternatives, counseling, social support, and knowing the risks pulled the other way. Participants wanted a clear tapering plan agreed in advance. The authors say deprescribing programs should build those protections in from the start.
pmc-11693358:
Jiaan Zhang studies internet use and worry among older adults in Shanghai, China, in a 2024 paper. Older people now spend more time online, and a flood of information can leave them anxious. Zhang asks whether a sense of personal control links time online to that anxiety, using fresh survey data from 428 users aged fifty-five and older.

Spending more time online went with lower information anxiety, and using the internet to talk and socialize helped most. People who felt more in control also felt less anxious. Control partly explained the link between time online and lower anxiety. Zhang suggests that support programs should build both digital skill and a sense of control.
pmc-11694658:
Yi-Xiang Chen and five co-authors defend their claim of a rare mineral in Alpine rocks, in a reply published in 2024. The mineral, coesite, forms only under extreme pressure, so finding it in surface-derived rocks proves the continental crust once sank to great depths.

Critics had suggested the signal could come from polishing contamination or from the host garnet crystal itself. The authors answer that no polishing material produces the same spectral fingerprint, and no silicon of the required kind touched their samples. Spectra taken on the garnet alone lack the disputed peak. They maintain their identification stands, with its implication that a slice of the Alps was once buried deep in a collision zone.
pmc-11696658:
Yashar Aryanfar and co-authors present a 2024 study on a hybrid heating system for Izmir, Turkey. The design pairs a geothermal heat pump with a wind turbine. Heat pumps draw on the ground's steady warmth, and the authors grade the combo on four lenses at once: energy, exergy, cost, and environmental cost.

The heat pump reached a performance coefficient of 3.916, and the system delivered about 119 kilowatts of net power. Total energy efficiency came to about 68 percent, with exergy efficiency near 45 percent. The unit cost of exergy looked competitive against standard options. An environmental factor of about 0.81 pointed to a large cut in impact. The authors present the pairing as a model for winter heating in mild coastal climates.
pmc-11697558:
Enshuo Zhang and co-authors publish a step-by-step surgical protocol for removing the lymph nodes that drain the mouse lung, while keeping the animal alive. These nodes matter for studying infection, inflammation, and cancer spread, yet working on them inside the chest is technically demanding. Few labs had a reliable in-place method.

The protocol walks through each stage: finding the lung-draining nodes, opening the chest, dissecting the nodes out, preserving the samples, and caring for the mouse afterward. Survival after surgery is a design goal throughout, so the same animal can be followed over time. The authors tested the steps in their own immunology and cancer work. They present the method as a shared standard that other labs can adopt directly. Better access to these nodes in living mice should sharpen studies of how lung diseases and tumors engage the immune system.
pmc-11698258:
Osama Eissa, Samira Diar-Bakirly, Humam Saltaji, and Tarek El-Bialy published a 2024 review of anchored spring devices for correcting Class II bite problems, where the upper jaw sits too far forward. The Forsus device pushes the lower jaw, but anchoring it to bone screws instead of teeth may change its effects. The team searched six databases for trials comparing anchored and standard versions and pooled the miniscrew studies, covering 93 patients.

Bone anchoring did not boost forward growth of the lower jaw. It did reduce the outward tilt of lower front teeth, a common side effect. Miniplate anchoring went further, even pulling those teeth back slightly, with a headgear-like effect on the upper jaw. The authors say anchoring buys tooth control, not extra jaw growth.
pmc-11698558:
A fourteen-author team reviews what happens when patients whose brain gliomas return receive a second course of focused radiation. Return of these tumors is hard to treat, and repeat radiation demands precise targeting to spare healthy brain. The team looked back at fifty-two adults treated between 2011 and 2021 at one center, most with high-grade tumors that came back a median of about twenty months after their first course.

Patients received either 30 gray in five sessions or 40 gray in ten, some alongside drug therapy and some after salvage surgery. Median survival after retreatment was twelve months. Tumors progressed inside the treated field in about two-thirds of patients, yet side effects stayed low, with severe acute harm in under six percent and lasting radiation damage in two patients. The authors judge the approach workable and tolerable, with results in line with earlier reports.
pmc-11700258:
Ruben Perellón-Alfonso and co-authors test whether the brain's excitability, measured electrically, tracks a blood marker of early Alzheimer's change. In the disease's first stages, amyloid deposits may overexcite neurons, prompting them to release the tau protein that later tangles. The team studied 658 healthy middle-aged adults from a Barcelona brain-health cohort, measuring a blood form of tau, a control marker of nerve damage, and brain-wave signs of excitability.

Both resting brain-wave markers and markers from a subsample of 47 people whose brains were briefly stimulated magnetically tracked the tau levels, especially in older participants. The stimulation-based marker predicted tau more sensitively than the resting one. No such links appeared for the control marker. The authors read excitability as a plausible early-warning signal, and a possible lever for slowing the disease's start.
pmc-11701258:
A large team led by Joachim De Jonghe keeps a living map of the gear that reads single cells and tissue maps in a 2024 review. The field shifts fast, and labs need a guide that shifts with it. The review spans bench tools sold today, from droplet rigs and plate methods to index tricks that tag many cells at once.

On the tissue side, it weighs read-by-sequence and read-by-image ways to map genes in place. New methods that could widen what drug hunts can measure get a closing look. The authors frame the piece as a working guide for labs and drug firms alike.
pmc-11701758: Dieter Schollmeyer, Paul Jirsch and Heiner Detert report the crystal structure of a small organic acid made from alpha-pinene in 2024. The compound, C12H20O4, was prepared in three steps. Its ester and acid groups sit on the same side of a slightly folded four-membered carbon ring. In the crystal, pairs of molecules link through their acid groups and stack into flat layers. Such structure reports pin down the exact geometry of terpene-derived building blocks.
pmc-11701858:
Chaochao Chen and co-authors review the two-way marriage of large language models and federated learning, in this 2024 paper. Big models hunger for quality data that privacy rules lock away; federated learning trains across owners without moving the data. Each side can also fix the other's weakness: models bring task skill to scattered training, while federation brings fresh data to models. The authors sort the fusion into three layers.

They cover part-level swaps, like using model tricks inside federated systems, through full mergers of the two frameworks. Healthcare, finance, and education get worked examples. Open problems include cost, uneven data, and attack surfaces. The review closes with directions the authors see as most promising for this fast-growing crossroads.
pmc-11708958:
Irem Seleoglu and Aynur Demirel sift in a set way lung fix-up care for lung ills that scar the lung and come from ills of the join flesh. Their 2024 review asks if care based on sport helps a group of sick folk. Their ill may stay firm with no stock drug care.

Just four studies met the bar in six stores, which shows how scant such care is here. Mid-grade proof backed gains for lung work and for how gas spreads in the lung. Work skill, grade of life, grade of short breath, and tired state all got more good with mid-grade proof. Proof was thin for gains in strength of breath and limb muscles. The team ends that such care can aid the care-based path back for these sick folk. They call for full trials to make the proof base firm.
pmc-11709458:
Michael Miller and co-authors study DNA changes in single brain cells after long-term head trauma in a 2025 paper. Repeated head impacts link to a degenerative brain disease. How that disease starts at the molecular level is still unclear. Past work showed lone neurons gain private mutations with age and in brain disease.

The team sequenced single nuclei from the front cortex of fifteen people with the trauma disease. Four more had impacts but no disease. Rates were compared with healthy and Alzheimer brains. One class of small change rose modestly, in a pattern like that in Alzheimer disease. Small insertions and deletions were far more common, mostly on one DNA strand.
pmc-11709558:
Natividad Olivar, Luis Brusco, and Daniel Cardinali review the records of patients with mild cognitive impairment who took melatonin at bedtime. Their retrospective study came out in 2025. Melatonin is the hormone that sets the sleep-wake cycle, which often frays in older adults.

Half of the two hundred fifty patients received a fast-release melatonin dose each night for twelve months, on top of their usual medication. After a year, the melatonin group scored better on standard mental status and cognitive tests. Most other test scores also favored the treated group, except one timed symbol task. Depression scores that started abnormally high improved, and patients reported better sleep and wakefulness. The authors suggest melatonin as a useful add-on treatment in everyday clinic practice.
pmc-11709658:
Qiulan Ma and a large team link an enzyme at nerve synapses to Alzheimer's disease damage and thinking decline. Their study came out in 2025. The enzyme releases a fat that the body converts into inflammatory signals, and animal work had hinted it helps destroy synapses.

The team isolated synapse preparations from donated human brains: healthy, mildly impaired, and Alzheimer's cases. The enzyme's beta form was clearly higher in both impaired groups than in healthy brains. Higher levels went with worse cognition and more of the tangles that mark the disease. The enzyme sat alongside key synapse proteins and tracked with the fat it releases and its inflammatory products. The authors ask whether dialing the enzyme down could protect synapses, a question still open.
pmc-11709758:
Aram Aslanyan and a large team give the first detailed chemical portrait of Alzheimer's plaques and tangles in living human brain. Their study came out in 2025. Brain tissue came from patients having shunt surgery for suspected fluid buildup, who had received a labeled amino acid before the operation.

Four of six participants had amyloid plaques. Different amyloid forms sat in different parts of each plaque: some concentrated in the core, others spread evenly. No labeled amyloid had been incorporated into plaques, suggesting they grow very slowly. Labeled tau, by contrast, appeared within hours, and its half-life in brain tissue worked out to about twenty-seven days. Knowing how fast these proteins turn over helps researchers judge how treatments that clear them should behave.
pmc-11709858:
Meenakshi Umar and co-authors present a 2025 conference abstract on folate shortage, a common gene variant, and COVID-19 in mice. A variant in the MTHFR gene is linked to worse COVID outcomes and higher dementia risk. The team infected normal mice and mice with one broken copy of the gene, then checked the blood-brain barrier.

Infected gene-variant mice lost slightly more weight and carried a trend toward more virus in the lungs. A key barrier seam marker dropped far more in their brains than in normal mice. Lab vessel cells grown without folate were also tested with virus spike protein. The work ties folate shortage to weaker barrier defense.
pmc-11710058:
Six authors, led by Matthew Welhaf, test in 2025 whether shaky reaction times in healthy older adults warn of coming Alzheimer's disease. Catching the illness at its first signs is a prized goal, and tests must be sharp to spot subtle change. Attention wobble, measured by how much response times vary, had already tracked with brain markers of the illness.

Nearly five hundred adults with normal thinking took a task that asked them to answer every number except one. Their response wobble was scored at the start. The study then checked who slid toward mild illness, and whether spinal fluid markers lined up with the wobble.
pmc-11710158:
People who pass eighty with their minds intact are rare and scientifically precious. Elizabeth Kaplan and co-authors studied thirteen Colombians averaging nearly ninety-five years in 2025, testing memory and thinking and scanning the hippocampus, a brain region central to memory. Seven participants were unimpaired, three reported complaints, and three met criteria for dementia.

Larger hippocampal volume went with better scores on a word list memory test, even after accounting for age, sex, head size, and daily function. The link to a general mental status score just missed significance. The authors call the findings preliminary and note the study continues with more participants and added biomarkers.
pmc-11710258:
Michiko Sekiya and co-authors searched blood samples for signs of the brain swelling tied to Alzheimer's plaques, in a study published in 2025. They used mice bred so that sticky amyloid builds up in the brain, much as it does in the human disease. A broad scan of small chemicals in blood plasma guided their search.

One chemical, a form of vitamin B3, was lower in the blood of the bred mice than in normal mice. In the brain, genes that make and use its partner compound were more active, mostly in support cells around plaques. The team suggests the blood level could serve as a sign of plaque-linked swelling. They also point to this pathway as a possible target for early treatment.
pmc-11710358:
Henne Holstege and co-authors, working with several large research consortia, studied how rare variants in the gene SORL1 affect the risk of Alzheimer's disease. The gene helps nerve cells sort and move proteins, and broken copies have long been suspected of causing the disease. Most known variants, though, are small changes whose effects were unclear.

The team first picked out the protein spots most likely to matter, then checked those variants in nearly nineteen thousand patients and close to twenty-two thousand controls. The chosen variants raised the risk of early-onset disease more than tenfold. Carriers fell ill on average more than eight years earlier than people with the normal gene. A few variants appeared only in patients and seemed to act in a stronger, dominant way. Carriers also had much lower levels of a protein fragment in spinal fluid.
pmc-11710458:
Emrah Düzel and co-authors evaluate a phone app for self-testing memory in routine care, in a 2025 paper. Mild cognitive loss needs early spotting, but clinic tests are slow and burdensome. An app called neotivCare lets patients test their own thinking at home over weeks. Doctors in German primary and specialist care offered it to about a thousand patients.

The study, named re.cogni.ze, asked doctors and patients how the app compared with standard paper tests. Satisfaction was the main measure, scored on a graded scale. Ease of use and added value in daily care were also rated. The project is described as the largest check of remote self-testing in routine German care so far. Results guide clinics weighing digital screening.
pmc-11710558:
Melissa Rosahl and co-authors explore in 2025 whether how older adults talk through everyday tasks can flag mild cognitive impairment. Small shifts in natural speech track with thinking skills. Script generation, describing the steps of making toast or coffee, offers a quick window.

Seventy-nine adults over sixty-five take part, twenty-one with mild impairment. Scripts are scored for length, key steps, extra steps, errors, and asides. The impaired group lists fewer key steps than healthy peers. Scores are set against lab thinking tests and a real-object meal task. Speech links to both test scores and real task performance. A brief talking task may thus aid early screening where full testing is scarce.
pmc-11710658:
Devaraj Chandrashekar and a large team of co-authors study in 2025 how heavy alcohol use and liver changes may drive Alzheimer's disease in mice. The liver clears a protein that builds up in the diseased brain, and heavy drinking harms the liver. That brain-liver link has been little explored.

Mice fed alcohol through the stomach for five weeks showed disease-relevant changes in brain and liver. The team checked liver levels of a key clearing protein, blood-brain barrier function, and brain immune cells. They also silenced the liver protein to test its role in brain buildup.
pmc-11710758:
Spotting who will slide from healthy thinking into mild cognitive impairment years ahead could focus prevention where it counts. Bhargav Tallapragada and co-authors draw on 2,853 cognitively healthy older adults from an international consortium. Instead of the standard memory-heavy test bundle, they let the data itself carve test scores into four domains: memory, executive function, attention and speed, and global cognition.

Over fifteen years, 309 participants progressed to impairment. The four data-driven scores, plus age and the APOE ε4 gene variant, predicted progression with 77 percent concordance, edging out the standard bundle's 74 percent. The authors argue that balanced, data-built scores catch decline spreading across domains, not just memory. The study appears in 2025.
pmc-11710858:
Yuko Denda and co-authors published this study in 2024 on patients in Japan who do not speak Japanese. Language gaps can mar every step of care, from check-ups to treatment. How patients see their own illness shapes how they cope, yet no work had tied that view to speaking skills in this group. The team sent a web survey in early 2024 and kept 354 replies.

Patients who got language help scored lower on speaking skills, yet saw their illness in a more hopeful light. Skill scores split by homeland, stay status, Japanese level, and the tools used to talk. Views of illness split by sex and like traits as well. A stronger sense of control over illness tied to better skill marks. The authors urge clinics to fund language help as part of care, not as an extra.
pmc-11712058:
Anna Rosicka and co-authors tested whether phone-based thinking tests reflect a gene risk for dementia, in this 2025 study. Carrying one gene variant raises risk, but its effect may differ by skill. Past work found strong harm on navigation tasks and mixed results elsewhere.

The study enrolled 87 healthy adults aged 44 to 67 who knew their gene status. They played game-like tasks on a phone app that tested planning, visual memory, speed, and flexible thought, plus self-ratings of memory. Carriers did not score worse overall. In raw checks they even scored better on visual memory, though that link faded after full adjustment. The authors urge care in reading phone tests as gene risk signs.
pmc-11712158:
Kenny Chi Man Chui describes a dementia care training package built in Hong Kong in a 2025 report. Stigma around dementia runs deep there, and respectful language is rare in daily care. Chui's team listened to people with dementia through interviews and observation in community and residential care.

From those voices they drew sixteen principles of proper caring attitude, branded as DemenTitude. The principles urge staff to listen more than they criticize, to trust feelings, to guard dignity, and to let care outrank speed. They were first written in Cantonese, then rendered into English. Training with the package raised positive views of dementia among staff who took part. Chui calls for wider promotion of attitude training alongside skills and knowledge.
pmc-11712258:
Reilly Moberg and Arshia A Khan study how people return favors to a humanoid robot in a 2025 experiment. Social robots work better when designers know how humans naturally act with them. Seventy-two students interacted with Pepper, a humanoid robot, while sensors on their faces read muscle signals tied to emotion.

In one version Pepper first did the person a favor by offering water. Later the robot asked the person to buy raffle tickets, and the team counted purchases. After removing outliers, the favor group bought more, which supports the idea that people repay robot kindness. Face signals for emotion rose and fell together, but they did not track ticket buying. The authors say social norms carry over to machines.
pmc-11712358:
Sinem Özçelik and co-authors compare symptoms and scan findings in early-onset Alzheimer's disease in a 2025 study. The early form, which starts before old age, often begins with language, vision, or behavior trouble rather than memory loss. The team reviewed nineteen patients whose spinal fluid confirmed the disease.

Patients fell into groups by first symptom: memory, vision and space, language, or behavior. Test scores lined up with activity on PET scans in matching brain areas. Memory scores, for example, tracked left temporal activity in the memory group. Attention scores set the language and memory groups apart. The authors say these links show how varied the early form is, and they argue for care plans fitted to each patient's pattern.
pmc-11712458:
Abeoseh Flemister and co-authors tested short sirolimus treatment in healthy carriers of the APOE4 gene, in a 2025 paper. That gene is the strongest known risk factor for late Alzheimer disease. Carriers show brain shrinkage and low blood flow decades before symptoms. Sirolimus, an approved drug that blocks the mTOR path, might restore those measures.

The trial ran at the University of Missouri. A low daily dose was given for four weeks to middle-aged, healthy carriers. Brain scans compared their volumes and flow with non-carriers. Memory-linked regions were the focus. Early results test whether a brief course can normalize the brain picture.
pmc-11712558:
Aditi Sathe and co-authors use a newer brain imaging method to study aging white matter in a 2025 paper. Standard diffusion imaging blurs areas where nerve fibers cross, which are common in the brain. Fixel-based analysis treats each fiber direction separately, giving a sharper picture of decline.

The team applied the method to see how crossing fibers shape age-related white matter change. Better measures of fiber loss matter because white matter health tracks memory and thinking in older adults. The work helps researchers choose imaging tools that reflect biology more faithfully.
pmc-11712658:
Benjamin Wolozin and co-authors report a drug-like compound, taken by mouth, that cuts tau damage in the brain. Tau tangles drive Alzheimer's disease and kin, and the protein's harm runs through RNA and stress granules, pockets that form in stressed cells. A company team hunted for small molecules that block tau's tie to those pockets.

A screen in human nerve-like cells flagged a family of compounds, and tests in rat neurons and in lab-grown human brain tissue confirmed the effect. The lead drug target sits in the proteostasis pathway, the cell's protein quality control system. Mice bred to develop tau disease took the drug daily for a month. Their brains showed strong drops in misfolded and harmful tau forms, measured by two lab methods.
pmc-11712758:
Brent Aulston and co-authors report a 2025 step toward a one shot gene therapy for Alzheimer's disease. Their lab edits the tail end of the APP gene, a gene at the center of the disease. Past work showed the edit cuts the protein's harmful cleavage and eases disease signs in animals. The open problem was delivery: all editing parts had to fit inside a single virus carrier to be clinic ready.

The team packed the editing enzyme, guide RNAs, and control elements into one such carrier. They injected it into mice bred to develop the disease. Brain tissue showed wide spread editing of the target gene end. Both plaques and insoluble amyloid, the sticky protein clumps of the disease, fell in treated tissue. The authors call the result proof of feasibility for a single injection treatment.
pmc-11712858:
Jonathan P Hulse and co-authors describe a 2025 study of vaccines aimed at tau, a protein that builds up in tangles in Alzheimer's disease and in related brain diseases called tauopathies. Each vaccine trains the immune system to spot tau at one exact site where it carries extra phosphate groups.

The team tested blood serum from vaccinated mice on slices of human brain tissue from people who had Alzheimer's disease or one of the related diseases. Serum from each vaccine did stain the tangles, but the pattern differed by site and by disease. The results suggest that a vaccine may need to match the tau form found in each disease.
pmc-11712958:
Stanislau Hrybouski and co-authors report a 2025 brain scan study of how tau buildup affects two networks anchored in the medial temporal lobe. One network serves object and face knowledge, and the other serves scenes and places. How tau relates to the working links of each network was poorly understood.

The team studied 125 people, from healthy agers to patients with clear symptoms, using MRI and two kinds of PET scans. Near links of the first network grew stronger as tau rose in people without symptoms, while the second network was affected more broadly. The contrast suggests the two networks fail in different ways as disease advances.
pmc-11713058:
Rory Boyle and a large team study brain networks and memory loss before symptoms of Alzheimer disease appear, in work from 2025. Some older adults with amyloid in the brain stay sharp, while others decline. Brain networks that support control of thought may help explain that gap.

The team used a large data set from many sites on care for people without symptoms. They tested whether links in a left control network changed the effect of amyloid on later decline. Other networks were tested as well. The work seeks signs of strength that protect thought, not just signs of disease.
pmc-11713158:
Kayla Le and co-authors link brain structure to money handling skill before dementia in 2025, using team framing since the catalog list ends with a study group name. Handling money is a key daily life skill. Its loss may warn of Alzheimer's disease early. The team studied three hundred forty four people with brain scans and a short finance test.

People with mild impairment scored far worse than healthy peers. Brain maps tied the finance score to the temporal lobe and a nearby memory area on both sides. One spot, the left parahippocampus, stood out as a predictor. The authors say these brain signs may flag early decline. Watching finance skill could help catch change before dementia sets in.
pmc-11713258:
Holt and co-authors present advances in array tomography, a method for imaging protein interactions inside human synapses at fine scale. Synapse loss tracks memory decline in Alzheimer disease, but normal microscopes blur with depth. Their 2025 work cuts resin embedded brain tissue into ribbons of very thin sections, images them in series, and rebuilds three dimensional views.

New add ons sharpen the method further. Energy transfer imaging profiled over a million synaptic spots in temporal cortex and signaled contact between amyloid and a candidate partner protein in control and Alzheimer tissue. Super resolution and DNA based imaging add more detail, and live human brain slices can be challenged with disease proteins. Analysis scripts are shared openly. The team frames the toolkit as a way to watch disease proteins meet at the synapse.
pmc-11713358:
Omonigho M Bubu presents early data and a trial plan on treating sleep apnea in Black and Hispanic adults, in a 2025 paper. Sleep apnea and heavy daytime sleepiness both raise Alzheimer's disease risk. Black and Hispanic patients carry a heavier load of Alzheimer's, worse apnea symptoms, and more sleepiness than non Hispanic white patients, yet treatment often fails them.

The proposed approach treats the whole person, pairing standard apnea care with action on the social and structural barriers that block steady use of treatment. Success is defined by breathing and sleepiness targets at three, twelve, and twenty four months. Brain imaging during an attention task and Alzheimer's markers in the body will track whether better sleep care slows disease signals. The trial targets groups usually missed by sleep research.
pmc-11713458:
Yazan Hammad and co-authors published this study in two thousand twenty-five on gene scores and amyloid build-up in the brain. APOE is the strongest known gene risk for Alzheimer's disease, but smaller gene effects are often set aside.

The team used a large Alzheimer's data set with gene data and amyloid scans for more than a thousand people. They built scores from many small gene effects, leaving out the APOE region, and a separate score that grades APOE risk by type. The APOE score tracked scan-proven amyloid strongly. A score built from spinal fluid amyloid genes also tracked it, even next to the APOE score. A tau-based score did not reach the same bar. The results say risk grading gains from genes beyond APOE.
pmc-11713558:
Terry Goldberg and three co-authors trace paths from a gene variant to psychiatric symptoms in dementia, in a 2025 study. The APOE e4 variant raises Alzheimer risk and is tied to several brain pathologies. The team asks which of those pathologies, or which losses in thinking, carry its effect on behavior.

They used an integrated national database covering 1,199 cases with behavior, cognition, and autopsy data. Layered mediation tests found many indirect paths from the gene through pathology to symptoms. Dense amyloid plaques and a tau staging measure drove the results, while diffuse plaque spread did not. Thinking limits also carried part of the effect. A direct link from the gene to memory appeared as well.
pmc-11713658:
Leticia Fernanda Palma and co-authors study what shapes thinking scores in older adults in Latin America in a 2025 paper. Poorer nations face high dementia risk, partly because schooling is often brief. Around seventy percent of cases there may go undiagnosed. Knowing which life factors track with test scores could help local clinics screen people better.

The study covered ninety-two people from one middle-income country in the region. Seventy-four were healthy older adults, and eighteen lived with Alzheimer's disease. The team measured schooling, health, and daily habits next to thinking scores. Work like this helps clinics tell normal aging from early disease in settings where most research data does not apply.
pmc-11713758:
Clemente Zúñiga Gil and co-authors reported in 2025 an early trial of natural killer cell therapy for Alzheimer's disease. The protein alpha-synuclein builds up in this disease, and natural killer cells can swallow and destroy its clumps. The treatment, SNK01, grows a patient's own killer cells outside the body without genetic changes. Eleven subjects with mild to severe disease received four infusions at rising doses.

No treatment-related side effects appeared. Nine of ten evaluable subjects held steady or improved slightly on a composite cognition score after treatment. Six of ten showed lower alpha-synuclein levels in spinal fluid than at the start. Most subjects were on the lower doses, which makes the stability notable. The authors present safety as the main proven point. Bigger trials must say whether the cells truly slow the disease.
pmc-11713858:
Bahar Niknejad and co-authors describe a community-led program that recruits Black Americans into Alzheimer's research in a 2025 paper. Black adults are often left out of prevention trials, though the disease hits them hard. One national trial aims for at least fifteen percent of members from groups usually missed. The local team built its outreach with the community, not for it.

The program grew from a partnership between a medical school, a historically Black university, and a local Alzheimer's group. Black community leaders and church leaders formed an advisory board in the Hampton Roads area of Virginia. Teaching events in trusted settings raised awareness of the disease and the trial. The paper shares a model other sites can copy.
pmc-11714058:
Luigi Lorenzini and co-authors study patterns of brain thinning in people without dementia in a 2025 paper. Different thinning patterns are known in the dementia stage of Alzheimer's disease, but less is known early on. The team used brain scans from more than thirteen hundred people in a European cohort. Most had no protein buildup in the brain, and some did. They grouped people by their pattern of thinning across brain areas.

Three patterns stood out, described as limbic led, typical Alzheimer's type, and spread across the outer brain. The team then modeled how thinning in one area may spread along brain links over time. Each pattern spread in its own way. Readers learn why early Alzheimer's may follow more than one path through the brain.
pmc-11714358:
Matthijs de Geus and co-authors used machine learning on spinal fluid proteins to tell two brain conditions apart in 2025. Alzheimer disease and normal pressure hydrocephalus can look alike in clinic, which makes diagnosis hard. Past protein studies of the second condition were small and shallow.

Fluid samples came from a neurology clinic's diagnostic taps. Patients were classed as controls, Alzheimer, or hydrocephalus by symptoms, response to a large fluid tap, and amyloid status. A deep protein scan measured thousands of proteins at once. Random forest models then searched for protein signatures that split the classes in pairs. Top features were ranked, and pathway tests showed which body processes were raised or lowered in each condition.
pmc-11714458:
Gilda Ennis and colleagues studied in 2025 how heart disease risk and kidney function relate to thinking skills in middle-aged and older Black Americans. This group faces higher rates of heart risk factors and kidney failure, both tied to dementia risk, yet the link to cognition in healthy adults was little studied. Data came from a Wisconsin study on Alzheimer's prevention.

About a quarter of participants had high ten-year heart risk. Higher blood pressure tracked with faster decline in processing speed with age, and higher past pressure with weaker language scores in older adults. Heart risk also tracked with worse attention and working memory, and poorer kidney function with weaker fluency and speed. Most findings faded after strict correction, which may reflect limited power.
pmc-11714558:
Rishabh Singh and co-authors present a 2025 study of tiny particles in the blood and the course of Alzheimer's disease. These small bubbles are shed by cells and can carry proteins from place to place. The team took blood from forty-five people in three equal groups. One group had the disease, one had mild loss of thinking skills, and one was healthy. The bubbles were drawn out and checked for size, count, and protein cargo.

People with the disease or mild loss had more of the bubbles in their blood. The bubbles also carried more of the two proteins that mark the disease. A protein that helps nerve cells connect fell step by step from health to disease. Proteins tied to swelling and immune response rose in the sick groups. The authors say blood bubbles may help track how the disease moves.
pmc-11714658:
Adults with Down syndrome face a high risk of Alzheimer's disease, so the genes behind its markers in this group matter. Kang-Hsien Fan and co-authors ran a genome-wide search in 2025 across 320 adults of European descent in a Down syndrome biomarker consortium. They linked gene data to brain tau scans and to blood levels of several tau forms.

One well-known risk gene variant showed no tie, while its protective sibling variant came with lower blood tau. Three fresh associations reached genome-wide strength, near genes on chromosomes 11, 21, and 7. Two of those spots have also been tied to tau traits in the general population. The authors present this group as a rich resource for finding genes that steer Alzheimer's markers.
pmc-11714958:
Katsumi and co-authors compare brain shrinkage patterns in a 2025 paper on Alzheimer's disease. The illness can start early in life or late, and the two forms may wear the brain down in distinct places. The team used scans from two large study groups, LEADS for early onset and ADNI for late onset. They measured cortex thickness across 211 early onset patients, 144 late onset patients, and healthy peers.

The team expected early onset cases to show more wear in side and top regions tied to space and language. Late onset cases were expected to show more wear in the inner temporal lobe, a memory hub. Scans were processed with FreeSurfer software to map thickness for each person. A head to head map of the two forms helps sharpen markers that tell the forms apart.
pmc-11715058:
Ziming Liu, Longjian Liu, Robert Heidel, and Xiaopeng Zhao use advanced machine learning to study how diet links to deaths from Alzheimer's disease. Their 2025 study draws on a large national health survey from 1988 to 1994, linked to death records through 2019. The goal is to find which food-related factors matter most.

The team compares newer transformer models with older methods such as random forests. They also use tools that explain which inputs drive each prediction. The newer models spot Alzheimer's cases with high accuracy and beat older methods on recall. Blood levels of a protein, vitamin B12, and selenium stand out as key factors. Diet patterns for this disease also differ from those for heart disease and cancer.
pmc-11715158:
How much dementia in Latin America could be dodged by fixing known risks is counted by Paradela and co-authors in a 2025 study. Global work ties about forty percent of dementia to twelve fixable risks, from low schooling to hearing loss and smoking. Rates of those risks vary by country, so the dodged share must be counted locally.

The team uses matched national surveys from seven countries in the region. Each risk's share is counted alone and in combination, with care for overlap. Prevention plans differ where schooling gaps dominate versus where blood pressure does. The counts give health ministries a ranked list for scarce funds, tuned to their own populations rather than global averages.
pmc-11715258:
Grace Tuatoo describes how a community based approach recruits American Samoans for dementia research in 2025. The study aims to find how common Alzheimer's and related diseases are in the islands. It uses blood and gene markers plus thought tests. Past abuse by outside researchers bred deep hesitancy in the community.

The team built the work on Samoan custom and respect. They first sought backing from the Office of Samoan Affairs and village mayors. That body acts as gatekeeper to villages. A mobile event in a remote village signed up ten people who could not reach the main sites. Random sampling was kept intact. More events were planned for the next year.
pmc-11715358:
Micaela Noelle Andreo and four co-authors asked whether daily well-being steers how well older adults stick with a brain game. The game, a bird-watch task played at home, trains working memory and focus shifts. Gains mean little if folk quit early. Sleep, mood, stress, and how busy a day feels could all bend play from day to day.

Fifty-six healthy adults past sixty-five played for about fifteen hours on the whole. The team logged how often each played and for how long. Time-series models then asked if past days of well-being could foretell the next day's play. For about a third of the players, it could. Group-level tests also set well-being and stick-with-it scores next to gains on a set of thought tests. The work backs care for daily life, not just game design, in home training.
pmc-11715458:
Haoqi Nina Zhao and co-authors present two tools that read diet and drug exposure from chemical fingerprints. Their 2025 paper uses untargeted metabolomics, which scans a sample's small molecules without a fixed target list. Two resources anchor the work. One is a reference set of some 3,500 foods with their spectra. The other is a drug library searched against over a billion public spectra.

The food tool traced a known Alzheimer's marker to lentils, and its diet score separated participants in a Mediterranean diet trial by their profiles. The drug tool found over a hundred drugs in brain samples from a long-running aging study, nerve, mood, and heart drugs the biggest groups. It found nearly two hundred drugs in stool samples from another cohort. A Parkinson's drug appeared in almost two thirds of one patient group. The authors offer both tools for exposure research in aging cohorts.
pmc-11715658:
Sigan Hartley tracks how cognition changes as amyloid-beta builds up in adults with Down syndrome. Adults with the syndrome tend to form amyloid plaques early and face high rates of Alzheimer's dementia later. Hartley asks when memory first starts to slip, counted in years from the point where the amyloid scan turns positive. The 2025 study drew on a shared consortium project built for this population.

The study held 167 adults with a mean age near 39, each scanned and tested twice, about 32 months apart. Memory scores began to fall about three to four years after the scan turned positive. From there, scores fell by about 1.35 points a year. On average, mild impairment sat about seven years past that point, and dementia about 13 years past it. The timeline can help trials choose when to intervene.
pmc-11715758:
Felix Michalik and co-authors studied whether a shingles vaccine can lower deaths from dementia, in a 2025 paper on England and Wales. A rule based on birth date created a natural experiment: adults just too old at the program start could never get the free vaccine, while slightly younger adults could. People on each side of that line should otherwise be much alike.

The team used death certificate data for more than five million adults over a nine year follow up. They compared the share of each birth group whose death was due to dementia, on either side of the cut off date. Their estimate was that being eligible for the vaccine lowered that share. The study builds on earlier Welsh record work that tied the same vaccine to fewer new dementia cases over seven years.
pmc-11715958:
Ma and co-authors present a 2025 review pooling cohort studies on mood disorders and later dementia. Anxiety and depression can surface decades before memory fails. Four databases were searched for long-run studies tying the two to mild impairment or Alzheimer's disease. Thirty-nine studies qualified, and pooled risk ratios were built with a random-effects model.

Anxiety raised the odds of mild impairment by about half but showed no firm link to Alzheimer's itself. Depression raised both: impairment by about a third, Alzheimer's by well over half. Evidence grades were scored with a standard tool. The authors urge doctors to treat midlife mood as a brain-health signal, not a side note.
pmc-11716058:
Heeyun An and co-authors pretrain a brain-aging model on unlabeled scans in a 2025 neuroimaging paper. Cortical thickness maps reveal how neurodegeneration thins the brain, but every prediction task used to demand its own large labeled dataset and bespoke model.

Borrowing the BERT recipe from language modeling, the team fed thickness values from sixty-eight brain regions, measured in over ten thousand MRI scans, into a model that learns by guessing masked-out values. Once pretrained on thousands of unlabeled profiles, the foundation model needs only a thin output layer to tackle classification or staging. Context-aware thickness fingerprints are the product.
pmc-11716158:
Masayuki Teramoto and co-authors ask whether calcium buildup in the heart's arteries forecasts thinking skills in midlife, in a 2025 paper. Calcium in those arteries signals vessel disease long before symptoms show. Midlife is a key window for brain aging, yet little was known about this link at that age. The team drew on a long-running study that began with young adults.

In the CARDIA study, artery calcium was measured by scan at years fifteen, twenty, and twenty-five of follow-up. Growth of the buildup was classed by set rules for people starting at zero, low, or higher levels. At year thirty-five, participants took six thinking tests covering speed, memory, and word skills. The authors compared scores between people whose artery calcium grew and those whose did not, hunting for an early heart-based warning of decline.
pmc-11716458:
Emily Hickey studies hard childhood events and the timing of Alzheimer disease in adults with Down syndrome in a 2025 paper. People with Down syndrome face a high genetic risk for the disease, yet symptoms start across a wide age range, from the late forties to the seventies. Hard early events have been linked to later decline in the general population.

Hickey checked 112 adults, with a mean age of 39 years. Eight in ten reported at least one hard childhood event, and about one in four reported four or more. More such events tracked with more anxiety, depression, and problem behavior. The study also weighed blood markers of swelling and brain scans for plaque and tau.
pmc-11716558:
Hyun Kim and co-authors published a study in 2025 on how the link between sleep and brain thickness changes with age. Poor sleep is tied to poorer brain health, but the tie may be strong at some ages and weak at others. The team looked for age ranges where sleep quality matters most for the cortex.

They studied 700 adults aged thirty-six to ninety from a national connectome project. Sleep quality came from a standard questionnaire and thickness from MRI scans. The link between sleep and thickness in two regions bent with age rather than running straight. A second data set was set aside to confirm the pattern. Timing sleep care to the right ages may protect the brain most.
pmc-11716758:
Matthew Kang and nine co-authors used data from the long-running Framingham Heart Study in a 2025 paper on schooling and brain health. Damage to the brain's smallest blood vessels is common with age and raises the risk of stroke and dementia. The team asked whether how far people went in school relates to that damage.

Brain scans from 3,367 adults were scored for five signs of small vessel damage, such as tiny strokes and bleeds. People without a high school diploma had far more damage than college graduates, and more high blood pressure and diabetes as well. After age, sex, and study group were taken into account, the gap in odds shrank and was not firm. The study hints that schooling ties into brain health partly through general health, which matters for prevention planning.
pmc-11716858:
Sakshi Kumari and Sharmistha Dey published a study in 2025 on a protein linked to swelling in the brain in Alzheimer's disease. The protein, called COX-2, rises when amyloid triggers immune cells and harms nerve cells. The pair asked whether blood levels of the protein could flag the disease early, and whether blocking it could help.

They measured the protein and its gene activity in blood from patients and healthy people. Levels were higher in patients with the disease or mild impairment, though they fell as illness wore on. A small peptide they designed bound the protein and protected nerve-like cells in the lab. Both a test and a treatment idea rest on these results.
pmc-11716958:
Dementia tests spoken in one language can misjudge people raised in another, so Rachel Yep and fifteen co-authors tried tests that need no words at all. Their 2025 study enrolled 54 unimpaired older adults in a Canadian multi-ethnic aging cohort, average age about 69, most of them women.

Each volunteer took standard paper-and-pencil cognitive tests plus two eye-tracking tasks. One asks the eyes to obey or resist a cue, probing executive control. The other watches where the eyes linger, probing visual memory. The team compared scores between white participants and those from underrepresented ethnic groups. The authors frame the study as a fairness check on a promising workaround.
pmc-11717158:

Success, complications, and procedure times were recorded, along with the newer technique's learning curve.

pmc-11717558:
Ambika Singh and co-authors hunt for the best dose of a blood shot for worn knees in a 2024 review. The ill burdens hundreds of millions of people, and shots of a patient's own platelet-rich blood have shown a power to slow the wear.

The most common plan gave three shots, a month apart. Dose size and platelet counts swung wide from study to study, as did how the blood was spun. Gains showed in pain and use scores, not in scans. The authors say the field needs one set recipe before a best dose can be named.
pmc-11721858:
Mary Higgins and co-authors explore how Irish medical students and trainee doctors approach crisis pregnancy in a 2024 qualitative study. A crisis may mean an unplanned pregnancy or a fatal fetal defect, and patients have a right to unbiased advice on all options.

The team used story completion: each participant finished a set story opening for both scenarios. Fourteen volunteers from a Dublin medical school and a national training body took part, yielding twenty-five stories. Thematic analysis found varied approaches, all anchored in the wishes of the person or couple. Stories ranged from continuing the pregnancy to ending it. The method let trainees voice sensitive stances safely, exposing training needs in counseling.
pmc-11725958:
Zhimin Chen and Xiansheng Zhang test blood markers for sorting types of premature ejaculation in a study published in 2024. The catalog lists 2025, but the text itself gives 2024. Doctors can name four types of the condition, yet they lack a lab test that tells the types apart.

Men with the lifelong type had lower serotonin and higher leptin and a stress hormone than the other groups. The other groups did not differ much from each other. Cut-off values for the three markers may help flag the lifelong type. The authors note the small sample as a limit.
pmc-11726758:

pmc-11726858:

Seventeen species showed clear killing power. The authors frame the screen as a map for follow-up work: pull out the active parts of the winning plants and test them against the resistant germs that worry health bodies most.
pmc-11726958:

pmc-11727158:

The pooled share with eye disease came to 31 percent. The review also weighs what drives the risk, such as how long a person has had diabetes.
pmc-11727858:

pmc-11727958:
Nitesh Pradhan, Deepali Chodancar, and Ugam Usgaonkar write to the editor about how two common diseases affect the aging eye's focus. pmc-11728058:
Sławomir Wojczyk and co-authors survey how 832 Polish doctors in one region cope with work stress, and how resilience shapes their habits. Their study appeared in 2024.
