Highly resilient doctors favored active coping: planning, problem solving, and engagement. Low-resilience doctors leaned away from such strategies. pmc-11728158:
Daniel Calegaro and co-authors tackled in 2024 a quiet failure mode of tiny motion sensors: the glue line where the moving part anchors can peel away under repeated shaking. They study an on-chip test device built to stress exactly that joint, and they search for the shape that stresses it most.

Full simulations of the shaking are costly, so the team used a reduced model that follows the device's natural motion surfaces. The shortcut kept the accuracy while slashing computing time. They report how the peak stress at the joint changes with the device's shape and the shaking rate. The method lets designers tune the tester before building it. The authors frame it as a reliability tool for the whole class of inertial micro-devices.
pmc-11728258:
Iwona Damps-Konstanska and co-authors review a rare form of collapsed lung that strikes around menstruation, in a 2024 paper. The condition links to tissue like the womb lining growing in the chest, though such tissue is sometimes absent. Diagnosis often comes late.

Care has two tracks: treat the acute collapse, then stop it returning, often with hormone or surgical steps. No global guidelines exist yet. The authors stress team care across lung, imaging, and women's health experts to speed diagnosis and pick the best plan.
pmc-11728458:

Readers were blind to which group each sample came from. The team found nerve endings that stayed multiply connected, with altered synapse cleanup. Such wiring may explain why the toxin stops helping and guide next steps for these patients.
pmc-11728658: Ekaterina Lyukmanova and Zakhar Shenkarev open a 2024 special issue on toxins from animal venom. Venoms hold a huge range of active compounds, called toxins, with a near-mixed spectrum of effects on the body. That range makes them a rich source of leads for new drugs. The short text serves as an opening note for the issue, which gathers work on how these compounds act and how they might be turned to medical use.
pmc-11728758:

These infections are frequent and debilitating, and avoiding antibiotics matters. The vaccine, MV140, is a whole-cell bacterial mix taken under the tongue. Its effectiveness in the Portuguese population was unknown. One hundred twenty-five patients with recurrent infections, complicated and simple, were treated and followed for twelve months. Infection frequency and severity were the main outcomes.

Thirty-eight percent stayed infection-free for the year. Another third had one or two episodes. On average, patients had about three fewer episodes per year than before. Effectiveness held across sex, weight, activity, and several risk conditions, the head text reports.
pmc-11736358:
Zeinab Ahmed and colleagues measured tick-borne pathogens in dogs and ticks in Egypt. Their 2024 study targets three agents spread by tick bites. Blood came from 110 tick-infested dogs across the study area. Five hundred fifty ticks were grouped into pools for testing. PCR assays hunted DNA of each target pathogen.

Lyme disease bacteria appeared in a few dog samples. Ehrlichia was the commonest find in both dogs and tick pools. Coxiella turned up only in samples from kenneled dogs. Some samples carried more than one pathogen at once. Overall rates stayed low but present in the region. Kennel settings showed a distinct risk pattern. The data support tick control as a health step for dogs and people.
pmc-11742458:
Shweta Parakh and five co-authors report eye inflammation after injections of a newer drug for wet macular degeneration. Their report appeared in twenty twenty-four. The drug, faricimab, was given to three patients who had stopped responding to older agents.

Two patients developed mild inflammation of the eye's gel within three days. The third showed front-of-eye inflammation the day after injection. No vessel inflammation or blockage appeared. All three settled with steroid eye drops alone. One patient had reacted before to a related drug, hinting at an immune link. The authors urge vigilance, since the same reaction can, in worse forms, threaten sight.
pmc-11742758:
Barrera-Hoffmann and co-authors report a rare labor complication in a case paper from two thousand twenty-four. Air leaked into the space around the heart and lungs during labor, a condition called Hamman's syndrome. It is often triggered by strong straining and is usually mild, but it must be told apart from more dangerous problems.

The patient was a woman aged twenty-one having her first baby. She developed air under the skin and shortness of breath during labor. X-ray and CT scans confirmed the diagnosis. She was treated with oxygen and pain relief alone, and she improved without further problems. The authors stress that fast, accurate recognition guides safe care.
pmc-11749258:

Turning the Wnt path up with a drug blocked the starter cells and the pouches they form. The team found two related genes switched on in the starter cells at just the right stage. Embryos missing those genes piled up a Wnt partner protein and failed to form pouches properly. A drug that calmed the Wnt path rescued the fault, which pins the genes as brakes on that signal.
pmc-11752858:
Bislenghi and coauthors trace 30 years of pouch surgery for ulcerative colitis. The surgery removes the colon and builds a pouch from small bowel. It is the top choice when drugs fail or pre-cancer appears. Technique and outcomes may have shifted a lot over time.

The team reviewed all pouch cases in Leuven from 1990 to 2022. The full set held 492 patients across three time spans. Main outcomes were leak at 30 days and pouch failure. New drugs before surgery grew more common in late years. The team weighed how care shifts tracked with patient results.
pmc-11770358:
Paul Erohubie and co-authors measure how often schizophrenia outpatients skip their antipsychotic medicine, and why, in a study from two thousand twenty-four. Three hundred ten adults at clinics were interviewed with standard scales for adherence, symptoms, side effects, and insight. Diagnoses were confirmed with a structured interview.

Just over half did not take their medicine as prescribed. Worse illness, substance use, and young age each raised the odds. So did weak social support, single-generation drug regimens, and sharper awareness of symptoms. The authors urge clinics to check adherence often and teach patients steadily. The fixable risks deserve the most focus, they say.
pmc-11772358:
İsmail İlbak and five co-authors explored why regular exercisers craved workouts after an earthquake disrupted their routines, in this 2024 study. When fitness centers closed and daily life broke down, committed gym-goers were forced to stop training. The team interviewed six people aged twenty-two to twenty-nine and analyzed their accounts thematically.

Two kinds of craving emerged. The first grows out of exercise addiction itself: people hooked on training feel the urge when sessions stop. The second is driven by anxiety, arising when training becomes impossible for reasons beyond a person's control. The authors note the second form carries a more clinical character. Their distinction may help support active people after disasters.
pmc-11773658:
Chettiyam Kandy and nine co-authors survey Ayurvedic doctors in Kerala, India, about millet-based diets. Diet holds a central place in Ayurveda, and interest in millets surged when 2023 was named the International Year of Millets. The online survey reached 386 practitioners with full responses.

Knowledge, attitude, and practice scores each averaged between about 5 and 6.4 out of 8. Doctors with better knowledge held far more favorable attitudes toward prescribing millet diets. Their reported practice was more positive still. The authors call practitioner knowledge satisfactory overall. They argue that education and awareness shape whether millets reach patients' plates.
pmc-11776858:
Xudong Liu and co-authors read body composition from CT scans to forecast survival in metastatic colorectal cancer treated with bevacizumab. The drug, which starves tumors of blood supply, also wastes muscle. Quantitative CT can measure muscle area and fat placement precisely, turning routine scans into a prognosis tool.

One hundred two patients starting first-line bevacizumab-based therapy were scanned a month before and a month after treatment began. Falls in muscle index and fat creeping into muscle tracked with worse outcomes. Combining those body changes with clinical features produced a predictive model. Watching the body, not just the tumor, may tell oncologists sooner whose treatment is failing.
pmc-11784058:
Alberto Elmi and co-authors test in 2024 whether richer cages change stress hormones in lab rats, using hair as the record. Hair stores hormones over months and needs no blood draw. Twenty Wistar rats lived for three months with either a standard tunnel or an extra hanging tunnel as well.

Two hormones, corticosterone and DHEA, could be measured in the hair; cortisol could not. After three months the two housing groups showed no overall difference. Females carried higher levels of all steroids than males, and males in the richer cages had higher corticosterone. The authors say bigger studies are needed to set normal ranges for hair hormones in rats.
pmc-11790558:
Pei Dai and colleagues tested brain stimulation in cerebral small vessel disease in a small exploratory study. Continuous theta burst stimulation was applied to the right prefrontal cortex. The team asked whether it could aid the brain's glymphatic clearance system. They also tracked brain network traits and cognitive function. Eleven patients took part over a two-week treatment period.

Six patients got real stimulation and five got a sham version. Clearance scores rose in most treated patients, but in fewer controls. Network measures improved in four of six treated patients and in no controls. Memory and attention scores rose for all treated patients. One backward span score was clearly higher than in controls. The authors say stimulation may aid clearance, networks, and cognition in this disease.
pmc-11790658:
Claudia Felicia Pop and a team of co-authors survey self-reported food allergy in Romanian schoolchildren, in two thousand twenty-four. Food allergy rates have risen worldwide in recent decades. Most European countries have such survey data, but Romania did not, so the team sent an online questionnaire to parents in one city.

More than seven hundred families completed the full survey. Just under nine percent reported a food allergy for their child. Cow's milk, strawberry, and egg were the most common triggers named. More than a third of allergic children had needed an emergency visit. The authors found poor sharing of medical details with school staff and call for better education.
pmc-11799258:
A first epileptic seizure late in life often has no obvious cause, and suspicion falls on the brain's small vessel disease, visible as white matter lesions. Adrian Nasca and co-authors compared MRI scans in this paper (published 2024). Their groups were 39 patients aged sixty and over with a first late seizure, patients with a mini-stroke, and other patient controls.

Total lesion volume did not separate the seizure group from the mini-stroke group. Location did: in seizure patients the lesions were shifted toward the rim just under the cortex, and statistical path analysis made that shift a significant predictor of seizures. Their gray matter was also locally thinner in movement-related regions. The authors argue that where small-vessel damage sits, not just how much there is, helps decide whether an aging brain seizes.
pmc-11805058:
Six authors, led by Nupur Dhanak, measured tooth proportions in dental students for this 2024 study. Smile design rests on a principle of gradation: front teeth should look narrower step by step as the eye moves from the center outward. Several math rules claim to fix the right widths for the upper front teeth.

The team tested how often three of those rules appear in real smiles. The rules are the golden percentage, the recurring esthetic dental proportion, and a new Tarulatha-Ruchi proportion. One hundred students from Gujarat state, aged 18 to 25 with pleasing smiles, were photographed from the front. Software then measured the widths of the upper front teeth and gums from the photos. The study reports how well each rule matches natural, good-looking teeth in this group.
pmc-11888658:
Kaliaperumal Poorana and co-authors hunt a suspect gum bacterium in plaque samples from healthy and diseased mouths, in this 2024 study. Filifactor alocis keeps turning up beside periodontitis, the gum disease that loosens teeth. Forty-five people split evenly among healthy gums, chronic disease, and the aggressive form. A PCR test measured the bacterium's load in plaque taken from under the gumline.

The germ appeared in every sample, but its load told the story. Aggressive disease carried the most, chronic disease less, and healthy mouths least, with clear statistical gaps. The deepest pockets held the heaviest loads. Clinical damage scores marched with the same order. The authors nominate the bacterium as a strong marker and likely driver of gum disease.
pmc-11891758:
Przemyslaw Wielemborek and co-authors compare hands-on therapy with surgery for moderate carpal tunnel syndrome, in a study whose head is dated 2024. The syndrome squeezes a nerve in the wrist, causing pain and weak grip. Sixty-nine patients were split into a surgery group and a manual therapy group, with five weekly therapy sessions for the latter.

Both groups had far less severe symptoms after treatment, at checks about a year later. Manual therapy improved hand function in women, and the therapy group showed higher grip strength, with clear gains in women. Quality of life also rose in women in that group. Nerve test measures showed smaller differences, with some positive trends. The authors present manual therapy as a real alternative to nerve release surgery for moderate cases, with effects that vary by sex and by outcome.
pmc-11960258:
Carminda Goersch Lamboglia and four co-authors tested the ActivityStat hypothesis in preschool children in a 2023 study. The idea is that children defend a set level of activity: move more at one time and they compensate by moving less later. Ninety-eight children in Edmonton, Canada, averaging four and a half years old, wore activity monitors for seven days.

Using a continuous-time statistical model, the team found each behavior predicted itself up to about half a day later. Light activity, vigorous activity, and still time each persisted on their own track. But no behavior predicted any other, so a burst of activity did not trigger later stillness within the window studied. The authors report no support for compensation in this age group.
pmc-11970158:
Obinna Dim, Chigozie Anene-Okeke, and Chinwe Ukwe survey herbal medicine use among pregnant women in Nsukka, Nigeria, in work from 2024. Herbal products are common in pregnancy, yet their safety is often unclear. Care teams need to know what patients use and why.

The team gave a survey to 400 women at prenatal visits in mid-2022. About two-thirds showed good knowledge of herbal medicine. More than seven in ten held a positive view of its use. Over half had used herbs at some point, though fewer used them in the current pregnancy. The results can help clinics ask about herbs with care and give safer advice.
pmc-11979758:
Eugenio Solchaga Flores and co-authors report in 2024 a surprise about how bacteria control their intake of iron. Small RNA strands fine-tune gene activity, and two such strands were already known to curb a receptor that pulls iron into the cell Escherichia coli. The team found five more strands that curb the same receptor, each switched on by a different cue.

Some strands pair near the gene's start, as expected, but others act through a folded loop far upstream, a new role for such loops. A helper protein and a cutting enzyme were both needed. Tight control by many hands, the authors argue, shows how vital the iron gate is to the cell.
pmc-12004358:
David Montefusco and colleagues trace how a fat-making enzyme subunit in the liver licenses the liver to make sugar, in this study from twenty twenty-four. High-fat feeding switches on SPTLC3, part of the machine that builds sphingolipids. Mice engineered to lack it only in the liver answered with lower fasting glucose.

Their liver cells produced less glucose, and isotope tracing showed the sugar-making pathway itself suppressed. The chain ran through signaling: without the subunit, a membrane messenger system dimmed, and the genes of gluconeogenesis lost their drive. Lipid chemistry supplied the link: a specific short-backbone sphingomyelin appears to partner with the messenger enzyme at the cell surface. The work pins a precise lipid-protein handshake behind a whole-body metabolic effect, with diabetes implications.
pmc-12118258:
Wenrui Xu and co-authors review a fainting-like illness in children in a 2024 paper. The illness, called POTS, makes the heart race when a child stands. Signs include light head, headache, blurred sight, and deep tiredness. The review sums up what drives it and how care has moved toward plans shaped for each child.

Low blood volume in the core, weak vessel squeeze, and an overactive stress response all play a part, the authors say. Good care starts with a full check of signs, body changes, and blood markers. That check guides the pick of drugs and daily habits for each child. The review traces gains since care plans began to fit the child, not just the label. It serves as a map for doctors who meet this illness in young patients.
pmc-12312158:
Wang and a large team boost solar water splitting with magnetic materials in twenty twenty-four. Splitting water with light could supply clean hydrogen fuel for the future. Performance suffers because charges recombine and oxidation is slow. Magnetic fields were an untried lever for improvement, until this work.

A thin magnetic coating was added to a bismuth vanadate photoanode. With an external magnetic field switched on, water oxidation improved clearly. Measurements showed better charge separation at the coating interface. Oxygen release at the surface was also promoted by the field. The trick worked on three other common photoanode materials as well. The authors present this as a general route to better results. It applies even to semiconductors that are not themselves magnetic.
pmc-12315758:
Walter Adame-Gonzalez and co-authors build a brain scan denoiser that does not care what scanner or resolution produced the image. Their 2024 paper introduces FONDUE, a nested network ensemble trained to clean structural MRI. The training spans three vendors, field strengths from low to ultra-high, and voxel sizes an order of magnitude apart, in healthy and diseased brains alike.

Pushing resolution raises noise, and noise corrupts the measurements morphometry studies live on. FONDUE matched or beat specialist denoisers on every test set on at least one quality metric. It also ran orders of magnitude faster on modest graphics hardware. The code, scripts, and trained weights are public. Large cohort studies process tens of thousands of scans; a fast, resolution-blind cleaner removes a quiet source of bias from all of them.
pmc-12453558:
Mazytha Kinanti Rachmania and co-authors describe a new bacterial species found in forest soil in West Java, Indonesia, in a 2024 paper. Three strains were taken from inside a decayed bamboo stem in a geothermal area. The bacteria are aerobic, stain positive, and form branched threads with spore like structures. Lab tests mapped the range of heat, acidity, and salt in which the lead strain grows, and what food sources it can break down.

Chemical study detailed the cell wall sugars, the fats, and the other molecules that mark this group of bacteria. Gene tree work placed the strains inside the genus Dictyobacter, closest to a known species. Genome size was much larger than in known relatives, and gene similarity scores fell below the cut offs for an existing species. On that combined evidence, the authors name a new species, Dictyobacter halimunensis.
pmc-12661758:
During a pandemic, a test only helps if people can reach it in time, and India had no map of that reach when COVID-19 spread. Sakshi Poddar and co-authors built that map in a 2025 study, using site lists from the national medical research council plus road and population data. They covered all states and more than seven hundred districts.

The map shows wide gaps. The middle travel time to a test site was long on foot and about fifty minutes by motor travel. Most city dwellers lived within an hour of a site by road, while rural coverage lagged well behind. Some districts had no one close to a site at all. The authors urge planners to place new sites where the gaps are worst, not where building is easiest.
pmc-12663358:
Yuxiu Yang and five co-authors wrote a 2025 study on two blood markers that together predict trouble during a heart attack hospital stay. The stress hyperglycemia ratio compares admission blood sugar with a patient's usual level. Albumin, a blood protein, reflects nutrition and inflammation. Each alone carries risk signals; their joint use was less clear.

The cohort drew 5,269 heart attack patients from a multi-center registry between January 2022 and October 2023. About 28 percent had high stress ratios and about 20 percent had low albumin. Patients with normal albumin and low stress ratios fared best, with major events in just 1.4 percent. Those with high ratios and low albumin had nearly seven times the adjusted odds of major events. Combining both markers sharpened risk sorting.
pmc-12663458:
Diego Carbonell and fifteen co-authors present a 2025 study predicting how many key immune cells a blood collection will yield for cell therapy making. The therapy, built from a patient's own T cells, has shown strong success in a fast growing lymphoma. The first step collects the cells, and a poor yield can doom the batch.

What drives yield was poorly understood, and classic statistics gave thin insight. The team trained three machine learning methods on patient records to find the markers that forecast yield. Pattern based models can weigh many clinical factors at once. The paper validates which markers hold up as predictors.
pmc-12663558:
Mehran Feizi-Dehnayebi and co-authors report a 2025 lab study of three new compounds built from isatin, a plant-linked chemical base. The team made the compounds with the help of a tiny catalyst, then checked their shapes with care. Such compounds are known for strong effects on living cells. The work pairs bench tests with computer models of how the compounds bind.

All three compounds cut the life of breast cancer cells in lab dishes, more so at higher doses and longer times. One of them also fought cell damage well, blocking up to 80 percent in the test used. Tests with DNA and a blood protein pointed to a groove-style fit on DNA. Two compounds mixed with fat more readily than a common cancer drug.
pmc-12663858:
Youn, Lee, Han, and Jeong report a rare case from 2025 in which a woman was found to have a mass in her windpipe during a routine health check. The growth measured 17 mm, and doctors removed it with a rigid scope passed through the airway. A team review of the tissue showed the cause was Rosai-Dorfman disease, a rare condition in which certain immune cells build up in tissue.

After the removal the woman had no symptoms, so doctors first watched the part of the growth outside the windpipe. Scans 20 months later showed that part had grown, and she then took steroid medicine for nine months. The growth shrank a lot and stayed stable for four years after treatment ended. The case shows that rare diseases belong on the list of possible causes of airway masses.
pmc-12664858:
Ahmed Abu-Zaid and co-authors review past reviews on resveratrol and body weight, in work from 2025. Resveratrol is a compound sold as a supplement. Past pooled studies gave mixed results, so the team gathered those studies and checked them again as one large review.

The review kept eighteen pooled studies and rated their quality with a standard tool. It found small drops in weight, body mass index, waist size, and body fat for users compared with control groups. The gains were small, not large. Readers get a careful summary of what the pooled data can and cannot prove.
pmc-12666158:
Denise Campbell-Scherer and co-authors study vaccine decision-making in immigrant communities in this 2025 paper. During the COVID-19 vaccine rollout, many people faced conflicting claims and hard choices. Cultural health brokers in Edmonton, speaking fifty-four languages between them, helped their communities sort fact from rumor. The team recorded how that help worked in real time.

Twenty-eight brokers logged 277 stories and met weekly to make sense of them. Trust stood out as the core need in most stories. Brokers built trust, kept relationships strong, and made safe spaces for group discussion. They also used community ties to remove practical barriers. Their work cut confusion and supported choices people felt good about.
pmc-12685458:
Yahua Chen, Xian Deng, Juan Wang, Qi Gan, and Guangcai Li pool trials on recovery paths and delirium, in a meta-analysis from 2025. Delirium after surgery is a common sharp drop in clear thought for adult patients. Enhanced recovery paths bundle care steps that may cut that risk across the surgery stay.

Trials compared enhanced paths with standard care in adults having planned surgery. Delirium rates fell by more than half in the enhanced care group overall. First episodes came later and lasted fewer days under enhanced care as well. Memory scores rose, walking started sooner, and hospital stays shrank in that group. Total complication rates also fell, which backs wider use of the bundled path.
pmc-12687658:
Nine authors, led by Jie Chen, built a DNA machine that times drug release inside cancer cells in this 2025 paper. Drug resistance is a leading cause of failed cancer treatment. A root cause is stemness: a subpopulation of stem-like cancer cells that shrug off chemotherapy and regrow the tumor.

The team traced stemness control to a pair of proteins, PRMT1 and SOX2. Their machine is folded DNA origami fitted with guides that home to a surface marker on stem-like cells. It carries two payloads: the chemotherapy drug cisplatin, and an inhibitor that blocks the stemness pathway. Inside the cell, the inhibitor bursts out first, triggered by a molecule abundant there. The drug follows on a schedule. Reprogramming the cell's defenses before the poison lands is the strategy, and the paper reports it can reverse resistance in their tests.
pmc-12689958:
Melanie Smith and co-authors study why some hornbill chicks starve in the nest while mates thrive in a 2025 paper. The bird's eggs hatch days apart, and the mother seals herself in a tree hole with the brood, safe from hunters. The team tracked growth and deaths in nest boxes.

First-hatched chicks grew faster and more often lived to fly. When the mother stayed in the box, later chicks grew better, as if she curbed fights over food. Small late chicks in big broods were the chief sign that a brood would shrink. Rain, standing in for food supply, nudged the odds in a smaller way.
pmc-12692658: Paramjit Tappia and Bram Ramjiawan introduce, in a 2025 editorial, a special issue on how health and disease take root before birth. A wide body of evidence now holds that the risk of adult chronic disease is shaped early, by molecular and genetic events in the womb and in infancy. The editorial frames that theme and points readers to the research the issue collects.
pmc-12692758:
Wojciech Poncyljusz and co-authors report mid-term results for a stent-plus-coil treatment of wide-neck brain aneurysms, both burst and unburst. Aneurysms are weak bulges in brain vessels, and wide necks make them hard to seal from inside the vessel. The study reviews 242 patients treated with a newer braided stent, LVIS EVO, that holds coils in place.

The stent was delivered in every case. Blood-clot events and other complications were uncommon and mostly managed during the procedure. Follow-up imaging in 228 patients showed good sealing in about ninety-five percent of cases, and most patients had favorable recovery scores. Deaths were concentrated in patients whose aneurysm had burst, reflecting the first bleed's severity. The authors call the device safe and effective for this hard aneurysm type.
pmc-12693558:
Chuangwei Wang and co-authors predict hole expansion in advanced steel in a 2025 paper. Hole expansion tests how far a punched hole can stretch before cracking. Many factors affect the result, from thickness to strain rate.

The steel is a vanadium-niobium bainitic grade for car parts. Samples were hot rolled and quenched with varied coiling temperatures. Lab forming curves and instability rules need many inputs. The team fitted a hardening exponent from mechanical tests. A necking instability curve then anchored the prediction. Readers in steel forming learn a leaner route to a key quality number.
pmc-12694458:
Sachi Tokunaga and three co-authors study zinc levels in children with migraine in a 2025 paper. About one in ten schoolchildren gets migraines, and many also feel dizzy or faint when standing. Low zinc has been linked to migraine in adults, but child data were scarce.

Records covered fifty-seven newly diagnosed patients with a median age of thirteen. Blood tests at first visit measured zinc, iron, copper, and a storage protein. Forty percent of the children fell below the zinc cutoff for deficiency. The team compared zinc status between children with and without standing intolerance. Clarifying this link could point to simple nutritional checks in pediatric headache care.
pmc-12696958:
Xiaopeng Gan and co-authors measure how steadily patients with idiopathic scoliosis hold their heads, in a spinal curve disorder that also dulls position sense and balance. Thirty patients and thirty healthy volunteers wore a triaxial motion sensor on the head through three standing tasks: firm ground, foam, and one leg. A ten-meter walk and stair climbs completed the tasks, with eleven sway measures computed.

Standing still, the patients swayed more, with sway path and jerkiness higher than controls, and the gap widened with eyes closed. Foam and one-leg standing raised the peak measures too. In motion the strategy flipped: head movement tightened during walking and stair climbing, though descent showed no gap. Some sway measures tracked spinal alignment angles on X-rays. The authors read the pair of habits as compensation for dulled position sense, and urge rehab plans that train both.
pmc-12698858:
Danila Valko and Jorge Marx Gomez share Lightning Network maps from 2019 to 2023 in a 2025 data paper. The net is the top fast-pay layer on Bitcoin, yet clean map data were scarce for study in past years. Snaps rebuilt from shared chat logs form the set, checked step by step for sound form. Each snap froze the net at a set date.

Town-grade place tags from net names enrich each node in the set for map work. The set tracks how the net grew in time and space across the four years of logs. Funds and form checks guard the build at each stage. A checked base for web shape work is the aim of the share.
pmc-12699158:
Tao Luo leads a team that tests a targeted nano drug for pancreas cancer. Their work from twenty twenty-five joins imaging and heat therapy in one. The rings carry a dye and aim at a cancer mark called uPAR.

Traits of the rings were checked in lab and in mice. After vein dosing, tumors lit up on both glow and MRI scans. The targeted rings beat plain dye and untargeted rings on contrast. With a magnet field, the rings heated and killed cancer cells. One dose plan was used in a mouse tumor model. Early stage proof is the aim.
pmc-12699258:
Nguyen Thi Mai Huong and co-authors report a 2025 food study on gluten-free cookies. The team swapped part of the rice flour in the cookies for a mung bean starch that resists gut enzymes, and used stevia in place of sugar.

They tried swap levels from fifteen to forty-five percent and checked size, color, hardness, taste, and how fast the body breaks the cookies down. More starch made the cookies darker and harder, and a thirty percent swap gave the best mix of looks and feel. That cookie held much starch that resists breakdown and scored a low mark on the blood sugar scale. Tasters liked it too, with mean scores near seven on a nine-point scale.
pmc-12700158:
Rebuilding a major vein during liver surgery calls for patch material that is safe, handy, and the right size. The eight authors report a case using the patient's own peritoneum and fascia as that patch. A 42-year-old man had an intrahepatic bile duct cancer invading two vessels. The vessels were the portal vein and the inferior vena cava. The team performed an extended right hepatectomy with segment 1 removal.

They cut out the invaded vein sections and rebuilt both vessels with a patch harvested from the left upper abdomen. The patch was sewn with fine polypropylene while keeping the veins open and at full caliber. Pathology confirmed a clear-margin R0 resection. The authors present the case, with figures and a video, as proof that this home-grown patch can enable curative surgery in advanced liver and bile duct cancer.
pmc-12700858:
Magali Vandevenne, Sara Mokhtar, Hans Bosma, Carroll Webers, Rudy Nuijts, and Tos Berendschot link air pollution to a cornea risk score, in a 2025 study. The score flags corneas prone to bulging outward, a condition called keratoconus. Data come from a large Dutch cohort of adults aged forty to seventy-five. Over six thousand eyes had detailed cornea scans. Yearly pollution levels came from a national consortium's maps.

Higher fine particle levels went with higher risk scores. Soot showed the same pattern. A related nitrogen gas showed no link. The team adjusted for age, sex, schooling, smoking, and drinking. Diabetes changed the strength of two links. The authors read the results as support for pollution as a risk factor. They also raise the idea that diabetes may partly protect the cornea. The study cannot prove cause, but it opens an environmental angle on eye disease.
pmc-12701258:
Muhammed Furkan Tosun and co-authors follow shoulder repair in non-contact athletes for at least eight years in a 2025 study. The repair sews a torn rim back after the shoulder slips out. Wounds fall into two zones of the socket track, mid or edge, and some doubted the edge zone would fare as well.

The group held 101 athletes, sixty-two with mid-zone wounds and thirty-nine with edge-zone ones. Both groups were checked for fresh slips, return to sport, and score sheets on pain and use. The title reports sound results for both zones, backing the view that zone alone should not bar the repair.
pmc-12702158:
Ianei de Oliveira Carneiro and seven co-authors study pet health in poor town zones of Salvador, Brazil, as a One Health case. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-five. Dogs and cats there face poor drains, thin food, and ill care, which keeps germ stores alive. Those stores threat pets, wild beasts, and folks alike.

Surveys plus blood and stool tests covered hundreds of dogs and cats in two zones. A paid clinic group served as the match set. Blood marks split clear twixt town and clinic beasts. Home and street facts tied to blood and germ marks in mixed ways. The team urges spay, food, worm care, and street curb steps.
pmc-12703058:
Wentao Li and co-authors review how reading single cells in their spatial context is changing disease research. Their 2025 review covers single-cell and spatial multiomics, methods that measure many molecular layers cell by cell while keeping each cell's address in the tissue. Together they reveal connections that bulk measurements blur away.

The authors first explain the tool families, then walk through uses in head and neck cancer, brain degeneration, and aging. Deep learning enters as the analyst that can digest these huge, layered datasets and trace cause chains through them. Clinically, the methods are starting to shape treatment plans and risk estimates for individual patients. The field is young and the data heavy, the authors concede. Their survey argues the payoff, a mechanistic view of disease in place, justifies the effort.
pmc-12705958:
Thuy-Tien Le and Thi Thuy Hong Nguyen published a 2025 study of workplace safety in industrial zones in Vietnam. Many factories meet safety rules on paper while workers still get hurt. The authors looked for the organizational and behavioral barriers that sit behind that gap.

They surveyed 486 employees in industrial clusters and analyzed the answers with statistical modeling. Two theories guided the work: one about how bureaucracies function, and one about how beliefs shape planned behavior. The results point to structural, cultural, and psychological factors that weaken safety performance, including safety routines treated as mere formality. Naming these barriers helps managers fix safety culture, not just paperwork.
pmc-12706058:
Lukasz Wylezinski and co-authors use machine learning to find high-risk multiple sclerosis patients and forecast their care costs. Rich claims data offer a chance to act before costs and harm spike. Multiple sclerosis care is costly relative to how few people have it.

The team studied de-identified claims for a large insured population over two years. Only a small fraction had multiple sclerosis, yet they drove a large cost share. Many regression and classification models were trained on monthly claims. The goal was to flag patients headed for the top cost tier. The models captured most of that top-tier spending in tests. They clearly beat forecasts based on past spending alone. The tool could help insurers plan support sooner.
pmc-12706658:
Angela Lee and co-authors show Americans wildly overestimate how many social media users behave badly online. Across three studies of just over a thousand people, respondents guessed that nearly half of Reddit users post severely toxic comments and nearly half of Facebook users share false news. Platform data put the true shares at a small, hyperactive minority.

The misperception held across different definitions of harm. In an experiment, people who overestimated the bad actors felt worse, saw deeper national moral decline, and misjudged what others want to see online. A short educational correction undid those effects. The authors argue that inflated villain counts quietly corrode social cohesion, and that fixing the numbers is a cheap antidote.
pmc-12706958:
Congcong Guo and co-authors study how cotton roots spread after early drought in a 2025 paper. Roots shape how well a plant copes with dry soil, but how drought at the bud stage changes root spread at later flower and boll stages was unclear. The team grew thirty cotton types in the field, with full watering for one group and cut watering for another.

At the flower stage, early drought lowered leaf green and light use values. Types were sorted into five groups from tolerant to sensitive. Tolerant types showed a sharper drop in side root angle, a smaller rise in root to shoot ratio, and higher yield than sensitive types under drought. Root shape thus links to saved yield.
pmc-12707058:
Yangyun Liu and co-authors measured in 2025 how summer flooding changes hormones and enzymes in a rare river plant during its autumn recovery. Leftover groups of the plant live on Yangtze River islands, sleep through summer floods, and regrow in autumn. Plants were flooded under controlled depth and length.

Flooded plants showed higher levels of three growth hormones and lower levels of a fourth during recovery. Two enzymes that drive carbon capture rose a great deal, while a third fell. Hormone and enzyme changes were linked in the analysis. The authors read the pattern as boosting light-based growth and easing breathing costs, which aids regrowth. Restored banks, they say, need yearly flooding.
pmc-12708658:
Hassan Karami and co-authors examine whether strains of HPV-16 differ in how they settle into the genome of Iranian patients. Type sixteen of this virus drives most cervical cancers, and its DNA often fuses into host chromosomes on the road to malignancy. The team tested one hundred twenty-five confirmed samples spanning normal tissue, precancer, and cancer.

Three lineages appeared, with lineage D making up about two thirds of cases. Viral DNA showed in three states: free-floating, fused, or mixed. The fused form grew more common with worse tissue grade and in women past forty, a statistically firm pattern. Lineage by itself, though, did not track with fusion state, leaving the integration risk spread across strains in this population.
pmc-12709758:
Ruomei Yang and six co-authors trace how frailty moves before and after diabetes begins in older Chinese adults in a 2025 cohort study. Diabetes and frailty are known partners, but the timing was murky: does frailty creep up first, or does the diagnosis speed the slide? The team used a long-running national survey of healthy longevity.

They followed nearly ten thousand adults aged sixty-five and up from 2002 to 2018, scoring frailty with a forty-three-item index. About four hundred developed diabetes. After onset, frailty climbed faster each year, above all in the skills of daily living outside basic self-care. The speed-up hit hardest the oldest, the unmarried, and the lean. The authors urge function checks right after diagnosis.
pmc-12711558:
Hermann Edlbauer and co-authors report an eleven-qubit atom processor built in silicon, in a 2025 paper. Single phosphorus atoms planted in silicon make fine qubits, since their nuclear spins hold coherence for seconds and can be read and steered precisely. Linking several atoms to one shared electron creates a small register, but a useful machine must entangle separate registers too.

Their processor joins two multi-atom registers through electron exchange. Careful calibration pushed all gate fidelities above ninety-nine percent, and Bell states between local and distant pairs reached state-of-the-art quality. The team also built shared entangled states across as many as eight nuclei. The work marks a step toward larger silicon quantum machines.
pmc-12713258:
Fen Liu and co-authors probe how poor sleep and low mood act together on high blood pressure in a 2025 study. The three states feed each other, but how they join up, and who is hit first, has stayed unclear.

The team read a large national health survey and matched the groups with care. Short sleep, long sleep, and sleep disorders each raised the risk of high pressure on their own, and so did low mood. The best span of sleep sat near seven hours a night. Cases that began early in life tied more strongly to all three risks. Where poor sleep and low mood met, they shared blame for about a fifth of cases. Computer models and a gene-based test backed the links.
pmc-12713558:
Qing Liang, Yuhuan Jia, Ruxia Shi, Dan Zhao, and Mei Luo present a 2025 study building gene markers for a rare and prized Chinese tree. The tree is valued for fine timber and good looks, and it is under national protection as an endangered species. Saving it needs knowledge of how varied its genes are.

Few gene resources existed for this tree, so the team read its genome and hunted for short repeating stretches of DNA. They found more than 790,000 such spots, which serve as markers. From a random pick of test pairs, they confirmed a working set of markers. These tools can now support surveys of the tree's gene diversity in the wild.
pmc-12714158:
The authors survey nurses who recovered from COVID-19 in three lands, asking how a sense of control and bounce-back strength relate to burnout. Their 2025 study spans Taiwan, Malaysia, and Indonesia. Pandemic strain left nurses worn out, and ways to blunt that burnout need proof.

Six hundred five nurses filled in online surveys on the three traits. Nurses in Indonesia scored highest on strength and control, while those in Malaysia reported the worst burnout. Both traits linked to lower burnout in all three lands. In Malaysia, control cut burnout head-on. In Taiwan and Indonesia, its effect ran through bounce-back strength instead. The authors urge bosses to build choice, mentoring, and sane workloads. They add that the best lever mix may differ by land and culture.
pmc-12714358:
Yetong Liu and co-authors compared heart disease risk models across many countries in a 2025 study. Doctors and policy makers use such models to estimate a person's risk over the next ten years. Yet the models may not agree, and they may work unevenly in regions with different health profiles. The team set out to map those gaps.

They used health survey data from fifty three countries and more than eighty six thousand adults without past heart disease. Three models gave very different average risk values for the same people. The gaps in who counted as moderate or high risk were large in several regions. The results warn against using one model's cut offs in a new region without checking them first.
pmc-12714758:
Zheng Li, Xiangliang Yang, and Zifu Li review in 2025 tiny gel particles that swell or shrink with their surroundings, and their uses in medicine. The gels are networks held by chemical links and by hydrogen bonds. At a set temperature they pass through a sharp change of volume.

The review explains how that change can be tuned in its position, sharpness, and range. Choices of building blocks, partners, links, shape, and even heavy water shift the switch point. Two uses lead the field: blocking blood vessels to starve tumors, and carrying drugs to tumors. Odd dips in gel traits near the switch point may themselves aid treatment. Tuned gels could one day release a drug only where the body is warm or acidic.
pmc-12714858:
Jamal Al-Saleh and four co-authors weigh the cost worth of biologic drugs for a stiff spine illness using real world data from Dubai. More than two hundred patients were tracked for two years, with costs and life quality tallied. A life long model adds a guess at long term value.

Biologic care cost far more, driven by drug price, which took most of the spend. Value per healthy year sat high but still in a range the authors call worth it, most for patients off target. Early illness and some added traits raised the ratio. Cheaper copies could lift value further.
pmc-12715058:
Syed Tawassul Hassan and co-authors track mind-loss death trends in old stroke cases in the US in a 2025 study. Mind loss adds weight to stroke harm, a top cause of death and ill in the land. Their ask is how stroke deaths in old folk with mind loss moved over time.

A land death base gives a span of over two decades for the counts at hand. Death lines name stroke as the root and mind loss as a co-cause in each case. Age-set rates per head and year shifts are the core reads.
pmc-12716058:
Kai Yan and co-authors mine two decades of US shot-harm logs for a four-germ kid shot. The study appeared in 2025. The shot guards kids past six years of age round the world. Harm logs for it in kids were thin read till now.

Near fourteen thousand logs fed the hunt. Most were mild, past nine in ten. One eye ill stood out with the top odd mark by far. Kids with lung spasm or fit ills bore high marks for wheeze and fits, most fits in two days of the shot. Kids with kidney ill showed no clear lift. Harm marks came soon past the shot as a rule.
pmc-12716558:
Timothy Nathan Kwan and six colleagues present a 2025 Australian study on the outlook for hospital patients with pericardial disease, disorders of the sac around the heart. Using records from every hospital in New South Wales between 2004 and 2021, they compared patients admitted mainly for the pericardial problem with those in whom it was a side diagnosis.

Of more than forty-five thousand patients, under half came in primarily for pericardial disease. Those patients were younger, more often male, and far less burdened by other illness, and their hospital death risk was fivefold lower, around one percent. Cancer, present in a fifth of all patients, sharply worsened the odds in both groups. The authors stress that the company a diagnosis keeps drives prognosis.
pmc-12716958:
Graders along the Welsh diabetic eye screening pathway agree only moderately, a 2025 study by Christopher Stewart and co-authors finds. Screening catches diabetes-related eye damage early, when treatment works best. Wales has run a national program since 2003, but agreement between its grading stages had not been measured.

The team reviewed 762 eyes from 486 patients referred between 2021 and 2023. First graders matched community optometrists on about sixty percent of disease grades. Community graders matched hospital specialists a little more often, and more strongly. Agreement ran higher for damage at the center of vision than for wider disease. The authors use the gaps to argue for training and quality checks.
pmc-12717058:
Julita Machlowska and co-authors map, in a 2025 study, how honey bee wings vary across southwest Asia. The bee's home range spans Europe, Africa, and that zone. Its gene wealth is worn in spots by trade queens and moved hives. Farm drugs, new pests, and germs add stress. Wing form is a cheap read of that wealth: no dear kit is called for. The team read 17,457 wings from 1,557 hives in nine lands. Each wing gave 19 set marks for a shape read, a morphometric path.

Most zone pairs split in wing shape by a clear span. The full set of wing shots sits in the open Zenodo store. Keepers and labs alike can use the path to watch bee wealth.
pmc-12717158:
Rigveda Bhave and co-authors describe a lab system that grows two kinds of immune cells from cord blood, in a study from 2025. The system makes B cells and natural killer cells, both key parts of immune defense. Older setups used mouse feeder cells, which are less like the human body. The new setup uses human bone marrow support cells and no animal serum.

The team started from stem cells found in umbilical cord blood. They tracked the growth with cell markers over time. The system yielded young B cells and mature killer cells in good shares. The stages of growth matched early human blood development in the womb. A serum-free setup keeps results steady from run to run. The platform can support work on immune disease, cancer care, and safe drug screening.
pmc-12717258:
Soon-Chan Kim and co-authors spray chemotherapy as a fine mist inside the belly to beat colon cancer in two thousand twenty-five. The method, PIPAC, pressurizes the drug aerosol so it sinks deeper into tissue than a wash can. Patient response varies, and lab models to sort that out were missing.

Mini-tumors grown from patient tissue, called organoids, were treated with the mist plus one of three classic drugs. Cisplatin gained the most, killing far more cancer cells under pressure. Gene reads showed the mist reshaping cancer pathways tied to cell spread and growth signals, plus cell-cycle gears. The organoid setup offers a test bed for picking who should get the mist treatment.
pmc-12717358:
Reham Aljalamdeh, Muna Barakat, Rami Mosleh, and Derar Abdel-Qader surveyed Jordanian pharmacy students about treating themselves with antibiotics, in a 2025 paper. Self-medication with antibiotics feeds drug resistance worldwide, and these students are future gatekeepers of the drugs. Two hundred fifty senior students answered a validated questionnaire about what they know, believe, and do.

Four in five had self-medicated with antibiotics, mostly bought from pharmacies. Amoxicillin led the list, and sore throats were the top reason. A third had changed doses mid-course, nearly a third saved leftovers, and most had recommended antibiotics to others without a prescription. Knowledge and attitude scores were good; practice was poor. The authors call the gap between knowing and doing the real finding, and a warning for training programs.
pmc-12717758:
Susan Waserman and colleagues study how subcutaneous C1 inhibitor therapy changed quality of life for Canadians with hereditary angioedema. The disease brings swelling attacks that can not be predicted and can risk life.

The study joined phone talks over one summer with a checked angioedema quality-of-life questionnaire. Twenty patients took part, half of them women, with a mean age in the early fifties, most with type one or two disease. A concept map from the talks showed what patients valued most, across physical, mental, and emotional parts, function, social life, and medical care. Patients told of better control since the therapy began. Most had fewer attacks, and many had none, or next to none. Gains for feelings stood out, with less stress and anxiety about attacks to come.
pmc-12717858:
Yuening Zhan and five co-authors test whether avoiding opioid pain drugs during chest surgery protects the mind afterward. Their trial is from two thousand twenty-five. Older patients who have keyhole lung surgery often wake with fuzzy thinking that lasts for days. The team used a drug called esketamine in place of opioids for one group.

Eighty older patients were split by chance into two groups of equal size. Fuzzy thinking within three days struck twenty percent of the no-opioid group. It struck more than forty percent of the standard group. Reaction times were also faster in the no-opioid group on the first and third days. Blood pressure and heart output stayed higher and steadier there too. The gap just missed the usual bar for firm proof, the authors note.
pmc-12717958:
Dilay Gök Korucu and five co-authors study in 2025 how seizures shape birth outcomes for pregnant women with epilepsy. Seizure timing and type may sway risks for mother and baby. Care teams need clear facts to plan delivery and drug choices.

Records cover 100 pregnant women with epilepsy and 200 healthy controls at one center. Cesarean birth runs high in the epilepsy group at 71 percent. Babies born small for their age are also more common there. Seizure type alone shows little link to most outcomes. A seizure in the year before conception stands out: those babies arrive earlier and weigh less. The authors urge close watch for that group.
pmc-12718158:
Mauro Spina and four co-authors report in 2025 on a two-stage operation for the most severe, stiff cases of teenage spinal curvature. Adolescent idiopathic scoliosis this extreme, with curves past one hundred degrees that barely bend, cannot be safely fixed in one pass.

Between 2019 and 2024, nine patients, most of them fifteen years old, had the staged repair at one center. First came dense screw fixation plus a temporary magnetically controlled growing rod to ease the spine straighter; the final correction followed. The team reviewed the X-ray and clinical results of this gradual approach to a dangerous deformity.
pmc-12718258:
Testing a fungus against drugs guides treatment, but testing every sample wastes effort when a whole species is sure to resist. Cornelia Lass-Flörl and Sevtap Arikan-Akdagli review when labs should run such tests, focusing on resistance built into a species rather than picked up over time. They draw guidelines and recent papers into a selective testing plan.

Some patterns are fixed: one yeast shrugs off fluconazole, the Mucorales fungi resist short-tailed azoles, and Cryptococcus species resist echinocandins. The authors note that the European and American standards bodies use different terms for these categories. They recommend reserving routine testing for deep or rare infections, failed treatments, outbreaks, and trials of new drugs, which saves resources while protecting patients.
pmc-12718458:
Christian Petitjean and Julien Labreuche ask, in a 2025 study, whether diabetes makes a dangerous dip in brain blood flow more likely during neck artery surgery. Surgeons repair narrowed carotid arteries to prevent stroke, and while the artery is clamped, some brains lack backup flow. That state, hemodynamic cerebral ischemia, shows itself during surgery when a shunt proves needed.

The team reviewed operations on 4,117 arteries in 3,745 patients treated from 1990 to 2019. A quarter of the patients had diabetes. Flow failure struck eleven percent of diabetic cases against about seven percent of others, a clear excess that held up in the odds analysis. The authors suggest this extra risk may help explain why strokes hit diabetic patients harder and why their surgery carries more danger.
pmc-12718558:
Umesh Kawalkar and co-authors explore, in a 2025 study, why type 2 diabetes is often found late in rural western Vidarbha, India. The team spoke with health workers, doctors, and patients in Akola district. They held key interviews, patient talks, and group talks with community health workers, then sorted the themes that came up.

Blocks the team found include gaps in staff knowledge, low health reading skills among patients, weak referral links, and short supplies. Helpful steps include staff training, screening at home, awareness work in villages, and support from specialists. The study builds a map of system, staff, and community factors that shape care. It argues that early testing and care need work on all three levels at once.
pmc-12719958:
Chan Mi Park, Hyeon Ok Kim, and Eun Jee Lee test a bundled care program for older adults living alone in rural Korea in a 2025 study. A public health sub-center ran art, craft, garden, and movement sessions. Health checks and lessons joined the mix. Thirty-two elders took part in a before and after design.

Thinking scores improved after the program, and low mood eased. Life quality tied to health rose clearly as well. Systolic blood pressure, though, climbed during the period. The authors urge wider roles for local health centers in elder care. Bundled social and health support can lift mind and mood even in small rural posts.
pmc-12721758:
Akunchan Shrestha and ten co-authors describe a rare tooth-related tumor in an older woman. Their case report was published in twenty twenty-five. The tumor, a dentinogenic ghost cell tumor, makes up under half of one percent of jaw tumors and mimics other lesions.

The seventy-one-year-old patient had facial swelling and pain at the front of the upper jaw, from below the eye toward the cheek. Scans showed a hollow, expanding lesion with dense contents and a thinned wall. Under the microscope, ghost cells with calcification, island-like growths, and dentin-like material confirmed the diagnosis. Wide surgical removal was the treatment. The report walks through the signs that separate this rarity from its look-alikes.
pmc-12722258:
Endale Alemayehu Ali and co-authors studied heat and pandemic deaths in Belgium in two thousand twenty-five. Extreme heat and the COVID pandemic each raised death rates. Their overlap may have pushed risk higher still. The team focused on Flanders, the northern region of Belgium. They asked whether the two threats amplified each other.

Daily death counts were matched with heat and case data. The study window ran from two thousand eighteen to two thousand twenty-one. A case-crossover design compared risky days with calmer ones. Models allowed heat effects to unfold over two weeks. Results split the period before and during the pandemic. The findings help cities plan for heat during future outbreaks. Protecting older residents sits at the heart of that planning.
pmc-12722358:
Thirteen authors compare centromere evolution in two sister plant genera in this 2025 study. Most species park a single centromere on each chromosome, the spot where spindle fibers attach. A minority spread it along the whole chromosome, and how such holocentromeres arise is an open puzzle.

One genus carries huge single centromeres; the other is fully holocentric. Both showed chromosome wide histone marks unlike typical species, and they shared an altered kinetochore protein, with further changes in one genus. Genome maps suggested the holocentromeres formed fresh rather than by spreading. The authors propose a model joining kinetochore mutations, changed histone patterns, and repeat DNA growth.
pmc-12722558:
Phoebe Asplin and four co-authors test whether Google search data can stand in for real illness counts. Their 2025 study uses a large winter survey of COVID-19 in England from 2023 and 2024. The survey gave a rare ground truth for symptoms in the community. The team turned survey rates into counts of new cases and matched them against Google Trends data, symptom by symptom.

For sore throat, the search data tracked the survey growth rate closely. For most symptoms, though, search trends lagged the survey by days, and the lag shifted by age group. The authors conclude that search data can help track illness, but it works unevenly and should back up, not replace, direct surveys.
pmc-12722658:
Colin Shing Yat Yung and co-authors question routine biopsies of broken hip bones in older patients in a 2025 study. After a hip fracture in someone with a cancer history, the removed ball of the thigh bone often goes to the lab by habit. Whether that habit helps patients or just burns money was unclear.

Twenty years of records at one center held over fourteen hundred such specimens, from patients averaging about eighty-two years old. Only a small share, roughly three in a hundred, came back positive for disease. Most positives already looked suspect on scans, lacked any injury story, or came with warning pain beforehand. Just over half of the positive cases saw any change in care afterward, mostly toward comfort-focused treatment. With each exam costing hundreds of dollars, the authors urge tighter selection.
pmc-12722858:
Ghaith Mansour, Ahmad Hajjar, and Muhammad Sajid review treatments that target iron control in blood diseases. Iron balance hinges on hepcidin, a hormone that works through ferroportin, the only channel that exports iron from cells. When this axis fails, iron builds up or reaches the wrong tissues.

The review explains the signals that tune hepcidin, including bone morphogenetic protein pathways and erythroferrone. It surveys new drugs such as luspatercept, matriptase-2 blockers, and anti-hemojuvelin antibodies. It also covers ferroptosis, an iron-driven form of cell death now eyed as a drug target. Trial results show promise, though the authors stress gaps in patient selection and long-term proof.
pmc-12723258:
A gene that tags proteins with fatty chains may also drive how fast a face ages. Xueyao Cai and four co-authors used genetic methods in 2025 to test whether the gene ZDHHC17 causes facial skin aging, and whether DNA methylation sits in the middle of that path.

Mendelian randomization, which uses gene variants as natural experiments, tied higher expression of the gene to greater facial aging risk in data from over 420,000 people. A second method confirmed the link. Mediation analysis then asked whether methylation marks on DNA steer the gene's expression, and so the aging. Sensitivity checks probed the result's sturdiness. The authors present the chain as a fresh angle on skin aging biology.
pmc-12723658:
Amine Sijilmassi and co-authors tested whether facts about immigrants' efforts soften hostility to immigration, in this 2025 study. Hostile views are widespread in Western nations. The team focused on perceived deservingness: intent to contribute and struggle to get ahead.

A survey experiment with 480 people showed low-status immigrants judged more kindly when such traits were clear. Two follow-up studies during the 2024 European and French elections gave voters a short fact treatment. False beliefs about immigrants fell sharply, opposition dipped modestly, and vote effects were smaller. The authors offer deservingness cues as a practical lever on prejudice.
pmc-12723858:
Ian Moura, Kaitlin Stober, Joseph Caldwell, and Teresa Nguyen measured how many adults with disabilities in the United States identify as LGBTQ+. Both groups face health gaps, yet their overlap has rarely been counted. The team used a large phone health survey from twenty twenty-two, with over two hundred seventy thousand replies across thirty-one states.

Thirteen percent of adults with a disability identified as LGBTQ+, against seven percent of others. Among those needing long-term daily help, the share rose to sixteen percent, the highest of any group. The link between such needs and identity was strong. The authors say better counts can guide fairer health care and support services.
pmc-12727758:
Francesca Caselli and co-authors uncover a fresh role for BPC gene regulators in shaping the female part of the Arabidopsis flower. That part, the gynoecium, guards eggs, guides pollen tubes, and ripens into fruit. Plants with several BPC faults grow weakly, bear small fruit, and form a faulty inner wall.

The team shows that class one and class two BPC proteins tune distinct gene sets for carpel growth and hormone paths. Two key genes for the inner wall and the pollen track fall quiet when BPC genes fail. As a result, the wall and track form poorly in mutant plants. A gene for auxin flow also drops. Naming direct BPC targets like these explains how one regulator family steers the whole reproductive chamber.
pmc-12729058:
Qinyan Xu and co-authors pool trials of nursing care for women in fertility treatment in a 2025 review. Assisted reproduction brings anxiety and depression to many patients. Single studies of nursing support disagree on how much it helps. The team gathered the trials in a systematic review and meta analysis, sorting support types against each other.

Outcomes tracked anxiety and depression scores across intervention kinds. Pooling can reveal which style of care earns its keep and which adds little. Fertility clinics run on tight margins, so evidence for where nurses help most guides staffing. The review also exposes where trial quality needs to rise before firm claims can stand.
pmc-12729158:
Zengshu Huang and co-authors published this fertility study in 2025. Embryos are often frozen for later transfer, and sometimes thawed ones must be frozen a second time. Clinics worry the extra freeze harms the odds of a baby. The team sifted more than thirteen thousand transfer cycles from one center, spanning 2018 to 2022, and matched like cases against each other.

After matching, 107 cycles used twice-frozen embryos and 214 used once-frozen ones. The twice-frozen group had far lower pregnancy and live birth rates. The harm showed most in women under thirty-five and in single-embryo transfers. Babies who were born looked alike in weight and health. The authors advise clinics to limit second freezes for younger women and to save the best-grade embryos when a refreeze is a must.
pmc-12729258:
Fatemeh Vakili and co-authors study how social conditions shape menopause symptoms among Iranian women, in a 2025 paper. Symptoms in midlife can cut deeply into quality of life, and their roots may lie partly outside the body.

The team surveyed 465 women aged forty-five to fifty-five at health centers in Kashan. A path model sorted direct from indirect effects. Domestic violence and higher child counts worsened symptoms directly. Social support and physical activity protected against them. Income, age, and a spouse's schooling acted through those middle factors. Higher body weight worsened symptoms both ways. The authors suggest screening for social risk alongside medical care.
pmc-12729358:
People react to hard life events in very different ways, and a 2025 study by Yanli Zhu and co-authors sorts those reactions into patterns. The work draws on self-determination theory and asks how well a person's basic mental needs are met when stress hits.

A survey of 1,596 people in China, most of them young adults, was sorted with a person-centered method into four groups. One group stayed self-focused, one turned stress into aggression, one mixed aggression with other drives, and one leaned toward helping others. The groups also differed in empathy and in how fully their basic needs were met. The authors say support programs should be shaped for each pattern, not offered as one size for all.
pmc-12729658:
Rui Cui and co-authors build a mattress that reads the heart's signal through bedding, in this 2025 paper. Skin-free sensing promises comfy, long-run heart watch during sleep. Older versions caught only the main spike of each beat.

Their layered pad uses cloth electrodes and tuned circuits to catch the full wave shape. Across four sleep poses, beat spotting hit near-perfect rates. Timing errors for wave points and gaps stayed in single-digit thousandths of a second, close to clinic gear. Users rated the pad comfy, and wear tests held up. The authors lay the ground for sleep labs to adopt the pad.
pmc-12729958:
Ragnoli and co-authors present a 2025 registry study on cancer types in patients with obstructive sleep apnea. Broken sleep and nightly low oxygen may feed tumor growth, above all in oxygen-sensitive urinary tissues. The team reviewed fifty patients in the Vercelli hospital registry who had both apnea and cancer. Diagnoses were taken at the time apnea was found, before airway therapy began.

Urinary tract cancers led the list at about a third of cases. Breast, bowel, and lung cancers followed at lower shares. A tenth of patients had cancers at more than one site. Those with urinary cancers were mostly men with high blood pressure and good therapy adherence. The authors urge vigilance in this group.
pmc-12730058:
Victor Abreu de Lima and eight co-authors redesign the crates that carry chickens to slaughter, using airflow simulation to cool the birds. Transport heat stress threatens poultry welfare and survival, yet crate engineering has seen little research. Four virtual crate designs were compared against the conventional box.

Computational fluid dynamics modeled internal airflow at three transport speeds, and scaled prototypes in a wind tunnel checked the predictions. One alternative design raised average internal air velocity by about a third over the conventional crate at highway speed. It also ran cooler and less humid, with the best thermal comfort indices of the set. Wind tunnel results confirmed real differences among designs. Better crates, the authors argue, are a cheap welfare intervention.
pmc-12730158:
Luo and seven co-authors report a study from twenty twenty-five on a germ behind udder infection in dairy goats. Outbreaks at a farm in Jiangxi Province had cost farmers heavily. The team took tissue and milk samples from sick goats for lab work. Stains, chemical tests, and gene reads name the germ as Staphylococcus caprae. Tests in mice confirm the germ is strongly disease-causing. They then screen thirty antibiotics and many herbal options against it.

Several standard antibiotics work well against the germ in dishes. Penicillin works worst among the drugs they test. Some herbal medicines and plant extracts rival the drugs in effect. The authors list options for treatment and prevention on the farm. They say the work guards goat health and dairy safety.
pmc-12730558:
Chenyu Pan and co-authors compare two ways of deliberately forgetting words. Volunteers saw words flagged to remember or forget. One group cleared their minds and let traces fade. The other rehearsed other words to crowd the unwanted ones out. Brain waves were recorded throughout.

Both tactics erased the flagged words equally well. The active group, though, remembered the keepers better, having shifted attention toward them. Brain signals told the same story in different rhythms for each tactic. The passive group's late cue signals carried the forgetting mark. The active group's mark moved to the test phase. The study shows forgetting style shapes what survives.
pmc-12730758:
Kaige Sun and co-authors count cancer risk factors among workers in China. Their 2025 study draws baseline data from 841 employees at fifteen workplaces in three cities. The survey feeds a workplace prevention trial, so the risks found set its targets.

Smoking touched over a third of workers, almost all of them men. Drinking was reported by nearly two thirds, and half were inactive. Almost everyone carried two or more poor diet habits. Regional quirks stood out, like betel chewing concentrated in one city. Screening and vaccine gaps were wide. The authors call for prevention tailored by region and job type.
pmc-12731058:
Efstathia Liatsou and seven co-authors review where artificial intelligence now stands in stomach cancer care, in this 2025 review. Models already help watch risky stomach lesions, read tumor tissue, sort patients by outlook, and plan treatment. The authors screened the latest studies across diagnosis, pathology, and prognosis.

The tools keep gaining ground in clinics, they find, but every study so far lacks the gold-standard design: a large randomized trial. Data quality, uneven algorithms, and hard-to-read outputs also hold the field back. The authors call for models trained on big shared datasets and then proven in multicenter randomized studies. Only that, they argue, will move AI from promising to standard care.
pmc-12731358:
Alexandru Oprita and co-authors report three separate cancers found at once in one patient in a 2025 paper, with a review. Triple primary cancers are extremely rare and hard to diagnose and treat. Their patient was a seventy six year old man with masses in the liver, left kidney, and right lung. Lab work confirmed three distinct cancers, one of each organ type.

A tumor board advised surgery for the liver and kidney tumors and focused radiation for the lung tumor. He had both surgeries but suffered severe complications and died. The review found eighty three relevant cases, none with this exact organ trio. Readers see why full workup and team based, tailored plans matter in such rare cases.
pmc-12731458:
Virag Bartek, Marta Csire, Greta Kiss, Reka Hodula, and Artur Beke study a virus infection that can pass from mother to baby before birth. Their study is from two thousand twenty-five, using cases from a university clinic in Hungary over more than two decades. The virus is a common herpes-family member that often causes no symptoms in adults.

In one hundred thirty confirmed cases, mothers were offered a test of the fluid around the baby. The virus was found there in eleven cases, about eight percent. Follow-up covered one hundred sixteen births. Eighteen newborns had complications, some with more than one. Brain and nerve problems were the most common type, followed by eye problems. The study links signs seen on scans during pregnancy with outcomes after birth.
pmc-12731758:
Vanesa Cabeza-Fernández and co-authors review new drug targets in a family of enzymes that tag proteins with a sugar based mark. Their paper from 2025 deals with PARP enzymes, which keep cells in balance and play a role in many diseases. Most past work centered on the members tied to DNA repair.

A smaller subset of the family, which adds a single mark rather than a chain, has drawn growing notice in the last decade. These members guide cell growth, early development, and disease paths. The cycle of adding and removing the mark must stay in fine balance. The review weighs drugs that block the adders or the removers as cancer care, and the hard parts of making them act on one target only.
pmc-12731958:
Stem cells from shed baby teeth are easy to gather and can form several tissue types. Marina Miteva and co-authors sorted those cells by two surface markers to see if the sorts differ in skill. Magnetic sorting split cells into marker-high and marker-low groups for each marker, one at a time. The groups were then pushed toward bone, fat, and cartilage. Stains confirmed the cells' identity markers.

Cells high in the first marker made bone less well than their low peers. Cells high in the second marker excelled at both bone and fat. Cartilage formation looked unchanged in flat culture. Picking the second marker's high group could enrich cells for bone repair work.
pmc-12732058:
Fan Huang and co-authors report a 2025 study that hunts for marker genes in ischemic stroke, where a blocked vessel starves part of the brain. The team focused on genes tied to a form of cell death called ferroptosis and to immune cells that enter the tissue. Few past studies had joined those two threads.

Computer checks found four key genes with strong test value for the illness. Rat tests after blocked and restored blood flow showed brain harm and signs of that cell death. Three of the genes rose in the rats, and all four tied closely to immune cell levels in the tissue.
pmc-12732358:
Yuqing Zhao and co-authors characterized a food-grade bacterium that breaks down uric acid, in a 2025 study. The strain came from traditional fermented vegetables and showed strong uric acid lowering in early tests. High uric acid drives gout, so a safe microbe that degrades it draws interest.

The strain proved harmless in blood and enzyme tests, stuck well to surfaces, and fought other germs. It degraded about 29 percent of uric acid in vitro and all of two related compounds. Its genome, about 3.2 million letters long, holds a complete cluster of uric acid breakdown genes, with eight copies of one of them. The authors call it the first such genomic map for its species.
pmc-12732658:
Tomasz Urbanowicz and co-authors ask, in 2025, whether a blood protein tied to immunity tracks coronary artery disease risk. Podoplanin is known from clotting and immune work, and its role in artery clogging was unclear. One hundred fifty patients with chronic coronary symptoms underwent angiography and blood testing at one center.

Patients with confirmed disease had clearly lower podoplanin levels than controls. The more arteries involved, the lower the level ran. In diabetic patients, the protein also moved opposite to a blood sugar marker, and it correlated with heart pumping strength. The authors read podoplanin as a marker of the immune side of coronary disease.
pmc-12732758:
César Cerecedo-Zapata and a large team wrote a 2025 report on fifteen years of work on myotonic dystrophy type 1 in Mexico. The disease stems from a repeated stretch in one gene and affects many body systems. In poorer countries, gene testing and full care are often scarce. Their center is the national reference site for such diseases.

The team tested more than eight hundred people at risk over the study span. About half were confirmed as carriers of the gene change. Classic and youth forms were the most common types seen. Repeat length tracked with the form of disease. A small share had broken repeat patterns and milder illness.
pmc-12732858:
Jeong Yong Lee and nine co-authors test gene variants in Korean women with repeated pregnancy loss, in a 2025 study. Losing two or more pregnancies in a row affects about five percent of couples, and over half of cases stay unexplained. The gene studied helps control blood clotting and plays a part in pregnancy.

The team compared 388 women with unexplained repeated loss against 377 healthy women. Six variants in the gene were read from blood samples. One variant's double-copy form came with a clearly higher risk of loss. Certain combinations of variants also raised risk, and the pattern held in larger combinations. The results add a clotting gene to the list of factors clinics may one day screen for after repeated losses.
pmc-12732958:
