Zubritskaya and co-authors present a 2025 study on telling how much radiation a stored potato received. Food irradiation extends shelf life, but dose checks usually need pricey gear and can miss low doses. The team tested a cheap chemical fingerprint method on raw tubers kept in cold storage. Potato extracts ran through plate reactions whose rates were read by light signals.

The method sorted doses into broad bands, none, low, and high, on the day of treatment and after two and six days. By day six the call was right at least ninety-seven percent of the time. Treated and untreated tubers split apart cleanly in the models. The authors pitch the test for routine food control.
pmc-12733158:
Di Feng and co-authors compare the meat quality of largemouth bass raised indoors in recycled water against bass raised in a classic outdoor pond. Both groups came from the same young stock and grew for ten months. The indoor system packed fish densely in concrete tanks, while the pond spread them thin over a large earthen area.

Indoor fish gave firmer, springier flesh with denser fibers. Their meat also held more protein and more of the prized omega-3 fats. A few taste amino acids ran lower, but off-flavor chemicals dropped sharply, so flavor read cleaner overall. The authors offer the trial as a guide for steering bass quality in the indoor system.
pmc-12734358:
Megumi Matsuyama and seven colleagues published a dental trial report in two thousand twenty-five on mouth splints for teeth grinding in sleep. Grinding, called sleep bruxism, wears teeth and strains jaw muscles. Splints can guide the jaw in different ways, and it is unclear which guidance works best.

Twenty-four adults with sleep grinding each wore two splint types in turn, one favouring balanced contact and one guided by the canine teeth. Each splint was worn at home for over a month. Muscle activity sensors and sleep recorders tracked the nights. Twenty-three people finished, and the two splints showed no clear differences in muscle activity, sleep pattern, or comfort. The authors treat the small trial as groundwork for a larger one.
pmc-12734458:
Min-Gi Kim and co-authors tune a press process for vinyl-coated metal sheets in work from 2025. Such sheets clad home goods, but pressing them can peel the coat or crease the sheet. Heat and damp air make both flaws more apt to form.

The team first set a safe strain line from dome tests and soak tests. They then ran press sims across four key settings and trained a deep network on the results. The network could call flaws with high accuracy without a fresh sim each time. A search for best trade-offs found settings that held both flaws in check at once. A check sim backed the pick. The method gives plants a fast, firm way to set press rules before real sheets are cut.
pmc-12734558:
Hubert Danielewski and co-authors evaluate laser welds joining two high-alloy stainless steels with a filler metal. The two steels differ in heat and strength traits, which complicates welding. A 309L filler may ease the joint between them.

The team compared welds made with and without the filler. Both welds showed pillar, cellular, and branched crystal forms. They differed in crystal growth direction and ferrite content. The filled joint showed a lower thermal gradient across the weld. Precipitates appeared near one steel side in the welds. Strength and structure tests weighed overall joint quality. The results support filler use for such mixed steel joints in plant service.
pmc-12735158:
Yaqian Liang and five co-authors sequence a hundred and one strains of the bacterium behind most cow udder infections, and census the dormant viruses hiding in their genomes, in this 2025 study. Staphylococcus aureus from dairy herds keeps evolving drug resistance. One suspected courier is the prophage, a virus genome stitched into the bacterium's own, capable of carrying cargo genes between strains.

The strains came from large dairy farms in Xinjiang. Resistance ranged wildly by drug, from none at all to eighty percent for one common antibiotic, and a tenth of strains resisted multiple drug classes. The team's genome survey found fourteen strain types, one dominating, and 398 prophages in total, with more than four-fifths of strains carrying resistance genes in or near prophage regions. The picture links the herd's resistance problem to its viral stowaways, which suggests watching prophages as an early warning of resistance on the move.
pmc-12735258:
Manal Bakeer and nine co-authors test two plant extracts against drug harm to the pancreas in a 2025 paper. The drug is metronidazole, and the model is rats. One extract comes from horsetail, the other from olive leaves. Both were checked for their chemical makeup first.

The drug alone raised pancreatic enzymes and blood sugar in the rats. Oxidative stress markers climbed while defenses fell. Inflammatory genes switched on and survival genes switched off. Tissue sections showed clear degeneration of the pancreas. Both extracts blunted these harms when given alongside the drug. Horsetail protected best, restoring enzyme balance and tissue form.
pmc-12735758:
Roman Altunin and co-authors report a 2025 study of ultrathin platinum films. Such films serve in sensors, contacts, and optical coatings. How the film first forms, layer by layer, shapes all of its later traits, so the early stage draws strong interest.

The team grew films from 0.2 to 20 nanometers thick and probed them with electron scopes, surface scans, light measures, and resistance tests. Near one nanometer, the film first carried current across gaps between islands. Near two nanometers it turned almost solid. Growth in the thin range mixed flat layers with 3D crystal islands. Scaling theory framed the results and tied the growth mode to the film traits.
pmc-12735958:
Natalja Bouwhuis and co-authors compare pharmacy-made capsules of a rare-disease drug with the licensed product, in work from twenty twenty-five. The drug, chenodeoxycholic acid, treats a rare fat storage disease. A hospital pharmacy in Amsterdam has made its own capsules for years. Little data existed on how the two forms move through the body. A fair head-to-head test was needed before wider trust.

Twelve healthy volunteers take both forms in a crossover design with swapped order. Both forms peak in blood at about one hour after the dose. Total exposure over six hours lands close between the two forms. Peak level, though, runs much lower for the pharmacy form. Both peak and total ratios fall outside the accepted match range. High variation between people blurs the verdict further. A larger study would be needed to settle match claims.
pmc-12736058:
Mercury in water is deadly at trace levels, and a color-change test built on silver particles and a DNA catcher may spot it fast. Haolin Wang and co-authors build the sensor in a 2025 paper. Bare silver particles clump in salt water and change color. A strand called an aptamer coats and steadies them. Mercury grabs the aptamer with high affinity, stripping the protection away.

The color shift then reports the mercury present. The test reads across a wide range with a very low floor. No labels or heavy gear are needed. The authors aim the method at quick field screening of water.
pmc-12736358:
Lisheng Wang and co-authors tune the switch point of a wide-gap chip switch with a fluorine gas wash. The study appeared in 2025. The stuff bears high fields well, a prize for power gear. Its switches oft leak in the off state, though, from flaws near the face.

The wash drives fluorine in at the face, where it ties to the base stuff and pays off flaw states. Off leaks fell to a low mark, and the on-off span held firm. Wash time set the switch point, with shifts past twelve steps at long wash. Sim runs showed less face charge and a wide dead zone. Break strength near twice its first mark.
pmc-12736458:
María-Angélica Espejel-Rivera and three co-authors detect breast cancer from heat movies in a 2025 paper. Infrared cameras watch the breast cool after a cold challenge, and tumors betray themselves by rewarming differently, thanks to their extra blood vessels and metabolism. The team turned those movies into numbers.

From twenty heat images, they extracted time series of five features at hotspots. The features were peak and average temperature, spatial unevenness, heat flow, and estimated tumor depth. The last two came from solving a standard bio-heat equation backward. Two machine learning methods then judged the sequences. A forest method scored eighty-six percent accuracy, while a memory network reached ninety-four percent. The authors argue the dynamic rewarming pattern carries the diagnostic signal, not any single snapshot. The approach is non-invasive and radiation-free, a possible screening complement where mammography is scarce.
pmc-12736558:
Oleg Stepanov and co-authors build a smoother for navigation data in a 2025 paper. Vehicles that fuse GPS, inertial sensors, and other sources must estimate their path from noisy readings. Here the math is nonlinear, and the best-guess distribution starts with several peaks, settling to one as data pile up.

Standard filters fail on such problems, and particle methods are too heavy for real time. The team proposes two recursive batch algorithms that revisit past data and straighten the curves at several points along the way. The result aims at near-best accuracy with a cost that real navigation systems can afford.
pmc-12736758:
Lottefier and co-authors rebuild walkers' and runners' paths from video to help engineers design for crowds. Footbridges increasingly sway under human loads, and sound load models need real movement data. Their method mixes color checks for marked volunteers, deep-learning detection for everyone else, and a geometric projection that maps image points onto the ground plane.

Trials at two city running events and in controlled setups, from fixed and moving cameras, recovered each person's path reliably in varied conditions. The output is fine-grained space-time data on how people space, pass, and bunch. The authors offer it as a hands-off way to study crowd flow and feed vibration models for structures people excite.
pmc-12737058:
Paul Park, Junseok Kim, and Juhyun Ko build a hybrid image sensor that removes motion blur at high speed, published in 2025. Hybrid sensors pair a normal image sensor with an event-style sensor that reacts to change. Earlier hybrids suffered from bad-pixel problems that degraded performance.

Their design reads frames very fast and derives the event-style frames by differencing the fast normal frames, giving an effective rate well over a thousand frames per second. A new pixel layout made the event pixels the smallest reported. Data from a high-resolution main sensor and the event channel streamed over a standard mobile interface without loss. Paired with a deblurring method, the event frames sharply reduced blur in test images, including a simulated jogging scene, the authors report.
pmc-12737158:
Four authors report a case in two thousand twenty-five of a vein variant found before birth. The inferior vena cava is the large vein that returns blood from the lower body to the heart. In this variant the vein is interrupted, and blood detours through a smaller vein called the azygos.

The variant was spotted on a routine second-trimester scan and confirmed by a detailed ultrasound of the fetal heart. The baby was born without problems. The authors review how to diagnose the variant and what it can mean over a lifetime. They stress telling isolated cases apart from those paired with other birth defects.
pmc-12737258:
Michael Vernon and four co-authors present a smarter growth cabinet for raising plants in lab studies. Their work appeared in twenty twenty-five. Plant scientists need steady, controlled rooms to test which crops cope best as the climate changes, but standard cabinets are costly and fixed.

The new cabinet runs saved climate recipes that copy real weather shifts. Cabinets can link together for larger trials, and the frame can be rebuilt for different species. It costs under ten thousand Australian dollars. Sensors record climate and plant growth on their own, ready for use with artificial intelligence tools. In tests, the cabinet held its target heat level well while copying weather from Hobart, Australia.
pmc-12737358:
Researchers test oregano oil in feed water for older laying hens in 2025 on two commercial flocks. About 7,884 hens aged 79 and 96 weeks got the oil for one week, with records kept before, during, and after. Blood checks track hormones, minerals, and stress marks tied to health and laying.

Egg output rose during the oil week, and deaths fell the week after, above all in the younger flock. Feed use per egg also dropped. Blood shifts point to a restored calcium balance and calmer liver stress, which may link the oil to better health.
pmc-12738558:
Huimin Wu and three colleagues published a sports science study in two thousand twenty-five on predicting force in incline push-ups. Push-ups build upper body strength anywhere, but how the slope changes the load was poorly quantified. Force plates can measure it, yet a formula would be handier.

Twenty-seven male students did push-ups at three slopes and three metronome tempos with feet raised. Body mass, slope, and tempo fed a regression model for the force through the hands. Predicted and measured forces agreed closely on average, with moderate spread. Tempo linked to peak force differently at each slope. The authors offer the model for setting training intensity without lab equipment.
pmc-12738658:
Piotr Gwiazda, Alexey Kazarnikov, Anna Marciniak-Czochra, and Zuzanna Szymańska present a new framework for fitting math models of living systems to data, in a methods paper from 2025. Calibrating such models is hard: data are scarce and noisy, and the models are costly to run. Classic Bayesian tools strain on systems with mixed or chaotic behavior.

Their method, built on a correlation integral likelihood, handles pattern-forming and individual-based models in one frame. They show its range through sample uses in math biology. They also compare random sampling with guided gradient-flow sampling, and show how the two blend. The result is a practical toolbox for model fitting.
pmc-12738758:
Laura Amaya-Pascasio and colleagues use score mismatch to predict early recovery after stroke clot removal. Their study from twenty twenty-five builds a formula from admission data. Stroke severity scores sometimes exceed what scans predict. That mismatch may mark salvageable brain tissue.

Patients with large vessel blockages treated mechanically were included. A derivation group produced the expected-score formula. Mismatch percentage compared actual against expected severity. Early improvement meant a large score drop within a day. The mismatch predicted that improvement in the analysis. Such bedside maths could refine patient selection for treatment. It may also set family expectations after the procedure.
pmc-12739158:
Yanghang Huang and co-authors power a tiny drone with an aluminum-air battery to stretch its flight time. Small quadrotors, only centimeters wide, serve in farm watching and rescue searches. Standard lithium batteries store too little energy, cutting flights short. Their 2025 study designs a pouch cell around the aluminum-air chemistry instead.

Fast corrosion of the aluminum plate, a known flaw of this chemistry, matters less when a drone drains the cell in one short run. The tuned cell beat commercial lithium cells on both energy and power measures. On a printed test drone, it flew for just over thirteen minutes, versus four and a half minutes on the standard battery. The team call the swap feasible for short, intense missions.
pmc-12739458:
Bushra Zahra and co-authors survey people with epilepsy in Pakistan on phone health apps. The study appeared in 2025. Such apps could bridge care gaps where funds are tight and stigma runs high. Yet their worth rests on whether patients will use them.

Over four hundred patients at one large site in the capital filled a set form. Most had heard of health apps for epilepsy care. A large share also said they would use such an app. The team links will to use with how much patients knew, how they saw the apps, and how fit the apps felt for daily life. Gaps in access still held some back.
pmc-12739858:
Mengya Wang and eleven colleagues track how viruses of gut bacteria interact with the bacteria themselves in the cow rumen across lactation, in a 2025 study. The team profiled rumen contents at peak, early, and later mid-lactation using metagenomics and metabolite analysis. They catalogued 780 bacterial phages and watched how their numbers shifted alongside their hosts.

Some phages rose and fell with their host bacteria, while others moved in the opposite direction. Early mid-lactation stood out: two phages linked to fewer of their hosts coincided with a bloom of Prevotella bacteria and stronger carbohydrate and amino acid metabolism. The authors model a chain from phage pressure to bacterial mix to milk traits.
pmc-12740758:
Oh and a large team review whether gut microbes can flag breast cancer risk in twenty twenty-five. Gut microbes shape hormone handling and immune response, both tied to the disease. The team pooled thirteen case control studies from several regions. They compared microbe mix in women with and without the cancer.

Over half the studies found lower gut richness in cancer patients. Community mix differed in most studies. One gut genus ran high and one ran low across studies with some stress. Shifts split by region, with distinct genera leading in the United States, Europe, and China. The authors see promise but call for bigger, standard long term studies.
pmc-12741158:
Sophia Åkerblom and four co-authors sorted people with endometriosis in two thousand twenty-five into subgroups by their whole-life profile, not just body symptoms. Care for this painful condition has leaned on a purely medical view, yet symptoms span body, mind, and social life. A latent class method searched for hidden groups in survey data.

Two groups appeared. One carried a high overall burden, with severe pain and heavy psychological strain, plus low felt control and weak social support. The other carried a low burden on the same measures. The authors say clinics should screen for life-wide burden and offer team-based care to those who need it most.
pmc-12742058:
Victoria Jenneson and co-authors lay out a plan to judge England's rules on where unhealthy foods may sit in stores in a 2025 protocol. Since October 2022, larger stores cannot place items high in fat, sugar, or salt at entrances, aisle ends, or checkouts, or their online equivalents. The aim is to cut impulse buys and excess calories.

The team will use daily sales and product data from several retailers, covering 18 months before and 12 months after the law. About 160 English stores form the treated group, and 50 stores in Scotland and Wales act as controls. Time series models will estimate effects on sales, product ranges, and fairness across areas.
pmc-12742158:
Antonia Gazola and co-authors set a Turing test for a care aid in a 2025 plan paper. Their aid, AVA, guides vent care for sepsis and lung failure in intensive care. Sharp forecast scores are not proof that its picks are safe at the bedside.

The plan asks if doctors can tell AVA picks from real doctor picks. Past notes of real care form the human side of the test. If AVA picks pass as human again and again, trust grows for live trials. The test gives a low risk gate before an aid touches real patients.
pmc-12743958:
Ricardo E Colberg and co-authors present a new ultrasound method for checking the ulnar collateral ligament on the inner elbow. Published in 2025, the study deals with a ligament often injured in baseball players. In the standard test pose, gravity pulls the forearm and loads the joint before any stress is applied, which can skew the resting measure.

The team scanned both elbows of healthy male college baseball players at rest, under inward stress, and under outward stress. The throwing arm showed a wider resting joint space under gravity, likely from adaptive laxity. Under inward stress, both arms matched closely. The authors propose that measure as a better baseline for future tests of injured athletes.
pmc-12745158:
Qiuyue Wu and co-authors published a 2025 study on a blood-and-fluid test for sorting gliomas, a type of brain tumor. Gliomas are classed by their molecular traits, which also hint at how a patient will fare. Spotting those traits without surgery is hard, because very little tumor DNA floats free in body fluids.

The team looked instead at how open the tumor's DNA packaging is at certain spots. Open spots can be read from free DNA in spinal fluid and blood. Using tumor tissue from four donors, they found seventy-two open regions that spinal fluid could reveal. Sixteen regions in blood DNA differed between low-grade and high-grade tumors. A classifier built on those sixteen sorted tumor grade well in training data, and less well in fresh test data. The authors offer the approach as a new kind of marker for glioma class.
pmc-12745458:
Baoxuan Wang and co-authors report a hard case of a rare abdominal tumor that returned and spread, in this 2025 case report. The tumor, pseudomyxoma peritonei, fills the belly with mucus and usually stays there. Spread to lungs and lymph nodes is rare, which makes treatment choices after surgery especially tricky. Their patient was a woman of eighty-three whose tumor grew from her appendix.

Two years after her first surgery, the disease came back in both lungs and many lymph nodes. Surgeons removed what they could and washed the abdomen with heated chemotherapy to ease a blocked bowel. As upkeep treatment, she then received a two-drug plan every two weeks. The report lays out how the team sequenced surgery and drugs, a path other teams may weigh for like cases.
pmc-12746758:
Clopidogrel is a drug that stops blood clots by damping platelet activity, and the gut microbe Lactobacillus paracasei may change how well it works. Xiaona Ren and Caicai Liu tested the pair in rats, giving the microbe before or after the drug and then triggering clots in a standard model. Blood tests showed the combined treatment lowered the drug's active levels and raised some platelet measures. Yet in the living animals, clots took longer to form, weighed less, and were blocked at a higher rate.

The combined treatment also lowered several inflammation markers, improved the gut microbe mix that the drug had disturbed, and strengthened the gut lining. The authors note a puzzle: the platelet tests and the clot outcomes moved in opposite directions, which they attribute to the many factors that govern clotting in a whole animal.
pmc-12747058:
Novillo-Del Álamo and co-authors report a rare brain disorder found before birth, in this 2025 case report with a literature review. In the disorder, knots of brain cells sit in the wrong place, near the brain's inner fluid spaces, instead of reaching the outer layer. It often brings seizures and heart valve problems.

Only 186 patients appear in past reports, and very few were spotted before birth. In this case, an ultrasound during pregnancy raised the flag. After birth, gene tests found a change in the FLNA gene, which follows an X-linked dominant pattern. The authors stress that full checks before birth help in three ways: counseling parents, planning the newborn's care, and guiding choices in later pregnancies. The case adds a rare prenatal record to a thin field.
pmc-12748058:
Jung Soo Son and co-authors compare traits of three common sexually spread infections in Korea, in a study from two thousand twenty-five. Gene-based tests found five hundred cases at one hospital over more than a decade. Most patients were women, with a median age in the late twenties.

The most common germ also had the highest rate of complications. The least common germ was most often felt as symptoms. Among patients retested, about one in seven still carried a germ. One germ type and having symptoms each raised the odds of failed clearing. The authors urge watch on drug resistance and better retreatment plans.
pmc-12748758:
Batteries are too expensive for every solar farm to own alone, so sharing one big store among producers is gaining ground. Marwa Hassan and Eman Beshr design the sharing rules for the grid of Egypt in a 2025 paper. Their framework repartitions the shared storage dynamically as demand, prices, and forecasts shift.

A Nash bargaining scheme splits the gains fairly between producers and the storage operator. A distributed optimization algorithm coordinates the leasing in near real time without a central solver. Simulations show utilization up more than forty percent over fixed allocation, holding up under forecast errors and battery wear. The authors present the model as a market-aware template for renewable-heavy grids in emerging economies.
pmc-12749058:
Lingling Yang and co-authors design a tiny broadband low-pass filter for microwave circuits, in this 2025 Europe PMC paper. Their design rests on spoof surface plasmon polaritons, structures that guide waves along patterned metal. A new unit cell blends square dumbbell and meander shapes to slow waves more strongly than older cells.

Joining two cell types widened the passband and sharpened out-of-band rejection. Simulations showed clean low-pass behavior up to a few gigahertz with strong suppression above. An equivalent circuit model matched the simulations. The filter was built with standard circuit board methods at a fraction of a wavelength in size, and lab tests agreed well with the design.
pmc-12749158:
Virginie Dubourg leads a team of eight authors in 2025 in studying how the stress chemistry of obesity strikes the muscle cells of blood vessel walls. Obesity dulls vessel function partly through one receptor on those cells, EGFR, and the damage may begin earlier and differ by sex.

The team exposed mouse vessel muscle cells, with and without the receptor, to three stress mixes: sugar and fat, pressure hormones, and both combined. Gene readings then showed how each mix rewrote the cells' activity. Comparing males and females and receptor-free cells tests whether the receptor truly drives the early harm.
pmc-12749258:
Wireless sensor networks die young when radios drain batteries, so squeezing data before sending it saves the network. Marwa Madkour and co-authors present a scheme that compresses and encrypts readings at once. Compressive sensing shrinks the data; elliptic-curve cryptography locks it, with the sensing matrix's seed doubling as a shared secret between nodes and the base station.

Prime-number routing paths and a cluster-head strategy trim chatter further. Seven recovery algorithms were raced across sparsity levels, and three, subspace pursuit, message passing, and a Bregman iteration, best preserved energy and delayed the first node death. Measured on leftover energy, lifetime, and throughput, the hybrid scheme beat plain compressive approaches. The authors aim it at secure monitoring where replacing batteries is impractical.
pmc-12749858:
Getie Beza and co-authors measured recovery time for young children with severe pneumonia in Ethiopia in 2025. Pneumonia still kills many children under five in poor lands. The follow-up study tracked 394 children in public hospitals in West Gojjam during 2023.

Median recovery took four days, with most children well within three to six days. Children with many prior pneumonia visits recovered more slowly. Children of parents with diploma-level schooling recovered faster. Other traits screened in early checks fell away in the final model. The authors say recovery data can guide bed planning and family advice in busy wards.
pmc-12750158:
Edward Zhou highlights in a 2025 article new drug candidates against a chromatin reader called BRD9 in blood cancer. BRD9 sits in a complex that opens genes, and it keeps a key growth gene switched on in leukemia cells. Blocking its reading pocket has drawn drug hunters for years.

Past blockers bind tightly yet show weak punch in disease models, which stalled their path to clinics. Fresh compounds add an imidazole group that lifts their cell level effect. Zhou frames that tweak as a leap that turns binders into real drug candidates. The piece sums the target's role in acute myeloid leukemia for context. It also weighs what proof the new compounds still need before human tests.
pmc-12750558:
Rachel Drbohlav Ollerton, Nadine Bol, Gwenn Beets, Frans Folkvord, and Emiel Krahmer surveyed Dutch cancer survivors, in a 2025 study, on how useful they find four healthy habits. A sound lifestyle can aid both general health and cancer outcomes after treatment. Survivors tend to follow advice on smoking and alcohol more than advice on diet and activity, and the team asked whether belief in the payoff explains the gap.

The survey covered 197 survivors with varied cancer types. People who saw more benefit in a habit were more likely to practice it. Not smoking and drinking little were rated as more helpful than balanced diet and exercise. Survivors who had been diagnosed recently, and those who felt less control, saw less benefit in the habits overall. The authors draw lessons for how health advice is taught and framed.
pmc-12750758:
Georgia Pierson and co-authors ask whether mental health researchers share study results with their participants in a 2025 review. People with lived experience increasingly expect findings back, yet practice in top psychiatry journals was unknown.

The team identified over one hundred forty primary-data studies in high-impact journals and emailed their authors about two years after publication. Two thirds replied. Among respondents, about a fifth had sent results to participants, and a further tenth had shared lay materials with lived-experience audiences. Under kind assumptions about silent authors, sharing still looks like a minority habit. The authors discuss methods like email and plain-language summaries and urge journals to normalize giving results back.
pmc-12751158:
Mohammad Alghosi and co-authors compare warm-up styles for athletes whose shoulders pinch painfully overhead. Their trial appeared in 2025. Twenty-five male athletes with shoulder impingement and twenty-five healthy controls each tried three routines in random order: static stretching, a dynamic warm-up, and both combined. Shoulder rotation range, balance reach, position sense, and strength were measured before, right after, and one hour later.

All three routines improved rotation range, with static stretching giving the largest gains for the injured group. The dynamic warm-up most improved balance reach. The authors conclude the routines are not interchangeable: stretching buys motion, dynamic work buys control. Athletes and therapists can pick by goal, and combining both remains sensible when time allows before training or play.
pmc-12751258:
Fredrick Kebaso and seven co-authors wrote a 2025 data paper presenting the first genome assembly of the camel ked. This blood-feeding fly parasitizes camels, causing painful bites, blood loss, and disease spread. No genome existed for the species, which blocked study of its smell and taste systems, the senses it uses to find hosts.

The team sequenced DNA from chest muscle of male and female keds with nanopore long reads. The male assembly spans 133.5 million base pairs and the female 135.6 million, both over 97 percent complete by standard checks. They catalogued the active smell and taste genes: odorant receptors and binding proteins, gustatory and ionotropic receptors, and chemosensory proteins. The resource supports molecular work on ked control.
pmc-12751358:
Ruiting Wen and co-authors recount drug-level guided antifungal care for a teen with bone cancer and a lung mold infection in a 2025 case report. Invasive aspergillosis stalks patients after chemotherapy, and antifungal levels swing wildly between people. The boy, aged fourteen, also took targeted cancer drugs that can clash with antifungals.

Blood checks showed the first drug, voriconazole, sat far too low even after dose hikes, and the infection stalled. A switch to isavuconazole put levels in range and the lungs improved. Level checks also flagged one pairing that clashed and one that did not. Testing levels, the authors argue, should steer such care.
pmc-12751458:
Shouki Bazarbashi and fourteen co-authors compare two first moves when prostate cancer turns resistant after modern doublet therapy, in this 2025 Saudi multicenter study. Patients whose cancer progressed despite hormone therapy plus a receptor-blocking drug in the sensitive phase form a growing group with no settled next step: another receptor drug, or chemotherapy with docetaxel.

The retrospective study covered sixty men at three cancer centers. Twenty-eight took the drug route, thirty-two the chemotherapy. Response rates were nearly identical, around thirty-eight percent. Chemotherapy trended better on progression-free and overall survival without reaching significance. One subgroup stood out: men with visceral spread lived significantly longer on docetaxel, a median 14.4 versus 5.9 months. Statistical modeling flagged prior hormone response depth among survival predictors. The authors call for randomized trials and biomarker-guided sequencing.
pmc-12751858:
Heavy bleeding after childbirth is a leading danger for new mothers, and a drug called tranexamic acid helps blood clot. Orna Reichman and six co-authors ask whether giving it after a vacuum-assisted delivery lowers the rate of severe bleeding in first-time mothers, in this 2025 study. Severe bleeding was counted as a steep drop in the blood protein hemoglobin.

The team reviewed all first-time mothers who had vacuum-assisted births at one large center in 2021 and 2022. Some received the drug within half an hour of delivery, at the attending clinician's choice, and others did not. Because that choice could bias the comparison, the authors matched women with like risk profiles and adjusted their models. They also tracked transfusions and extra steps taken to stop bleeding.
pmc-12751958:
Hatice Kübra Başkan and Beyhan Başkan present an evaluation study, published in 2025, pitting seven leading chatbots against a real dental specialty exam. The questions came from a decade of Turkish dentistry specialization tests in pediatric dentistry. Experts split them into fact recall items and case based ones, and they were fed to the models in Turkish without edits.

Accuracy differed sharply across the models. The top system answered about nineteen of every twenty questions correctly, while the weakest managed under two thirds, and one search flavored model collapsed on case questions. Fact questions proved easier than cases for most systems. The authors offer the ranking as a reality check on using chatbots in specialist medical study.
pmc-12752158:
Ibrahim Maman Laminou and a large team test Niger's front-line malaria drug in kids and hunt gene marks of drug proof. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-five. The drug pair was tried in kids aged five to fifteen with plain malaria at four sites in late twenty twenty-two, with day checks for twenty-eight days. Gene tests told fresh ills from back-sliding ones.

Raw cure rates swung wide by site, from near half to near full. Past gene fix, cure held at or past ninety-three percent at all sites, past the WHO bar. Proof gene flaws ran high in two genes, but none in the kelch gene. South sites showed strain, the team warn.
pmc-12752258:
Xiaogang Hu and co-authors tested a simple blood ratio as a warning sign for severe pancreas attacks driven by high blood fat, in work published in 2025. The ratio divides white cell counts by protective cholesterol. More than four hundred patients at one hospital were studied.

Patients with moderate or severe attacks had clearly higher ratios than mild cases. High ratios also came with longer hospital stays and more fluid and dead tissue collections around the pancreas. The ratio stood as an independent risk factor and slightly sharpened the prediction model. Its link with severity ran in a straight line. The authors offer it as a cheap early marker, while noting its added accuracy is small.
pmc-12752858:
Ronique Gordon and eight co-authors ask whether a short wait before clamping a newborn's cord pays off months later, in a 2025 study. Waiting half a minute to a minute gives the baby extra blood rich in stem cells and immune proteins. The team reviewed charts of full-term babies born in 2022 at one city hospital. About a third had the wait, and the rest were clamped at once.

Babies in the wait group came back to the emergency room with breathing infections far less often in their first six months. They were also admitted to hospital less, and fewer showed the yellow tint of a strained liver. Stays, when they happened, lasted about the same in both groups. The authors read the results as one more reason to keep the brief wait as standard care for healthy newborns.
pmc-12753458:
Hyunjae Yu and co-authors put a commercial brain-scan tool on trial across many centers, in a 2025 study. The tool, Neurophet AQUA, carves brain scans into regions on its own, a job clinics need for diagnosis and follow-up. The long-standing free tool in this space is slow and fiddly, which limits its use in busy wards. The trial ran two checks: region carving on one scan type against the older tool, and lesion spotting on a second scan type against hand-marked truth.

Large shared datasets of aging and Alzheimer's scans fed the tests. Expert readers graded the quality of the carving, and repeat scans checked whether the tool gives the same answer twice. A second dataset tested whether results hold across different scanners. The study frames the tool as a faster, easier path to the same measurements, pending the graded results.
pmc-12753658:
Shiori Takeuchi and co-authors report, in a 2025 study, a new antibody that kills an aggressive lymphoma by punching large pores in its cells. Natural killer and T-cell lymphomas are fast and commoner in East Asia and Latin America. Fresh treatments are badly needed.

The team immunized mice with two lymphoma cell lines and screened the resulting antibodies on a third. One, named ANAP, killed cells immediately without help from complement or other immune cells. Its target is a surface adhesion protein. Death depended on the cell's internal skeleton and proceeded through pore formation. A directly lethal antibody sidesteps the resistance tricks tumors use against drugs that work through slower pathways.
pmc-12753758:
Labelling tissue in microscope slides pixel by pixel is slow, expert work that limits how much data pathology AI can learn from. Zhilong Weng and co-authors propose a semi-supervised method that learns from many unlabelled slides as well as a few labelled ones. Their swarm-of-models approach keeps several specialist models, each tuned to a tissue type, and picks the best-matching specialists for each new slide by similarity.

The chosen specialists then label the unlabelled slide, and those labels feed further training. On a large international dataset for colorectal tissue, the method beat standard supervised and semi-supervised approaches, raising tumour scores by 3.6 points and tumour-plus-stroma scores by 2.1 points. Tests with varied amounts of labelled data and single-centre training confirmed the gains hold up. The work shows that using likeness between cases can make pathology models stronger and more general.
pmc-12753858:
Deep inside Earth, a boundary layer called the transition zone may store slabs of ancient seafloor and sediment. Rong Xu and co-authors tested that idea in 2025 with mercury isotopes in young basalts from northeast Asia. Those rocks carry a mantle signature thought to come from that deep store, and their mercury showed odd, mass-independent patterns.

The patterns point to very old land-derived sediments that sank, kept their strange mercury signature for over a billion years, and later rose again in wet upwellings or plumes. The work shows mercury isotopes can trace recycling between Earth's surface and its deep interior across immense spans of time.
pmc-12754058:
Xuzhao Li and co-authors tested whether a common antidepressant, fluoxetine, combined with a gut acid called butyrate, can ease both low mood and constipation caused by long-term stress in mice. Stress is known to disturb the gut as well as the brain. The team built a mouse model that combined unpredictable mild stress with functional constipation.

Treated mice showed less depression-like behavior and passed stool more normally. The team measured gut transit time, gut hormones, the gut barrier, and swelling markers. They also read the gut microbe mix and the levels of helpful acids the microbes make. The pairing may work better than the drug alone, pointing to gut care as part of mood care.
pmc-12754858:
Jussara Almeida de Oliveira Baggio and co-authors profile stroke in Brazil from a national survey in this 2025 paper. Stroke ranks among the top killers and disablers in the country. A 2019 health survey lets planners see who carries that burden.

Nearly two thousand respondents reported a stroke diagnosis, about two percent of adults. That scales to more than four million Brazilians living post-stroke. Women and urban residents formed the majority of cases. Average age at diagnosis sat in the early fifties. About a third lived with functional dependence afterward. Maps and models flagged regional peaks and factors tied to dependence, guiding where rehab support should go first.
pmc-12755158:
Cristian Robayo-Cuevas, Howard Junca, Sandra Uribe, and Andrés Gómez-Palacio catalog the bacteria living in mosquitoes from Colombian rainforests, in a study from 2025. Rural mosquito species there are diverse, and their microbes may shape how well they spread viruses. Yet these communities are barely mapped.

The team mined RNA sequencing data from many mosquito species caught at two sites in Antioquia. They pulled out ribosomal sequences to profile the bacteria, and also assembled full gene fragments for a second view. Culex types held the richest, most even communities. Wolbachia dominated, reaching 60 percent of reads in some Aedes and Culex types. Common environmental genera like Pseudomonas and Acinetobacter followed at 10 to 20 percent. Some rarer finds could matter for disease spread.
pmc-12755758:
Felipe Rodriguez and Jeroen Saeij published a 2025 study on how the human body first fights the parasite Toxoplasma gondii. The parasite infects tens of millions of people in the United States alone. Mice rely on defense tools that humans do not have, so the early human response was poorly understood.

Working with human blood cells, the pair found that a special group of T cells senses infected cells through a receptor called BTN3A1. These T cells release signals that switch on natural killer cells, which then make more of the defense protein interferon gamma. Blocking the pathway that makes the sensed molecules weakened the response. The findings name a clear first line of defense in people.
pmc-12755958:
Janae Rasmussen and co-authors asked joint replacement patients how they felt about getting nutrition advice straight from their orthopedic surgeon, in a 2025 study. Poor nutrition, smoking, and obesity worsen results after hip and knee replacement, yet surgeons rarely lead those talks. The team surveyed patients treated at one private practice over twenty years.

Alongside the survey, they reviewed charts for complications, other conditions, and surgical outcomes. The study records how many patients recalled nutrition guidance, whether they felt it aided their preparation and recovery, and how they viewed surgeons raising the topic at all. A subgroup check compared ages between diet adopters and others.
pmc-12756658:
Xiaohong Lin and co-authors pool studies on mobile health tools for people living with transplanted organs, in work from twenty twenty-five. Good follow up after transplant is vital for graft survival. Phone based tools promise support between clinic visits, but firm proof was lacking.

Twenty-three studies with more than two thousand recipients were reviewed, most of them randomized trials. Mobile tools improved self care skill by a clear margin and cut rehospitalization by about half. Death, rejection, and infection rates did not differ firmly between groups. Story based synthesis added gains in drug and care routine adherence. Bias checks used standard tools for both trial types. The authors back mobile support as part of transplant follow up.
pmc-12757358:
A common stomach bacterium may quietly raise a risky form of cholesterol that standard panels overlook. The authors study adults attending routine health checks at one Chinese hospital, testing each for Helicobacter pylori with a breath test and measuring remnant cholesterol in the blood. Two possible middlemen are tracked: an index of insulin resistance built from triglycerides and glucose, and a sedimentation rate that reflects chronic inflammation. Statistical models then test both the direct link and the paths through the middlemen.

Infection ties significantly to higher remnant cholesterol, and the link holds across subgroups. Mediation analysis shows both insulin resistance and inflammation carry part of the effect. People whose infection persists over time show a marked rise in the cholesterol measure. The authors present the stomach infection as one more thread in cardiovascular risk, working partly by stirring insulin resistance and low-grade inflammation.
pmc-12767258:
Cesar Ramos-Gregorio and co-authors review a rare mouth condition called multifocal epithelial hyperplasia, also known as Heck disease, in a paper from 2025. The condition causes many small, painless bumps on the lining of the mouth. It is benign and is strongly tied to two low risk types of human papillomavirus.

Cases occur most often in children and teens in Indigenous American communities, but reports from other regions are rising. The review sums up what is known about spread, virus action, and the look of the bumps under the microscope. It also covers tests, including molecular and staining methods, and the options for care. The bumpy, cobblestone look is a classic clue, the authors note.
pmc-12767458:
Adalberto Campo-Arias and colleagues validated a mental health literacy scale in two thousand twenty-five. The scale measures attitudes and knowledge about mental health. It was first built for adolescents. This study tested the Spanish version in Colombian adults. Participants were adult high school students. Statistical factor analysis checked the scale's structure.

Two broad parts emerged: attitudes and knowledge. Attitudes split further into help-seeking and stigma. Fit statistics supported that structure well. Consistency scores were computed for each part. A valid local tool matters for research and programs. Schools can now measure mental health literacy reliably. Stigma tracking becomes easier across adult learners.
pmc-12768658:
Sumeyye Samur and six co-authors test whether generative artificial intelligence can rebuild a published health cost model. Cost models help decision makers judge new treatments early, but building them by hand is slow. The team fed a model of a bowel disease into a smart platform that reads papers and pulls out structure and numbers.

From the journal paper alone, the tool found costs and quality of life inputs well. It stumbled on health states and on the odds of moving between them, since the paper described them thinly. A fuller technical report fixed much of that gap. Some odds still could not be rebuilt from the printed formulas. The authors call for clearer model reporting so such tools can help more.
pmc-12768758:
Ana Luiza Cabrera Martimbianco and a large team count court-driven drug claims for rare diseases in Brazil in a 2025 study. When care is dear or hard to get, patients sue for access. Brazil set up centers that write science reports to guide judges. The team read those reports from 2019 to 2024 in a national system. They sorted reports by disease using a global rare disease list.

In all they read 235,546 reports, and rare diseases filled a small share. Motor neuron disease led the rare list with 501 reports, and most asked for two named drugs. Cystic fibrosis came next with 415 reports, with three-drug packs in six of ten asks. Muscle wasting and Gaucher disease claims were also common. The counts show where court paths bear most weight in rare care.
pmc-12771058:
Nine reviewers catalog how blood cancers and their treatments show up inside the chest, in a 2025 narrative review. Chest findings can be the first sign of a blood cancer or a side effect of its therapy. Infections cause the most lung findings, yet up to half stem from the disease itself or its treatment.

The review sorts the non-infectious patterns by site. Swollen lymph nodes and fluid around the lungs are common, and the fluid may be cancerous or treatment-linked. Lung tissue can host lymphoma, leukemia spread, or rare protein buildup diseases. Airway disease is rare, while vessel problems range from cell-clogged flow to clots and high lung pressure. Treatment damage forms its own group. The authors stress that these patterns need different care than infection, so early recognition at diagnosis matters.
pmc-12771858:
Xiang Cao, Zhencheng Ge, and Yiqing Gong report a frightening but fully reversible complication of a routine eye anesthesia technique. Sub-Tenon's anesthesia is considered the safer alternative to needle blocks for eye surgery. During combined cataract and macular surgery, though, a seventy-one-year-old man woke with vision loss, a drooping lid, a frozen eye, and a dilated pupil in the operated eye.

MRI showed mild fluid around the optic nerve and swelling of the fat behind the eye, with no compression or nerve thickening. Supportive care with oxygen and circulation aids followed. Within twenty-four hours every sign had resolved and vision partly recovered. The case report argues for counseling patients about even rare orbital apex syndrome risk, and for fast recognition when it strikes.
pmc-12772558:
Dominic Charles Townsend and co-authors review in a 2025 paper whether film can spot concussion in sport. A blow can leave few signs that the eye catches live. Film review lets staff rewatch the hit and hunt for set signs of a shaken brain.

The team swept four archives for work since 2001 where film signs or hit kind were set next to a true concussion call. They weighed how often each sign shows and how well it sorts the hurt from the hale. Such a sweep can firm the role of the replay booth in head care. Sport teams gain proof for a tool they now use by feel.
pmc-12775658:
A fatal brain disease caused by prions is notoriously hard to diagnose because its early signs mimic many other conditions. Virgilio Failoc Rojas and co-authors present one patient path to diagnosis in this 2025 paper and back it with a review of past reports. Their patient was passed between several specialties before the disease was suspected.

The review sorts the diseases most often confused with this one and the points where delays creep in. Because the disease has no cure, a fast, correct diagnosis matters for sparing families futile treatments and for infection control around brain tissue. The authors draw lessons on which test results should raise the alarm sooner. Case plus review gives front-line doctors a sharper eye for a rare but devastating illness.
pmc-12775758:
Sayegh and co-authors survey residents of the Jazan region of Saudi Arabia about burn injuries and what to do first when one happens. Burns from hot liquids, flames, and electricity are common in homes there, and poor first aid can turn a minor burn into a lasting injury.

An online questionnaire reached 404 adults. More than half showed poor knowledge of burn causes and first aid, and the internet was their main source of information. Over half had been burned before, most often by hot water or fire, usually on the hand or arm. The authors call for community education programs to teach prevention and correct first steps after a burn.
pmc-12779958:
María del Carmen Marín and co-authors characterized in 2025 a light-harvesting protein from an Antarctic cyanobacterium that had never been grown in a lab. Microbial rhodopsins are light-sensing proteins that drive and sense in microbes. One family, the xanthorhodopsins, carries two light catchers, retinal plus a carotenoid antenna, and pumps protons outward.

They had been studied mainly in a salt-loving bacterium and in one early cyanobacterium, leaving their spread in blue-green algae murky. The team surveyed cyanobacterial genomes for the genes, then studied the Antarctic protein, which binds a hydroxylated carotenoid antenna. Lab work covered its spectrum, its binding choices, and its pumping in function tests. Readers get a polar member of a sunlight family: an antenna-tuned pump from the cold end of the world.
pmc-12780058:
Zhongqing Sun and five co-authors present a 2025 data study on whether food nutrients can blunt asthma harm from indoor air pollution. Indoor pollutants trigger asthma through stress and inflammation in the airways. The team mined a large toxicology database for links among chemicals, genes, body traits, and disease. They traced how selected nutrients touch the same molecular targets as the pollutants.

The search surfaced about sixty key genes and over two hundred traits tied to cell stress, inflammation, and immune control. Resveratrol, a compound found in grapes, stood out: it shifted fifty-one genes and many traits, easing inflammatory signals. Vitamin A, zinc, and related nutrients also hit shared targets like IL6 and TNF. The authors call diet a promising side strategy against pollution-driven asthma. They stress that cell and animal tests must confirm the database picture.
pmc-12780258:
Emre Cem Eraslan wrote this solo 2025 study on squeezing the most medicine from a tinder fungus, a mushroom with a long folk history. How the fungus is extracted, with what heat, time, and alcohol mix, decides its strength. Two optimization methods went head to head: a classic response-surface design and a hybrid of neural network with genetic search.

Each method named its own best recipe, differing sharply in alcohol share. Extracts made both ways were then run through a battery: antioxidant power, enzyme blocking tied to memory drugs, killing of three cancer cell lines, and a chemical census of phenolic compounds. The classic method's extract won on most measures, including antioxidant scores and cancer cell effects. The author concludes the optimizer itself shapes the medicine, and backs the fungus for pharmacy and functional food research.
pmc-12780458:
Xiwen Liu and a large team of co-authors review hyperreactivity as a stand-alone clinical idea, in a paper dated twenty twenty-five. The term names an oversized body response to a normal trigger, seen after surgery, lung transplant, and COVID-19. No shared frame for it existed before.

The review roots the state in a four-way imbalance across nerve, hormone, immune, and local tissue systems. Traits include early onset, staying power, and wide person-to-person spread. The authors sort its forms by setting and propose marker-based tiers for care. Their goal is sharper spotting and tailored treatment.
pmc-12780658:
Kexing Xi and co-authors find how many lymph nodes doctors should check after pre surgery chemoradiation in rectal cancer, in work from twenty twenty-five. Standard rules push for at least twelve nodes checked. But the pre treatment shrinks node counts, so that rule may misfit treated patients.

Data covered more than sixty-six hundred patients from a Chinese cancer center and a United States registry. In both sets, the twelve node split did not separate survival in a firm way. A data tool set the best cut at seven nodes. Patients below seven nodes fared worse on disease free and cancer specific survival. The node count at that cut stood as an independent outlook factor. The authors back seven as the working floor.
pmc-12781958:
Mary Casey and co-authors reported in 2025 a case of a chronic skin disease flaring in a patient who was then found to have lymphoma. The skin condition causes yellow, thinning plaques and ulcers, most often on the lower legs. The patient also had a known enzyme deficiency that affects red blood cells.

After the skin diagnosis was confirmed by biopsy, doctors found a virus-linked lymphoma in the throat area. Treatment for the lymphoma, its complications, and the skin disease together brought relief from pain and healing of the ulcers. Such skin reactions are common near lymph system cancers but rarely involve the skin itself. The authors urge checking for hidden lymphoma when these skin lesions keep returning.
pmc-12783258:
Damla Arslantunali-Sahin and co-authors build a nerve tissue model on a patterned surface to watch single axons regrow after injury. Published in 2025, the study uses PC12 nerve cells on a PDMS surface with tiny pillars and channels. The pillars hold the cell bodies in place while axons are guided into the channels, one by one.

A growth cue, netrin-1, was placed at the far end of the channels, and Schwann cells were grown with the nerve cells. Axons grew far longer with both aids together than with either alone, reaching about three times the base length. After axons were cut, injury markers rose, then fell over the next weeks as regrowth began.
pmc-12784058:
Sung Jin Kim and five co-authors study night-time urination, blood uric acid, and death risk. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five. Night waking to urinate grows common with age and with body-wide ills. It is tied to a higher risk of death, but the path of that link was not clear.

They use a large population data set that spans a decade. Night urination tracks with higher death from all causes and from heart disease, after other factors are held in check. Uric acid shows a J-shaped link to death: both low and high ends carry risk. A path study finds uric acid carries part of the night-urination effect. Care that targets metabolism may cut the risk.
pmc-12784758:
Alvaro Sanabria and three co-authors review chemotherapy given before main treatment for throat cancer at the back of the mouth, in this 2025 paper. Cancers of this type driven by the HPV virus respond well to treatment, so doctors hope lighter regimens can spare patients harsh side effects. Early chemotherapy might shrink tumors enough to allow that lighter path.

Older studies, run before HPV testing was routine, showed mixed responses and no survival gain. Newer series in HPV positive patients report strong tumor shrinkage and high survival after early chemotherapy plus surgery or reduced chemoradiation. Patients also needed feeding tubes less often and swallowed better. The authors caution that these series are small and not randomized, so the approach stays promising rather than proven.
pmc-12785258:
Anna Kiełtyka-Dadasiewicz and four co-authors analyze the seeds left over from berry processing in this 2025 study. The seeds came from blackcurrant, strawberry, and raspberry pomace, the pressed waste of the food industry. The team measured their size, color, swelling, and basic makeup, from protein and fiber to fats and minerals.

Raspberry seeds stood out for their gelling slime and strong swelling, close to linseed, which makes them a candidate thickener for foods and cosmetics. Oils from all three seeds were rich in the n-6 fatty acids prized in skin products, and strawberry and raspberry oils also carried useful n-3 acids for diets. Fiber made up more than half of each seed's weight, and blackcurrant seeds led on antioxidant strength. The authors present the waste seeds as a resource for food and cosmetic makers rather than refuse.
pmc-12785858:
Rongying Chen and nine co-authors published a study in 2025 on measuring body fat with ultrasound, checked against MRI in lab-made models. Fatty organs are usually graded by an MRI measure of fat fraction, the reference standard, but scanners are costly and slow. Ultrasound machines can estimate how strongly tissue absorbs sound, a value that tracks fat content.

Twelve phantoms with fat shares from zero to one hundred percent were scanned by three commercial ultrasound systems and by MRI. The MRI values matched the true fat shares almost perfectly. Ultrasound readings from all three systems agreed with each other and rose in a straight line with fat content, repeatable across operators. The team derived a conversion formula, a step toward cheaper fat checks in ordinary clinics.
pmc-12785958:
Tarek Benameur and three co-authors survey student activity during the pandemic in a 2025 paper. Lockdowns closed gyms and shrank daily movement for many students. The team studied students at the University of Foggia in Italy. They used a long standard questionnaire on activity in daily life.

Just over three hundred students answered the survey. Two thirds reported high activity levels despite the closures. Work and leisure were the main sources of that activity. Men reported more leisure activity, while women moved more in travel and housework. Activity also varied with income, housing, and job status. Small living space and low income stood out as barriers. The authors urge lasting plans to keep students active in crises.
pmc-12786158:
Josko Osredkar and co-authors compare kidney function formulas in a 2025 study of real clinic patients. The filtered rate of the kidneys is a core sign of kidney health. Standard formulas estimate that rate from one blood marker, another marker, or both together, and each can be swayed by factors apart from the kidneys.

Records covered 435 adults with chronic kidney disease who had both markers measured at the same visit. Three standard formulas were applied to each person. Patients were then grouped by the results, to see where the formulas agree or part ways. The findings help labs pick the formula that fits their patients best.
pmc-12786558:
Nicoleta Sgavardea and colleagues examine whether filtering the blood calms the cytokine storm of severe COVID-19 sepsis. Plasma exchange is a rescue move meant to wash out inflammatory drivers. The team reviewed 102 ventilated patients who got at least one session.

The key marker IL-6 fell after treatment in every group, whether patients had one session or several. More sessions did not clearly beat fewer, and timing mattered little in the data. A clotting marker, D-dimer, dropped mainly after single sessions. The authors sorted patients into inflammation types to hunt for who benefits most, a question still open.
pmc-12786858:
Yan Wang and co-authors test how a heat-resistant superalloy behaves when worked hot. Their twenty twenty-five paper studies GH2787, an iron, nickel, and chromium alloy. Samples were pressed across a range of high heats and strain rates.

A math model of the Arrhenius type predicted flow stress well across the tests. A working map marked two zones where shaping used power to good effect. No unstable flow showed up in the range tried. Under the microscope, new small grains formed more as heat and strain rate rose. Grain edge bulging was the main way new grains began, a detail that guides factory practice.
pmc-12786958:
Andres Köster and co-authors test whether tongue and face exercises, delivered by web, move the airway's support bone in sleep apnea in a 2025 trial substudy. Myofunctional therapy trains the muscles of the mouth and throat, and it is gaining ground as an add-on treatment. Its effect on the hyoid bone, the floating anchor of the tongue, had never been measured.

Thirteen Estonian adults with mild to moderate apnea were randomized: nine to twelve weeks of online exercises, four to a waitlist. Three-dimensional scans and three-night home sleep tests bracketed the program. Breathing indices did not budge significantly in either group. The bones told a subtler story: waitlist patients' hyoids drifted backward and downward over the weeks, while the exercise group's stayed put, and that drift tracked worse breathing numbers. The authors read therapy as bracing the airway's scaffold, pending bigger trials.
pmc-12787158:
Giovanni Arrica and co-authors published a surgical study in 2025 on a new way to wrap tissue matrix around breast implants to cut fluid buildup. In reconstruction above the chest muscle, fluid pockets are a leading complication. Their unit changed the wrap over time: the back sheet is trimmed away, only front coverage stays, and small holes are cut in the front wall. One hundred and thirty-eight reconstructions were compared across both styles.

Complications ran about twenty-eight percent with the full wrap versus ten percent with the new style. Fluid pockets fell from nine percent to two. The difference cleared statistical testing. The authors credit pocket shaping plus a structured drainage routine for the calmer recoveries.
pmc-12787258:
Ellenberger and co-authors probe a placenta to brain pathway in a 2025 mouse study. Drugs that block serotonin uptake are often prescribed in pregnancy, yet they may affect the placenta and the fetal brain. Certain giant cells in the mouse placenta are thought to pull in the mother's serotonin through a transporter protein. That supply may seed the growing brain early on. The team bred mice lacking the transporter only in those placenta cells.

Levels of serotonin in the placenta and fetal brain did not differ between the altered mice and normal ones. The altered placentas did hold fewer of the giant cells, though. Gene activity also split by sex in both placenta and fetal brain. The results complicate the simple story of the pathway and point to backup routes that keep serotonin steady.
pmc-12787358:
Byung-Sik Ohm and Tri Ho Minh Le test a recipe for recycling old polymer-modified asphalt in a 2025 study. Reclaimed pavement from such roads is stiff and crack-prone because its binder aged and its polymers broke down. The team blends recycled engine oil, which softens the old binder, with a rubbery polymer that restores spring.

They compare plain, oil-only, and hybrid binders for stiffness and elastic recovery, then pave test mixes with thirty percent reclaimed material. The oil alone made the binder softer but less elastic, while the polymer brought the spring back. The hybrid mix resisted moisture damage, rutted less, and cracked less readily than the control. A working recipe matters because roads agencies want more recycled content without giving up pavement life.
pmc-12788058:
Chenglong Guo and co-authors build in a 2025 study a cheaper, faster version of a label-free sensing camera used to watch molecules bind in many channels at once. Standard wavelength-swept systems need pricey tunable filters. Their rig swaps them for five light-emitting diodes spanning the needed colors and a smart fitting routine.

The routine scans coarsely, then picks the best three diodes for a fine fit, rebuilding the resonance position with no moving parts. A full cycle takes about a tenth of a second with fine resolution. It tracked antibody binding live and read a cartilage wear marker in joint fluid, elevated in an arthritis sample as expected.
pmc-12788358:
Alejandra Gomez-Rivera and co-authors present a network that reads imagined movement from brain waves in a 2025 paper. Brain-computer interfaces based on motor imagery could aid rehabilitation and assistive devices. Yet brain signals are noisy, blurry in space, and vary widely between people, so many users fail to gain control.

Their method fuses raw signals with brain maps built from connectivity between regions, inside a learning design that also rebuilds its input. Training balances rebuilding quality, classification accuracy, and tidy internal structure. In tests the system topped rival methods on average accuracy and varied less across users. Strikingly, it wiped out the group of users who previously scored below sixty percent, lifting them by about a fifth.
pmc-12788558:
Priyatam Karade and six co-authors run a trial from 2025 on two silver-based treatments that prevent tooth decay in children. Decay is common in young children, and both treatments paint fluoride and silver onto teeth. One is a long-used liquid, the other a newer mix with tiny silver particles. The trial enrolled ninety children aged six to nine who already had active decay.

Children got one of the two treatments or plain water, twice over a year. Both treated groups gained far fewer new decayed surfaces than the control group. The older liquid did slightly better, but the gap between the two treatments was not firm. Both are judged useful.
pmc-12788958:
Yutaro Naka and four co-authors report a rare and dangerous complication of a preventive stent, in a 2025 case report. During a common bile duct procedure, doctors often place a small pancreatic stent that is designed to fall out on its own, lowering the risk of pancreatitis afterward. An eighty-seven-year-old man received such a stent during treatment for bile duct stones. Nineteen days later he developed a fever, and scans showed the stent had migrated and pierced his descending colon.

Stents of this type are widely used and generally safe, which makes a perforation easy to overlook. The case walks through the imaging and management. It reminds endoscopy teams that new fever after the procedure deserves a search for the stent, not just for infection.
pmc-12789458:
Cherop and co-authors study how working mothers at a hospital in eastern Uganda manage exclusive breastfeeding. Feeding only breast milk for the first months is key to infant health. Yet jobs often make that hard to sustain. The study ran at Mbale Regional Referral Hospital, where local data had been scarce. A total of 221 working mothers with infants under six months filled in surveys. Ten mothers also gave in-depth interviews.

About 68% of the mothers fed their babies breast milk only. Interviews showed wide gaps in what mothers knew about the practice. Some workplace and family factors helped, while others got in the way. The study gives the hospital a base for better support programs.
pmc-12789558:
Zhaoming Cao and co-authors trace a coffee effect in a 2025 study on blood sugar. The question is whether how people drink coffee changes a long term sugar marker in blood, and whether gut germs carry that effect. The team used a genetics based method that mimics a trial, drawing on large UK and gut germ datasets.

One clear path stood out. Drinking unsweetened filter coffee raised the level of a gut germ called Veillonella. That germ, in turn, linked to lower levels of the sugar marker. The germ makes a short acid that may help sugar control. Extra checks backed the main result, hinting at diet advice worth testing in trials.
pmc-12795458:
Mickaël Maziero and co-authors published this microbiology study in 2025. The pneumonia bacterium can flip into a state called competence, where it absorbs foreign DNA and gains new traits, including drug tolerance. Many signals can trip that switch, and they converge on one gene cluster. Earlier work showed that crippling the cell's protein shredder also flips the switch, by an unknown route. This study identifies the middleman: a toxin called RipA, half of a toxin-antitoxin pair.

The toxin attacks the sliding clamp, a ring that holds the DNA-copying machinery on the strand. That sabotage creates replication stress, which the cell reads as a danger signal and answers by switching on the competence genes. The poisoned cells themselves lose viability, yet stay active enough to release the chemical shout that spreads competence to healthy neighbors. The authors frame it as a sacrifice play: doomed cells warn the colony.
pmc-12796258:
Tonci Ivanisevic and ten co-authors trace why some lung tumors shrug off RAS blocking drugs from the start in a 2025 paper. KRAS gene faults drive near a third of lung gland cancers. New RAS drugs help many patients, but some tumors resist from day one, and the team hunted the cause in the protein's own disposal path.

They found that normal KRAS protein piles up when its disposal tagger, LZTR1, is lost or stalled by the drugs themselves. The surplus sparks a growth pathway by dragging an amino acid ferry complex to the cell's recycling hubs, which rewire nutrient sensing. Shallow cuts in the LZTR1 gene ride in up to forty percent of these tumors. Blocking the growth path or the ferry restored drug response in cells and animals.
pmc-12799658:
Vrinda Dimri and five co-authors published a 2025 study of whether uneven thinking speed predicts falls in older stroke survivors. After stroke, both movement and cognition suffer, and falls are common. The team reanalyzed a trial of 120 community-dwelling adults aged 55 and older. Each person took a computerized Stroop test, which measures reaction time under conflicting cues. The key measure was how much a person's own reaction times scattered from trial to trial.

Over six months, participants averaged 0.61 falls. Greater scatter on the simpler test condition predicted more falls: each unit of added scatter came with about a 20 percent higher fall rate. Average reaction time did not predict as well. The authors suggest that scatter in thinking speed could join fall risk screening after stroke, pending work on whether training can reduce it.
pmc-12800058:
Group decisions under deep uncertainty, several judges, many criteria, hesitant judgments, need math that respects fuzziness. Xiuqin Ma and co-authors build in 2025 a decision method inside dual hesitant q-rung orthopair fuzzy sets, a language where each judgment carries ranges of support and doubt. They fuse a flexible Dombi norm with Hamy mean operators, which notice when criteria lean on each other.

A new distance measure skips normalization, avoiding repeated information, and entropy sets the criteria weights from the data itself. A trial on diagnosing sleep disorders in Chinese medicine produced sharper score separation than rival methods, while keeping both flexibility and correlation in view.
pmc-12801058:
İzzet Karakulak and co-authors build in a 2025 study a scale that measures motivation and addiction together in extreme sports, where misery somehow becomes reward. Existing scales split the two or ignore these athletes. Over a thousand participants in sports like mountaineering answered the new items.

Factor analysis settled on sixteen items in three groups: hedonic deprivation, tolerance, and hedonic opposition. The structure held under both first- and second-order checks, with validity and reliability numbers in accepted ranges. The scale gives researchers one tool for the pull that keeps athletes returning to risk and hardship.
pmc-12801758:
Cervical cancer is Ghana's second most common cancer in women, and prevention starts with what teenagers know. Josephine Nsaful and co-authors surveyed nearly ten thousand high school students across fourteen schools in two regions. The questionnaire covered causes, warning features, risk factors, and screening. Knowledge in each domain was scored as adequate or not.

About fifty-eight percent of students had adequate general knowledge. Risk factor knowledge scored a bit higher. Knowledge of the disease's features lagged badly, at about twenty-two percent. Just over half understood screening and prevention. Gender, school type, and region all shaped the gaps. The authors argue for school-based teaching built on these numbers: strong where students are weak, not generic. Early knowledge, in a country with this burden, is a vaccine of its own kind.
pmc-12801958:
Honghong Yan and co-authors set out the plan for a clinical trial in acute myeloid leukemia, a fast-growing blood cancer, in a 2025 protocol paper. First-round drug treatment is the key step in care. The classic intense regimen works but brings heavy side effects, long hospital stays, and high costs, while a gentler two-drug option can fall short for some patients.

The trial adds a third drug, chidamide, to the gentler pair and tests the trio against both older options. Patients fit for intense treatment are split between the trio and the classic regimen. Patients not fit for it are split between the trio and the pair. The main measure is the rate of complete response, with survival, remission length, cost, and quality of life also tracked. Results are not yet reported in this protocol.
pmc-12804558:
Ruize Qin and co-authors map how the industrial chemical 2-naphthylamine may drive bladder cancer in a 2025 paper. The chemical is a known human carcinogen with a strong link to bladder tumors, yet its molecular route was poorly mapped. The team combined gene-expression analysis, learning methods, and docking simulations.

From several data sets they picked twenty-nine candidate targets, then narrowed them to fourteen core genes. Two genes stood out as the strongest predictors of cancer advance. Docking and dynamics simulations showed the chemical binds those two target proteins tightly. The findings sketch a gene-and-pathway route by which the chemical may push bladder cancer forward.
pmc-12804958:
Yusuf El-Khaled and nine co-authors measure how much heat and cold three Red Sea corals can bear before they bleach, in a 2025 study. Bleaching is best known as a heat harm, but cold snaps can bleach corals too. The team adds a cold threshold score to match the standard heat score. They test coral pieces in a fast stress rig in both summer and winter, and profile the microbes that live with each coral.

One coral type bore the most heat in summer, while another bore the least cold in winter. Each coral kept its own set of partner bacteria across seasons. In one type, more of a common partner family meant a lower heat threshold. Recovery after stress also differed by type. The paired scores give a fuller view of coral risk as seas change.
pmc-12805458:
Four authors, led by A. Larkum in the byline, look back in 2025 over twenty years of a conference series on light-based energy research. The meetings began in 2004 in Canada, set up as a smaller mate to the large world congress in the field. Their name grew over time to add hydrogen work and, later, a stress on lasting energy.

Twelve meetings ran across three continents in that span. Each drew experts with fresh work on how plants split water, how the twin light systems in cells run, and how hydrogen can be made from light. The piece gives the key events of each meeting in turn. It frames the series as a hub where basic plant science meets clean fuel aims.
pmc-12806658:
Ho-Sook Kim and co-authors compare three stomach acid regimens in healthy adults over fourteen days, in a phase one study from two thousand twenty-five. Thirty-six people took a low dose of tegoprazan twice a day, a higher dose once a day, or famotidine twice a day. Stomach pH was tracked around the clock.

The low twice-daily dose held acid down longest, keeping pH high for about three quarters of the day. The once-daily dose and famotidine trailed well behind by day fourteen. Famotidine also faded over time while both tegoprazan plans held steady. No side effects were reported in the low-dose group. Readers get a dosing case for split low doses.
pmc-12807958:
A brain scan that takes a minute instead of eight would ease patients and cut motion blur.
