Lindsay Hanford and co-authors tune in 2025 an ultra-rapid compressed-sensing scan for measuring brain structure. They varied the acceleration, up to eightfold, and the reconstruction's smoothing strength, then compared the brain measures against a full-length reference scan in the same sessions.

Even the fifty-eight-second protocol spread its repeat measurements no wider than the reference, and its volume and thickness estimates agreed closely with the full scan at every speed. Smoothing changed looks more than numbers. The team concludes such quick scans can serve morphometry studies without giving up trust.
pmc-12808358:
Badminton at the top level is a lunge game, and Hirotaka Nakashima and co-authors ask which leg strength makes a player quicker across the court. Their study, published in 2025, tested fifty national-team players from Japan on a court agility drill and on knee extension strength at two speeds. The leg opposite the racket hand turned out to matter most.

Stronger extension in that off-side leg tracked with faster agility in both men and women at both speeds. The racket-side leg counted only at the slower test speed. The asymmetry fits the sport: the off leg brakes and pushes out of each deep lunge.
pmc-12810158:
Bahammam and Rady checked in twenty twenty-five stains and roughness on made white crowns for kids' teeth. They watched twenty young kids with white crowns on top teeth and steel crowns on low teeth. In the lab they ran crowns in a chew sim to read rough change by pair kind.

White crowns that bit on steel crowns had the most stain and rough shift. Metal rub through films on the crowns drove that change, they find. White on white pairs fared far better in the same tests. Pair pick thus shapes how long such crowns last and look, they warn.
pmc-12811958:
Marisa Cunha and co-authors present a case report, published in 2025, on a common painkiller causing a rare and dangerous blood disorder. Metamizole is widely used for severe pain and stubborn fever, yet it can trigger agranulocytosis, a collapse in the white cells that fight infection. Their patient was a woman aged seventy who had cosmetic abdominal surgery, then developed an abscess with lasting fever.

When standard drugs failed, metamizole was started, and five days later her protective white cell count had crashed. The drug was stopped at once, and isolation, growth factor treatment, and broad antibiotics brought recovery. The authors use the fast onset and clean recovery to argue for caution and blood checks with this everyday drug.
pmc-12812658:
Salceda and Vidu study violence in teen romantic and sexual relationships, and how girls can break free of it. They link the problem to social pressure and coercive talk that push girls toward unequal partners. Their study tested a group reading and dialogue program built around the book Radical Love. Fifteen girls aged 15 to 18 took part in the sessions.

The team assessed impact through recorded talks, life stories, and focus groups. The sessions helped the girls push back against coercive talk. Participants reported more freedom to choose safer and more equal partners. The authors present dialogue groups as a practical prevention tool for schools and youth programs.
pmc-12812758:
Ya Yuan and co-authors present a study, published in 2025, of ultrasound-based learning models that sort follicular thyroid tumors by risk. Telling a benign growth from a borderline or cancer form before surgery is hard with scans and needle tests. The team drew image traits from inside and around each tumor.

Records held 277 patients with tissue-proven tumor types. Three learning methods were trained on mixes of clinic, scan, and image traits. A plain regression model with rim traits stayed the most stable, while a forest model scored best on plain traits but over-fit when image traits piled up.
pmc-12813558:
Soichiro Okamoto and co-authors test whether sealing a needle track with saline cuts the risk of lung collapse after lung biopsy, in a 2025 study. Guided lung biopsies help diagnose suspicious spots. Their most common side effect is pneumothorax, air leaking around the lung. A simple seal might block that leak.

The team reviewed hundreds of biopsies done at one hospital over three years. Some cases used saline injected while the needle withdrew. Others used no seal. Groups were compared on collapse rates and related outcomes. The biopsy systems and needle sizes were recorded as well. Radiologists gain direct evidence on a cheap safety step. Patients may face fewer chest drains if the seal proves effective.
pmc-12815758:
Dongling Luo and co-authors trace in this 2025 study how cigarette smoke tilts helper T cells toward inflammation through packages shed by dendritic cells. In dishes, smoke extract drained a guardian protein, SIRT1, from dendritic cells over time, disturbed their self-cleaning, and raised cell-death markers. Exosomes from those cells then pushed T cells toward the inflammatory Th17 type and away from calming Treg cells.

A drug that wakes SIRT1 reversed the pattern: cleaner self-maintenance, less death signaling, and a rebalanced T cell split. The authors link the chain to the immune imbalance behind chronic obstructive lung disease. Smoke-free lungs keep the balance by default. The chain starts in the nose and lungs.
pmc-12816058:
Yexia Guo and co-authors study in 2025 how packed loess soil in Yan'an, China, slumps when it gets wet. Such slumps drive frequent ground harm on the Loess Plateau, so knowing how the soil fails helps towns guard against it.

Stepwise wetting tests tracked how the soil sank under load at two packed densities. Scope images and pore probes showed large pores caving in and grains shifting as water rose. Loose soil sank the most, while dense soil, held by stronger bonds, barely moved. The team frames wet slump as pore cave in plus grain shift toward a more stable state.
pmc-12816258:
Chuanxiang Zhao and Juxiang Shen review how transfer RNAs and one of their chemical modifications help switch T cells on in 2026. When a naive T cell meets its antigen, it must suddenly build millions of new proteins, and that surge depends on the tRNA supply.

The review explains how tRNAs are made, how the m1A58 modification tunes each step of protein production, and how tRNA fragments add further control. New sequencing methods show the tRNA mix changes dynamically during activation. Understanding this layer could point to fresh ways of treating diseases where T cells misfire or fall short, from immune disorders to weak responses against infection.
pmc-12817458:
Julian Ganter and ten co-authors build a machine learning model to place defibrillators where they save the most lives, in a study published in twenty twenty-five. When a heart stops outside hospital, minutes matter, and a nearby defibrillator can double survival odds. Yet clear rules for placing the devices are lacking, and records of past arrests are often patchy.

The team worked in Freiburg, Germany, with over five thousand alerts for suspected cardiac arrest and ninety-five device spots. Their model predicts arrest risk from population and building data alone, with no need for past arrest sites. A greedy search then picked fresh locations step by step. Checks against real arrest records confirmed the picks, and scenarios measured how coverage would grow.
pmc-12817758:
Li and six co-authors trace how a surface protein lifts fat burn in bone cells in this twenty twenty-five study. Fat use gone wrong in bone cells can thin bone and feed weak-bone ills. The protein in scope links to a range of cell talk paths in past work.

Inside, gene tweaks that boost or cut the protein shift fat burn in bone cells. With more of it, a cell power switch flips on and stays on in cell tests. That switch speeds the burn of fats and backs fresh bone growth as a result. The protein holds the switch in its on pose by blocking a self-off fold. Mice with more of it lost less bone, which marks it as a cure lead.
pmc-12819558:
Xuanang Wu and a large team wrote a 2025 study on a sibling rivalry between two calcium sensors at nerve endings. Synaptotagmins sense calcium to trigger vesicle release, the step that sends signals between neurons. The star sensor Syt1 binds calcium. Its relative Syt11 does not, yet still shapes transmission by an unclear mechanism.

The team found Syt11 clings to acidic membrane lipids and is pushed off by calcium. Syt1 does the opposite, inserting into the membrane when calcium arrives. At rest, Syt11 occupies membrane sites and competes with Syt1; a calcium pulse clears it away. Mutations mapped the binding styles of both proteins. In neurons, Syt11 slowed early release and recycling while peak release stayed intact. The pair act as a calcium-operated switch on the membrane.
pmc-12820058:
Arega Zenaw and co-authors report a 2025 study of the hormone prolactin in men with type 2 diabetes. The work took place at a large hospital in Gondar, in northwest Ethiopia, during 2024. Prolactin comes from a small gland in the brain and helps with reproduction and body chemistry.

The team compared 165 men with diabetes to 165 healthy men, using surveys, blood tests, and standard lab work. High prolactin levels showed up in 9.1 percent of the diabetes group and 6.1 percent of the control group. Average levels were also higher in the men with diabetes, and the gap was firm by the usual tests. The study gives local data on a hormone that is rarely checked in this group.
pmc-12820358:
Waqas Ali Shah and co-authors report a 2025 chemistry advance in making sunlight split water for fuel. Their catalysts marry clusters called polyoxometalates with porous frames called metal-organic frameworks. The key lesson is fit: when the guest cluster matches the host cavity size exactly, charge flows well and wasted recombination drops.

Their best pairing locks a cobalt cluster inside a zirconium frame so it cannot leak or clump. It drove water oxidation at 283 turnovers, past prior versions of its kind. Light tests confirmed clean charge separation, and the used catalyst kept its structure for reuse. The authors offer size matching as a design rule for this catalyst family. Solar fuel work gains a clear target from the result.
pmc-12821258:
Fan Zhang, Chenbing Wang, and Jiaxuan Ren study how peach seeds wake from dormancy in a 2025 paper. Peach seeds sleep deeply, so they sprout slowly and unevenly, which limits nursery work. The team set up four groups with water, plant hormone plus other chemicals, and bleach based or fluoride based mixes, all with heat control. They tracked body measures, gene activity, and plant hormone levels over time.

Treatments raised sprouting and shifted levels of several growth hormones. Day forty five stood out as a key control point in the balance between a sleep hormone and a growth hormone. Thousands of genes changed, clustered in hormone signaling and sugar use pathways. Eight key compounds also shifted. Readers get a gene level map for shortening peach seed sleep.
pmc-12823558:
Abadi Atsbaha and six colleagues measure child wasting after war in a town in northern Ethiopia, in a twenty twenty-five survey. Wasting means a child is far too thin for their height, a grave risk in poor regions. Little data existed for Adigrat town after fighting stopped in Tigray. The team surveyed 325 children aged six months to five years in early twenty twenty-five, measuring arm size and asking carers questions.

About seventeen percent of the children were wasted, with five percent in the severe range. Skipping the first milk after birth was among the linked factors the authors report. The rate sits above emergency thresholds. The team calls for food and health support aimed at the youngest children in postwar areas.
pmc-12823658:
Yiming Zhang and co-authors build a model that predicts whether a drug compound will bind a protein, in a paper from 2025. Such forecasts speed up drug discovery by screening pairs before lab work. Past deep learning models leaned on letter sequences alone and on scarce labeled data, which hurt their accuracy on new cases.

Their model, called GenSPARC, reads proteins through their three-dimensional shape. Shape codes come from a structure predictor and a three-dimensional alphabet tool. Compounds are read by both a graph network and a trained chemical language model. An attention step then models how the pair fits together. Tests across several benchmark sets showed strong results, including on hard splits where test pairs differ most from training pairs. Screening tasks also scored well.
pmc-12824058:
Antoine Dubray-Vautrin and co-authors compare surgery first with other care for throat cancer that has not spread. Both paths are seen as valid, yet no trial has split patients at random between them, so the best first step is still not known.

The study covered 432 patients treated at two centers from 2012 to 2020. The surgery group was younger and fitter at the start, with less advanced disease. A weighting method was used to balance the groups. After that step, the surgery first group showed a lower risk of death and of disease return over five years than the other group.
pmc-12824158:
Wei Fu and co-authors studied how heat changes coal dust wetting in a 2025 paper. Wetting coal dust with surfactant sprays is a main dust control in mines, where dry dust harms lungs and can explode. Heat in deep shafts runs high, yet most past wetting work was done at one mild temperature.

The team tested three surfactants, one of each charge class, from about 18 to 35 degrees Celsius. Contact angles fell as heat rose, so sprays wet the coal better warm. Atom-level simulations showed why, at the level of molecule pull. The work helps mines tune sprays for hot faces.
pmc-12824258:
Sidsel Pedersen and co-authors report five-year outcomes from a trial combining a cancer vaccine with a checkpoint drug in advanced melanoma, published in 2025. The vaccine targets two immune-suppressing proteins, IDO and PD-L1, and was given with nivolumab as first treatment for metastatic disease. Short-term results had been promising, but durable benefit needed proof.

At five years, the combination showed durable efficacy, with a median time without progression measured in years rather than months. Blood protein profiling found immune signatures tied to the vaccine. Rises in three signaling proteins marked patients with long progression-free survival. Those rises were not seen in a matched group given the checkpoint drug alone, suggesting the vaccine modulates immunity in a distinct way. Lab studies confirmed the vaccine targets certain immune cells.
pmc-12824358:
Haorui Wang and six colleagues published a mining safety study in two thousand twenty-five on water bursting through a coal mine floor. Mining extra-thick seams shakes the rock below, where pressurised water may wait behind a weak barrier. Tiny rock cracks, called microseismic events, can warn of danger.

The team monitored one working face in a Chinese mine. Most events clustered in one rock layer beneath the seam. Daily energy release, failure depth, and the reach of mining influence all tracked measured water inflow and rock pressure closely. They built a risk scoring model from these live signals rather than fixed geology. Its verdicts matched field readings. The authors offer the approach for mines over strong aquifers.
pmc-12826858:
Poudineh Moghadam, Bazi, Esfahani, and Emadi reviewed virtual clinics for remote care in this paper from twenty twenty-five. Distant and underserved regions suffer more preventable illness and death. Virtual clinics promise to bridge that distance with telehealth tools. The team gathered the published evidence using a formal scoping method.

Thirty-eight distinct benefits emerged from the literature. Better access, lower costs, and less patient travel led the list. Gains also appeared in governance, staff training, and record keeping. Digital prescribing and local technology use showed strong effects in richer countries. The authors conclude that virtual clinics can narrow health gaps. They frame the review as a map for planners.
pmc-12827158:
Mikayla Jackson, Lauren Porter, and Robert Oakes wrote this review on tools that steer the immune system in the brain. The head of the record dates it to 2025, though the catalog lists 2026. Brain tumors, wasting diseases of the nerves, and autoimmune inflammation differ in cause. Yet they share deep immune dysfunction.

The review first lays out the immune biology common to these conditions. It covers both innate and adaptive immune cells. Next it surveys diagnostic tools, from molecular assays to nano-scale platforms, that image and screen for brain inflammation. A final section covers therapies that tune the immune response. These are sorted by whether they act inside the nervous system or across the body. Biomaterial platforms that deliver treatment with precision get close attention.
pmc-12827258:
Bahare Noohi and Mansour Zahedi present a computational chemistry study, published in 2025, on how the placement of DNA damage shapes the molecule's response. Oxidative stress in inflamed and cancerous tissue attacks the DNA base guanine, creating a lesion tied to cancer formation. Using reactive molecular dynamics on a standard short DNA segment, the team modeled five patterns of that damage, from a single site to the whole strand.

They tracked measures of twisting, stretching, and end separation in each case. Fully damaged strands stretched and unwound broadly, while damage clustered at the ends, aligned in one orientation, left the helix nearly native. Crossed patterns forced the ends to fray. Placement and symmetry, the authors conclude, matter as much as the damage itself.
pmc-12827658:
Gonçalves presents a review dated 2025 in the text on a membrane protein, TMEM165, and inherited heart muscle disease. Some children are born with cardiomyopathy, where early genetic diagnosis can guide care and family checks. A group of sugar-chain disorders, called CDG, often includes heart muscle thickening or stretching. Mutations in the TMEM165 gene belong to that group.

The review gathers recent basic and clinical work on the protein's disease variants. Certain amino acid spots prove critical to its function, the highlights note. The author argues the gene deserves a place in cardiomyopathy testing panels. Links to nerve and muscle signs in the same patients also get attention.
pmc-12829058:
Zhiguang Fan and four co-authors test a mindfulness questionnaire on Chinese nurses in a 2025 paper. The scale, CAMS-R, claims to measure attention, awareness, and acceptance, the parts of a mindful mind. Before hospitals use it to judge staff well-being programs, it must measure the same thing across ranks.

Over a thousand nursing graduates, interns, and registered nurses filled it in alongside scales for well-being and quitting intent. The Chinese version held ten items in three parts, and a two-layer model fit best. Scores were steady, linked to higher well-being and lower wish to leave, and meant the same across the three groups. The team clears the scale for nursing research.
pmc-12830758:
Maryam Mehrabani and co-authors present a computing paper, published in 2025, on predicting which drug pairs will work well together against cancer. Pairs that reinforce each other can raise gains and lower harm. Older prediction tools often model drugs two at a time and miss the wider web of links among drugs, proteins, and cell lines.

Their system, SynergyGraph, first builds a knowledge graph tying drugs, proteins, and cell lines together. It then learns features for each item and groups known strong pairs with the cell lines they act on. A deep learning model reads these features and predicts a synergy score for new pairs in a given cell line. The authors aim to cut wasted lab tests and point researchers toward safer, stronger drug pairs.
pmc-12830858:
Jennifer Marlon and co-authors show that Americans' sense of heat danger often misses the expert map in a 2025 paper. Heat illness is largely preventable, but people act on what they perceive, and perception leans on personal experience and mental shortcuts. The team built a framework comparing perceived risk from a multi-year national survey against assessed risk from a federal heat-health index, county by county.

Misalignment was substantial, especially in the Pacific Northwest and Appalachia. Places can carry high assessed vulnerability while residents feel safe, or the reverse. The authors offer their alignment maps as a targeting tool for risk communication, adaptation planning, and policy. The point is not that experts are always right, but that the gaps themselves are diagnostic.
pmc-12830958:
Poppy Joaquina Romera and co-authors test a classic ecology rule in soil food webs, in a 2025 paper. The energetic equivalence rule says populations of small and large species should use about the same total energy, since numbers fall as body size grows. The team checked size and energy patterns across 183 soil invertebrate food webs from many places, covering more than fifty-five thousand animals.

Size-density patterns did not back the rule in these soil communities. Whether the rule seemed to hold depended on how energy use was estimated, on the feeding level of the animals, and on the web's structure. The authors argue that energy flow and feeding links must be read together to explain body size patterns on land.
pmc-12831158:
Fayaz Hussain and co-authors follow serum albumin levels as shin bone fractures heal in a 2025 prospective study. These shaft fractures are common because the bone sits close under the skin and can be hit directly. Albumin is a blood protein tied to nutrition and healing, and the team asks whether its change tracks good or poor union.

The study, run at a teaching hospital in Gilgit over several years, enrolled about a hundred ten patients with simple shaft fractures. Staff took histories, examined each patient, and drew blood for albumin, then checked whether the bone united. About one in six patients had impaired union. The change in albumin differed clearly between the normal and impaired groups, a link the authors say could help guide fracture care.
pmc-12831258:
Jesper Biesmans and co-authors report a 2025 study on bringing a Dutch dementia care approach to three Caribbean islands: Aruba, Bonaire, and Curaçao. The approach, called DEDICATED, trains staff to give person-centered care near the end of life. Seventy-two health workers were trained, and the team surveyed their needs beforehand and ran focus groups on each island to hear how the rollout felt.

Staff voiced strong needs around knowing the person and planning care ahead. Death and palliative care came up as taboo topics in island culture. Still, the approach raised awareness and got staff raising end-of-life needs more openly with families. The team calls for local tailoring to root it deeper.
pmc-12831358:
Md Masud Rana, Farjana Tasnim Mukta, and Duc Nguyen present DeepGGL, a 2025 deep learning model that predicts how strongly a drug candidate binds its target protein. Good guesses at binding strength steer the search for new medicines, and learned models now beat older scoring rules when rich structure data is on hand.

DeepGGL reads the pair as a geometric graph, split by atom colors and weighed at several scales, so small atom-to-atom contacts are kept. Extra links inside the network and an attention step help it focus on the contacts that matter. On two standard test sets it set new marks, and it held its accuracy on two more sets, which the authors cite as proof it travels well.
pmc-12834958:
Katarzyna Zdanowicz and four co-authors tracked immune signals in children with ulcerative colitis in a 2025 paper. The disease inflames the colon, and blood levels of signaling proteins called cytokines might mirror its course. The team studied 33 children, most newly diagnosed, alongside 29 healthy children.

Blood was sampled at diagnosis or flare, then again at three and six months of treatment. Several signals, including IL-8, IL-17, and eotaxin, ran high at the start. Three of them were higher at baseline in children whose disease later settled than in those still active at six months. The authors urge care in reading the pattern, since treatments varied, but suggest these signals may help forecast the disease's path.
pmc-12835158:
Gang Li and co-authors published this study in 2025. It tracks how water moves through ion-adsorbed rare earth ore. The team used a dense electrical resistivity method alongside sensors on a test block. Resistivity readings map where water spreads underground.

Lower layers neared saturation while the topsoil stayed dry, forming a possible slip zone. Strength also bottomed out at full saturation. The authors urge close checks in mid and late injection.
pmc-12835458:

pmc-12835958:

Blood patterns pointed to blocked bile flow, while tests for viral, immune, and metabolic causes came back empty. He carried no known risk factors for the benign disorder. The overlap delayed the true diagnosis. Such reports sharpen suspicion when a supposed vascular disorder behaves oddly.
pmc-12836658:

pmc-12836758:
Abdelrhman Refaey and co-authors screen Washington-area communities for hidden kidney disease in a 2025 study. Forms captured background, other conditions, and contact with care.

pmc-12836958:
Rina Putri Noer Fadilah, Rasmi Rikmasari, Saiful Akbar, and Arlette Suzy Setiawan present a two thousand twenty-five study of an artificial intelligence app spotting tooth decay in schoolchildren's mouth photos. Accuracy was measured with standard detection metrics. The work tests whether automated photo screening can triage children toward the limited dental care available.
pmc-12837058:
Xiaohui Tian, Leibing Ji, and Reyisai Abudulamu report a swollen vortex vein in one eye with no underlying cause, in a case study from twenty twenty-five. pmc-12837558:
Mohammadbagher Sharifkazemi, Zahra Hooshanginezhad, Leila Ahmadi, and Marjan Jaladat compare two imaging methods for muscle shortening in a heart condition, in a 2025 study. Either tool can track the disease, with care at the base.
pmc-12838358:

pmc-12838458:
Bertrand Pavlovsky and ten co-authors study the pressure needed to reopen collapsed airways in patients on ventilators. The lowest regional value tracked the whole-lung value closely. Lying flat raised the highest regional pressure compared with sitting partly up, and tests on cadavers tied the rise to pressure from the abdomen. pmc-12838558:

Three test cases proved the fix: a bright dye at low concentration, dim particles troubled by solvent scattering, and a camera-like detector with hot pixels. In each, the correction restored accurate counts and repeatable results. The authors present the scheme as a general answer to a long-standing flaw in the technique. pmc-12841558:
Karen Florez and Emma Gutierrez explore what shapes body weight among Mexican immigrants in New York City. They use network data from a small group and the many people named in their circles. Each person said if they wished to weigh more, less, or the same.

People unhappy with their weight who also felt high stress from fitting in had much higher weight scores. Oddly, seeing more heavy people in one's circle went with lower own weight. The authors say norms in both cultures may pull in mixed ways and need more study.
pmc-12844558:

pmc-12847858:
Yixi Wu and co-authors present a 2025 structure of the flu virus copying machine bound to a viral RNA signal. The machine makes two kinds of RNA when the virus copies its genome. pmc-12847958:

pmc-12848058:

The assembly is large, highly complete by standard checks, and on par with kin species. pmc-12848158:

Using a mouse model of joint damage, the team lowered or raised the enzyme in cartilage cells. Losing it hurt DNA repair, woke an inflammatory pathway, and aged the cells faster. pmc-12849058:

pmc-12849258:

Ferroptosis, an iron-driven form of cell death, offers a way around resistance, yet its link to lenvatinib failure was unclear.

pmc-12849558:
Zhenhua Xu and three co-authors built a machine learning model to forecast injuries in football players in a 2025 paper. Injuries cost teams matches and players their health, so early warning has real value. The team followed 300 professional male players, aged 18 to 28, across two seasons.

Daily records covered training load, recovery, wellness, heart-rate measures, minutes played, and past injuries. Three model types were trained with cross-checks and cleaned data. Random forests won, reaching about 86 percent accuracy and strong scores across measures. Explanation tools named prior injury, training intensity, and recovery time as the strongest warning signs. The authors present the model as a practical aid for tailoring training to each player.
pmc-12852958:
Dadmehr Yaghoubi and colleagues wrote a 2025 case report about a seventy-nine-year-old man who became seriously ill after a COVID infection. Doctors suspected a rare, life-threatening overreaction of the immune system in which immune cells begin destroying the body's own blood cells.

Steroid treatment brought rapid improvement. The case shows how several insults stacking together can push the immune system past a tipping point.
pmc-12853858:

pmc-12854158:

pmc-12855958:
Yiyuan Zhang, Jirui Liu, and Jia Liu study how wiring density shapes what the brain can recognize, in work from 2025. Seeing an object well means both telling it apart and grouping it with its kind. Brain and machine vision both face that trade-off.

Sparser wiring in a neighbor area went with a richer space and finer detail. A model built with real wiring lengths found a sweet spot between the two. pmc-12858658:

pmc-12860058:
Clément Gouraud and co-authors set out in this 2025 paper the plan for a trial of intensive rehab for long COVID. Lasting symptoms after COVID lack proven rehab paths. The main yardstick is physical quality of life at six months, with mental scores, symptom load, and satisfaction tracked at three and six months. The protocol is published in full, tests and all, before results exist, so readers can judge the trial's fairness once the data land.
pmc-12860158:

pmc-12864558:

pmc-12864758:

pmc-12864858:

pmc-12866058:

pmc-12866458:

pmc-12867858:

pmc-12872858:

pmc-12874858:

pmc-12875558:

pmc-12887858:

pmc-12893958:

pmc-12894358:

pmc-12901458:

pmc-12907358:

pmc-12913858:

pmc-12916658:

pmc-12953558:

pmc-13018358:

pmc-13018458:

pmc-13070258:

pmc-13086258:

pmc-13120658:

pmc-13125158:

pmc-13126458:

pmc-13130758:

pmc-13135258:

Scan and body checks agreed in full. All kept bodies and most fresh ones held a well-placed tip. The team says the method let staff check and shift tips with care, though live trials must come first.
pmc-13136458:
Vanessa Campos Guedes and co-authors tested, in a 2026 study, how light color reshapes the chemistry of a workhorse microalga. Scenedesmus obliquus is farmed for proteins and pigments, and light is the cheapest dial growers control. pmc-13138758:

On three public cough sets, scores ran near perfect, about two points past the best past methods. Under noise, scores sagged by less than three points. Part-removal tests credit both new parts. The frame is offered as a reusable pattern for medical sound work where trust needs a visible trail.
pmc-13141458:
Taketoshi Fujimoto wrote a 2026 comment on a study of ultrasound diagnosis for gallbladder cancer. That depth matters: shallow growth can still be cured by full removal, while deeper growth is more grave.

pmc-13143058:
Hongjing Chang and co-authors study how readers receive translations of a Li Bai poem in this 2026 paper. Classical Chinese poetry crosses cultures with loss, since rhythm and imagery differ across tongues. Four English versions of one poem were compared head to head.

The versions used prose, free verse, rhyme, and literal styles. A total of 403 American readers rated them through an online survey. Questions covered content, theme, feeling, and character views. Rhymed translation proved most popular with this audience. It seemed to balance sense and beauty best. Open replies were coded for themes, and the poems were also read closely as texts.
pmc-13143158:
Weijing Chen and co-authors mine Chinese social media to map life with a weakened, stretched heart in younger patients, in a qualitative study from two thousand twenty-six. Nearly nine hundred posts and answers from a question platform were coded by theme.

Five themes emerged: losing control of the body, emotional turmoil, broken family and work roles, unmet care needs, and rebuilding life. Guilt over burdening family and worry over survival ran through the posts. Peer sharing helped many cope. The authors urge care shaped to life stage and culture.
pmc-13144258:
Thomas Pendergast and six co-authors survey herbicide resistance in a cosmopolitan weed in a 2026 paper. pmc-13144858:

pmc-13145058:

The trial will enroll 906 patients at centers in many countries. Half will get the clot drug and half will get best drug care alone. All had taken the pill in the past two days and had a disabling stroke. Main checks are function at ninety days and severe bleeding in the brain.
pmc-13145158:

pmc-13145558:

pmc-13145758:

pmc-13145958:

pmc-13146258:

pmc-13146558:

pmc-13146658:

pmc-13146958:

pmc-13151958:

pmc-13154458:

pmc-13154758:

pmc-13155658:

pmc-13156158:

pmc-13156258:

pmc-13156758:

pmc-13156858:

pmc-13156958:

pmc-13157458:

pmc-13158358:

pmc-13159958:

pmc-13161858:

pmc-13163758:

pmc-13164258:

pmc-13167058:

pmc-13174858:

pmc-13175858:

pmc-13175958:

pmc-13177458:

pmc-13177858:

pmc-13179058:

pmc-13179458:
Shima Ghasemi and co-authors compare blood levels of two vitamins and omega-3 fats in people with lasting gum disease. Their paper from 2025 works with thirty six patients at set disease stages. Gum state was scored by a gum index, pocket depth, and tissue loss measures.

pmc-13182158:

pmc-13182358:
Rodrigo Yanez-Sepulveda and co-authors compare fitness and body measures in Chilean teens by where they live in a 2026 study. Past work splits on whether town or country teens run fitter or leaner, so a national sample can settle the shape of the link.

pmc-13182958:

pmc-13183158:

pmc-13183458:

pmc-13183858:

pmc-13184558:

pmc-13185258:

pmc-13185758:

pmc-13185858:

pmc-13185958:

pmc-13187858:

pmc-13187958:

pmc-13190558:

pmc-13201258:

pmc-13202458:

pmc-13202658:

pmc-13203358:

pmc-13204358:

pmc-13204458:

pmc-13204758:

pmc-13206158:

pmc-13207858:

pmc-13208758:

pmc-13209358:

pmc-13209558:

pmc-13209958:

pmc-13210258:

pmc-13211258:

pmc-13211558:

pmc-13211758:

pmc-13213858:

pmc-13215458:

pmc-13224158:

pmc-13250658:

pmc-13251158:

pmc-13251258:

pmc-13251758:

pmc-13251858:

pmc-13252758:

pmc-13253258:

pmc-13253658:

pmc-13253758:

pmc-13254758:

pmc-13254858:

pmc-13254958:

pmc-13257158:

pmc-13257458:

pmc-13257658:

pmc-13258758:

pmc-13258958:

pmc-13259358:

pmc-13259658:

pmc-13259758:

pmc-13260158:

pmc-13260458:

pmc-13260858:

pmc-13262158:

pmc-13262958:

pmc-13263358:

pmc-13263558:

Quality ratings told a matching story: every review scored low or critically low on the standard scale, and none scored high. The authors demand concrete steps to curb spin in orthopedic publishing, since surgeons lean on reviews for daily choices.
pmc-13263758:
Sean Li and colleagues re-analyze a back pain trial to ask whether how treatment was delivered, not just whether, predicted success. The RESET trial's sixty-day nerve stimulation beat usual care for chronic low back pain. Their 2026 post-hoc study isolates patients who received the full intended protocol.

Proper delivery meant stimulating both sides of the spine, covering most of the painful region, for six to twelve hours daily. Patients treated that way had roughly triple the odds of halving their pain at three months. Ordinary clinical traits like age and pain duration predicted nothing. Fidelity to protocol, they conclude, separates responders in this therapy.
pmc-13263858:
Joffroy Rogier and co-authors report a hard treatment choice: giving immune-boosting cancer therapy to a kidney transplant patient with lung cancer. Checkpoint inhibitor drugs have improved outcomes in locally advanced lung cancer and now anchor standard care. Transplant patients were excluded from the trials, though, because the same immune boost can trigger organ rejection. Reported rejection rates in kidney recipients run from 25 to 45 percent, often with permanent graft loss.

The patient, a 69-year-old man transplanted in 2012, shows two lung masses that prove to be squamous cell cancer at stage IIIA. After joint discussion between cancer and kidney teams, he receives chemotherapy plus the inhibitor nivolumab before surgery. He tolerates it well with no kidney harm. Scans show clear tumor shrinkage, and surgeons remove the left lung. The authors present the case as a guide to balancing cancer control against graft safety.
pmc-13264058:
Marina Prat-Carreño and co-authors publish a 2026 systematic review in Spanish on social effects and controversies of artificial intelligence in primary care. Following standard review methods, they searched major databases and screened hundreds of publications from 2015 to 2025. Sixty-three studies using qualitative, quantitative, mixed and conceptual approaches were included, while purely clinical studies were left out.

Ten themes emerged, covering views of professionals and patients, ethics, the doctor-patient relationship, management, bias and equity, and job insecurity. Most evidence came from prototypes rather than routine care. The authors find a wide gap between studies of hopes and perceptions and studies that measure real social effects. Primary care planners gain a map of questions that still need field evidence.
pmc-13264258:
Yupeng Zhang and colleagues target a force-sensing pathway to protect the eye drainage tissue during pressure spikes in a 2026 study. Glaucoma damages vision, and eye pressure is its main treatable risk factor. The drainage meshwork that lets fluid leave the eye reacts strongly to force. Its response to sudden pressure rises was unclear. The team therefore combined single-cell sequencing with lab and animal models of acute pressure elevation.

Pressure spikes killed meshwork cells, rearranged their skeletons and raised scarring markers, while two signaling proteins fell. Mice engineered to carry extra activity in one of those proteins resisted cell death and tissue disruption. Restoring that signaling axis could shield the drainage tissue during dangerous pressure surges in glaucoma care.
pmc-13264358:
Victor M Marwin and colleagues report six-month results for ultrasound-guided carpal tunnel release in a 2026 registry study. Nearly nine hundred patients covering over one thousand hands received the minimally invasive release at twenty-two United States sites after non-surgical care failed. Most procedures used wide-awake local anesthesia without a tourniquet, incisions averaged about five millimeters, and follow-up captured symptom scores, pain, quality of life, satisfaction and return to daily routines.

Median return to normal activities took three days and return to work four days. Symptom and function questionnaire scores improved substantially by six months, with follow-up nearly complete. Bilateral same-day treatment was common. Registry evidence of this scale shows how the technique performs in everyday practice beyond single-center trials.
pmc-13264558:
Catalina Aguilera-Flores and Carlos F Arias wrote a 2026 review on DPP4, a protein on cell surfaces that helps control metabolism and immune action. Some viruses use this protein to enter cells or to bend immune responses. The review maps those tricks and asks whether blocking DPP4 could treat infections.

Coronaviruses such as MERS bind DPP4 directly to get inside cells, and human astroviruses use it as part of a two-receptor route. HIV and hepatitis C instead exploit its enzyme and non-enzyme roles to alter T cell action and aid persistence. The authors weigh drugs that block DPP4, antibody treatments, and decoy versions of the protein. They frame DPP4 as a broad target for future antiviral work.
pmc-13264858:
Mônica Cristina da Costa Drago Souza and a large team present a 2026 trial protocol on genitourinary syndrome of menopause, a set of vaginal and urinary symptoms from low estrogen after menopause. Vaginal estriol cream helps many women, yet symptoms often persist. The trial tests whether adding a gentle erbium laser treatment beats cream alone.

All women in the trial get the cream daily for two weeks, then twice a week for 16 weeks. Half also get three real laser sessions about a month apart, and half get sham sessions, with neither side told which. The main measure is a vaginal health index four months after the last session. Other checks cover symptom severity, vaginal germ mix, quality of life, and sexual function. Women aged 45 to 70 with clear symptoms can join.
pmc-13264958:
Abdur Rahman and colleagues review evidence linking ultra-processed food with stomach cancer risk, in a 2026 systematic review. Consumption of such foods has risen worldwide. Links with several chronic diseases are known, while evidence for gastric cancer stayed mixed. The review gathered observational studies published over three decades.

Seventeen studies with about 277,000 participants were included. Eight found higher risk with higher ultra-processed food intake, three found none, and six found mixed results. Processed meats, fried foods, and sugary drinks were tied to risk most often. Differences in diet measurement explain part of the variation. The authors see a possible link that needs stronger studies.
pmc-13265158:
Zhongshun He and colleagues investigate baicalin, a plant compound, against melanoma cells, in a 2026 laboratory study. Melanoma is among the most aggressive skin cancers, and treatment options remain limited. Baicalin had shown anti-cancer promise in earlier work. How it acts on melanoma was not fully known.

Melanoma cells treated with baicalin grew, moved, and invaded less, while cell death rose with dose. Computer analyses predicted targets, and docking tests pointed to a growth receptor called EGFR. Further experiments showed baicalin dampened a growth pathway driven by that receptor. Forcing the receptor higher had the opposite effect. The findings suggest a mechanism worth testing further.
pmc-13265258:
Jinjia Zhang and colleagues test a small RNA as a predictor of lymph node spread in stomach cancer, in a 2026 study. Node spread strongly shapes outlook after surgery. Scans detect it with limited accuracy. Data from a public cancer database and a Chinese hospital covered 416 patients.

Four factors independently linked to node spread, including tumour stage and grade. The RNA, miR-1287-5p, added predictive value beyond clinical factors. A chart combining all four estimated spread risk for each patient. Accuracy was strong in the main cohort and moderate in the support cohort. The tool could aid surgical planning.
pmc-13266158:
Ji-Yeong Ku and the team compare gut microbes in Korean Hanwoo calves with viral diarrhoea (2026). Newborn calf gut mixes are still forming, making diarrhoea common and disruptive. Faeces from seven healthy calves and eight with diarrhoea were checked. Two viruses, rotavirus and coronavirus, were found in sick calves.

Overall variety differed little between healthy and infected calves. Cases of the first virus showed lower variety scores than cases of the second. Community make-up split clearly by group. Each virus shifted germ classes in its own way, and a helpful genus fell with both infections. The results support pathogen-by-pathogen gut work in calves.
pmc-13266258:
Qiang Gao and co-authors describe in 2026 DynaTOF, a software system that reads heart ultrasound scans to spot tetralogy of Fallot and judge risk after surgery. This birth defect of the heart is serious, and early, correct detection shapes survival. Data came from four centers and covered 1,986 children: healthy controls, look-alike conditions, and confirmed cases.

Five modules did the work in sequence. They sorted scan views, measured key heart widths, merged video with those measures to make the diagnosis, and predicted later risk scores. A last module split patients into high-risk and low-risk groups. Scores were strong across tasks, so the team sees DynaTOF aiding screening, surgical planning, and follow-up care for babies with this defect.
pmc-13266358:
Youngmin Kim and colleagues rethink the one-hour surgery target for regional trauma centres in South Korea, published in 2026. The metric demands emergency surgery within an hour for bleeding abdominal trauma with low blood pressure. Records covered 425 patients at two centres from 2019 to 2022. Matched comparisons tested the threshold.

Just over half reached surgery within the hour. In-hospital death did not differ between early and delayed groups, even after matching. Age, consciousness, blood pressure, transfusion volume, and injury severity predicted death instead. Complications rose as delay lengthened. The authors propose metrics that capture whole resuscitation quality, not one clock.
pmc-13267158:
Woon Teen Sia and colleagues wrote a 2026 study on how well ultrasound predicts a baby's weight before birth in Malaysia. Guessing fetal weight guides many delivery choices, yet scans are not always on hand in basic care. The team followed women with single babies at a large hospital near the end of pregnancy.

The study covered 153 women scanned at 37 to just under 39 weeks. Estimated weights were within 10 percent of true birth weight for about 69 percent of babies. Accuracy was best when the scan came within a day of delivery. Mother's weight, past births, and diabetes in pregnancy affected accuracy. The authors stress examiner training and wider scan access.
pmc-13267258:
Manal Alqahtani and five co-authors survey urine leakage among women in Saudi Arabia in a 2026 study. The condition is common yet often hidden, since shame and wrong beliefs keep women from seeking care. Its toll on daily life in that country had barely been measured.

Adult women across the country filled out an online survey on their health, birth history, and any leakage, plus its effect on life quality. Women who were pregnant or had nerve disorders of the bladder were left out. The authors aim to size the problem and show how it drags on daily life, work, and mood.
pmc-13267558:
Maureen Walton and a large team test in 2026 a phone app designed to cut cannabis use among young adults who use regularly but rarely seek treatment. Over thirty days, 122 participants answered surveys twice daily and were randomly sent, or not sent, support messages chosen by a learning algorithm. Follow-up checks came one and two months after the trial began.

The app proved workable: most participants downloaded it, completed most surveys, and rated the messages as caring and respectful. Receiving a message lifted short-term engagement with the app, though it did not directly lower next-step cannabis use. People who engaged more tended to report fewer use days later. The authors see promise and call for refining the messages to turn engagement into behavior change.
pmc-13269358:
Yusuke Saito and co-authors identify in 2026 an enzyme from a soil bacterium that breaks down polyamide 4, a bio-based plastic prized for strength and natural degradability. A marine version of the enzyme was known, but the land-based counterpart had never been characterized. The team found the gene in a soil bacterium, then produced the enzyme inside two different host microbes for comparison.

One host, a Brevibacillus strain, secreted enzyme with more than double the plastic-degrading activity of the E. coli version. Computer modeling split the enzyme into three parts: a binding region, a middle region, and the cutting region, with the outer two closely matching the marine enzyme. Similar genes turned up in ocean environmental DNA, hinting at a wide family of plastic degraders in nature.
pmc-13270058:
Jueun Oh, Yoon-Seok Chung, and SangJoon Lee published a review in 2026 on recent advances in mpox, a viral disease whose recent outbreaks spread widely between people. Disease severity, they note, cannot be explained by virus amount alone. The review draws together virus genetics, early immune sensing, inflammation, and immune evasion.

Host factors shape outcomes, including the strength of interferon signaling, control of inflammasomes, which are inflammation switches, and natural killer cell function. People with weakened immunity, including advanced HIV infection, face more severe and prolonged disease. Genetic diversity in the virus and its tricks for dodging immunity are also covered. The authors aim to explain why cases vary so much and to guide care of high-risk groups.
pmc-13271058:
Håkon Reikvam led a 2026 pilot safety study of hypoxic red blood cells, blood stored with oxygen and carbon dioxide removed to keep it in better condition, given by transfusion. Two patient groups were studied: people with blood cancers who need regular transfusions, and people with acute burns having surgery.

Twenty patients aged 27 to 96 received the stored blood, ten in each group. No adverse events linked to the hypoxic blood were reported within 24 hours or up to seven days. Haemoglobin, the oxygen-carrying protein, rose by an average of 1.2 units in the blood cancer group and 0.3 in the burn group soon after transfusion. The authors call the product safe and well tolerated here.
pmc-13271258:
Nada Abu-Shraie is lead author of a 2026 economic analysis of upadacitinib for moderate-to-severe atopic dermatitis, a long-lasting itchy skin disease, in Saudi Arabia. The study used mathematical models to judge whether the drug gives good value to the public payer and what wider use would do to budgets.

Over a lifetime model, upadacitinib at 15 milligrams gave 0.21 extra quality-adjusted life years, years lived in good health, and cost less than the comparison drug dupilumab by an amount given in Saudi riyals. Raising its market share over five years was linked to estimated savings of 1.5 billion riyals. The authors caution that model inputs and local data limits add uncertainty.
pmc-13271558:
Ankush Kawali and colleagues write in 2026 about gene sequencing tests for epidemic retinitis, an eye inflammation that follows a fever. Doctors have long suspected rickettsial infection, partly because patients improve on doxycycline. Standard blood tests, though, rarely prove which germ is responsible.

The team ran a broad sequencing panel on fluid drawn from the front of the eye in cases with inflammation there. None of the samples held the rickettsial or typhoid germs the panel covered. Only three patients tested positive, and those results looked like false alarms from very low read counts. The letter questions how much sequencing adds in this disease.
pmc-13271958:
Zhuqin Xiang and coauthors test in 2026 whether pairing two tissue features predicts survival in mouth cancer better than either alone. Tumor budding, where small cell clusters break away at the tumor edge, signals aggressive spread. Tertiary lymphoid structures, organized immune clusters, signal the opposite.

Records from 510 patients with oral squamous cell carcinoma were scored for both features on stained tissue. Heavy budding matched worse survival, while mature lymphoid structures matched better outcomes. A combined index separated patients more sharply than either feature alone. A prediction chart built on the index plus standard factors performed reliably in validation checks.
pmc-13272158:
Rong Hu and coauthors trace in 2026 a pathway linking iron imbalance to early aging of the placenta in preeclampsia, a dangerous pregnancy condition. The placenta in this disease shows signs of premature senescence, and the protective protein SIRT1 was found reduced in patient tissue. Its partner p53 is a known driver of cell aging.

Lowering SIRT1 in placental cells increased aging markers and harmful secretions while slowing growth and movement. Activating the protein in animals eased both placental aging and disease-like features. Removing excess iron also calmed aging, and clearing aged cells partly restored iron balance, showing the two processes reinforce each other.
pmc-13272358:
Mihajlo Bosnjak and coauthors review in 2026 a paradox at the heart of Parkinson's disease: cells need energy to run their cleanup system, yet energy failure is a hallmark of the disease. The cleanup process, autophagy, normally rises under energy stress, but completing it consumes ATP, the cell's fuel. In Parkinson's, faulty mitochondria drain that fuel supply.

The authors propose a two-phase pattern where mild early energy loss stimulates cleanup while severe loss stalls it midway. Undigested cargo, including worn-out mitochondria, then piles up and deepens the energy crisis. This vicious cycle framing suggests treatment must restore energy, not just prod the cleanup machinery.
pmc-13272858:
Shanshan Xu leads a 2026 study of drug pairs that can cause serotonin syndrome, a dangerous reaction from too much serotonin. Such risks grow as drugs that raise serotonin spread into pain and infection care. The team used a review of past work, United States safety reports, and a check of five drug interaction tools.

High-risk pairs went beyond mood drugs to include the antibiotic linezolid, the pain drug fentanyl, and methylene blue. Strong signals showed for linezolid with sertraline and fentanyl with venlafaxine. The five tools often disagreed, and 10.16 percent of pairs appeared in none of them, so one tool alone can miss real risk.
pmc-13273058:
Pascal Hauff leads a 2026 study using large language models to maintain a database of branded food products. Branded food data help track modern diets, but the data are vast, fast-changing, and uneven in quality. The team built a fully automated pipeline to collect, standardize, and enrich product data down to ingredient level.

A fine-tuned model beat human experts at parsing and mapping product data. Models without fine-tuning performed poorly, while even modest amounts of tuning data improved results a lot. The authors say language models offer a scalable way to keep food databases consistent, and can help estimate ingredient amounts and nutrients not declared on labels.
pmc-13273158:
Osama Abdallah and co-authors test chars made from farm waste as filters for two pesticides in water, in a study from 2026. The chars came from date palm stalks and eucalyptus leaves, both cheap local residues. The target chemicals were a common insecticide and a fungicide that wash into water supplies.

Batch tests varied dose, acidity, heat, time, and starting concentration to find the best recipe, which sat at neutral acidity and a day of contact. The palm char beat the leaf char in quick treatment, removing most of both chemicals. Two standard models fit the uptake curves well. The process released heat and ran on its own once set. The authors pitch the palm char as a low-cost, green sorbent for farm regions.
pmc-13273258:
Thomas Braun and colleagues studied how alpha-synuclein fibrils affect mitochondria in a 2026 cell study. Clumps of alpha-synuclein mark Parkinson's disease and related disorders, and mitochondria, the cell's power units, are also damaged. How the two connect is still not fully clear.

Using electron microscopy, they examined human nerve like cells exposed to alpha-synuclein fibrils. Treated cells showed defects in the folded inner structure of mitochondria. The mitochondria also shed more small bubble like vesicles, a conserved response that echoes how bacteria release membrane vesicles. Protein analysis backed the images, finding shifts in proteins that shape the inner folds and guide vesicle traffic. The authors suggest this shedding may matter for diagnosis and treatment research.
pmc-13273358:
Amy McDermott wrote a 2026 news feature on hydrologic whiplash, sudden swings between very wet and very dry conditions, driven by climate change. She opens with California at Christmas 2022, when severe drought gave way within days to a series of atmospheric rivers. Nine strong storms in three weeks caused flooding, 22 deaths, and billions in losses.

Researchers argue that droughts and floods should no longer be studied only in isolation, since back-to-back extremes can amplify harm. Such swings strain water storage, and forecasting models trained on older data anticipate them poorly, because rapid flips were rarer in the past. The piece urges water managers to plan for whiplash events.
pmc-13273858:
Ventimiglia and colleagues follow men whose PSA stayed stable on prostate drugs after a negative biopsy. Their 2026 journal article is a nationwide Swedish population study. PSA is a blood marker for prostate cancer.

The study used the PCBaSe Xtend database. It included 1,248 men who started 5-alpha reductase inhibitor therapy. These drugs shrink the prostate. Of the men, 901 had stable PSA and 347 had rising PSA. At ten years, cancer incidence was 8.3 percent with stable PSA. It was 18 percent with rising PSA. Most cancers in the stable group were low grade. Prostate cancer death was very low with stable PSA. The standardized mortality ratio there was 0.19. The authors say PSA trends could tailor follow-up intensity.
pmc-13274158:
Xiaoyan Chen and colleagues report a 2026 journal article on how single-color light changes a prized medicinal herb. Salvia miltiorrhiza, known as danshen, is grown for root compounds used in heart remedies. The team exposed plants briefly to ultraviolet, blue, red, or far-red light, with white light as the comparison.

All single colors switched on defense responses, and overall chemical levels mostly fell versus white light. Red light raised the most individual compounds, though. Ultraviolet, red, and far-red light each boosted two key tanshinone compounds while lowering salvianolic acid A. Blue light cut the variety of microbes around the roots. The authors suggest light recipes could raise herb quality.
pmc-13274458:
Mariah K. Hermary and co-authors studied surface layer shedding in a methane eating bacterium in a 2026 paper. Some methanotrophs wear an S-layer, a protein shell over the cell surface. Their species, Methylomicrobium album BG8, turned out to shed this shell in unusual amounts.

Electron microscopy showed constant shedding in this species but not in seven relatives, even one with a similar shell. Shedding continued under every food, metal, and growth condition they tried. Protein analysis of the shed units found shell subunits plus transporters for calcium, vitamins, and iron carriers, which hints the shell helps gather metals. A strain adapted to strong acid lost its shell through gene damage. The authors suggest harnessing the secretion system for industry.
pmc-13274858:
Siqi Zhang and co-authors report a 2026 journal article reviewing adverse events reported after HPV vaccination in the United States reporting system VAERS. Such systems collect voluntary reports and cannot prove a vaccine caused an event, but they can flag patterns. The team mined reports from 2006 to 2024 and required a signal to pass four different statistical tests.

In total, 77,909 reports were analyzed; 68.4 percent involved females and nearly half involved people under eighteen. About ninety percent of events were reported within thirty days of vaccination. Headache and fatigue were the most common complaints. Fainting was the most frequent statistical signal, while a racing-heart condition called POTS showed the strongest signal strength, meriting further study.
pmc-13275558:
Yunzhong Liu and colleagues report a 2026 before-and-after study of a fast-track recovery protocol for elderly hip fracture patients at a traditional Chinese medicine hospital in China. Such fractures bring long stays and many complications. The protocol, called ERAS, bundles early feeding, pain control, and quick mobilization, here with added traditional medicine elements.

Three hundred patients aged sixty-five and over were split by era: 146 treated conventionally from 2022 to 2023 and 154 under the new protocol from 2024 to 2025. The protocol group left hospital about 3.86 days sooner and suffered complications at 7.79 percent versus 15.07 percent. They also stood up far earlier, about twenty-nine versus fifty-three hours, reported less pain, and cost less overall.
pmc-13276458:
Fanny Chereau and a French outbreak team report a 2026 investigation of Cryptosporidium parvum infections. The parasite causes gut illness and spreads through water and food. Cases of one genotype jumped in France during 2025, far above the usual yearly count.

Standard gene typing could not split the outbreak further, so the team added a multi-locus repeat analysis. That method revealed two large, distinct strain profiles. Patient interviews tied one profile mostly to goat milk cheese and the other to packaged lamb's lettuce. Purchase records and traceback work located the product origins, and producers received preventive advice. The authors urge hygiene monitoring for raw milk goods and fresh produce.
pmc-13276558:
Si Wu and co-authors report a 2026 journal article on a signaling chain in stem cells that may worsen or heal gum disease. Periodontitis, severe gum inflammation, destroys the tissue and bone holding teeth. Bone marrow stem cells can calm immune responses, and the team probed how an inflammation signal, interleukin-6, steers them.

In mice with induced gum disease, both interleukin-6 and a small RNA it controls were raised. The signal switched the RNA on through a partner protein called STAT3. Blocking the RNA eased an imbalance between two T cell types that drives inflammation. Stem cells pretreated with the RNA blocker were then injected into diseased mice. Treated animals regrew more periodontal tissue, with fewer bone-eating cells and less bone loss. The authors propose this chain as a treatment target.
pmc-13276758:
Barbora Lujka and colleagues study fat-like membrane molecules in colon cancer cells in a 2026 laboratory paper. These molecules, glycosphingolipids, help build cell membranes and steer growth and death signals. Their building block, lactosylceramide, is made by two enzymes that cancer cells may depend on.

The team dialled down each enzyme in a human colon cancer cell line using gene editing. Levels of lactosylceramide and several complex downstream lipids fell as expected. The altered cells then died more readily under oxaliplatin, a standard colorectal chemotherapy drug. Stress responses inside the cells also shifted. The authors frame the enzymes as possible levers for making chemotherapy bite harder.
pmc-13276858:
Di Hu and colleagues look for warning signs of severe Chlamydia pneumoniae pneumonia in children, in a 2026 study. The bacterium causes a share of childhood lung infections, mostly mild, but some cases turn severe. Records came from Hebei Children's Hospital for cases treated between 2023 and 2025.

One hundred thirty-three children were split into non-severe and severe groups under current national guidance. Severe cases ran higher, longer fevers and showed more inflammation in blood tests. Two measures stood out after full statistical adjustment: a lower lymphocyte share and higher IgA antibody levels. The authors suggest these markers could help flag children at risk of worsening, pending wider confirmation.
pmc-13278458:
Dengue is among the world's most widespread mosquito-borne diseases, and its four virus types keep expanding into new regions. Ravindra Shinde and co-authors review the disease end to end in this 2026 paper, from its history and virus biology to how it spreads and harms.

They explain how a second infection can turn severe through antibody effects, and how a viral protein loosens blood vessel walls. Testing options from rapid antigen kits to gene sequencing are weighed, with emphasis on India's burden. The authors call for stronger routine tracking of virus lineages, which hospital studies still largely skip.
pmc-13279558:
Parvin Kalhor and co-authors test whether two heart measures together predict bad outcomes in patients whose chest pain comes without blocked arteries. One measure, coronary flow reserve, gauges the small vessels of the heart. The other is an AI-read ECG marker of the heart's filling pressure, a sign of strain. Among nearly two thousand such patients studied after invasive testing, about a quarter had poor flow reserve and a small share had the pressure marker.

Over eight years, about ten percent suffered major cardiovascular events. Both measures stayed tied to higher risk after adjustment, the pressure marker more strongly. Adding the marker to standard models improved fit and slightly sharpened risk sorting. The authors argue the cheap ECG marker adds prognostic power beside the invasive flow test.
pmc-13279658:
Nenad Filipović and colleagues published a 2026 editorial opening a journal collection on what is new in bioresorbable materials. These materials do a job inside the body and then dissolve into harmless products. They remove the need for a second operation to take out an implant. They also avoid the long-term risks of permanent foreign material. A device must stay strong for its working life. It must break down at a steady rate and yield only body-friendly products.

The collection spans electronics that degrade, magnesium implants, and polymer systems for heart and vessel use. It mixes perspective pieces with lab reports. One review covers electrodes made from metals such as magnesium, zinc, and molybdenum. Others use polymer-metal mixes, made by casting, printing, or electrospinning to meet soft tissue. The editors present a fast-moving field still short of designs that meet every need at once.
pmc-13280058:
Ewelina Wojciechowska and colleagues published a 2026 case report of a teenager whose high blood pressure traced back to an anatomical band squeezing two arteries. Median arcuate ligament syndrome usually compresses the celiac artery and causes gut symptoms such as pain and weight loss. Their patient, a 15-year-old boy, had none of those complaints. Instead he showed asymmetry between his kidneys and hypertension that stayed uncontrolled even as his amlodipine dose doubled.

Imaging revealed the ligament and the diaphragm's pillars compressing both the celiac trunk and the left renal artery, starving that kidney and driving renovascular hypertension. Surgery released the compression, restored flow in the renal artery, and normalized his blood pressure. The authors stress that this syndrome belongs on the checklist for young patients with hard-to-control hypertension and uneven kidney sizes, even without abdominal symptoms. Early decompression can prevent damage to the kidney's blood supply.
pmc-13280258:
Zhilong Li and colleagues report a 2026 lab study that tunes thulium fiber laser settings for kidney stone work. Lithotripsy uses laser pulses to break urinary stones in dust or fragments. Three parameters were varied: peak power, average power and pulse energy. A decoupling platform and fake BegoStone models let each factor shift alone. Fragmentation, dusting, heat harm and stone kick back, called retropulsion, were all scored.

High peak power with low average power and pulse energy boosted fragmentation and dusting. It also kept heat harm at the low end. Low peak power with high average power and pulse energy cut stone kick back, with no loss in fragmentation or dusting. The multilevel plan can tailor settings to stone site in the urinary tract. Personal settings may raise yield and cut risk in stone surgery.
pmc-13280458:
Carlos Enrique Calvache Benavides and team report a 2026 case of breakthrough fungus infection in a lung transplant patient. Two Aspergillus species, niger and calidoustus, caused the harm. Such fungi are uncommon causes of disease, most in people with weak immune defences. Their patient was a sixty one year old man with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, a lung scar illness.

He had a one lung transplant with no early problems. Despite a preventive fungus drug, voriconazole, he developed aspergillosis in his airways. One species is hard to name, as it looks and reads like kin species in standard tests. DNA based tests proved key for exact naming in this case. Exact naming guides the fungus drug choice that can save life in transplant care.
pmc-13280558:
Sameer Lamichhane and team report a 2026 case of a penetrating neck injury, with an arrow impacted at the top of the neck. Penetrating neck injuries are rare in trauma care and need prompt, sound assessment. Selective care has replaced mandatory exploration for such trauma. Their patient was a forty one year old man with an arrow in his neck and no signs of neurological deficit.

The arrow sat in the right posterolateral neck, just behind the sternocleidomastoid muscle, at the C1 C2 vertebra level. It was freed after the entry wound was extended, and removed with a gentle move in the operating room. His post surgery course and follow ups were uneventful. Direct withdrawal in a controlled setting may suit stable patients when the object lies away from neurovascular and aerodigestive tracts, the nerve, vessel and airway paths.
pmc-13280658:
Yuanze Luo and Assam El-Osta wrote a 2026 commentary on a new cancer drug called rezatapopt. The drug targets p53, a protein that guards cells against cancer but is broken in many tumors. One broken form has a small pocket that a drug can fit into. An early trial in patients with that form showed tumors shrinking.

The authors explain why the drug fits only that one form and not others. They note that blood tests for tumor DNA could help track how well the drug works. They also flag side effects such as nausea and a need to take the drug with food. The piece frames the drug as a precise tool, not a broad cure.
pmc-13280858:
Ciera A Price and colleagues tested a battlefield leg brace in a 2026 study. In war zones, care can stretch for long hours before a wounded soldier can be moved. Broken lower leg bones are common and now call for simple splints and a stretcher. The team built a wearable frame that steadies the leg and lets the person walk. They tested two early models with medics and with users acting as the wounded.

Twenty people tried the frame on set tasks in a lab. Twelve more used it in a mock mass-casualty drill in the field. Users rated it well overall, though fit and adjustment need work. Talks with users raised themes of comfort, weight, and strength. The team plans to compare the frame with splints and refine the design.
pmc-13280958:
Candice Y Lumibao published a 2026 perspective proposing resurrection ecology as a tool for understanding how plant-microbe partnerships evolve under global change. Plants interact with microbes around roots, inside tissues, and on leaves, from harmful to helpful partnerships. The interactions feed back between ecology and evolution, but long plant generations make evolution hard to watch. Resurrection ecology revives long-dormant seeds or eggs from deposits, seed banks, or herbarium collections, growing ancestors beside descendants.

The author argues this comparison is powerful for plant-microbe questions, because both partners can be revived across time points. pmc-13283958:

pmc-13284058:

pmc-13284458:

pmc-13284558:

pmc-13285558:

pmc-13291058:
