pmc-13291258:
Immune cells in breast tumor tissue may warn against chemotherapy. Zak Kinsella leads a 2026 study of hormone-sensitive breast cancer. Such tumors often look safe for five to ten years. Late return of disease is still common. Mid-range risk scores leave hard calls for doctors.

Tissue from hundreds of patients was mapped in fine detail. Gene and protein maps showed stroma and tumor nests differ. Inflamed stroma carried signs of worn-out immune cells. More killer immune cells in stroma linked to worse outcome. That link held in a treated trial group. It also held in a second tissue set. The marker may help spare some women harsh drugs.
pmc-13291358:
A rare hernia after bladder surgery is repaired in a 2026 case from Yusuke Sato and colleagues. The patient was an 80-year-old man. Four years earlier, a robot had removed his bladder for cancer. A routine scan then found bowel slipping through his pelvic floor.

He felt no symptoms at first and was watched. Signs of a partial bowel blockage later forced surgery. Doctors worked through the perineum from below. They freed the bowel and closed the small defect with a cross-shaped mesh. The patch was fixed to pubic bone on both sides. No return of the hernia showed at six months.
pmc-13291458:
A simple blood ratio may predict arthritis drug success. Jingru Zhu leads a 2026 study of adalimumab in rheumatoid arthritis. The ratio compares neutrophils to lymphocytes in blood. High values mark stronger body inflammation.

The study followed 189 patients to week 24. Response was scored on a 28-joint disease scale. High starting ratios predicted a good response. Good responders saw their ratios fall after treatment. Patients reaching remission started with higher ratios. Far more high-ratio patients hit remission than low-ratio ones. A cheap blood test could thus guide drug choice. More work must confirm the cut point.
pmc-13291558:
A strong antibody against mpox is found and mapped in fine detail. Shimeng Bai leads a 2026 study targeting a surface protein, A35R. That protein helps the virus spread inside a host. Blocking it could curb severe illness.

Mice were primed with mRNA shots to raise antibodies. A light-based sorter fished out the best binders fast. One antibody, 17H1, neutralized real mpox virus well. Cryo imaging showed it gripping the protein’s far ends. A web of bonds locks that grip in place. Treated animals were fully protected from infection. Lung virus counts and tissue harm both fell. A fresh treatment candidate emerges here.
pmc-13291858:
Fulu Gao and colleagues report a 2026 genome-wide study of the ABC transporter gene family in sweet potato. These membrane proteins burn ATP to move substances such as metal ions and hormones across cell boundaries. The team catalogued the family's members, their chemistry, chromosome positions, and tissue activity, then measured gene responses under metal stress.

Seedlings faced iron, aluminum, zinc, and copper treatments, with expression checked by RT-qPCR. Most family genes changed activity under at least one metal. One gene, IbABCC14, switched on under all four metals and resembles known detox transporters in Arabidopsis and rice, hinting it locks metals away in vacuoles. The authors propose it as a lead candidate for breeding metal-tolerant sweet potato varieties.
pmc-13292058:
Jinhui Che, with co-authors, reports a 2026 study on why liver cancers that resist sorafenib stay aggressive, focusing on mitochondria and sugar metabolism. Resistant cells were checked for mitochondrial shape, oxygen use, glucose uptake, and lactate output. The team also tested drug combinations in orthotopic mouse tumors.

A protein called Drp1 drove mitochondrial splitting and a switch from oxygen-based energy to aerobic glycolysis in resistant cells, and that pattern tracked with poor prognosis. Blocking Drp1 curbed invasion and spread but sped cell growth by flipping metabolism back toward oxygen use. Pairing the Drp1 blocker mdivi-1 with the OXPHOS inhibitor IACS-010759 hit both sides of that trade-off and slowed tumors markedly. The authors frame the pair as a route around sorafenib resistance.
pmc-13292158:
Mingqiang Lin and colleagues compare treatment timing for advanced esophageal cancer in a 2026 matched study. Patients had resectable squamous tumors staged cT3 to cT4a. One path gives chemoradiation before surgery, the other after it. Records for 223 patients were balanced into fifty-nine matched pairs by propensity scores. Survival and side effects were then compared head to head.

The before-surgery group lived longer, with median survival near sixty-two months against forty-six. Five-year survival reached about sixty-seven percent against about forty-eight percent. Time without progression also favored the earlier treatment, though its five-year gap missed significance. Side effects looked alike between the paths. Treatment choice, body mass index, and nodal stage each predicted survival. A simple score from weight and nodal stage sorted patients into risk bands, except within the before-surgery group. The authors back chemoradiation first for this stage.
pmc-13292258:
Weixing Liu and co-authors trace a 2026 mechanism by which a circular RNA drives head and neck squamous cell carcinoma. The molecule, circ_0008777, runs high in these tumors and matches poorer patient outcomes. Most cases of this cancer, arising in the mouth, throat, and voice box, are caught late, so fresh targets matter.

Experiments in cells and animals show the circular RNA lifting levels of c-Myc, a powerful growth driver, through two routes at once. It binds the protein PC4 to boost c-Myc gene transcription directly. It also soaks up miR-185-3p, a small RNA that normally restrains c-Myc. With both brakes off, tumors grew and spread more readily. The authors propose blocking circ_0008777 as a possible treatment strategy for this cancer.
pmc-13292558:
Burak Ulkumen, Sabri Mutlu, and Onur Celik ask a 2026 question most nose surgeons never test: do spreader grafts protect the voice during rhinoplasty? Reshaping the nose can narrow the internal valve and shift the resonances that color speech and singing, especially the F3 and F4 formants. Their prospective randomized study, described as double-blind and the first of its kind, compared patients with and without the grafts.

Patients lacking spreader grafts showed significant acoustic deterioration after surgery, while grafted patients kept their essential formants intact. Voice handicap scores on the VHI-10 scale rose postoperatively only in the ungrafted group. The authors argue the grafts defend the singer's and speaker's formant clusters, not just breathing and looks. They recommend weighing voice outcomes when planning structural rhinoplasty.
pmc-13292658:
Mengfei Xu and co-authors develop a 2026 urine test angle for cervical cancer, hunting microRNAs that could triage women who test positive for high-risk HPV. Screening is shifting toward self-sampling, which rules out the usual cytology follow-up, so objective molecular triage is in demand. The team optimized a workflow, called IsoSeek in its profiling arm, for squeezing sensitive small-RNA sequencing out of whole urine.

Two microRNAs stood out as disturbed in cancer: miR-143-3p and miR-204-3p, detectable from urine rather than tissue. Their ratio separated cervical cancer cases with promising discrimination in the reported analysis. The authors frame urine microRNA profiling as a patient-friendly route, since samples can be collected at home without a clinic visit. They position the pair as candidate triage markers pending wider analytical validation.
pmc-13292758:
Shenao Wang and co-authors compare two chicken breeds in a 2026 study of egg laying and liver gene activity. White Leghorn hens lay many eggs, while Wenchang chickens lay far fewer, and the liver makes the yolk material that drives output.

Gene activity in Leghorn livers favored fat handling, with genes such as CPT1A and ACSL1 more active. The three-dimensional folding of DNA was mostly alike in both breeds, yet local switches differed. Some fat genes moved into active zones in Leghorns, domain borders were looser, and DNA loops linked more strongly to fat genes. The findings link genome folding to breed differences in laying.
pmc-13292858:
Zhanwei Zhu and co-authors build a gene-based risk score, reported in 2026, for liver cancer known as hepatocellular carcinoma. Blood vessel growth feeds this cancer, so genes tied to new vessels may help sort patients by outlook.

Using large cancer datasets, the team formed a score from four genes: APOH, SLCO2A1, SPP1, and VTN. High-score patients lived shorter lives in test groups from other cohorts. Single-cell data showed which cell types made each gene, with SPP1 coming mainly from macrophages and liver cells. Lowering SPP1 slowed vessel growth in lab and animal tests. High-score tumors also responded less to the drug sorafenib.
pmc-13293258:
Yingjie Zhang presents a 2026 case report on a hard hospital course after heart valve surgery in a woman aged 57 who had severe rheumatic mitral stenosis. She also had atrial fibrillation and class III heart failure before surgery.

Surgery replaced the mitral valve and fixed other heart issues, but the left ventricle tore during the operation and was repaired at once. Her heart then pumped very weakly and needed balloon pump support, followed by stomach bleeding and later a clot on the new valve. Stronger blood thinning and team care steadied her, and heart strength had improved markedly by day 29. She stayed well at later checks.
pmc-13293658:
André S Alves and co-authors map, in a 2026 bibliometric study, research on fat-derived stem cells for peripheral nerve repair from 2000 to 2025. Nerve grafts from a patient's own body remain standard, yet they cost a second wound and give uneven recovery.

The final set held 555 articles by 2750 researchers in 54 countries, citing 16,466 sources in all. Output rose steadily after 2011 and peaked in 2019. Adjusted for population, Switzerland led in research intensity, ahead of Sweden and Belgium. Topics shifted over time from building tissue scaffolds toward cell signals, tiny vesicles called exosomes, and steps toward clinic use.
pmc-13293758:
Shan Tian and co-authors simplify, in a 2026 food study, the making of smoked jujube, a traditional Chinese treat whose drying and smoking take great labor. Their shortcut pairs brief roasting with sealed aging to build flavor and health compounds faster.

Four batches were compared: plain, sealed only, roasted only, and the combined method, roasted at 190 degrees for 2 minutes then sealed for 14 days. The combined batch tasted best and held more phenolics than the plain batch, at 13.2 versus 9.2 units the authors report. Chemical scans found 854 changed compounds, with richer flavor and antioxidant types. The treat matched the traditional one overall.
pmc-13293958:
Si-Yi Lei and co-authors issue an expert consensus on laparoscopic liver biopsy in a 2026 statement. The technique takes liver tissue while the surgeon watches the organ's surface directly. It backs up needle biopsy when that route is unsafe or impossible. Practice varied widely between centers for lack of shared standards, so a global panel set out to write them.

Forty-five experts from six continents, spanning liver medicine and several surgical fields, worked through three Delphi rounds. The statement covers when to use the method, which cases count as high risk, and how to prepare patients. Steps of the procedure itself are also standardized. The goal is safer sampling and more reliable diagnosis for hard cases.
pmc-13294058:
Yesnely Anacari Flores and Don Operario write a 2026 perspective on structural harm facing Latinx public health students in the United States. About 68 million people identified as Latinx in 2024, and applications to master of public health programs from Latinx students surged early in the pandemic. Recent anti-immigrant, anti-diversity, and anti-public health policies now press on study, mental health, and careers at once.

An intersectional lens shows how racial, immigrant, and student status combine under those policies. Gains in grants, scholarships, and anti-racism pledges risk reversal. The authors outline campus and professional steps to protect students and keep the future workforce diverse and stable.
pmc-13294158:
Tehseen Riaz leads a 2026 lab study on whether zinc particles kill breast cancer cells more than healthy cells. Standard cancer drugs spread through the body and cause harsh effects, so selective particles draw interest. Spherical zinc peroxide particles in two size ranges, commercial zinc oxide, and four-armed zinc oxide microparticles were tested on MCF-7 cancer cells and RMF-EG fibroblasts.

Zinc peroxide harmed cells in a dose-dependent way, killing far more cancer cells while fibroblasts kept over 75% viability at matched doses. Flow tests showed cancer cells also took up more particles. The authors call for tests in more complex systems before any therapy claims.
pmc-13294358:
Margareta Ramström and colleagues compare sugar patterns on dog blood proteins in infection versus pregnancy for a 2026 study. Pregnancy itself shifts inflammation signals, muddying diagnosis of womb infection and other illness. Serum from ten dogs with pyometra, ten with respiratory infection, ten pregnant dogs, and nine healthy non-pregnant dogs was mapped with a tuned glycan method.

No clear split appeared between pregnant dogs and pyometra cases. Respiratory cases and healthy dogs shared higher levels of some glycan types and lower levels of the dominant glycan than pregnant dogs. Overall sugar patterns thus fail as a test to tell pregnancy changes from infection, a useful negative result.
pmc-13294458:
Yannick Mahlich and coauthors present spammR, an R package for spatial multi-omics, in a 2026 software article. New instruments map transcripts, proteins, metabolites, and chemical marks across tissue slices at fine detail, yet most tools assume sequencing data and fit mass spectrometry awkwardly. Their package aims at end-to-end handling with mass data at the center.

Workflows import, clean, visualize, and integrate several omics layers plus microscope images from the same tissue. Open code on GitHub invites reuse and extension. Bridging data types in place can reveal tumor or organ patterns that single-layer maps miss, such as protein hotspots sitting over quiet gene zones.
pmc-13294658:
Mahbobeh Zamani-Babgohari and co-authors wrote a 2026 study on the wax coating of two poplar tree species. Waxes form a water-repellent skin that guards leaves and stems against drying and stress. The two species are close kin with wide ranges across North America, but their wax mixes across that range were little known.

The team profiled waxes from stems and leaves at three growth stages, using a standard chemical method. Both species shared a core set of wax compounds. Other compounds were tied to tissue, species, or stage: young tissues held more phenolic compounds, while mature ones were mostly fatty. Some compounds appeared only in leaves and split the trees into two groups. A genome scan of 174 trees from one species found a gene cluster tied to wax traits.
pmc-13294858:
Kim, Cho, and Yun argue for one shared scale in lab tests as lands age fast in this twenty twenty-six review. Old lands face more long ills that need the same test read the same way in all wards. A shared scale lets a sick guest's grade mean the same from ward to ward.

Inside, the trio maps the state land's scale hub and its grade checks for test shops. Key long-ill tests get their own scale plans in the review's run. Gaps that stay are named in plain form, from proof stock to law force. The team calls for more proof stock, hard law, pro drills, and steady funds. Those steps, they say, lift care grade in a gray land.
pmc-13294958:
Gabriel C. Bueno and co-authors screen 134 candidate coating molecules for perovskite solar cells entirely by computer, in a 2026 study. Coating the crystal surface can stabilize these efficient but fragile cells, yet picking a coating has been trial and error. The team calculated how each organic cation sticks to a small perovskite fragment, then grouped the results with clustering methods to find what separates good stickers from poor ones.

No single trait predicted success. Stiff, flat molecules paid a heavy distortion penalty when they bent to fit the surface, canceling their strong attraction. Bulky, saturated molecules hugged the surface through weak dispersion forces with almost no penalty, and flexible amines anchored cheaply. Electronic analysis added a warning: ring-rich molecules planted energy states inside the crystal's gap that could trap charges, while saturated ones behaved as harmless insulators. Flexibility plus saturation, the authors conclude, marks a good coating.
pmc-13295158:
Jason Liu and colleagues count exercise injuries across the United States in a 2026 national analysis. Weightlifting and bodyweight training both build strength, yet their share of emergency care was not well measured. Records came from a national injury surveillance system covering 2014 to 2023.

National estimates reached 546,655 weightlifting injuries and 108,001 bodyweight injuries over the decade. Weightlifting harm centred on the trunk and fingers, while bodyweight harm hit limbs and dislocated joints more often. After accounting for age and sex, the odds of hospital admission did not differ by exercise type, guiding prevention toward lifting form and safe joint angles.
pmc-13295658:
Amy Leestemaker-Palmer, Stephanie Nuss, and Luiz E Bermudez test antibiotic order against a stubborn lung germ in a 2026 study. Mycobacterium avium infections need long three-drug treatment that still fails often. Bacteria react to first drug contact by changing their workings, so arrival order might shape the final result.

In free-floating growth, order made no difference to drug effect in the tests. Inside biofilms and inside immune cells, order mattered clearly. Starting with the wall-acting drug ethambutol, then the other two, matched giving all three at once, while other orders worked worse. The finding argues that sequencing deserves a place in treatment design.
pmc-13295758:
He Xiao, Mingqin Shao, and Zeng Jiang model winter homes for white-naped cranes under change in a 2026 study. Records from 71 wintering sites between 2015 and 2025 grounded the maps. Height above sea level, distance to big water, driest-month rain, slope, and temperature patterns shaped where the birds settle.

Good habitat today clusters along the middle and lower Yangtze River and North China coastal wetlands. Under low, medium, and high emission futures for 2050 and 2070, the centre of suitable ground shifts southwest overall. Use concentrates in the middle Yangtze while other regions shrink sharply, guiding protection toward that refuge.
pmc-13296158:
Sh. M. Abdo and co-authors make, in 2026, a cellulose-based gel for pulling zirconium out of acidic waste liquid from zircon processing. The gel mixes plant cellulose with polyvinyl alcohol and fumaric acid, giving a porous material dotted with binding sites.

Batch tests found uptake peaked in strong acid within ninety minutes, reaching a high capacity per gram. The pattern of uptake pointed to chemical binding, and the process absorbed heat while running on its own. A dilute acid wash recovered about ninety percent of the metal. The authors pitch the cheap gel for metal separation and purification work.
pmc-13296558:
Víctor Muñoz-Hisado and co-authors census the microbes living in Pyrenean ice caves in this 2026 study. These caves hold ice year-round and starve their residents of food and warmth, much like the buried habitats guessed at on icy moons. What lives there hints at how life persists in such places.

The team sampled four caves and read the gene tags of bacteria and small eukaryotes alongside water and ice chemistry. Each cave kept its own community. Liquid water favored ultra-small bacteria, while two kinds of ice held layered or stream-carried groups. Tiny eukaryotes thrived most in sunlit ice and least in one cave where fungi ruled. Acidity, salts, and simple organic acids tracked the community patterns best. The authors offer the survey as baseline data for judging life's chances in cold, starved worlds.
pmc-13296958:
James G. Lyman and colleagues report seven cases of a single-position spinal operation that removes a damaged vertebra in a 2026 series. The prone-transpsoas route reaches the spine from the side and back at once, so the patient never needs turning mid-operation. Cases covered trauma, severe deformity, and revision surgery.

All seven operations were completed without major complications, and every patient kept stability afterward. Three deformity cases gained large corrections of spinal curvature. Pain and function improved by the latest follow-up in the whole group. One complex revision case drove the longest operating time and highest blood loss. Larger studies are needed, the authors say.
pmc-13297058:
Amira Guirguis and colleagues weigh how methamphetamine acts in the body against related drugs, to inform court sentencing in the United Kingdom, in a 2026 review. The drug sits in the top legal class, yet the main sentencing guide sets no amount thresholds for it. The team weighed human studies, brain scans, poison data, and death records against amphetamine, cocaine, and heroin.

The drug sits closest to amphetamine in how it works, the authors find. It reaches the brain more readily, lasts longer, and shows higher death risk in the reports. Smoked use hits with a force closer to crack cocaine. Treating the two drugs as equal gram for gram is not backed by the data. A raised amphetamine scale is proposed instead, with gaps in human data flagged.
pmc-13297258:
Marco Cascella and colleagues trace a conceptual shift in chronic pain science, from single brain regions to whole networks, in a 2026 narrative review. Older teaching pictured a fixed pain matrix of areas lighting up together. Newer work treats chronic pain as disturbed communication among large-scale brain networks.

Salience, default mode, executive, and sensorimotor networks all show altered interactions in the reviewed literature. Children's chronic pain may involve developmental changes to the same networks, although long-term imaging studies are scarce. Artificial intelligence tools promise objective pain measures and personalised treatment choices in this framework. The authors present network thinking as the route toward precision pain medicine.
pmc-13297558:
Anqi Dai and colleagues review the use of large language models to detect depression, in a 2026 article. Depression ranks among the world's top causes of disability, and early spotting stays hard. The review maps rating scales and public datasets, then traces detection methods from single signals, such as text or voice, to combined streams and language-model systems.

One gap stands out. Real clinics rarely hold every signal type, and methods that cope with missing or noisy inputs remain scarce. The authors call for language-model systems that adapt when a channel drops and draw on medical knowledge to stay readable to clinicians. Ethics and human-centred design close the survey.
pmc-13297658:
George Triantafyllou and colleagues report a rare cluster of extra ankle bones found on a scan, in a 2026 case report. A forty-three-year-old woman was imaged after a fall down stairs, on suspicion of fracture. Fine-slice computed tomography with layered and three-dimensional rebuilds mapped the bones around her ankle.

Alongside a small heel-bone spur, the scan showed an extra bone below the fibula and a navicular bone split into three parts, an exceedingly rare variant. All the extra pieces were rounded and neatly shelled, marks of lifelong variants rather than fresh breaks. Telling such variants from fractures matters, the authors stress, since mistaking one for the other can drive needless treatment.
pmc-13297758:
Tomáš Taubner and colleagues compare the chemistry of hemp and linseed varieties grown side by side in the Czech Republic, in a 2026 study. Both oilseeds feed industry and nutrition markets, but varieties differ. Twelve hemp and eleven linseed lines, from shop catalogues and new breeding, grew under one regime for a season.

Fat content spanned a wide range in both crops, and the fats were rich in two prized unsaturated fatty acids. Broad gaps appeared across most nutrients measured, showing how much variety choice alone can shift a harvest. Both seeds could partly replace soybean meal in animal feed, the authors say, pending digestion and feeding trials. Hemp variety choice also steers levels of the unwanted compound THC.
pmc-13297958:
Melody Moezzi and Bjørn M. Hofmann examine how AI tools for dental diagnosis are sold, in a 2026 ethics-focused study. Promotional material from leading dental AI firms during late 2025 underwent qualitative thematic analysis. The authors read the marketing through principlism, professional ethics, and virtue-based lenses.

Marketing often framed the tools as ways to raise case acceptance, revenue, and practice growth, not only as testing aids. Images and results numbers presented the systems as authoritative and objective, which can press patients toward accepting treatment and hide uncertainty. The authors warn about autonomy, overtreatment, and professional integrity, urging safeguards so the technology stays a clinical support.
pmc-13298258:
Burn care in poor-resource settings needs guidance that bends to what is actually available, argue Hongyu Tang and colleagues in a 2026 evidence synthesis. They mined guidelines, consensus statements, and systematic reviews worldwide to assemble recommendations for the first phase of adult burn treatment.

Fifty-nine high-quality sources yielded 77 recommendations across 13 domains, from scene safety and stopping the burning through airway and circulation support to wound care and transfer preparation. The authors found a gap between written protocols and the staff, supplies, and systems that decide survival on the ground. Their framework tiers actions by resources, prioritizing the ABC steps that save lives while patients await transfer.
pmc-13298758: An earlier paper on heart cell growth from stem cells has been pulled, this 2026 notice states. The paper had claimed that the ISL1 protein drives stem cells to become heart muscle cells. Doubts arose over three figures, 1, 2, and S1. In one, error bars look too much alike from point to point. In the rest, gel lanes show sharp breaks, and bands in unlike rows look too much alike. The item here is the withdrawal note, and it says why the claims can no longer be trusted.
pmc-13299358:
School screening flags suspected scoliosis more often in girls and in leaner teenagers, while some sports link to lower odds, report Josipa Glavaš and colleagues in a 2026 cross-sectional study. They screened 18,216 adolescents with the forward bend test during the 2019/2020 school year and modeled the associations.

Female sex more than doubled the odds (OR = 2.49), and odds climbed with grade level, reaching 2.98 by eighth grade. Higher body mass index lowered odds, as did playing soccer, gymnastics, or martial arts and training more often. The authors stress these are screening associations, not proof of cause, and back school screening with attention to body composition.
pmc-13300158:
Two plant flavonoids, fisetin and pinocembrin, kill leukaemia cells more strongly together than alone, report Narawan Kaewthawee and colleagues in a 2026 laboratory study. The team tested the pair on Jurkat and K562 cell lines, tracking survival, programmed death, and cell-cycle proteins, with computer docking against the Fas receptor.

Fisetin alone cut viability and switched on caspase-8, a marker of death-receptor signaling, while lowering CDK4. A Fas-blocking compound confirmed the receptor's role in the effect. Adding pinocembrin produced synergy scores above 10 in Jurkat cells and sharpened caspase-8 activation. In K562 cells, the pairing also shrank colony growth in soft agar far more than either compound by itself.
pmc-13301058:
J Cravo and co-authors compare starting ventricular tachycardia ablation from the heart's outer surface alone against the conventional combined inside and outside approach, in a 2026 retrospective study. Scans beforehand suggested which patients carried mostly outer surface substrate. Fifty-four patients treated between 2015 and 2025, most with dilated cardiomyopathy and defibrillators and many arriving in electrical storm, split into thirty-one outer only procedures and twenty-eight combined ones.

Complications touched about twenty-nine percent of procedures overall, with major events less frequent in the outer only group, though not significantly. In about five percent of procedures no abnormal substrate turned up at all, meaning the outer access was unnecessary. Over a mean follow-up above two years, recurrence and survival did not differ between strategies. The authors credit imaging triage with picking the right door into the heart and sparing some patients the second route.
pmc-13301958:
Anna Prokopowicz and co-authors measure how ready new mothers feel to care for their babies, two to three days after birth. Their 2026 study joins two hundred women in rooming-in care. Readiness is scored for day care, night care, and breastfeeding on ten-point scales.

Breastfeeding readiness is the strongest correlate of both day and night care readiness, with a steep gradient. Higher anxiety on day two drags all three scores down. Poor sleep lowers daytime readiness, while drive despite low mood lifts it. Focus under strain lifts night readiness, which falls sharply where suicidal thoughts appear. Prior births and active breastfeeding raise feeding readiness. The authors argue early support should target anxiety and sleep to steady new mothers confidence.
pmc-13302158:
H Fukaya and colleagues compare airway methods during cryoballoon ablation for atrial fibrillation in a 2026 retrospective study, focusing on a rare but dangerous complication. Air entering a coronary artery can be fatal, and deep sedation may let air be sucked in through large sheaths when chest pressure dips. A laryngeal mask with positive-pressure ventilation should prevent those dips.

The series covered 491 patients treated between 2017 and 2024 at one university hospital. Symptomatic coronary air embolism struck five patients managed with an adaptive ventilation device, and none managed with the mask. No brain embolism or deaths occurred, and other complication rates were similar. The authors argue that airway control deserves the same attention as the ablation itself.
pmc-13302358:
Corneal transplant surgery in frail, elderly patients got a gentler anesthetic recipe in a 2026 case series from Margita Lucic and colleagues. Fifty consecutive high-risk patients, aged fifty to ninety, received penetrating keratoplasty under a sub-Tenon eye block plus a dexmedetomidine drip given without the usual loading dose. Heart rate, blood pressure, oxygen, and sedation depth were tracked across nine phases of surgery.

Sedation stayed exactly in the cooperative target range for every patient, with breathing unaided throughout. Heart rate eased from 76 to 57 beats per minute and pressures drifted down from hypertensive levels into a comfortable band. Nobody needed opioids. The authors call the results preliminary but promising enough for randomized trials.
pmc-13302758:
Two fungi living quietly inside Thai Itea shrubs include a species new to science, Jutamart Monkai and colleagues report in a 2026 taxonomy study. Strains from healthy stems of Itea japonica and Itea riparia were grown out, examined under the microscope, and placed on family trees built from four gene regions. Close nucleotide comparisons separated look-alike members of the Apiosporaceae family.

The Itea japonica isolate became Nigrospora iteae, formally introduced as a new species. The other matched Apiospora vietnamensis, a first record on that host. The team also reclassifies a Ficus fungus as Apiospora fici, renames a homonym, and appends an updated checklist of Nigrospora species with hosts and activities.
pmc-13302858:
Twelve papers map where ceramic matrix composites stand, Rodrigo Moreno and Oscar Rubem Klegues Montedo introduce in a 2026 special issue overview. The collection spans ten research articles and two reviews on materials built to survive extreme heat and hostile chemistry. Topics run from additively manufactured graded ceramics for armor to carbon composites armored with ultra-high-temperature ceramics against oxidation.

Research contributions cover rocket thruster modeling for green propulsion, silicon nitride boron nitride ceramics tuned by particle size, MAX-phase coatings on silicon carbide fibers, and polymer-infiltrated networks, among others. The editors frame the set as a snapshot of a field balancing performance, reliability, and sustainability.
pmc-13303358:
Hot root-filling settings can push a tooth's outer surface past the safety line, Mihai Paven and colleagues measure in a 2026 laboratory study. Twenty extracted single-rooted teeth were filled with warm injectable gutta-percha at device presets of 180 or 230 degrees while infrared cameras watched three root zones. A bench experiment separately checked what temperatures the devices actually deliver at their tips.

The hotter preset drove middle-third surface readings significantly higher, and three of ten teeth crossed the 47-degree threshold tied to periodontal damage, peaking at 49.6 degrees. Tip output also lagged presets sharply. The 180-degree setting gave the more predictable, safer profile, especially for thin-walled roots.
pmc-13304558:
A fungal lung infection can quietly seed the brain, and catching that spread early saves lives. Xiao Dang and seven co-authors reviewed 101 patients without AIDS who were treated for pulmonary cryptococcosis at one hospital over twelve years. Most patients had no symptoms at all, and over half had another underlying illness, mainly high blood pressure or diabetes.

Eighteen patients, about 18 percent, also had cryptococcal meningitis. That group carried more underlying disease and showed lower blood counts, protein, and potassium levels. Statistical modeling picked three independent warning signs: having an underlying disease, low globulin, and low potassium. Combined, they predicted meningitis well. The authors urge thorough brain evaluation for lung patients showing this risk pattern, even when the lung disease seems silent.
pmc-13306158:
Shu-Peng Dong named a new plant species from Hainan Island in a 2026 taxonomic account. Argostemma baotingense belongs to the coffee family and grows in southern China, joining nine known members of its genus in the country.

Closest likeness is to A. bachmaense, yet the new plant differs in low or creeping stems, narrow leaves pale beneath, and hairless flower clusters and cups. Photographs and a key separate all nine Chinese species for field and herbarium use. The genus favours damp shade near streams and wet rocks, a habitat note that helps locate further populations.
pmc-13306858:
Giuseppe A. Malfa profiled chemicals and bioactivity in white mignonette extracts in a 2026 study. Leaf, flower, stem and unripe fruit extracts were made with ultrasound help and scanned by high-resolution liquid methods.

Thirty main compounds appeared across flavonoid, glucosinolate, phenolic acid and fat families, with four reported for the first time in this genus. Fruit extract led on calming inflammation and trapping radicals, likely from richer flavonoid content in reported results. Flower extract cut cell growth most strongly, showing plant parts differ sharply in useful chemistry. The part by part split shows why whole plant tests can mask strong plant drugs.
pmc-13306958:

Live spectroscopy confirmed earlier and wider surface rebuilding under the gallium effect.
pmc-13307158:

Teamwork across borders hit 22.55% of papers, with the United States, United Kingdom and China as top partners. pmc-13307758:
Solomon Monday Jacob and co-authors check in 2026 odd shaped schistosome eggs in urine from Abuja, Nigeria, to learn which species made them and whether animal forms play a part. Urine came from 1887 people aged five years and up, and eggs were first found by microscope checks.

pmc-13309558:

pmc-13309658:

pmc-13309958:

pmc-13310658:

pmc-13310758:

pmc-13311158:

pmc-13311758:

pmc-13311858:

pmc-13311958:

pmc-13312058: Min Zhang and co-authors published this 2026 correction notice for their earlier review of miR-17 and its role in development and cancer. pmc-13312158:

pmc-13312358:

pmc-13312658:

pmc-13315058:
Lena Easton-Calabria and colleagues measure indoor heat in New Orleans homes in their 2026 study. Extreme heat is a growing health risk, and the worst harm lands indoors, yet most research watches outdoor air and neighborhoods.

The team surveyed residents and logged indoor temperature for 2-week spans in 114 households across two heat-vulnerable wards, across the warm seasons of 2023 and 2024, as the design states. The aim was to learn which homes overheat and what predicts it, inside the real limits of high bills and patchy air conditioning. Their findings point to cheap, fair fixes for a city where heat and poverty overlap.
pmc-13315458:

pmc-13315558:
Marcel Bawej and colleagues tested artificial insemination in 2026 for the grey partridge, a European bird whose wild numbers have fallen fast. pmc-13315758:

pmc-13316158:
Yingmei Wu and co-authors modified cassava starch in 2026 to make it better at wrapping olive oil in tiny capsules. The combined starch beat ester-only starch on modification gains. Structure, thickening, and flow traits were tracked to judge the new material for food and delivery uses.
pmc-13316258:

pmc-13316558:

pmc-13316658:

pmc-13316758:

pmc-13317158:

pmc-13318258:

pmc-13318558:

pmc-13318658:

pmc-13319058:

pmc-13320458:

pmc-13320558:

pmc-13321158:

pmc-13321458:

pmc-13321658:

They weighed uptake against age, sex, and race, schooling and income, chronic illness and smoking, and access traits like insurance and a usual source of care. pmc-13322858:
Xue Lv and co-authors test spectral CT as a way to track bone change linked to fructose intake in rats, in a 2026 pilot study. Eighteen young male rats were split between normal food with fructose water and normal food with sterile water, for eight weeks.

pmc-13323058:

pmc-13323158:

pmc-13323558:

pmc-13323858:

pmc-13325158:

pmc-13325858:
Takumi Kagawa and colleagues expose mice to device-like environmental noise to find which part harms the kidney in a 2026 study. Human surveys link noise with kidney trouble, but the guilty frequencies were unknown.

pmc-13325958:
Synnøve Næss Sleire and colleagues track iron stores in Norwegian mothers and infants across pregnancy and after birth in a 2026 longitudinal study. Iron shortfalls threaten mother, fetus, and child, yet local data were thin.

pmc-13326058:

pmc-13326458:

pmc-13326558:

pmc-13327658:

pmc-13327858:

pmc-13327958:
Pavel A Solopov and co-authors test a phosphatase blocker against alcohol-amplified lung injury in mice in a 2026 study. The target looks druggable for drinkers facing severe lung insults.
pmc-13328458:
Roberto Navarro Quiroz and a large team grade the mechanisms of severe dengue in a 2026 systematic review. Severe disease brings vessel leakage, falling platelets, bleeding, and shock, yet which drivers rest on the firmest proof was unclear. Studies from 2020 to 2025 were sorted into six mechanism families and graded on a five-tier evidence scale.

Each claim also received a ceiling grade capping how strongly it may be stated, and readiness for meta-analysis was checked against standard criteria. An agent-based model then served as a logic tester, asking whether the three best-supported families together could generate connected vessel barrier failure in simulation. The design separates what evidence shows from what it merely suggests.
pmc-13330058:
Ogechukwu Samuel Obi and co-authors review whether sex shapes outcomes after catheter ablation for atrial fibrillation in a 2026 paper. Guidelines offer no sex-specific advice, and long-term recurrence and safety differences were unclear. The team pooled only studies that matched patients on baseline traits.

Twenty-one studies covering over one hundred thousand patients were included, about a third of them women. Recurrence at one year did not differ significantly by sex, and neither did the combined recurrence outcome. The authors frame the matched evidence as reassuring on efficacy, while noting that safety and longer-term gaps remain open. The review follows standard reporting and bias-grading methods.
pmc-13330258:
Andrzej Nowakowski and a large team compare two ways in 2026 to screen for cervical cancer risk in Poland. One way tests for HPV, the virus that causes most cervical cancer. The older way checks cells under a microscope, called cytology. New European guidance favors the virus test.

It also sent more women for follow-up exams, since more tests came back positive. The authors say a switch needs good follow-up rules and more clinic capacity, but it catches more danger early.
pmc-13330658:
Sydney Dougan and co-authors track use of safety net programs by low income California families in this 2026 paper. The programs are SNAP, WIC, and Medicaid. Use rose and fell during the COVID-19 pandemic. The team asked how patterns of use over time related to family health.

Data covered 361 families from 2019 to 2023. The team found six distinct patterns of program use. The largest groups used all programs or moved in and out of them fast. That in and out pattern is called churning. Families with stable full use reported fewer poor health outcomes. Families facing more paperwork burdens tended to fare worse.
pmc-13331458:
Ali Sovari and co-authors describe a 2026 case report about a 90-year-old woman with lasting atrial fibrillation and slow heart pauses who needed pacing support. Her right ventricle was small, and a standard ventricular leadless device kept losing contact with the heart wall.

The first Aveir VR device also interfered with her tricuspid valve, and its pacing thresholds rose until capture was lost again. Doctors removed it and placed the smaller Aveir AR device, built for the atrium, into the right ventricle instead, where it fixed firmly. The authors say the swap, reported here for the first time, shows why device choice should follow a patient's anatomy, especially in older patients with small chambers.
pmc-13331558:
Wenqi Wan and co-authors test whether a citrus honey calms the gut, in a 2026 study that pairs computer mapping with fruit fly trials. Honey from Citrus aurantium blooms is a folk food in China. The team wanted the pathways behind its gut effects, not just the effects themselves.

Inside cells, the honey dialed back an overactive growth pathway by shifting two partner genes. The work gives folk honey a measured, testable mechanism.
pmc-13332058:
Adrian Puello and co-authors chart fifteen years of cancer trends among older adults in Martinique in this 2026 registry study. The island's cancer registry covers all cases from 2008 to 2022. The team tracked new cases and deaths for people aged sixty-five and older, by cancer site and sex.

Lung cancer in men and stomach cancer also declined late in the study. Female breast cancer, by contrast, rose steadily. The authors link the patterns to screening, treatment gains, and pandemic disruption.
pmc-13332158:
Yi Zhang and co-authors used energy accounting to pick the best width for the coal pillar that guards a mine roadway, in a 2026 study. In deep mines, a new tunnel is often driven beside an old, emptied seam, leaving a pillar of coal as the wall between them. Too thin, it crumbles; too thick, it wastes coal and stores dangerous energy. The team built computer models of pillars from four to fourteen meters wide.

They tracked two kinds of energy in the rock: stored elastic energy and energy spent in damage. The ratio marked the shift from a crumbling pillar to one that bears load soundly. At six meters the balance was best under their mine's conditions. Wider pillars hoarded energy in a risky central zone. Field readings backed the choice. The authors say the energy ratio reads stability better than stress maps alone.
pmc-13332358:
Manasi Anbazhagan and colleagues describe a 2026 diagnostic challenge posed by a recurring skin sarcoma that mimicked benign lesions. Dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans is an uncommon, slow-growing skin sarcoma that invades local tissue and tends to return if not fully removed. Spread to distant sites is rare, yet the tumor can look like benign spindle cell lesions both at the bedside and under the microscope.

A 54-year-old man first presented in 2019 with a painless swelling over the right shoulder blade, first read as a benign spindle cell lesion. It returned at the same site in 2022, again reported as a spindle cell lesion with the sarcoma among the possibilities. The case shows why repeat lesions at an old scar need full workup with staining, and why a benign first reading should not close the question.
pmc-13332458:
Sheng Liu and colleagues mapped cardiac arrests and defibrillator placement across Deyang, China, in a 2026 geospatial study covering 2021 to 2023. Survival after arrest outside hospital is very low in China, and survival falls fast with every minute before a shock, so where devices sit matters.

The city logged 3,273 arrests, peaking in morning hours and on public holidays, and clustering grew stronger across the three years, with Jingyang District a steady hotspot. Homes produced 82.22 percent of arrests but held only 6.29 percent of devices, and existing units sat within 500 m of just 31.87 percent of past arrests. Modeling cabinets at round-the-clock primary care sites showed full redesign could pass 50 percent coverage with 100 added devices, against 200 under simple expansion. The authors call the clinic-based plan a cheaper route to a resilient response system.
pmc-13333358:
Zhifang Zhang and co-authors tested a tumor-killing virus against stomach cancer that has spread through the belly lining, in a 2026 mouse study. Such peritoneal spread is the main reason treatment fails and patients die in stomach cancer, and options once it appears are bleak.

Immune profiling of belly washings and tumors showed richer entry of white blood cells, including helper and killer T cells, after treatment. The authors offer CF17 as a candidate immunotherapy for this spread pattern and a base for optimizing the approach.
pmc-13334758:
Joseph J. Amon and colleagues write a 2026 piece on crisis science, human rights, and the US ICE siege of Minneapolis. Before its leaders and staff were gutted, the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention provided technical help and crisis science training to state and local public health workers. Public health tools such as tracking to detect new threats, risk assessment and risk mapping, and outbreak probes could be applied wherever crises, natural or human-made, emerged.

Practitioners guided by relief also developed strategies for crisis relief and help, designing models to model disease spread through crowded shelter shelters and to estimate medical supply needs. Core crisis-science principles such as defining groups at risk, measuring health outcomes in a system, and finding causes are applied in the piece to the siege context. The article frames ICE enforcement as a human-made crisis open to public health analysis.
pmc-13335958:
Junyu Chen and co-authors build a blood-test platform in 2026 to tell apart lung diseases that look alike. Asthma, chronic bronchitis-type disease, lung scarring, and lung cancer share symptoms that delay the right call. Chemical fingerprints in blood could split them, but standard lab tools are slow with raw serum.

Their platform grows layered nanomaterials from sponge-like crystals, pairing five metal mixes with a titanium base. One pairing won on light uptake, charge flow, and heat release, and it tolerated messy blood samples. Fingerprints from 776 clinic samples split all four diseases from healthy controls, they report, and staged lung cancer sharply with machine learning. Test scores sat near 0.95, a strong mark for a drop of blood.
pmc-13336358:
Jintao Wu and co-authors mapped an immune-damping cell network that protects prosthetic joint infections in a 2026 study. Infections around artificial joints fail treatment and recur largely because the local immune system is stalled, and reversing that state had no practical strategy.

A drug screen then picked out alendronate, a bone drug, as a direct inhibitor of these quieting cells through STAT3. Paired with vancomycin it performed strongly across infection models, pointing to an add-on immunotherapy for stubborn joint infections.
pmc-13336658:
Jian Yao and colleagues proposed a knowledge guided artificial intelligence method in 2026 for printing nickel superalloys by laser powder bed fusion. These alloys are vital for hot, high stress parts, yet they crack easily during printing and tuning the process by trial alone is costly. Past data models also hide their reasoning and suffer when data are scarce.

The team let a large language model apply known metallurgy rules, such as aluminium to titanium ratios, to cut 76,800 candidate settings by more than 95 percent. Those distilled rules then gave a reinforcement learning agent a warm start for fine tuning. The hybrid approach promises cheaper, clearer process design for crack prone superalloys in aerospace and energy parts.
pmc-13336858:
Phillip Glass and co-authors magnetize soft rubber while it prints in a 2026 fabrication study. Soft magnetic actuators serve medical robots, artificial muscles, and wearables, but setting their magnetic pattern after making them limits what they can do. Their printer applies a controlled magnetic field during printing, locking local domains in chosen directions inside one solid piece.

The method is sensitive to curing speed, material thickness, and magnet placement, all mapped by theory, tests, and simulation. Demo builds include a dragonfly with oppositely magnetized wings, an octopus-like swimmer, and a bending catheter with 6 magnetic nodes in the demonstration setup. Printed-in patterns also support strain sensing and information encoding, widening design freedom.
pmc-13337658:
Hanhua Sai leads a 2026 intervention study on teen obesity in Inner Mongolia. Earlier work supports school programs that mix diet advice and activity, yet bilingual teaching in minority language areas had little study. The team focused on Mongolian middle school students in Ar Horqin Banner.

Screening of 2,210 students identified 155 students with obesity for a six-month program taught in Mongolian and Chinese. Teaching covered sensible eating, healthy habits, and moderate exercise. Height, weight, fasting blood tests, and diet questionnaires were taken before and after. Comparing those measures shows whether bilingual teaching can shift weight scores and blood markers in rural and pastoral settings.
pmc-13338058:
Haipeng Xu and co-authors search for a gene signature that tracks damage to mitochondria after spinal cord injury, in a 2026 study. These cell power plants fail during the second wave of harm that follows the first injury.

The team mined gene data from 113 mouse spinal cord samples and let machine learning pick the strongest signals. Five genes formed a signature that separated injured from healthy tissue with high accuracy. A scoring chart built on the five genes measured how far the damage had gone. All five genes rose in a second, separate mouse model as well. The signature tied closely to immune activity and to loss of nerve cell function.
pmc-13338158:
Home care visits across rival centers can share staff under a two-layer planner, Xinmiao Shao, Zhong Wu, and Qing Guo propose in a 2026 paper. Centers left alone end up lopsided: some swamped, others idle. Their model prices travel time, service cost, lateness penalties, and imbalance in one score.

Skill matching and labor rules bound the plan. A genetic search assigns clients to centers at the top layer. A hybrid swarm method then routes each center's own visits, with repair steps for time windows. Sharing staff across centers could cut waits for elders who depend on home care.
pmc-13338758:
Minsub Shim, Jaegu Kang, Kyung-Sang Yu, and Ki Young Huh build automated checks for handling errors in drug level data in a 2026 simulation study. Swapped time points or swapped samples can quietly ruin pharmacokinetic analysis. Two detection methods were compared on simulated vancomycin profiles.

A total of 12,500 simulated profiles tested a run-based method against a distance-based method with leave-one-out checks. The distance method caught 79.7 percent of errors versus 59.6 percent for the run method in the reported results, with stronger overall accuracy. It held up across another drug model and messy training data, supporting automated screening before analysis.
pmc-13340658:
Herpes simplex infection of the esophagus in a healthy adult is documented in a 2026 case report and literature review by Hoi Hang Yu and coauthors. Their patient, a 49-year-old woman, came in with painful, difficult swallowing and fever, and endoscopy showed ulceration in the middle and lower esophagus.

Tissue tests confirmed herpes simplex virus, and intravenous acyclovir plus a strong acid blocker brought marked healing by two months. Reviewing cases from 2009 onward, the authors found tissue examination confirmed most diagnoses and most patients still received antivirals despite the illness often clearing on its own. Rare complications included perforation and recurrence.
pmc-13340958:
Jeniffer Viviana Ramirez Hernandez and co-authors review in 2026 the use of flavonoids through the nose. Flavonoids are plant compounds with wide effects in the body, usually taken by mouth as sugar linked forms.

Second, treatment of nose and breathing diseases and other illness through the nose route. Third, delivery to the brain along the nose to brain path, to prevent or treat brain disease. Delivery problems and formulation tricks for each level are covered.
pmc-13341058:
Jianping Zhao and co-authors test FOXA1 as a marker to confirm prostate cancer, even in hard cases. These forms often lose the usual prostate markers, so pathologists need new ones.

It showed in eight of ten primary small cell cases and twelve of twenty-one spread cases. It also appeared in some breast and bladder cancers, so it works best as an added marker.
pmc-13341158:
Organizing huge biomedical image collections on a local workstation is the purpose of PixelDeck, presented by Benjamin L. Kidder in a 2026 software paper. Labs in histology and fluorescence microscopy generate overwhelming piles of images and videos that plain file systems handle poorly.

Benchmarks on libraries up to 1000 assets showed import speeds above 500 files per minute and typical search answers in milliseconds. Keeping everything local-first suits sensitive research data and ordinary hardware.
pmc-13341358:
Yunmin Han and colleagues studied body health, obesity, and activity in 2026 in 442,666 Korean adults from national health screening data from 2009 to 2012. Body health used modified NCEP ATP III rules, with at least two faults marking unhealthy status. Obesity meant body mass index at least 25. Four groups resulted: healthy lean, unhealthy lean, healthy obese, and unhealthy obese.

Deaths from all causes and heart disease were weighed across groups. The team tested single and joint effects of body health, obesity, and physical activity. The huge cohort splits weight from body health in death risk. The findings back activity and body health care even when weight alone looks reassuring.
pmc-13341558:
Injured knees stay measurably behind in elite wrestlers, in a 2026 study by İmge Nas and colleagues. Twenty wrestlers, ten women and ten men, who had returned to full training after one-sided knee injury were tested for joint position sense, dynamic balance, and hopping.

The injured limb made bigger position errors at 15 degrees of bend, reached less far in the posteromedial balance direction, and hopped a shorter distance. Subjective knee scores and pain levels tied moderately to performance gaps. Returning to sport, the authors warn, does not prove the neuromuscular system has fully recovered, so clearance tests should probe both legs.
pmc-13341958:
Team-based support plus technology could remake dementia care, argue Esther V. Loseto-Gerritzen and colleagues in a 2026 UK-US commentary. Over 55 million people live with dementia worldwide, a figure set to triple by 2050, straining systems and families.

Artificial intelligence could tailor diagnostic workups and monitoring plans to each person. Without such connective work, the authors warn, new drugs and devices may widen the very inequalities they should close.
pmc-13342158:

Wide necks (27%), branches arising at the neck (19%), and tiny size under 3 mm (8.6%) led the reasons catheters would not do. Bystander aneurysms were often clipped alongside the main one. pmc-13343158:
Liqun Xu and co-authors test mitochondrial transplantation in aged lab cells in 2026, using the human neuroblastoma line SH-SY5Y as a stand-in for sick neurons. pmc-13343258:

pmc-13343858:

pmc-13346058:
Vishwanath S. Khadye, Rodrigo Costa, and M. Teresa Cesário rework bacterial bioplastic production for cost and scale in 2026. Seaweed residue sugars fed the bacteria as well as store-bought glucose, and enzyme recycling trimmed costs further. Waste-fed, low-sterility production moves this bioplastic closer to market sense.
pmc-13347058:
Xinyue Du and co-authors release a large set of heart tracings meant to train AI tools that flag acute coronary syndrome. The ECG is the first test for patients with suspected heart attack, and blocked-artery cases need care within minutes. AI readers shine on some heart faults, but open data for this syndrome has been scarce.

Labels sort the cases by attack type and by where the damage sits. Two doctors also read the set, giving a human benchmark. A baseline deep learning model ships with the data for occlusion detection.
pmc-13348058:

Lake water on the Ontario side faces farm and factory inflows, making it a One Health watch site. Colonies grown from litre samples were purified, read for DNA, and scanned for resistance traits.

Both drafts carry several heavy metal resistance factors, a notable load for lake bacteria that also often harbour drug resistance in polluted waters. Publishing the drafts lets health and environment teams track how metal pressure in the lake may co-select tougher bacteria at the human-animal-water meeting point.
pmc-13348358:

No isolate was linked back to a named donor.

Skin bacteria steer skin balance and health, so open drafts for common forearm kinds give a base for comparing healthy skin sets against diseased skin in later work. Careful ethics cover and clean lab handling are stressed, since skin samples sit close to personal identity even when names are removed.
pmc-13348858:

Synthesis linked psychological distress, unhealthy coping, early life adversity, and emotional trauma to persistent pain. pmc-13349058:

Through a national external quality programme, the team took reports from 34 labs for three simulated samples. They weighed gene panels, variant finding and sorting, and handling of primary versus secondary findings. Structured forms and content checks showed marked shifts. The findings give practical proof for national reporting rules that would make gene newborn screening results clearer, safer, and more alike across labs.
pmc-13349358:

pmc-13349758:

pmc-13350158:
Erick dos Santos Ribeiro and co-authors study three genes in paricá tree seedlings exposed to cadmium and a plant hormone, in a research paper from 2026. Paricá, an Amazon tree, stores cadmium in its roots and may help restore damaged land. How its genes respond to the metal is poorly known.

Seedlings grew under four cadmium levels crossed with three doses of the hormone. The team tracked two genes that help make the hormone and one that builds metal-binding proteins. Sixty test units filled a growth room in a fully randomized design. The work links hormone dose to the gene response, informing plans to use paricá on polluted soils.
pmc-13350258:

Health systems everywhere face tight resources and rising demand, so the collection asks how to gain the most health for a given social cost. Studies are grouped around welfare and institutional economics and statistical evaluation of policies and interventions. The editors aim for a shared framework that lets economists and health researchers judge programmes by both fairness and value for money.
pmc-13350458:
Hao Zhang and Jian Wang analysed COVID-19 timing patterns in a 2026 study of case data from March 2020 to February 2023 at world, hemisphere, and country levels. They used an advanced signal-splitting method to pull cycles out of noisy incidence curves.

pmc-13350658:

In treated patients, home checks flagged uncontrolled pressure tied to stroke risk.
pmc-13351158:

Newer work covers custom implants and printed braces. Research on metals that dissolve in the body hints at implants that merge with growing bone. pmc-13351958:
Narrowing of the spinal canal high in the back is tricky to operate on because the working space is tight and the joints that stabilize the spine sit close. The aim is to free the pinched cord while preserving the approach-side joint that keeps the spine stable. A straight scope view acts as a control strategy, the authors argue, limiting how much bone the surgeon removes by habit or by awkward angles. Over-removal can leave the spine unstable and lead to fusion surgery later. The note explains the steps and the reasoning for other spine surgeons.
pmc-13352158:
Ethan Bendayan and co-authors told in 2026 that self-inflammation syndromes in chronic hives are rare but distinct. The data came from a look-back cohort at a certified urticaria centre. Blood counts, thyroid antibodies, and linked tests were used to split self-inflammation cases from typical hives. Self-inflammation patients showed distinct systemic traits and treatment needs. Spotting these rare cases early avoids long futile therapy.
pmc-13352658:

pmc-13354158:

Development risk and uncertainty drop when cost-effectiveness thinking starts at the design stage. Long-run viability and fit with health systems improve as well. pmc-13354958:

Xiangyu Li's team boosted crystal-organic tandem solar cells by adding a clumping-induced output compound to the organic sub-cell, tackling its large voltage deficit from non-light merging. Mainstream non-carbon-ball acceptors suffer clumping-caused dimming and low glow yield.

Paired with a wide-band gap crystal, the tandem reached 26.5 percent power conversion efficiency, confirmed at 25.8 percent.
pmc-13392658:
Siti Rakhma Afriana, Widagdo Sri Nugroho, and Widodo Suwito screened Australian beef cattle held in quarantine in Indonesia for a dangerous strain of Escherichia coli that can cause severe food poisoning. Between March and November 2025 they gathered six hundred eighty samples, nearly all dung, from five quarantine sites in West Java and Banten. Lab work confirmed the strain and hunted for toxin and resistance genes.

Sixteen samples carried the target strain, and about two thirds of those isolates held genes for Shiga toxins. Most isolates still responded to common antibiotics, with tetracycline resistance the most frequent exception. Worryingly, resistance genes often sat hidden in bacteria that looked sensitive in standard tests, ready to wake under drug pressure. The authors argue quarantine checks should include gene screening, not just growth tests.
pmc-13393258:
Xiaoyan Tang and eight colleagues mapped how nicks at every position of a split DNA activator change the behaviour of Cas12a, a CRISPR enzyme used in ultra-sensitive tests. Split activators promise fast, programmable detection without copying the target first, but design rules were guesswork. The team built over two hundred configurations, cutting each strand at successive points, and measured the enzyme's collateral cutting activity for each.

Cuts in the strand the guide reads suppressed activity to degrees set by position, while cuts in the opposite strand boosted it. Applying those rules produced an activator pair that detected a microRNA at attomolar levels, roughly four hundred eighty times more sensitive than an intact activator. The boost enabled profiling of five microRNAs inside living cells for machine learning classification of cancer cells, and the trick extended to an enzyme and a chemical target as well.
pmc-13394458:
Lanhao Qin heads a 2026 team that built an eye-inspired chip for spotting motion, modelled on birds of prey. Drops of oil in a raptor retina focus light, and the chip copies that trick with gold cores wrapped in a mineral shell. The shell turns light into hot charge carriers with great speed. A full wafer held a grid of 32 by 32 sensing points.

Every point in the grid worked, with small spread between them. The array answered in just over two milliseconds and stored light levels in five-bit steps. After brief training it named motion direction with near-perfect scores. The authors pitch the chip for cars, traffic watch, and guard systems.
pmc-13394558:
Anastasios Makris leads a 2026 twin study of breath holding, asking how much genes shape the skill. People vary widely in how long they can hold breath with the face in cold water. Twelve identical and ten non-identical twin pairs each did five longest-possible holds. The team compared pairs to split gene effects from shared home effects.

Genes explained most of the spread in hold time and in blood pressure rises. They also explained much of the spread in lung size. For heart rate and some flow measures, the maths needed for a firm split did not hold. The authors stress that heritability is about spread, not fate.
pmc-13394858:
Yaxiang Jia and colleagues review, in 2026, virtual reality exercise for children and teens with autism. Beyond social traits, many young people with autism struggle with planning skills and movement. The team gathered fifteen studies with 439 youths who did active games, motion-sensing training, or augmented reality exercise. Nine studies fed into pooled maths.

Pooled results point to gains in planning and self-control skills. Proof grade was moderate, though the range of true effects crossed zero. Effects on social behaviour and repeated behaviours were mixed across the few studies that checked. Movement gains are covered in the full review. The authors call for larger, more alike trials.
pmc-13394958:
Anpei Li and others test a SETD2 block to boost a menin drug in MLL-fusion blood cancer in a 2026 study. SETD2, a gene-marking enzyme, has played a two-faced role in this blood cancer, curbing tumors when lost yet marking grim odds when raised high.

Gene typing of lost SETD2 marked it as a half-dose tumor curb, while SETD2 and menin blocks joined forces to kill cells, halt growth, ripen cells, and drive cell death. SETD2 block made cells keen for menin block by cutting H3K36me3 marks. The paper backs a drug pair for a blood cancer that spurns most cures.
pmc-13395158:
Qian Huang and a team of co-authors review progress in screens that show true three-dimensional images using holograms. Their review is from two thousand twenty-six. A hologram records and rebuilds the full light wave from a scene, so the image has real depth. That makes it one of the most sought-after display ideas.

Two limits hold the field back: holograms are slow to compute, and each display can show only so much detail. The review sums up fast methods for computing holograms on a computer. It also covers ways to widen the detail a display can hold and to cut grainy noise in the image. Uses range from near-eye displays and virtual reality to secure optical codes. The authors close with trends they expect next.
pmc-13395258:
Tianya Liu, Ji Wu, and Ivan Steenstra test, in 2026, how sharing blame with AI shapes doctors' judgement. Ninety-six doctors worked ten case puzzles in a mock clinic. Each group got a different rule for who answers for errors: the doctor fully, both equally, a shifting split, or no AI at all. Only the rule changed between groups.

The shifting split won clearly, lifting accuracy and trimming overconfidence. Full blame on the doctor added nothing over the control group. Equal sharing hinted at worse accuracy and clearly worse confidence balance. The authors say who carries the risk changes how closely doctors check AI advice. Design of blame rules is part of safe AI use.
pmc-13395358:
Rebecca Pabst and co-authors build, in 2026, a trait-based forecast of which mosquitoes may invade new lands. Only a few species have spread so far, but invasions have sped up with world trade. The team logged 26 traits for 184 species of medical concern. Forest models linked traits to the odds of travel and of settling after arrival.

Species from Asia and Australia scored as most likely movers. Love of human-made breeding sites, heavy rain zones, and harsh heat also raised the odds. The models flagged 24 fresh species as likely travellers, and 17 of those as likely settlers too. The authors urge guards to watch the flagged list first.
pmc-13395458:
Elena Spinetti and co-authors model, in 2026, how a cell stress sensor grabs unfolded proteins. The sensor, IRE1, sits in the cell's folding workshop and fires a rescue program under strain. No clear picture showed it touching unfolded chains directly. The team ran long atom-level simulations of the sensor's sensing part.

The sensor's head did grip unfolded protein bits in two pockets at its centre. Those grips could steady larger sensor clusters that switch the program on. A helper named BiP was also shown blocking the cluster face, which keeps the sensor quiet in calm times. The model settles clashing past claims, the authors say. It maps the first step of the stress alarm.
pmc-13396058:
Hanie Raufi and others review CDK9 as a drug target in blood cancers in a 2026 paper. CDK9 drives gene copying stretch-out, feeding short-lived cancer genes and anti-death proteins, and its wild activity shows up in blood cancer, marrow cancer, and big B-cell lymphoma.

Inside the P-TEFb crew, CDK9 tags RNA polymerase II and histones, keeping cancer programs on and breeding drug spurn. Blocking CDK9 hits cancer cells' need for fast gene copying. The review tours first drug blocks and the snag of hitting a cell engine used all over the body with care.
pmc-13396558:
Sercan Özkaçmaz and co-authors asked whether a liver cyst's density, read from a CT scan, can separate two look-alikes. One is a harmless simple cyst; the other is a hydatid cyst, a parasitic sac that needs different care. Their 2026 study tackles a real diagnostic knot, since the two look nearly identical on scans.

Cysts were included only when the diagnosis was settled by tissue tests, blood tests, or the look of the removed sac. Density was measured in Hounsfield units on contrast-enhanced scans for 51 hydatid cysts and 36 simple ones, and the averages compared. A clean density cutoff would spare patients extra tests and steer surgeons correctly before anyone operates.
pmc-13396658:
Xing and co-authors explain, in 2026, why formamidinium perovskite solar cells decay, tracing the damage to the interface where the working alpha phase meets the inert delta phase. Their microscopy and diffraction work shows the boundary between the alpha phase's 011 plane and the delta phase's 110 plane carries tensile strain. That makes it the active site where the alpha-to-delta transformation ignites and spreads.

Acting on that mechanism, they seeded the perovskite with two-dimensional perovskitoid material that bonds preferentially to the delta phase's 110 plane, forming a strained 2D-delta interface with 4.24 percent lattice mismatch in the reported analysis. The large strain scrambles delta-phase orientation and blocks formation of the dangerous alpha-delta boundaries. Cells built this way reached 25.61 percent efficiency, and unencapsulated devices kept 90 percent of their initial efficiency after 1,000 hours at 70 percent relative humidity. The authors offer the interface rule as a universal stabilization strategy.
pmc-13396758:
Davide Monopoli and co-authors built mirrors on a chip that can steer light across a wide range of colors. The mirrors use a repeating groove pattern, called a Bragg grating, placed beside a ring-like cavity on a silicon nitride chip. By shaping the grooves, the team widened the band of light the mirror reflects to more than 70 nanometers and gained control over how the light's speed varies with color. Tuning the cavity length and the gap beside it raised the sharpness of the resonances and the strength of the reflection.

Such mirrors could serve inside hybrid lasers built on chips, where a tunable reflector is needed. The same control over spectrum and sharpness suits sensors and systems that mix light in nonlinear ways. The work shows that groove shaping can turn a side-coupled cavity into a flexible mirror for integrated photonics.
pmc-13396858:
Enrico Prajiante Bertolino and co-authors report a ruptured, infected aortic aneurysm caused by a bacterium better known in horses, in a 2026 case report with a literature review. Streptococcus equi rarely infects people, and an infected aneurysm seeded by it is rarer still, as well as often fatal.

A 72-year-old man had emergency open surgery: the diseased aorta was rebuilt in place with a polyester tube graft soaked in the antibiotic rifampin, with a ready-made branch for the kidney artery. A false aneurysm later bulged at the upper join, and cultures from surgery grew the horse bacterium. He left hospital on long-term antibiotics meant to suppress any remnant.
pmc-13397658:
Brian Otaalo and others gauge antibiotic prescribing rightness among people with HIV in a Ugandan outpatient clinic in a 2026 study. Sub-Saharan Africa bears high antimicrobial resistance driven by wrong antibiotic use, yet outpatient prescribing data for HIV patients were thin.

Reviewing prescriptions from 2016 to 2022 across general, urgent care, and tuberculosis clinics, the team judged rightness by noted indication, drug, dose, frequency, and duration against national guidance. The audit counts where prescribing strays and why. Stewardship programs gain a baseline for guarding antibiotics in HIV care across Ugandan outpatient clinics.
pmc-13398158:
Qorinah Estiningtyas Sakilah Adnani and co-authors examine why involving local stakeholders in global health research so often falls flat. Their 2026 viewpoint draws on published work and experience inside a multinational respiratory research programme. Funders increasingly demand engagement, especially in low- and middle-income countries, yet what it looks like on the ground is rarely inspected.

Structural limits, fuzzy ethics, power gaps and cultural mismatches can hollow out the exercise until it becomes theatre. The authors argue engagement only turns real when it is reflective, properly funded and backed by institutions over the long term. Flexible models fitted to each setting, they say, serve communities better than a tick-box shaped far away.
pmc-13398758:
Yu Zhang and colleagues let an AI evolve dye molecules that glow in the second near-infrared window. Their 2026 study builds the AI4NIR-II pipeline, joining quantum chemistry calculations, transformer prediction models and generative design. Such dyes (glowing between 1,000 and 1,700 nm) pierce tissue deeply with little background haze, prized for imaging and light therapy, but finding them by hand is slow trial and error.

Starting from two fragment families, the model trained on about 16,000 molecules with computed absorption and emission values. It then proposed, scored and refined new candidates in rounds, a self-driven loop needing far less bench work. The authors present the loop as a template for smart molecule hunting generally.
pmc-13399158:
Amy M Kemp reports the first year of BRAIN-FIT in 2026, a community program offering brain-health screening outside clinics in mid-sized cities and nearby rural areas. Rural adults often face long distances and few specialists when they want checks that might catch dementia risk early. Screening commonly turned up raised cardiometabolic measures, weaker physical endurance, poor sleep, and hearing or vision problems. Thinking and language scores mostly stayed in the functional range. Sixty-three participants answered a follow-up survey four weeks later about behavior changes. Kemp presents the model as a workable way to flag changeable risk before serious decline sets in.
pmc-13399358:
Nanako Tomioka and co-authors used a large Japanese longitudinal study to test whether social capital protects older adults against oral frailty, in a 2026 analysis. Oral frailty, a decline in chewing, swallowing, and remaining teeth, threatens nutrition and independence. The data came from the Japan Gerontological Evaluation Study, with 31,378 community-dwelling older adults assessed in 2019 and again in 2022.

Over the three years, 21.6 percent of participants developed oral frailty risk by the study's predictive model. The share was higher among lower-income participants, 24.6 percent, than among the better-off, at 19.9 percent.
