Community-level civic participation also helped, and its protective association ran stronger for lower-income participants, a statistically significant interaction. The authors suggest that encouraging social participation could narrow the income gap in oral health among older adults.
pmc-13399458:
A hearing aid can only be judged with word lists the patient actually struggles with. Rathna Kumar and co-authors tested Telugu lists on thirteen older adults whose hearing fades at high pitches. They compared ordinary words against high-frequency words, under plain amplification and a frequency-compression strategy, in quiet and in noise.

Ordinary lists flattered everyone, hiding both the deficit and the difference between strategies. The harder lists exposed real perception problems and revealed the compression strategy's advantage, which the easy lists missed entirely. Noise dragged every score down. The authors argue for tests built for speech in noise, and for Telugu specifically, before claims about hearing-aid benefit can be trusted.
pmc-13399558:
Gu and Xu present a study from twenty twenty-six on white noise plus coaching for new mothers with late milk onset. The study reviews one hundred twenty first-time mothers at one hospital. Half got standard breastfeeding guidance alone over four weeks. The other half got the same guidance plus white noise sessions. The team compare feeding rates, latch scores, anxiety, and milk measures. Baby stress and growth are tracked as well. After care, the combined group shows a higher exclusive breastfeeding rate.

The combined group also scores better on latch and milk onset speed. Anxiety in mothers and stress in babies run lower in that group. Babies gain more in weight, length, and head size by four weeks. The authors back the low-cost add-on for wards.
pmc-13399858:
Siddharth Padmanabhan and co-authors present a repair for radial tears of the meniscus that adds the patient's own fibrin clot as biological mortar, in a 2026 technique paper. A fibrin clot, made from the patient's blood on the back table, carries platelets and growth signals into exactly that dead zone at almost no cost.

Thirty milliliters of blood are drawn and left to clot undisturbed for seven minutes, then stirred with a textured glass rod until a firm clot forms. It is trimmed, lassoed with braided suture, and delivered into the tear through a cut-down pediatric endotracheal tube used as a cannula. The tear is then closed with polydioxanone sutures in horizontal and vertical mattress passes arranged as a hashtag, or ripstop, grid that resists pulling through. The authors pitch the method as low-complexity biological insurance for any high-risk meniscus repair.
pmc-13400158: The notice is a correction only. It amends a 2023 Cell Reports Medicine article by Ori Fridlich and colleagues on where cell-free DNA in blood after exercise comes from. In Figure 1C, the pie chart for Runner 1 at rest was accidentally duplicated from Runner 2. The corrected figure carries the right chart, and the legend to Figure 1D is also corrected. Falastine Das, Susmita Parashar and Aparna Kulkarni review, in 2026, how high blood pressure disorders in pregnancy affect heart health in mothers and their children for years afterward. These disorders affect about one in ten pregnancies worldwide and remain a leading cause of harm around birth.

Shared genes, womb programming and lasting immune changes may explain the pattern. The authors call for checks starting right after birth, lifelong follow-up and care plans that treat mother and child together.
pmc-13400658:

Nine needed revision surgery, most often because the radial part loosened within three years. Wear after injury was the top reason for the first operation, and half the patients had prior elbow surgery. Estimated ten-year survival was sixty percent. The authors urge careful counseling and trial-based use.
pmc-13401158:

It also changed the study of immune pathways in cancer, inherited disorders, infections, heart disease, and autoimmune illness. They also cover gene editing, nano-scale drug carriers, immune-based therapy, biologics, and targeted drug delivery. These tools can hit tissues more precisely and cause less off-target harm. pmc-13401458:
Li, Dohan, and Abramson argue, in 2026, that time deepens inequality for terminal cancer patients. Patients had to triage colliding demands of treatment, work, family, and paperwork schedules. They reconcile disease trajectories with official timetables that assume different speeds, and anchor today's decisions in a future they could plan for, one that cancer keeps dissolving. The authors name three forms: schedule conflict, trajectory mismatch, and anticipation uncertainty. Advantaged patients found this labor resource-draining and goal-displacing as disease advanced. The analysis, combining fieldwork with correspondence analysis, reframes time as a ruptured relation between agency and context.
pmc-13402258:
Glória M C Lacerda and co-authors give the first genetic portrait of Micropleura vazi, a worm parasite of caimans in Brazil, alongside fresh detail on the female body. pmc-13402358:
Dipak Patel and co-authors test a plant oil fuel spiked with tiny zinc bits in a diesel engine. The study appeared in 2026. Blends of the oil with diesel ran from a fifth to full strength. The two-fifths blend gave the best trade of work and clean air.

With the zinc bits in that blend, heat work rose and fuel use per work fell a bit. At full load, key smog parts fell by clear shares next to plain diesel. One gas fell by more than a third, while smoke fell by near a third. A heat-loss read gave the spiked blend top marks for how much work it kept and for long-run worth.
pmc-13403358:

pmc-13403458:

pmc-13403758:
Vindhya Prakash, Nishanth S, and Kashish Goyal told in 2026 of a man whose pierced eye hid its own wound. A stone strike left the 58-year-old with pain, redness, watering, and sudden sight loss in one eye. A leak test came back negative, and no torn tissue showed at first look.

pmc-13403858:

pmc-13404858:
J Jane Pillow and colleagues present CIRCA DIEM, a 2026 protocol testing day-night light and sound cycles for very early babies. Assessors who score the children will not know each child's group.
pmc-13407758:
Kathryn C. Collins and co-authors test, in 2026, whether brain-stimulation measurements give the same answer twice in healthy adults. The authors counsel caution in interpreting single readings.
pmc-13407858:
Rebecca Blue and co-authors review the infection record of NASA's health program for astronauts in a 2026 study. The team gathered records from US missions from the Apollo era through 2024. They counted cases where a breach, a slip in protocol, or an exposure during the health period led to crew illness. In the large set of missions they reviewed, they judged how often such events occurred and what raised the risk. The findings test whether decades of strict routine have worked, and where the routine still leaks.
pmc-13408058:
Chumin Ni and co-authors build, in 2026, a smarter funnel for finding hidden diabetes in heart patients. People with coronary heart disease carry high rates of undiagnosed diabetes. pmc-13408158:

pmc-13408358:
Zheng-Yuan Zhang, Han-Chao Chen, and a large team demonstrate in 2026 the quantum Zeno effect acting on a single atom's movement through space. The group used an optical trap as a repeated measurement pulse and tracked atom loss.

Measurements held back the spreading of the atom's quantum state, and the team mapped how pulse frequency, strength, and position change the outcome. Varying the protocol prepared distinct motion states on demand. Moving the trap during measurement even carried the atom in a chosen direction faster than gentle adiabatic dragging allows. pmc-13409558:
Cristina Benites and co-authors gather in 2026 every reported case of an inflammatory myofibroblastic tumour inside the jawbone, thirteen in all, and add a fourteenth of their own. Her tumour was removed and the jaw rebuilt in the same operation using the approach nicknamed jaw in a day, restoring normal mouth function with no recurrence at one year. Across the reviewed cases, complete surgical removal likewise produced favourable outcomes. The authors detail the imaging features. They name the look-alike diagnoses pathologists must exclude, and the molecular markers that secure the identification. Oral surgeons gain a compact reference for a tumour most will never see.
pmc-13411158:
Yiming Liu and co-authors survey in 2026 how nanotechnology might calm the misdirected immune attack behind Sjögren's syndrome. Platforms covered include polymer and fat particles, mineral particles, body-mimicking shells, and gels. Goals stretch beyond quieting inflammation toward restoring immune tolerance and regrowing working glands, with smart, computer-designed carriers flagged as the next wave.
pmc-13411358:
Peng-Yu Chen and co-workers test in 2026 a sponge-derived compound against aggressive mouth cancer cells. Oral squamous cell carcinoma spreads readily and ends poorly for many patients. The compound, stellettin B, comes from the marine sponge Jaspis stellifera.

Spread slowed as cell identity markers flipped back toward a settled, less mobile state. Gene scans also showed quieter growth signaling. pmc-13415558:

Most loci were already tied to pain, thinking, autoimmunity, or general health. Modeling placed fibromyalgia mainly among pain and autoimmune traits, with nerve mechanisms underneath.
pmc-13415658:

pmc-13415758:
Mathou and colleagues compare the brains of four shrimp species at hydrothermal vents, asking how nervous systems adapt to darkness, pressure, and plumes. Vent shrimps occupy niches around the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, from dense swarms to loners farther out. Their 2026 study uses tissue staining, antibody markers, micro CT scans, and 3D rebuilds. It maps the brain and its blood supply in the four vent species, plus a coastal relative.

Their visual centers shrank against the coastal shrimp's, fitting the near dark, while the retina stretched along the back, longest in swarm formers. A visual satellite center was missing in vent species, hinting they barely track motion. Smell lobes kept one layout but varied in size and count by species, matching each niche's chemistry and diet.
pmc-13417858:
Sanchit Mehta and co-authors trace a fatal course of methotrexate poisoning in a 64 year old with lymphoma, in a 2026 case report. The chemotherapy drug had been tolerated before, yet prior heart damage from anthracycline treatment changed its handling. After infusion for brain directed therapy, the patient developed kidney shutdown, low blood pressure, and shock.

Drug levels stayed extremely high despite an antidote enzyme and dialysis. Fluid around the lung held a large drug store, a third space trap that kept leaking drug back into the blood. Clearance took 35 days of continuous dialysis, and the patient moved to comfort care. Heart failure is flagged as a key risk.
pmc-13418458:
Chail Shah and colleagues reviewed in 2026 a lethal overlap syndrome that strikes intensive-care patients on cancer immunotherapy. Checkpoint drugs can unleash a triple attack resembling myasthenia gravis plus muscle inflammation plus heart muscle inflammation, mimicking sepsis, pneumonia, clots, and heart failure at first glance.

Early antibody tests and heart imaging often look normal, so the review urges fast multi-system checks with muscle enzymes, serial troponins, heart tracings, and imaging, alongside infection screening and prompt drug withdrawal. Critical-care teams gain a structured rescue path for a syndrome where hours and missed heart inflammation decide survival.
pmc-13418558:
Preeti Sinha and a large team run a pilot trial of probiotics added to standard care for depression in older adults, published in 2026. Fifty eight patients aged 60 or more with moderate unipolar depression were randomised at two centres to daily probiotics or placebo for 12 weeks, with 12 more weeks of follow up. The strains were Lactobacillus helveticus and Bifidobacterium longum.

Depression and anxiety scores improved over time in both groups, with modestly lower overall scores in the probiotic group, though change patterns did not differ significantly. Quality of life rose in both groups equally. A brain growth factor rose higher with probiotics. Over half the participants dropped out, limiting conclusions.
pmc-13418758:
Felix Seelemeyer and colleagues weigh reusable against single-use flexible scopes for bladder checks in outpatient urology. Their 2026 study comes from a German center that performs 337 of these checks each year, many for bladder cancer follow-up. The team counted the full cost of each route, from purchase and repairs to cleaning and staff time.

Cost models covered both a basic setup and full gear replacement, with break-even points worked out for each. A survey added the views of 13 physicians and 25 nursing staff across five practices, scored on set scales. Staff rated both scope types on image quality, handling, and daily workflow fit. pmc-13419958:
Fang-Hui Zhu and colleagues pool studies comparing catheter valve replacement in patients born with a two-leaflet aortic valve against the usual three-leaflet form. The pool held 31 studies and 192,691 patients in total, a very large base for this question. Death from any cause at one year ran lower in the two-leaflet group, with pooled odds of 0.84 in the reported model, while heart-related death showed no firm gap between groups. Safety and benefit profiles otherwise looked alike. The results ease fears that the catheter method suits only standard valve anatomy.
pmc-13420258:
Mu Qin and colleagues build a tiny drug carrier that releases its cargo in acid, aimed at retinoblastoma, the main eye cancer of childhood. Care for this cancer is hampered by the blood-retina barrier, drug resistance, and harsh side effects on the whole body. Their carrier wraps the repurposed drug nitazoxanide inside a metal-framework shell that breaks down where tissue turns acidic.

Acid-triggered release kept the drug held at body-neutral conditions and freed it in tumor-like acidity. Two effects at once, carrier plus drug, slowed tumor growth more than either alone in the study's tests. The system offers a template for gentler eye cancer care in children.
pmc-13420858:
Victor Ogutu and colleagues pooled 25 studies with 1624 children in 2026 to estimate how often clubfoot returns after Ponseti treatment. The casting and bracing method corrects most feet at first, yet relapse during childhood varies widely across reports, leaving families and clinics unsure what to expect.

The paper gives orthopedic teams a global relapse benchmark and a risk-factor synthesis for targeting follow-up and brace adherence, and family counseling in follow-up care.
pmc-13420958:
Jane Rich and a large team report what Quitline counsellors learned while helping drug and alcohol clients quit smoking, in work from twenty twenty-six. A trial gave clients twelve weeks of vaping products or standard nicotine aids. Counsellors on the phone line carried much of that support.

Themes cover staff readiness for new quit tools and the strain of multi-drug recovery. Client likes and product use, care gaps after discharge, and training needs also stood out. The talks show phone services can adapt fast and partner well with trials.
pmc-13421358:
Parner and colleagues report a 2026 study of worry after major emergency abdominal surgery at a Copenhagen hospital. Patients rated their degree of worry at discharge and at one, three, and six months. The team linked worry levels to days alive and out of hospital.

High worry was common but uneven over time: about a third of patients at discharge, a fifth at one month, then nearly half at three months, and a third at six months. Fear of relapse was the most frequent worry, followed by disease itself, daily function, and daily living. Worries about the body stayed prominent across the period. Tracking worry itself could help teams time support to when anxiety resurfaces.
pmc-13421458:
Y. N. Vashisht Gopal leads a large team testing, in a 2026 preclinical study, personalised drug combinations for melanoma that has stopped responding to BRAF and MEK inhibitors. High starting BCL2 predicted success, while high MCL1 — another family member — predicted failure, confirmed by engineering MCL1 upward. Pairing an MCL1 blocker with the standard drugs overcame that resistance and softened the heart-toxicity markers linked to MCL1 blockade.
pmc-13421558:
Ker Ke Jun and co-authors studied in 2025 how Malaysian older persons divide their time among daily occupational activities, and how that split varies with social and demographic traits. Occupational activities here mean the tasks of a day: personal care, paid work, study, housework, childcare, shopping, volunteering, social life, and leisure. Population aging is speeding up, and active aging depends on how those hours are spent.

Readers get planning evidence for health and policy teams: support can be tailored to the daily shape of a group's life, rather than offered as one flat program for all older people.
pmc-13421758:
Christy Bills and five colleagues tell, in a 2026 paper, how citizen scientists found flashing fireflies across Utah, where their presence in the American West was long an open question. A public outreach campaign and an interactive reporting website invited sightings over nearly a decade.

Reports passed 135 distinct localities, verified where possible by site visits and collected specimens. The flood of public data brought headaches — sightings outside the target area and worries about private land — handled by refining the reporting protocol and outreach as the project grew. Media and school engagement widened the haul. The authors plan a western-states expansion with partner organisations, and they present the project as a model for community-engaged species mapping.
pmc-13422358:
Harmke van Kooten and colleagues compared heart risk in 2026 between 78 adults with late-onset Pompe disease and 78 matched controls. The muscle-wasting disease may carry extra heart risk, yet whether risk factors or actual heart events run higher was unclear.

Patients showed faster resting heart rates, larger waists, and more hypertension history, yet past heart events, 19 versus 9 cases, did not differ significantly. The paper advises heart-risk monitoring in Pompe care without overstating event risk, pending larger cohorts. Clinicians can still act on the risk profile with standard heart prevention.
pmc-13422858:
Karar Zunaid Ahsan leads a six-author team asking, in a 2026 study, whether better-equipped health facilities close the wealth gap in Bangladeshi mothers' care. Overall use rose substantially, yet the gains were unevenly shared: equity improved only modestly for antenatal care and complication management. The authors conclude readiness alone does not deliver fairness.
pmc-13423158:
Caterina Matucci-Cerinic and five co-authors systematically review anakinra, an inflammation-blocking drug, for Kawasaki disease that resists standard immunoglobulin treatment. Searching seven databases to October 2025, the team found 32 publications covering 81 patients, mostly single cases or small series plus two early trials. Fever and inflammation settled in 94.9% of treated patients. Existing artery aneurysms fully resolved in 32% of cases and shrank or stabilised in a further 56.3%. No serious safety signal appeared, though the authors stress how thin the data remain.
pmc-13423958:
Liao and co-authors introduce a training-data-free method for restoring damaged images, in this 2026 computer science paper. Such images are degraded by some mixture of blur, downscaling, noise, and missing pixels. Most modern restoration tools learn from huge paired datasets; their framework, MG-SpaIR, instead fits each corrupted image individually using an implicit neural representation, a network that encodes the picture itself.

The method refines the reconstruction in grades. It recovers broad structure first and fine detail later. That counters the known tendency of such networks to blur high frequencies. A sparsity penalty applied directly in the full-resolution image domain suppresses invented textures while keeping genuine edges sharp. The authors prove convergence of their alternating optimization under standard conditions. They report that the method consistently beat strong training-free baselines on mixed-degradation benchmarks. Deep Image Prior was among the baselines beaten.
pmc-13424258:
Yuta Hasegawa and nine co-authors report a rare case of pancreatic cancer in a thirty-nine-year-old woman. As a newborn, she had surgery to widen her stomach outlet, a fix for a feeding block in infants. She came to hospital with worsening nausea and vomiting. Scans suggested a tumor at the stomach outlet, possibly from stray pancreatic tissue or stomach cancer spreading into the pancreas.

Surgery showed the tumor had grown into the head of the pancreas, so the team removed the pancreatic head and nearby organs. Lab study showed the cancer had arisen from pancreatic tissue embedded in the muscle wall of the stomach outlet and bowel. The authors think the odd placement traces back to her newborn surgery. She later received drug treatment, but cancer spread within two years. The case warns surgeons to expect odd anatomy in such patients.
pmc-13425458:
Mechati and colleagues published a 2026 study on making dye-cleaning particles from olive waste. Olive pomace, the pulp left after oil pressing, served as the natural helper. With it, the team grew magnesium oxide particles just nanometers wide. The particles were then tested on Congo red, a stubborn textile dye.

Lab checks confirmed clean, round crystals with a porous, active surface. The particles cleared more than nine-tenths of the dye within 30 minutes. Under tuned settings, removal passed 95 percent in their test runs. Computer models showed strong electric pulls between dye and particle surface sites. The work turns farm waste into a tool for cleaner wastewater. The method needs no harsh chemicals, which keeps the whole process green.
pmc-13425958:
Clio Berry and colleagues design a mentoring program to lift hope among young women in deprived coastal England who are out of school, work, and training. That group fares worse for mental health and social outcomes than peers who work or study, and coastal disadvantage deepens the gap.

The co-developed program, called HOPEFUL, is flexible and modular, helping each woman set and chase goals that matter to her, with a mentor she may pick from her own circle. This paper is the feasibility-stage protocol, testing whether a full trial can recruit and run. Services get a hopeful, person-led alternative to one-size-fits-all job schemes.
pmc-13426058:
Anton A. Gladkov and colleagues describe a light-driven route to aryl indium reagents in a 2026 chemistry article. Shining visible light from LEDs at 400, 455, and even 520 nanometers on indium(I) bromide mixtures generates a highly active low-valent indium species. pmc-13426358:
Ammad Ahmad Farooqi and coauthors review natural products that target the NRF2 and KEAP1 pathway in a 2026 article framed around gentle, precise pharmacology. NRF2, discovered in 1994, sits at the center of a wide molecular web controlling cell defense responses, with many regulators upstream and targets downstream. Interest has surged in compounds that can tune this node for disease prevention and treatment.

Natural products with distinctive structural features and multipronged actions receive special attention as candidate modulators. The review maps the pathway landscape so drug hunters can spot where plant-derived chemistry might intervene safely.
pmc-13427458:
Yoshihito Mima, Masako Yamamoto, and Ken Iozumi report sleep gains with nemolizumab in prurigo nodularis in a 2026 retrospective study of 22 patients with refractory disease. This intensely itchy nodular skin condition wrecks sleep, mood, and social functioning, and easing itch is most patients' chief goal. Three patients stopped by week sixteen for asthma flare, swollen redness, or acute eczema, leaving the rest for analysis of sleep duration and night awakenings beyond standard itch scales. Real-world sleep data extend trial findings for a symptom patients rank first.
pmc-13427658:
Nana Li leads a huge multicenter team that built, in 2026, a tool to predict low blood oxygen during gut endoscopy under sedation. Such dips in oxygen are common and can turn serious, yet clinics lacked a purpose-built risk score. Data came from outpatients at seven hospitals across China between May 2020 and November 2023. The eight cover body mass index, throat and jaw features, tongue size, snoring history, neck shape, and starting blood pressure. Standard checks for sleep apnea and difficult airways fed the comparison work behind the model. Performance was judged on accuracy, calibration, and whether using the score would help real decisions. A separate patient group tested the model independently, a step many risk tools skip.
pmc-13427858:
Calegari and colleagues published a 2026 study on repeating DNA in two true bug species. Satellite DNA is stretch after stretch of the same short DNA code. The other held less, with older copies drifted further apart over time. The biggest families filled the ends of chromosomes in both species. pmc-13428158:

In lab studies, these compounds slowed tumour spread, reset the cell cycle, and pushed cancer cells toward orderly death. They also helped tumours respond again to standard chemotherapy drugs that had stopped working. Jia flags real limits, including liver harm from some compounds and poor uptake in the body, and urges better delivery designs.
pmc-13428258:
Iterbeke and colleagues test whether texture in muscle MRI scans can separate two genetic diseases that both waste muscle. One is myotonic dystrophy type 1, a muscle disease. Both patient groups carried more fat in every leg muscle than controls. The geography differed: dystrophy hit the back compartment hardest, while the nerve disease hit the front outer compartment and faded from ankle to hip. Adding texture to standard maps, the authors argue, sharpens non invasive diagnosis.
pmc-13430858:

Staff caught 250 mozzies in Kwara State, in three local areas. Gene tests named Anopheles coluzzii in 31.2 percent, Anopheles gambiae in 16.8 percent, and Anopheles arabiensis in 13.6 percent, while 38.4 percent gave no gene read. pmc-13431858:

Fifteen triage nurses from three Melbourne emergency departments were watched for two to two and a half hours each between January and May 2025, with lapel microphones recording the work. Transcripts were coded deductively against the HIRAID nursing framework, covering history, danger signs, assessment, actions, tests, re-checks, and talk. Managers get a grounded picture of triage work for staffing and training.
pmc-13432858:

Trials show low rates of the grave immune storm that haunts this drug class, and fit patients can take doses as outpatients. Shouse walks through the drug's build, its mode of work, gains, and harms. The review frames the drug as a model of immune care gains in lymph cancers.
pmc-13432958:
Selma Kronsteiner-Gicevic and co-authors mined a vast British cohort in 2026 for ties between salt intake and fresh asthma in adults. More than four hundred thousand adults free of asthma at the start gave urine spots and notes on salt added at the table. Health records caught new cases across near eleven years.

Near twelve thousand new cases arose. The top fifth for urine salt marks met asthma at half again the rate of the low fifth. The tie ran stronger in women than men, in never-smokers than in past or live smokers, and in people with low counts of one white cell type. Always adding salt at the table also tracked with more new cases. The authors urge diet trials to test the salt link.
pmc-13434558:
Gaige Wang and colleagues scramble the atomic order of a fuel cell part in 2026 to make it work better on hydrocarbon fuels. Solid oxide cells turn fuels such as methane straight into power. Carbon buildup and slow fuel use have held back the anode, the fuel side part.

Those traits speed fuel cleaning and carbon removal at once. The cell gave strong power and ran past 1,000 hours on wet methane at 700 degrees. Disorder becomes a design tool.
pmc-13434658:

pmc-13434758:

Layer patterns hint at fresh water pulses into the North Atlantic. Paired timing ends a long mismatch between land and sea records. Both ice sheets grew large far earlier than once thought.
pmc-13435258:
Gomeni and Bressolle-Gomeni test deep learning as a partner for traditional drug development modeling in this 2026 paper. Model-informed drug development usually relies on hypothesis-driven models built from biology and chemistry, which can miss complex nonlinear patterns in data. A neural network, by contrast, learns such patterns directly without a preset structure. It reached that performance while needing far fewer assumptions about the underlying system in advance. The authors argue the two styles are complementary: mechanistic models offer biological interpretability, deep learning offers flexible prediction, and combining them should strengthen drug development decisions.
pmc-13435758:

Breaks at the greater trochanter struck 25.0 percent of front route hips versus 3.3 percent of back route hips. Within the front route, patients with breaks carried higher body weight scores. Hip function scores ended alike for both routes. Cup shift past two millimeters tracked worse function. Surgeons may weigh route and weight together when planning.
pmc-13436558:

The team searched three large databases for studies on case-based learning in obstetrics training, weighing gains, weak points, and open questions. Studies linked the method to stronger engagement, clinical reasoning, practical skills, and teamwork among residents. Results still hinged on teacher skill, case quality, and school resources, and most studies tracked only short-term gains. Chen sees promise in blended learning, simulation, and artificial intelligence tools, but notes that solid proof of long-term benefit is still missing.
pmc-13437658:

pmc-13437958:

pmc-13438758:

That guides empty vehicles toward stations where riders are likely to appear, with charging in mind. Mock trials compare the method with classic routing and solvers. The team also tests a reverse annealing step for better answers than a single forward run gives.
pmc-13439058:

With those parts, the group built a three-input logic gate, a half adder, and a full adder. pmc-13439358:

pmc-13439558:

Diagnosis also lagged at every step for that group, from first symptoms to confirmed imaging. Back-of-brain artery involvement ran higher, and rising blood pressure percentiles preceded diagnosis by months. A year on, children with Down syndrome carried more disability and muscle stiffness. The authors urge earlier vascular checks in this group.
pmc-13439758:

pmc-13440458:

pmc-13440758:

pmc-13441158:

pmc-13444258:
Xuran Zhou and colleagues fix sound-speed warps in 3D photoacoustic scans without extra gear in a 2026 paper. pmc-13445958:

pmc-13446358:

pmc-13447058:

pmc-13447158:
Francisco Fernández and colleagues revisit in 2026 how much of the drug eculizumab is needed in blood to fully block a part of the immune system called complement. pmc-13447358:
Ziyi Yan and a large team review how pneumococcal vaccines reshape antibiotic resistance in a 2026 mini review. pmc-13447558:

pmc-13447858:

pmc-13448658:

pmc-13448858:
Yan Jiang and a large team examine in 2026 whether swings in blood sugar leave marks on the eye even in people who do not have diabetes. Their choroids were thinner, with a smaller share of large vessels yet a higher overall vascular index. pmc-13449058:
Umur Anil Pehlivan, Gurcan Erbay, and Elif Karadeli write in 2026 to the editor about the stubborn misuse of two old names for vascular anomalies in children. pmc-13449458:
Chengjian Wu and colleagues tested a small surgical trick for tight knees in 2026, aimed at making meniscus repair safer. pmc-13449658:
Bincheng Tang and co-authors run in 2026 a multi-omics hunt for the genes behind erectile function in male geese, a trait that decides mating success in breeding flocks. pmc-13450558:
Alexa Kwang and colleagues gather a 2026 case series on a slow skin lymphoma that posed as a common flaky scalp-and-face rash. The lymphoma, mycosis fungoides, is the most frequent skin T-cell cancer and is known for copying mild skin diseases. Late labels raise the risk of wrong care and spread.

When creams failed and the spot thickened, deeper checks told the true story, a lesson in retesting stubborn patches.
pmc-13451258:
Robert Olek and Zsolt Radak review in 2026 a gut-made compound long cast as a heart risk, asking what exercise does to it. The compound, TMAO, forms when gut microbes process certain foods and the liver finishes the job. Levels also depend on how fast the kidneys clear it.

Hard sessions and muscle damage nudged levels for a short while in some studies. pmc-13451358:

pmc-13451858:
Shuo Pang and co-authors set out in 2026 a gut-prostate link for a lasting pelvic pain illness in men whose cause stays unclear. The illness mixes pelvic pain with urinary and sexual trouble, and care often stalls. New work hints that a skewed gut germ mix may prime the body toward it in some men.

pmc-13452158:

pmc-13453158:

pmc-13453458:

pmc-13454258:
Raneem Darraj and others built a design-led HPLC test in 2026 for two syrup preservatives, methylparaben and propylparaben. pmc-13454458:

pmc-13454558:
Javeria Anees (2026) writes a letter to the editor about a study of heart tracings after orchiectomy, the surgical removal of a testicle. pmc-13455258:

pmc-13455358:

pmc-13457058:

pmc-13457458:

pmc-13457858:

pmc-13457958:

pmc-13458758:

pmc-13459058:

pmc-13459158:

pmc-13459358:

pmc-13459458:

pmc-13459658:

pmc-13459958:

pmc-13460058:

pmc-13460558:

pmc-13461158:

pmc-13461458:

pmc-13461658:

pmc-13462058:

pmc-13462258:

pmc-13545658:

pmc-13546658:

pmc-13546758:

pmc-13547058:

pmc-13547158:

pmc-13547258:

pmc-13547458:

pmc-13547658:

pmc-13547758:

pmc-13548058:

pmc-13548258:

pmc-13548358:

pmc-13548658:

pmc-13548858:

pmc-13550058:

pmc-13550958:

pmc-13551258:

pmc-13553658:

pmc-13554758:

pmc-13555058:

pmc-13555158:

pmc-13556058:

pmc-13556158:

pmc-13556358:

pmc-13556458:

The adapted shot aimed to beat the original on neutralizing the matched variant, judged by antibody ratios and the share of participants mounting a response. Two-dose results in vaccine-naive participants were compared against the original vaccine's earlier trial. Safety and soreness data complete a picture regulators used for variant update decisions.
pmc-13570958:
Xuan Zhao and co-authors measure how people walk after tearing the main ligament that steadies the knee. Their 2026 study deals with rupture of the anterior cruciate ligament, which leaves the knee loose. How the legs adapt matters for planning rehab.

Forty people took part: twenty-two with a fresh tear and eighteen healthy peers. Each walked on a treadmill at a set pace while wearing seventeen motion sensors. The team compared joint angles at the hip, knee, and ankle across ten strides, on both sides of the body. The patients turned their hips and ankles less on both sides, and bent the hurt knee less at its peak. The shifts on the sound side show the whole body adapts, not just the hurt leg.
pmc-13571158:
A large Dutch team tested whether iron given by vein helps kidney transplant patients walk and live better in 2026. Many such patients lack iron, but no one knew if fixing that lack would lift daily function. The trial ran at two Dutch hospitals over more than four years.

Adults at least six months past transplant got four doses of the iron drug or a placebo. Among 148 people in the main count, walking distance after 24 weeks barely differed between groups. The drug fixed iron levels and raised blood counts, yet heart, muscle, thinking, and life quality did not improve. Harm events were much the same in both groups.
pmc-13571658:
Diego Amarante-Silva and co-authors build a self-rolling film that delivers anti-inflammatory medicine straight to a radiation-injured colon. Radiation therapy saves cancer patients, yet it can inflame nearby healthy bowel, and systemic drugs expose the whole body. A local, gentle delivery route could calm the injury where it sits.

First they built a rat model of radiation proctitis with targeted, split-dose irradiation and full tissue checks. Then they engineered a two-layer PEG-PLA film, loaded with prednisolone, that curls into place through an endoscope. Placed in the injured bowel, the film cut inflammatory signals such as IL-1β. Local dosing like this may spare patients wider side effects.
pmc-13571758:
Zhen Zhang and co-authors published a study in 2026 on a protein called SENP7 in lung adenocarcinoma, a common form of lung cancer. The disease kills many people each year, and some patients do not respond to, or become resistant to, existing treatments. Novel therapeutic targets are therefore in strong demand.

The researchers analyzed gene and protein data from large databases and examined lung tissue in the laboratory. SENP7 was markedly more abundant in cancer tissue than in normal lung tissue. High levels were associated with worse outcomes for patients. When the team reduced the protein, cancer growth slowed in cell cultures and in mice. They found that SENP7 protects a second protein, SP1, by removing molecular tags that would mark it for destruction. That action is central both to tumor growth and to resistance to chemotherapy. The pair is proposed as a fresh target.
pmc-13571858:
Hye Hyeon Kim and co-authors read mood from daily speech in a 2026 study. Four hundred call center workers, a group heavy in emotional labor, recorded three short voice entries a day for two weeks in a phone app. Language models and a classic word-count method scored the transcripts for sentiment, while standard questionnaires tracked depression.

Model-based scores separated workers by depression level, beating the word-count method. Morning entries separated groups best, and a running score peaked on day ten. Self-rated mood faded and failed to separate groups. Language-based personality scores also tracked symptoms better. Readers get a passive, low-burden mood signal.
pmc-13571958:
Siying He, Junqi Wu, and three co-authors pool studies on a DNA trait in bladder-area cancers. Their review, from twenty twenty-six, looks at aneuploidy, an abnormal count of chromosomes in tumor cells. Urothelial cancer is common and deadly, and good marker tests are scarce. DNA count tests have grown faster and cheaper of late.

Fifteen studies met the bar for pooling. Tumors with odd DNA counts tied to far worse survival overall. Disease-free and progress-free survival were also worse. The trait linked to higher stage, worse grade, and spread to lymph nodes. Oddly, the survival link held in Asian and American groups but not European ones.
pmc-13572058:
Makoto Asaeda and co-authors test seated aerobic exercise for care home day visitors in a 2026 analysis. The trial ran at ten Japanese daycare sites. Older adults needing care did usual rehab, and half the sites added seated stepping and arm swings. The added work came in short bursts at a brisk beat, over six months.

Of 252 finishers, the exercise group clearly out-stepped the usual group on a two-minute step test, gaining about nineteen steps on average. Felt effort during exercise ran slightly lower too. Grip, mobility, daily living scores, and frailty class did not differ significantly. The authors conclude the cheap seated program builds endurance, a base benefit, even where other measures stay flat.
pmc-13572458:
Manogna R. L, with two colleagues, benchmarks 2026 computer models for winter wheat yield forecasts across India. District-level forecasts guide food plans and policy in the world's second largest wheat producer. The team tested nine model types on 23 years of data from 275 districts in seven states.

The data joined soil depth profiles with weather and satellite series from 2001 to 2023. A hybrid model that routes each data kind through its own path won, with a mean error of 273.2 kilograms per hectare. That cut error by 43.8 percent against a random forest base model. A plain forecast that just repeats last year's yield nearly tied it, though. The hybrid pulled ahead in the dry 2023 season, and its edge centred on the February to March grain-filling window.
pmc-13572558:
Jun Lei Gao, with seven colleagues, reports a 2026 mouse study of breathing hydrogen sulfide, a toxic gas found in industry and farm waste. The gas can harm the lungs, immune system, and nerves, but the gene-level picture in lung tissue was unclear. The team varied the dose and read both body markers and lung gene activity.

At set doses, the gas raised an inflammatory signal and two defence enzymes, while high doses shifted more immune signals and stress measures. Some markers of cell damage fell, a mixed pattern the authors note. Lung gene reads found 963 genes whose levels changed across groups. Those genes cluster in immune response, DNA change, enzyme work, and cell cycle control. Four genes, among them FGFBP1 and GATA3, look central to the response. The data set seeds later work on how the gas harms lungs.
pmc-13572858:
Jingzhi Zhang and co-authors map the molecules that give foods their smells, in this 2026 study. A food's aroma comes from a blend of odorants, yet how blends hold a stable identity was unclear. The team built an atlas of key odorants from more than two thousand food aroma profiles. In all, eight hundred ninety-six molecules made the key list, and every aroma needed at least three of them.

Plant foods drew on wider sets of key odorants than animal foods. Some unlike foods turned out to share smell building blocks in telling ways. The atlas shows mixture-level order: identity sits in the blend, not in single stars. With that map, the authors show a generative tool can design new aromas on purpose, a step for both flavor science and the food trade.
pmc-13572958:
Shaobo Li and co-authors study thyroid hormones and weight-loss surgery in a 2026 paper. Bariatric surgery helps many patients lose weight and remit diabetes, but results vary. With new weight drugs rising, spotting who benefits most from surgery matters more.

The study covered over 1,500 adults with normal thyroid function, and about 1,000 were followed after surgery. One hormone, free triiodothyronine, tracked fat-free mass and levelled off past an age threshold. Patients starting with higher levels were more likely to hit strong weight loss and diabetes remission at one year. The link was stronger in women, and sex-specific cutoffs were reported. Low starting levels predicted weaker results over three years. The authors propose the hormone as a planning marker.
pmc-13573158:
Yunxuan Jiang and co-authors report, in a 2026 battery study, a zinc anode design that breaks a long trade-off between stability and use. Water-based zinc batteries are cheap and safe, but their zinc anodes grow spikes, waste metal, and die early. Surface coats alone have not fixed the cycle.

Their anode sprays zinc grains onto a copper mesh, each grain wrapped in a bismuth inner layer and a carbon outer shell. On discharge, the grain core empties and leaves a shell with a hollow inside. On charge, zinc plates back into that hollow, guided by the bismuth, instead of spiking outward. The design held near-perfect charge efficiency and ran over 10,000 hours at a set current. Confined growth may unlock long-life zinc storage.
pmc-13573358:
Gad and co-authors test in 2026 whether melatonin loaded nanoparticles raise rosmarinic acid output in basil plants. The compound is a valued bioactive product of basil. Melatonin was packed into chitosan particles and dosed to plant cultures at three levels, beside plain melatonin.

Leaf phenolic and flavonoid content rose under both treatments, and rosmarinic acid rose too. The middle dose gave the strongest gains, near 3.5 and 3.8 fold for the two content measures, with acid at 19.73 milligrams per gram. Key pathway enzymes ran faster under treatment. Pathway genes switched on more strongly as well, which ties the chemistry to gene control.
pmc-13573558:
Some germs break down oil waste with no air, and one enzyme starts that work by joining two small compounds. Maciej Szaleniec and co-authors trace that enzyme's steps in a 2026 study, joining lab tests with a full maths model of the run. One clue is how much slower the enzyme works with a heavy form of one compound.

The model matched the real slow down well. It showed the gap comes less from a quantum shortcut than from how the enzyme grips light and heavy forms at unlike rates. The team also tracked a slow swap of atoms in the end goods and set out how that swap could run. The work firms up views of a germ tool that helps clean oil waste.
pmc-13574558:
Min Gon Kang and co-authors present a case of Fanconi anemia with a liver mass in a thirty-seven-year-old woman in a 2026 clinicopathological report. She came in with stubborn mouth ulcers and pain after seven years of follow-up for low platelets and large red cells.

Short stature, a café-au-lait skin patch, and a thumb fixed by four childhood surgeries all pointed to the inherited marrow failure syndrome. She had long refused marrow biopsy and gene testing. A neck lump, removed and shown to be a benign nerve tumor, finally prompted full workup. A chromosome breakage test showed marked fragility, and gene analysis confirmed Fanconi anemia from two FANCA faults, one mosaic. The case then turns to her liver mass.
pmc-13574858:
Luping Qiu and colleagues built a model to flag severe drug-induced liver injury without biopsy. Severe injury carries a poor outlook, yet blood markers are vague and biopsy means cutting into the liver. Their study at many centres signed up 305 patients who had both liver biopsy and dual elastography, a scan method that yields activity and scarring scores. Eight machine-learning models were tried, with the best tuned by cross-checks.

The best model, a tuned regression, scored 0.862 on the standard accuracy scale in testing, with 81 percent sensitivity and 75 percent specificity, and the scan scores were its top predictors. The team also put out an online risk tool. The authors present the model as a clear aid for sorting risk and guiding early care choices.
pmc-13575158:
Luyu Wang and co-authors pack a terahertz transmitter onto a chip, aiming at the ultra-fast wireless links future networks will need. Terahertz waves offer vast capacity, but today's photonic systems are benches of separate parts, with lossy couplings and bulky footprints. Their 2026 paper bonds two chip technologies together to shrink the whole transmitter.

A photodiode grown on indium phosphide is fused onto a thin-film lithium niobate modulator chip. The marriage pairs the modulator's crisp electro-optic response with the diode's strong terahertz generation. The diode reached a bandwidth of 240 gigahertz, a benchmark figure. Over the air, the transmitter sent forty gigabits per second at 150 gigahertz and thirty-two at 200 gigahertz. The authors present the bonded design as a scalable path toward compact, high-capacity wireless interconnects for data-hungry networks.
pmc-13575358:
Zachariah Whiting and co-authors report how often athletes return to sport after combined hip surgery in a 2026 study. Hip dysplasia, a shallow socket, can sideline young athletes. Two operations are often paired: one reshapes the socket bone, the other repairs inside the joint with a camera.

Records from one center covered eighty-four patients and one hundred three hips treated between 2016 and 2023. The patients were young, averaging about twenty years old. Nearly nine in ten hips returned to sport, at roughly ten months on average. X-ray measures of socket cover improved after surgery. Return rates did not hinge on the factors the team tested. The series adds weight to the combined approach for active patients.
pmc-13575958:
Juan He and four colleagues review bedside bronchoscopy for the sickest COPD patients, those on breathing machines during a flare. A scope through the tube can clear mucus, sample infection, and guide care. When to run it, though, has no firm rulebook.

The narrative review gathers guidelines and trials from Western and Chinese databases. Evidence hints at better oxygen levels, fewer ventilator days, and less lung infection with well-timed scopes. The authors propose four timing windows, from just after intubation to failed tube removal. They also set out standard steps for risk checks, sedation, and monitoring, with notes for smaller intensive care units. Trial proof stays thin.
pmc-13576458:
Churun Jauharoh Al Aryachiyah and co-authors distinguish folded from denatured hemoglobin with a printed circuit board sensor that uses the same metal for all three electrodes. Their 2026 paper deals with electrochemical sensing of a key blood protein.

Denaturation lowers a protein's stability and changes its redox behavior. Standard sensing uses three electrodes of differing materials. Their board-based sensor uses gold throughout, yet still produced the characteristic hemoglobin profiles. In buffered saline, the oxidation and reduction peaks sat close together. A cheap, single-metal board that can tell native from damaged hemoglobin could suit point-of-care testing and teaching labs alike.
pmc-13577858:
Ibtissam El Bqaq and six co-authors report a groin lump that was not a hernia in a 2026 paper. The true cause was endometriosis inside the inguinal canal. This rare form affects the right round ligament most often. Its cyclical pain and swelling mimic a hernia closely.

The patient was a 38-year-old woman with months of right groin pain. Ultrasound and MRI pointed to inguinal endometriosis pre-surgery. Surgeons removed the lesion with the ligament segment by keyhole surgery. Tissue study confirmed endometriosis, not a hernia defect. Early imaging can spare women the wrong operation, they stress. A linked review covers the reported cases.
pmc-13578358:
Kamil Shah and co-authors build a math model of how measles spreads, fitted to real case counts from China from 2005 to 2017. The model sorts people into groups by health state, from open to infection through sick, held apart, and healed. Shots, a waiting phase, isolation, and treatment all enter the setup.

The team checked that the model's answers stay sound and found the key spread number that marks when the disease can take hold. A neural network tool then solved the model fast and matched the case data well. Runs showed that higher rates of shots and isolation cut spread a great deal, which can guide control plans.
pmc-13578758:
Arianna D'Ulizia, Alessia D'Andrea, and Riccardo Denni refine a way to rank the best spreaders in a network when some kinds of nodes matter more than others, in a 2026 study. Classic peeling methods strip a network layer by layer to find its core, yet they score every category alike. Their version peels with a priority order over categories, honoring a user's ranking of which groups count most.

The method raced seventy nine rival measures on seven real networks. It placed the true top spreader highest on five of the seven sets. Ties were its weak spot, since many nodes shared top ranks. Pairing the peel order with a simple degree count broke ties best, reliably lifting true spreaders into the top group. The code is shared freely for other teams to test.
pmc-13579058:
Four doctors report cascade screening in a Syrian family with a hereditary tumor syndrome in a 2026 paper. The syndrome, MEN2A, runs in families and brings thyroid cancer, adrenal tumors, and parathyroid overgrowth. Finding it early lets doctors screen kin before disease advances.

The first patient, a 37 year old man, had both adrenal glands and his thyroid removed, and pathology confirmed the classic tumor pair. Screening by symptoms and labs, without gene testing, then found his 39 year old sister with the same tumor pair. A younger brother held two distinct thyroid cancers of other types. The family shows the value of symptom driven screening where gene tests are lacking.
pmc-13579458:
Satoshi Sagai and six co-authors reported a 2026 case where two ways of measuring lung volume swapped places after a transplant. Alveolar volume is measured by two breathing techniques, a repeated-breath and a single-breath method, and theory says the first should always read higher. Their patient, with severe emphysema, received one transplanted lung. After surgery, the readings came out reversed.

The team ruled out machine error and sloppy technique. The likely cause is physiology: the new lung and the remaining emphysematous lung work so differently that gas mixing behaves in a way the standard theory does not cover. As a result, the combined numbers may misstate how well each lung actually exchanges gas. The case warns against trusting pooled indices after single-lung transplant.
pmc-13579758:
A protein that shapes bone and blood vessels may also foretell how a patient fares after artery surgery. Sofia Skroder and seven co-authors test that link in a 2026 study of 210 patients set for open repair of blocked leg or neck arteries. Blood levels of the protein were read before surgery.

One year on, the team counts new cases of a chaotic heart rhythm, major heart and vessel events, and deaths from any cause. Risk models weigh whether high levels track with worse ends. Most patients were men, and most had leg surgery. Women were older and held higher levels of the protein. A blood read that flags risk before the knife could steer who gets closer watch after surgery.
pmc-13579858:
Maryam Adelipour and colleagues tune a cheap polymer method for harvesting healing vesicles from stem cell broth, in a 2026 study. Stem cells release tiny packets called exosomes that calm immune attack and aid repair, yet pulling them out cleanly at scale has lagged. The team tried three weights of a common polymer, polyethylene glycol, which crowds the packets out of solution so they can be collected.

The middle weight won on yield and purity. Its packets measured under two hundred nanometers and carried the right surface badges. A deep scan counted hundreds of proteins and over a thousand small molecules inside, proof the cargo stayed intact. Extra rinse cycles through a sizing column stripped away stray junk. Cancer cells bathed in the packets stayed alive and, at high doses, thrived a bit more.
pmc-13580058:
A blood transfusion can flood the lungs with inflammation in a rare, deadly reaction, and Jiani Gao and nine co-authors trace one driver of that cascade in a 2026 study. The driver is a signaling chain in immune cells: a surface protein called CD36, a partner kinase, and chemokine signals that summon neutrophils, which then cast toxic nets.

Single-cell gene reads from a mouse model tied CD36 to aggressive macrophage behavior. Blocking the chain at any of several links calmed the macrophages and cut the neutrophil response. The team also built a delivery system modeled on platelet vesicles that releases its cargo where reactive oxygen runs high. In mice, the system homed to the lungs, damped the same signaling chain, reduced net formation and oxidative stress, and left lung tissue and breathing improved.
pmc-13580258:
Jisha Kuttiani Ali and Emad Alhseinat build a membrane from porous organic cages whose holes widen or shrink with the solvent, in a 2026 study. The cages were cast onto a plastic support film from two building blocks at room temperature. Solvent choice flips the pore size, a switch confirmed by crystal pattern checks, and the change runs both ways.

In water the tightened pores let only a trickle of heavy metal ions through while blocking most test dye. Looser pores in alcohol passed more of both. Metals trapped upstream could then be washed back out, with about half the nickel and slightly less of the zinc recovered. The authors pitch the switchable film for pulling valuable metals from waste water while sorting molecules on the side.
pmc-13580458:
Yuntian Chen and co-authors ask, in a 2026 study, whether living near greenery protects the lungs, whatever a person's genes say. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease is driven mainly by smoking, but place and inheritance also play roles. The team followed more than 385,000 UK Biobank members and mapped the green, blue, and natural land around each home.

More green space and natural land near home came with a lower risk of developing the disease. Water features showed weak, uneven links. The greenery benefit appeared at every level of genetic risk, low to high, and gene scores did not change the link in either direction. The authors read place as a lever of its own: greener neighborhoods may prevent lung disease across the whole population, not only for the genetically lucky.
pmc-13580658:
Yiqing Yu and four co-authors survey obstetricians in Xinjiang, China, on their readiness for prenatal genome sequencing in a 2026 study. Whole-exome sequencing can find gene causes of fetal problems before birth, but general obstetricians must know when to refer and how to counsel families. Xinjiang is vast and has thin resources, which makes the gap worth measuring.

Most of the 666 doctors who answered felt least sure about sequencing and single-gene disorders, though support for testing in clear cases ran high. Specialists in maternal-fetal medicine felt far more ready, yet few felt very sure when reading results. The authors see a clear training need as testing spreads faster than skills.
pmc-13580958:
Thomas Slavens and Hamid Shabgard refine a nature-inspired design method in a 2026 paper on heat management. Engineers borrow tricks from living things to cool devices, but picking which species to study is tricky. Heat load on an organism depends on wind and radiation as well as air temperature, a fuller measure called operative temperature.

The team clustered places by growing-season operative temperature for a North American tree species. Air temperature alone split the range into two broad groups; the fuller measure resolved four, including coastal and mid-latitude pockets. Leaf edges from one hundred three pressed specimens were then measured across the groups. Cooler groups showed distinct leaf traits. The method sharpens the hunt for heat-driven traits worth copying.
pmc-13581458:
Robert Raffa, Joseph Pergolizzi, and Eugene Vortsman warned in 2026 about internet sales of so-called research grade compounds, using the opioid SR-17018 as a case study. Sellers claim buyers promise lab use only, yet the products come as tablets, a form handy for human use and awkward for research. The drug agency has flagged such compounds as emerging abuse risks.

SR-17018 was made at Scripps Research to test whether a biased opioid could give pain relief without slowing breathing. It never entered human trials, so almost no human safety data exist. The review gathers lab and animal pharmacology and recounts one emergency doctor's case of a suspected overdose, to show the uncertainty clinicians face.
pmc-13581758:
Wenneng Liu and a team of co-authors review artificial intelligence in obesity care, in a paper dated twenty twenty-six. They searched major databases through June twenty twenty-six for studies since twenty fifteen. Each study was weighed by design, checking, and real patient benefit.

Direct proof for AI-led obesity care stays thin and mixed, they find. The strongest results come from mixed digital programs where the AI part was never tested alone. AI drug hunting remains at the lab stage. Text tools can flag drug safety chatter but cannot prove cause. The authors set priorities for closing the gap to clinic use.
pmc-13581858:
Seven authors, led by Mary Shen, review in 2026 new drug options for opioid use disorder and withdrawal. Three proven drugs exist, yet many patients drop out, cannot reach care, or still struggle. The review looks at drugs that act beyond the main opioid target in the brain.

Ketamine has early trial support for easing withdrawal and craving. A cannabis compound may blunt cue driven craving, while another may soften withdrawal signs. Psychedelic drugs show early signals but carry safety and legal bars. Gut hormone drugs used for diabetes are also under study. The authors weigh promise against proof for each class.
pmc-13582358:
Brandon Feole, Denis Grouzdev, Emmanuelle Pales Espinosa, Guillaume Cacot, and Bassem Allam show that how a sample is taken changes what oyster blood microbes look like. Their 2026 study works with the eastern oyster, whose blood, called hemolymph, is a handy window on health. Much past work does not say clearly how the blood was drawn.

The common notch method pushes a needle through soft, seawater-exposed tissue, risking contamination. Their hole method drills the shell and draws blood straight from the muscle, avoiding that path. Comparing the two, they test whether the bacterial communities found differ by method. The results push for standardized sampling in oyster microbiome research.
pmc-13582658:
Ro Osawa and four co-authors test a personal fiber picker: a lab screen that ferments a person's gut microbes against many fibers and names the best match. Their 2026 trial starts from a known puzzle, that fiber supplements help some people and not others. No proven way existed to choose a fiber ahead of time.

Eight healthy adults took both their best-match and worst-match fibers in turn. The matched fiber raised helpful gut acids over baseline at group level, while the unmatched one did not. Seven of eight people did better on their match. Yet the screen's score gap did not predict how big each person's gain would be. The authors call the results a proof of concept that needs larger trials.
pmc-13582858:
Bing Liu and colleagues solved the crystal structure of USP15, an enzyme that strips ubiquitin tags from proteins, caught in the act of gripping ubiquitin. USP15 shapes immune responses and cancer, but how it recognises ubiquitin and switches shape was poorly understood. Their 2026 study reports the catalytic domain at 2.3 angstrom resolution, covalently bound to a ubiquitin probe.

Binding flips the enzyme from a closed, inactive shape to an open, active one, realigning its catalytic trio and swinging a finger-like subdomain outward. Two conserved parts, an alpha-8 helix and a loop, proved essential: deleting the helix killed activity, and a cancer-linked mutation in the loop weakened binding. The authors point to these parts as targets for selective drugs against this enzyme family.
pmc-13583058:
Wang Hui, Wang Jing, and co-authors pool studies on muscle loss in folks with diabetic foot sores, in work from 2026. Muscle loss can slow heal and raise fall risk in this frail group. Its true rate and drivers in foot sore cases were not yet summed in one place.

Seven studies with more than one thousand cases were pooled. Close to a third of cases had muscle loss by joint counts. Long years with diabetes linked to more loss in the few studies that could be pooled. Proof on other drivers was too thin to sum. Early muscle checks are urged in foot care.
pmc-13583358:
Raj Whitlock, Robert NL Fitt and the Darwin Tree of Life Consortium, with several Wellcome Sanger Institute teams, published this 2026 genome sequence note for Hypericum pulchrum, slender St John's-wort. The plant is a hairless perennial herb of heaths and open woodlands, widespread across the British Isles and western Europe but declining in central England. The assembly forms part of the Darwin Tree of Life project, which is sequencing the eukaryotic species of Britain and Ireland.

The assembly resolves two haplotypes, the two chromosome sets, totalling about 373 and 368 megabases. Most of the first haplotype, about 95 percent of its length, is organised into nine chromosomal pseudomolecules. The team assembled the mitochondrial genomes, at about 218 and 277 kilobases, and the plastid genome at about 149 kilobases. Annotation through Ensembl identified 29,497 protein-coding genes. The authors present it for studying the species' ecology, including its antifungal seed coat and poorly known insect relationships.
pmc-13583458:
Robert Roy and co-authors scanned the reward wiring of the brain in methamphetamine addiction in a 2026 study. Brain circuits that handle reward sit at the center of addiction theory. The fiber bundles that link those circuits are a necessary part of them, yet how much they change in meth addiction was unknown.

The team gathered several kinds of magnetic scans from just over ninety people with problem meth use. They measured the white matter tracts of the reward system and matched them against thinking and behavior tests, including responses to non-drug rewards. Blunted pleasure from ordinary rewards is the so-called dark side of addiction. Linking tract damage to that blunting could guide treatments that rebuild reward balance.
pmc-13583858:
Dan Lewer and co-authors measure teen mental health gaps in Bradford, UK, in a 2026 study. Surveys from 2023 and 2024 covered ages twelve to fifteen. The data come from the Born in Bradford birth cohort.

Poverty is a known driver of teen mental health problems. Ethnic patterns are less clear and often debated. Validated scales measured anxiety, depression, and well-being. Loneliness and eating problems were also included in the survey. Inequalities by income and ethnicity were quantified side by side. Readers see which gaps persist in a diverse city, guiding where school and health support should land.
pmc-13584058:
Chun-Lin He and five co-authors mine United States drug harm reports for heart defects at birth, in work from twenty twenty-six. Their aim was to flag drugs whose reports link to congenital heart disease more than expected. They also mapped which defect types show up in the reports.

Reports came from the national adverse event system, spanning from twenty oh four to late twenty twenty-five. Four distinct math methods hunted for signals, with a strict correction for many tests at once. Hundreds of drugs showed some signal, and a smaller set held up as robust. The authors stress that a signal is a flag for more study, not proof a drug caused the defect.
pmc-13584158:
Kamran Arshad, Muhammad Arif, Apilak Worachartcheewan, and Dong-Jun Yu present BAN-SDBPred, a predictor that sorts DNA binding proteins into single strand and double strand binders. These proteins run key cell jobs, and lab tests to type them are slow and costly. The study came out in twenty twenty-six.

The method reads traits from two large protein language models plus a trait set built from pair energy patterns in the sequence. A sampling plan fixes the lopsided class counts. A bilinear attention network then makes the call. The authors say it beats other deep models on this task, which can aid drug search work that needs these proteins typed fast.
pmc-13584358:
Changyou Zhong and co-authors compare two planning styles for lattice radiotherapy in bulky tumors in a study from 2026. Lattice therapy plants high-dose spheres inside a tumor like seeds. When the tumor stretches far head-to-foot, standard arc plans need wide-open jaws. Wide jaws leak dose and blur the lattice pattern.

Their pipe-joint method segments the beam path lengthwise, guided by the beam's-eye view. Nineteen patients with bulky tumors were replanned four ways each. Dose maps for tumor and healthy tissue were scored side by side. Sharper longitudinal control should spare the valleys between dose peaks. Big tumors, the hardest radiotherapy cases, are exactly where such gains matter.
pmc-13584958:
Jianfeng Chen and Leyu Tao wrote this review, published in 2026. It surveys how artificial intelligence is being used to predict medication risk in older adults who take many drugs at once. Simple counts of pills and fixed rule lists miss how risk shifts for one person over time.

The review covers machine learning, deep learning, text mining, graph models, and large language models, plus the data sources behind them. It highlights uses in clinics, nurse-led programs, and care handovers between settings. The authors are candid about the weak points: models that no one can explain, patchy data, and little proof from live trials. They call for models that track risk as it changes, and for testing across many hospitals before these tools guide real prescribing.
pmc-13585158:
Gregory A. Hosler, Matthew S. Goldberg, and Etan Marks present eight hard-to-call skin cases in this 2026 series. The growths at issue are melanocytic, meaning they arise from pigment cells, and some are melanoma, a dangerous skin cancer, while others are harmless moles. A stain test called PRAME often helps, yet its readings can clash or stay unclear, leaving experts split.

Each case drew four or five separate expert opinions. The team then ran a 23-gene test, which reads the activity of a set of genes in the tissue, to see if it could tip the balance. In cases where the stain was muddy or conflicting, the gene results pushed the final call up or down in risk. The authors offer the test as a tiebreaker, not a replacement for expert review.
pmc-13585258:
Qiusu Wang presents a 2026 study on why university teachers keep using generative AI tools. The survey covered 615 teachers in Qingdao, China, and builds on the technology acceptance model, a classic frame for why people adopt tools. Wang split teachers' sense of their own AI skill into parts: basic grasp, and skill for teaching, research, and professional engagement. The analysis traced how each part feeds beliefs about ease and usefulness, and then the wish to keep using the tools.

Skill for teaching, research, and engagement each linked to seeing the tools as useful. Basic grasp linked only weakly to ease of use. Seeing the tools as useful, in turn, predicted wanting to continue, while ease showed no direct effect. Wang concludes that AI skill is not one thing. Training that shows real professional value may matter most for lasting adoption.
pmc-13585458:
Stefan Schmollinger and co-authors count the protein machines inside an alga's chloroplast across its day in a 2026 study. Modeling a cell's metabolism needs real numbers: how many copies of each complex, and in what proportions. The green alga Chlamydomonas is a favorite test bed for photosynthesis research, but its parts list was mostly relative.

The team used the total protein approach, weighing the whole protein mass of a sample to anchor absolute amounts, and cross-checked with metal and pigment measures. They computed abundances for more than seven thousand proteins, over two thousand of them at every time point of the diurnal cycle. The census covers the light reactions, photoprotection, protein housekeeping, and fat building. A counted cell can be simulated honestly.

Hannah Van Ryckel and co-authors present a 2026 study of phosphorus in tired tropical soils where iron and aluminium oxides lock the nutrient away. Farmers mix organic matter with mineral fertilizer to free it up, but results vary. The team asks what soil trait predicts how much sorption falls.

Their answer is how full the soil already is with carbon. The fuller the soil, the weaker its grip on phosphate. The effect grew stronger as soil sat after treatment. Weaker grip also meant phosphate spread further around the fertilizer spot. Past accounts blamed acidity shifts. This study puts carbon fullness at the centre, with clear advice for soil care.
pmc-13586358:
Francisco M. Nadal-Nicolás and colleagues established the thirteen-lined ground squirrel as a translational model for head-injury vision loss. Rapid head acceleration damages the optic nerve and visual system, but mice and rats, being nocturnal with rod-dominated retinas, translate poorly. The ground squirrel is diurnal, with a cone-rich retina, dense retinal ganglion cells, and an astrocyte pattern shared with primates and humans. Their 2026 study tested repeated closed-head impacts in this species.

Impacts caused lasting harm, including abnormal seasonal weight control and persistent visual dysfunction, with retinal thinning, reduced ganglion-cell function, dorsal cell loss, and late optic-nerve glial change. The authors present the squirrel as a strong animal stand-in for human head-injury vision loss, capturing systemic, behavioural, and visual effects of human closed-head injury.
pmc-13586458:
Hannah Lee and co-authors reviewed artificial intelligence for early esophageal cancer in a 2026 paper. Cancer of the esophagus often kills because it is found late. Endoscopy can catch early lesions, but tired or less practiced doctors miss some, and early growths can be subtle.

The review explains how deep learning systems now help at several steps. They flag suspicious areas during the exam, judge how deep a lesion grows, classify tiny vessel patterns, and outline tumor edges. Reported miss rates for one cancer type reach 4 to 17 percent by eye alone. The authors present these tools as support for doctors rather than replacements, with accuracy gains that could shift survival.
pmc-13586558:
Amar Shah, writing alone in 2026, traces how quality assurance in health care grew up over four decades. His article argues the topic is oddly unstudied beside its flashier sibling, quality improvement. The story starts with the first frameworks that made hospital boards answer for quality, then moves through the clinical governance systems of the 1990s, which bundled scattered duties into one structure.

Later decades taught managers that assurance alone is not enough: it must be balanced with improvement, control, and planning. A case study from an East London health trust shows the modern form, with patients leading, improvement science informing checks, and clinicians brought inside the process to cut pointless burden. Shah closes by urging the same care in documenting assurance as the field gives to improvement.
pmc-13587058:
Ramzi Ibrahim, a lone author, makes the case in a 2026 essay for teaching heart health long before hearts fail. He came home from a forum on prevention with one hard question. If artery clogging starts in childhood, why does his field spend most of its force on hearts that have already broken down?

Ibrahim notes that clogging grows in silence for decades and can be found in many adults in their forties with no signs. Care that waits for risk factors misses the chance to keep them from forming at all in youth. What harms arteries, he says, is the load of bad cholesterol held over a whole life, like pack-years for smokers. Small cuts held from a young age can push off disease for years.
pmc-13587158:
Sounira Mehri and Josef Finsterer write a 2026 letter that questions a recent case report on exercise training. The report told of a man with MELAS, a rare inherited disorder of cell energy, who regained strength after a stroke. The letter's title states its claim: one case cannot support training as therapy.

The writers ask how the stroke was told apart from stroke-like episodes, which are common in this disorder and look alike on scans. They list missing facts, such as blood pressure, heart rhythm, smoking, and clotting checks. They also note that a single case cannot rule out natural recovery as the cause. Their letter urges more care before case reports guide treatment.
