Mandy Berndt-Paetz and eight co-authors tested a light-based therapy, alone and with radiation, against bladder tumors in rats, in a 2026 study. Bladder cancer care still needs options that spare the organ. The light therapy uses a drug that turns toxic inside tumor cells when lit by near-infrared light.

In lab dishes, flat cell layers showed no added gain from pairing the two treatments, but three-dimensional tumor balls did, at every drug dose. The team then grew tumors in the bladders of rats and treated each group three times. Light therapy alone doubled survival time over no treatment. Radiation alone, and radiation before light therapy, left every rat alive at the study end point. Tissue checks backed the gains, and the authors urge further work on the pairing.
pmc-13588958:
Spine surgeon Ercan Yılmaz questions a study about back pain after scoliosis surgery in this 2026 letter. The study looked at teens whose curved spines were straightened with metal rods, some of whom also had a defect in a lower back bone. It found more pain years later when the rods reached low into the spine, and it advised stopping higher up when possible.

Yılmaz argues the result may not be the fault of the low rods. The study never reported how much pain each group had before surgery, yet pain before an operation is one of the strongest signs of pain after it. If the low-rod group hurt more from the start, the gap at follow-up would say little about rod placement. The letter asks the authors to adjust for that starting point before changing practice.
pmc-13589158:
Seven authors report a 2026 case of a rare blood cancer that grows inside blood vessels and hid as repeat strokes. The patient was a 69-year-old man with strokes of no clear cause. Many tests for clotting and cancer found nothing, and CT scans showed no masses.

A vessel flaw on a CT scan of the head and neck led to a tissue test that named the cancer. Drug treatment with the R-CHOP mix improved his nerve symptoms. A gene-based test for tiny traces of disease later came back clear, which gave the team a way to track his response.
pmc-13589258:
The nose's lining is both a sense organ and a wall against germs, and a rare brush-like cell helps run both jobs. Sai-Sai Zhang and seven co-authors broke the brush cells' taste-signaling parts in mice in 2026 and watched the wall. With the signals gone, the lining sat inflamed even at rest. Its resting stem cells woke too early and too often.

A flu hit then landed harder: more swelling, more germ-fighters, more cell death, and a slow calm-down. Stem cells rushed to rebuild and made floods of the brush kind. Sprays of the very signals that ran high in the broke lining could wake stem cells in dish-grown lining. The team read the brush cells as peacekeepers who also pace the rebuild after a hit.
pmc-13589358:
Isabel Heidrich and a team of co-authors followed tumor DNA in the blood of melanoma patients over time in a 2026 paper. Advanced melanoma is usually watched with scans that give coarse categories at long intervals. Blood-borne tumor DNA might report change sooner, but its dance with true tumor volume was poorly charted.

The team studied 42 patients on immune checkpoint drugs, with 241 blood time points. Tumor DNA levels rose across worsening scan categories and tracked measured tumor volume. They also probed how the gap between blood draw and scan affects agreement, and catalogued cases where the two disagreed. The authors argue frequent DNA sampling can sharpen real-time monitoring of treatment.
pmc-13589658:
Dilek Yildirim and co-authors build and test a scale that asks cancer patients how they view AI in their care. AI tools are now common in cancer care, and nurses guide patients in their use. Older scales were made for health care in general and miss the trust and work issues of cancer care. The team wrote a pool of items, had experts judge them, and gave the scale to 382 adult patients.

The final scale has 33 items in three groups. One group covers knowledge, awareness, and trust in the tools. The other two cover felt benefit and readiness to accept and use them. Checks showed a strong fit and very high scores for how well the items hang together. Felt benefit partly linked knowledge to readiness to use the tools.
pmc-13590258:
Pim-1 is a protein that helps some cancer cells grow, and blocking it is a goal for new drug design. Rufaida Al Zoubi and co-authors, writing in 2026, searched for fresh compounds that can block this protein. They screened close to nine hundred thousand compounds on the computer, then tested six of them in the lab.

One tested compound, built on a shape not reported for this target before, blocked Pim-1 at a modest strength. Further computer work showed why some high-scoring compounds failed in the lab: their flat shapes were hard to reach in real terms of energy. The active compound also formed two key links with parts of the protein. The hit gives drug designers a new starting shape to improve.
pmc-13590458:
Pregnancy with a heart defect that has already flipped blood flow the wrong way is one of the riskiest states in medicine. One young woman's case ended far better than the odds suggest. Mohamed Mukhtar Mohamed and co-authors report her care in a 2026 paper with a review of past cases. She arrived at thirty-four weeks, breathless and swollen, with blood oxygen far below normal.

Heart scans showed large holes between the chambers and a great vessel rising mostly from the wrong side, though key details could not be pinned down with the tools at hand. Labor was induced, and she delivered a live baby within hours. Blood loss after birth was replaced, and she left the hospital a week later, stable. The authors stress the case proves survival is possible, not that the path is safe.
pmc-13590958:
Randall Nett and co-authors argue in a 2026 paper that West Nile virus needs stronger prevention in the United States and beyond. Since the virus arrived in 1999, it has settled in and causes about thirteen hundred severe brain cases and one hundred thirty deaths each year. Current defense rests on personal habits and mosquito control, which have not cut cases enough.

The authors call for added tools, such as a human vaccine and lab made antibodies for people at high risk. Faster detection of infection also matters, they say. They urge partners in government, universities, and industry to work together so proven and new measures reach people. Readers get a concise case for widening the fight beyond spray and sleeves.
pmc-13591158:
Paola Ruška and five colleagues published a children's bowel study in two thousand twenty-six on drug choices for ulcerative colitis. When the standard drug mesalazine fails, doctors must pick the next step. One older option, sulfasalazine, is cheap but less often used in children.

The team reviewed records of children diagnosed over a decade who relapsed on mesalazine alone. Ninety-nine children qualified; about a third switched to sulfasalazine. The switch worked for four in five of them, and over half stayed relapse-free for a year. Time without relapse did not differ clearly among the three drug paths compared. Children switched to sulfasalazine had wider disease than those staying on mesalazine. The authors call the switch a fair option for mild to moderate cases.
pmc-13591658:
A steady rhythm in brain waves, the alpha peak, has been proposed as a marker of how strongly a person feels pain. Carolina Ceruti and co-authors test whether reward and punishment settings shift that rhythm, in a 2026 study. Twenty-nine healthy volunteers did a hearing task while pressure pain was applied.

Feedback on each answer set the context: errors could bring relief or a stronger squeeze, while pain itself was held matched. Brain waves were recorded throughout, and the alpha peak was read at front, central, and back sites. The peak ran lower after errors in the reward setting than after correct answers in the punishment setting. The work warns that context, not pain alone, shapes this proposed marker.
pmc-13591858:
Eye drops that relax the eye's focusing muscle are used before some eye exams, but they might change corneal measurements. Navid Elmi Sadr, Leila Ghiasian, Yasaman Hadi, and Ramyar Hariri tested that question in 2026 in older patients with type 2 diabetes who also had age-related focusing loss. Eighty-eight eyes were measured with an automatic device before and after drops, at two dose strengths.

Corneal power, astigmatism, and the white-to-white width of the cornea barely changed after the drops. None of the changes reached statistical significance at either dose. The authors conclude that such measurements can be taken reliably after the drops are given, which simplifies exam flow for this patient group.
pmc-13592358:
Pramathes Das Mahapatra and co-authors review whether antioxidants can aid fertility in women with a common hormone disorder. Their 2026 review deals with a syndrome of ovaries and metabolism that often blocks conception. Oxidative stress in the ovary is thought to harm egg quality. Four antioxidants get focus: a mitochondrial cofactor, a sulfur compound, melatonin, and a pigment from algae. Trials from 1990 to 2024 were searched in three databases.

Of 198 records screened, twenty eight studies qualified. Reviews, animal work, and duplicates were shut out. The cofactor improved cell energy function and cut oxidative stress in the reports. It was also tied to higher pregnancy rates and better insulin response. The authors weigh the other three agents on the same terms. They present the set as add on options beside standard fertility care, with evidence still uneven.
pmc-13592458:
Clarissa Dine leads a protocol for a feasibility study on spotting depression relapse early with a smart ring. Magnetic brain stimulation can lift treatment resistant depression, yet many who improve slip back within a year, and no firm warning marker exists. Their pilot will enroll 25 outpatients at two Ontario hospitals. Each will wear an Oura ring through treatment and six months of follow up, with mood, anxiety, sleep, and well being scales taken at set points.

Success will be judged on recruitment, ring adherence, retention, missing data, and ease of use. Exploratory checks will probe whether ring derived signals track treatment response or herald relapse. Dine and the team stress the work is a groundwork step toward larger relapse prevention trials.
pmc-13593558:
Robert H. Anderson, Richard Sutton, and Damian Sanchez Quintana dispute a claim about where a pacing lead was placed in the atrium, arguing from the anatomy itself. In their 2026 commentary they contend the images in the report show the lead sitting in the front wall of the right atrium. It is not in the septum between the atria, as the report's authors suggested.

They follow the path a signal would take from that site. It runs through a recess of the right atrial appendage and then along a bundle between the atria before reaching the left atrial walls. Neither structure belongs to the atrial septum, they point out. Their message is practical: work on new ways to pace the left atrium will only succeed if the underlying anatomy is described correctly.
pmc-13593858:
Aimei Feng and co-authors map polyamine states in acute myeloid leukemia in a 2026 study. Polyamines feed cell growth, and leukemias lean on that feed, yet how the lean spreads across cell kinds was unclear. The team joined single cell reads from 41 cases with bulk profiles from 712 patients.

A 76 gene score showed polyamine action richest in blast cells, tied to stem like traits, fast growth, and weak maturing. Two subtypes split by metabolic and immune marks. A survival model sorted patients by risk with fair strength. One gene, CCT6A, ran high and held the polyamine pool in check in lab tests.
pmc-13594258:
Qingwu Du and thirteen co-authors report a 2026 study on why small cell lung cancer shrugs off immune therapy. This fast cancer builds a suppressive shield of immune cells around itself. Working with mouse tumors and patient samples, the team traced the shield to a shipping protein that moves cargo out of the cell nucleus.

That shipper expels a second protein, which then orders the shredding of a defender that would raise an immune alarm call. With the call silenced, guard cells drift into a state that blinds tumor cells to attack. Blocking the shipper restored the alarm, curbed the guard drift, and made a standard immune drug work far better in mice. The authors propose the pair as a joint drug target.
pmc-13594358:
Lees and thirteen co-authors describe a mouth condition linked to Crohn's disease in this two thousand twenty-six study. Orofacial granulomatosis causes swollen lips and mouth inflammation, and it often travels with Crohn's, yet its pattern and best treatments were poorly mapped.

Gathering one hundred seventeen patients from two British centers, the team compared them with a large Crohn's control group. The mouth condition came with earlier diagnosis, more disease spanning the ileum and colon, and more perianal and upper gut involvement. Common biologic drugs brought remission in roughly half to three-fifths of patients, often needing dose increases. Newer drug classes helped about half of those who had already failed biologics. The cohort is the largest yet for this condition.
pmc-13594458:
Yohei Kikuchi and colleagues asked whether electrical signals measured before implanting an atrial leadless pacemaker predict pacing thresholds three months later. Thirty-nine consecutive patients received the Aveir AR device at one Japanese hospital between February and September 2025, mostly as part of dual-chamber systems. The primary outcome was atrial capture threshold at three months.

Premapping pacing threshold tracked with the three-month threshold, but the link was confounded by operator-driven site selection and was not an independent predictor. Waveform measures such as amplitude, current of injury, and voltage change added no further discrimination. Atrial tissue and anchoring differ enough from ventricular pacing that dedicated prospective markers are needed.
pmc-13594658:
A gentle exercise test on a treadmill might help sort horses with asthma from healthy ones without invasive sampling, and a field study tested that hope. Lia Meiseberg and co-authors ran the study in this 2026 paper. Twenty-six privately owned leisure horses of mixed breeds took part.

Eight horses were healthy, and the rest had mild, moderate, or severe asthma judged by history, exam, and lung wash results. All took the submaximal exercise test, and its measures were compared across the groups. Leisure horses are rarely tested like racehorses, so a simple field tool has real value for everyday vets. The study checks whether test variables separate the severity bands cleanly enough to guide treatment.
pmc-13594758:
Sayaka Nishihara and co-authors review how patients take part in preventing falls in hospital in a 2026 paper. Falls are a major safety risk for inpatients worldwide. Staff-led programs dominate, yet patients themselves can own part of the effort, and how that sharing is spread across the care process was unclear.

The review sorts patient involvement into three levels, from passive receipt of advice to fully self-led choices. It then tracks four phases, from grasping one's risk to managing it day by day. Involvement clustered in the early phases, with shared choices reached at times. Later phases, such as setting goals, drew far less patient ownership. The authors note the roles of family, clear information, and mental demands in closing that gap.
pmc-13594858:
Alexandra Power-Hays and co-authors check measles shield levels after shots in children with sickle cell anemia on a common drug, in a study from two thousand twenty-six. Records came from a past trial of the blood disease. Shield was judged by a set antibody line after each of two doses.

Alice Doubinsky and five colleagues report a case of probable Alport syndrome passed down in a dominant pattern. Alport syndrome harms the kidney's filtering membrane and stems from faults in collagen genes. Dominant forms are often missed because their signs stay mild and varied.

Though formally of uncertain meaning, the variant fits her picture and family history well.

İbrahim Yıldız and co-authors draft a risk-based playbook for stage III lung cancer in the immunotherapy era, in a 2026 review. Eight authors present a systematic review dated two thousand twenty-six on pregnancy in women with complete heart block. The authors pooled twelve studies covering two hundred ninety-four pregnancies in two hundred twenty women. Two-thirds received temporary or permanent pacing during pregnancy. pmc-13595558:
Erica Nerbonne, Scott Magelssen, and Wolfgang Muhlhofer describe a teaching partnership where drama students play patients for neurology trainees, in a 2026 paper. Over two and a half years, forty-one residents ran forty simulations with thirty-two drama students as patients and family members. Residents and faculty rated the sessions highly, with nearly all faculty recommending them. Months later, most residents reported meeting real cases that resembled a simulation, and felt readier to counsel patients and read diagnostics. The authors present the model as a durable, mutually beneficial curriculum worth copying.
pmc-13596458:

Meridiana Dodaj and co-authors report a 67-year-old man whose atypical carcinoid tumor, a slow neuroendocrine cancer of the lung, returned beneath his vocal cords almost twenty years after the original surgery. pmc-13597358:
Xinchao Jiang and eight co-authors tracked in 2026 what happens in the gut after fecal transplants in teenagers with obesity. Changes faded fast. Donor strains settled only briefly, the teens' own core microbes bounced back, and the virus community wobbled only in the short term. How much rebuilding happened depended on the donor. The authors urge smarter donor choice and personal matching over one-size treatment.

Nikolay Shakhpazyan and co-authors study immune patterns in colorectal cancer in a 2026 paper. Most past work counts immune cells in tissue or checks fixed inflammation signals. pmc-13597658:
A daughter's vaginal microbe mix resembles her mother's more than a stranger's, a Belgian citizen-science study finds. pmc-13597758:
Lauren Borges, Jacob Farnsworth, Sean Barnes, and Robyn Walser wrote a 2026 paper on moral injury and a therapy called acceptance and commitment therapy. Moral injury is the deep distress that can follow acts that clash with a person's values. It is common in soldiers and health workers.

pmc-13598158:
Lorenzo Testa and co-authors present a method for counting protein forms in a 2026 paper. One gene can make several versions of a protein, called isoforms, and each can act in a unlike way. Their Bayesian method, PAQu, joins peptide data with transcript data to estimate each form. It also gives a measure of doubt and a firm way to test ideas. In tests it beat rival methods. Applied to schizophrenia data, it found one immune protein form raised while a close form was not.
pmc-13598958:
Shuo Yang, Xi-Can Liu, and Jing Chen present a 2026 review on why a chronic dizziness disorder refuses to fade. pmc-13599158:
Anne-S. Helvik and three colleagues present a 2026 systematic review asking how often people with dementia who live at home are in pain. Reports of any pain in the past month ranged from 36 to 76 percent. Studies used very different definitions and rating tools, which made direct comparison hard. pmc-13599258:
Furkan Çiftci and co-authors compare eye measures in patients with lichen planus, a skin and mouth rash state, against healthy peers, in a study from 2026. Whether the state touches the eye was little charted.

pmc-13599458:
Esraa Mohamed and co-authors test leaf extracts from a mahogany tree in a 2026 paper. The tree, Khaya senegalensis, was grown with different waters and fertilisers, including farm drainage water that is often reused in dry regions. The team asked whether its leaves could fight plant fungi.

pmc-13599858:
Chryssa Grylli and nine colleagues study how the COVID-19 pandemic changed referrals for suspected child abuse at a forensic exam center in Vienna. During the pandemic, referrals for suspected physical abuse fell by about fifty-five percent. Referrals for sexual abuse held steady. After the pandemic, physical abuse reports went back to their old level. But suspected sexual abuse cases rose, and the victims' median age climbed over time. The need for mental health support jumped during the pandemic and stayed high. The authors say a plain return to normal is not likely.
pmc-13600158:
Grace Malheiro and co-authors review what is known about watching hearing health in adults who live with diabetes. pmc-13618858:

pmc-13621558:

pmc-13623258:

pmc-13631958:

pmc-13632658:

pmc-13632758:

pmc-13634058:

Pilot interviews, read through a human-factors framework, supplied the friction points the stopwatch missed. The authors judge supervised night delivery feasible.
pmc-13634158:
Shelja Mohan and co-authors presented a 2026 case series on odd root canal shapes in lower molars. Mandibular molars often hide complex canal anatomy, which makes root canal treatment hard. Precise access, cleaning, shaping, and three-dimensional filling are all needed for success. The report covers three unusual cases with rare canal configurations.

Each case was diagnosed with cone beam computed tomography, a 3D imaging method. Sonic activation was used to disinfect the canals. The authors stress that careful imaging and canal identification make such rare anatomy treatable. Because these configurations are rarely documented, the series adds practical guidance for dentists facing similar teeth. It shows how modern imaging changes the odds in difficult endodontic work.
pmc-13634458:
Teratomas are odd tumors that can contain fat, hair, and even teeth, and they almost never start in the adrenal gland. Muhammad Rifki Setiawan, Johan Renaldo, and Wahjoe Djatisoesanto report a 37-year-old woman with a very large one above her right kidney. She had lived with on-and-off flank and stomach discomfort for seventeen years, with bloating that had lately worsened.

Scans showed the mass held fat and calcified parts and had grown greatly since imaging seventeen years earlier. Surgeons removed the whole adrenal gland in an open operation without complications. Lab study of the tissue confirmed a mature cystic teratoma with no cancerous elements. The authors stress how slowly such a tumor can grow. They urge doctors to keep it in mind for long-standing masses in that spot.
pmc-13635658:
Kaoyan Feng and co-authors report a 2026 lab study on a protein called RNF113A and its role in colorectal cancer spread. The protein is found at higher levels in this cancer. The team asked whether it acts on a second protein, SNIP1, which normally holds back a growth signal pathway tied to how the disease advances.

Using patient tissue samples and cancer cells in dishes, the team found that high RNF113A went with low SNIP1. Extra RNF113A helped cells grow in colonies and move, while cutting it back raised SNIP1 levels. Tests showed the first protein tags the second one for breakdown. The authors name RNF113A as a possible drug target, while noting that more proof is still needed.
pmc-13635858:
Soawapak Hinjoy and eight colleagues adapted a United States disease-ranking tool for province-level use in Thailand. The tool helps governments rank animal-to-human health threats under the One Health idea, which treats human, animal, and environmental health as one system. National rankings can miss local realities. The team ran four-day participatory workshops in two provinces during 2025, each drawing about seventy people from health, farming, environment, government, and community groups.

The provinces ranked threats quite differently because they weighted the criteria differently. One province prized biomedical severity and cross-sector impact, putting emerging infections and rabies on top. The other prized workable governance, so air pollution, open waste burning, stray dogs, farm chemicals, and climate disasters led its list. The authors conclude that community-led adaptation makes rankings legitimate and useful. Local lists, they argue, strengthen early warning and prevention better than a single national table.
pmc-13637058:
Saadat and a large team combine two molecular layers in this 2026 study of Wilms tumour, the most common childhood kidney cancer, which arises from derailed kidney development. They profiled DNA methylation, chemical tags that switch genes off, alongside gene activity in 27 primary tumours and matched healthy kidney tissue from the same children.

Roughly 9,000 methylation sites split tumour from normal tissue and from other childhood cancers, forming a tumour-specific signature. Cases clustered into three methylation groups matching gene-expression subtypes with different immune landscapes and predicted drug responses, one favoring paclitaxel and another doxorubicin in the models. More than 900 genes sat under such control in the combined analysis. Tumours with a methylation gain at the classic 11p15.5 imprinted locus showed the deepest epigenetic damage, while shrinking tumours with a normal locus were least affected.
pmc-13639158:
Al Jadeedi and co-authors ask which patients who carry drug-proof germs on or in the body go on to get a blood infection from those same germs. Their study compares patients who did get such an infection with similar patients who did not. The setting is a teaching hospital context in Oman.

Only a small share of carriers, about six in a hundred, went on to a blood infection from the germ they carried. Some patients carried two or more drug-proof germs at once. When blood infections did occur, the germ matched the carried one in just under half of cases. Care in an intensive care unit and having a tube in a large vein stood out as risk factors. The findings help staff watch the carriers most at risk.
pmc-13639558:
Shota Miyakuni maps the published evidence on therapeutic software in Japan in a 2026 scoping review. Such software, including digital therapeutics and software classed as a medical device, delivers treatment through apps, yet the Japanese study record sits scattered across diseases and designs.

Searching PubMed records from 2015 to early 2026, the author sorted each publication by how rigorous its evaluation was and how clinical its main outcome was. The resulting maturity map shows where solid trial evidence exists and where only early feasibility work has appeared. The snapshot gives developers and regulators a shared picture of remaining gaps.
pmc-13641458:
Natalia-Guillemina Target and five colleagues present a 2026 study comparing physical activity in short daily home dialysis against standard in-center hemodialysis. Dialysis for kidney failure burdens daily life heavily, and treatment setting and schedule may change how active patients can stay.

The international prospective study enrolled patients in French and Belgian centers between late 2018 and mid 2021, with each person's dialysis route chosen outside the study. Alongside activity, the researchers tracked treatment effectiveness, tolerance, acceptability, and side effects. The design reflects a patient-centered view that the best dialysis plan should fit individual lives, not only lab targets.
pmc-13642458:
Two artery-blocking treatments for liver cancer are compared head to head by Mosconi and colleagues. Hepatocellular carcinoma that cannot be removed by surgery is often treated through the arteries feeding the tumour. Treatment either blocks blood flow alone or blocks flow while releasing chemotherapy from drug-loaded microspheres. The team ran a multicentre randomised trial in 111 patients with early or intermediate unresectable disease, testing whether plain embolisation was non-inferior to the drug-loaded approach.

Time until the disease progressed was similar in both arms, at roughly eight months, and formal equivalence testing confirmed the treatments matched within the preset margin. Overall survival, tumour response, severe side effects, and hospital stay also showed no meaningful difference between the groups. Mosconi and colleagues conclude that plain embolisation performs comparably for these patients, which matters because simpler treatment may ease cost and complexity without sacrificing outcomes.
pmc-13643458:
MHD Osama Srour and five colleagues report a 2026 project to cut overuse of heart rhythm monitors in hospital wards. Extra days on a monitor raise costs and alarm fatigue. They bring no clear gain for the patient.

At their hospital, staff ran talks and put up posters based on the 2017 heart group rules. They then compared early 2025 with late 2025. Mean monitor time per patient fell by about a fifth. Doctors also knew the rules far better and scored much higher on case questions. The team says steady teaching plus checks in the record system could lock in the gains.
pmc-13644758:
Geng, Li, Zhang, Hou, and Lin build a low-cost camera sensor that sees in a band of infrared light tied to chemical traces. Light in this band reveals the marks of bonds found in pollutants and waste. Cameras that see it now rely on pricey crystals that are hard to merge with standard chips.

Their sensor uses carbon-based materials laid down from solution, a cheap coating method. It is paired with thin-film switches on the same base to form an imager. The materials absorb far into the infrared band and waste little of the signal. The sensor responds across a wide span, from near visible light to deep infrared. A cheap imager of this kind could bring chemical-spotting cameras to farms, dumps, and water checks.
pmc-13645558:
Hua Chen and seven colleagues report a 2026 cross-sectional survey of older patients with osteoporosis in Henan Province, China, about how well patients grasp their own fall risk. Staff at two campuses of a bone specialty hospital collected 294 valid questionnaires. Patients answered scales on fall awareness, daily function, frailty, mood, and felt social support. The team then looked for factors tied to awareness scores.

Awareness of fall risk differed across the scale's dimensions and linked with many factors at once. Age, sex, marital status, household income, and living alone all played a part. Fall prevention teaching, daily function, depression, and social support also mattered, and together the factors explained a large share of the score spread. The authors suggest nurses shape fall prevention work around these patient traits. Better awareness, they argue, could cut fall injuries in this group.
pmc-13647058:
Yan Wang and co-authors present a 2026 basin-wide study of fish variety in the Nu-Salween River, one of Asia's last big free-flowing rivers. Nearly twenty-seven thousand place records cover 445 native fish kinds across 382 sub-basins. The team mapped four faces of variety: kind counts, family-tree depth, trait spread, and how much each place holds found nowhere else. Each face peaked twice along the river's length, a twin-hump pattern no one had called before.

Climate and lay of the land drove the pattern most. Warmth, height, and distance from the mouth shaped kind counts and tree depth. Trait spread rose with warmth and rain. The report also weighs threats pressing the basin. Free-flowing status is the asset to guard, the authors imply.
pmc-13648358:
Elaida D Dimwamwa, Nelson H Chang, Christian Waiblinger, and Garrett B Stanley watch a feedback layer of the cortex at work in awake mice. Layer 6 corticothalamic neurons send heavy input to the thalamus, the brain's sensory gate, and are cast as gain knobs for incoming signals. Most evidence for that role came from anesthetized animals. Their 2026 study uses new tools to identify these neurons precisely during live recordings in awake, behaving mice. It shows how the neurons engage during real touch sensation.

Awake data matter because anesthesia itself retunes the circuits under study. A feedback knob that behaves one way asleep and another awake changes theories of perception. The authors work in the mouse touch system. Their findings refine the picture of cortex talking back to its own gatekeeper. The question could only be asked once the tools improved.
pmc-13648958:
Roslyn Harold and co-authors run a pilot study on brain chemistry and thinking in women who carry a fragile X gene variant in a 2026 paper. The variant raises risk across mental health, movement, and fertility. What sits between the gene and those outcomes is unclear.

Fifteen carriers and fifteen matched non-carriers took part. A brain scan method measured GABA, a calming chemical, in the cerebellum. Thinking was tested with a brain-wave marker of error spotting and standard paper tests. Carriers showed an odd scalp pattern for the error signal. In non-carriers, the error signal tied to GABA levels and test scores; in carriers it did not. The break hints the variant rewires the error network.
pmc-13649458:
Carolina Valle and seven colleagues tested whether the main scent compounds in rosemary oil act on the brain's serotonin transporter, a key target of antidepressant drugs. Rosemary oil has shown calming and mood-lifting effects in past work, but the molecular route was unknown.

Computer models placed all three compounds, pinene, camphor, and cineole, into both binding pockets of the transporter. Lab tests then showed each compound pushed a labelled drug off the transporter, with pinene the strongest. In living cells, all three partly slowed serotonin uptake, even at high doses, but never blocked it fully. The authors propose these scents as mild, partial blockers that may help explain rosemary's effects.
pmc-13649558:
Jesper Qvist Thomassen and a very large team split Alzheimer's genetics by APOE type in a 2026 study. The APOE gene's variants remain the strongest known genetic risk for late-onset Alzheimer's. The risk-raising form also blunts response to new amyloid drugs and raises their side effects, yet its mechanism stays murky.

Genome-wide scans were run separately for carriers and non-carriers of each key variant. The split design aims to expose risk genes that act only in one genetic setting. Early named loci include genes tied to blood pressure control and sugar transport. The authors hope such context-specific genes explain how the main risk variant tilts the brain toward disease.
pmc-13650558:
Zemin Qing and thirteen colleagues build a framework that connects autism genetics to behavior across three layers of biology. Autism varies widely. Its syndromic forms are tied to a known genetic condition, while non-syndromic forms may share some mechanisms while differing in others, a puzzle the review tackles by comparing both groups.

The first layer lists gene functions, the second groups them into core pathways, and the third maps onto clinical traits. Genes range from local parts of the synapse, the junction between nerve cells, to global controllers that repackage DNA and switch whole gene programs. Chromatin control and synapse building recur as shared ground, while each subgroup also carries enriched factors of its own that ripple into circuit-level integration problems. The authors offer the hierarchy to guide biomarker hunting and to sort patients by biology rather than behavior alone.
pmc-13651458:
Jaume Noguera-Gómez and three co-authors build a field-diagnostic method that watches outdoor perovskite solar cells with cameras and electronics at once, to separate passing weather effects from genuine, irreversible failure. Perovskites are efficient but fragile, and ordinary output records blur reversible daily and seasonal swings into permanent decline.

Encapsulated cells were monitored in Alpine and Mediterranean climates with matched electrical, spectral, temperature, humidity, and color image streams. Using two healthy reference cells to cancel the shared environmental response exposed four persistent failures at the Alpine site, while the winter slump of the reference cells themselves reversed with the season. Color changes sometimes came days before electrical ones, yet the audit showed the lead depended on the marker chosen and was not unique to failing cells. At the Mediterranean site the timing did not reproduce. A hidden test confirmed the cameras read surface wetness and thaw reliably.
pmc-13651558:
Ignacio Silva-Llanes and seven co-authors test whether high blood pressure worsens Parkinson-type brain damage in mice, a plausible fear since vascular disease and inflammation travel as a pair in aging brains. Their model forces mouse brains to make too much alpha-synuclein, the protein that clumps in Parkinson's disease, inside the substantia nigra on one side.

Chronic infusion of angiotensin II produced hypertension, yet neuron loss in the dopamine system matched normotensive animals exactly. Support-cell activation in astrocytes and microglia also refused to budge. The inflammatory gene program switched on by the protein, including the inflammasome machinery that matures inflammatory signals, ran no hotter under hypertension. The pyroptosis executioner protein rose where the protein was made in excess, mainly inside microglia, whatever the blood pressure. The authors conclude that synuclein pathology drives this inflammation, and that hypertension may need aging or other vascular partners to matter.
pmc-13652358:
Alexander Muacevic and four colleagues describe a difficult diagnosis of DRESS syndrome, a severe drug reaction, in a man being treated for a bone infection in his foot. The patient, a man in his thirties with major burn history and bipolar disorder, had failed home antibiotic infusions and was admitted for stronger treatment. On the fourth hospital day he developed a spreading rash, rising liver enzymes, and high eosinophil counts.

His medication list made the culprit hard to pin down, since it included two psychiatric drugs and two antibiotics at once. The team stopped the suspected drugs, started high-dose steroids with a long taper, and gave N-acetylcysteine to protect the liver. DRESS can turn fatal when recognition comes late. The case shows how a new rash plus blood changes in a patient on many drugs should trigger fast action even before every test returns.
pmc-13652458:
Rasheed Altwiher and five co-authors report a grave surgical emergency in this 2026 case report. A forty-three-year-old man had long-standing scarring of the liver's portal area from schistosomiasis, a parasitic disease, which had swollen his spleen and raised pressure in the veins of his gut. A clot then formed in those veins, starving part of his small bowel of blood.

At emergency surgery, the team freed the trapped bowel by cutting dense adhesions, and the bowel segment survived in full. In the same course they removed the spleen and cut the veins feeding dangerous swollen vessels, easing the pressure at its root. The belly was left partly open for two days, then checked again and closed. A leak from the pancreas healed without more surgery, and the patient recovered fully.
pmc-13652658:
Alexander Muacevic and eight colleagues report a case where a large abdominal mass in a teenage girl turned out to be something other than what scans suggested. Imaging pointed to a tumor of the mesentery, the tissue that supports the intestines. She had arrived at the emergency department with acute abdominal pain, and the uncertain diagnosis led the team to operate and look directly.

During surgery the mass proved to be a mature ovarian teratoma, the most common benign germ cell tumor of the ovary, and the surgeons removed it completely. Lab examination of the tissue confirmed the finding. Teratomas usually affect women of reproductive age and can present in misleading ways. The report reminds clinicians that a confident scan reading can still be wrong, with surgical exploration sometimes the only route to the right answer.
pmc-13653658:
Quanlong Lu and co-authors present a 2026 study that builds a risk chart for high grade vaginal cell change. The condition lacks clear signs and has no routine screening path, so diagnosis often lags. The team mined a large colposcopy population for its trait pattern.

Records covered 3,259 women seen at one center from 2012 to 2024. Of those, 1,192 women had the high grade change. Older age, HPV infection, worse cell test results, and paired cervix or vulva lesions ran higher in that group. Five HPV types led the list. A chart built from ten firm predictors was checked in training and validation sets for accuracy and clinical use.
pmc-13654158:
Yanni Yang and four co-authors study in 2026 how to check the salivary glands of thyroid cancer patients treated with radioactive iodine. The treatment, given after surgery, lowers the chance of the cancer returning, but the radioactive iodine also gathers in the saliva glands and can damage them.

The team combined dynamic gland imaging, which watches the glands work over time, with a fused tomosynthesis view for sharper anatomy. Together the scans measure both shape and function without invasive tests. Tracking gland damage early matters, since dry mouth and dental trouble follow when saliva fails.
pmc-13654358:
Irene Li Peng Ooi and co-authors weigh whether gene-guided statin use pays off for heart disease prevention in Singapore. Some people at mid-level risk miss statin therapy today despite high genetic risk. A polygenic score sums many small gene effects into one risk number. Their 2026 model followed forty-five-year-olds at intermediate risk and compared standard checks with gene-guided ones over up to forty years.

Gene-guided care was not worth its cost over short spans. From thirty years on, it turned cost-effective at the local pay threshold, as avoided heart events piled up. A probability check put the chance near fifty-four percent. The authors frame genes as a long-game tool for prevention.
pmc-13657758:
Olufenwa Milhouse, Paige Bird, and Denis Mesa Cruz ask if social media finds real ills in men or makes patients of the well, in work dated 2026. A young man sure he has low testosterone opens the piece. Hours of forum posts had set his mind before the visit. He came for a yes, not a workup. Such visits grow common as health feeds reach men first.

Feeds broke old silence and shame around men's ills, a real gain. They also sell plain traits as disease and strain the doctor bond. The piece weighs both sides and their clinic fall-out.
pmc-13658258:
Eve Piekarski and co-authors tell of a rare side sign in a gut nerve tumor: a vast clot-cell heap with no blood ill. The study appeared in 2026. Such tumors oft bring a flush tale, yet clot-cell heaps as a side sign are rare. A late-50s wife came with weight loss and sky-high cell counts.

Scans showed spread to liver and bone, and a gut scope found the source tumor. No blood ill bared the heap's cause, so the tumor was cast as its source. A cold drug held the ill at first, then liver growth came with worse counts. A tag-drug run then set counts to the sound band in two months, held for a year and a half.
pmc-13659558:
Chunjie Li and Kian-Huat Lim write an editorial on a pancreatic cancer trial in a 2026 piece. Pancreatic cancer is among the most deadly cancers, with gains tied mostly to better drug care. Giving drugs before surgery has grown over the past decade for operable cases. Early spread, hard surgery, and weak recovery after surgery all drive that shift.

The trial compared two drug plans given before surgery across many centers. One plan used a strong drug mix alone for a set number of rounds. The other paired a single drug with radiation, then more drug rounds after surgery. The editors say the head to head data force a fresh look at how to time care around surgery.
pmc-13660558:
Yoko Tominaga and co-authors map how bisphenol A and its cousins disturb signaling in the brain's memory center, pixel by pixel. Such chemicals may nudge neural circuits in subtle, spread-out ways that single-point measures miss. The team built an imaging pipeline around voltage-sensitive dyes in mouse hippocampal slices.

Stimulus-evoked glow is turned into normalized maps, averaged within anatomical regions, and compared between control and dosed tissue pixel by pixel. Two relatives of BPA are run through the same pipeline. The maps show where each compound strengthens or dampens circuit responses, a spatial fingerprint that could separate safer substitutes from regrettable ones.
pmc-13661758:
Lauren Lynn and co-authors pair two enzymes that together free far more cellulose nanocrystals from plant fiber than either can alone, in a 2026 study. One enzyme here nicks the fiber surface by oxidation while the other, an endoglucanase, cuts chains from inside. Alone, the first freed no crystals and the second only a few.

Together they raised crystal yields by up to 81 percent beyond simple addition. Tuning their ratio chose between making crystals and making sugars. The surface enzyme also opened the fiber so a third enzyme could bind better. The work sketches a greener route to the nanomaterial.
pmc-13662458:
For skin cancers that are not melanoma, a treatment that lays radiation right on the skin can spare surgery on delicate sites. They review the traits that bend the dose: skin curve, target depth, pads, and air gaps.

Layered and patterned setups can cover the target while cooling hot spots at the surface, they report. Newer dose math handles mixed tissue better than the older standard, and printed guides shaped to the patient can sharpen fit. The authors stress that a gentle treatment still needs exact planning. Their tips aim at safer, steadier care.
pmc-13668958:
Zebo Kudratova and co-authors comment on how aging studies measure body function, in a 2026 paper. Population aging is speeding up worldwide, so aging well is a public health priority. A study by Zhuang and Gao linked average grip strength over time to aging well in three global cohorts. The multi-cohort design gives useful cross-country insight.

Kudratova and co-authors raise several cautions about the methods used. Grip strength alone may miss other drivers of function, such as standing up from a chair. Self-reported disease can bias results, and cohort gaps in timing add more risk. A thinking score cut-off set inside each cohort also hampers fair comparison. The paper urges stronger designs for future multi-cohort work.
pmc-13669358:
Natasha Lie and co-authors trace genes behind a deadly child malnutrition form in this 2026 study. The edematous form, marked by swelling, differs from plain wasting and still kills many children under five. Faulty one-carbon metabolism, a folate-linked chemical web, is a suspect.

Data from Jamaica and Malawi tied six gene spots to the swelling form. Four spots touch the web's core chemistry, and three also moved related blood compounds in gene-based tests. Together the spots linked strongly to the disease. Population patterns pointed to shared East African roots and past selection. The authors say the finds strengthen the metabolism case.
pmc-13669558:
Zhe Wang and co-authors teach a model to predict handedness outcomes in a key reaction. Their 2026 paper studies iridium-led asymmetric C-H borylation, a route to prized boron compounds. Guessing which mirror form a catalyst will favor is hard, since many parts interact. Knowledge about the process lies scattered across papers.

Their model reads both molecule shapes and the literature itself. A graph encoder handles catalyst, substrate, and product in three dimensions. A language model pulls atom-level notes from source papers as extra input. Trained on 800 reported reactions, the model beat standard rivals on held-out tests. Cutting the literature notes hurt it in set ways, which shows they carry real signal. The team then screened about 100,000 pairs for fresh candidates.
pmc-13669758:

In practice, patients often fast far longer, which adds thirst and discomfort. Their unit handed out fasting cards that told patients to drink until called.

After the change, most patients knew they were allowed to drink before sedation. Those who knew fasted for about an hour, far less than uninformed patients. They also drank more that morning and felt less thirst on the day. More of them took their morning medicine as well, the team reports.
pmc-13670358:
Yu Qin and five co-authors checked in 2026 how trustworthy a timed backward walking test is for people after stroke. Walking backward taxes balance and control in ways forward walking does not. Stroke survivors finished far more slowly than healthy adults, and a cut-off near seven seconds separated the groups well. Repeat and rater agreement were all excellent. Times tracked closely with mobility and gait speed, and moderately with balance and leg strength. The smallest real change was about four and a half seconds. The authors offer the test as a sound partner to forward gait checks.
pmc-13671258:
The flowers of Cassia alata, a plant known for useful compounds in its leaves, get their first close chemical look in a 2026 study by Adonai Yin-Anaab Kunduzore and co-authors. The team made extracts from the flowers with water and two alcohol mixes, then profiled what each extract held.

Using liquid chromatography with high-resolution mass spectrometry, they tentatively named 42 compounds, mostly flavonoids and phenolic acids. A standard lab test then measured how well each extract could calm free radicals, the unstable molecules tied to cell damage. The work suggests the flowers may be an untapped source of antioxidants for foods or supplements, though the findings rest on lab tests rather than trials in people.
pmc-13673058:

Blood samples from stroke patients held more of these parcels than samples from healthy people, and the same rise appeared in mouse brains. Inside vessel cells, circMagi1 helped a partner protein mark a repair protein, ANXA2, for destruction, which held back new vessel growth. In mice, timed treatments that blocked parts of this chain improved recovery, with a delayed second treatment working best in their tests.
pmc-13674858:
Bacteria growing in narrow channels organize themselves into lanes, and Ing Xhu Lim and co-authors ask how cell shape steers that order. In earlier experiments, two bacterial populations sharing a channel either merged into one or settled into long-lived side-by-side lanes. Here the team simulated the contest with agent-based models, varying cell shape and division speed. The boundary between populations wandered like a simple drift-diffusion process, and that law lets them predict how long coexistence lasts even when the contest runs too long to simulate.

Round coccus-like cells invaded and took over more readily, while rod-shaped populations could hold their lanes almost indefinitely. Shape, in other words, is a competitive weapon in crowded microbial worlds.
pmc-13675158:
Fatemah AlAhmari and co-authors test an oxygen-releasing mouthwash on gum germs in 2026. Two bacteria drive gum disease, and a standard rinse is the benchmark for killing them. Whether the oxygen rinse matches it, and for which species, was unknown.

Lab tests gauged killing in liquid, on agar, and inside biofilms. One species fell at low rinse strength and was fully killed at set doses. The other needed near-full strength just to slow down. Biofilm bulk shrank under the rinse for both, and gene activity shifted at low doses. Docking studies probed how the active ingredient might bind its targets.
pmc-13675458:
Giulia Vatteroni and co-authors report, in 2026, how women with a past breast cancer diagnosis felt about a contrast-based mammogram. The women were in routine follow-up after surgery. The scan type was used in place of the standard mammogram inside a larger trial.

Soon after each exam, women filled in a short anonymous survey with sixteen questions. It asked about pain, exam length, worry, the dye injection, and how clear the staff's explanations were. It also asked how this scan compared with their past standard mammograms. The answers help clinics judge whether a more detailed scan is one patients will accept year after year. That acceptance matters for any follow-up program built on the method.
pmc-13675658:
Hyung-Gun Kim and four co-authors test whether a melt-in-the-mouth version of an acid-blocking drug behaves the same as its ordinary tablet, in this 2026 study. The drug is zastaprazan, a potassium-competitive acid blocker for reflux and ulcer disease. The disintegrating tablet is meant to be easier to take, with or without water.

Blood levels of the drug matched closely across all three ways of taking it, inside the accepted bioequivalence range. Peak timing and early exposure also lined up, with no extra surge in the first half hour from the quick-melting form. One volunteer reported two mild side effects and nothing serious occurred. The authors conclude the disintegrating tablet, taken either way, is pharmacokinetically equivalent to the standard tablet.
pmc-13676158:
Khoa Le and co-authors present, in a 2026 study, snapshots of the energy-making machine inside a drug-resistant hospital germ. The germ resists many drugs, partly by pumping them out using cell energy. It cannot ferment, so it leans fully on this energy pathway.

Using a freezing microscope method, the team caught the machine's head section mid-action as it built ATP, the cell's energy coin. The parts twist and shift together, and new energy coins form as the motion completes. Computer simulations backed up and extended what the images showed. Seeing the machine move points to fresh spots where a drug could jam it. That offers a new angle against a germ that defeats many current drugs.
pmc-13676358:
Soeda and co-authors studied a painful spine change in elite athletes, in a paper published in 2026. The change affects the bone next to spinal discs and is strongly tied to lasting low back pain. The team asked whether where it appears reflects how each sport loads the spine. They reviewed athletes whose pain had lasted over three months and whose scans confirmed the change.

Each athlete's pain had been pinned to the changed level by a targeted test. The team measured how the lower spine moved and where the change sat. Athletes over 60 and those with past spine surgery were left out. Comparing sports may show that twisting, bending, or impact loads leave distinct patterns. Such patterns could guide training and treatment for athletes. They may also help explain why the change hurts in some people and not others.
pmc-13676558:
Lamia Barakat and co-authors describe making emotional screening a routine part of childhood cancer care in a 2026 paper. The forms probed symptoms, quality of life, thinking and school needs, caregiver strain, family risk, and unmet resources, in English, Spanish, or Arabic. Follow-up documentation varied by site, the honest gap the authors say implementation must keep closing.
pmc-13676658:
Mohamad Rustom, Balazs J Denes, Stavros Kiliaridis, and Gregory S Antonarakis offer a two thousand twenty-six study of a notch on the lower jaw across growth.
